Yeah it's overpriced (I got this on sale for next to nothing), but the game is highly enjoyable and, in my opinion, a good way to spend an hour or two relaxing. If you enjoy anything to do with Ancient Romans/ancient history then this game is even better. You start with three Aurigas (charioteers), their horses and chariots. Depending on what faction you choose to race under, their starting statistics such as speed or strength vary - the Roman Army have strong chariots and horses but are slower, the Nobles splash out on some of the finer horses, etc.
I'm not going to pretend that actually winning a race to earn those much-needed Denarius is easy, but this makes it all the sweeter when you actually do manage to propel your hapless Auriga to victory. My most exciting win was when my rookie Auriga, Aurelius, turned the last corner on the last lap with a rickety wheel which gave out and flipped the chariot. He was quite a way ahead of the competition, but could he survive being dragged across the remainder of the track? A few nasty bumps later and he was over the finish line, beaten and bloody but alive and a winner. From then on he became Team Excelsior's champion Auriga with numerous victories under his belt. It's building this legend up that makes Qvadriga so fun. When the funds come in, you can upgrade the chariots and horses to make your team better and better - and hence, the races become slightly easier. I say -slightly- because there's still the ever-present danger of your Auriga's getting killed. No matter how many victories they have under their belt, they're still mortal and one unlucky flip of their chariot or brutal lashing from another Auriga with a grudge can spell death. In that sense it's historically accurate; many a star rose to fame in the circuses of the Roman Empire, only to be killed in a bad race.
The races themselves are turn-based - in a way. You select an action for your Auriga to perform, such as whipping the horses on, maintaining control or even deliberately smashing into an opponent's chariot, and then everyone on the track moves at the same time. It gives you time to think out a strategy which is nice, but unfortunately in many circumstances these plans never survive first contact with the enemy! xD (And by enemy I don't just mean the other Aurigas - there's♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the track as well from those that have tried and failed to keep their chariots and horses in one piece.)
Overall it's a good game with no glaring problems save its exorbitant price and, perhaps, a lack of some kind of multiplayer? Otherwise a solid buy on sale and much recommended.

Would I recomend this free game? Absolutely. Would I recomend paying anything for this? No. This is a weird jumble of barely playable games and a showcase of failures and worries, but I want to be clear, that is not a bad thing.
Pros:
This kid tore his heart out and displayed to anyone walking by who would give him the time of day. It's some real raw stuff. Really brought me back to when I was young. That feeling of nothing working out ever for you so you just put on the mask and try and get on with your life. That sort of life just destroys you little by little. It was pretty refreshing to see something like this. This sort of thing is really difficult to just throw out to the world.
-------------------------------------------
Cons:
Good art is worth money. Bad art is for other artist to roll around in each others egos like an orgy of confused personas. Good art conveys a clear and concise message. Bad art is a convoluted. This is bad art. But he's a kid. Still lots to learn in that department.
Art Problems:
If you're going to make an art game, focus on the art. This game spent too much time talking about game development.
Many of the levels made no sense until I looked at the commentary. I shouldn't need to do this. There is always a way to convey this information without commentary.
Gamplay Problems:
Needs a better run option. Either toggle run on the stick, or use one of the buttons. Holding down the stick while trying to run can be really annoying.
The stealth level needs better definition on the parameters of where the light sees you. It was hard to judge just how close you could be without getting noticed.
The one where you wake up in the room. You made rules to leave the level by a door. This one broke that rule and really frustrated me.
(Sorry if this seems a little harsh. Sometimes, when everyone is being encouraging and helpful, you need a couple people to play it straight and tell you how you messed up so you can grow.)

One of two sides of the Earthbound coin, but mostly drawing upon the darker, creepier and trippier aspects of it.
It's the story of Brad, a complete nobody, who while living his days in a depraved, post-apocalyptic world where women have ceased to exist, stumbles upon a baby girl, giving him purpose in his useless life. As you travel through the desolate wasteland that used to be the world and interview some of the colorful characters here, you'll be asking yourself "wtf could happen to the world to make it like this?"
Unlike Earthbound, the game plays out as a side-scroller RPG rather than a top-down one, but plays well and feels like an RPG. NPCs are authentically disgusting, miserable, cruel, pathetic and pointless - the worst side of humanity is well portrayed here. Combat plays just like in Earthbound, with enemies just as absurd. Graphics are simple, cartoonish, and pleasant.
The soundtrack is pretty atmospheric, conveying feelings ranging from constant pointlessness (God's Call), to a Lovecraftian feeling of dread (Devil's Bath Boys), to even the peace of a sunny afternoon in an isolated village (Summer Love).
The plot will require you to make choices, and your choices will have impact in the plot. It's a cruel story, I will say that much. It has some great twists, some of which will require deep digging into the game. But it's not for everyone. If you like everything to make sense, you better avoid this game. While I have no complaints, can't say I fully enjoyed the direction the DLC went by its end. But it was definitely worth the time and money spent.

LISA is polarizing by design, and simply playing through it's introduction alone is enough to give you an understanding of why so many people never finish or play it at all. The plot is a pitch black, grim, and hopeless affair filled with only occasional forays into light hearted and humorous territory. But the catch here is that these moments are designed to make the inevitable fall back down into the blackest pits of human cruelty imaginable even more devastating and impactful. You see, while LISA is a deconstruction of many common JRPG tropes, it's main deconstruction is that of a trope found in many forms of media, not just video games. That trope is the notion of protagonist centered morality. What this trope means is that in a story, when the protagonist causes innumerable amounts of death and destruction in their quest, they'll still be a hero and still be loved and praised by the populace, because although they've caused all this, their goal is noble so they're relieved of consequences or responsibility for their actions. LISA disposes of this folly almost immediately. The main character, Brad, is not only suffering because of the awful events that have happened in his life which he has no control over, but by his own decisions and actions as well. Brad has what sounds like an entirely noble goal at first, save his surrogate daughter Buddy from all the people in Olathe who want to use and abuse her for sexual pleasure and stop them from turning her into just a tool to repopulate the earth with. Save his surrogate daughter Buddy from the people who kidnapped her. Except the things he does to accomplish this start to get increasingly worse as the games plot unfolds. Not only that, but the regular people of this world do not look at Brad as if he's some divine hero that must be showered with praise, most of them look at Brad and see this sad old washed up has been and loser, who's just another nobody and a drifter, and then they proceed to ignore him, harass him, try to rob and kill him, make fun of him, and just treat him like garbage in general. And as his actions grow larger in their notoriety and scale, Brad becomes a demon in the eyes of the world. So much so that people either attack him on sight out of pure hatred, or retreat from him out of pure fear. And all the suffering that befalls on his companions and loved ones during the games events are all at least somewhat Brad's fault as well, and at many times Brad will be made to pay for it with mortal injury and failing at all his goals. In the end, this is not a story about someone conquering their demons and becoming a better person, this is a story about how someone is completely consumed by them and not only destroys themselves, but those around them as well.
While I for one never found LISA's gameplay to be outright impossible even on Pain mode (the hardest difficulty) I can see why many are repelled by it as well. Unlike most JRPG's, you have a large pool of party members (30 to be exact) that are not only fragile and expendable, but are actively encouraged by the game to be used up as resources in decisions and situations that are either dangerous and risky, or ask you to give up some of your protagonist Brad's strength or items for the life of a party members. Another feature that is in LISA is one you usually don't see outside of roguelikes, certain strategy games, and CRPG's. And that is permanent death. Whenever you are fighting a particularly powerful enemy, sleeping at campfires, or being faced with a decision, there's a random chance or a conscious decision on the player's part as to whether or not a party member will be killed off forever. There is one thing that makes it all easier on you. There is no grinding required whatsoever in LISA. How is this possible? Simple, you gain enough exp from exploring and fighting pre set enemies you can actually see and walk into. Consequently gameplay is now spent venturing into as many new areas as possible instead of fighting the same enemy in the same caves or same forests for hours. After all, the largest  amounts of exp will only be found by exploring and fighting enemies that are well off the beaten path.
LISA isn’t perfect though. While it’s obvious that a lot of passion and care went into the game, the aspect of it that causes almost all of it’s problems is simply the engine itself, RPG Maker. RPG Maker is a widely used engine for a lot of indie games, mostly because it requires next to no scripting or coding, but unfortunately this comes at the cost of performance. Numerous bugs and optimization issues tend to plaque RPG Maker games, and LISA is no exception to this. Even in fullscreen, LISA will have black borders on the right and left hand side of the screen no matter what. Characters will sometimes be found  floating in the air or simply stuck in the terrain, Brad can climb on parts of the scenery in certain areas and start walking or biking through the air and can cause a glitch on ropes that causes him to walk faster then the bike, and in certain areas like Snow Mountain the framerate will drop down severely depending on your hardware. Part of these issues stem from LISA being a top down game which uses various tricks to make it look like a sidescroller, due to RPG Maker being incapable of making sidescrollers. Essentially the game is pretending to be a sidescroller in a engine that was never meant to make one and it really shows at times. Part of it might also stem from the fact that RPG Maker renders everything as an object and also renders things offscreen at all times. It’s just incredibly sad to see a great game get held back somewhat by a buggy and unstable engine.
At the end of the day, when all of the above elements (besides the bugs) combine, they form an experience that's both foreign and strange, yet so human and relatable. For those of you who are easily offended or disgusted, or for those who subject matter such as this brings back unpleasant memories or experiences, you will most likely not enjoy this at all. But if you're willing to try something that's truly unique and impactful despite everything mentioned here, you might just have an unforgettable ride ahead of you.

A Story About My Uncle is a narrative focused, first person platforming adventure developed by Gone North Games and published by Coffee Stain Studios. The game has great sound and music design, surreal environments, jaw-dropping visuals, and much, much more.
The story not only puts emphasis on the main plot and characters, but also on the side plot and side characters. You play as a dad telling his daughter a story about how his uncle, Fred, goes missing and how the dad goes after him. The father comes across his uncles' invention, a suit which has a grappling hook and lets you take no fall damage, to help the dad find his uncle. On your journey you will traverse through a multitude of different environments, while meeting numerous side characters that will help you on your way. The narrative is the soul of the game, but it's done in a simple and subtle manner that you, the player, have to explore and ultimately piece it all together.
The game focuses on movement, speed, freedom, and light puzzle solving instead of violence. Movement is the core element of the game. With the help of your grappling hook, you feel so free and fast; flying without restrictions and at uncontrollable speeds. It feels so genuine and fluid that it immerses you into this unique world. WASD moves your character, shift to sprint, LMB to use your grappling hook, Space to jump, hold RMB to power jump, and Shift and hold RMB for powerleap. Almost every new platform is a checkpoint where it gives you a certain amount of charges for your grappling hook. And then you have to use your charges and your skills wisely to get to the next checkpoint. Also, Later in the game you get rocket boots to help you through the harder parts of the game.
Like I said before, the graphics are very stunning. ASAMU runs on the Unreal Engine 3 and by god this game looks fantastic. It has gorgeous lighting effects, great world design, phenomenal texture work, and a fantastic attention to detail. Also the art style is very vibrant and dark at the same time; using greens, blues, and browns to convey the mood of the game. Sadly, character models are pretty outdated.
The sound and music design is absolutely brilliant. The sound is very immersive and completely engages the player into the game itself. The "Whoosh" that you hear when you soar through the massive levels is incredible and gives the player a huge adrenaline rush. The game exhibits an emotional, heart-felt, and melancholy symphonic, fantasy soundtrack. Voice acting is somewhat good and somewhat bad. The protagonist, the daughter, and the town elder are voiced well, while everyone else is poorly voiced.
Additional Notes: This game has an FOV slider that can be adjusted from 60-120 FOV. There are 15 Steam achievements and the game is about 5-7 hrs. (depending on playstyle) and has a time trial mode. The game also features gorgeous water effects, best looking vegetation I've ever seen, beautiful architecture/ cityscapes, and stunning rock designs and textures. The devs are SO nice and are on the forums to answer questions and complaints!
Final Thoughts: A Story About My Uncle is Gone North Games' very first game and it is a masterpiece with phenomenal sound, music, atmosphere, immersion, graphics, gameplay, and a gorgeous world to explore. However, the game does suffer from character models that are not up-to-date, ok voice acting, and a poorly translated script. Overall, I can recommend this game to anyone looking for an immersive first person adventure with an unique world and tale to tell. And is most definitely worth $12.99.
*Review copy was provided by Gone North Games; Thank you very much!*

BIT.TRIP Runner 2 (forgive me, but I'm not using the full name of the game) is a really fun... platformer? It's not really a platformer, more like a crash course of obstacles to avoid. Which might sound boring, but it's actually pretty fun!
The gameplay is relaxing, yet challenging; there hasn't been anything that made me ragequit, just try harder; the normal difficulty setting seems to be really balanced, and also implementing checkpoints makes the frustration factor go waaaay down. One note though, if you don't have a controller, you might have a bad time.
There is a lot to do here. 100 levels, with collectibles, chests, keys and other stuff. You can go for all the items, try the high score or try the deceptively tough warp zones (3 lives...) If you're a stickler for collecting, prepare to get sucked in.
Visuals are top-notch, the art style is really pleasing and in a sense idyllic. And of course, the most important factor in such a game, is the sound; I cannot praise the sound enough. The combination of your inputs and the visuals and the music, wonderfully composed of variously pitched sounds, make this game feel really complete and suck you in.
All of this makes this one of the "one more level" genre games. And sure, it won't last you forever, as there is an end to all the challenges, but I'll be damned if you don't have lots of fun on the way there.
Strongly recommend. Pick this up now, or on the nearest sale (it was really cheap in December, but I never got around to playing it)

Definitely enjoying this game. I haven't run into the technical bugs some players have mentioned, so I can't comment on that. I can say that the game brings back the beat'em up joy of the original, while like the original has some more texture ("depth" might be a stretch) than a lot of brawlers. The game ran just fine for me in private, online play, and is perhaps best enjoyed with friends.
Bad points: the game definitely starts as a bit of a grind- characters start feeling like they are missing some basic moves, and end up feeling more like punching bags than "Bad Dudes" until some techniques are bought and stats improved. Also, the moves list can be a little misleading, and some techniques feel a little clunky to execute.
Good points: the references to the original game are fun, but not over the top to the point of cheesy- feels like a sequel rather than a homage. The many techniques, the varied maps and hazards, and the distinct playstyles of the multiple characters make for a less shallow experience than the original; the game builds on it's predecessor, rather than simply emulating it. Even in the pixel art, it feels like the perfect 16 bit sequel we would have wanted on the SNES to the 8-bit original.
Upshot: if you enjoyed the original, and especially if you have a friend on Steam who is also a fan, then confidently buy this one. You may enjoy the game solo, but the grind may feel slower without a friend.

This game is incredibly broken.  It's very fun to play, no doubt, and the teamplay is excellent.  But don't let anyone convince you otherwise, there are a TON of problems with this release.  As follows:
- SAVE FEATURE IS BROKEN IN MULTIPLAYER.  Not sure what the issue is, but 50/50 shot whether your progress will be kept or not.  It's EXTREMELY frustrating to co-op for an hour and find nothing you did was saved.  Huge issue for multiplayer enjoyment.
- Friendly fire doesn't work.  Yes, it says you can turn it off.  Except weapons, special moves, and even some knockdowns will still knock your teammates to the ground.  Now, this may not do damage, but it's annoying, disrupts teamplay, and leaves you open to "down" attacks from enemies.
- Menu features are an absolute joke.  They barely work, the UI is completely unintuitive, and character progression is mystifying.  In multiplayer, the map barely functions, and character swapping is an absolute joke.
- Can't have more than one player shop at a time during multiplayer.  Archaic, poorly thought out, and frustrating.
- Stat upgrades/changes and special move upgrade are NOT clearly explained or labelled.  Must be fixed.
Again, this game has immense promise.  For 20 bills it's a solid buy for the single player but as soon as you start adding players it all falls apart.  If the devs put in the time to fix at least 50% of the extreme issues, it could be a great game.  Until then, pass on this and keep an eye on the updates.

Altrough making a damn 180 turn in the story, SRIV remains one of the funnest sandbox games that I've played recently. The superpowers are fun to mess around with, weapon costumization (swappable skins) and nice additions to clothing. Altough it puts you back into the lack luster city of Steelport, this city actually works for Saints Row 4. However, this Steelport still doesn't put justice to Stilwater from Saints Row 2.
SRIV does some things really well. The superpowers are really balanced (except ♥♥♥♥ing Freeze Buff), the story has some funny and memorable moments, albeit not
memorable and the overall style of over the top sillyness gets carried over from Saints Row 3.
But let's talk superpowers for a moment. The superspeed and superjump features are amazing, I've actually ran and collected clusters for 30 mins straight with the basic upgrades. Once properly upgraded, the other combat powers are rather well balanced and usually kill the lower tier enemies in 1 blast. Telekenisis is amazing, chugging things from the start to the end of a street is entertaining and tossing a tank to a UFO is satisfying af. The only thing that is overpowered is the Freeze Buff ability, it basically cripples hostiles in a minigame.
Other notable things that I like are the simple addition of an on foot radio. Destroying stuff at the beats of The Mix radio station remains one of my favorite things to do. The minigames are designed around having superpowers, which is nice, and the missions are well detailed (altough you can't visit the locations later). The stunting has been improved ALOT compaired to SR3, you can now turn, twist and flip your car around. Sadly the main way of going around town is by sprinting alot, but every small thing helps. Gunplay is solid once you invested upgrades. Actual good clothing DLC. And of recent; mod support!
Rain comes after sunshine too! And SRIV is no exception.
What I still don't enjoy is Steelport, I don't like it and it's a bland, small city without any good momuments. If you want a reference on what I mean, try summing up places you know of in Steelport. You have that statue on an island, Kinzie's warehouse, a monument at a pier and some copy paste towers that you have to climb. But I do think that this city is better suited for SRIV than for SR3, more on that below.
The story has turned a 180. Saints Row 1 and 2 was gangster based, with dark moments and really made The Boss look like a sociopath. Saints Row 3 rolled in and
. And Saints Row 4 follows up with becoming the president. If you want a story, go ahead and buy Saints Row 2. It's going to be forever better at telling the story of The boss than SRIV will do.
Other dislikable things are the fact Cribs are gone. In Saints Row 2 you could have costumized cribs, SR3 brought it back in the form of these penthouse things. SRIV has doorways made out of light, turning your crib into a menu screen. There's also a lack of day progression. Sounds picky, but having one makes the game alive. Peds are still boring...
In my opinion, Steelport is a terrible city. Compaired to Stilwater, Steelport is a hunk 'o junk. The only memorable thing in SR3's city is the huge metal dude and the stripper pole building. SR2 on the otherhand, had graveyards, a trailer park, a suburbs, campus, grotto's... SRIV adds copy paste towers into the skyline of Steelport. But, Steelport works waay better in SR4. Everything is a blurry mess when you sprint and you wanna keep going fast. That's why there's so much detail in the missions wher
I almost remember all of the mission locations. SR3 had the same thing, but not that much as SRIV.
Altough having a fast type of gameplay, destoyes the chance of having little tagging spots in the city where you have to spraypaint a wall or something. This was a feature in SR2, but sadly removed in SR3 and SRIV. However, in SRIV you have data logs, clusters and stuff, so there is exploring to do, but you're probably will be spending attention to the orbs, rather than the city.
The DLC is really nice, there are mods and there's a modding community on Steam and on the SR Forums. The Penetrator's back, plenty of funny nods to things...
For a recap, or if it was TL;DR: Saints row 4 is a fun game with well tailored superpowers, altough it lacks when compaired to SR2.
The superpowers are nice, location works out pretty well (altough ugly when running like normal), has funny moments in the story and there's room for costumization.
Anyways, this game is more aimed towards having fun. So, have fun playing it

Pretty fun, honestly. The strategy layer and base management are definitely the best parts and the most familiar to the X-COM roots, but the combat felt a little lacking. Most of the time the game played itself, ending interceptions after only destroying one or two UFOs because the rest of the squadron already took out the rest. Since they're mostly autonomous aside from a few vague orders you can give them, they usually do most of the work without any input. However the environment was rather immersive and despite the shortcomings in combat I still enjoyed it. Also the story is nice, does a decent job of establishing a bridge between the plots of the first two games and that of X-COM: Apocalypse.
Alas, it's old, so it crashes constantly and requires extreme vigilance in saving whenever you do anything. I don't know if there is an ironman option but I wouldn't highly advise against using it if there is. I'm giving this a Recommended rating, but I honestly wouldn't recommend to anyone other than fans of the original who would like a little more plot and lore and don't mind the lacking gameplay. It doesn't have anything to do with Julian Gollop though so those die-hard fans would be probably be disappointed by that.

Shadowrun Hongkong is a great turn-based strategy game combined with role playing elements.
Btw, this is my first time playing Shadowrun series. This game made me interested in playing the other series (Returns and Dragonfall)
Pros :
- Good character creation. There are 6 distinct classes, but you can make your own customized class if you want.
- Beautiful level and environment design.
- Memorable characters with great background story for each.
- There are tons of choices you can make in this game. That makes you really involved inside the game. Not to mention that your choices have consequences.
- Good writing. Every conversation is interesting. Even without voice actors, you will always get hooked into what the characters are saying. Seriously, it's like you're acting as a character inside a novel.
- Good, balanced, and challenging combat.
- I love the fact that sometimes you can complete your mission unscratched by talking your way through. But of course, some conditions must be met. A high amount charisma and some other status will be required.
- Okay story, but not that great.
Cons :
- I encountered a few small glitches, but not game breaking.
- If I already scrolled to certain point of the stash and I dragged an item to change my equipment, the scroll keeps coming back to the top of the stash. This is a bit annoying. If I want to drag multiple items and those items are located near each other, I must drag, scroll again, drag again, scroll again.
Overall, I give this game 9/10. A must have for turn based strategy fans.

Another excellent addition to the Shadowrun series. UI and gameplay overhauls abound, making for the most complete experience yet. Admittedly, the plot wasn't as enjoyable as Dragonfall, but the rest of the gameplay elements more than made up for it. This is a great installment to the SR series.
The storyline had me locked into the game for long periods at a time.
The available dialogue for each character between missions was great to read.
The characters themselves made for diverse team builds; all bases are pretty much covered, and there is a workaround for almost every situation during each mission.
The new UI is aesthetically pleasing; as is the new Matrix build.
Matrix sub-missions are much more challenging, and gaining access to nodes feels more rewarding with the new system.
The available missions themselves also tie into the actually storyline quite well.
I noticed a couple of typos early into the game, but these are minor, and I personally noticed no real flaws in the gameplay itself.
Whether you've played through the previous two campaigns or not, I'd say this is worth your money.
Thanks HBS for another great campaign - keep 'em coming!

While I still have a few issues with the game on a mechanical level (honestly calling them issues is overblowing it), this incarnation of the franchise is quite possibly one of the best cRPGs I've played in a long while.  Certainly the best of anything current (though it will never live up to Planescape: Torment of course, nothing can).
The closest thing I'd call to a complaint (and it really isn't a complaint, more of an observation) is that I suspect it will be perceived as being a little too verbose.  Certainly the game is FAR richer for it, but I suspect the average player will get rather impatient with the almost extravagant florid descriptions and dialogues, which concerns me in that I want more games to take this level of textual effort over something like eye-candy, but reality is unlikely to reward cerebral quality these days.  As far as I'm concerned, this is a good thing, I just worry that it will work against the game's success.
At any rate, this game is a more than worthy successor/expansion from HBS, despite a few niggling bugs and more than a few proofing/editing errors.  I'd have liked to see a little more character interplay (especially among the secondary and tertiary characters), but what's in the game is more than appetizing.  There were also a few missed opportunities, but I suspect deadlines played a factor into a few of those.
Definitely worth the asking price, especially if you like cRPGs and doubly so if you like the IP.  I just wish there was more on the way, but I suspect we'll need to wait on the community for the next couple of years, at least until HBS is done with Battletech.

They told me I solved the Scoggins case. They told me my job was done. They were wrong. I saw Isaac Davner being dragged away. But the factory was running again, so I was done.
All the puzzles I was handed since felt lacking, gum always tasted stale. Like a maze with no exit, something was amiss. I couldn't take it anymore.
I took some time off, a nice vacation. Booked a passage west. Where there's snow. Where there's a lodge. Where I left something unfinished.
When I got there, it's was as if I had never left. Everything was still wrapped in puzzles, the whole town a huge question mark. It was almost as if I was in a Professor Layton game. Funny as hell, it was the most horrible thing I could think of.
The town greeted me with the warmth of a cold morning. Monosyllables and riddles, shoos and puzzles, lots of ABC gum. But the answers were clear: more missing people. All lost in the woods. Just like Isaac.
I could tell that, while everything looked the same, everything was different. There was a sense of urgency about the people. Folks who made little to no sense before had now lost all but one of their marbles. Something was going to happen soon.
I'm still not sure I believe what I saw in the woods. The Hidden People are just a bad fairytale, like the boogeyman or the shockmaster.
I have to solve this mystery. Scoggins may very well depend on it. My life certainly does.
I just hope I can stay sane long enough to do so.

The dev is a middle class highschool student, who's struggles seem to be some combination of romantic and academic pressure, along with a contrived sense of persecution for his hobbies manifest as teenage angst. The author is clearly in the second panel of this comic:
He's yet to experience the true horrors of capitalist commodity production and wage labor, and is still in the mindset of "aspiring ruling class".
This aside, some of the level design and creative decisions were very well executed. There were some beautiful and varied environments. I loved how the floating orbs in the garden scene had a shader effect on them that made it difficult to tell how far away they were when you looked directly at them. The game has an interesting concept, merging a space trading game with some first person action elements and missions, and even a bit of mystery (Where the heck is Lieutenant Dan?), however it falls short on many levels.
Firstly, as a trading game it is pretty weak.  The economy simulation has a very limited number of commodities and the pricing mechanics are reasonably predictable.  Go to destination A, buy the highest priced goods that have the most recent lowest price, possibly split the cargo hold between the two top picks, then travel to the next destination to hopefully (and almost always) sell it at a higher price then repeat.  It's fairly tedious, and there is no buy/sell commission/overhead so you just sell off your entire inventory whether it is a profit or loss, then buy up whatever is the best deal on the current planet even if it is one of the things you just sold them, fairly unrealistic compared to any other trading games I've played as there is no buy-ask spread whatsoever.  There are 5 missions in campaign mode and the first 4 are more or less like tutorials more than anything and have only 2 or 3 destinations which is pretty suboptimal for a space trading game really.  The real game is campaign mission 5 which has 4 destinations and a bit of a story to it (albeit a weak one).  The biggest mystery in the game is trying to find Lieutenant Dan, which is a bit challenging, but also rather disappointing when you do find him.
You then go on contract hitman jobs to kill various bad guys you've been either sent to take out, or that you opted into by taking a job through the bartenders.  The contract hits are incredibly repetitive due to there only being about 3 or 4 small maps that they play out in.
The FPS enemy AI is 1990s quality, and the action isn't that great.  The meat of the game is in mission 5 which is the longest and has the most trading destinations (4 total).  You're on a countdown timer from 500 hours with each travel you take consuming some number of hours with which you must meet the trading objectives.  Problem is, from the start you can't trade anywhere due to a military presence halting trading, so you have to travel around to make money from hit jobs to then pay off the authoritarian police state guys to leave so trading can resume.
The rest of the time you end up running around the levels collecting crates full of random commodities like Super Mario and selling them.  It's very tedious and gets boring quick.
I finished this game just to see if there was anything at all exciting about it, but it was somewhat disappointing.  If it is a space trading game you're looking for, this sure isn't it.

X-COM: Interceptor was the fourth game developed by MicroProse and released in 1998. MicroProse decided to the previous installments had too slow of combat so they decided to stick you into an spaceship instead of controlling units and moving them slowly turn by turn.
Basically this has all the same base construction, slow paced strategy building, but instead of the strategy-game-element used in the battles they replaced those elements with a space ship simulator where you fly and shoot down enemy UFO's.
Remember how in the last game you were fighting to protect the plannet? And then you were forced to fight under water to protect the planet? Then you fought to protect one single city? I'm under the impression that we must have lost there too
So now where do you go when you can't hide underwater, or in one city? You get the heck out of dodge and go to the moon. So welcome to *speaking in a deep narrators voice* X-COM in space! You must do your best to keep the aliens at bay by using your super powers of ocd fine tuning control!
Most of the controls and mechanics in the previous two games are the same you have a crazy amount of base customability, ship/vehicle customization, freedom to choose where you want to construct new bases. The biggest features I noticed in this version is that there's actually a "help wizard" that pops up whenever you enter into a new window or UI you've not seen before. You can then toggle the wizard to give tool tips over each user interface portal
and button to help you learn what does what. (That's pretty big, seeing as the first two games didn't give you any explanation and assumed you had the paper manual that came with the game.
The controls still feel very much like a 1990's game though, you can see they really were coming up with some clever ways to keep the game feeling fresh. Do remember that when I say "controls" I'm specifically talking about the controls and menu's you navigate in the base-view. Once you enter into flight combat that's a whole different ball game.
Full disclaimer, I played this game on an older windows 7 laptop which has a habit of over heating, I also played with only a keyboard. In the past I could get away with that, because it was turn based. This time things got a bit more interesting.
You can control the game with keys, and you can rebind them! But you turn WAY too sharp and you can't pull off any of the close shots you need to pull off in a flight simulator. But you can also aim with the mouse
I learned to use a system of switching between the keys and the mouse pad to get some kind of "flight simulator work flow" going, which ended up working for me, at least slightly.
I'd highly suggest getting a joy stick or controller
The controls feel really good actually! I think this would be a pretty fun space ship flyer simulator. However I was having flashbacks to playing X-wing alliance, and TIE Fighter...
So I had a look at some dates, and it seems that X-Wing was the first of the space fighter simulator series and was released in 1993, so it's possible there might have been some influence, but it seems the greatest influence came from a game I haven't played: Wing Commander, which has released games from 1990 based on space combat simulation.
As always, older games have problems. I've seen several other reviews mentioning glitches with drones, I can't speak from experience about them because I never played the original game.  I can say the steam overlay wasn't working for me, and since I'm playing this on a windows 7 machine, that doesn't bode well at all. I also couldn't exit the game after starting a game. It felt like I was playing the game Hotel California, "You can check-out any time you like, But you can never leave".
There ya go, a 1976 song for a 1993 released game. Now if you'll excuse me, I'm going to go rant about woodstock and other dated references that make me sound older then I really am.
All in all, I can see why this game gets mixed reviews. I could thumbs it up or down. As a reviewer it was nice to have a game that introduced something new to the series, however it's still very difficult to get into, even with the addition of a helper-wizard. Wizards does not magic make.
I could see myself enjoying this game far more on my desktop computer because I like the idea of combining a strategy game AND a flight simulator.
There's a very good chance you'll probably pick this game up with an X-COM Game bundle deal. I think it's worth your time if you're looking to play something different. But the X-COM UFO Defense is the staple for the series, and the reboot X-COM: Enemy Unkown is the game which will bring in a new generation of X-COM fans.
I'd suggest those other two games before this one.

X-COM interceptor is a bad game, but in some peculiar way, enjoyable. Put simply: it's so bad it's good.
I can not in good faith recommend it, because it's bad, on the other hand I can't not recommend it, because it's possible that you may enjoy it.
On strategic side, it's a typical X-COM styled game, adapted to specific environment. You build bases, expand them with modules, research techs (story-wise you download them from Galactic Science Corps, gameplay wise it's just like research in every other such game), you hire pilots, buy craft, weapons and equipment, and send them to intercept UFOs.
Combat is centred about classic dogfighting, with "air drag", max speed and other such elements which are staple of oldschool dogfighting, but make no sense in space. Not that it's unusual for "space" flight sim, a lot are guilty of that and it's not necessarily a bad thing.
Word of warning, combat is very fast paced, so fast that it takes some time to get used to. That's not a problem though, your wingmen are very capable and will win fights for you, until you start carrying your own weight.
That's about facts, but what makes it enjoyable?
Hard to say, attempts at humour are corny, reading "news from Earth" will make you groan or facepalm, interface is clunky because it pretends to be retro-futuristic in-universe screens/displays, combat repetitive and simplistic which leaks into strategic layer also making it simplistic.
Still, campaign is short, individual missions rarely take more then minute, big chunk of which is "fly in", and "hyperspace out" animations, and this is probably what saves Interceptor: it's too short to bore you (too much).
All in all, it's very subjective, I give negative review because it's bad, but I did enjoy it in a way, maybe you will too?
Side note: there's a bug that makes enemy installations impossible to kill, it's solved in unofficial .exe patch, but launching Interceptor with this exe prevented Steam from properly logging my playtime, hence so low value - contrary to what Steam says, I did play game from start to end.
Takes a bit of work to get going good, but worth it.

Characters can be unlocked with points rewarded for your progress after each death or by completeing a certain feat. You can use these points to get a vault and add space to said vault. The Vault NPC is in the set spawn for each character. I recommend always keeping a Key of Seals in the Vault if you manage to come across one. Keys of Seals are used on Temples and can give you Holy Artifacts. My first holy artifact was an Axe that crushed everything before me. By the time it had worn down i found another temple and another key of seals, and got a Holy Spear and Holy Chest Armor. Made it the last 80 km to the Demon Loard and killed him with no struggle.
I've only gotten 2.8 hrs of playtime in the time of this review, but i could easily put 200 hours into it. It's cheap for it's value of entertainment, and if you end up in a poor spawn you can always just continue again.
More tips
-Always buy from a Chef When/If you reach a town. They seem pricey but in actuality they are cheap and extremely valuable.
-This game is about Trade-offs, you may end up choosing things that are detrimental to the world you spawn on.
-More expensive is not always better, especially when you do not have a high enough Item-Appraisal to know what you are buying.
-Randomly Generated worlds always have their problems, the largest map wrecker in this game is large mountain walls that you have to climb. They take a great deal of turns to climb and eat your stamina, if you find yourself having to climb mountains frequently you will die, and you may want to explore a different route or a new world entirely.
-Chests in the water are also death-traps but if you can manage it, they may offer useful loot.
-Teleportation Pills will save you from Bandits, Bears, or Golems.
-Axes will destroy walls and chests with ease for better dungeon navigation.
-Bows and Lances will help you kill your enemies from a distance, very beginner friendly weapons, unless you have no arrows.
Negatives about this game -
The loss of your character after completeing the game is without a doubt a loss, but the ability to save his gear makes up for it, despite the fact it is battered and will probably have to be repaired despite my deep loathing of the brittle debuff.

A pretty simple game, you have up to four chariots, charioteers and groups of horses each, and your goal is to conquer the whole ancient world of charioteering. During the race you pick from many different moves that will make you shift your lane, attack your opponents, accelerate, slow down, or just hold your reins a bit more firmly. What may seem a rather simple idea, shines because of how it is done. There are MANY different race tracks in several of the main regions of the Roman Empire - covergin such main provinces as Italia, Gallia, Hispania, Aegyptus, Syria, Macedonia, Achaea, Africa, and several others. Each of the regions contains many different stadiums, which are not only of different size, but also differ in whether they are Greek or Roman style, as both nations had a different idea about how to start a race.
There are many possible combinations of how good your chariot or horses are. Do you prefer stronger ones that can run for a longer time, or faster, but less durable ones? Do you prefer a stronger chariot that will allow you to ram your opponents or a light one that will accelarate well but at the same time will be easier to break? The choices are yours, and together with a random event that happens just before race, such as drugged horses, assaulted auriga (charioteer), or corrupted praetors that stolen some prize money, it makes every race unique. You really need to adjust your strategy often, although the best one (and was in the ancient times) is to block your opponent behind your chariot and try to anticipate his moves so as to keep him trapped, as changing lane takes quite some time.
Overall, I can heartily recommend it to anyone who likes either fun sports games and/or ancient history. Spent a lot of time playing it on my iPad and it's just as fun on your PC. The only con is the price - I don't really think that it's worth it. Therefore I must also recommend that you wait for the next sale. If it's at least 33% off, don't hesitate.

A really interesting, original strategy game - but not worth the price tag.
Turn based Roman chariot racing - good original subject. And a really nice, simple mechanic, easy to understand, quick to get into, but really intriguing to play. That sounds great, right? Well, it is. The apparent simplicity of chariots trundling around the track actually creates a really interesting set of challenges, where the positions of chariots around you mean you have to carefully consider every turn, with different races unfolding to reward different tactics. It's like a really, really good board game.
Except...
The graphics are super-simple, 2d. That isn't a problem, but it feels more like a five dollar mobile game.
The individual races are interesting, but there is no sense of story or progression, no apparent end-game, no rivalries to develop with other teams, and little ability to develop your drivers. Further, there is no Hall of Fame where you can compare your drivers' achievements nor mourn for those who have died. And all of that is a shame.
Also, there is no multiplayer. Given that this plays like a boardgame - like the sort of thing you'd want to get out for half an hour to play with your friends around the coffee/dining table - it's a real shame that there is no internet multiplayer option (nor any other multiplayer).
So, if you're interested in an unusual little strategy game - one that you can keep coming back to and dipping into for an engaging coffee-break distraction - then this is absolutely worth having. But it's hard to justify much more than $5 for it.
Recommendation: add to wishlist; wait for it to be reduced.

That's a great mobile or office game, one of the very best of them, but sadly it totally lacks any endgame content or storyline, or characters so it's not the best choice for PC gaming, still I've had enough of fun with it to recommend it to every turn-based strategy fan at least to try it out. Good realistic AI & carrieges' physics model along with 10 second real-time turns with pauses between them make it an ultimate gambling entertainment where you can simultaneously identify thyself with a brave rider, wealthy horse owner & an affectionate rooter.
The gameplay is simple yet effective. You get gear: horses (speed & endurance), carriage (acceleration & endurance) & rider (turning skill & endurance), when they lose health their quality lowers so you want to get leading the race without losing too much of those resources. Every 10 seconds you have to make one decision - speed up or down, change lanes (1, 2 or 3 to each side), bash or whiplash rival moving at your side. You also get a random condition either good or bad which significantly changes your strategy. You can also bet on yourself. The whole point is to make money & become a prominent stabling. The Mediterranean region with lots of towns is at your service, every town has it's own hippodrome, their configurations & sizes are different, so you have to change your habits. When you become a champion at smaller arenas you can go to Rome, Constantinople or Alexandria to compete with the best & earn even more money - that's all, no logical game ending here.
Still if you are fond of things like 'King of Dragon Pass' where your decisions are regularly put to the test of random outcomes & you can follow the mechanics of your triumphs & catastrophies in detail - you should by all means try out this small game with perfectly balanced risk-reward gameplay!

The first Puzzle Agent combined a unique artstyle and an interesting story with some interesting puzzles to make it a short but memorable puzzle solving experience in an era of "brain/sudoku" sytled puzzle games. It was reasonably entertaining but was left on a cliff-hanger with many questions in the story left unresolved that leads to the sequel, Puzzle Agent 2.
The problem was this game feels exactly like the first game. While there are some new locations to the game, because of using exactly the same engine and artstyle, it is really hard to distinguish itself from the first game. The story element though, was expanded quite a bit as this concludes all the mysteries from the previous installments that were left behind. While the story was quite well done, it slows down the game play quite a bit and makes it less of a puzzle game and feels more of an adventure game.
This leads to the main problem for Puzzle Agent 2. To have 'puzzle' in its title, the puzzles were extremely disappointing. There were only about 30-odd puzzles and most of them are not hard to solve. And to make matter worse, a lot of them are just rehashes of the exact same puzzle mechanics. This leads to quite a few repetition and uninspiring gameplay. Most, if not all of the puzzles aren't terribly ground-breaking and a number of them you would have played before if you are even a semi-regular puzzle player. So for a game that is centered around solving puzzles, it failed miserably.
Overall it is hard for me to recommend this game because it is just a sub-par puzzle game. Unless you really want to know what happened to the story after the first Puzzle Agent, I would just skip this game.

I just want to preface with a sidenote that I am a long time nintendo fan.  Especially the Zelda series.  I have a strong emotional attachment to those games like many others.  As I'm sure everyone knows, a new entry was released yesterday and it is being hailed by many as the new high point in the series.  I've been playing it and I agree.
And yet I'm still playing River City Ransom: Underground.  For me personally, that's saying something.  I could list the many flaws with the game, but I think others have that covered already.  In spite of those, I am absolutely addicted to this game.  It's all about the combat, and it's so damned satisfying!  The developers clearly put a lot of focus and effort into making the fighting system as fun as in depth as it coukd possibly be, and it's an astounding success.  It requires patience, however, as you do begin the game underpowered and a far cry away from pulling off the amazing combos you will be doing later in the game.
Of course, while I did say the game is all about combat, it might not be entirely accurate.  Part of the game's weak points revolves around non combat missions, as others have explained.  Chasing Tex through the sewers can be particularly irritating.  But when it's all said and done and you're Acro Circusing your way into crowds and playing hacky sack with downed enemies, you know it's well worth it.  Not perfect, but hopefully with some balancing tweaks and bug fixes this game can become a true classic.  Of course I recommend it.
A tip if you're having a hard time getting into this one.  Find Mao's restaurant early in the game.  As soon as you accumulate $5.55, go there and purchase / use edamame.  It will boost your defense by a bit.  Rinse and repeat a few times until you're able to comfortably save up $13.85 for the Octopus Roll to boost your strength.  Yes, it's a bit grindy, but that would only be a problem if, like I said, combat wasn't incredibly fun.  When you're getting more comfortable with these stats, then go to the dojo where Purple Bee is / was and then start learning new moves.  It becomes a lot of fun when you power yourself up a bit, so don't let the early game discourage you.

I'm not quite sure what I expected before I played Runner2, probably another obstacle course with the same clear-cut pixel graphics and simple charm of the prequel Runner, perhaps with a bit more underlying menace or excitement pursuant to a Rhythm Alien which apparently featured in it. What I got was something with the same basic gameplay, but with a lot of extras.
Extras? Extras are good, right? If you played the first Runner, there was almost nothing more satifying than getting an extra, then speeding along with the music at full audibility, collecting gold with a rainbow contrail stretching to infinity. Sadly though, in this version, extras result in a watery rainbow which trails sadly in your wake, and the music doesn't really noticably change throughout the course of a level. I suppose that anything less wouldn't fit the new 'style' of the game.
No, these extras are the normal sort of game extras, extra characters and collectable outfits and a 'reward' system. Collectible outfits? If you're still thinking of the first BIT.TRIP Runner, you may be wondering how that works. I could tell you the first outfit was a pair of earbuds, and you might wonder if that meant whitining a couple pixels on the Runner's ears. Not to fear though, it's all part of the new 'style'.
At the beginning of the game, a smarmy narrator informs you that CommanderVideo has been sucked into an alternate dimension, while fighting in some manner of justice league. A new world awaits, with a lot more living things, and more importantly, real 3D graphics.
I don't feel that 3D graphics really do much for the game. I felt that my runner was not a s responsive due to the slower nature of the jump animation. In fact, starting out, the overhangs on staircases would always make me trip, as I was used to a more 2D perspective from playing the first runner. Moreover, when I tripped, the runner would swim backwards like an octopus, at a constant rate no matter where I was in the level, which was really irratating if I tripped towards the end (compare Runner, where returning to the start took a fixed amount of time, no matter what).
The presence of a lot more living things is worse for the feel of the game, though. In the first runner, the living things include huge tunneling worms, fish, clouds with mustaches, and trampolines with eyes. What all of these have in common though is that they are separated from your gameplay. None of them are beneficiaries or detractors to your Herculean run. Your enemies, such as they are, are robots. In Runner2, the first thing you see is a spike-thing sitting in the road. Then, as you go further on, a drunken pickle registers you at a checkpoint. This makes the aesthetic lonliness which the first game had impossible to acheive. End the level, and a sign flips to tell you it's an "Amazing Acheivement!". If you've collected all the gold, you no longer get to go to a fiendishly difficult bonus level, but instead get fired out of a cannon.
As the game mechanics were introduced I noticed another thing I didn't like about this sequel, namely, the trigger keys no longer did what they used to. I really enjoyed using A+RTrigger to Jump-kick in the first Runner, but in the second it was not to be.
All in all the game comes off as extremely patronizing, with it's hollow achievement system (called 'rewards' for some reason) and its collect all the costumes mentality, which bothers me much more in the face of the sink or swim of the first Runner. It has some promising new mechanics that the first one did not, but they don't necessarily play out. An example is tracing a circle with your right stick, an idea I thought was pretty novel until I realized it had absolutely no impact on the game besides earning extra points.
In an effort to enjoy the game more, I switched to the drunken pickle as soon as I possibly could, so that I might be able to enjoy the game for what it was, instead of comparing it to the first runner. A fine idea, though at the character change screen I was briefly greeted by the monstrousity that is CommandgirlVideo. For heavens sake, I believe that collection of black pixel which comprised the protagonist of the first Runner was gender neutral, for that matter, so is the word 'Commander'. Is there any purpose for a second amalgamation of pixels with secondary sexual characteristics other than to alienate half the population from the main protagonist? Do the words 'separate but equal' ring any bells?
In any case, I continued playing the game, pretending now that it was the adventures of drunken pickle. I was plesantly releived that noone seemed present at any of the checkpoints, but drunken pickle's extra mode was an all-green rainbow, which should, in any reasonable game, be an oxymoron. I finished off the level, and defeated the boss.
But then came a cut scene, featuring CommanderVideo going pointlessly into a whale, even though I'd been playing with drunken pickle the whole time. And then the checkpoints were populated again, by a crab man in a hut. And then I lost interest, and let the game run on to give me Steam Card drops while I wrote this review.
So, in conclusion, Runner is better. If you were thinking about playing this game, play Runner. If you've already beaten Runner, go back and do all the challenges, or do it on Perfect mode. If you've already beaten it on perfect mode, then grab your square frames, put them on, and meet me in the cafe down the street, which serves 100% economically sourced coffee-flavored foam, and we can chat about how the first Runner was so much better, before BIT.TRIP went mainstream.
Bottom line: Though Runner2 may be better played with a controller, it's better to play the original Runner with that contoller.

Runner2 is the game that you didn't know you wanted. Gameplay is of a platforming-meets-rhythm persuasion, where your character runs forward at a fixed pace and you have to clear obstacles that spawn in time with the soundtrack. The soundtrack is gorgeous, by the way.
Bad at rhythm games? That's fine! Runner2 uses clear visuals with vivid colors to help you know exactly when you need to jump, duck, kick, block, or dance your way to victory, and it gives you the entire first world to become familiar with those mechanics. Bad at timing in general? That's also fine! There are three difficulty settings to give challenge for those who want a challenge, without the frustration for those who don't.
The Runner2 experience is that when you are doing well, you feel it. You are rewarded with pleasant changes in music, sound effects, and visuals. Your senses are bombarded with happy things, and you can't help but enjoy yourself. Unfortunately, when you perform poorly, you feel that as well. Stages that you just can't seem to get past are frustrating, though there is some satisfaction in finally figuring them out. There is no redemption, however, for the times that you stupidly mess up the very last step in a stage and have to start over. At least there's checkpoints this time around.
Is this game for everyone? Pretty much yes, though maybe not at its original asking price. Buying this with the soundtrack was a good decision for me, but so was waiting for a sale. You can complete the story in 5-10 hours, with 100% completion taking closer to 20-30 hours. If you're a quantity-over-quality type person, wait for the price to drop down a touch. Otherwise, put on your running shoes and join Commander Video as he tries to reach the right side of the screen.

It's X-COM but in SPACE!!!!!
This game has not aged especially well from 1998 but it does have some charm left deep inside it's husk.  Changing up the formula after three terrestrial X-COM games, Interceptor takes the fight to the aliens.
While the classic base building, research and soldier management are all present.  The core gameplay is a space flight sim, which if you can convince it to play well with modern controllers can still be fun if silly time.

X-COM is remembered by many old-school gamers as the uber-difficult, tactic-heavy, turn-based strategy game of earth's defense against aliens.
While it is still all of these things, it is very difficult to play this game today when there exists the new X-COM games with modern day conveniences. If you've played this game before, it may still get a playthrough thanks to nostalgia. However, if you have never played this game before, it is doubtful that you will both understand how to play this game, nor find it worthwhile to actually play through it. Not to mention, Interceptor was probably the weakest of all the original X-COM games.
While it may not really have stood the test of time to be playable to the masses, it is a title that will always be remembered by those who enjoyed it many years ago.

Game play wise, it is a fairly tactical game. Be prepared to look for cover and plan your moves carefully. Combat can be slow, especially if you play it like a game of chess. However, it gives you a great deal of options. The matrix section can depend a bit on your tastes. If you like stepping away from combat to solve puzzles you will probably enjoy them more. For the most part, though, the matrix is skippable if you don't want to bother with it.
Your actions will have consequences in the game. Some more long term than others. You can choose to fight or talk your way through many situations. Who you let live or ally with can impact the story later on. While I would have liked to have seen more hard moral choices, over all the options presented seem believable and organic.

Civ V is an absolute masterpiece that will immerse you for hundreds, or thousands of hours with its beautifully addicting gameplay mechanics.
As the sole leader of an empire, you will be tasked with shifting priorities and making concessions to navigate enigmatic, and sometimes impossible waters. Throughout your many playthroughs, you will always have a different experience; you will grow in patience, relish in your micro-victories, and learn from your mistakes. The seemingly endless variety of gameplay sytles and strategies you can choose to incorporate give this game a staggering amount of replay value.
Gameplay aside, Civilization V also walks you through iconic empires, eras, and technologies that have all culminated to form our modern day. Sure, an expert historian could point out many faults in historical accuracy or cohesion, but as a casual appreciator of world history, I found this game to be a very enjoyable gateway to further learning.
Long story short, if you can appreciate turn-based strategy games, this game has exceptional depth and quality, and it is certainly worth your time and money.

I call this game a "Time Warp" game, because you can start playing it at the crack of dawn, look out the window and think "Huh - the sun has been rising for awhile now", only to realize that it's the sun setting instead. Most of the complaints I've ever heard of this game stem from biggering over how there should be more RTS style micro-managing, or how OP certain systems are for certain objectives, but I'm convinced that these work in the game's favor, rather.
Cov V is a blast, it's a great experience seeing your nation flourish and grow, nurturing your people from disjointed bronze-era peasants at the bottom of the leaderboard, to a technological master-race at the top of the wrold.
There's lots of work for personal lore here too, which I love. You can name a city and specialize it how you want - make one city the "trade center" and another a "military" city; which can actually be a solid strategy in the long run.
There's so much fun to be had here in single player alone. With mods, you can put even more aspects of thegame to the test - or try out dream civilizations in strange scenarios of your own design. Or, you can hop online and slug it out with human nations - which is always good fun. Befriending someone knowign that they're your friend - or getting betrayed by your IRL best friend and not seeing it coming, they're all amazing additions to the experience.

You think it ends there? I wish, there's mods for the game that enable players to easily see who's a good or bad captain live in-game during a battle. What this means is that anyone who has the mod can actively target any good/great players in the battle untill he/she is destroyed. Sounds fair right? Not so much if you even exceed the expectations of the average playerbase's skill level; everyone will target you, accuse you of cheating, complain, teamkill, attempt to screw up your shots etc. Especially in World of tanks where such a mod has existed for decades.

I played several thousand battles on the WG launcher over the past couple years. Same as then I can't recommend this game at all.
++Ship models are pretty
++Effects of guns firing full broadsides (sound, visual) is so unbelievably satisfying and never gets old
++Ship classes play very differently
++In my opinion the grind/f2p system is not at all bad, but I love naval combat so I'm probably biased
++Slow nature of gameplay is a fantastic change to instant random respawn multiplayer that soy boys love so much
--You have to employ wonky workarounds to use your previous account through Steam.
--UI options are hidden away in an arcane menu system that requires googling and client restarts to fix
--Premium ships are hilariously overpriced, and from my perspective vastly more than WoT. For example one ship I wanted more than the others is the USS Indianapolis. Its cheapest model runs at $35. The Tirpitz is $55; the Hood is $44; the Dunkerque is $25. These are the BASE models, mind you. Yeah, $35 for one ship, in a game with dozens and dozens of them. That's comparable to paying $35 for one character or gun in whatever childish pew pew orgy people like these days. If $35 or $55 unlocked ALL the ships, I would pay that happily and consider it a fantastic value. But yeah, no. In contrast I purchased the box tank in WoT for eighteen bucks and even then I feel that's highway robbery--albeit more Robin Hood than Comcast.
--Lastly, and the point which absolutely ruins the game for me: everyone is terrible. WoWS, WoT, AW, WT all have a brilliant and groundbreaking feature called a "minimap" which is handily provided for everyone, free of charge. And yet no one ever looks at it. Ever. In all games you will play, at least half of your teammates will go to the wrong place, stay too long, or run too fast. In a game where it can take several minutes to recover from poor positioning, it will lose you more games than you can bear. I must emphasize that I'm not remarking on the skill of players (ie, shooting the correct ammo type, accuracy, repair timing, etc), but only on the overwhelming propensity of people to just...ignore the minimap. And if you complain or ping the map--just as in those other games--YOU are suddenly the troll or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Really convulses my cortices.
BOTTOM LINE: No. Even were all the above problems fixed, you will still grow to loathe Wargaming in every possible way. Just like
, Gaijin, and so on, they have made a fundamentally sound product but are far more concentrating on ♥♥♥♥ing it up than making it fun or enjoyable. RIP in peace.

The first Puzzle Agent combined a unique artstyle and an interesting story with some interesting puzzles to make it a short but memorable puzzle solving experience in an era of "brain/sudoku" sytled puzzle games. It was reasonably entertaining but was left on a cliff-hanger with many questions in the story left unresolved that leads to the sequel, Puzzle Agent 2.
The problem was this game feels exactly like the first game. While there are some new locations to the game, because of using exactly the same engine and artstyle, it is really hard to distinguish itself from the first game. The story element though, was expanded quite a bit as this concludes all the mysteries from the previous installments that were left behind. While the story was quite well done, it slows down the game play quite a bit and makes it less of a puzzle game and feels more of an adventure game.
This leads to the main problem for Puzzle Agent 2. To have 'puzzle' in its title, the puzzles were extremely disappointing. There were only about 30-odd puzzles and most of them are not hard to solve. And to make matter worse, a lot of them are just rehashes of the exact same puzzle mechanics. This leads to quite a few repetition and uninspiring gameplay. Most, if not all of the puzzles aren't terribly ground-breaking and a number of them you would have played before if you are even a semi-regular puzzle player. So for a game that is centered around solving puzzles, it failed miserably.
Overall it is hard for me to recommend this game because it is just a sub-par puzzle game. Unless you really want to know what happened to the story after the first Puzzle Agent, I would just skip this game.

This is even better than Puzzle Agent 1. It has built in humor and farcical attitudes, all complimented by the cartoon-based design. The story continues to be puzzled all over and sometimes it can get repetitive. Nevertheless, for the puzzle fans out there who enjoy point and click funny adventures, I whole-heartedly recommend it! It is also worth the price and replay value.

The original River City Ransom was one of my absolute favorite games growing up, so I was elated when I learned that Conatus was doing a follow-up. While I don't have much multi-player experience with this one so my review will be mainly from a single player perspective.
PROS:
1. This game does a great job at capturing the "nostalgia" aspect of things for me. There are familiar characters, places, items, mechanics, you name it. It just creates a "feel-good" atmosphere to see some of these things and the way that they were implemented into this game. Doing things like visiting the old River City High School and taking Saunas, to how the character eats the entire plate when consuming food items just really takes you back to the classic days of running around River City.
2. Different Characters - I love how there are many different characters to choose from, all with their unique fighting styles, strengths, and weaknesses. This add a nice amount of depth and a ton of replay value in my opinion.
3. RPG elements - Although, I know some may disagree but I actually rather enjoy how grind-heavy this game is. This may be the JRPG fan side of me speaking, but I enjoy feeling like I actually earned my upgrades and level-ups. The constant stream of enemies allow you to not only grind, but perfect your fighting style and strategy as well.
4. Easter Eggs - There are quite a few Easter Eggs in this game and a lot of them are pretty cool.
5. Combat - While it's not perfect by any means, it still is enjoyable pulling off combos and finding ways to implement new moves into your play style. There are a decent amount of upgrades that expand combat quite nicely and allow you to rack up some major damage on your enemies.
6. Soundtrack - Again this is just another thing that just brings home that old school feel of the original.
7. Humor - If you ever have time to read some of the comments at the bottom during figths, some of that stuff is hilarious. I know it's hard to take your eyes of the action when you're surround by like 10 dudes trying to kick the crap out of you but, it's still worth a look.
CONS:
1. I think my biggest issue with this game is the lack of information. This game does a TERRIBLE job at explaining even the simplest things and by TERRIBLE I mean basically non-existent. There's not really detailed explanation for anything really outside of the few tutorial points that  are easily skippable by mistake since they pop up out of the blue, mid-fight and if you're pressing the button you're going to skip it. And even worse, if you're playing multi-player ANYONE can skip them. So Imagine up to 4 people pressing buttons vs a tutorials that pop up in the middle of action that are skippable by a simple button press by ANYONE lol. It's basically a recipe for disaster. My wife an I were playing and we maybe only saw like 2 tutorial messages because we kept skipping them accidentally.
But unforunately, it gets worse. Item descriptions are minimal to non-existent as well, so not only do you not know what you're buying a lot of the time, but the game gives little to no information on what the item actually does or how it is beneficial. This is a huge problem because it puts the guess work on the players and you have to learn what some things do by trial and error. There are certain moves that I can't purchase because my Special Move attribute is too low, but It's hard to know what to buy to boost it because the game doesn't tell you what stats the food/novelty improves until after you've eaten it. And then the added kicker is you have to sit through and wait for the text to get done scrolling to actually know what benefits you received from the item lol.
This same problem plagues you when you're upgrading your moveset. The does and extremely poor job of explaining what moves do and how to do them. The moveset is kinda all over the place and again leaves players to do a lot of guess work and experiementing to figure out how moves even work. There is no animation to allow you to see what the moves look like when they are performed, it's all just a trial and error fest that places the work on the player. Admittedly, It was frutstrating at times trying to figure out how things worked.
2. The GTA Style Heat system - While I do think it's wrong to just go around punching random pedestrians in the face all willy-nilly but this game kinda takes it overboard and not in a good way. Allow me to explain. First off pedestrians are EVERYWHERE and they are mixed in with the 10 or so gang members that immediately start attacking you as soon as you enter the screen, it can be hard to fight without some innocent by-stander being caught in the crossfire. Not to mention that a lot of the times through all the chaos, the innocents will position themselves directly between you and the enemy and pause as if to say "PLEASE DROP KICK THE F*** OUTTA MY FACE SO I CAN CALL THE POLICE MISTER!!!" This happens quite often so you'll end up with the police on your tail for acciental assaults. The vandalism is pretty bad too. I remember I kicked a guy out of the air and he landed on a parking meter, and GUESS WHO GOT IN TROUBLE FOR IT. lol
I think this would've been a funny easter egg to unlock (and made a LOT more sense) if they took the same "NO ENEMIES ALLOWED IN SHOPPING AREAS" approach as the original RCR. This way, if you willingly decided to go around punching innocent shoppers in the mouth or intentionally breaking stuff, THEN you'd get in trouble with the law (kinda like how in Zelda if you continously abused that poor chicken, then you'd get swarmed). But the way things are set up, the game punishes you for accidents. For Christ sake, I didn't mean to Haymaker all the change out of Little Timmy's pockets, i'm not a monster. lol
3. Player/Entrance/Exit Markers - This is a small thing that would've really gone a long way. Just simply putting a red arrow at entrannce and exit points. For stores especially, because some stores close at night, while others are open. A CLEAR indicator would've been nice. I can't tell you the amount of times I got my a** kicked and robbed of HALF my money in an entryway of a closed store while fleeing for my life lol. Also there are parts of the game where the exit is not clear, and this feature would've been extremely useful. Secondly, adding a marker over your player would've been awesome. It's easy to get lost in all the chaos especially with so many characters on screen at times.
4. Chase Sequences - These are probably some of the most annoying and frustrating sequences in the game. I miss the old days of beating the information out of your enemies. Not having a "Crash n' the Boys" foot race. It just feels awkward and out of place in a game like this. I really question the design choice, as I don't mind the boss running, but I would've rather had to fight my way through his crew and eventually corner him instead of having to chase him down.
5. Platforming - wtf?.....no
WHY? There is absolutely zero need for platforming in a game like this. The Forest Log thing was beyond rage inducing because of the poor jump tracking. Uness there is a game-breaking, holy grail, UP-UP-DOWN-DOWN-LEFT-RIGHT-LEFT-RIGHT, B, A, SELECT, START level cheat code item or something that's being hidden, then there is NO need for this type of platforming in this game.
IN CONCLUSION:
Despite some technical flaws and lack of explanation on a lot of the game's mechanics, this game is still awesome. It combines two of my favorite genres (rpg and old school beat 'em ups) and mixed them into one. I've had a great time with it so far, and I would recommend it to anyone who's a fan of classic beat 'em ups.
