If you were a fan of the original, this is a damn good game.  The controls seem tighter and slightly faster.
It's an old school beat em up, so know what to expect.  As for people complaining about the "grind", do you remember the original game?  It's the same mechanics.  Buy food, buy training to get extra moves, etc.  It feels totally like how it should for being a RCR game.  The openness of the world seems metroid-like as shops are closed at different parts of the day.  Be careful doing bad deeds, as it can get cops after you.  Remember when you wanted to punch the NPCs in the original but couldn't?  Well, you can now, but you might find yourself in trouble.
Controls feel super tight, I feel myself getting better the more I play.  The enemy AI is great, sure the enemies are generic beat em up targets, but it feels like they are a bit smarter than most, the bosses I've seen so far are quite fun.
Graphics are perfect for the game, and capture a sense of the nostalgia quite well, while providing more variety and looks than the old NES could handle.
This is the RCR you've been waiting for.
EDIT: I hear other reviewers not liking the tutorial and/or explanations.  They are entirely sufficient.  Pause the game and you can see the moves.  It's not big thing that the moves aren't descriptive, that's part of the charm, finding out what they do.
If I could change one thing about the game it would be that the moves list would detect if you had a controller plugged in and list the controller button instead of "s" etc.  The game is brand new, so hopefully the dev will address this in an update.

Strictly for fans of the original.
I'm not going to lie - I enjoyed playing through this game to the end with a friend, but I am a huge RCR/Kunio fan, and a lot of the fun for me was references and nostalgia. It's not that you can't have fun with RCRU, but it has so many unforgiveable problems.
It's riddled with bugs that have no place in any release title, let alone one at this price point, the user experience and interface are strictly amateur hour, and some design choices are flat out player-hositle (hiding information from the player about items and moves, the milk quest, etc). That said, the graphical style is very cool, the music is fine and nostalgic, the story is serviceable, and the combo system is fun. It also has online co-op, which I feel like you don't really see enough of, and was a big selling point for me.
But, ultimately, you'll likely be so frustrated the first time it eats your save, or you get locked into an infinite combo, or you can't open a menu, or an objective disappears completely - or any of the myriad other problems the game has - that none of that will matter anymore. Instead, you'll ultimately realize that the game is more frustrating than it is fun, and that's a bad, bad verdict for button-mashing brawler.
If you love RCR - I'd say go ahead and grab it. For everyone else? Wait for a sale. A BIG sale.

One of the most enjoyable strategy race games in many years. The worst part is the non-sensical pricing strategy of the publisher ($19.99 on PC, $9.99 on Android, $4.99 on iOS - all for the same game). Put it on your wishlist and wait for the price to hit $9.99 or less on Steam. Most negatives about this game center on the price, not the game itself. This is mispriced gem.
This game was so enjoyable, I spent dozens of hours experimenting with factions, upgrading my drivers, chariots, and horses, developing racing strategies and collecting game data about different cities, just so I could successfully manage teams to the Circus Maximus at Rome.
The game is deceptively simple - each "turn" of play you pick one order for your driver. The trick is dealing with the other drivers while positioning your team for the next corner. Drive too close inside, especially with an inexperienced driver, and you might suffer a costly crash. Horses, chariots and even your driver can suffer damage. Flipped or wrecked chariots result in the driver being dragged by the horses until he escapes, crosses the finish line, or dies.
Each individual race takes 5 to 10 minutes to play. However, it takes multiple races to get the "feel" of the hidden variables and probabilities, so you can race intelligently and make money - instead of losing your toga (like I did the first few times). But the real game starts when you play the campaign.
The campaign starts in your choice of a (probably distant) Imperial province, in a small city, with a few drivers, horse sets and chariots. It's your job to make enough money racing that you can cover the inevitable damage costs, upgrade your team and build your fame. With fame comes access to higher status cities with better rewards and better equipment. Eventually you'll want to travel to new provinces with more cities, on your way to the ultimate racing venue: the Circus Maximus in Rome.
The game's user interface and graphics are indie in spirit. The track and chariots are in top-down view. Gentle tints on the driver, chariot (wheels) and horses show exhaustion and/or damage. Despite this, the game oozes atmosphere, from the type fronts, to the crisp clear icons, to the blood smear on the sandy-tan track marking the death of a charioteer. Everything about the game reminds you of Imperial Rome.
From a game design standpoint, the inner workings are excellently balanced. Chances of damage or disaster change with multiple variable. Even a risk-averse manager will find rare, random event can set back the best laid plans, or provide an unexpected success. Incautious, wild racers are heavily punished -
you cannot rely on "good luck" or constant aggression to win this game. The AI drivers are intelligent, and occasionally unpredictable. If they have no hope of winning themselves, they may even block your chances out of pure malice or spite! The temptation to bash them off the track is strong, even though it won't profit you.
This game reminds me of chariot race boardgames from 30 to 40 years ago. However, Qvadriga is vastlymore playable than those clunky endeavors. Those old boardgames had fewer variables, took 1-3 hours per race to play, and had no AI players! Besides, Qvadriga's campaign game is infinitely more interesting and playable than anything available in those old boardgames.
Yes, it would be nice if the game had beautifully animated isometric or 3D racing graphics. We all dream about drivers that animate appropriately in response to your orders, or when victims of attacks, not to mention chariot wheels coming off, chariots flipping, horses dying in collisions, and chariots bouncing over the wreckage of other chariots and dead horses, plus drivers being dragged or running away, sometimes to a gruesome death. However, the chances of that game being made is infinitely small, given the current state of strategy games, publisher investment resources, and the technical limitations of building games for mobile as well as the PC.
Yes, it would also be nice if the game allowed for human opponents. But do I want to wait hours until another human player is available? Am I expected to run a private serve? Do I expect the poor, cash-strapped developer (or publisher) to maintain a multi-player server for me and the nineteen other English speakers in the world who just might want to play each other? Do I expect an online chat system as well? For a niche game like this, it is quite understandable that we're limited to offline play only.
The only REAL fault with this game is publisher's (Slitherine's) inane pricing strategy. Today (July 21, 2016), the very same game costs $19.99 for the PC (on Steam), $9.99 for Android (at the Google Play Store), and $4.99 for iOS (in the iTunes store). Yes, the game is priced lowest on the platform that has the richest customer base! If I were the developer, I'd be outraged by this inconsistent pricing. As other reviewers have noted, the $19.99 price needlessly discourages PC purchases. Personally, I believe the publisher has simly lost track of any rational pricing strategy for this two-year-old title.  It's really a shame. This is a timeless, great, little racing game. Put it on your wishlist and wait for $9.99 or less.

LISA is polarizing by design, and simply playing through it's introduction alone is enough to give you an understanding of why so many people never finish or play it at all. The plot is a pitch black, grim, and hopeless affair filled with only occasional forays into light hearted and humorous territory. But the catch here is that these moments are designed to make the inevitable fall back down into the blackest pits of human cruelty imaginable even more devastating and impactful. You see, while LISA is a deconstruction of many common JRPG tropes, it's main deconstruction is that of a trope found in many forms of media, not just video games. That trope is the notion of protagonist centered morality. What this trope means is that in a story, when the protagonist causes innumerable amounts of death and destruction in their quest, they'll still be a hero and still be loved and praised by the populace, because although they've caused all this, their goal is noble so they're relieved of consequences or responsibility for their actions. LISA disposes of this folly almost immediately. The main character, Brad, is not only suffering because of the awful events that have happened in his life which he has no control over, but by his own decisions and actions as well. Brad has what sounds like an entirely noble goal at first, save his surrogate daughter Buddy from all the people in Olathe who want to use and abuse her for sexual pleasure and stop them from turning her into just a tool to repopulate the earth with. Save his surrogate daughter Buddy from the people who kidnapped her. Except the things he does to accomplish this start to get increasingly worse as the games plot unfolds. Not only that, but the regular people of this world do not look at Brad as if he's some divine hero that must be showered with praise, most of them look at Brad and see this sad old washed up has been and loser, who's just another nobody and a drifter, and then they proceed to ignore him, harass him, try to rob and kill him, make fun of him, and just treat him like garbage in general. And as his actions grow larger in their notoriety and scale, Brad becomes a demon in the eyes of the world. So much so that people either attack him on sight out of pure hatred, or retreat from him out of pure fear. And all the suffering that befalls on his companions and loved ones during the games events are all at least somewhat Brad's fault as well, and at many times Brad will be made to pay for it with mortal injury and failing at all his goals. In the end, this is not a story about someone conquering their demons and becoming a better person, this is a story about how someone is completely consumed by them and not only destroys themselves, but those around them as well.
While I for one never found LISA's gameplay to be outright impossible even on Pain mode (the hardest difficulty) I can see why many are repelled by it as well. Unlike most JRPG's, you have a large pool of party members (30 to be exact) that are not only fragile and expendable, but are actively encouraged by the game to be used up as resources in decisions and situations that are either dangerous and risky, or ask you to give up some of your protagonist Brad's strength or items for the life of a party members. Another feature that is in LISA is one you usually don't see outside of roguelikes, certain strategy games, and CRPG's. And that is permanent death. Whenever you are fighting a particularly powerful enemy, sleeping at campfires, or being faced with a decision, there's a random chance or a conscious decision on the player's part as to whether or not a party member will be killed off forever. There is one thing that makes it all easier on you. There is no grinding required whatsoever in LISA. How is this possible? Simple, you gain enough exp from exploring and fighting pre set enemies you can actually see and walk into. Consequently gameplay is now spent venturing into as many new areas as possible instead of fighting the same enemy in the same caves or same forests for hours. After all, the largest  amounts of exp will only be found by exploring and fighting enemies that are well off the beaten path.
LISA isn’t perfect though. While it’s obvious that a lot of passion and care went into the game, the aspect of it that causes almost all of it’s problems is simply the engine itself, RPG Maker. RPG Maker is a widely used engine for a lot of indie games, mostly because it requires next to no scripting or coding, but unfortunately this comes at the cost of performance. Numerous bugs and optimization issues tend to plaque RPG Maker games, and LISA is no exception to this. Even in fullscreen, LISA will have black borders on the right and left hand side of the screen no matter what. Characters will sometimes be found  floating in the air or simply stuck in the terrain, Brad can climb on parts of the scenery in certain areas and start walking or biking through the air and can cause a glitch on ropes that causes him to walk faster then the bike, and in certain areas like Snow Mountain the framerate will drop down severely depending on your hardware. Part of these issues stem from LISA being a top down game which uses various tricks to make it look like a sidescroller, due to RPG Maker being incapable of making sidescrollers. Essentially the game is pretending to be a sidescroller in a engine that was never meant to make one and it really shows at times. Part of it might also stem from the fact that RPG Maker renders everything as an object and also renders things offscreen at all times. It’s just incredibly sad to see a great game get held back somewhat by a buggy and unstable engine.
At the end of the day, when all of the above elements (besides the bugs) combine, they form an experience that's both foreign and strange, yet so human and relatable. For those of you who are easily offended or disgusted, or for those who subject matter such as this brings back unpleasant memories or experiences, you will most likely not enjoy this at all. But if you're willing to try something that's truly unique and impactful despite everything mentioned here, you might just have an unforgettable ride ahead of you.

LISA, or to give it its full name, LISA The Painful RPG. Painful is right, as you adventure with Brad to save his adopted daughter you'll struggle with addiction, meet characters who have been through hell, maybe even watch some of your favorite ones die before you. Worst of all you'll feel like a lot of it will be your fault as LISA forces you to make tough decisions with no right answer; dismemberment or death? Sacrifice all your items or sacrifice your only friend? The story is a simple and personal one. There's no world to save, just a very important girl. It hits hard and it's wonderfully engaging. You'll always want to know what happens next. Having said that, it isn't always so downtrodden in tone. LISA also manages to work a lot of humour into its setting and characters. A bunch of middle aged men doing bad Power Rangers impressions, the Mexican guy whose main attributes are crying and hitting enemies with a truck and so much more.
The story is complimented by a soundtrack that is often sombre and occasional lighthearted, thus it fits the mood of the environments and the events perfectly.
Of course there's more to the game than the story. The gameplay is great for those who like turn based RPGS, especially Earthbound as this game is heavily inspired by it. Though there is more to the combat than just "choose enemy, choose attack." The different character, and there are a lot of different characters, have different combat styles. For Brad's attacks you have to input button combinations for example. Outside of combat the gameplay is very simple. You mostly just move left and right without any platforming. Moreoever the story and combat are meshed together very well. Certain choices you make will affect how characters behave in combat. It's difficult to say without spoiling it. One example is that
To summarise, LISA is a tough experience that'll make you laugh and maybe cry. It'll make you feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥at times but you'll always want to come back for more because of the endearing characters that yuo'll no doubt want to see succeed.

I have played this game since the open beta. It has grown quite a bit since then, in good ways and bad, but there are some major factors with this game that have driven me to write this negative review.
Note, while I did put around 2000 battles into the game before the steam release, I have not played the game for around 3 months, and the developers have given me no incentive to do so. For added context, I was a carrier main; about 60-65% winrate overall.
Positives:
The game has rather pretty ship models, even though the developers haven't been able to figure out anti-aliasing and sometimes make historical mistakes (and sometimes even fix them). In general, the ship modelers are very good and this is probably the one place where the game shines. I would include sounds here, but they are largely hit or miss. Aircraft sound terrible. AA effects are bad.
Major problems with this game:
- The engine Wargaming runs this game on is horribly overtaxed. It was not designed to simulate water, so your ships will float along driving like a tank on a flat 2d plane with little water animations moving up and down the sides. Watch Dev Diary #8. At a glance, it looks fine. But once you start to see it, you realize how much more this game could be with a full engine built for it. It's a bathtub, not an ocean. No dramatic pitching and rolling, no waves crashing over bows, no distinctly different weather - this will become
noticable during "cyclones" which puts a little curtain of light rain over your ship and lowers your draw distance. It's really disappointing in 2017. The devs are trying to improve it.
-  Like most free-to-play games, WoWs relies heavily on RNG to pad out their content and add a false layer of "depth" to the game. For example, the game will add rng to all of your shooting as dispersion, so hitting a ship at mid-long range has miss chance to average player skill levels. This was because their decision to make gameplay speed of ships on a 2D battlefield slow enough that they seem to have "weight" also makes a point-and-click interface insanely easy to hit targets. You will find it in almost all mechanics- Map choice (no pick/ban), team makeup (no lobby w/o training room mod!), DoT chance is RNG based, direct DPS has rng miss chance, AA and dive bombing is all RNG based. Not to mention everyone's hated "feature" - Detonation -  you have an RNG chance of exploding when hit.
Naturally then, things often considered "strong" in the game are the things that players CAN control, aka are not based in rng, like HP regen, stealth, smoke, radar, hydro, defensive fire (which pushes some AA rng% up to 100% in some cases) - though defensive fire isn't considered strong because CVs are not guaranteed to appear in matches due to smaller playerbase, and nobody really should be playing them until Wargaming actually does a rework.
Because of this, developing new ships and premium ships generally centers around this handful of mechanics: armor is more a factor of gun penetration, ship speed does not have enough visual variation between the classes to really matter (again, if they made things move
in the game, they could have more visual differentiation here!). So we have "balance" and "new" ships based on their consumables. It used to be the case that a ship would have to choose between slotting certain ones, but newer ships basically all get some variation of hp heal, radar, hydro, smoke, or defensive fire. Put simply, the game devs have run out of 'depth'. Everything for the last year can be described as "Basically like ship X, but with Y consumable!" Carriers were basically abandoned by the devs after launch.
- Despite the pretty models, maps are mediocre skyboxes; they look ok at first glance, but if you play more than a few games on a map, you will find it getting boring. Some of them are hilariously unbalanced or promote extremely boring playstyles.
- The entire gameplay has been a patchwork stand-in mechanic, from rng-based accuracy and anti-aircraft fire, to planes lacking actual armor and hull values, having infinite fuel and yet limited ammo. This has been a beta mechanic since the
, something developers have continued to lie about until this last fall.
They promised in 2016 that 2017 would be "the year of the carrier" with a rework. They then proceeded to sell 3 premium carriers (ending with the scandal this fall) before finally coming out and admitting a month ago that they haven't even started working on the rework, and that nothing should be expected until somewhere in 2018.
So, if you want to play this game for carrier play, you shouldn't bother. The mechanics as they play now are boring, repetitive, and while you can trick yourself in thinking you are having fun, they are shamefully lacking in any sort of tactical depth. At low tiers you can no longer manually control your planes, which was a patch introduced this year, by the way, to make it "easier to learn"  (the devs are are still under the delusion that the low number of carrier players is because they are "difficult" to play, and not because they never actually put in real CV mechanics). At higher tiers your planes will be shot by AA fire before you spot the ship.
The UI has NEVER been improved to include anything useful for CV players - you have no way to tell in the UI how close your planes really are to something, aka if you are flying into AA range or if your planes have been spotted by enemies. The UI in general is incredibly buggy - it was so bad they actually attempted to patch it earlier this fall so you could actually consistently input commands to your planes (and with a logical keyboard layout, so be lucky you didn't wait 2 years for that!). Carrier Captain skills are still cookie-cutter options with no depth of play because Air Supremacy is basically a required take, even though it
air loadouts in higher tier play.
Poor Community Relationship & Cash-grab at Gamescon 2017- This fall the developers released the "Graf Zeppelin" premium CV, despite the fact that it was an unfinished, unbalanced, and exhorbinantely overpriced mess. Despite widespread (and I do mean widespread, from the community contributors down to forums in every region) outcry and criticism, Wargaming berated the community by calling them inept, kicked out community contributors, and declared that everything was fine, locking threads and deleting comments showing bugs. They turned around and admitted a few days later that things were not as they were intended, and offered refunds for the ship (the first time they have done this). This is sadly the norm, as it has been for years, they are incredibly tone deaf to the playerbase.
If you take it on the nose as a free-to-play game, then you should NEVER buy premium ships - the devs will tweak and edit their stats and abilities again in the future, guaranteed. They tend to retire the horribly balanced ones from the store (Nikolai, looking at you in particular), but that just leaves them in the hands of the abusers.
I would also make you aware as a steam user that the ENTIRE reason Wargaming released this game on Steam is because they have been loathe to take on the burden of paying the bandwidth costs for downloading the bloated client. Up until this release, you were REQUIRED to download their "manager" which forced players to use p2p torrenting to download their game. With a dwindling playerbase, matchmaking was awful; another reason to add steam users.
Daily rewards became lootcrates (meh, more rng mechanics), and store purchased "christmas lootboxes" will be back this winter season to make big bucks off gambling.
All in all, play the game if you want to enjoy a relatively niche naval wargame, but

Puzzle Agent 2 picks up so flawlessly from where the first finishes off that it feels like an episodic series which should be longer than it is. And that's not because it feels unfinished, it just feels like a story universe that could expand into so much more and be relentlessly interesting.
I've heard this described as "Professor Layton if written by David Lynch" which I assume is a reference to Twin Peaks. That is indeed an accurate assessment. This game mixes a hilariously dry wit and a surreal, dark undertone that simultaneously treats itself seriously while being aware of the ludicrous nature of its elements.
Having not played much Professor Layton, I can't make a ton of comparisons, but the puzzle-heavy adventure definitely feels more gratifying than the inventory-heavy nature of many contemporaries. It's nice to never be in a situation where I have to try the verb on every noun until something clicks.
The art style of the game is very unique, and after playing the two games I looked up the artist's (grickle) work, which can all be found on his YouTube. If you're not into mindgames, you probably won't get much out of this, but for those with a cerebral persuasion, the gameplay and story both heavily play to your need to "solve puzzles".

After playing Puzzle Agent 1 and 2. I want Puzzle Agent 3, if it ever happens, and they can expand a bit on the story. The game is kinda like a rather innocent "Fargo" like setting, with fitting animations, decent story and logical and enjoyable puzzles. There is no quality dif between 1 and 2. 2 is just a continuation of the story with the same engine.

This is a step back from Puzzle Agent 1. While it still kept the original aspect and feel of the game, it was worse in almost every other way: heavy reuse of assets, low variation in puzzles which had clunky explanations and a story which lacks intensity and has a lot of loose ends. Play Puzzle Agent 1. If you want more of the same but done on a lower level of quality, try PA2 as well but I would not recommend it as a stand alone.

Puzzle Agent 2 is a decent title by itself, but it is mainly recommended for those who played the first game. They not only can watch the rest of the story, but can enjoy the increased puzzle difficulty.
A typical sequel usually does nothing but brings you more of the defining elements of the first instalment. Puzzle Agent 2 is no exception.
The artwork is yet again based on Graham Annable’s Grickle series, but one of the defining elements, the eerie small town mystery is quickly abolished by the new plot, leading into an overcomplicated government conspiracy thriller that in the end just cracks under its own weight.
The puzzles received a large overhaul. There is no more ambiguity, and the number of 5-second riddles have been reduced considerably to give room for more difficult and more computer game-like types. There is also a new incentive system for replay value: you can only access the final enigma if you successfully complete all puzzles without hints or wrong answers, a feat which is nearly impossible on the first try without a walkthrough.
Thanks to these simple design improvements Puzzle Agent 2 is a little more fun to play than the first game, especially for returning players.

I had this game in my library far before reviews were a thing on Steam (even before they tracked hours, remember that?)-- I remembered the game as being entertaining and was shocked to see all of the negativity. So naturally, I had to go back.
Space Trader is best described in four steps:
1) Find a starship
2) Get seriously deep with the wrong people
3) ???
4) Profit.
It's not a global marketing simulator, it's a game where you Han Solo your way through a gunslinging, profiteering, not-quite legit smuggling career. The only thing that matters in this game is making enough profits to survive the stage. There's a lot of fun to be had doing the very simplistic FPS missions while trying to grab the most profitable deals while racing against the clock (though you'd wish that clock were either shorter to keep the pressure on or longer to stretch out the experience).
This was one of the first Steam purchases I'd made and, despite leaving the game to gather etheral dust in cyberspace, I have a lot of fun memories playing it. You won't put 100+ hours on this game but, if you're the sort of person who enjoys the above, you'll get a kick out of the short time you do spend with it. 7/10

is another triumph from Harebrained Schemes, just perhaps not always as consistent as it's predecessor, Dragonfall. The new Matrix gameplay is fun and can be actually challenging, the characters are deep and realized as usual, and the final sequences where all the mysteries of the game start to get wrapped up are engaging.
If you've played a Shadowrun game before, you should know what to expect. Isometric point-and-click, turn-based combat, it's all pretty consistent, although throughout several points I found that the combat dragged on for some encounters far more than was necessary. Also, what's up with 70%+ to hit, I take three shots, all three miss. I understand that sometimes these things happen occasionally, but it's happened to me several times now. Normally I wouldn't nitpick on this, but because the previous two Shadowrun games didn't have this problem for me, I'm just a little disappointed with this. Other than that, the gameplay is still solid, with a new stealth+puzzle Matrix for deckers to jack into.
You are invited to Hong Kong by your foster father, who wants to speak to you on a matter of utmost importance. However, both parties, you and your brother, Duncan, and your foster father, Raymond, are ambushed. The story unfolds from here as you discover that you have an entire city full of police out for your head, as well as strange dreams plaguing your sleep. The characters that accompany you on this journey are fleshed out and realized, and it's well worth talking to them between missions. However, if you hate reading, you will definitely miss out on the best parts of the game. It's not a game that you should always go with the 'attack' option. There is a lot of dialogue in this game, I like that, but be warned. The previous two games have less dialogue, which can be either good or bad.
Graphics are better than from last time, walking around Heoi (your home-base area) it is all very well done, with the graphics letting Harebrained Schemes get the most out of their environments and characters.
The atmosphere, is, as usual, impeccable. The game really draws you in, with detailed descriptions, awesome character portraits, interesting characters, usage of Chinese magics such as Qi and Feng Shui, and every environment feels just that *bit* different, and that's a good thing.
The sound is, again, still awesome. With gunfire, splatters of blood, exploding of heads with critical kills, and another epic soundtrack to accompany the game, it's up high on the scale of 'what's great about this game'. My favorite tracks are Bad Qi, DeckCon, The Walled City and Welcome to the Grid.
This was easily the most frustrating moment in the game, and I'd like to outline it for anyone who is looking to buy this game. The mission called 'Misdirection' in which you have to steal from an Ares corporation and dodge Knight Errant Soldiers, has an infuriating bug if you take along Racter. You have to find a keycard to open a safe, and, on the lab level, be sure not to trip the Matrix alarms or bring in extra security *before* you reach the other Runners. If that happens, a dialogue will be missed and you won't receive the keycard. Unfortunately I didn't realize that the keycard couldn't be gained after fighting off extra security, so after completing that long battle I realized I had to start the entire mission again. You have been warned, there may be other glitches like this throughout the game.
A fun, detailed, immersive game that, although it has it's problems with gameplay and glitches, I'll still let it go because I found myself enjoying the game more than I was hating on it. If you are looking for one Shadowrun, buy Dragonfall, but if you are looking for another Shadowrun adventure, buy this, just acknowledge that there will be some problems. But, after all, what game doesn't?

I hope the playerbase grows a lot more, because it really deserves it.

Crazy. Insane. Quirky. Super depressing with some black humor.
Preface: If you are going to play LISA, you should look up LISA The First. You do not necessarily have to play it, but just read up the story on it, even if it's creepy.
Now for this LISA: Go buy it. Further, make sure you buy LISA The Joyful as well, meant to be played after you complete the main game.
This game is one which is best played going in blind, so I do not want to say much about what happens. But if you are alright with witnessing some pretty terrible events and having to make some pretty terrible, screwed-up choices, then seriously get this game. Even if you are afraid of having to make bad choices, still try the game out - open yourself up and don't be afraid to give it a shot.
The game has its ups and downs, but the environment and story was just so strange yet organized in a way that it kept me focused and playing it all for a good long while. I never wanted to stop playing LISA despite what bad events kept occurring (exception: there is 1 single point in the game that is bad random number generation and really annoying).
The game is certainly not an easy one, especially because there are difficult RPG battles, which I did not know about when I first started it out. But I have more than enough experience with RPGs so I lived through it all. And if you play it right without wasting some items, you should have enough luck to make it through, or grind if you need to. Just read up on some of the guides.
But really, you should just give the game a shot - go in blind, and just push yourself through it. Make sure you get LISA The Joyful because you really need it to "wrap up" some parts of the storyline more. In fact, LISA The Joyful turned out to be a great culminating point for everything.
I got so connected to this game way beyond what I imagined. I got extremely angry at the characters, happy when certain obstacles were passed, and well, really sad when a ton of the bad events occurred.
It had me hooked from the beginning.

LISA is a wonderfully painful experience. Some games get under your skin; LISA goes for bone. This is ultimately a difficult game to recommend to most people. Its humor is bizzare and macabre, its gameplay is sometimes purposefully confusing and challenging throughout, and, at the end of the day, it left me feeling heartbroken. However, if you are someone who looks for a rich, emotionally compelling story set in a harsh world with hilarious characters and utterly soul crushing decisions to make, LISA has your number.
The world of LISA is without heroes. This is a depraved post-apocalyptic world scattered with destroyed homes and populated only by pent up men. Roving gangs conquer the wasteland, drunks and drugs are abundant, wrestling is worshipped, pornographic literature is the currency, there is a cult that lifts heavy things, men are used, and hope is forsaken. This is a brutal world where you are absolutely going to die and lose a lot of progress because you weren't paying attention. You are Brad, a depressed, middle-aged, bald, former martial arts instructor with a traumatic past and nothing to live for. Brad is addicted to a drug called Joy, which makes him feel nothing. One day, Brad finds a crying baby abandoned in the wasteland. He and his friends discover that this baby is the last girl in the world. She disappears, along with his friends, and Brad embarks on a quest to find her. What follows is a tale of perverts, inept characters, hard choices, and disappointment.
The soundtrack of LISA is brilliant and just as ecclectic and strange as the characters you'll meet. It is rather amazing how much detail the game has considering the limitations of the technology at hand. There is so much to explore and so many characters to meet I scoured the world, and there is much that I somehow missed.  My only qualm with the game is that is can be very difficult to determine your next course of action. The world is vast and navigating it can be a challenge. Yet, there is a weird mystique to it all. Something that, despite its gloom, kept me asking for more. It is peppered with much humor and little victories that LISA makes you quest for the brighter side of things; for a better life. It's hopeless, but it's feeling alive that counts.
LISA is one of my favorite games. It is sometimes not the most plesant game, but that is the point. I recommend it to anyone looking for an experience as dark and twisted as themselves.

Unlike the first game, many of the puzzles lacked proper descriptions, forcing the player to make guesses on the rules of certain puzzles. While the first Puzzle Agent relied more on logical and 'puzzle' puzzles, this game tended to use more visual puzzles without much logic at all. The game held some kind of promise on release, but with every patch the game was affected negatively. The original single player campaign was balanced for the state of the game as it was released, and then promptly was ignored and orphaned.
If you must buy a game, the original Company of Heroes is a much better choice, as is the original Dawn of War. With, of course, all the expansions for both games. Given the age on both of these titles, you should wait for a sale.
If you MUST buy Company of Heroes 2, do so on a sale, particularly because of the IN GAME STORE with MICROTRANSACTIONS (not listed in the store page) on each and every little thing. Pretty much every decent commander is realistically held behind a few extra dollars EACH. The scary thing is that underneath all of this, a good game could be beaten out of what's here, but as far as I've seen, modding support is not to the point where one could totally convert the game into solid gold - unlike the titles listed previously in this review. Its likely this is the case because of the microtransactions.
I've already put too much effort into this review, so to keep it short - don't waste your money or time on this title, you'd be better off trying to mod DOTA 2 into Warcraft 3.

If you liked the first Company of Heroes and enjoy WWII strategy games - then Company of Heroes 2 is the game for you. I can definitely understand others being upset over all the DLC and balancing issues for competitive play - however, these issues don't personally effect me because I usually only play against the A.I. with the help of some friends or another A.I.
Compared to the first Company of Heroes, the second installment (to me) is much more fluid and the user interface is clean and provides a lot of helpful data. Also, with the introduction of the Steam Workshop - the mods have really made my experience that much better. Mods that add up to 140 different units for all factions, maps, game modes, population cap increases, etc.
If you're not good enough to play on a competitive level like me, and just want to amass a bunch of WWII-era units into war and watch and enjoy the carnage this game is great for that. Especially when the Master Collection can go on sale to as low as $10 USD. A must buy for any RTS fan.

Additionally, the overall pacing, length and cohesiveness of the story weren't nearly as strong as they could've been, and I think this is where the majority of complaints about the plot stem from. Not necessarily that the plot was bad per se, but that because of its awry execution, people were not able to fully appreciate it.
Nonetheless, there were still a number of noticeable improvements made to the actual gameplay and the music was quite stellar too, especially the main menu theme. All in all, I believe people are having a difficult time judging HK objectively due to their rose coloured lens tinting their experience with DF.
Personally, I find the biggest flaw with HK not to be how badly ( or well ) it sizes up with DF, but with how it seemingly passed up on a lot of easy/simple potential to improve the game.
Ultimately, if you consider their budget, the development time frame and the size of their team, you really can't fault them...as they need to cover their bases financially first and foremost, as a smaller independent studio.
HBS' hard work has paid off all the same, and their surging fame and popularity can be witnessed in how quickly their recent kickstarter gathered steam. I wish them all the best, for so long as they remain passionate and grounded in their work, a successful HBS means a successful Shadowrun series.
And from what we've seen and what we know, HBS is very much down to earth and in touch with their community.
Now, enough of this doom and gloom...GIVE ME THE NEXT SHADOWRUN ALREADY
Edit: Whatever discontent I had with the base SR:HK game have been completely dispelled by the Shadows of Hong Kong mini campaign, and transforms SR:HK into the clear better as compared to SR:DF.
This, here, is the complete Shadowrow experience, and the feels this game gives you by the end, all the personal and tough choices you will have to make throughout, the blurred lines of morality and the shades of grey, all of them resound with you. Though it saddens me to say goodbye to the game for now, it couldn't have ended more poignantly. This game has captured the essence of cyberpunk and made it its own.
I'll miss my team :')

The thing you have to keep in mind when looking at Shadowrun: Hong Kong is that it is not Dragonfall. They have similarities, and many of the mechanics are the same, but they are not the same game both in feel and in gameplay.
I really liked the amount of dialogue you get from the NPCs. It is clear as you talk to these characters that there was a lot of writing that had to be done. I'd say that for each major NPC (the party, the townsfolk, etc.) there is at least 2-3 hours of dialogue available. Not only that, but the options and conversation was much more advanced and flowed much more realistically than Dragonfall. In prequels, you would bombard NPCs with dialogue options until you exhausted all they could tell you; in Hong Kong, NPCs will remember what you tell them and conversation will follow a life-like pattern.
The companions are really amazing in Shadowrun: Hong Kong as well. They all have an interesting and developed backstory, and their behavior ties into the setting of the Sixth World. The only one I didn't quite like was Is0bel, as I found her behavior childish and she was abnormally quite. Then again, this was what she was supposed to be, if you look at her backstory.

One of the major issues is you'll notice up front is that this game loves inadequately explaining anything to you. The game is infuriating for new players to get into, feeling like it was designed to experienced testers standards instead.
What few tutorial messages that do pop up, there's going to be a good chance you're in a middle of a fight and you'll just mash the prompt away and you'll never see it again.
Once you get some cash you'll do one of two things.
Buy Moves:
Moves that aren't explained to you in the Dojo. Moves that aren't properly explained in the move list. A good chunk of these moves are variations on your basic combos (So you can Punch, Punch, Kick now.) so it feels like a waste of your money and time getting that cash.
Othertimes you get a Not High Enough Level message when trying to learn a move but it won't tell you what level you need to be.
Once you get a good set under your belt it evens out, it's just that it's stuck behind a few hours of frustrating grinding for a new player.
Buy Food:
Eventually you'll feel under powered even though it flashes on the screen that you're leveling up and you're buying moves.
What you need to figure out then is you need buy items to actually increase those stats and that leveling up just increases the Max cap for the stats. The system isn't bad but again it's not explained to you.
Buying items is terribly slow, only displaying one line.  Even on the fastest text setting you still have to wade through:
-You Bought Food. Pause.
-Funny Text About food. Pause.
-Stat Y went up by AMOUNT. Pause.
-Stat Y is Maxed Out. Pause.
-Stat X went up.
Etc.
Skipping the text doesn't skip the line, it skips the entire thing so you have to sit and stare through it again.
The game doesn't track what stats that item actually increased either. This isn't the NES days, are you trying to sell game guides? The Community Pages thankfully already have a guide up on what items increase what but again there's no reason to be forced to have this open all the time when the game could just tell you.
A few more sucker punches too. There's a bunch of gimmick items in stores. Again the issue is the game doesn't tell you what they are. The Comic store that has extremely useful stat-gaining items has this one alluring expensive item. Being the most expensive item in the store it must be even better?
You buy it and nothing happens, it takes your money but it doesn't appear in your Inventory. You try to buy it again but it tells you that you already have it. Did it glitch out? Did you accidentally skip the text? No. What you wasted your starter-money on was a poster for one of your hideouts.
Healing:
Mostly a New player problem. You can only heal through store items, leveling up or a refill by dying (and losing half your cash). You just don't have the cash flow to constantly stop to get items when starting, but you don't want to die and lose your money because you need it for moves/stats.
The Quests:
Variety is fine, it's how they've been implemented. You have the simple RCR classic 'Beat up the grunts and the Boss appears' ones.
Later you get a 'Chase this people down and hit them' quests, they'll sprint through the screen and you just have to whack them once to stop them. But they move almost as fast as you do. And you still have to contend with all the grunts. Plus the platforming they want you to do. They give you three of these quests in a row, having to fend off the grunts as they give their spiel one line at a line.
Eventually you get to the Milk bottle quest:
You need to carry, over your head, which slows your movement, a bottle of milk through at least 7 screens without getting hit or running into something even once. If you get hit once it will break and you need to try it again. You can place the bottle down but it's still fragile and a single hit will break it, you can also easily get hit while placing it down or picking it up. A beaker thrown from the Nerds, bats from the Necroemokids, a grunt hitting you as you put it down, a respawning grunt hitting you as you go to pick it up, the instant sudden diving attack from a Luchador or Bomber, or just getting hit as you walk into the next screen. There's a boss fight right at the end too once you get right infront of the door of the delivery place.
Later on you have to fight through a rather long and tough gauntlet with tough grunts. Hope you stocked up on healing items because you if die you have to go through it all again, all 7+ screens of them.
The Combat:
But in the end the combat must be fight right? Just beating guys up and using your moves and all that? Yes. The combat is fun once you get all your moves and you know how to use them. The animation is pretty great overall. The controls are responsive and it never feels like it ate your inputs.
But starting the game you'll notice something, you figure it will get better as you learn but it really doesn't. Through the entire game, a large chunk of the grunts kite you.
Constantly.
They'll back away from you the same speed you walk at them.
They'll expertly jump/back out/block your strike/grab when they're right in your face then punish you back right away.
Wait for you to finish your combo for them to instantly punch you back in the face. Or even better you'll just plain outright strike you in the middle of a combo anyway.
Back out of strike range by a few pixels then dash in to punch you in the face.
Later in the later they'll Block more and more. So not only are constantly trying to chase them down but when you finally get them they're Blocking. When you try to Grab them or chip down their Block, another enemy will punch you in the back of the head. Turn to attack the ambusher? The first guy will stop kiting/blocking to hit you. You might have a back-attack move but that doesn't stop the front grunt from Blocking/Cheap shotting you.
The easiest way to play through mid/end game is to stand in one place, hold Block and let them come to you, tap them a few times then just Block again. You can actually kite the kiting enemy into attacking by quickly letting go of Block then holding it again since there's a good chance they'll attack the split-second you let go of it.
It's slow and boring.
There's a bunch of other smaller problems too, the Police system is irritating and at the current time the Over-Internet Multiplayer is busted.

I've played at least 40 hours (including some time spent during the beta) and while the lustre is starting to fade a little bit, I'm still excited to play more, and I guarantee that RCR:U will be a game that I dig out and play every year or so.

Also, the game will have mod support, so I can't wait to see what the community will do when they get ahold of it.
All that said, if you don't have the patience to wade through the bugs and usability issues, then by all means put the game off for a few weeks. But don't let it drop off your radar, it's absolutely worth playing.

It's short, a little under two hours for my first playthrough, but it's still plenty good enough to recommend. The story is told from the perspective of a dad to his little girl, so it's a bit light and the wording is easy for little kids to understand. I rarely find PVP games that interesting. They tend to be fun in the first, generously, day or two, but then they start looking like just a reskinned copy of some other PVP game and that's it. Novelty worn off.
Blade symphony is something unique from the ground up, and due to being based around duels in the first place, and while some sort of singleplayer or co-op mode with story would definitely add positively to the experience, it is not designed to need one to be fun.
The defense is pretty active, so you don't have a lot of people turtling up with a block button making no attacks safe. you really have to judge your distance so you can both parry and attack in the same sequence. If you just go wild, you may get in a lucky win, but you'll lose most of the time, because the game requires you to actually fence. This isn't a fighting game, its a fencing game.
The combinations of the weapon types and the character mechanics works well, I could only hope that they might add more in the near future though its got a solid basis now.

This game is quite a gem!  It is strange how a game like this fell under the radar.  I quite enjoyed the story and humour.  The story can be quite emotionally taxing to some, as it is not a very happy one and does not skirt away from topics such as depression and drug abuse.  For some people, the constant switching between humour and seriousness may not be a selling point, but it should not affect the enjoyment of the game in any extreme manner. The colourful and bizarre world and characters, however, are some of the best that I have seen in a game.
As for the gameplay, it is quite solid and the combat can be challlenging at times (mainly on Pain difficulty).  The only problem that I had with Pain difficulty is the removal of save points after use, which can extend a gaming session longer than one may wish.  Sleeping is dangerous and hard decisions concering one's party are to be made.  The biggest pain in the♥♥♥♥♥would have to be the cliffs.  If you do not move cautiously near cliffs, you will fall from them and have to load back to a previous save.  I find the cliffs to be needlessly punishing, as one is only punished for trying to get through the levels without paying attention to them.
Overall,  I would highly recommend this game to anyone wishing to experience emotional duress and an engaging story with plenty of humour (mainly of the dark variety).  Also, if you like nipples and man♥♥♥♥♥♥ then this game has MANY!

I know everyone wants a rating or something, so lets say it rates like an 80%

First off, as someone who lives in Hong Kong, as well as a fan and Kickstarter backer, I was truly psyched to play the game and thoroughly enjoyed it.
Despite the UI enhancements, more developed Matrix, slightly better graphics, I honestly felt the whole premise was a carbon copy of Dragonfall: We start off solving a mystery, take random side jobs and then tackle the final part of the story where you're given a decision to affect the ending. But all in a different setting with different characters. But hey, if it ain't broken don't try and fix it. I still enjoyed it, especially reading the little quips related to Hong Kong's political situation. The writers really did their research. But the feeling I got from the game afterwards was just all too familiar like Dragonfall and secretly I was hoping for a whole new experience.
Just *one* minor gripe I have about the level design - all the MTR (subway) stations have the same name, Kowloon Bay!

Shadowrun Hong Kong is the third game in the popular cyberpunk RPG series. I really enjoyed the previous two games, Returns and Dragonfall, so I've been looking forward to playing Hong Kong ever since it was announced, and I'm pleased to say that Hong Kong lived up to my expectations.
The story is excellent. Your character has received a mysterious message from your foster-father, indicating that he's in trouble and asking for your help. After arriving in Hong Kong, you get dragged into a massive conspiracy involving organised crime, corporate espionage and supernatural wierdness. There are lots of interesting characters and the dialogue is well written.
The turn based combat system is pretty much the same as previous games. You have a team of 4 characters, and each round they spend action points to move, attack (with guns, melee or magic) or use items such as medkits and grenades. Its a system that I really like because there's a lot of tactical depth, especially now that you can customise your companions' abilities when they level up (a feature that was also added to the director's cut of Dragonfall).
Most missions are designed to allow non combat skills to be useful, for example using dialogue options to avoid fighting guards, or hacking a computer to unlock a door.
The biggest new feature for Hong Kong is the improved matrix system. There's more of a stealth element - some enemies patrol along a set path and they won't attack until you enter their vision cone, so if you're careful you can avoid them. And hacking nodes within the matrix is now a two part mini-game involving remembering sequences of numbers and symbols.
My only disappointment is the continued lack of voice acting. It didn't spoil my enjoyment of the game, but its something that I would like to see added if there's a fourth Shadowrun, because I think it would elevate a good game into a great game.
It took me 20 hours to finish the main story and I think I completed all the side quests as well. I didn't encounter any bugs or crashes. I also want to say that the music is pretty good and matches the oriental theme.
Overall Hong Kong is a really good game, fans of the series will certainly enjoy it, and its worth a full price purchase. The story is not connected to the previous games, so if you're new to Shadowrun, you could choose to play the games in any order.

The story is rich in characters- and places- background information, and there is a whole lot to do. I thoroughly enjoyed it.
The decker overhaul made me cringe at first until I got the hang of the new approach to cyberspace, but it works well in my eyes and makes you think twice before jumping into a system.
Again, as with the other games, this game's only flaw is that the main campaign is too short. Having made this into a third game forces community creators to take their creations from Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun Dragonfall and port it over, leaving those other two games with abandoned or broken content. This could have really been done better.
Here's to hoping the next Shadowrun game combines the previous three campaigns under one banner and releases more official campaigns as DLC, allowing community creators to use content from new DLC in their workshop builds without having to port to yet another game with changed GUI.

As many other negative reviews note: this is an interesting concept that becomes repetitive all too quickly. I first heard about Qvadriga via Rock, Paper, Shotgun that called it the Best Racing Game of 2014. I find my tastes often align with RPS so I was looking forward to trying this out.
Qvadriga is a one-man effort from Daniel Soria at Turnopia games, "a humble attempt to achieve the ideal of turn based games". He delivers a relatively unique concept in his chariot-racing game: your charioteer has a pretty decent chance of dying. And there's often not much you can do about it. You're often at the mercy of the RNG. In many ways it feels like a rogue-like. I finished 37 races in my (unfinished) campaign. I came in first on about 33% of them. I had 8 charioteers get killed in the line of duty.
If you embrace that, it means you sometimes are rewarded with more interesting stories than most racing games will give you. Let me tell you about the time that my top-ranked charioteer had his chariot disintegrate underneath him rounding the corner on the final stretch; he was in first place and rather than lose, let his horses drag him the last stretch across the finish line. Or the time my rookie charioteer gambled it all on a risky inner-lane turn to take first place. Or the time, just seconds after the race started, my #1 charioteer got whipped, stunned, and then was whipped to death before the first turn!
Unfortunately, moments like those -- great as they are -- don't make up for the short comings. There seems to be no relationship between "famous charioteers" and their skills in the races. I consistently beat the globally famous guys with 16 wins....and lose out to some no-name guy in the backwaters of Syria. The game seems to level-up your competitors so they are always approximately the same skill as you.
Despite playing for hours, I never once had a charioteer level up. The game gives some indications it is possible but I never saw it happen. That lack of progression contributes to the sense of sameness. I went from Hispania to Gaul to Italy to Macedonia to Syria and the races felt the same no matter where I was. There are a few varieties in track (some are narrow with just 4 chariots, some are wide with 12 chariots) but that's about it.
The "sports management sim" part of the game is pretty thin, as is the campaign. If these were better developed it might make up for the repetition and randomness/lack of skill of the races themselves. I quickly amassed more money than I knew what do with (80,000 denarii and nothing much to spend it on) and often spent it travelling the world just to see if anything was different anywhere.
The core racing is fun but just doesn't offer enough variety. You also have to accept that some races are unwinnable through no fault of your own. If you start out in the middle of a pack of 12, and get lashed by a neighbor, you're going to have difficulty placing. Likewise, sometimes you'll get a random event -- like the one where your charioteer gets bribed to brake after the first turn -- that makes it hard to come out on top.
Those aren't the end of the world, since the game does give you a kind of rogue-like feeling of failure being okay. But it often made me feel like success and failure wasn't really up to me or my tactics. I won around 1/3 of my races but in 1/4 of my races I didn't place in the top three and I had essentially the same team the whole time. (Sure, I went through various charioteers but their stats were all similar.)
There's a lot of potential here but as-is, the novelty wore off for me after a few hours. I'm glad I picked it up on sale and only paid $5, so I feel like I got decent value from the game.

This is neither a massive nor a complex game. Instead, it is simple, elegant, and surprisingly dramatic for a turn-based game.
The premise is that you manage a chariot racing team, from humble beginnings on the outskirts of the Roman Empire, through to fame and glory in the Circus Maximus of Rome itself. Races are broken into ten second turns. On each turn you can give a single order to your charioteer, which could be speed management, a positioning manoeuvre, offensive, or devensive action. You need to play to your strengths at any given moment, and maintain a high level of situational awareness. I was particularly impressed by the AI. It's smart, but will still make risky decisions which can make for the kind of bloody and brutal chaos one would expect from any Roman sport.
While at its heart, there is a fairly simple press your luck mechanic (i.e. do I push the horses and risk injury, can I take a tight turn or go wide, should I protect myself or go for position, etc.), the systems are well designed to create emergent situations where finding the right balance between risky and safe is a constant learning experience.
Between races you spend your winnings on keeping your team in good order, and upgrades when you can afford them. There's not a ton of complexity to this management layer, but it is still nice when a better component to your racing team comes up for sale and you can afford it.
Having sunk over 10 hours into Qvadriga, I'm not sure I'll be dedicating a great deal more. But that was more than enough for me. I felt that the game respected my time. There was a progression, but it felt like it was far more about my skill in the game improving than it felt like I was grinding to go forward. When I got over my initial hump early in the learning curve and gained some confidence, then I was able to bet heavily on myself during most races and plough through the mid and late game relatively quickly. Even late in the piece though, random events at the start of a race (annouced before placing bets), a single bad move or dramatically unlucky roll could easily lead to a disastrous outcome in a particular race.
This is definitely not a game for everyone. The RNG can feel really harsh while you are learning the game. It's definitely possible to mitigate its effects with skill, but at least for me that skill took several hours to properly cultivate. I came close to giving up, but I'm glad I didn't, because it turned out to be well worth my time. I also felt like I had to be willing to take more lost races than I was used to in a single player game. Early on, just coming out ahead in terms of earnings to expenses is really the order of the day.
My one tip for anyone who does end up playing this game, never whip the horses while at the end of a high speed turn. Every time I did it I crashed the chariot. Even if there was just a few degrees before opening up into the straight, whipping my horses just before fully opening out into a straight was invariably a recipe for disaster. Most of the time in this game any advice will be based on relative positions between you and other racers, as well as the exact condition and abilities of your Quadriga. But in this one case though, it's a 100% bad call to attempt this kind of manoeuvre. Many a race was lost stubbornly confirming the futulity of this move.
Fun game, but would benefit greatly from some more features and character development.

A strong focus on small units; giving a guy a bazooka or an MG42 turns a mundane unit into a mid-game powerhouse; the presence of just one tank reshapes the whole game. The AI is pretty unforgiving too, creating a cerebral, engaging and pretty challenging offline skirmish even for veteran players. In-game unlockables and customization on unit stats to boost the units you use the most.

Mafia II. Note that I have, at this moment in time, never before played Mafia I.
Although I have played other such titles, for example Mafia Wars, The Godfather games, Omerta City of Gangsters and of course GTA and also Saints Row.
This game, has by far one of the most gripping main story lines I have come across for this genre. (Personally)
I played this first on Xbox 360, and I have many many hours clocked.

Now I shall tell you about a few features.
Car mechanics;
the driving is lovely and realistic. No manual gear changing or first person head turning ( I belive there is a fine working modification for first person) but everything works smoothly as it should. You can turn on or off a speedomiter on as far as I know all cars. There is also an option to turn on or off realistic driving ( more slipping when it's wet with rain and snow, realistic breaking, that sort of thing. ) Car damage is very well done and there is a car mechanic shop at your service, as well as a few other types of shops : ) you as the player cannot shoot out of windows as far as I know without some sort of modification to the game, but other NPCs in the car can and will if need be ( if they use a gun normally  xD ) You can open the bonnet and boot of most cars, which is a lovely feature :) they really did well on the cars, I mean you can take the hubcaps off from damage.. taking out the lights and tyres is very fun and rewarding.. shooting through the windows is very nice.. the bumpers bounce about nicely when they partly come apart.. spinning out and drifting is very nice, aaandd, you can shoot the sirens to stop them xD! There are many many vechicles to see and drive, from armoured vans and trucks to small sports cars and hotrods : D.
Next is the violence mechanics;
Shooting is very well done, you can also punch up enemies with your fists.. the fighting is well done!
You can kill someone instantly if you shoot the head, so there is minor locational damage, and all animations are very good. There is blood also.
There is a good cover system, alowing you to take cover on most objects however they are. You can also destroy most objects as you please.
Atmosphere;
It feels veryy genuine. The music, crisp textures and wonderful lighting provides a truly nineteen thirtys to seventys feel. Something perhaps out of The Italian Job, or a James Bond movie..
There are many many songs out on the few radio stations.. from home radio to car radio you can listen all the time :D
Oh, voice acting is absolutly top notch. For the most part there are no hiccups!
You can dress differently, answer phones and use rest rooms, buy drinks and food, and take a stroll out and about.
I love this game. I hope you will or do too :)

Man, this one was pretty crazy. As far as gameplay goes, I wouldn't expect much as you dive into this, but it definately packs a lot. I like to consider this as more of an interactive walkthrough of Steven Harmon's thoughts and memories than a structured
, but it is regardless very encapturing. You explore scenes from Steven's nightmares, fantasies, regrets, and much more. You can feel a sense of melancholy throughout the game, but it honestly hits a little deeper and at points feels like it's beyond one kid's sadness. To me, this is an outlet of feelings, artistic expression if you will. As an artist, I understand the aspect of this expression, and it was honestly kind of cool to see somebody else's life through

One Way Heroics is a nice little game created in Wolf RPG Editor. When I first played it, I was excited. Games like this always caught my eye and the dialogue the characters/NPC's have only made it more fun. A tad bit silly, but nonetheless still great. So, I started it up and was ready to play. I thought it would be rather simple. It looked easy enough to do; Avoid the darkness consuming the world. In other words, avoid getting scrolled off the screen. I fought monsters along the way. It was very tedious, sure, but entertaining. Then, finally, I encountered the boss, the Demon Lord. I swear, I have never been defeated so quickly by a boss in my entire lifetime.
Eager to defeat him, I retried. And thus started the endless cycle of trying to successfully defeat the Demon Lord.
This game is a bundle of joy, frustration, and addiction. You are provided with numerous classes to choose from and to defeat the Demon Lord with. Each world is randomly generated so there are always new surprises to look forward to. You are also given opportunities to save here and there, so if you are absolutely certain this particular world is suitable for you to achieve your goals, then save at a save point and viola! No need to worry about losing your progress. There are also a number of skills you can obtain, as well as weapons, armor, items, partners - you name it. In addition to the gameplay, the soundtrack is beautiful, enjoyable, and is certainly enough to keep you motivated. Obviously, the graphics are pixelated (with the exception of when character dialogue pops up), but the art is nice and I will admit that I find some of the monsters rather cutesy.
I somehow managed to hop off this game for a while (which was good because if I hadn't, it would've been an unhealthy addiction for me), but I have taken note that the One Way Heroics Plus DLC is coming around Steam sometime soon, so I'll definitely be playing soon again. Do I recommend this game? Of course I do! If you choose to purchase this game, I now wish you all the good luck on your journey to defeat the Demon Lord!

Lisa is without a doubt one of the darkest and funniest games I've ever played. The game itself is a turn-based RPG in a 2D side-scrolling world, and looks a little unpolished/bland from the outside in, but don't let that fool you. Austin Jorgensen has delivered a hilarious game with substance to match.
You control Brad, a guardian/adoptive father of Buddy, the last unknown female in the known world. Years before the setting in the game there was a mysterious event called The White Flash which brought upon the end of the world, wherein all women died out. To some this may seem like heaven, but this left behind a strange society of men who sold themselves and their bodies for "Joy", so other men could sleep with them and satisfy their needs.
Oh, I didn't mention what "Joy" was. "Joy" as it is ironically known is a drug which most people are addicted to in the game, including Brad. Brad is a drug addict, which is one of his better traits believe it or not.
Brad is scared for Buddy, as he sees the world for what it is, even as a drug addict he knows what men in this world will do to her if they found out she was a girl, and not a boy in a mask.
Brad unfortunately is not able to prevent Buddy's identity and gender being discovered and near the beginning of the game she is kidnapped, this is where the story begins, and Brad sets off on his way to save his Buddy from the world at large.
Throughout the game you're made make decisions which effect your party, or Brad himself, none of the decisions make you feel good, and the game really makes you think about your decisions and what you'll do.
I don't want to go into too much detail about the story as its fairly linear and a normal game would take up to 6-8 hours. Its a seriously fantastic game which is worth the full price.

I got this game as part of a bundle awhile ago and just found it in my library. When I first fired it up, it reminded me a lot of Freelancer in terms of graphics and feel. Which is great, except that Freelancer is from 2003, and this game is from 2008, so the graphics are terrible by that standard.
This game focuses almost exclusively on trading with a few FPS missions thrown in. You have a few other side missions you can do (acquire goods for someone for a potential payout later). Each of the spaceports lets you wander around and explore, and there's hidden side missions and goodies at every port (some require a bit of platforming as well). Unfortunately, you can't actually fly your ship. You choose where you want to travel, and you're there. No space flight at all, which is a major disappointment.
The FPS missions remind me of the oldschool shooters where the guns, health and shields were just lying around the map for you to pick up. Unfortunately you can't buy any kind of upgrades to help you with these FPS missions, you basically learn the maps and go get the guns/health/shields before the boss arrives. This is probably the weakest aspect of the game, but at least it pays well and is the fastest way to earn cash and loot to sell for more cash.
Overall, not a terrible game, but definitely has its issues, especially with how repetitive it gets since you basically do the same few things the entire game (do FPS missions initially to buy all the cargo capacity upgrades, then travel around hauling the highest profit goods). The exploration and side missions in the ports help relieve some of the tedium, but I really wish I could actually use my money to buy more than just goods and more cargo space.
I tentatively recommend this game simply because it's cheap and relatively fun if you like trading style games and it brings back the nostalgia of the classic space games that have been largely neglected for the last decade.

I love the world of Shadowrun, but much as I love it, it's just not enough to make up for lame game design.
The writing is sometimes interesting, but rather than feeling like I'm part of the story, I usually feel like I'm being talked at. I don't feel like my choices really matter. The many curious conversations available in the game hub should have been connected with small playable storylines and quests. The fact that they (mostly) are not, means that these conversations ultimately feel hollow.
Worse, the game mechanics often feel awkward. Why can't I use Is0bel's mine skill before battle, to prepare the battleground? Why can't I use medkits after battle? And what's up with the stealth? Stealth is a fun mechanic, and a huge part of the Shadowrun world ... but the implementation is terrible. The realtime controls are so loose that I sometimes can't get my characters to do what I want, and alarms are raised - not because of any tactical error on my part, but because the controls just didn't support my needs.
Which brings me to technical issues. The most obvious issue is the level load time. Even with a mid-level SSD, levels require 10-60 seconds to load. This wouldn't be so bad, except that I in the stealth sections of the game, I often have to reload a lot, because I'm unable to control my characters well enough to stealth effectively.
The other big technical problem is the AI. In one of the side missions, I gained the support of several NPS's, but they were almost useless in combat. Mostly, they lagged behind my team, such that they weren't even useful as damage sponges. When they did get near the front line, they made terrible choices. For example, the physical adept would power up ... then run back and forth till he ran out of AP.
So, sorry Harebrained Schemes. I love the world, and I love the idea of this game, but I can't find much to like about the execution. I like the art, but I wish you'd spent more time on story and gameplay, and less time on graphic art.

After Returns and Dragonfall they keep giving great Shadowrun turn-based rpg. Each game also keep improving, this one really giving a lot of required engine improvement. Each game also show you different part of the Shadowrun universe so it's a good idea to start with the first but they can be enjoyed in any order.
Hong Kong is also really full of dialogue and text to read but you can skip most. I probably spent half my 20 hours in the hub interacting with the many npcs there. This game give a lot of information on the universe and different part of the world.
For those that played the previous games, you can now trade between your party member when you want, you can even loan them equipment and not only consumables. You can even pick between two "perks" for them when you advance the story that gives them interesting abilities. They also were my favorite of the three games, really interesting party members this time around.
I feel there is also more non-violent option this time around, I was able to do the first run without any fight because I had the right etiquettes and attributes. Overall the runs were really varied and interesting with usually a few options how to do them.
The Matrix needed an update and they finally did it. It might not be an improvement for everyone but personally I really like what they did. It's now kind of two real-time puzzle minigames instead of a big battle. But when you fail and get found it can turn into the old fight.
The Hong Kong area is also really beautiful, they really pushed those isometric graphics to the max. Characters model are not the best and leg animation still looks a bit weird but the portraits and maps are really nice and shiny, giving a great cyberpunk feel.
The best Shadowrun game and one of the best turn-based rpg of the last few years.

The Shadowrun series just keeps getting better. Once again, Hare-Brained Schemes delivers an enthralling tale full of mystery, conspiracy, and just a dash of fantasy to enrich its cyberpunk universe.
