The campaign is long yet effectively paced, and the only downside of its conclusion is the fact that it ends at all. I can only hope HBS intends on revisiting the Shadowrun universe again, because they've got it nailed.
Again, a wonderful game. Exciting story, great characters and even better game mechanics than Dragonfall.

If you only play one Shadowrun game this year... play Dragonfall.  Otherwise, Hong Kong is a good addition to the series.
I think my experience with Hong Kong suffered a little from playing it immediately after finishing the amazing Dragonfall.  Having to exist in the shadow of the near perfect second game in the series it suffers a bit.  The characters, with a few exceptions, just didn't pop like the memorable party members and NPCs in Dragonfall. I suppose it's unfair of me to think so when I immediately assigned the new party names like "Not Glory" and "Not Billy Idol Punk Rocker Shaman dude".  Hell, I even missed Blitz.  The two exceptions are the Red Samurai Ghoul you can pick up and the Russian Rigger Guy.  I never really felt and interest in learning much about the NPC denizens of Hong Kong.
Dragonfall allowed you to make tough choices that resonated into the ending of the game (and beyond).  In contrast, Hong Kong seems to be far more linear with little variation in how you handle the overall campaign.  While the individual Shadowruns in Hong Kong are very well done and interesting with different set pieces, you never really are afforded the same level of choice you had in the previous game (i.e. walking away from Lofwyr and SK or not).  I would have loved the choice to walk away at the end and go back to Seattle.
Finally, the conclusion to Hong Kong ends with a bit of a wimper when the game falls into the old trope of killing the same boss over and over (and over) again until it finally relents.  My party members made note to tell me at the very last that I had never really taken the time to talk to them.  Which I suppose is telling in and of itself.
Despite not living up to the former game Hong Kong is still a very good squad tactics game.  If you have already played Dragonfall and are looking for a new flavor then you can't really go wrong with Hong Kong.

All in all a good experience and a must have for Shadowrun Returns fans.
It's better than A Dead Man's Switch and on par with Dragonfall.
The side missions were very interesting with different ways to solve.
A weakness was the hub. Whereas Berlin in Dragonfall was quite interesting, the Waterfront in Hong Kong was quite boring.
Total score: 8/10

I feel I need to write at least a quick review for this because the game is getting a lot on undeserved flak over difficulty and a few technical issues.
Look. This is a game where you can grab a cop, pick him up, and throw him into another cop, and then proceed to breakdance under the second cop while he's airborne in order to juggle him across the screen. The game is comic beat-em-up cheesefest made of game mechanics. It's goofy, it's hammy, and it is at its core very much gamey.
If you don't like this, there's plenty of Minecraft clones, iPhone games, and games about the struggle of transgender lesbians or... Whatever. This here isn't that. This is a loveletter to an NES classic, and beat-em-ups in general. It's going to require you to stick with it, and get good with it. It will reward you for doing so, both with more power, and practical application of skill.
Yes, it's hard. It's supposed to be. This isn't a walking simulator, it's a beat-em-up. No, it's not *that* hard. The mechanics are mostly smooth and responsive. Enemy AI is counterable.
Yes it's a bit slow to get started. This could use some work, but it's only a speed bump. The game has RPG elements, but it's not dicerolls and random chance. Get good and grind a bit, then proceed to breakdance through swarms of gangers and cops with impunity.
The game has some stability issues, and yes this is a legitimate issue. They'll be fixed. At the very least, Arcsys is the publisher, and as of late they have a great track record on PC when it comes to this sort of thing.

For  design  flaws the first is  level limitations on moves. Before I begin I'm going to preface this review by saying that at the time of writing, March 3rd, 2017, there are a good number of bugs that hamper the play experience. Online multiplayer for example will not save progress. Also at the time of writing that bug is acknowledged and is in the process of being fixed as well as the other bugs in the game that are known. If you're sensitive to bugs I would say hold off for a little bit until the team patches the game a bit more. Also as a point of transparency, I was a backer of the Kickstarter, had beta access, and helped beta test the game.
With that said, I still think this game is incredible. It's one of my favorite beat em ups of all time if not outright my favorite. It's not a perfect game, but the core of the game is so solid that every time I play the game hours just fly by and I have a blast every single time. I feel like lots of things this game does are evolutions to the beat em up genre that we never got to see because after the hay day of the arcade sidescroller the genre morphed into other genres and all attempts at making classic style beat em ups never attempted to add to or improve the formula, everyone was content doing the most basic by the numbers game with maybe a gimmick here or there. Not to say that all modern beat em ups are bad, but none of them really stuck out as awesome new interesting ideas. On the surface, River City Ransom Underground follows the steps as its predecessor, but once you start getting into the nitty gritty, the game opens up and fully comes into its own. Despite some big efforts to stay faithful to the original, this game is not a clone of the original River City Ransom, it takes the spirit of the original and takes it in a new direction, inspired by some of the potential the original game had that wasn't immediately obvious to the player as well as Technos' lineage of fantastic beat em ups.
To start off, the game puts you right at the end of the original River City Ransom, making the final run to the rooftop of the school to confront Slick. Here the game teaches you the basics of the game and some of the mechanics to get you into how the new system works. You punch and kick your way to the roof, defeat Simon, and all the gangs go back to class and become honor students. From there, you jump ahead to the present day where you are introduced to your new main characters for this game, The Flock. You're running late for class so you have to sprint to your classroom before you're tardy, which will have its consequences. Upon reaching the classroom you see a TV broadcast from Merv saying that the leader of The Flock has kidnapped his beloved and is offering a bounty to anyone who can bring you to justice. Vigilante justice. The story isn't going to win any prizes, but it's got a lot of charm to it and has a lot of fun. It sets you off in a world feeling straight out of The Warriors, your gang against the world. Along the way you can recruit members to join your gang by helping them out as they try to survive the world becoming overrun by gang activity. This is also where the differences start to show up with the original game. After the broadcast you must escape from the school, and once you do so every gang from all over is hunting you down, no matter where you are. In the original you could always go to the shopping malls to get away from conflict because the gangs were just protecting their turf and their gang leader and you were stomping their grounds to get the attention of the gang leader so you could get information about where Slick was hiding Cyndi. In this game however, the gangs don't care about their turf, they're after the bounty on your head, so they will chase after you in shopping malls. Some people won't like this change, however personally I feel like it keeps the action pace of the game going and really makes you feel like you're being hunted, giving The Flock two choices wherever they go, fight or flight. It's a warzone and you're doing everything you can to survive. It fits the tone of the game and gives you ample opportunity to get your beat up on. Because the town has become so overrun with gangs, the police are now on high alert, watching the town like it's on Marshall Law keeping an eye out for any crime going down and ready to jump on it in full SWAT gear. The police system can use some polish but I absolutely love the idea of it from a gameplay perspective. During your play you're asked to grind money so you can buy things from shops and dojos to improve your character. Along the way you might be a little short to buy that new move you wanted, so you've got to plan how you're going to get the money. You can be a good boy or girl and beat up gang members, or you can get some quick and easy money by mugging a civilian or jacking a parking meter. The money is easy, but by doing so you bring the full force of the law down on you. Is it worth it to get the couple bucks from the construction worker on his lunch break so you can have the thing right now or do you move a screen and work a little harder? The risk/reward on this mechanic is both really interesting and fleshes out the world a lot more, and if you want to have some fun and a couple laughs, you can use the police as a pseudo survival mode to see how long you can last against the constantly increasing police task force. The system can be too aggressive at times in regards to when it decides to trigger and it's not uncommon to be fighting a thug and have a civilian walk in the crossfire, but if this mechanic gets some cleaning up it's one of the things I like most about the world. When the police action gets too hot or you just want to relax or maybe just save your game, you can stop by one of your hideouts hidden along the way. Hideouts act as a checkpoint for your progress as well as give you the ability to store items and weapons. You can dress them up in various ways and make it so that you've always got your favorite weapon ready to go.
The actual combat is where this game really shines. Just like the original River City Ransom you start off with a very basic moveset of punches and kicks and slowly build up to a wrecking ball in a very inconveniently placed China shop. The juggle system is so freeform and open that you're basically allowed to do whatever you want. Every character will have combo chains that they can do in a very Tekken style manner, weaving between the punch and kick buttons as well as special moves that work in a very Street Fighter way with Smash Bros. inputs. You do a chain and then special cancel into a launcher then juggle and then wrap up in an air combo, there is so much creativity to be had in the combat that I'll often stay on one screen not even grinding just to see what I can come up with. It's one of the core defining features of the game and in my opinion greatly extends the replay value and longevity of the play time you'll get out of it. As I said though you do start off with a very basic moveset. The craftier players should still be able to make fun things happen with the limited moveset but for most it won't be obvious what you can do. In the same vein however, the actual character strength balance could use some work. Some characters are very weak in the early game and don't start to come into their own until the late game and some characters are just harder to play in general for less effective results than some of the other characters. Part of this has to do with the dojos and which moves you unlock and when. Some characters have basic things you don't get until very late in the game and some characters get tons of combo moves in the very first dojo. It wouldn't be that big of a task to rearrange these better so I do hope that gets changed in a future patch. It's an issue that can be fixed and I trust the team behind the game to clean it up some more. Apparently Steam has a review size limit so I'm going to wrap up here.

This game is not bad, but it deserves a mere "meh"
Civ 4 was way better.
The fact that you cannot stack units anymore dramatically changes combat.
Before, you could stand against a much more technologically advanced ennemy as long as you had a superior production.
Now, whoever is the most advanced is going to take it all.
But even then, it is half made : aircraft can still be stacked, so whenever you reach modern time, whoever stack the most place win it. Not quite sure what's the logic there?
Civ 4 was more deep and had more complexity.
First, you had to handle religion. Sometime, you would change your state religion to avoid angering a powerful neighbor. Or you would rush in to build the holy cities for that one very popular religion so you could cash in on the donation.
Civ 5 completely removed religion... unless you buy that particular DLC, that is.
Second, the economy was better. There was several ressources that provided a small bonus (health, hapiness, etc) that you could trade around. Not every resources were war/units related like iron or oil.
In Civ 5, you use the resources to make units. That's it. To trade resources with another player? Why would you do that, do you want them to make powerful units??
Finally, in Civ 4, you could see the state of your relation with others. It would tell you WHY that particular NPC hates/loves you. Maybe they dislike your religion? Maybe they do like your politics? Maybe they are getting afraid of you because you grow too powerful? That would affect you choice toward them.
In Civ 5, everyone hates you or will soon.
No, seriously: weaker NPCs will hate you because you are too strong. Stronger NPCs will hate you because you are weaker. The rest will hate you because their weaker/stronger allies hate you.
After one or two game you won't bother about diplomacy anymore; no matter what you do, how many gifts you send away, they WILL attack you. Better to kill them first.
That's about it... I was very disapointed on this game.
Simplistic and no deep. It is kinda fun, but no big "wow".
Buy it on sale if you have to.

When the first
released, it was an unexpected but welcome change from developer
's typical point-and-click adventure game that they are know for. Given it's cliffhanger ending and complete lack of closure it was inevitable that a sequel would eventually emerge, and thus we are presented with
, a direct continuation of Nelson Tether's previous escapades in the odd little town of Scoggins and a fitting end to the story that was begun in the last game.
Although it's marketed as a full sequel, PA2 is far more akin to a second episode, which is fairly typical of
. It ties directly into the ending of the original game, tying up loose ends and finally shedding a light on what happened to Issac Davidson, what have Nelson's visions been about, and who the heck are the hidden people. While many of the revelations are absolutely absurd taken in context with the rest the series they don't feel at all out of place, instead just one more bizarre happening in the day to day occurrences of a puzzle agent. I was very pleased to finally get some answers for the many questions that had previously been asked, and in the end everything tied up quite nicely (or as nicely as anything this unusual could).
Gameplay is identical to the original game, mixing Professor Layton-like puzzles with the Twin Peaks-esq setting and dialog to great effect. The puzzles are a bit fewer in number this time, but as a whole they are better designed and effectively tied into the story than before. Many characters return, with better writing and voice acting while still retaining the original off-kilter charm that made them what they are. I never did adjust to the stilted animation style, but like everything else has a unique appeal to it that works with the rest of the game.
If I had any problem with the game it's that it's short, shorter than it's predecessor, and yet costs twice the price. I couldn't say that the quality of either of the two games is far apart (I think both are excellent for what they are), but at double the cost of admission with less content, it's hard for me to recommend purchasing PA2 at least outright, and would definitely advise waiting for a sale.
Other than the length,
is a treat for fans of the original. You're getting more of the same, and that's a good thing as so far there isn't anything else like the series available on Steam. Playing the first game should definitely be considered a prerequisite, and if you didn't like it then this won't change your mind. For those wanting for more this is a worthy sequel who's biggest flaw is actually being called one. Think of it instead as
and you're unlikely to come away disappointed.

Years before the setting in the game there was a mysterious event called The White Flash which brought upon the end of the world, wherein all women died out. To some this may seem like heaven, but this left behind a strange society of men who sold themselves and their bodies for "Joy", so other men could sleep with them and satisfy their needs.
Oh, I didn't mention what "Joy" was. "Joy" as it is ironically known is a drug which most people are addicted to in the game, including Brad. Brad is a drug addict, which is one of his better traits believe it or not.
Brad is scared for Buddy, as he sees the world for what it is, even as a drug addict he knows what men in this world will do to her if they found out she was a girl, and not a boy in a mask.
Brad unfortunately is not able to prevent Buddy's identity and gender being discovered and near the beginning of the game she is kidnapped, this is where the story begins, and Brad sets off on his way to save his Buddy from the world at large.

OK, first, I have a lot more hours on this game, but they were in the non-Steam version as originally published by Matrix Games.
As related in other reviews, this is a turn-based (with optional real time) top down chariot racing simulator. Conceptually it goes back to a board game origin, but it has been quite successfully brought to the PC. The rules aren't too complex, but there is strategy in the development of the drivers, the horses and the chariot. And there is likewise a lot of tactical decision making during a race. The inclusion of random events keeps the game from getting stale.
There is also a business aspect in that doing well in races (and making smart bets!) will give you more money which allows for chariot upgrades, better horses and more qualified drivers. Also money is needed to care for injured horses and drivers and repair damaged chariots.
One of the great aspects of the game is that it can be played in small blocks of time, a race not taking more than ten minutes at a time. So you can do a race or two, or really dive into the campaign mode if desired.
Post if you have questions!

So, let's get the bad stuff out of the way:  This acts like a converted boardgame.  The graphics are from the 90s if not late 80s.  The game will not hold your hand - if you act stupidly, the game has no issue with punishing you.
That said, this is the best racing game I've played in a very long time.
In Qvadriga you control a team of charioteers (aurigas).  You're responsible for selecting them, buying and upgrading horses and chariots, and paying for medical care/repairs when things don't go well.  Your sponsor will give you certain advantages:  Perhaps your aurigas are tougher than average, or your horses faster.
Once you've taken care of maintenance and the like, it's time to race.  Simply put it's three times (usually) around an oval track, with rewards for finishing first, second, third, or even simply finishing.
The commands are intuitive enough once you've played a few games:  You can accelerate by shaking the reins, whip the horses (which might hurt them and lower their overall speed), pull back on the reins, change lanes, whip to the left or right to try and injure enemy drivers and horses, or ram your cart left and right for the same reason.  Action by default is turn based.  There is an option where the turns run together, simulating an RTS, but I feel it's not worth it.
Since the commands are simple enough you can focus on strategy.  Whipping the horses is a great way to surge past the enemy ... but if you hurt them too badly it'll hurt their base speed and you'll be paying for a vet later.  Sometimes beating the crap out of your enemy is the answer, but that tends to slow you down.  Do you take the turns at full speed and hope you don't crack a wheel?  Or do you focus on stabilizing your chariot or even slowing down to make sure everything you make it?  Having your chariot shatter under you and being dragged is no fun.   Letting go of the reins and getting run over by an opponent is even worse.
Strategies are affected by random events.  For example in a recent race my auriga was so mad at the world 'he' decided that accelerating by shaking the reins wasn't an open, and if I wanted to win I'd have to rely on the whip much more than I like.  In another event drunken spectators thought throwing trash on the outer lane of the track was great fun and several drivers got hit in the head.
Don't let the graphics scare you off.  This is an intuitive racing game with good strategic potential.  Enjoy!

Okay, Qvadriga doesn't even look old, it looks completely
, and the concept of a turn-based top-down simulation of chariot racing isn't exactly mainstream. But don't judge a game on your first impression as you wouldn't judge a book by its cover (I have a feeling you'd like books as much as I do if you've come here).
, and truly deserves its sale price if not its full price.
The core gameplay is based on managing your speed and taking the decision to whip your horses to push them over their limits, or whip your opponents to incapacitate them, ram their chariots, cripple their horses, trample your dismounted rivals - playing it brutal is all part of the games, and the capable AI will use every trick in the book.
Campaign-wise, racing is rewarded with denarius (the currency of the Roman Empire) to build your team with upgraded chariots, horses and skilled drivers-slaves. Good results also increase your fame which will open up the doors of more prestigious stadiums, several dozens of them available in seven provinces, up to the great Circus Maximus of Rome if you prove worthy. Completing a campaign requires about 10 hours of gameplay, more if you invest time to skill up your team of slaves and acquire the top quality chariots and horses.

This was the first game from Hairbrained studios that finally felt a bit like actual Shadowrun.  They fixed the issue of magical characters having no way to buy cyberware/bioware and the character building interface is much better.  Dialogue was much stronger than previous releases.  Unfortunately the game still suffers from some short comings which prevent it from delivering a true Shadowrun experience including:
-- Negotiation with Fixers for run pay based on social skills is completely missing. The lack of an effective social system makes "Face" type characters non-existent.
-- The main drive of Showdowrun is to make money to pay for lifestyle, and as a Runner is sucessful gain a better lifestyle with access to better accomodations and services.  This element is completley missing in this game.
-- There is no stealth engine at all which is a critical aspect of Shadowrun.  Public Recognition is a non-factor.  Cleaning up signatures in the matrix and astral space is non-existant.
-- There is no non-lethal system (gel rounds etc) and no penalty of any kind for giant body counts that would bring a megacorp down on a shadowrunner and end his career.
-- There are no Fake Sins, social checks at border crossings, etc.
-- The game is completely missing a legal engine.  Folks can walk around the mall with a tank gun and there is no consequence.  The game is missing the license system for weapons which renders highly concealable weapons, low calibur, and legal weapons worthless.  There is no point in developing skills or learning to use any but the biggest weapons.  This makes the game two-dimensional.
-- The system of contacts is completely missing. One of the most enjoyable aspects of shadowrun is developing contacts and building their loyatly to leverage for future runs.
-- There is no legwork in the game which makes non-combat builds superflous.
Hopefully the developer will slowly chip away at these deficienices as time and budgets allow.  Despite the above issues the game is still worth buying.

I was hyped by the game back when it got announced on Kickstarter, and getting to play it some years later almost feels like a dream. It has its rough parts, but it's still a very retro fast paced action brawling piece I'd really like to recommend to fans of brawlers. It has cheesyness in spades and many small details that will make you chuckle.
As a fighting game, it doesn't disappoint. Fighting gangs of enemies while slowly but steadily improving yourself feels so good. There's plenty of characters, each with their own movesets to master. I ended up playing first as the boxer, which felt like a drag for a while because of how "limited" his moveset looked like, but once I bought the special skills, he felt more fast paced. There's also a grappler, the crowd-control breakdancer, and others with movesets all over the place.
The sense of humor of the game is of my liking. Not in-your-face, and mostly subtle references. I loved the store with the Apples, Grapes and Grapples, for example. Also, go to Merv's burger and order the Free Smile. The description is priceless (pun intended, with the quality of those that you can find within the game). Heck, the descriptions of many items are a treat on their own.
The problems arise when it comes to actually advancing in the game though. Early on, you'll have to grind for survivavility, and it'll be a while until you can consistently get recovery items. You'll also want to buy the good moves (which, by the way, are loosely explained, so you might not even get to see them often). Then, getting from one point to another is a mess because the map does a poor job indicating where the objectives are exactly. For example, if you want to go to the old University (right of the map) you have to go through a town, walk left, pass the fitness centre, continue left, and suddenly, you're right.
As other people have pointed out too, there are a few objectives that feel out of place. Specially the persecutions. 3 of them, one after another. They're not that hard, and I didn't need more than 3 tries on any given one. But still, maneuvering through some maps and guessing where you can enter and where you can't is still a sour point.
Regardless, I'm satisfied with the game. RCR and RCRAdvance are two of my favorite games of all time, and RCRU does a great job at being follow ups. It adds many things to try and revitalize the franchise. Many work, some others don't, but overall, I believe I'll be playing this one for a good time before I burn up.

Guess what guys, I beat the game.

Want to know why?
Because I figured out how to beat all the parts people are complaining about because they want their hands held.
Platforming? No issues here.
Milk Escort - Did you know you could set the milk down by pressing the same button you use to pick it up? It's amazing! And the milk doesn't break! Scary what you can find out by experimenting!
It's got RPG elements for a reason - Don't like RPGs, don't play this game. You WILL need to grind.
----
Sarcasm aside, yes I can see why people don't like this game.
I only ran into a few bugs, and they were not game enders.
Until someone puts out a walkthrough, the devs wanted people to experiment in this game just like the old NES one.
The enemies are also close to the NES era - They are programed to read your button presses, that is what made the original so difficult.
However, like the original you can learn to manipulate the patterns.
As I DID finish the game and got Provie (A character with a BROKEN move list at this point in time, I learned how to do everything by experimenting.) at level 40 with almost all her moves.
So heres the pros, neutrals, and cons:
PROS -
Great music
Controls very well (Don't use keyboard, you NEED to use a controller for this.)
Lots of characters with variety.
If you like RPGs/Fighting games, you'll love this game.
NEUTRAL -
Lots of experimenting - Took me a hour to figure out how to get to the final area.
Story - It's kinda there.
Lots and lots of grinding - However, if you know where to look, you'll be fine
Nasty Difficulty - Enemies are programmed to respond to your button presses, but can be manipulated
No Direction - Like the NES days, you really are not given much direction on where to go. The map helps though.
BAD -
BUGs - Ran into a few bugs which reset missions
Milk Escort - Yes, I hated it. But I got through it after figuring out that you can set the milk down to fight.
Broken Move list - I played Provie, some of the moves listed have the wrong buttons under them.
Multiplayer - Yeah, it's broken... but it's still a great single player experience at this time.
All and all I enjoyed the game, I plan on doing new game plus with some of the characters I unlocked.
I do recommend this game. :)

Okay, so I may have not played Blade Symphony as long as Sader or some of the other people in the game with Master rank.  However, I do think I have a decent-enough understanding of the game to recommend it.
I began playing Blade Symphony when it was on sale for $3.  For the price, I thought "what the heck, it's cheap."  I fell in love with the game!  However, there are a few issues.  I'll list the pros and cons as I currently see them.
Pros:
-The combat system in wonderful.  It reminds one of the old Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast combat system, except much more complex and fluid.
-Good community (sort of).  There are a lot of really great people that play Blade Symphony and love to help new people learn the ropes.  Also, there are community-driven tournaments that provide some extra excitement to the game.  I'll hit on the "sort of" in the cons.
-Steam Workshop integration.  The fact that anyone can make weapons/masks/maybe eventually capes for this game is extremely satisfying and provides a level of personlization that many other games do not have.  I, for one, enjoy beating people with a Candy-Cane Wielding Batman every once in a while.  The Steam Workshop integration makes that possible.
-Open Developers.  The developers of Blade Symphony are very open with the community regarding what they are working on with the game.  They have been hosting developer hangouts every Saturday night to provide updates, and I personally enjoy them.
Cons:
-Some balancing still needs to be done to a few attacks, but it's minor.
-Large learning curve.  It took me quite a long time and many, many losses to get somewhat decent at this game.  This is not necessarily a bad thing but I just want people to recognize that this game requires some time to learn and they should not just play for a couple of hours, get frustrated and never play again.
-Some dedicated players are jerks.  Now, this will be the case with ANY competitive game.  So please- if you run into someone that is a jerk, do not think that person is representative of the whole community.
-The pricetag of $15 dollars seems excessive to me.  I would think it should be more like $10.
All things considered, I would recommend this game.  $15 dollars may be a bit much, but it is a very enjoyable and fun competitive swordfighting game, the likes of which I have not seen before now.

As you can tell by my playtime, I’ve played a lot of this game. Hundreds and hundreds of hours and thousands of duel matches. At the time of writing this my current ranked game number stands at 2594 Wins, and 1298 losses for a total of 3892 matches which is 11,676 individual ranked fights.
Eleven thousands individual fights, and for some reason I find myself warning you dear reader that this is not a $15 game. I purchased Blade Symphony back in December 2013 for around $7 dollars; my brother purchased the game for $3, and I can tell you right now based on the current game I overpaid.
So let’s start with the good: If I’m writing a negative review, then what is keeping me playing.
Workshop Integration:
The current game allows me to create (using various modeling and texturing programs) my own weapons and items. I am one of the more active and prolific workshop creators in this game. This is one of the main reasons I have continued to play this game, as I love to create custom items for people to use. Without this workshop Integration I would have quit the game a long, long time ago.
Deep Combat System:
This game has the framework for a fantastic combat system, giving you a true feeling of skill when you defeat an opponent. There is a lot of depth here.
And… that’s it for the good.
This game has a severe lack of content in the form of game modes as well as characters. I personally have played only one of the four characters in nearly all of my 11,000 matches. The character I chose was unfinished as of December 2013, and is now being released unfinished in May 2014 (the game’s current release date). You heard me: This game is releasing an UNFINISHED character and charging you $15 for it.
There are currently only four characters in this game (or 3.5 considering the unfinished/unbalanced character I play. There is also only one way to play the game: 1v1 duel. This is the only game mode you will be able to play at launch and unless you have a competitive streak like me; you will eventually grow bored of this, as 99.98% of the current community has. This game currently has over 30,000 people who OWN the game, yet at peak times US East you will barely find 30 people playing.
The asking price for this game is $15, I urge you not to buy until it is at least HALF this price, or even a quarter of this price; because the vast majority of you will not be able to play this nearly as long as I have and you will likely quit within the first 5 to 10 hours once you’ve seen all this game has to offer. I want to reiterate; it was my Workshop projects that have kept me here so long, not just my competitive dueling.

I have to say--I'm surprised I hadn't heard of this game at least in passing before the Summer 2015 Sale. Considering the fact that it was purchasable for less than a dollar--as well as its high approval rating--I figured I'd give it a try.
The game's concept is a fun play on a classic video game trope--the left side of the screen is literally a huge wave of annihilation, and anything that is consumed by it is obliterated. It's up to a multiverse-travelling hero (the player) to face this apocalyptic force and save the world!
For the price, I've found the game to be thoroughly enjoyable and surprisingly diverse. As many others have mentioned before me, the soundtrack is great. There's a large number of tunes for each biome, enemy encounters, and structures in the world. The number of potential classes to play as and the different ways to win also gives it a nice boost to replayability. A large variety of variables can be changed to make the game easier or harder, depending on your preference.
---GRIPES
There's only a few personal gripes I've had so far (and they are small). First, while there is a large number of biomes for the world, I would have liked more types of natural and constructed obstacles. Water is one such element present in the game, but it tends to be little more than a mild variation in the terrain. Occasionally, lakes will spawn with chests in the middle of them, but otherwise they're fairly generic and feel a little short of their potential in the game's unique setup.
Another minor issue is that some classes are noticeably harder to play with. I'd like to play more as an Adventurer, for example, but the class's physical weakness and emphasis on running away makes it difficult to level up and increase their equipment load (something this thief-like class desperately needs in order to maximize their chest-looting!).
---OVERALL
Overall, it's a fun game that I'm still enjoying at the point of this review. I should warn that--like every other game--it's not necessarily for everyone. If you're not a fan of roguelikes or RPGs, you might have some difficulty getting into the live-grind-die-repeat cycle you'll quickly recognize in the game. There's also a noticeable manga/anime influence in the art and storytelling style,  which might clash with some players (personally I enjoyed it, particularly the game's humor).
I should also mention that the game seems to have an expansion that adds content such as more companions, classes, and gameplay elements. I unfortunately haven't had the chance yet to try it--it's currently unavailable on Steam--but the presence of its Achievements here hints at its eventual release.
Personally, I've enjoyed this little hidden gem, and feel that my less-than-a-dollar was well-spent.

A Story about my Uncle - Gone North Games & Coffee Stain Studios
Always check settings and controls!
Do you know what one of the hardest challenges for a single player Game developer is? The answer: creating a videogame that's a first-person platformer. This is because there's something incredibly difficult about aiming invisible feet on an inch-wide surface while moving airborne at tremendous velocity. And here's the collaboration of Coffee Stain Studios and Gone North Games to accomplish exactly this nigh impossible feat.
Welcome to the game. We enter a first room of a small house. A voice starts talking: It's us! We're telling our daughter about the day our Uncle Fred went missing. Upstairs we find a suit that apparently improves our jumping capabilities. It's a weird and clunky exoskeletal armor, but I'm sure it'll become fashion within time. Another staircase. This leads to Fred's observatory tower. In their is a switch that will activate the garbage disposal pad and sent anything flying into the great unknown.
The game is divided in a handful of stages, which all feature an upgrade to the exo-skeletal jumpsuit. There's a grapplebeam and rocket boots. The big challenge lies within finding the quickest way through the level and let me tell you, jumping from ceiling to rock like spiderman is massively hilarious! Each level teaches us about one of the steps of how to handle grief, which is a promising premise and executed perfectly. Personally, I learned about the anxiety I inflict when hiding in the renown mancave.
What do I always say about the music? A good soundtrack gets stuck in your head and makes you want to come back. The soundtrack isn't extraordinary enough to be a stand alone album. A few months later and you'll have forgotten every song, though it is ambient and merges well with the environment.

Tl;dr version:
Despite having won this game multiple times on higher difficulties, a friend and I recently lost together on easy against Byzantium, one turn away from our vicctory, because the uranium needed for my friend to nuke their capital (and for my ships to capture it) was unavailable because a city-state nearby my friend was so unhappy that barbarians spawned, crossed his borders and raised the uranium mine.
GG would underestimate the complex interactions again.
(Much) Longer version:
Don't be fooled by my play time. I probably spent more than double that offline.
I'm a big fan of politics. I love it so much I went and studied it. Even before I did so I fell in love with Civ5 and now, with a better grasp of politics, I can say that Civ5's diplomacy - although obviously not perfect - is definitely extremely underrated. Many reviewers sometimes speak bad of the AI. I disagree. I've found that in games where I keep out of conflict, give when the AI ask for help and refrain from irritating them, I have a way more peaceful game. Being friends with everyone not just prevents war against ME, but also acts as a mediating influence on the AI, leading to less war between my AI friends. In fact, befriending an AI's enemy, although that AI will be irritated with me at first, eventually leads to both AIs becoming friends. Yet, again in a game with a friend, I found that my friend had false friends. He invaded his neighbours, stole their territory and did not give them help. Yet in time he became "friends" with them. Yet when he went to war with Rome I decided to send ships and troops to support Rome without my friend knowing. These troops sapped my friend's army which led to all of his so called friends declaring war on him and destroying his economy, making him abandon the game like a sore loser. In contrast, in most games where I have spent hundreds of turns improving my relationships with my neighbours, they are less inclined to invade me if I go through difficult times. The AI is rational here and yet personal. In most games there are always at least one civ who always hate you, no matter what. And yet, there are deliciously rare times (it's good that they are rare) that the AI will eventually, if you don't take revenge on their aggressive actions, come over to your side. In one game Russia was a threat, we had war, we hated each other. But I was never the cause of it. Eventually I put up a resolution of sanctions against her. Yet before we voted on that Russia changed her mind, forgave past issues, adopted the same ideology and wanted to become friends. So I agreed and we became the best of allies.
This final year of college we studied nuclear deterrence. Never before did I use it in Civ. Yet in this one game I was surrounded by civs, all of them having war with me at one time or another. I decided to use my knowledge to my advantage: get nukes as soon as possible. If you have nukes and your neighbours do not, they are lot less inclined to war with you. This way I only need two or three nukes. Then I don't have to spent time and money on a huge army just to DETER my neighbours. Instead I could use the money to buy space ship parts. I lost the game by only a few turns, but I'm confident that was the right choice. The AI is smart enough.
Obviously and yet necessarily geography is also mixed into the politics. In my most recent games I had way more wars than usual simply because of my geography mixed with personality. In one of them, Poland I (Germany) shared a small area. This led to competition between us and extremely devastating wars that dragged on until the end of the game. Usually Poland is not so tenacious and hateful. Yet in this game the slightly randomness of the AI (this time around a more aggressive Poland) mixed with a small territory led to eternal hatred between us. Although I did not win the game as by then it was too late, I "won" it in my eyes by finally, at our fourth war, breaking him.
The game manages to have a near perfect blend of personality with randomness. That's what I like. Always something new and unpredictable, yet always predictable.
I appreciate how the world becomes smaller over the ages. In the beginning the ten turns needed to travel between your first two cities seem immense. Little later you begin to solidify and consider your neighbours and their attention. By the mid game and beyond you slowly start to think globally. All the while through this process you have this fear in your mind that those around you will progress quicker: that my neighbour will start looking outward while I'm still fighting barbarians or struggling to build up my new cities. This is a hell of a balance. Because of this meta-balance war is not always the best choice. One of the most devastating things to happen to you is a war staying beyond its welcome; to fall behind other civs because you are too busy building units. And yet - also a balance - fight well and the benefits you reap in that war will win you the game.
To give an example, in a recent game I was playing as Denmark. I was smothered by civs on three sides, with the ocean - and across it England on her own continent - on the other side. I could only manage two cities. That is not enough to win the game. You need at minimum 4, preferably 5 or 6. If I stayed the course I would have lost one way or the other. But Engalnd, being weak, and I having a naval advantage, had no choice but to invade and take over London and another city. Usually I would have avoided war until the end game. But this was a matter of absolute importance. I also knew if the war dragged on I would fall behind. I also knew that having a war and taking London would sour relations with my stronger neighbours, maybe they would even declare war on me - the AI is rather opportunist (a good thing). But the gambit paid off: I conquered much of England and solidified my gain. This one move led to me slowly rising to go beyond civs hundreds of points above me.
^^^ These long stories is why I love the game. If you like my examples, buy the complete Civ5. Buy it on special or NOT on special. It is still worth everry cent. If the above sounds boring, after all, you have to plan a hundred turns ahead, then this is not for you. Yes the game has its issues, although I think it only has few issues, but really they are negligible.

Calling this game a rhythm game is disingenuous. It's certainly a musical game, but it is not a rhythm game. It's a musical action game.
The goal of Runner 2's levels is not to have your button presses be in time with the music, or to match the music. The goal of Runner 2's levels is to -create- music. You don't play the levels, you perform them. Much like reading music from a sheet of paper, you read the levels as they scroll by, and you respond to what the level tells you. Looking at the obstacles directly in front of Commander Video is going to make you lose. A musician does not look at the note he is playing, because he's already playing it. You can't react to the obstacle that you should already be dodging. This means that even though your actions reflect the music, it's not in the sense of pressing the button in rhythm. In a strict rhythm game, the music is already happening, and you simply follow the beat and are graded based on how well you do. In Runner 2, the beat follows you. The music and the rhythm is created by your actions- it can't exist without you playing it.
Many people go in to this game expecting it to be a timed-button rhythm game. It frustrates them because they feel a dissonance when the beat or note that occurs from their input happens after they had already done it. The game doesn't allow for failure either. The level never slows down for you or allows you play a wrong note. You're performing the level, you're not allowed to mess up.
This all sounds kind of difficult, and it can be if you play on the harder difficulties (which are the fun ones). Making music isn't supposed to be easy. But when you learn how to play, it's a very calming experience. Even though you're quickly pressing buttons and reacting to dozens upon dozens of obstacles that will halt your momentum in one hit, you're also listening to the rhtyhm of your actions, and you get the feeling that you're actually playing a song.
Visually the game looks great and it's got a good art style. The amount of stuff to unlock gives good reason to replay levels and adds value to the experience. One thing that makes this game great for anyone is you can choose to make it easy on yourself through optional checkpoints and difficulty that can be changed any time outside of a level. My one complaint is sometimes looking at the screen intently, which you often have to do during tough parts, can be a strain on the eyes. My other complaint is that the scoring system can sometimes get wonky, but that only affects my ego, and not the gameplay.
In conclusion, music is art, this is a game where you perform music, this game (and therefore all games) is/are art.

After his exploits in the previous BIT.TRIP games Commander Video is back to running in everyone’s favourite retro themed series and now available on the PC. To try and describe the madness of the plot is somewhat pointless but we can say it’s something to do with our hero crashing his spaceship in a strange place and then deciding to run a lot.
Unlike previous entries into the BIT.TRIP series, Runner 2 is no longer 8-bit styled in terms of how it looks. The stages are now rendered in a glorious array of crystal clear colours and everything is also much bigger on screen. There are still retro looking levels to be unlocked but the majority of the time you will be screaming along at breakneck speed in a more HD friendly landscape.
Gameplay is based on a fairly simple concept. You start at one end of the course and run continuously to the other. Players have no control over Commander Video’s running and he continues on until you reach the end of the stage or crash into something.
As you run along different types of obstacles will appear which need to be negotiated. This starts out with players simply needing to jump over things but, on an almost level by level basis, the obstacle count increases and thus, so do the moves needed to get past them.  Soon you’ll be locked in a rhythm of jumping, sliding, kicking, spinning and dancing in order to reach the end of each course.
As well as avoiding obstacles you also need to pick up the gold bars that are in each course. There are normally between thirty to sixty gold bars in each level and collecting them all triggers the chance to get bonus points by Commander Video being fired, head first, into a target at the end of the course. If you think the course is too easy you can also jump over the mid-point checkpoint to put the game into challenge mode for even more points. Still not enough? Then you can spend your fleeting free moments making our hero dance to gain even more points. The score attack aspect of Runner 2 is here to stay for a very long time.
Once you master that even more moves are introduced and everything keeps getting more hectic to the point it all begins to blur into a state you aren’t quite sure the human brain should be able to deal with. It’s at moments like this that you realise where the ‘rhythm’ part of the title comes from. Perhaps deceptively, Runner 2 is not really in the same category as endless runners such as Canabalt. It should really be grouped with games like Frequency, Parappa the Rappa and is perhaps most similar to Vib-Ribbon.
Courses are also deceptively packed with things to find and navigate. Many of them have multiple routes with some leading to hidden objects such as new costumes, while others will take you to a different exit. This in turn will lead you to hidden levels or the much sought after ‘Key Vault’. Conquering the Key Vault will then open up even more routes and collectables in the courses found in that world.
An array of map icons is present for each course to help keep track of your progress with the ultimate goal to have each level completed, with all collectables found, the bonus bull’s eye hit at the end of the course and the mid-point checkpoint jumped so the game goes into challenge mode. Levels get hectic very early on so it’s a relief to find that each course gives you infinite lives to get through it. When you hit something you will move back to the last checkpoint and lose any points or objects you have acquired. The unlockable retro levels remain hardcore and give you three lives with which to navigate them.
The game can still be maddeningly frustrating at times as once you lose your rhythm in a level it can be near impossible to get back. You will persevere though as everything is fair and each collision results in a lack of skill from the player or in the fact you haven’t reacted to something quickly enough. Learning each level does come into play but we rarely came up against the sort of ‘memory test’ gaming with objects you had no way of avoiding first time that games like Donkey Kong Country used to employ. Just one thing though – do make sure you are playing with a gamepad as the keyboard controls are a bit tricky.
Overall, it’s easy to recommend Runner 2 on any system. It fits nicely onto Steam among the other high profile indie games and is the perfect game for PC gamers to take short blasts at on their lunch break. The charm and fun present are not easily found elsewhere and it’s great to see something which sets itself out as a pure gaming experience without the pretentious overtures that many bigger budget games now have. It’s both something old and something new and you should stop reading now and go and buy it.

Puzzle Agent takes place in the morose corners of the Midwest. Sure it's a clichè setting for mystery thrillers, but how this setting is expressed in a "children's book" art form turns that clichè into an interesting contrast. Graham Annable's art profoundly brings the story to life, and what a strange story it is. I say that in a good way.
The main gameplay draw in Puzzle Agent are obviously the puzzles, which are interspersed throughout the game as the story unfolds. The formula is basically narrative-puzzle-narrative-puzzle-narrative reminiscent of the Professor Layton games for the Nintendo DS. No, Puzzle Agent is not a Professor Layton rip off. Both titles are really just video game versions of puzzle story books that anyone born before 1990 grew up with. Also, although this is a Telltale game, this is not really a point-and-click adventure since there are no branching paths. Just keep on clicking the next obvious thing to progress the story.
There are a good variety of puzzles ranging from logic to spatial reasoning. I would say just over half of the puzzles offer a solid challenge for the average Joe. The puzzles that are easy are indeed the weakest aspect of this game, but they're so easy that it can literally take 10 seconds to finish them, getting you straight back into the intriguing narrative or better puzzles. It only gets frustrating when an easy puzzle is a slight variation of a previous one. The game could seriously use less of those rotating tiles, piece fitting and pathfinding puzzles which often can be solved by simple brute force. The piece fitting puzzles in particular are somewhat broken because the pieces automatically latch onto the correct position when in close proximity thereby essentially solving itself for you.
I do like how a few puzzles meld with the narrative. At certain plot points, the game interrupts you midway through solving a puzzle with an animation happening on the puzzle pieces directly, momentarily bringing you back into the story. In one part, someone off-screen steals a puzzle piece while you solve that puzzle. You can't experience narrative like this in puzzle story books. Here Telltale have shown us an example of what they do best: how they can transform traditional forms of media into a better experience through new technologies. I just wish there were more moments like these.
The one other issue I had with a few of the puzzles is that sometimes the rules are vague. For example, one puzzle asked you to determine the winner of a tournament with nothing more than statements made by the contestants. However, the format of the tournament was never mentioned (spoiler alert: it's single-elimination). Another involves fish and food chains, but it was never clear what eats what and whether there can be a fish within a fish within a fish... ya know, fishception. There are 72 puzzles (37 in Puzzle Agent 1 and 35 in 2) and I counted no more than 5 that suffered from ambiguity or outright misses necessary information to be solvable. It's a small percentage so I don't think it's that big of a deal. It just sucks when a brilliant puzzle was spoiled because the rules weren't crystal clear.
Overall, I enjoyed Puzzle Agent's story, art and most of the puzzles. Also, you should know that this review covers Puzzle Agent 1 and 2 since they are each half a game and half a story. Telltale really should've called them Episode 1 and 2.

Shadowrun Hong Kong provides a hefty amount of tactical combat, cRPG mechanics and a decent dash of choice & consequence, fixed around a pretty good story. There is not that many additions for those who've already played Shadowun: Dragonfall, but the developers seem to have improved the overall gameplay nonetheless.
> Combat is straight-forward but more dynamic than SR: DF due to more abrupt means of enemy elimination, such as Duncan's Subdue, allow for much speedier resolution.
> NPCs are well fleshed-out and impressive in their backgroudn stories. The game's take on the Walled City is quite interesting and deserves praise.
> The game features some new character art (presumably via Kickstarter backer portraits), which are quite an upgrade on the diversified stock portraits from SR:R and SR: DF.
> Martix system seems to be overhauled (as per KS stretch goals) but it's a moot point whether it's better or worse. Aesthetically it's much better than in previous games but gameplay-wise it's often frustrating to get +20 Trace (increasing the alarm status) per round.
> Game length is acceptable, considering the side missions et cetera. Harebrained will also release an extra campaign to resolve some loose ends from the original campaign. Even without that, as per previous SR games, alternative means of gameplay are visible to the player (i.e. if you need a particular skill for a dialogue but don't have it, it'll often -not always- appear to you, so you may try that out during you next play-through).
> The soundtrack is very well executed and fits the game's theme extremely well.
Overall, the game is definitely worth every penny paid for it. There is also the level editor in the pipeline so further gametime can be obtained via Steam Workshop.

Since SR:R I always vote these games 10/10 even before they come out. Therefore the expectations for SR:HK were high and I can't really say if the following list of mostly disappointments is a valid evaluation of the game. While reading please keep in mind that I rated the previous SR games exremely highly and had, due to the success on Kickstarter, the believe that this would get rid of some of the quirks of the previous game, but instead added some.
Matrix: The best comes first. I was shocked, positiveley, how well you can do the matrix. I really thought what we had in previous games was good enough, given the scenario and the game engine limitations. This is so much more fun. It feels intense. And you really need to apply some skills software developers and hackers need to employ, like recognizing patterns, looking for that one spot that isn't covered by your assertions (or IC) yet, and memorizing seemingly irrelevant details like numbers. There is also real skill involved, because sometimes the spot that is not covered by the watchers is dynamic and you need to move on fast to really not be spotted. The sounds for the number pad at first are really confusing which stopped me from getting more than 4 numbers. But after you get used to them they start to help you and you can sometimes complete the number game, even though it's not really necessary for the pattern game that follows. A huge plus, this whole new matrix thing. I'm so happy I played a decker.
Size: All the SR games are way too short. Maybe because of my expectations this one felt the shortest. The missions are very short, often just contain one little quirk and then you are done with it. You don't have enough character dialogues for all the missions. And how many missions were that, 10? When all the dialogues were finished and I could head out to the final mission there were about 3 or 4 runs left. But I felt like I just warmed up and started. All RPGs are rather boring in the beginning. Only after you develop some of your skills and get some better items you can really start playing. But that's when you were almost finished. Due to the sucess of Kickstarter and co I can't understand that.
Story: It's basically the story from SR:R. Even the endboss looks like a bug. After the runs were finished it got really really boring for me and I just wanted to be done with it. That's the first time this happened in SR to me. Sad.
Characters: I like to take a Shaman on every run. Because of that and the general dialogues Gobbet was basically the only character I really liked here. If the rest lives or dies, I can't say.
Fights: They were also quite boring. In every fight with the end boss I killed in at most 3 rounds. Maybe it's time to play on higher difficulty, I don't know.
Environment: Maybe it's because the Shadowrun Pen&Paper designers didn't know about China and HK, but the representation is much worse than with Berlin. Simplified Chinese characters here, wrong characters there. Everything looks like a Chinarestaurant in the US, not like China. Some of the jokes are a copy&paste from the internet, some even are jokes that foreigners make about Chinese not jokes that Chinese people make. I don't know. Getting an HK intern to do your due diligence on the language and cultural stuff is quite cheap. Why do people never do it?
RPG Engine: Can't say, because I only completed my character only about 60% percent. But it seems at least from the items there is not more to get. There was one better uniform to buy than what I had, but there was only one opportunity. Money and Karma wasn't even close to enough to get done with my char.
Replayability: For me, none. The game isn't free enough to try different things. It feels really scripted. You can choose between different paths, but each one of them is layed out clearly in front of you and often has no real impact on the result.
Conclusion: For me it was not a good game. Just something I finished because I'm a real fan of SR world and the previous games. The new Matrix was top, but nearly everything else was "mamahuhu". I really hope there will be a Dragonfall version with that Matrix though. I can't choose to give no opinion if I recommend it, so I can only give my personal opinion which is: I can't recommend it. Objectively it might be worth it. Can't say.

A new twist on the classic RPG beat'em up of the original NES days. Far more characters and a more robust environment, yet still paying homage to it's original completely. This game has been something I've been looking forward to for a long time, and it delivered exactly what I was hoping for. Slap-happy brawls and goofy fighting abounds. There are a few issues I've noticed: there is some odd slow-down in parts with heavy animation, which strikes me as odd as this isn't a particularly taxing game. Additionally, on the onset, fighting is basic and sometimes frustrating, as your character will stand and just take a beating if you get locked into it. However, these problems alleviate themselves pretty quickly, and on the whole I would recommend this game to anybody looking for a modern beat-em-up with an NES feel.

Such a missed opportunity.
The original River City was one of my first NES games. I bought it new as a kid with saved allowance and played it with middle school friends and family members many, many times to completion over the years. It was unlike anything we all had ever seen, an RPG/Beat 'em up with some strategy and even a little locker room humor, in a setting right out of the the book the "The Outsiders" which is/was huge at that point in your life as a kid. I cannot overstate how much I love this game and have followed it for years, playing imports and even fan translations of the other games in the series.
And that's why this game is just so incredibly DISAPPOINTING...
Unfortunately I think the flaws are more design than play balance, which means there is not going to be any type of magic patch that fixes this one. This game is fatally flawed and a total bust for me and it seems a lot of other players. How could this have been done so poorly???
Example: You start the game confused almost immediately due to tutorial messages that cancel with the punch button(!) in a fighting game. I must have punched the first boss for ten minutes doing no damage at all due to him being invulnerable except to special attacks, even starting over thinking it was bugged. Nope, just poor design and no player direction. This is less than 30 seconds into the game. You begin the game so weak, and spend so much time on the ground, you will assume your controller is not working correctly.
As the game progresses, you are joined with other main characters that give such brief and poor explanations as to what is actually going on, you aren't sure if they are now your enemies or trying to help you or what. This is compounded by the fact that they can and do injure you (and kill you) repeatedly, even if you don't attack them or do so accidentally. I had no idea if I was to join them, follow them, attack them... It felt like I had been dropped in a random save state or that perhaps the game was glitching the story presentation. Nope, just bad design. Even the map is confusing and poorly explained!
Add to this that my character was listed as a luchadore and starts out with ZERO grappling moves. You are a wrestler with a dedicated grapple button, and cannot do a single wrestling move until you buy one from a vendor to learn. WHAT? Again, I thought it was bugged but that is how it was intentionally designed. Who play tested this???
There are a lot of nods to 80's properties (DeLoreans in traffic, Akira motorbike in the shop, etc) that are appropriate to the era, but other touches like modern indy game characters lurking in the background or graffiti that is too new school in appearance is totally jarring and hurts the rest of the theme. The original characters are in it, but they look so drastically different (imo) they might as well be entirely new. I guess the music is well done, and the sprites look nice?
Honestly the only positive thing this game has going for it is that it will remind you of the much better original, which is vastly superior in every way despite being more simplistic and almost 30 years old.
RCR:U is grindy, confusing, unfair, cheap, has art styles that clash drastically (nothing was in "Chibi" style on the NES version, but the cut scenes and menu screens here are, and it is just so stylistically WEIRD looking), possesses a button layout for my NES30 that crashes the game in a repeatable error, has an unnecessary GTA wanted style mechanic that is not explained and poorly implemented, and much, much, MUCH more. Bottom line, If this was not attached to the original property the word of mouth would have killed it day one.
I would have much rather this game never came out than to do so and be as unplayable of a mess as this.

2. Running out of the screen in co-op mode doesn't save your friend (which saves money) like in the original.
3. There's about 10 million enemies on the screen with special moves when all we can do is punch/kick.
4. Leveling up seemed to not have any obvious benefits considering we were always dirt poor.
5. What's up with the tool tips? We're in the middle of fighting and the tool tip is GONE the second it appears, so maybe some of the questions I had above might have been answered, but there's no way of knowing.
6. You're taught in the tutorial to punch vending machines for items, but then you're punished for vandalizing in the real game and you don't even GET anything from them.
7. Chase scenes????  HOW MANY CHASE SCENES DO YOU NEED?!?!
8. Why the hell do you lay on the ground for so long?  Knock downs feel like a million years to recover from.  Are we to believe that down the road in the game, we can improve our speed of recovery?
9. Getting flanked by enemies seems impossible to fight naturally without trying to exploit some angle or position.

11. Who makes vans so thin that you can't jump on them?
12. We understand that you're trying to make the feel of the original where there's not too much exposition and guidance, but hot damn, it's hard to figure out how many zones you need to clear before initiating the next boss sequence.

14. My heart wants to like this game, hell I'm a backer, and I had a lot of expections.  I'm hoping future patches and changes will allow me to come back to this game and actually enjoy it.

I am not having any fun with this game.  I know that 80 minutes is not near enough to get a grasp on this game but I don't want to go past the point where I cant get a refund.
The simple fact is that if this game was not River City Ransom I would have refunded this without a second thought.  As I meandered about desperately trying to have fun, it occured to me that if not for the nostalgia, I would have refunded this turd right away.
Combat feels clunky, maybe this changes as more moves are unlocked, but the enemies don't drop tons of money and you lose half of the money you have upon death.  This makes the game feel incredibly grindy, and I have always been of the opinion that a game that requires grinding is a poorly designed game, especially if that game is a beat em up.  If the combat was fun, grinding may not be an issue but based on your early move sets, combat is not fun at all.
You get a punch and a kick(no combos to start), a dash move, a jumpkick, and a grapple.  Each screen typically has mobs of about 5 enemies and fighting them with such a limited moveset grows tiresome very quickly.  Then you have moronic gimmicks like the cop system.  If you accidentally punch a NPC then you become wanted by the cops and have to do something boring to get rid of your wanted status(ie; return to your hideout, hide in a dumpster etc). I've been playing this game since closed beta, started around May 2015. And I have to tell you, don't listen to the salty people that left their reviews. Try the game for yourself, it's free. Just be sure to learn the mechanics if you like the it, iChase on YT is the best source for info, watch his captains academy vids(all of them).
If anyone is interested in my opinion, here you go:
Credibility: 2.5 years played, over 5k games combined(not that much but still some), 61%+ WR on my main account, and 1450+ WTR
TL;DR: The game is good, try it, you won't be disappointed.
The game has had and probably will have it's ups and downs, but despite that it's really enjoyable. The grind is nowhere near WoT, WoWP or Elite: Dangerous. In fact it's quite enjoyable, as most ships are at least decent, and almost all tech trees have their gems. The devs are not the antichrist, nowhere near. They listen to us a lot more than most devs I've seen. Most people are just the usual doom sayers whenever their favorite ships get rebalanced. Balance is mostly good, there are some ships that are too strong, but WG at least tries to keep it balanced with changes to ships that are OP/UP. P2W is almost non-existent in this game. Sure there are strong premium ships(the ones that you buy with real money), but there are plenty of strong silver ships(the ones you research with XP). And if a premium is considered overpowered they remove it from sale, and they eventually disappear, or you see them once in a blue moon. You can play the game for completely free if you have the time and patience, but investing in premium time is recommended, as it makes a lot of things so much easier. It only costs around 10 euros a month, or even less if you buy in bulk. The game is also well optimized, so even the average russian toaster can run it. It also gets updated with a major patch every month, the devs are working hard, even if their ideas sometimes are questionable at best.
Of course the game has it's flaws too, in no particular order: The CVs are a huge mess, there is little to no counter play, you entirely rely on RNG with your AA, or RNG to get a competent CV on your team. They are really strong, being able to carry the team, but if the one you got on your team sucks, you are out of luck. The battleships are just too strong, and that probably won't change, as it's the easies to do well in, so most bad players(there's a lot of them) just play those. WG also caters to battleship players, even if they say otherwise, it's quite clear. The whole UI is a joke, it's flash based, slow, unresponsive, a pain to use, and likes crashing when in port(not that often though). WG is also terrible at teaching their players how to play, so there are lots of poeple sailing around in T10 ships not knowing about core mechanics, yelling "HAX" when they get killed by something they don't understand. The community can be toxic sometimes, but it's mostly okay.
BUT, and this is very important: the game is getting better over time, if some salty dude tells you otherwise, just go watch vids from older patches. Sure there are updates which are considered one(or more) step(s) backwards, but I can tell you it's much better than it was 2 years ago. The average skill level though, let's not talk about that.

This game was a slow disapointment. At first, it was farely enjoyable, but it soon occured to me it what was a waste of time and especially money.
This game is a story of a boy who follows his uncle into a mysterious world but given as telling his daughter about it. The story is very akward. The boy goes to his uncles labratory and next thing he knows, he's in a suit and in a strange cave world. He spends no time to go through the cave until he finds a village of traditional fish people. It's pretty mysterious and strange. Eventually, he travels through dark caves with one of the fish people, a girl named Maddie. Together they go past the caves and into Starport, where Maddie decides to stay. He continues to an ice place where he thinks is uncle is. Eventually he finds his uncle and his uncle is glad he came, but suddenly wants him to go back.
It is upsetting. After travelling through caves, sky areas, and ice caves, that the uncle attempted to have his son travel through, he just wants him to leave and go back to his world. He comes to be with his uncle, and his uncle won't even go back with him or better, or work with him in the things his uncle is about to do. While this game seems to advertise the story, but implements a very boring one with very boring characters. Maddie is a steroetypical excited girl. The cave village people are a steroetypical traditional no advancement group. The uncle is a steroetypical fun inventor guy. The boy is a stereotypical hero brave person. A Story About My Uncle has charcters that aren't exciting or interesting in anyway. The plot is a "travel through a dangerous place and avoid the enemies to save someone even though the hero is a child a should have no chance mentaly and physically". It is the epitome of a uncompelling, unrealistic, irrating, and bland adventure story. The singular path in the game only helps the feeling of a bad plot line.
Gameplay wise, A Story About My Uncle is okay overall. The grapling hooks are amazing and feel great to use. The air pulls are fun. And so on. While the magical grapple hook is great, the other tools aren't that interesting. The jump, jump dash, and jetpack could have been much better. The jetpack holds you in place and then rockets you forward in the direction you are pointed. It is often obnoxious and moves you further than needed. It would have been much better if it blasted you up smoothly and it had a set amount of gas that would reset when you touched the ground again. The jumps are simply boring and simple. More tools interesting tools and/or a replacement to the jumps would have been better. More things like the grapple would be excellent
Another thing is the enviroment/map, which isn't so good. There is only one way to go for basically the entire time and occasionally side paths. More of a sandbox, more open area with more places to grapple to and go would work much better. It is puzzle with only one solution. I also would say, I either went through something first try, or had a ton of difficulty with it. There isn't much of a middle ground of difficulty for the game.
The graphics and music were beautiful. It was one of the good things about the game. But with time spent ther, it spawns the biggest problem in the game, at least for me.
There is so little content. There is so little to do. After spending a few hours to beat the game, there is almost nothing to do. Either you can replay the game, which is so short it feels like a repeat, or you can do the speed challenges. Again, the speed challenges are a repeat of the game. It makes me pretty upset. This game costs $13, and all you can get out of it is a few hours of enjoyment. Perhaps some people aren't as cheap as I am, but I don't like spending money on RPGs for reasons like this.
If they added a working steam workshop where levels could be made and played by anyone, I would overlook the short campaign, bad story, and cringy gameplay, and I would instantly rating it up.

An enjoyable action adventure game, with a plainly charming background story, delightful attention to detail, and appropriately atmospheric world, graphic, and level design. I would love to see future games in this world, perhaps with a different gameplay style.
And here's the caveat, and why this recommendation must come with a warning: 1st-person 3D platforming is an abomination, and though
offers an original take on this rightfully uncommon gameplay genre, it cannot fix its essential problems. As you whoosh through the air in big parabolas you have to use your mouse to see around you, while also using the caret to aim and grapple a limited number of times before you plummet to your death. These awful controls coupled with unnaturally confusing visibility and restricted grapple distance are a recipe for frequent frustration. Perhaps there are some amazing gamers out there who always jump just right in three dimensions, and always grapple just the right surface at just the right angle, but I imagine most of us will have to try and try again until they succeed. Furthermore, those of us with a fear or apprehension of heights will find it not only frustrating, but also nerve-wracking.
This would all be OK if the game were forgiving of slips and bounces, but it's not. As you progress it becomes increasingly difficult, with the last level being purely evil. Persevere and keep trying (30 times for me in one section) and you will be rewarded with a certain degree of satisfaction at beating a challenging game. I say “certain” because I feel that this genre always involves a certain amount of luck in addition to skill. It's kinda like winning at poker.
If this warning doesn't turn you off -- it might even turn you on! -- then do buy this game. It pulls you quickly into its originally realized world, and will leave you with a smile when you finally reach the end.
