There are two things you need to know before loading up Awkward Dimensions Redux. First, this game is about dreams which is a word with more than one meaning. Second, this a personal game meaning an outside audience wasn't always taken into account during the design process.
Many of the varied levels are stunning in their own way, but they all carry the hallmarks of an amateur Unity project. As one would expect from such a project, it plays like a walking simulator with a little platforming and a few puzzles thrown in for good measure. The soundtrack, though, is one that I would consider listening to outside of the context of the game, which is unusual for me.
When faced with the amount of randomness present in this game, I have to ask myself if it adds to the overall message or only serves to distract the audience from a lack of depth. In this case, it's the former.  Though it isn't trying to invoke these feelings in its audience, the game is raw and emotional. Awkward Dimensions Redux seems to be an honest attempt to communicate the developer's feelings in the order – or disorder – in which they come up. Whether – given the format – that effort is brave or pointless is up to the player to decide.

Ok, here's my review of Lisa. I absolutely love this game, I would recommend this game, but I have a few dislikes.
Here is what I liked about Lisa; the music, the story, the characters, the money currency (magazines), and the dark humor. All of this made me want to buy and play this game. Also, this game is very addicting once you get into it.
Here is what I disliked about Lisa; the repeated enemy encounters, the random generator, and no rewards afterwards.
Let me explain using other role playing games. Paper Mario, Final Fantasy, the Tales of (video game series), and many more role playing games (rpgs) have this formula where if you encounter a enemy and beat it in a fight, you gain a small reward for your efforts. I'm not just talking about experience points to level up characters, though it's important to level up the characters.
I'm talking about like money to buy items or weapons, items or weapons (sometimes you get very lucky if you beat a rare type of enemy), materials to help upgrade your items or weapons, keys to enter other rooms in dungeons, etc... These things are the sole purpose of an rpg type of game.
What I'm getting at is I don't hate Lisa, Lisa is a great game, but it could do better.
In my opinion, here's how Lisa could be better if you add the rpg formula to the game.
Here's an example, let's say you are about to fight the first boss in Lisa, Smiley. Now, your party is probaly level 8 or past level 10 and you need the child's bicycle to travel a bit faster to get through the first part of the game. Let's say you beat Smiley, after a long or short fight, your party gains experience points, and your rewards are 200 magazines, 2 domestic jerkys or 2 diet coco cola's (you can only have one or the other), and you gain access to the child's bicycle.
I would like Lisa to have this formula, so you don't have to fight repeated enemies like the shadow figures to gain 10 magazines per round, so you can buy better equipment for your party, or just buy healing items for your party's hp or sp. I rather fight other enemies or side quest bosses, so I can get good rewards to help me get better items or equipment for the tough trials ahead.

If you're old enough to remember light sabre dueling in Jedi Knight II: Outcast, then you will understand why Blade Symphony is so good.  It has it's quirks, but is still being actively developed.  It should be a good finished product.

First impressions:
Aww yeah, Blade Symphony! I've played this game far too much over the past few weeks, and I've gotta share my thoughts.
Blade Symphony is alright on its own. You can jump in and enjoy yourself, dueling against others and all, but the real fun is when you get a couple of friends to play it with you. I happen to have three other friends who also picked up the game, and boy is it fun. The true way to play the game is in a dueling fashion. You go up against another player in a one-on-one duel, which are very fun to do. There are three stances to take: fast, medium, and heavy. The heavier the attack, the more damage. I start off my fights with a heavy attack, quickly switching to fast attacks afterwards, then back to heavy after I've backed up a bit.
The sword fighting is excellently crafted, huge props to the work that went into it. We had a lot of fun stabbing each other for a good hour or two. After that, we took the game in a very different direction. The game has two modes: FFA and duel. You already know what duel is, but FFA is a bit different. FFA will take any of the duel maps and make it a large, open-world map for you and some buddies to mess around in. In this mode. you're able to parkour around the level, wall-running and such.
Due to the various parkour features, we ended up playing hide-and-seek for several hours. It sounds ridiculous, sure, but it was so good. Specifically, there was one map we spent a ton of time on. This map resembled a mall, and it was HUGE, much larger than any of the other maps. The parkour features allowed us to find some pretty interesting spots to camp out at, one of my favorites being the very top of the mall, higher than the top floor. The best spot, discovered by a friend of mine, happened to be above the elevator in this map. It was a small, black room that a few of us hid in whilst playing.
Blade Symphony is a fantastic game. It's still in development too, so there's much more to come, even in its already glorious state. I look forward to future additions to the game and highly recommend it.

Short version: Very nearly a great game, but with some serious (though fixable) flaws.
The original River City Ransom is, by far, my favorite NES game. In most respects, this game is a worthy modern follow up. The graphics are fantastic. The fighting system is mostly great, if a little confusing in terms of move sets. The basic gameplay is close enough to the orignal to scratch the nostalgia itch. I have some quibbles about some of the changes to the gameplay mechanics, but they're pretty minor. Overall, RCR:U goes a long way towards building on the existing RCR world.
But there are a few problems. At least in the early part of the story, for instance, it's hard to know exactly what to do. I don't need my hand held, but I do need some general indication of where to go and what to do. Some elements are completely inintuitive, like having to jump over a random fence on the bridge -- not a mechanic that's hinted at, explained, or used again -- in one of the earliest missions. It's a reference to a similar spot in the original game, but without any visual clues as to what you need to do. Once you do figure it out, it's hard to imagine how this ever got past playtesting. Are the devs trolling us, or was this just some oversight?
There are also chase missions that just don't work, such as going after Tex in the sewers. There's a "Milk" mission that is already becoming notorious for being arbitrarily hard, rather than challenging. No explanation is given in most cases, making it hard to tell if you're even still in the mission or not. RCR is fundamentally a beat-em-up game with open world, RPG, and other bits thrown in, and it should never be a mystery about HOW you are supposed to progress through the story.
These are all relatively small issues, yet exceptionally frustrating in the moment. It's not a matter of being "NES hard," it's a matter of game design and playtesting. I don't want to feel like I'm a playtester. I paid $16 for this thing, and I want to enjoy it without caveats.
If these small issues could be fixed, this game would arguably be superior to the original. It has the potential to be. I could see this being a DLC machine, with plenty of stories and expansions worthy of a more of my money. But it's not there yet. As it stands, it's not worth $20, because it simply doesn't feel like it's ready to be called "complete." If the devs fix the outstanding gameplay issues -- and there really are only a handful of them that I've seen -- it could easily be called a masterpiece. As it is, it's more a promisingly good, but flawed, follow up to the original.

Online play doesn't save data, so if you want to play with friends and gain levels that remain permanently, you can't. The game is based on an NES beat'em up, yet they added excessive kiting, dodging, reacting to all player action, and a lot of other things that will have your brain say, "I am not playing River City Ransom." Remember in NES when a mob blocked and you were surprised? Or it was a special boss? The weakest mobs in RCR:U Block, Dogde, Kite and throw projectiles, so if you wanted that old school feel of mobs basically just coming at you, it's completely gone. This is not an old school game, not like that.
Yet I agree with basically everyone who recommends it, and I do repeat, saving does not currently work in online, yet me, and many people are still recommending this game. That should tell people something, seeing as how many Triple AAA games will be launched into Triple AAA purgatory for something like 30 FPS.
I like the new school approach they took, it takes balls to take something so beloved and try to redo it when the player base isn't THAT big. It's not like River City Ransom for NES was hot or anything. They added levels and slamming and other modern conventions that are really nice. Beating people up feels fantastic, it's just a shame that 50% of the time the computer response will be to evade, or move backward, and it only gets worse toward the latter stages of the game. So compared to the NES version you will do FAR LESS for the amount of attacks you put out. This is a good idea because it adds character and strategy to all the enemy mobs, but what ended up happening was the opposite. Since ALL mobs block/dodge/kite/spontaneously move MUCH faster than sprint speed, while going backwards, to evade, it makes all mobs kind of bleed together. The Jocks are just as scared as the nerds, who are just as scared as the other mobs, and so on.
Mobs will never MOB you, which is the worst part about this new AI, they'll constantly try to take either side of you with one person each, minimizing damage taken, maximizing damage dealt. So if 8 dudes are on the opposite side of the screen, 2 will actively attempt to engage you, and the rest will get to about half screen and start cheer leading. In terms of AI making a player think, it's great. In terms of AI emulating a River City Ransom experience, probably the worst decision they made. The last 15% of this game is catch-a-gnat simulator, where in the NES version, the last 15% was "I am a golden god, now I shall go forth and triple smack the world with this stick". I think everyone loves that end-game powerful feeling, and don't mind that the game gets somewhat easier. You're every bit the golden god, statistically, in RCR:U, it just doesn't feel like it when you have to chase everything down (Made worse by the fact nothing can remotely hurt you, so you just want the sheep to die)(Except that one guy in the thing I don't wanna spoil, he totally hurts, it rhymes with Mighter Get). RCR:U also has a super off-brand final boss that wasn't as good as the first.
The saving grace for the late game is how good the moves are, the move kits in this game are genuinely amazing. The move list on the other hand, is top to bottom full of errors, still totally recommending this game. It's RCR, but better (for the most part) and it has RPG like levels for individual characters now, and my lizard-brain appreciates that.
I bet folks want a recommendation with less complaining, buy this game, get to Act 2, do the Milk fetch quest, and tell me you don't need to vent. Great game, lots of room for improvement, but thanks for another RCR :)

Puzzle Agent 2 is a sequel that tries to fix the shortcomings of its predecessor and does so - but only by being less ambitious.
My review of the first Puzzle Agent lambasted the varying quality and difficulty of the puzzles. The second game does not have as many issues - only a few puzzles are ones that I would consider unfair (specifically, a few puzzles that require the player to have a cursory understanding of mathematical concepts that are not universally taught to all students, such as what an integral symbol from calculus looks like). In their place are more simplistic, traditional puzzles (many of which are used in the first game) that repeat several times through the game: sliding tile puzzles, "cut all the lines" puzzles, and programming puzzles to name a few. It feels like the developers got rid of the whole "FBI man solving challenging puzzles" conceit and just made the game using puzzles no more challenging or unique than those found in typical adventure games - except the puzzles don't integrate as tightly into the narrative as they do in the better examples of the genre.
That being said, I'm actually going to recommend this game for one reason: the storytelling is a step-above the first game. The writing for the character dialogue is more enchanting (though it may be because the Scoggins universe has already had a game to set up its universe... or it may be because there is a much larger dialogue tree this time around). The story also goes into mysterious, unpredictable directions, riffing on government conspiracies with engaging results. And the humor (while still subdued and at times subtle) is more on-point this time (particularly in the hero's exchanges with Korka Tetirdottir, the closest the game gets to creating a love interest for Agent Tethers).
The story is improved enough that I'd recommend this game for anyone who made it through the first one or anyone who likes adventure games. Those who aren't keen on adventure games should probably just skip this return trip to Minnesota.
Note:
For those who didn't play the first game, there is a synopsis of the story in Nelson's journal under the puzzle file menu - I'd recommend skipping the first game and just reading that as it isn't worth playing through the first game just to get a few in-jokes.

It is another Shadowrun game. I must admit however, that even though I really enjoyed Dragonfall (playing through it twice - upon original release and later the directors cut) Shadowrun Hong Kong just didn't click for me. It might be that I am simply tired with the same formula and engine, or that recent excellent and more ambitious RPG like Pillars of Eternity & Wasteland 2 make me want a more complex game.
The good stuff - there are many tweaks to the game which are welcome. The UI is much better this time around. You can also enter turn based combat mode at will, so if you spot an enemy you can set up and get a drop on them. There is also the new decking system however it does not bring changes I hope for. It would be nice if decking allowed player to interact with enviroment in some interesting way, but all it changed is the way Matrix works on the inside. It plays a bit like a stealth game but it is very basic and not very fun.
The story is weaker than in DF. You end up chasing after a person you never met ingame, which makes it very difficult to care about him. It doesn't help that writing isn't as tight. There are interesting ideas and missions, some cool characters but most of the conversations go for too long after they finish. It seems the script could use a rewrite of two. So does the whole game for that matter. Some conversation in the game (the hub area) kept repeating everytime I talked to that person and I don't think it was supposed to happen. Nothing game breaking but certainly felt "unfinished."
Also, just like in the Shadowrun Returns, I found that many of my skills and my etiquete weren't really usefull throughout the game. DF improved on it making frequent use of different skills and background giving you an impression that who you are matters. Here the design seems sloppy again.

The game itself is nice and I like this futuristic sci-fi fantasy stuff ... but:
NEGATIVES:
* Why are there no translations available? This game is 100% text based. Is it that difficult to translate?
* The leveling-system for the character looks very boring and feels pretty unfinished. Why did you change the last one?
* The game itself has not really improved ... I don't expect a game to be totally different to the previous ones ... but a little enhancement would be very nice.
* Why is the text/dialogsystem on the right side? If I play full hd on my monitor then I have to move my eyes from one side to another to follow the dialog and scenery. I mean ... in any other rpg etc. the dialog is on the bottom and it's fine this way.
* Text is sometimes to long for a single dialog ... especially if you are in hurry (school or work) and can not save in between.
* How does the save-system work? I nearly never am able to save the game except I exit it. If this is how it's meant to be ... so why don't just use an autosave-checkpoint-system during whole game?
* Do I see some propagandistic tries to connect russia with the ukraine? Such stuff does not belong into a game. (The guy living under your room who tells this funny fairytale about the european war.) Or is it this way in the books? This one I am really not sure about.
POSITIVES:
* Atmosphere is A+ ... the environment is pretty nice.
* The characters seem to be worked out very well (not fully finished the game).
* The story is (till now) very interesting.
* The hacking stuff for the decker is super ... but I nearly always triggered some of the security drones (maybe too difficult for the strange controls)
These seems to be some minor topics ... but if you played the other both games then you will see that it somehow sucks that the game seems not to improve. If it stays this way in the future ... I won't buy it.
EDIT:
I'm not sure about this game ... it looks more like an community MOD or something. I won't say it is bad ... but not worth the full price.
Maybe I'm just too stupid for this game but why am I not able to upgrade the weapons etc. of my teammates? I was a shaman and bought some ESPs for my decker ... but I was not able to replace the existing ones. Is it supposed to be this way?
In my opinion this sequel is the worst of all the three ... but not bad. It's okay. I wish there were a little more improvements (like building/equipt the ship - your base - etc. ... making new rooms).
Aw yeah ... I figured out that you can not save while any of your characters is moving. And one thing I don't understand:
* What is the difference between Rewinding and Loading a savegame? I tried both some times and I ended up restarting the whole level ... yeah ... nice ... T.T

At first I wanted to say that if you liked the first two "reincarnations (:P)" then don't wait and go play them. But I can't say that now. I can't force myself to play it anymore, so I can't even finish the damn game. So be aware.
Disclosure: I backed both kickstarter campaigns. I played the first one three times in a row, which is unprecedented for me. Maybe because I prefer RPGs and most of them are 50-100 hours long, so even after three playthroughs I still had time to spare. So I liked Shadowrun Returns very much. The Dragonfall not so much, although I still enjoyed it and got through the campaign.
So what's different now? Well there are few changes in GUI (some I do like, some not so much, but that's not important) and there are some game-play changes as well. The Matrix now works differently, it's more stealth oriented. The game doesn't tell you anything about the changes and it took me three attempts at hacking minigame to find out that there are actually some characters which should help you break the code. The lack of introduction was grin-worthy, but not a mayor fault.
You level up your runners now, after every run you give them one of two skills. And you can give them some equipment. Bud I was so poor that I could barely buy new weapon for myself, so I don't know what's up with that.
Generally, I really like the writing in these new Shadowrun games. Hong Kong is no different, in the way they are written. The problem is the content. Most of the times the reasoning of the characters, why they are doing said things, is just stupid. I've never noticed that before in these games, but this time it was a big problem for me. That said, there were occasions where I really enjoyed the dialogues and I had to think about stuff afterwards.
In the SR Returns, the controls were unresponsive at times till they fixed it. Dragonfall did not have this problem. Here comes Hong Kong and the unresponsiveness is back.
For the more serious problems: they are building on the thing that I didn't like in the Dragonfall. In SR Returns all of the shop keepers were in your hideout. So if you wanted to buy something, you just run around for few seconds and you had everything. In Dragonfall they spread it out to a whole city block. For someone like me who has to constantly check if there is something new, better, it was mayor boring waste of time and really bad design. I get that they wanted to put some stories into it, but for me the positives didn't out-weight the negatives. Here, it's the same.
The biggest problem for be is the combat. They added armor indicators and different kinds of cover. Which sounds nice, until you see it in action. The combat is really long, and boring. I was inflicting small amounts of damage to character out of cover. I had a long fight with enemies which were mostly unarmed, they were running around like crazy, and hitting me harder with fists that I did with weapons. I don't know how else to say it, but I couldn't enjoy combat when I saw what a little damage I was inflicting, waiting minutes and minutes for the boring fight to end.
I really like the SR formula, but I think that the evolution of a combat is a bad one. They should make a bigger game, with free roaming, exploration, better item progression and faster combat. I loved the combat in the first game, all the possibilities and combinations. The only problem was that there wasn't enough of it. And now? Now I hated it.
I really don't like to do this, I really really don't, but I can't recommend this game :(

Ok, here's my review of Lisa. I absolutely love this game, I would recommend this game, but I have a few dislikes.
Here is what I liked about Lisa; the music, the story, the characters, the money currency (magazines), and the dark humor. All of this made me want to buy and play this game. Also, this game is very addicting once you get into it.
Here is what I disliked about Lisa; the repeated enemy encounters, the random generator, and no rewards afterwards.
Let me explain using other role playing games. Paper Mario, Final Fantasy, the Tales of (video game series), and many more role playing games (rpgs) have this formula where if you encounter a enemy and beat it in a fight, you gain a small reward for your efforts. I'm not just talking about experience points to level up characters, though it's important to level up the characters.
I'm talking about like money to buy items or weapons, items or weapons (sometimes you get very lucky if you beat a rare type of enemy), materials to help upgrade your items or weapons, keys to enter other rooms in dungeons, etc... These things are the sole purpose of an rpg type of game.
What I'm getting at is I don't hate Lisa, Lisa is a great game, but it could do better.
In my opinion, here's how Lisa could be better if you add the rpg formula to the game.
Here's an example, let's say you are about to fight the first boss in Lisa, Smiley. Now, your party is probaly level 8 or past level 10 and you need the child's bicycle to travel a bit faster to get through the first part of the game. Let's say you beat Smiley, after a long or short fight, your party gains experience points, and your rewards are 200 magazines, 2 domestic jerkys or 2 diet coco cola's (you can only have one or the other), and you gain access to the child's bicycle.
I would like Lisa to have this formula, so you don't have to fight repeated enemies like the shadow figures to gain 10 magazines per round, so you can buy better equipment for your party, or just buy healing items for your party's hp or sp. I rather fight other enemies or side quest bosses, so I can get good rewards to help me get better items or equipment for the tough trials ahead.

But on a more serious note, LISA is an amazing game.
Described as "The miserable journey of a broken man", LISA is one of the most understated games I have seen in a loooooong while. The gameplay is solid (although the movement system takes a lot of getting used to, but that's understandable given the engine limitations), the characters are diverse and interesting, there are many different events and finally a complex moral choice system, through sacrifice and general actions, which all have a lasting effect on story, the world around you, and even core gameplay mechanics. The soundtrack is great. I have spent many an hour listening to Widdly 2 Diddly's rad beats. (boy oh boy is the best song btw)
But as much as I would like to proclaim this a perfect game, sadly it has a couple of drawbacks.
First up, the aformentioned movement system. Now, I will admit, I fell prey to the movement system more times than I'd care to admit, often many times over on the same location, but really it's an understandable drawback. Since the game is  made using a top-down square based engine, having a 2-D adventure platformer-ish game is going to be a little odd, to say the least. If you can get used to it though, it becomes very easy to navigate, especially in Joyful.
The second main drawback, for some people, is the high difficulty. Now, this wasn't really a problem for me, but I did get stuck on a couple of bosses, and some of my good party members abandoned me for next to no reason, but if I'm being honest here it adds to the whole "miserable journey" thing.
My favourite part of the game would have to be the disturbing fights with the mutants. Oh, there might be some minot spoilerage ahead, so yeah. Fights with the mutants like Baby and Chester in the Joyful expansion really bring with them a creepy atmosphere, and that really helps add to the tension of these potentially party destroying enemies.
All in all, LISA is a sometimes hilarious, sometimes soul crushing experience, with a high difficulty curve and a deeply interesting world that is full of lively NPCs and is affected by the choices you make throughout your gameplay.

Fans of rhythm games should already be aware of BIT.TRIP series, but they also probably know about how mostly hardcore they are. Runner2 changed that: while expanding on BIT.TRIP Runner gameplay, Runner2 offers friendlier learning curve and adjustable difficulty, which is a welcome change for all those non-hardcore gamers who wish to actually enjoy the game without regular rage-quits. And that doesn't mean that experienced BIT.TRIP-ers won't be satisfied with the challenge: set the difficulty level to "Rather hard" and go for those Perfect+'s! And don't forget beating all the Retro levels, too.
So, overall, a great game.

Mäng on üldse külgvaates ja mängus ta ise jookseb, aga nuppe vajutades väldid takistusi. Takistuse vältimiseks on funktsioonid: Hüppamine, Libisemine, Blokkimine, Batuudi pealt tõukamine, löömine ja nende combod. Üks funktsioon on veel, tantsimine. Sellega saad lihtsalt punkte ja sellega ei läbi sa ühtegi takistust. Võrreldes eelmise versiooniga on see edusamme teinud. Mäng on hea kui võtta üldiselt. Muusika on mängul hea ja on syncis sinu tegevustega. Takistuse möödudes tuleb täpselt sama heli tagataustal, mis lõpuks muutb päris heaks muusikaks kui oled 4/4 tähte veel eriti kokku kogunud. Seal on 5 maailma ja igas maailmas on leveleid. Osades levelites on kaks võimalust sul edasi minna. Tavaliselt on üks nendest raskem ja teine lihtsam. Osades raskemates teedes võid leida ka preemiat. Igal maailmal on kujunduses omale omased väiksed graafilised uuendused. Sul on erinevaid karakterid ja karakteritel on erinevad skinnid, mida saad lahti lukustada. Mängul on ka achievementid, et teha natuke su mängu lõbusamaks. Mäng kogub ka põhilist infot. Nt mina kasutasin X nuppu 15 tuhat korda, ehk tegin 15 tuhat hüppet. Nüüd on levelites ka 1 checkpoint, mida saad sa vältida ka üle hüppates ja saad lisa pointe. Iga maailma lõpus on see sama boss, kes oli sul ka esimest korda, aga teises masinas. Mängu mängides tuleb mängule keskenduda ja see ei ole ajaviitmis mäng, et rahulikult aega veeta. see mäng võib vahepeal sind tõesti närvi ajada. Soovitan seda mängu, aga ei garanteeri, et saate sellest lõbu tunda. Mängus on kolm raskustaset ja mina mängisin keskmise peal. mäng on väljakutsuv.

Gameplay - The gameplay is very easy to get used to, from stealth missions to full out combat, this game gives you some brilliant gunfights, robberies, boss missions and car chases. The police evasion is a very tedius, but over all more fun method, Unlike games like GTA where, you loose the police and you can then drive past them with a car thats smashed up, covered in blood with bullet holes in it and they won't beat an eye, this game requires you to get your car fixed up, new plates added, and a change of clothes to get the police to not suspect anything next time they see you.
Controls - The controls are very nicely done, as far as combat is concerned, the aiming, the slow motion, everything is brilliant. As for driving, They have gone for realism with it, Some people might like it, I wasn't really a fan of it, it takes a bit of time to get used to meaning I spent most of the beginning of the game crashing into things and getting shot up in no time, but with a bit of practice you become a good driver in no time, But then again, its realistic, its how cars where back then.
Story - One of my favorite stories of all time, I can't really describe it, but you will have to play it to find out. Its a whole story of betrayal, emotion, sadness but at the same time, partying, trust, money. The story is a crazy mix of family life and gang life. The best way to describe it, is sort of on par with Breaking bad. A hardworking man taking up illegal tasks to help support his family.
I can't actually believe I got this game for free by voting in a contest, The fact that it was a free giveaway made me think quite poorly of this game and it took me a while to get round to playing it, and that was a big regret. This is by far one of my favorite games.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants to have a fun little adventure down through forest, plains, snow mountains, towns, and of course dungeons. Each world in this rpg has its own little treasure and with rogue gameplay so were looking at something different each time that your hero can use or be abused by. Replayability is infinite as you can choose the way you wish to play your character with perks, abilities, and classes, and you are rewarded with points that can be used to obtained items from your earlier via a Dimension Vault.
Milling about in one area is a sure way to lose in this game. Your hero stands against grave danger between the force of darkness that constantly ravages the land, represented by a roving darkness that forces is way through the game on the left side, with each action growing the encroaching danger. Creatures with mal intentions stand in your way to keep you from your heroic quest to face the source of evil. If you like rogue-likes then you'll love this game. You start off with a few classes of characters and can choose a few perks to augment stats or gain abilities, and your goal is to defeat the demon lord who appears to be the cause of a darkness swallowing up the lands. Literally. The game has you constantly running to the right as the darkness behind you swallows up everything. Time only moves when you're moving or performing an action however, so don't be worried about being idle. This provides an interesting mechanic and a rather unique gimmick to this game similar to what Half Minute Hero does with having a time limit to defeat stuff.
This game is also highly replayable; With each death you gain hero points and can use a thing called the dimensional vault to store some of your fallen hero's goods for the next hero. You can use hero points to expand said vault or unlock more classes or perks.  Each day there are new "dimensions" basically randomly generated worlds that are downloaded each day, for you to explore and play with others, well, not with others like a party of folks to fight, but you can go through the same dimension as everyone else and see their current progress in the dimension, which is pretty neat.
The music is great, and surprisingly enough is all public domain music you can use if you want, and while the art might not be the absolute best, it has an endearing charm to it that is only enhanced with the characters themselves. For so cheap, this game offers a lot of hours of fun times for anyone wanting a rogue-like with a lot of content.

Qvadriga, developed by Turnopia and published by Slitherine, takes on the topic of Roman Chariot racing, applying Slitherine's usual love and care in bringing out a turn based, tactical approach which makes racing strongly reminiscent of Avalon's Circus Maximus boardgame. I get the distinct feeling that it was inspired by it, and it's taken that as it's base and then developed from there, iterating on it and improving and extending on that for the computer and tablet platforms.
You take on the role of a manager of a Chariot stable, home of anything up to four Aurigas (Charioteers) and their associated Chariots and Horses. Before each race you'll get a chance to manage your stables, purchase specialised repairs if necessary for your stable, and make bets on your charioteer if you feel confident enough that he'll win.
Additionally in the campaign mode you'll be racing around the empire of Rome, building up reputation in smaller venues at first and buying and selling progressively more skilled and expensive items for your stable, eventually working your way into the Circus Maximus itself. The campaign comes in normal and epic mode, depending on how much of a challenge you're up for.
Static turns are the way to go, allowing you plenty of time to assess the field and figure out your next move, you've a slew of options to control speed (Hint, you want to go fast, it's a race you know), to move across the various "tracks", the inside tracks are narrower and afford tighter turns but you'll need to take them slower unless you want to wreck the chariot and end up with a dead rider.
The outer tracks mean more distance but you can maintain that speed, this means there's a clear risk and reward involved in working out the optimal place to be on each turn, particularly in the early stages when the field is packed, and you really, really don't want to wind up fighting with another charioteer.
Combat happens as well, there's two options, lacerate (which means using your whip to whack at the horses and the rider, it's more frequent, but less damaging) and crash, which will hurt far more, but can only be done once or twice per turn. Needless to say, the better chariots come with wheel blades, making Crash a far more temping option, especially when a well timed crash will either shred the poor horse to pieces or the wheel on the cart, instantly taking out the rider.
There is also a "watch" option to avoid an attack if you expect one to happen, and a "control" option to better ensure stability if you think you're coming into a turn too fast. There's a lot of control here, and turn by turn as the race unfolds, you'll be required to continually think and re-adjust as you're going along. A few tutorial races will help you get into the swing of things.
Whilst the various events can impose weather effects which do show up in game, a nice touch, graphically the best way I can phrase this is as "Vanilla", along with the sound and music, it's functional and decent. But it's not exactly going to amaze or thrill. One problem I had was that the unity engine used (4.3) kept failing and crashing until I performed the D3D9.DLL fix (Payday2 vets will know what that implies), if you're getting unity failover errors, this is definitely the first thing to look at. It seems that the Unity engine is a bit finnicky. Worth examining if it's a problem.
Functional presentation aside, this is a really, really good game. It's one for strategy buffs though, don't expect heart pounding action, but if you like the concept of a thinking Roman's race through the Circuses. And managing your Chariots and building up an excellent stable whilst gambling those coins to help keep you afloat whilst hoping that your Chariot's wheel stays on for this one last lap... well, this one definitely gets the thumbs up.
Verdict

In rare form, Slitherine has (as of this writing) temporarily slashed the price for this game in half.  While I might normally say go get the mobile tablet version (on which I have countless hours), this is the perfect price point for this time suck of a game and make no mistake, it's unlikely they'll slash it more.  So if you've been on the fence, pick a side now!
Like the very best of games out there, it's a mechanically-simple approach to turn-based racing - chariot racing, mind you - that has clearly been inspired by similarly-themed board games of old.  Also like the very best of games out there, its simplicity belies its depth.  While races last about 5-10 minutes of real-time at most - making it the perfect pick-up-and-play game - you only have a handful of actions you can do on each turn, Qvadriga provides a tactical experience that gives you the right 'feel' of racing around in ancient Rome.
Unlike the staggered starts of the Olympics, chariots will line up side-by-side or even one behind another with random start positions, leading to seemingly unfair, foregone conclusions.  However, unlike the Olympics, it's perfectly okay to kill your opponents or their horses by whipping them to death or smashing your chariot into them, which might also damage their wheels enough to throw the driver out, only to be dragged to near-certain death.  Not satisfied?  It's also perfectly okay to position yourself to block opponents, often causing them to violently smash into your backside, hurting their horses, and therefore their overall speed.  Just be mindful that what you can do to others can also be done to you.
While there are similarities to other racers like Gallop Racer or Derby Owner's Club in that you must manage your horse's stamina during the race (too much damage and they slow down, whip 'em to make 'em go faster at the risk of hurting or killing them), the true depth of the game comes from tactically positioning yourself and upsetting your opponents to get ahead.  This will be difficult at first, but you will soon be able to second-guess the guy behind you with a pretty good degree of accuracy.  Do you try to take the inside lane and make the turn at speed, risking your chariot flipping over?  Do you hang back a little bit so you can whip your opponent from his chariot?  Do you smash your own chariot into his horses, hoping to drop his four-horse team to a three?  Or do you sacrifice the health of your own horses and whip 'em for that extra burst of speed, possibly slowing you down for the remainder of the race if you bleed them?
With single races available, the meat of the game is actually its campaign mode where the goal is to gain enough fame for your team to be invited to the Circus Maximus, the most electrifying arena in Roman entertainment where you can race for the millions (AND MILLIONS) of your team's fans.  Essentially you will start off by picking one of the available historical factions which will give you various starting bonuses, but don't worry too much about that as you will eventually replace all of your drivers, horses and chariots over time.  From there, you start racing, hoping to survive those early moments until you can make enough money to afford some good stuff.  Nothing will stop you from winning, mind you, if you've got the wherewithall to do so.  In between races, you will be able to see your team's fame on the local level (with several cities to make your name in) and on the global level.  Then you can manage your team, from pure maintenance to purchasing upgrades with your winnings which includes faster, stronger horses, higher quality and more durable chariots, and tougher and more skilled drivers.  Each stat for each component of your entry plays into your tactics for the upcoming race.  If you front a team of toughness, chances are you'll want to do your best to take out the city's top leaders (who are easily identifiable by their faction color and the number of wins they hold) whereas a faster team will be more dead set on getting a podium finish.  Finally, before each race, should you choose to do so, you can place a bet that your team will win and the payouts are tremendous if you manage to do so.  Keep it going and if you don't manage to kill all of your drivers, eventually new venues will open up to you for more glory and fame and money.
Overall this is a wonderful little gem of a title and while it won't necessarily hook you with its bland visuals and minimal sound design, once you figure out its magic, you'll be drawn in wholesale.

River City Ransom: Underground's primary goals were ambitious, and I had serious doubts as to whether they could be achieved. Could it expand and evolve River City without losing its spirit? Could it carry on the good-natured daftness of the original? Could it add complexity and nuance to the original's fighting system without sacrifing the overall feel? The answer is yes. Holy mackerel, yes.
...Which makes it all the more baffling that some of the more mundane elements of the game are kind of a wreck. It provides almost no direction as to your objectives. The moves list is indecipherable: many moves show the same button or sequence to activate, but there's no indication of the circumstances when each move will be used or even what the move looks like so you'll know when you perform it. The stun duration is frustrating. The lack of restaurants or other stat-boosting shops in Grotto Mall make the early game needlessly difficult. The easiest difficulty setting is about twice as hard as the original's default difficulty; I love the whole "Nintendo hard" vibe, but not giving an option for a slightly more manageable experience makes the game fairly unapproachable for even average players.
I'm hoping future patches can help iron out these kinks, because they seem like pretty low-hanging fruit compared to the wonderfully realized big-ticket items. As it stands, I find myself growling in frustration about 5% of the time, and grinning in nostaligic elation the other 95%.

Trying to defeat the AI in harder dificulties is like trying to defeat a monkey with better weapons: It still has no idea what to do with it.
The game is pretty cool, I spent days, if not weeks, testing and discovering its concepts.
However it lacks a lot when it comes to reaching the real objective that is to become a challenging game in a trial to archieve one of the victory conditions.
Of course we all get at some point to the point in which defeating the AI is much more like a very well know routine than anything else, and of course every game has that one bug which we find and spoil it so much that we lose the concept of the game, but let's talk about the victory conditions here: There are 4 victory conditions:
1 - Political Victory, which is archieved once a player get enought votes on the "international congress" to be the next world leader by having most if not all City-States as allies: The AI simply do not try to archieve it at all. You can ally all the city states in front of them and they would barelly send a spy to steal some reputation points. They still ocasionally accidentally please the city-states by destroying a barbarian camp that the city-state gave a quest for. They won't try to accomplish the quests given to them, and they will actually even sell their very own vote for world leader for something way too trivial in latter eras. The madness continues: Even though you are clearly getting close to the victory condition, the AI will still keep being your ally and helping you. They won't send a single army to stop you. (and I am not talking here about all the nonsense that happens during other votes in congress. The AI will always make a proposal that is clearly trying to destroy your economy, and if you ever counter it, they will get mad with you because you denied their agressive proposal: wtf?)
2 - Cultural Victory, which is archieved by conquering enought tourism points (which you mostly start to be able to get at latter ages by constructing the right buildings and is multiplied by your cultural power) and is countered by having more culture points then the other players (which you are able to get since the start of the game by constructing the right buildings, wonders, policies, and allying cultural city states). Does the cumputer even try to have some decent culture or tourism? For sure they rush those early artists in the end of reinascense era, and then what? And same thing from the political victory: even though you are clearly getting close to the victory condition, the AI will still keep being your ally and helping you. They won't send a single army to stop you.
3 - Domination Victory, which is archieved by capturing all the initial capitals of other players by using military power. In this one the mess is quitte interesting: The computer really strive about expending every single economic point it have in making a huge powerfull army, which it mostly uses for suicidal missions. The AI does not only destroy his eco in amassing weapons, as it also destroy the weapons, like as if you had a basooka and you want to destroy a wall by hitting the wall with the bazooka as if it was a stick. There is no terrain utilization or any strategy of any kind at all from the part of the AI. But it does not stop here. Lets talk about diplomacy: Lets say that you are player 1 and player 3 is atacking player 2. If you ever atack player 3 to help defend player 2 that is your ally (or even worse, if you capture one of the cities from player 3), your ally that is player 2 might end relationship with you and become your enemy. The funny part is that probably player 3 might want to have a friendly relationship with you for some reason: but if you ever try, then, to atack AIs to make them friendly towards you, they will just probably all get mad and declare war against you together. If you are clearly in front of their cities with the Army of Death and demands tribute in exchange for peace they will always deny, untill the last moment (that is when they clearly lost everything already) and at that point there is clearly nothing they can give you that is fair enought to exchange for peace (They declared war for no reason and kept creating so much problens just so that when you are going to give the final blow they realise that giving those 200 out of theirs 2000 gold coins would have been a good idea? they don't even have 200 anymore right now!)
4 - Science Victory, which you archieve by constructing a spaceship and sending it to space. Now, if you don't disable all the other victory conditions you won't ever get to the point in which you win a Science Victory against an AI (and probably against other players as well, probably). The reason for this is that to get a Science Victory you need the lattest technologies discoveries first and a good production power, which means that you probably already have first all the tecnologies and buildings needed to be ahead as a Cultural Victory; that you have all the production and techonological superiority to have a bigger and stronger army than your enemy to win a Domination Victory; that you have all the army production, wonders and buildings and economy that you probably needed to have a Political Victory. In other words: the Science Victory is extremally redundant, and it would only happen in a player vs player game in which both are struggling untill their limits.
5 - Score Victory: After reading all the other 4 above there is nothing needed to be explained. At higher dificulties the AI start with higher score, however it just don't have a single idea of what to do and eventually loses; making thus the next one: the Timed Victory unfair and nearly impossible if too fast in huge maps agaisnt a "Harder" "AI".
There is religion in the game. But it sounds more like a waste of effort if not for those early game pantheons (this could really be worked out better), and if not for the Religion Victory that you can add from the Worshop, by modding the game.
The game mechanics are not well built. Each action and each end of a turn is so slow that a single "Quick" paced game (in which everything was supposed to happen faster) can become a daylenght game against an AI. Making thus unpractical to play against online players, unless both of you are really really fan of civilization and are willilng to let the game awake in comptuter background while doing something else, and ready to load hudreds of saves due to internet disconections; and this could take whole weeks, if not months for 2 players - making thus nearly impossible to play with more than 2 players.
A very good and common adjustment for this would be to have a good AI, what we already noticed above that is clearly broken.
These are the main problems. Many other game balances and concepts are still pretty broken, but nothing you can't fix by your own by using some mods.
The Steam workshop is amazing and just makes the game so much easier to be moded. You can study the inner game mechanics by your own and make your own adjustments in most XML files, correct what you want, or find many other cool ideas and mechanics resolutions online.
There is even an interesting patch that is being developed right now by fans willing to work on improve and correct the major problens by creating a better AI.
If you are one of those who already found yourself working in modding a game during hours and days just to find out how would it be like after all that chemistry, then this game can be a great pack for you.

If you liked the previous shadowrun games, then this latest installment will also be to your taste. A new story, new equipment and new characters as we've come to expect harebrained schemes shadowrun games all come as standard, and I have no complaints. What has changed significantly from the previous games however is the decking system (hackin if you are unfamiliar with the shadowrun universe). Whereas in previous games it was merely an extention of the combat system, in SR Hong Kong it has been revamped as stealth based, requiring you to time your movements aroung patrolling ICE. While I am still not convinced it works in a turn based strategy game, it did none the less provide a refreshing chane of pace. The story is to the usual high standard, and while I personally preferred dragonfalls, Hong Kong's story will keep you gripped from begining to end. All in all another great HBS shadowrun game.

I found blade symphony surprisingly enjoyable. a small-league early access game about pure, unabridged swordfighting. i figured that it was infinitely better than torchlight (I was right) and tried it out
my first impresions were bad because the game was laggy, and had more bugs than a starship troopers movie. it was in its infant stages though.
I picked it back up so see if it improved and did it?
it has its own workshop, if thats not testament enough, I don't know what is.
The game has a really simplistic art style and theme that is more or less a combo of cyber-martial arts in a modern setting, not much to scream about but thats because its background. Blade symphony's main call is gameplay.
its a multiplayer only game where two or more people must duel with swords until one wins
. there is no simpler way to explain, no story, no war, just simple, one on one sparring with swords.
the selection of swords is satisfactory, with the player being able to choose between four styles of blade, each with their own attributes and styles, and to then extend that, a selection of four characters who again, have their own fighting style, making for 16 different combos of ways players can fight.
the best thing about the game, however, is that there is no overruling tactic. every style has a weakness (several, in fact), and every sword has a counter. its all up to player skill to beat the other guy in pure unbridled sword combat.
should you buy it?
Yes. it really tests your wit and is quite fun.

One Way Heroics is a side-scrolling rouge-like turn-based RPG in which the Player attempts to claim victory by defeating their evil adversary. However, even in defeat, one can carry over items and gain hero points, which can be used to unlock new perks and classes. The game even gives you advice based on how well you did on your run.
As for playtime, the game varies on a case-by-case basis. Although there's a wide range of things to do- find companions, unlock epilogues, beat the game without using x, maniac mode, and other achievements, one may find themselves interested in some things more than others.
For the people who run out of these things, the game offers daily campaigns, all with unique aspects, whether that includes no level ups, a companion off the start, or all NPCs being merchants.
All things considered, there's a lot of value here for a game that's only $3.49, and One Way Heroics Plus, a DLC expansion, is coming soon. How soon? As of this review, the acheivements are up for the expansion.
I highly recommend the game. The amount of content and humor in this game is definitely worth the money, especially when it goes on sale.

While it may feel easier than other rogue-likes out there, One Way heroics is a fun, fast paced and addictive game. In a way, every time you play you make your next plays a bit easier and every difficulty level add new complexities to the game and more information is revealed about the true nature of the evil you're fighting against. For it's low price it's a very nice addition to my steam library, probably would be to yours as well.

A top-down racing/strategy game based on Roman chariot racing.  The game plays in either
(real-time) where you give your aurigas orders on the move, or
which plays as turn-based control over sections of the course (rather like a board game).
You start the game with three men, their chariots and horses belonging to one of 6 factions (each with its own strengths/weaknesses and a couple of extra upgrade points).  You visit the shop for repairs and upgrades, then kit out and send one team into a race at a time, allowing other teams to recover from your last folly (if you can afford the fees and repairs, that is)!
When playing the turn-based variant, each 'turn' lasts for a highlighted section of track around the circus.  Looking at the section and the positions of your opponents, you have a choice of moves you can click (only one action is allowed per turn).  Crucially, these include speeding up or slowing down, switching lanes, taking a defensive stance or whipping, blocking or even crashing into your opponents (no-one said this was a clean fight)!  If you're playing the dynamic version the chariots never stop so you have to think fast and give orders with good timing.  What you choose is pivotal to your survival and your success.  If things go bad (and they will), your man's chariot will break up, leaving him dragging face-first in the dirt.  Do you risk everything by insisting he hangs on until the very end (after all, a finish IS a finish...) or do you tell him to run away while he still has his life?  Your escapee causes the race to be forfeit but at least your man is still alive (if he didn't get trampled...).  New men are expensive to recruit, and no racers means no more game.  You have been warned!
To keep things fresh, each circus has its own pros and cons, there are random events that help or hinder you, crowds might lob objects at you, or the debris of other casualties might just finish you off.   While it might seem that luck plays a hand, strategic moves will win the race.
The game is entirely mouse-driven and is accompanied by a decent PDF manual.  The races are simple and intuitive (all choices are displayed on screen in front of your horses and you simply click the move to be made that turn).  However, the user interface for the shop and upgrades is a little confusing (the game could really use some tooltip text help for its buttons as well as mouse-over feedback to show what can and cannot be clicked) but once you understand how to use it and how to buy the most suitable upgrades, everything is fine.
]The game brings that level of addictiveness associated with any game where you upgrade and then progress a bit further each time to earn more upgrades.  Your campaign is lengthy and is retained between sessions so you can pick up where you left off last time.   This is no 10-minute throwaway game.
The idea is genius and it's a unique and original game.  Production quality is best described as 'functional' with no added polish (there is no fun commentary as was advertised in the video, and it lacks any graphic touches like cut-scenes of a win (or a tragedy).  This by no means affects the enjoyment of the game and will mean it can run on any level of kit, but it's sat firmly in the £15 territory where a little bit more polish is usually expected.  This is a minor gripe only as the game is otherwise excellent.  If you have doubts, there is a free demo you can download.  The game can also be bought on Android/iOS (full game with no in-app purchases).

This is a fun, but simple strategic chariot racing game.  The graphics and sound are purely functional, but they do serve their purpose.  I always play in turn-based mode, and the fun comes from analyzing your situation during each of your turns and trying to choose the optimal action to improve your situation.  These actions include things like: Do I flog my horses for a brief burst of speed now at the cost of horse endurance?  Do I flog my oponent and risk losing my whip, or crash my chariot into him and risk becoming stunned?  What's the closest lane that I can safely take a turn and set myself up nicely afterwards?  And so on.
If you enjoy lite strategy, you will probably find some enjoyment here.  But it is lite and probably best enjoyed in small doses.  Doing pre-race team management and completing a single race probably takes about five to ten minutes.  You will be frustrated when things randomly go wrong, but also elated when you round that last corner a bit too fast, overturn your chariot and grin as your driver is able to endure long enough to be dragged over the finish line, winning you the race.
However, the price seems a bit steep.  At $10 I could wholeheartedly recommend buying it, but at $20, you might want to wait for a sale if you're on the fence about it.  Matrixgames has a demo on their website, and you might want to watch a "Let's Play" video to see the game in action.

This is the most addictive, fun racing/strategy game in existence. If you are even remotely interested in this game BUY IT! You'll have hours and hours of enjoyment. Don't be put off by the screen shots, when you zoom in on the action the animation is more than adequate, the mechanics are near perfect, the thrill of victory is extremely satisfying. The price is on the high side but the pure enjoyment is worth every cent.

The game really does have the best turn-based racing mechanics in a computer game (and no, it's not the only one). And, what's just as important, there's a clean interface that helps avoid struggling with them. You learn the basics and you're off, and then you have quite a gentle learning curve until becoming a master charioteer.
Once you're a bit more accustomed to the game, there's a pleasant semi-trance state that you can fall into during the races. It's good and bad at the same time. While there still are decisions to make, you've probably encountered similar situations before and know a good way out of them. After you've reached this point it is nice to zoom out and see the chariots go, and admire how believable their movements seem.
Unfortunately there's not much else to do outside of that. The campaign is very welcome if a bit barebones, but in the end it becomes a comfort game that you can Alt+Tab to and run a race or two to before getting back to work.
I do hope the developers use the great design in place for a more ambitious game, be it historical, fantasy or any other kind of racing. It simply needs more content and variety to mix things up a bit.
What is there is very well balanced and thought-out, though, and is definitely preferable to a chaotic mixture of bits and pieces that don't really gel together or a feature creep that tends to plague other games. Nevertheless, in the end you are left wanting more.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a simulation/RTS game.  You take control of a ship, part of the Federation to deliver important info on a Rebel Army coming to attack.  You must travel through different sectors to get to your base and deliver the info.  However, the ride there wont be easy as you will encounter many dangers.  The game is kinda bit on the survival side as he can run out of fuel and may have to wait in space for soemone to give you some.  Random events can happen like invaders attacking your ship, resucing people who agree to join your side, people offering weapons and parts for your ship.  Your ship can be upgraded use scrap, which is this games version of money.  You can even assign people to different systems of your ship to give them a boost like putting someone in your weapons bay so your weapons charge faster, or putting some in your engine room so you have a better chance at dodging shots.  The game is smooth at first, but begins to get harder and harder as you go, but you get better rewards for it.  There are multiple races as well and each have their own advantages.
FTL is a fun game and quite addicting as no one gameplay will feel the same.  Every time I played the game, I had found a new weapon or had a different outcome in some way.  This game will want you to keep coming back and has amazing replayability.  Too bad it isnt free though.

First, I use an XboxOne Controller and recommend you use it to fully enjoy this game from the start!
Now, for the review...
I will simply say this. This was a crowd funded game and FOR GOOD REASON, because the old school gamers wanted an old school game that was EPIC! This is not a typical predefined game that just fits into one type of genre. So do not go in expecting it to play like something you have played before or something similar. This game is a direct sequel to the original NES game and was unique and original for it’s time. River City Ransom for the NES created waves and was the first game of it’s kind combining all of the elements that it did. “R.C.R. Underground” has done everything right in staying true to all the traditions and features of the original while expanding and creating a whole new dynamic fighting system based on the original game, and it’s GORGEOUS!
THIS GAME pays perfect homage to the original and much more (another reason it had such massive success in reaching it’s crowd funded goals from regular people). It's an old school game made new with many expanded elements.
Check out this Video, it's a great let's play:
**NOTE:** There are some bugs at the moment, however, the developers have already addressed the community of the bugs and glitches, “and have announced patches.” These series of patches are expected to come through out this week and the next. In addition to announcing those patches, they also dropped a bombshell of awesomeness with the ability to mod the game in the coming future.... THAT'S HUGE that they would give the community the power to do this and so early on at that.
IF YOU ARE NOT FAMILIAR WITH RIVER CITY RANSOM, BE PREPARED...
This game is not like any other games. It has secrets. It has very hard to figure out story-pathing. It is as it should be. This game is NOT intended to reach the broadest target market, as such, some younger generational players don't like it because it’s too hard and uses A LOT of quirky old school logic (secret passages like doors and paths and such that blend perfectly in the back ground of the game… *priceless*). As the game progresses, the enemies difficulty increases exponentially and WILL overwhelm you and WILL punish your every mistake from skill to tactical errors just like old school games were best at! “However,” a great many do love this, and pride themselves on being good at it, like myself. This game is extremely challenging in both the enemies difficulty from AI, logic, toughness, tactics to the dynamic fighting system and how you have to chain combo’s together while at the same time play defensively and carefully, “ESPECIALLY” as you progress the game more-and-more.
This game is not what you would typically expect just from looking at it if you have never heard of River City Ransom before- especially if you didn’t grow up playing the most challenging Nintendo Entertainment System games on the market. “Back in my day we didn’t have the internet to tell us how to do things, WE HAD TO FIGURE IT OUT!!!” And boy do they ever pay tribute to that in this game (though the internet will ruin that fun pretty quick *sad face*). They have expanded on so much and truly created an "artistic video game master piece" with how much they honor the original and stay true to just how original, the original was at being original!  : D
There are guides, and the community for this game is awesome. MANY old school players meeting new school ones, and all of them being able to show down in the arena and just having a blast either duking-it-out against each other or playing together in the co’op. ***THOUGH WE COULD SURE USE A KICK FEATURE! THAT COMES WITH SOME WARNINGS FIRST, LIKE A 3 STRIKE RULE FROM THE HOST***
I also want to point out I normally don’t leave positive reviews on games, if it’s a good game but not perfect, I just don’t leave a review, but if it’s a bad game then I let state as such in as much detail as possible in my negative review so hopefully the developers will take note of it.
There are only 3 developers I have ever truly blindly had faith in to do 100% right by their gaming communities, and I’m proud to say “Conatus Creative” is one of them. The other two are “Payload Studios” and “17-Bit” and this is because of how they listen to their communities but don’t fold to the pressures and deviate from the grand vision and design of what made their games great as they develop.
In conclusion, this game “as a sequel” to the original River City Ransom is a masterpiece in it’s own right. Make no-mistake, this game is in-fact, “SEQUEL!” Many new elements and game aspects to enjoy and I personally can’t wait to see what mods introduce to this game as the community grows.
Feel free to leave comments asking questions about the game if you are on the fence on whether or not you should buy it and need to be directed to any sources that may help you decide if this game is for you or not. I will try to respond within 12 hours of the comment.

Great game if it could get a few things out of the way. Vague instructions popping up when you're busy concentrating in the middle of combat. The least the devs could've done is to halt the game, do a pop up and make the interactive button unuseable for a bit so that we don't accidentally just click by it.
As for the combos you buy, I'm really having a hard time finding a way to execute the combos. There's no description for the skills nor is there a preview. There's also no proper description to execute some of the skills you buy. So you end up buying it but not knowing how to use them.
Also, the grind spoils the pacing of the game. I don't expect an unreasonable rate of advancement but the grind is real with this game.
And finally, what the hell is up with the vagueness of the game? There's no specific objectives or clear descriptions of what to do next. Sometimes to the point where you accidentally advance into the next part of the game without being able to completely explore the previous area because you didn't know that enterance led to a new area in the story.
I don't know if I wasted my money or not. But  as of this point, I don't recommend buying the game.

Overall, this is a really fun game to play, even with the current bugs/issues.  What it does really well:
-Really fun combat mechanics and tight controls
-Great overall visuals
-Sound track is fantastic

-I personally don't find the money/level grind that bad for most characters once you get the hang of combat and using safe houses
-I think its a great follow up to the original RCR that I love!
-Looks of charm in this one :)
Issues I have:
-I think the Dojo's should show you what level you need to purchase a special skill
-The level up indicator seems to be bugged so I am never quite sure how much longer until I will level up
-As others have pointed out, mis-labeled moves or moves that dont work.  They really need to focus on this as a big priority to make things clearer to players.
Issues aside, there is a really fun beat em up with level up mechanics, diverse characters and awesome local multiplayer (cannot speak to the online experience).  I wholeheartedly recommend knowing that the devs will continue to work on ironing out the issues moving forward.

tl;dr Oh my GOD, they listened to the fans!♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at how stupid the UI was in the first 2 with the lack of interparty trade and/or ability to control your team? Its fixed now!
I remember writing somewhere in the Shadowrun:HK forums before it came out how annoying and stripped the UI was of the older games. That you couldn't trade items within missions, and that you had no way to position your party tactically before battle, not so bad if you're a street sam - really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ if your main guy is a squishy mage or decker.
I believe my exact words were something like ...do you see real-world SWAT or military have the tech specialist wander up and open the door with all the burly armored dudes with assault rifles randomly grouped around behind picking their noses?
The UI is still stripped. But now its got the ability to ambush, giving you a few rounds to place your team before the shooting starts. You can trade items inter-party too while on missions, and give found items to anyone with a free inventory space. Its way better. People had been complaining about how stupid the inability to trade and the inability to control your party out of combat was, so Harebrained fixed it. Good on them! Now to get them to put some kind of minimap, especially since the levels have gotten huge.
They cleaned up the models too, so dwarves and orks dont look so ridiculous. Overall, the models are much cleaner. The running animation kind of reminds me of The Venture Bros though...
Some sequels suck. This one does not. HS has learned from the first 2. Theres more of everything, including plenty of awesome char portraits for each race/gender, unlike the first one where female trolls had what...5? You can see that HS has found their stride, listened to their fans, and cleaned up some of the glaring flaws of the engine and game.
If you liked the first 2, even if you thought they were flawed - get this game. If youre a fan of Shadowrun, get this game. Its way better than the others. Dragonfall:DC was good, this is better. If you havent played the first ones, pick up Dragonfall:DC first, otherwise I can pretty much assure you you'll be disappointed going backwards.

Another great example of what a sequel should be, BIT.TRIP Runner2: Future legend of Rhythm Alien does a great job of maintaining the expectation of the first game while improving and adding more to the series to make an even better game than the first. Not only is there more content, but the game overall has had a massive overhaul. The music is still just as great and is even more prominent in each level and it instantly becomes a joy to start running regardless of level and the sound design in general is greatly improved and it’s even narrated by Charles Martinet! The style and graphics have taken a huge turn for the better; the world is filled with even weirder worlds, colors, style than the previous game and, overall the game now resembles something more like a modern cartoon. The gameplay is still simple and more or less the same from the first, however levels have been improved, aside from the checkpoints now at about the mid-point of each level (which you can skip for bonus points) most levels have extra or various routes to take, some more difficult with greater rewards vs. easier routes or ones that will give you access to other levels. You can now also play different characters and unlock a great variety of costumes for each one. The game also has added more abilities you unlock to give greater variations to the scores you can earn in each level and it also has effortlessly combined leaderboards and scores from Steam friends right into the game and each level has different variations depending on the difficulty set; all this combined makes it a joy to play through each level and go back through ones you’ve beat to try to achieve a greater score or top friends who have also played.
BIT.TRIP Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien is a great sequel and if you’ve already played the first game the sequel should be a no brainer purchase. For those of you interested in the first game, I recommend picking up Runner2 as it offers a lot more and it is only $15.00 USD, only $5 more than the first game. BIT.TRIP Runner2 is a great game, it’s challenging, easy to play, difficult to perfect and master and it has loads of unlockable stuff and, can easily entertain you with its fast action and great music. Definitely pick this up if you enjoy arcade styled games, fast paced games, games that capitalize on music or family friendly games, it truly is a game everyone can enjoy and for the asking price you really can’t get much better than this.
-Double Thumbs Up from Royial

Like Star Trek simulator in a way.
FTL: Faster Than Light is a simulation/RTS game.  You take control of a ship, part of the Federation to deliver important info on a Rebel Army coming to attack.  You must travel through different sectors to get to your base and deliver the info.  However, the ride there wont be easy as you will encounter many dangers.  The game is kinda bit on the survival side as he can run out of fuel and may have to wait in space for soemone to give you some.  Random events can happen like invaders attacking your ship, resucing people who agree to join your side, people offering weapons and parts for your ship.  Your ship can be upgraded use scrap, which is this games version of money.  You can even assign people to different systems of your ship to give them a boost like putting someone in your weapons bay so your weapons charge faster, or putting some in your engine room so you have a better chance at dodging shots.  The game is smooth at first, but begins to get harder and harder as you go, but you get better rewards for it.  There are multiple races as well and each have their own advantages.
FTL is a fun game and quite addicting as no one gameplay will feel the same.  Every time I played the game, I had found a new weapon or had a different outcome in some way.  This game will want you to keep coming back and has amazing replayability.  Too bad it isnt free though.

When I first saw the trailers for Runner2, I thought to myself, 'Wow, that looks nothing like the original...I don't know if I like that."
Obviously, I am an old man afraid of change, because Runner2 is excellent [if not better than] the original.
It IS more of the same gameplay from the first, but that's not a bad thing; they had all that right the first time 'round. The platforming is still as smooth as a freshly opened jar of peanut butter.
The new elements of Runner2 add a bit of freshness to the affair, like having to break open 'Key Vaults' to make keys appear in other levels, which allow you to open up alternate pathways and find hidden goodies that you may have missed previously. Unlock other runners! Unlock SKINS for said runners! It's all good new stuff.
The soundtrack is amazing, the visual style is gorgeous, it has the same teeth-gritting difficulty from before [but with optional checkpoints, for those who aren't masochistic], and - despite all of the graphical updates - feels so familiar to RUNNER that I found myself feeling at home with it right away.
And boy, is it good to be back.
Except for a few select levels on hard and a final boss made artificially hard by making you run to the left instead of the right, this game is great. Definitely pick it up next time you can.

I couldn't make it through the first Runner game; I ended up permanently rage-quitting somewhere around World 3 and never looked back. With that in mind, I approached Runner 2 with a lot of trepidation, expecting to encounter a lot of the same issues. Runner 2, however, is so much fairer, less punishing and more enjoyable than its predecessor, mainly due to the addition of mid-mission checkpoints (which you can skip for a bigger score). It's amazing just how much of a difference it makes when you know you've only got to hold out 'til halfway rather than start the whole thing from scratch. And whilst it is more forgiving than the earlier game, perfectionists will find that it still provides ample challenge. The key difference is that Runner 2 lets YOU dictate just how difficult you want to make the experience, rather than the other way round. I ended up perfect+'ing every level and adored it the whole time.. and once you get that music melody stuck in your head, it doesn't leave for days.
