I put off reviewing the game for some time fearing the negative backlash I'd almost surely recieve. Nowadays it's become a bit more accepted to dislike Undertale, or simply have it be "not your thing", but giving criticism to LISA, its darker, more "mature" counterpart it's often compared to, seems to be entirely blasphemous.
That said, I tried my very best to like this game. I thought I would abslolutely love its handling of serious topics, gameplay, and story. The reviews on the front page affirmed my assumption, with one in particular I recall describing the game as...
"If Earthbound and Mad Max had a baby, and then David Cronenberg became that baby's abusive alcoholic stepfather."
Earthbound and Mad Max, I suppose I can see. Like Earthbound, the game has some rather fun and engaging gameplay, more innocent and simplistic visuals despite a dark plot, and odd humor interlaced between the game's seemingly more serious segments. It's Mad Max in the sense of its setting and world, and that's about it.
But there is nothing "Cronenberg" about this game aside from its body horror. It's missing the artistry, actual decent writing, and above all, subtlety, that makes Cronenberg so great.
Here lies the biggest problem in this game, which so many others regard as being its greatest strength  -- LISA's writing. Despite masquerading as something meaningful, the experience is artificial and lacks the competence to actually pose any real or unsettling questions. It hides behind its simplicity of plot behind a deep-curtain comprised of extremely out-of-place humor, and lazy absurdity.
Prior to writing this review I read several interviews with the game's creator, Dingaling, and was especially hooked by and interested on a particular write-up he did regarding his process of telling stories. Seeing as I hated how he told stories, I felt it would give me insight and explaination as to how his methods succeeded so well with so many others, and not with me. Having read it, I got just what I was looking for. If you're interested in taking a look yourself, the link is below:
It pretty much told me what I already knew -- Dingaling is not a subtle storyteller. He tells things only as they appear to be, rather than what they imply. For many people this is enough, but for me it doesn't work. There is no right or wrong way to tell a story, but in the context of LISA, with its serious subject matters (abuse,♥♥♥♥♥♥ genocide, death, etc.) these kinds of subjects are just not suited to such a simple approach. This is why the game fails, and why its unfitting absurdist humor, on top of its lack of subtlety, is the nail in the coffin.
Earthbound, I believe, succeeds where LISA fails. Its dark tones were a very fascinating juxtaposition to its upbeat and innocent exterior. Its off-the-wall oddball humor added to its themes, rather than muddled them. LISA is all over the place, and on a narrative level doesn't work on any front it sets out to explore.
What can I say. Great story. Great combat. Funny content.

Earthbound is one of my favourite games of all time.  It's a classic RPG that makes fun of the genre's tropes.  It's filled with humor and heart.  Undertale is a fantastic example of how Earthbound's setting and feel stand the test of time.  But in 2014, alot of us overlooked another title that took a whole new mature look on the lighthearted SNES classic.  LISA...  If you are looking for a game that will make you fell absolutely terrible (in a good way, believe it or not :P), pick up LISA.  It takes place in a world without women, about a drug-addict named Brad, whose life is terrible.  But when he finds a baby, the last woman on the planet.  He's given a second chance...  For what?  That's all I have to say, I don't want to spoil the experience.  It's an RPG Maker game, but it's different.  It plays like a 2D platformer.  It has choice, by that I don't mean multiple endings (well it does...), but I mean choice in gameplay.  Throughout LISA, you will be forced to make major changes.  Whether its
, it does an amazing job at making you feel hopeless and that you really are in a world on the verge of collapse.  For all of you grown up Earthbound fans or people that just finished Undertale, try LISA; you won't regret it.

This game looks like it could be something, but it really needs some more work.
The game recommends what is clearly an Xbox controller, yet the tutorials and move lists instead all use a single color system with letters corresponding to what the moves are instead of the standard buttons on an xbox controller. This means going to your move list, then back out to the options and controller setup to figure out which buttons G, P, K, and S mean.
Speaking of the tutorials, good luck reading them! In a game where you are hitting buttons rapidly to perform attacks, having it so any button press clears the message screen during tutorials is terrible game design. Simply forcing tutorial messages to be cleared with the start button, or any button not used commonly in combat would make it so people could actually read the messages.
I actually restarted, twice, once so I could try and remember when a message would pop up, but I still missed out. The second restart was because my game actually froze when fighting the first tutorial boss. After playing for about an hour I decided that this game clearly needs more time and effort. That being said this is my first ever Steam refund request... congratulations!? For anyone else I would strongly recommend stepping back, letting some patches come out (hopefully a UI/Menu overhaul can take place). I might look out for this game down the road during a heavy sale or if it gets some major work done, otherwise I am fine with a refund and watching an LP at this point.

I've put a few tens of hours in on this before I moved it to Steam, on both the pc version and the iPad.  This is one of my "Game of the Year" picks.
Qvadriga is a single-player chariot racing set in the Roman Mediterranean. You choose one of seven factions to race for, and your "stable" is one of several your faction may operate in each city.  There are many cities to race in across the various provinces.  Each city offers it's own special bonus, like half-price drivers, or cheap chariot repair.
Each city has it's own racing stadium, varying from 8 lanes wide to 4 lanes wide, and generally either an oval or a U shape. Your tactics have to change to reflect the number of teams racing and the width of the track - a six-team race on four lanes is very different from 8 teams on 6 lanes, and so forth.
You can have up to four teams in your stable; you start with three.  Drivers, chariots and horses each have two skills to be gained, at up to two points for each skill.  For drivers, it's constitution and driving skill; for horses, speed and endurance; and for chariots, acceleration and durability.  So there are 9 combinations for each skill, and three sets of skills, for 729 different driver/horse/chariot combinations.
Each race has a special condition, given before the start, which mixes things up.  You might have corrupt Praetors drinking up some of the prize money, or fog making everyone more cautious, or two teams fighting at the start line, or even a track littered with previous race debris for the crowd's amusement.  Add to that the various chariot/driver/horse combinations and the width of the track, and each race is different and unique.
Your faction gives you a set of skills to begin with.  For example, the military faction favors skillful drivers and horses with good endurance, along with heavy chariots.  Other factions have different mixes.  This provides the initial differences between teams in a race.  You must learn to adapt to your equipment and drivers - is your team going to win based on fighting other teams, or getting ahead early and holding the lead, or coming from behind in the final lap?  And bear in mind, as your gear and horses and drivers change, your tactics will have to adapt as well.
Once you are in a race, you have a number of actions you can take each turn.  You can slow or speed your horses, or really goose them by whipping.  You can change lanes (subject to someone being in the way, or your momentum in a turn) and you can crash into other teams or try to whip their driver.  Most actions, including cornering and even just driving, carry a risk of damage, which increases as you take damage through the race.  So you really have to consider every turn carefully; even if you are far in the lead coming into the last turn, one mistake can see you with a destroyed chariot being pulled along the track by your runaway horses.  Each race has it's tense moments and you can go from being on top to crashing out in an instant.
Once the race is over, you get money if you finished; more if you placed in the top three, and then if you win, you can collect your private bet if you placed one.  Your teams will need repair, rest and healing, which cost money; this is why you start with three, to let them come back to full strength over several races.  Your drivers will be ranked by victories, and as your fame climbs, you'll gain access to other cities and regions, and can compete across the empire.  Eventually, the goal is to become the leader of your faction empire-wide, and in Epic game mode, to become the most successful rider in the empire.
In short, this is a great racing game with a good deal of bloodshed and heartbreak, and more than a little historical accuracy.  It's well worth it if you like racing games and history at all.  There is nothing else like it out there.  Highly recommended.

If you were a fan of Circus Maximus by Avalon Hill, this is the game you want.  Played in Dynamic mode, its plays like a real time chariot race, and it is brutal.  Very little quarter is given, and in the campaign game you will very soon develop a champion driver that lives on the edge of disaster each race.  When played on Epic mode, this is old school, with no saves, no going back for your body, no fluff.  Like in real life, your champion gets all your best gear to give him that edge, and in flash of hooves and blood, it could all be gone.  If you ever wanted to manage a team of chariots for a faction and race them with the final hope of getting them to Rome and the Maximus, this is the game for you.  The graphics aren't stunning.  The sounds are adequate, but nothing more.  This is a simulation and racing strategy game.  Crash your opponents?  Lash them with your whip into submission?  Go for speed and try to out run the mayhem?  It's up to you.  Well done Turnopia, I look forward to your next release.

This is a great little game! There is a lot of strategy involved. The learning curve is pretty steep, but as you get the hang of it, you really get sucked in. Usually set backs are not game breaking. On my first play through, I lost my drivers and chariots quickly, and could not recover, but only because I didn't know what I was doing. I went back, looked over the tutorial, started a new game, was more careful this time, and I've been having a great campaign. I've had my set backs still, but always have recovered from them and surged to new levels despite them. A word to the wise: don't imagine this is a game you can easily win on your first race. You will have to work hard for each victory. But they are all the more rewarding when they come.
You will also quickly develop rivalries with other teams' charioteers (called auriga in the game). Currently, I've got a very heated rivalry going with a fellow named Alpheaus. After he took out two of my horses and almost killed an auriga at the very start of a race, I've had it out for him ever since. And he likes gunning for me, too. Makes the races very interesting when he's around.
In response to critics who say there are only two types of track: first of all, each type has many variations within. Some are longer, some are shorter, some are wider, some are thinner. No two tracks are exactly the same, and each one has unique strategies required to be successful. Second, in ancient Rome this is exactly how it was. Two types of track (Greek style and Roman style), but with variations all over the place. Each race also will have a random event at the start, sometimes good, sometimes bad, to add to the variation. There's also different combinations of auriga skills, chariot types, and horse quality.
In total, this is a great game. I think it is worth $20. But if you can pick it up on sale, that's always good, too. I give it a 9/10.

For a game that is all about grappling, they sure could have spend a little more time on the actual grappling mechanics, as of right now, it's rather rubbish.
- It's never clear what the actual reaching distance of your grappling hook is.
- 9/10 grapples result in you banging either against (bad) collision meshes (killing momemtum instantly) or the edge of a platform without the ability to climb/grapple up.
The power jump often won't fire because of how platforms are often irregular shapes resulting in the player going in falling state (even though it's just a 5 cm step.)
Graphics and art direction are okay, pretty much looks like every other Unreal Engine based indy game out there.
The checkpoint system is complete and utter rubbish, forget about backtracking for achievements, as falling down will respawn you all the way back at the last checkpoint that could be activated (you can't reactivate checkpoints on your trek back.)
Unskipable cutscenes (which are bad enough on their own) but with the added illusion of movement, which on top of that is twice as slow as normal movement in the rest of the game.
Audio and music are decent.
Bloom and mouse smoothing can be turned of (thank you dev), but there's not much else in the sense of visual quality adjustment (you'll need to edit the engine.ini for that), but I doubt you'll need to fine tune settings much as the game runs smooth on high even on my old HD7950.
A small nitpick is the scale (either from the scenery or the character controller), at times it feels like I'm literally just a head with 2 hands sticking out of my ears.
This game to me is a missed opportunity, of all the things that would have been acceptable even if they had been mediocre, the core game mechanics are not one of them.
This is a fun game, with a memorable expierence, some levels are challenging but that's what makes it fun. I give it a 7/10, overall it's a great game.

I purchased this game way back during the Steam Summer Sale of 2015. I played it for about half an hour, put it down, and didn't pick it up again until today (7/1/2017). That said, because I couldn't remember how to play the game, I started from scratch and ran through it in one sitting.
To be honest... it's an all right platformer. Far from bad, but not neccessarily great, either. Because of how many buttons you have to press at once, results are pretty inconsistent. The sprint key could have just been removed entirely and the game would have been a lot easier to control. But even then, that's really only half of the problem. You don't really get that much of a margin for error when it comes to distance jumping. There was one level in the middle of the game where I just grew plain frustrated because of how many times I had barely missed the end of the platform I was trying to get to.
Of course, the end level was laughably easy in comparison. It's also riddled with unintented ledges where you can sit on and try again halfway through a jump. Where on the previous level, I was stuck and frustrated, this one I eased right through with little to no problems. It made the ending really anti-climatic. There just wasn't anything to make the player feel changed like how there was in previous levels. By the way, there are 5 levels if you count the tutorial level.
The artwork for the levels is really pretty and there are more than a few "Kodak moments" to be had. It's honestly the highlight of this game. The design and gameplay is really inconsistent and the story was so bland and silly that it was almost pointless. Character conflicts get resolved within a 2 minute bit of dialogue. Conflicts, which you never get any warning or reason with. They just happen and get resolved. And these are not small little conflicts, either. These are life changing conflicts. It would be like if I walked up to a bank and decided in the span of 2 minutes on getting a $50,000 loan for a house.
Inconsistent is just such a perfect descriptor for this game. When it works, it's really great. There's a few really great moments in gameplay, but they never great repeated again. The story starts off mysterious and adventurous, but just ends with disappointment and a totally lame with no true closure to the build up that the story starts you with.
On sale, I can recommend this game, but at full price, I cannot. This is a 2 hour game and while it is a fun little adventure, the only big positive it has is nice environments and some occasionally fun platforming.
A very beautiful game with a great stroy and game mechanic, I enjoyed every second of it and I hope the Devs can make some sort of second/sequel to this.

A Story About My Uncle is a hidden game among the thousands of game on steam and it's incredibly fun.

The story isn't really that in depth and the reason you might want to check out this game is the gameplay itself and the game is rather fun. The best way I can describe this game is imagine Mirrors Edge without the parkour element and you got up to the high places using a grappling hook.

I've played a lot of adventure and RPGs - this one surpasses all of them!
I'm going to start out with my verdict: I had a blast with SRHK, I was so deeply immersed in it! And I'll play it again and again - it has quite a bit of replay value!
This one is to me more like a book made into a RPG (with a twist - initially you choose something like a "profession"  - which you can expand upon - that give you initial stat bonuses, but at least there are no class restrictions - yay!) with turn-based combat (somewhat like XCOM, but not as strategic IMO, but at least allows you to use cover, as a strategic element, plus you have special abilities).
It has a deep, developing story with a blend of organized crime (gang / chinese mafia), sci-fi, fantasy and some mysticism all very well blended together. All the main characters have a strong personality and personality development (some of which you have somewhat an influence on).
Dialog and dialog options are also very well done - more about that below.
The RPG element (character stat system) IMO is very well done - it doesn't just consist of strength, intelligence, stamina, ... like in most RPGs - instead, these are the main stats, and then they have somewhere between four to seven (I think) sub-stats. Very cool, adds additional strategy and customization elements.
SRHK is VERY story-rich - so, if you're not into reading a lot, then this might not be your thing. Well, you don't have to read everything, but you'll lose out on a lot of story.
Its main elements and their strengths:
* RPG
Certain "activities" (main "quests", side-quests) earn you points that you can then use to increase the stats of your character (NPCs don't level up their stats, but get new abilities, which you have to choose then, one of two each time, similar to XCOM). Stat points are not just handed out generously - you really have to decide which direction you want your character to develop, if you level up all the stats more or less evenly, then they can use any and all type of equipment, but will in the long run just be mediocre in the use of those. Additionally, some stats and a certain level of them unlock additional conversation choices. So, as a tip, it's advisable not to allocate any stat points unless absolutely necessary!
* Cybernetics
Part of the RPG element - but, you don't use stat points for those, instead money. Also, there's something like a "life force" that starts out at a certain number and almost all cybernetic implant decreases that by a certain amount - the resulting number can not fall below 1 (1 basically means, you're almost more machine than human). Cybernetics either give your character additional abilities, or, in most cases, increases their stats.
* Conversation
Most other RPGs have one-liners. Not this one (in most cases) - it seems like the characters actually have full-fledged conversations going on. Which adds to the realism aspect and immersion factor, SRHK therefore doesn't just seem like a turn-based combat game with some story slapped on, but rather the opposite. Also as mentioned before, some conversation options are unlocked based on your stats (and some on your "trait" that you initially choose).
* Story
Games trying to blend realism, sci-fi and fantasy together usually end up in a huge mess, story wise at least, because things just don't add up... logically there are just things that don't make sense. This one even adds "mysticism" to the mix - and it all works! It seems to me that the writers of the story didn't just "force" all these elements in there, but rather, elements were added to support the overall story.
* NPCs
There are quite a wide variety, even some "supernatural" ones - I'm not going into detail here to avoid spoilers, but trust me, it makes sense and is actually really well done, ties well into the story! At least I had a blast, laughing quite a lot because of the turn of events and the explanation of those... so well done!
Last but not least (and literally, that is the weakest, yet still not terrible, part of SRHK):
* Combat
Sometimes you can avoid getting into a fight by choosing certain dialog option(s) and overall approach to a situation, but often combat is unavoidable. It's turn-based and you have weapons to use - melee or ranged - and some abilities. You can (and should) make use of cover, which is divided into three categories: weak (pretty much non-existence), low (partial cover) or high (strong cover). You can use certain abilities to improve damage, but you can't target certain parts of the enemy's body, nor can you blow up cover or items (such as furniture) - again, it's not as sophisticated as XCOM and of course a long shot (no pun intended hehe) from Jagged Alliance. Yet, all in all, it's satisfactory and for those who just really don't care for combat, they still have to though but at least on lowest difficult setting, it's a breeze and quickly over with.
Also, a quick note, combat can also take place in "virtual reality", which, although slightly different, is in general the same as non-vr combat. And can in most if not all cases all together be avoided.

Playing Shadowrun: Hong Kong left me feeling somewhat conflicted. Firstly, the writing was great, but that's never been a problem for Harebrained Schemes, generally the dialogue is witty and funny and excellent, even if the "plotlines" for missions do tend to resemble each other a bit and things go wrong so often it's more of a surprise when things go to plan.
The basic gameplay also wasn't any worse than the original SRR or SR: Dragonfall, with a few noted improvements(decking has been improved somewhat), but it felt like it was just too easy. Playing on Normal, I think I had a total of one challenging battle(mostly because I was lazy) and zero challenging choices or puzzles. It simply felt too hard NOT to do the right thing, I'd have had to be blind and an idiot to screw something up, I never really felt like I had to think, which is a damn shame.
The game also really felt very short. The actual core plotline, which has a very creative premise, consumes about four missions, counting generously... while there's about twice as many side missions. Which is a damn shame, because I wanted to dig more into the actual premise, and I wanted to drag it out a bit so they could actually do something with the atmospheric writing they were getting into, maybe do a bit of horror. Instead the climax they've been setting up consists of about three fights with a short corridor in between each, none of which are as big or challenging as the ones at the end of Dragonfall(...or even really the original SRR). The shortness and lack of fights is also a bit of a shame because the nice level-up system for the companions gets little play as a result, Gobbet had some handy powers for manipulating enemy spirit summons... but I think I had a total of two enemies in the entire game who ever summoned a spirit.
Which, again, is a shame, because I really liked most members of my team(except for Wu and Is0bel, which... is kind of a shame, because he was supposed to be core to the plot, instead he just comes across as kind of dull, and you'll basically always be stuck with Is0bel if you're not a decker yourself, but mostly what she does is complain about how bad her past was) while Racter, Gaichu and Gobbet are all fun to deal with and talk to.
In general, the core plot suffered from a few major issues. Firstly, it was never really given any time to work itself out, it was over too quickly for any impact. Secondly, it was hard to care about Raymond when he was a character you were only told about, basically never met, the game could have done with more flashbacks, or maybe even an intro gameplay segment set BEFORE the current era. Thirdly, as a result of it being hard to care about Raymond, it became hard to care about Wu, because his entire thing is basically just Raymond Raymond Raymond Raymond My Dad Raymond My Dad.
I genuinely dug the side missions, but I can't help but feel that SR:HK would have been better if they scrapped them and put all those missions into the core plot instead.
Still, the writing was fun enough that I don't feel like I wasted my time playing it.
Except for one thing.
WHERE'S MY GODDAMN GOBBET ROMANCE, YOU NERDS.
OR AT LEAST KU FENG.
BOO.

Runner2 is a major improvement from the first Runner game and addresses a lot of the problems that the last game had. The mechanics are expanded upon to further the depth of your interaction with the game. Dancing is possibly one of the best move mechanics added, being a purely optional mechanic that tests how well the player can plan out their actions for extra points. Levels are much better composed in terms of layout and rhythm, feeling much more thought out and rhythmically pleasing. The levels are much more consistent in length and difficulty, and the optional checkpoint system takes a lot of the more painful frustration out of playing while keeping the level still challenging. There are also multiple paths, marked with which path is harder or leads to an alternative exit. The sound effects that generate the random notes are much better sounding and match the key of the background music. While the game does build with difficulty, there are now three ACTUAL difficulty levels to Runner2, and a lot of the precise jumps are pushed to the collecting gold and hard mode instead of being forced to make those precise jumps in every mode. I personally like the ascetics of the world design and the more general electronica music. Also, the boss battles, which were the weakest part of the first Runner game, are very well done in Runner 2.
There are some problems Runner2 still has. The bonus game at the end of a perfect run is a bit contrived. It's very different from the rest of the game, and, if you mess up on it, will require you to play the entire level again if you are aiming for a Perfect+. At the end of most levels is a point of no return, where there is only gold and no hazards; if you miss any of the golds, you cannot hit yourself to restart at the checkpoint and are forced to reset to the beginning of the level. The secret retro levels are more well done but still only have the one level background, making them a bit repetitive to the eye. One of the level mechanics, the loop-de-loop, controls very differently if your are using a controller versus a keyboard; with a controller, you have to rotate a stick to point at Commander Video, but with a keyboard, all you have to do is mash the space bar, which is much less fun and possibly easier to achieve.
None of these problems should deter you from purchasing this game. I have had a very fun time with this and I hope you do too.

Pros
- Nostalgic music, sounds like arranged tunes from the first game that most people recognise, RIVER CITY RANSOM (NES)

+ While the graphics are nothing special, they seem to have aged well
+ Top-shelf voice acting for the entire cast
+ Getting in trouble with the police is much more interactive than many other products of this genre, allowing you to pay fines, bribe officers, or attempt resistance on-site
+ Fist-fighting mechanics are cinematic, intuitive and entertaining
+ There is a speed-limiter key for toggling "safe driving mode;" a massive quality-of-life feature that every free-roam game should have
+ Game boasts very competent storytelling, with an even pace and solid character development
+ Has a great cliffhanger ending; seeing the story through to the end felt worth it
+ Every aspect of the aesthetics, from the clothes, to the vehicles and music, is period-appropriate and has a pervading feeling of authenticity
+ Vehicle handling feels realistic and smooth
+ Stock, reliabe cover system and shooting mechanics; nothing you haven't seen before, but the devs seemed to have settled with the 'less is more' approach, and it complemented the gameplay nicely
+ Engine optimization is excellent
+ While the explorable area is more of a medium size compared to competitors, there is still much to explore throughout the game world, and it feels appropriately sized for a small city
+ Active modding community, and the game itself is easy to alter
+ Some minimalist stealth mechanics that are well-implemented, though it isn't often revisited
- Many crashes; I've heard that this game has problems with AMD cards, though, so NVIDIA users may not have these issues
- Poor weapon selection (only about 7-8 usable firearms)
- No side missions, and little in the way of collectibles or extra content (though I cannot speak to the DLC); little replayability
- NPCs feel flat and generic, doing little to liven up the atmosphere of the city
- Lack of post-campaign free-roam (though a simple mod can fix this if you don't mind the small hassle)

This review is really simple - just refer to my review of Puzzle Agent 1. PA2 is essentially the same exact game (same engine, same characters, same setting, same types of puzzles). The main thing this one brings to the table is a continuation of the absurd story that began in part 1. So if you enjoyed the first game and/or just want to see how the story ends, then by all means, go ahead and pick up PA2. However, be warned - the puzzles aren't terribly brillaint or clever, and for the most part (as in PA1), the solutions are ridiculously easy. On only a few occasions will you be truly stumped for more than a few minutes, and that will likely be due to the instructions not being clear enough. Although, oddly, there are a couple of harder optional puzzles that require a more-than-casual familiarity with mathematics (which I felt was a bit strange). But aside from that, anyone should be able to solve the main puzzles required to complete the game. All in all, it's a fun, short game.

A rouge-like/rpg hwhere you must keep moving to avoid the darkness (AKA the dark void of death).
You first begin the game with the hero (you) selecting a class and a variety of perks to aid you on your quest. You can enter a randomly generated world or scenarios that change in real time. Depending on what mode you choose, the dark lord will appear at a certain time during your playthrough. You must defeat him to beat the game but this is no easy feat without proper equipment or items. Of course, there are dungeons and towns but you have to plan how to get in and out safely throughly without being eaten alive by the void. If you die on a playthrough, you can store items you had in the dimensional vault and use them on the next playthrough. You also accumulate hero points after each playthrough in which you can spend these points on extra vault space or hidden perks or classes for your next run. The amont of points you get depends on how well you did on your last playthrough.
A nice, time-killing game overall with buckets full of replayability but try not to swim in lava. Can you reach the end of the world?

from 2008. That's the year
came out. Think about that for a second.
gameplay was out of date by over a decade even back then.

If you enjoy sport manager simulators in the vein of Football Manager and its ilk, and have a fascination for Roman sport and spectacle, then buy QVADRIGA now! Be warned however, it's a time sink, this game will grab your interest and won't let go. You manage a stable of up to 4 aurigas (charioteers) and enter them in chariot races around the Roman empire. The campaign mode is great, and ends only once you accomplish 3 wins at the Circus Maximus, which is easier said than done. You are then scored based on how well you've done up to this point. If you want a greater challenge, then tackle the Epic Campaign.
You start the game by picking which faction (color) you want to represent. Each has a set of three attributes it values over others, and will determine the way you play the game. Your aurigas (charioteers) have two attributes, Skill and Constitution, your chariots' two attributes are Quality and Size, while the horses are rated by Speed and Endurance. You must pick a faction that fits your play style. If you want to be aggressive, then pick a faction that focuses on Size, while if you prefer to stick to the innermost lane and outpace the other charioteers, then pick a faction that focuses on Skill. Your first several games will definitely be a learning process, and you might end up being defeated by the arena.
There's much more to be discovered, but go out and give QVADRIGA a try now!

The genre of "turn based chariot racing game" should however have been my first hint of how this was going to go.
The truth is that neither the management side of the game, nor the actual racing is that great.
On the management side of the game there is no training. You effectively just need to pay for repairs as appropriate and select the squad that has the highest health. There is nothing on this side of the game that is even noteworth. Every skill is reduced to a three point scale, where you either have zero, one or two of each stat. With the racer, chariot and horses each having some skills.
Because there is no variance in the types of races there is no question between whether you put in the horses with higher endurance or not. You race your healthiest and highest scoring squad every single time, no question.
Also, the time played on this game is screwed up because there's a start menu that counts as the game. So that was open after I stopped playing and added way a good amount of time to my playtime.
So the game doesn't offer much on this side of the game, what does it offer in terms of racing?
Unfortunately there isn't much here either.
Each turn you choose between accelerating, whipping ("advance acceleration"), lane changes, stability for turning corners or some form of attack on your opposition.
That doesn't sound like an issue until you start to see how much of a grind that actually is. There is always a clear best decision, I think the only time there's debate of which decision is best is when choosing which attack. Unfortunately the attacks are too strong. One bad attack against you and you've almost certainly lost the race and might as well give up.
I don't know what you should pay for this game. But I'd certainly be waiting for at least 70% off.

How deep depression can bring us and what seems like an impossible climb back out. Love, loss, regret, and the random irrationalities that occur. How striving to "be better than what we once were" is really the only thing we can do to overcome our past.

FTL: Faster Than Light is one of those games that are so difficult to explain, so unique, inventive and intelligent that it is.
FTL is a space management simulator focused on resource management, where each game is unique and does not last More than an hour - probably ending up with his ship in pieces. Yes, FTL is also a difficult game even when played at the lowest difficulty level. The result is always unpredictable matches, where you are required to act as the action unfolds and, almost always, to improvise strategies and experiment.
The spacecraft is divided into different compartments: motor, weapons, shields, oxygen, direction, monitoring systems, etc. Taking care of a component enhances its operation, but like everything else in FTL, resources are scarce and you need to manage them According to each situation.
Throughout the game you can upgrade your ship and depending on the ship you choose at the beginning of each match, your style of play varies.
Facing opponents means fighting ships strongor or equivalent to yours, with the same types of compartments and capabilities (including those you do not have, by choice or lack of resources), although different in structure, crew, etc. Destroying an opposing ship means making money from your wreckage. Still, sometimes it seems to be more advantageous to negotiate with the enemy rather than destroy it completely.
Navigating through each point of the different sectors of the galaxy where the game takes place is like taking a card from a stack to determine the random event that will happen. Through texts, you get a description of an event, usually involving space pirates, allied bases in danger, caves inhabited by giant spiders, crews in trouble and so on. You choose what to do from the description of each event, with options that vary according to your own equipment and crew. Of course, it is common for some events to recur throughout the game, causing you to anticipate the outcome of some events, but the chain of events is always unique for each match and, over and over, you come across things you never had Seen before.
Although the luck factor is high, your FTL success depends on good planning and quick decisions. This requires not only attention to manage each element of your ship, but a good understanding of the system as a whole: following a plan, knowing how to act in each situation, knowing the different resources available and how to combine them efficiently, evaluate properly each opportunity, manage your ship according to the progression of each game, etc.

I really enjoyed this one. Interface problems aside (controls are kind of cumbersome, controller support is... not great), this is an experience worth having.
The designer was really creative with the scenarios and situations the game puts you in - there are lots of interesting choices and dark moments. The "setpieces", if I can call them as such, were really effective. One great positive is that the game don't bind itself to rpg "rules". There are unfair moments, there are moments where the difficulty curve kinda doesn't make sense (both to the easy and to the difficult side), but all of it contributes to the opressing atmosphere.
The amount of curveballs, traps, wrong decisions you can make is staggering, and the game doesn't become impossible or unbeatable because of it, which is a great achievement.
If you really want a dark story and a heavy experience (I can't even play long sessions, the atmosphere really becomes exhausting at points), I absolutely recommend LISA.

I would defianetly not recommend buying this game. The movement is very hard to get used to, it has no sense of flow. For instance the roll works like a normal roll during the roll itself, but instead of transitioning into a standing position in front of where the roll stops, you just stop immediately and in a flash of the eye you are sudenly standing up. It is hard to explain, but it defianetly does not feel rigth at all.
Another problem is that it does not give you a lot of features. I do understand that the game is in a pre-launch state, but I can't see what they can add. With what they have there is nowhere to expand, except for bug fixes, adding new cosmetics, and more weapons (which will most likely just be skins of already existant ones). This game has little replayablility because it lacks diversity of strategies. I honestly don't see why they allow each character to use the swords not meant for their play style, it never works out.
Another problem with the weapons is that you only have one sword for each type of play style, making it so there is basically nothing to unlock. I mean some of the skins seem to be worth unlocking beacause they are joke weapons and it is funny to see them in combat, but they are not a driving force to keep playing the game. There is honestly no reason not to have unlockable weapons with different stats. Each play style has so much room to expand, the current set of swords only are the tip of the iceberg of what is possible.
I also have a problem with the maps, they are all the exact same. Which is really disappointing, because I could imagine a lot of things that you could achieve with different levels. I think the main reason the maps aren't more than just a flat plain is because the jumping in the game is very flat and hard to control. By flat I mean that it doesn't do a good job at getting you anywhere, and you feel extremely heavy when you preform it. WARNING: IF YOU ARE A SELF-CONSCIOUS WHITE TEENAGE GIRL DO NOT JUMP! My biggest gripe with the levels is that I thought there would be a lot of diversity amongst them when I saw on the store page that there was a level editor. There is absolutely no point in a level editor when all of the levels are the same thing with different backgrounds. Most games don't have level editors when they probably should, but I never even imagined that the opposite would ever happen. Why would you put time and effort into making a level editor for this game!
Overall this game needs HUGE improvements. The biggest problem is defianetly the lack of different swords. This not only limits the action in-game, but also the replayability of entirety of the game. The next most important thing that needs to be fixed is the movement needs to be fixed, it always feels like the gravity is twenty times stronger then normal. Once the the movement is fixed I assume that the community would start making more creative maps for this game, and possibly even the developers. So if you intend to buy this game I would hold of until they fix the problems I have mentioned.

Great game. I am a picky player, but this one got me hooked up.
I will go and review the game mechanics, so hopefully it helps you get started if you decide to play this game.
TL:DR Game's good, give it a try. Slow paced game, but sometimes gets your blood rushing.
In short - you have large map and usually teams of ~10 ships in each. Players are matchmaked pretty well-balancedly, both teams will be technically equial. Ships are divided into several types: Destroyers, Light Cruisers, Heavy Cruisers, Battleships, Aircraft Carriers. All those types are pretty interesting to play:
- Destroyers are fast, nimble ships with weak artillery compared to other ships. What makes them stand out, are TORPEDOS! Those ships sneak all around the battlefield and try to get close (close means withing torpedo range, 4-8km) to camping ships and blow them up with torpedos. Destroyers are deadly if unnoticed (and being smallest ships, they are), however blowing other ships out is not only what they do. Destroyers are great scouts, who can find enemies for your battleships to shoot down. They also can set up smoke screen, which hides your allies from enemies. In a game, where if you get shoot at, and where ships take ages to change course/retreat, smoke screen is amazing thing.
- Cruisers are versatile ships. They tend to have decent anti-air guns, more or less powerful main calibre and speed, some cruisers have torpedos just as well. As you play with T1-T4 cruisers, you will get matchmaked into mostly "Cruiser vs Cruiser" fights. Everything is simple in that matches - you have cruiser, enemy have cruiser, who shoots and drives better wins. However as you get T5 cruiser and higher, you will be participating in matches where teams will have several battleships (sometimes even more than cruisers) and sometimes an aircraft carriers. Did I mention cruisers have good AA? Congrats, you are a support ship now. Cruisers have very hard time duelling with battleships due to weaker armor and guns, however they make up as a great escort ships, assisting in shooting down wounded targets, airplanes and defeding battleships from sneaky destroyers.
- Battleships. Tanky and powerful ships. They are not much bigger than cruisers, however they have high-calibre guns and very high armor. They are generally slower than cruisers, and do not have torpedos. Their main role is tanking when necessary, pushing enemy lines and just taking out enemies from afar, thanks to very high range of their guns. The downsides of Battleships is that it lacks proper AA (not all of them, Yamato has good AA) and their primary guns' reloading time is huge. Also, they are not quite maneuverable, and while cruisers can wiggle from side to side while under fire to avoid getting hit, battleships can hardly pull that off. Also, battleships have very big detecteability, meaning that they are seen all across the map.
- Aircraft carriers. I haven't played those yet. So far I see them hiding behind teammates, and launching several fighters: bombers, torpedocarriers and air superiority fighters. Torpedo carriers are devastating by the way, saying from my own experience :D Aircraft carriers are very squishy and shouldn't be anywhere near enemy's shooting range, otherwise it's as good as dead. Oh, and fighters are GREAT scouts! They have lesser spotting range than ships do, but they fly around quite fast and it isn't a big deal.
Next are damaging mechanics. Almost all ships with guns have 2 firing options: HE (high explosive) shells and AP (armor penetrating) shells. First one are general purpose shells, they can take out external modules (guns/steering/engine/etc), they can cause fire. APs are way more fun though - they can penetrate enemy and take out the "heart" of ship, called "Citadel". Citadel is a section of ship, located right in the middle of ship around the waterline, or underwater. It contains most important ship systems, and getting a penetrating hit into citadel causes great damage. Battleships, having biggest guns (and so having very good AP), can oneshot cruisers if they hit their citadel. But there's a trick - the AP shell should hit the citadel preferably at 90 degrees, otherwise if enemy ship is angled towards you (facing you with their nose +-30 degrees), then your AP shells are likely to just bounce off without doing any damage. Also, using AP is suggested against enemies you can actually penetrate (no point in using AP on destroyer vs battleship). The opposite situation is also not advised - when you have high calibre gun and you try to penetrate enemy with paper armor - AP shells just will pierce it through (instead of exploding inside of enemy ship) and fly out from other side of enemy ship leaving tiny hole.

Harebrained Schemes' keep making amazing strides with each release.  Hong Kong improves on the gameplay, level design, and art of Dragonfall and SRR before it.  I haven't decided if I prefer the story elements of Hong Kong over DF:DC yet, but the final levels of SR:HK provide an incredible ending.  Keep up the good work, HBS!

I'll keep it short.
I love this game. What I loved about Dragonfall was feeling like part of a community, advancing characters and their storylines. There is so much more of that in Hong Kong. I'm enjoying walking around more and talking to others...although if you're just into the missions, you can just skip most of the character development.
The decking is better, and more tense. Dodging those roving scanners in real time, the improved system for hacking nodes, and the feeling of being totally screwed when you get black IC called down on you, which I didn't feel in Dragonfall.
Missons are very good, which there seems to be at least one good twist per mission...not one had gone how I thought it would go. Side missions for your team are not necessary but intriguing, I especially liked IsObel's, when your chosen dialog is handling TWO verbal confrontations at once. Just got started playing this iteration. So far, love the story. Dialogue is good and so forth. There is however an issue in how this version handles critcal hits. Like Dragon Fall Director's Cut they are non-existant if the target is in any sort of cover. To understand why I have a problem with this you have to understand a few things: 1) The difference between a critical hit and a regular hit 2) What basic things affect causing one. 3) What things are considered cover. 4) How cover affects hitting a target in combat. So here it goes.
1) A regular hit is simple you fire a shot and it miraculously hits it's target either through dumb luck or skill. This is a hit anywhere on the body ie., arm, leg, chest, pinky toe. Critical hits are in essence hitting vital areas of the body that cause extra damage ie., Head, heart, gonads, spleen so forth. A bit harder to achieve in general, but much greater in effect.
2) I feel that three basic things affect critical hits. 1. Dumb luck. 2. Intent. 3. Opportunity.
1. Dumb luck. This is the base. Even blindfolded at midnight with a target behind a wageslave's desk, firing in their direction you just MIGHT hit their head. This is my biggest problem with the critical hit system since it was changed in DFDC. Dumb luck can not be eliminated. It just is.
2. Intent. This offers a way to increase your chances of hitting that sweet spot. You take the blindfold off and turn the lights on and now you actaully aim for their head, heart or gonads. This obviously is harder to accomplish then hitting in the center of body mass, but ultimately more effective and should to some degree be affected by the fact that the wage slave keeps ducking behind his desk.
3. Opportunity. This offers a great amount of latitude for chances scoring a hit. Lets say our wage slave, whom we will call Bob, decides to come out from behind his desk to try and pick up his favorite red stapler that was shot off his desk. Now you have a clear chance to frag his face no holds barred.
3) What things are considered cover? Cars, plaster and stucco walls, trash cans, motorcycles, desks, office plants, road barricades, a moose. These are all things that you can hide behind.
4) What though does cover ACTUALLY DO? Simple, makes you harder to hit. It does not however stop the bullets, or magically prevent all chance of a bullet finding it's way into your frontal lobe. Light cover, a large office plant for example will make it hard to make out where exactly their head is, but you can still most likely assume it is on the upper part of their body. Medium cover, a desk turned on it's side does not stop bullets, but can make it harder to hit you in the chest. Heavy cover, hiding behind a moose can stop bullets, but you have to pop your pretty little head out sometime to shoot back you will be less likely to be hit with that little exposed, but it is still your head.

I'm not sure whether to recommend or not.. I mean, this review will largely be negative, but ultimate it isn't a bad game, and might be worth a play...
I already own and have played Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun Dragonfall. I enjoyed both of those games at the time and reviewed them very positively, especially Dragonfall which felt like a fully realized Shadowrun Returns.
So what do I have to complain about? Is Shadowrun: Hong Kong somehow worse than Dragonfall? No, in some ways it is an improvement. I think my problem with the game is, it is just more of the same; Hong Kong feels like just Dragonfall but with names and setting changed. Same sorta contrived story, same sorta hamfisted characters, etc.
I can get past all that, but maybe the big difference is that, in Dragonfall I felt invested; the opening where an old friend/partner dies tragically, you are left to pick up the pieces with interesting characters dealing with her loss. In Dragonfall I *wanted* to find out what happens, I wanted revenge, I wanted to develop my relationships with my team and city. But in Hong Kong, I can't be arsed to care about this father-figure, I can barely be arsed about the team or conflicts facing them, it just feels so bland and boring to me.
I want to say that the combat also feels bland and uninteresting, but it seems much like the same combat in Dragonfall which I recall reviewing as better than Xcom's combat. Did something change that I just can't put my finger on? Or maybe my tastes have shifted between Dragonfall and Hong Kong.
Ultimately, this game just feels like a cookie-cutter of Dragonfall, only with a story I can't seem to be interested in. It largely feels like the same game, when I guess I might have wanted more out of it.
If you like the Shadowrun series (boardgame or videogame) you will probably enjoy this game, but not as much as I would hope.
TL;DR: Play "Shadowrun: Dragonfall" instead. If you've already played Dragonfall, then I'm not sure If I could recommend Hong Kong until it goes on sale. It is decent, but lacking in interest.

TL:DR - Its too expensive for what you get. Its not terrible, in fact the first hour or so is fun, but definitely not worth the price. Especially once you realize that when you've seen the two types of track youve pretty much seen everything the game has to offer.
So I love ancient Rome. An ancient Rome chariot racing game is an awesome idea. It reminds me of the chariot race missions in Shadow of Rome. (A really really fun PS2 game. If you are a fan of gladiator games, get it!  And enjoy cutting people's arms off, beating them with it, then tossing it into the crowd..) But this review isnt about Shadow of Rome. Its about Qvadriga. Which unfortunately, is no where near as cool as the concept could be.
Now, I wouldnt have as much of a problem with it if it wasn't 20 freakin' dollars. So what do you get for 20 dollars? A tiny-graphic boring game. I normally dont really care about graphics if the gameplay is engrossing, but this game unfortunately lacks that quality, so all you keep on thinking were damn, this would be cool if it actually had decent images of the action.
So a basic rundown. You start, and pick your faction. Different factions have different abilities that are explained in tooltips. Some are stronger, faster, can handle their chariots better. Then a map appears with different regions. There are many different regions, each with different tracks in them. Lots of tracks to run on with many random events is a giant plus, except for one issue which shall be explained later.
When you start, you can pick one region, and each region has 1 track unlocked. Then a screen where you can look at your  charioteers, get vet services, repairs and healing, and upgrade your horses and chariots. Heres the kicker. Once you pick your first track, you cannot leave it until you get your "fame" up enough from racing. So if you pick a hard as hell track (as I did my first try), youre pretty much stuck. Pick which charioteer you want to race with, and you are off.
The graphics are really simple, a top down view of chariots on a track. Looks like tiny mobile game graphics. There are two modes, one where the action stops every 10 seconds to give a command, one where it doesnt but you still only are give a command every so often. The commands are accelerate (to a certain level, then you can't), brake, crash right/left (slam your chariot into an opponent a la ben hur), lacerate (whip an opponent), small/medium/large move left or right (each one moves you farther across the lanes), watch for attacks (basically a block) and control (basically do nothing, but it makes your control go up), and finally whip (allows your horses to get a burst of speed, but you can hurt them).
There are many different tracks to race on, some narrow, some larger. Each track has a brief paragraph about its history. Every time you race there are slighty different variables on the track, described in a simple sentence before the race. Theres lots of these, both bad and good and they provide some variety.
Youre going to need it. This game is grindy as hell.
See, you get money for racing, more if you win. You use this money to buy better guys, horses and chariots. You also need to pay for vet and repairs from racing damage. Each wheel, horse, and charioteer has a life bar. Take too much damage, and a horse dies, leaving you to pull with 3. Go too fast, and your wheel gets damaged. Go too fast around a corner and you can topple your chariot, leaving your guy to be dragged by his horses. You then have the option of running (and the other guys can hit you, or hanging on till youre in a safe spot to run.
There are stats, represented by icons. The different stats ccombine to make the upgrades (say a horse with two speed icons vs a horse with 1 speed and 1 endurance - which one do you want.. The two speed will be faster but weaker than the 1 speed 1 endurance)
But theres only 6 guy types (stats: skill - how good of a driver you are, and constitution - how much damage you can take) and 9 horse types (stats: speed - top speed, and endurance - same as con but for the horse) and 9 chariot types( stats: acceleration and size, again same as con but for the chariot). And they are expensive as hell.
It also costs money to travel from track to track, and you can't race certain tracks till you get more famous. So you will probably doing the same race over and over just to get enough cash to go somewhere else.
Theres two types of track, a tight oval type and a longer wider type. Except for this, there is absolutely nothing to differentiate them.
A $20 game this is not. It can be fun for a little bit, and if it had some kind of multiplayer it'd be pretty fun. But as it is, its just boring after the first hour or so.
Recommended if you enjoy horse related mishaps and chariot shenanigans.

I bought this game direct from the publisher before it was made available on Steam and lately I have transferred my license to Steam. This game is based very much on an old Roman chariot racing boardgame called Circus Maximus where you have to design your team and you then do a single race or a series of races. But this game adds more to that premise.
For one thing the game introduces factions which all have their own concentrations, some build quality chariots, some have the best drivers other have tha fastest horses, there are quite a few of these traits that are introduced in the game which makes choosing your faction quite intriguing.
Another thing the game adds is random events at the start of each race which might affect just you/someone else or everyone equally. For example you miught be prevented from whipping for the whole race which will penalise horse teams where endurance is high but speed is not. Also you might ahve a race where all the old wreackage is still on the track from the previous race making it far more deadly. Or you can be forced to start from a certain lane or have a rival in a race. These add loads of variety to each race.
It also introduces faction leaders and leaderboards where each faction leader is ranked. You may make it you strategy to assassinate your faction leader in order to get your own best driver on the leaderboard adding extra strategy to the already packed with excitement races.
You get many different authentic Roman and non-Roman race circuits from basic ones where you start off, up to the Circus Maximus, where you have to win three times to complete the game.
As for the races themselves these follow the boardgame quite closely in that you can whip horses to make them go faster for a short time but this can damage them, you can try to whip other adjacent drivers or ram them or their horses, you can get damaged travelling over wreckage, you can be dragged and trampled to death etc etc. Its all very very Ben Hur in the most ruthless way possible. Of course though there is also a racing game in here and you can just try to win races through skill and speed.
There is loads to enjoy in this game, I have to say I was very pleasantly surprised when I played it as to how much variety, strategy, and fun there is in here. Its probably one of my top twenty most favourite games of all time actually, and definitely one of the best purchases I have made over the last few years of gaming.
Definitely recommended.

An amazing free-form fighting game.  There are elements of a traditional fighting game like frame traps, positioning, and combos, combined with the freedom and nuance of Jedi Academy.  I played a LOT of Jedi Academy back in the day and although I had a lot of fun with it, I can't honestly say that there wasn't a lot of randomness in how some fights played out.  Saber clashes weren't always consistent, and sometimes you just got lucky.  There's very little if any of that here.  The Fast/Balanced/Heavy stance system creates a very logical rock-paper-scissors type system to sword clashes.  In this game I can almost always say exactly things turned out the way they did and there's a logical way to combat different strategies.  It really does a great job of capturing the "easy to learn, hard to master" environment that most competitive games strive for.  Speaking as both a traditional fighting game fan and a fan of Jedi Academy back in the day, this is a fantastic sword fighting game that I'm going to be putting a lot more hours into.

And ofcourse, he's back, my favorite event, Professor Genki has returned with new maniacal events.
The game also adds a number of fun weapons to use, being that It is hard to pick which one is the funniest, but I believe the Singularity one is the most fun one, when It does not bugs out (When doing the mayhem It appears, leave the place the activity starts to make the Singularity blackhole be able to pull people and vehicles inside).
I believe that the major letdowns on the game, are the Super Powers, which are unlocked from the beggining, beside they are useful and fun to use, they are too op, making the game too easy most times... Why you need a car? If you can infinitelly sprint? Or why would you need a jet? Just use a abduction gun to send you higher and then glide your way to the destination. Also, after playing for longer, even the guns will turn to useless, since your character will be so op that
almost every enemy will be wiped out by your character super powers.
Another let down the game have, is that in the simulation, there seems to be nowhere safe for you to reduce your notoriety other than going to the ship, even more since the cribs are destroyed, and they removed the notoriety wipe from stores.
The game in some missions also have problems with higher resolutions, since It has the fps freak out in some cases, like the mission where the boss is driving a spaceship out the Alien's spaceship, and has to pass through the doors closing, If you are running the game with low fps, the doors will eventually crush your ship, failing the mission, to solve the issue would only be necessary to lower resolution. Such a bug is ridiculous If you think about it.
The game have also a number of coop activities, which I didn't had the chance of trying out, since none of my friends are playing the game currently, and neither looked in the server hub for open rooms to play, so I let them go.
Overall, the game Is fun If you want to pass the time and explode everything, If you want to try It out, be sure to take your mind of what you've seen on Saints Row 2 and Saints Row The Third, or else you will certainly give a not recommended to the game right on sight (Was going to do that at the intro areas, then decided to go ahead in the gameplay).

First & most important: play this game with a gamepad. Do not try to play with a keyboard. You will make yourself miserable.
That being said, this is what you want from a sequel: a game that improves upon the original in every way. I haven’t yet finished this one but I’m about halfway through and it has already exceeded my expectations.
I’ll start with the only negative point I have right now: the Reverse Merman’s ball sack. He’s a character with the upper body of a fish, the lower body of a man, and testicles that hang down to his knees. I’m not a prude, but I think it’s needlessly disgusting in an otherwise lighthearted & fun game. If you have kids, you probably don’t want them seeing that. I’m an adult and I don’t want to see that. At least he is an optional character so you don’t have to unlock him, and if you unlock him you don’t have to use him.
Aside from that blemish, this is an incredibly polished & enjoyable platformer for both casual gamers and hardcore, leaderboard chasers alike. The way they designed the point system is ingenious because while they added checkpoints into each level, if you don’t use them you will get a point boost and a challenge boost since your experience will be a lot like the first game where you start all over from the beginning of the level each time you die.
If you don’t care about your score, though, you can take full advantage of the checkpoints. They make trying to collect the gold bars scattered throughout each level a lot more fun. Ditto for the secrets and unlockables, of which the first game had none. Speaking of unlockables, there are quite a bit in this game from extra characters to extra outfits and even more of the Atari-style, ultra retro challenges featured in the first game. Levels also routinely feature multiple paths, one of which will be more difficult (but could contain a treasure or secret) or will lead to a secret level exit.
The graphics are much nicer than the original and are 3-D while still keeping the original’s retro, 2-D feel. It makes the game look much sharper and gives more life to the characters you can play as they have more than bare bones animations this time around (the cheeseburger guy is especially fun in this respect).
Oh and if the optional checkpoint challenge isn’t enough, there is also a new “dance” button that causes your character to dance for a split second during the level. You get points each time you dance, but your guy can’t do anything else while dancing, so you’re taking a risk when you do it. Also, getting a perfect run with all the gold bars gets your guy put in a cannon at the end where you have to try and hit a bullseye for maximum bonus points. The addition of these factors plus the checkpoint boost will keep a lot of leaderboard fiends busy for quite a while, I’m sure.
I got this for 50% off at recent Steam sale but I’d say it would also be worth full price, especially if you enjoy competing on the leaderboards. Can’t wait to finish it.

Puzzle Agent 2 is, in many ways; the second half of the first game. But despite reusing alot of the assets of the first game. it still feels fresh and current by virtue of it be so cleverly crafted as well as being as short as the first Puzzle Agent. The story does take on a quicker pace with the assumption that the player had finished the first game. The unforunaale thing is it fails once again to conclude all the plot points in a good fashion. Leaving you flummexed in the end about why certain significent plot points are left out.
The puzzles this time seem to lack the variety and consistency of the first Puzzle Agent's. Too often types of puzzles are reused too frequently, And although its been a while since I played the last one, it feels like there were fewer puzzles to solve in total this time around.
So what is Puzzle Agent 2? Well I would not call it a haphazad afterthought sequel meant to sum up the first game's glaring cliff hanger. But on the other hand its doesn't do much to improve or build on the series. Perhaps than Puzzle Agent 2 is a well crafted, somewhat rushed stopgap, made to bind this part of this series' narrative with the inevidentable third and possibly fourth entry (which is hamfistingly implied at the very end).
I liked it, but I'm not satisified with the end product.

Space Trader Merchant Marine was released in Oct 23, 2008. It boasts a score of 89% from a review by GameFocus saying, ""One of the best indie games of 2008. An innovative and addictive experience. Addictive, very fun and innovative are the best words to describe the game and the bottom line is this is a welcome addition to any gamer's library so buy this game and enjoy it."
This is very akin to the how 'reviews' reflected Bubsy 3D on its own packaging, to those that remember.
The game is broken down into four different areas, exploration, trading, time management, and fighting/bounty hunting.
The exploration is very limited, your only goal being to find crates of goods floating about, merchants, and the bar keep. The problem is that once you've gone through it once, you know where it all is, no variation, same boring bland walls, ect., and it honestly starts to feel like a chore.
The time management is very simple. Go to X location from y location = z time spent. You have a set amount of time in every 'chapter' to complete a set $$$ quota. Besides the time spent traveling through the travel menu, any time spent at a location does not diminish the time that you have left. And as thus, does not really give you any time pressure.
The trading is a joke, as, all you do it buy what's not doing well, and travel, and get guaranteed profit. It hardly reflects actual market value in the real world and makes the game largely unchallenging.
The fighting/bounty hunting is terribly bland and cycles through the same maps. Stupid AI, overpowered guns, and cheap kills, makes it horrid.
Now, all that said, this was made in 2008, 2-0-0-8, to be sure. Other games that were made in this period were:
Fable 2
Fallout 3
LittleBIGPlanet
Rock Band 2
Gears Of War 2
Spore
Grand Theft Auto IV
No More Heroes
Left 4 Dead
Professor Layton & The Curious Village
Compared to that list, the time period the game was released, and actual content in the game... it makes it look mediocre, a joke, something that belongs in a 2000 release.

The fps shooter aspect was actually a fun side aspect to the trading that got my blood pumping surprisingly. While the game resets your money and cargo capacity every chapter, it makes sense to give it the mission challenge feel.

But what happened to me is when I traveled away I ended up running out of time and failed the entire chapter.
The reason I kept failing to kill her is because she is unfairly strong (combined with the crappy FPS gameplay and unfair AI). So why doesn't she just blow up your ship? If your failure happens in real time then she should be aware that you're trying to kill her and it would make sense for her to just blow up your ship and kill you - except she doesn't. But the time factor still remains and you can still lose by running out of time (remember the time limit was for you to make $20,000,000 for the woman you're now trying to kill).

That being said; this game has one of the darkest, most intriguing story-lines of any game I've played in a long while. This game is funny and dark in a way that is really unprecedented in the world of video games; and although the dialogue isn't overly complex, the ideas in the story are something I would expect to come from an author like Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥ rather than a low-budget dev. All in all, I'm extremely excited to see what is next to come from Dingaling, hopefully Ninja Tears will deliver the same combination of irreverence, cynicism and soul-crushing despair that I welcomed into my life while playing this game.

The fact that the game is buggy means that meeting criteria will not cause doors to open, etc. But the fact that objectives are not well communicated means that you will not know for sure that you're actually doing the right thing until you do literally EVERYTHING in a nonlinear game without finding a way to advance.
Example: I just spent an hour playing a very brief section of a level over and over again, unable to get a door to open, so I kept reloading the save and trying again.  Went online, saw I was doing it RIGHT and then reloaded a slightly older save to finally achieve the objective.

Let me first say, I love Dragonfall. It was a fabulous game and I pre-ordered Hong Kong anticipating a similar experience. However, as some others have correctly pointed out -- Hong Kong's balance between interactive reading and actual gameplay is dramatically lopsided to me. I love a good story and the game does well to pull you into its world and characters. However, my karma points, weapons, armor and cyberware feel almost pointless as the last two missions I've accepted -- and completed -- were done without any need for them. Both missions were completed by clicking between endless dialogue windows between characters.
While it makes for sometimes intriguing story-telling, it does little to satisfy my interest in video game interactivity. So far, it's been little more than a choose-your-own adventure book with some beautiful static artwork. Even stranger is that for a game that chooses to focus so heavily on written word, there are a remarkable amount of typos, missing words and other seemingly obvious grammatical errors. To me, Dragonfall struck a better balance between story-telling and interactive gameplay than Hong Kong seems to (so far). I will say, I have not finished Hong Kong (I'm 35+ hours in) as I'm finding it a little difficult to do so at this point. However, should I complete it and discover a different result, I will gladly modify my review and recommend it. I will say, if you haven't yet played Dragonfall, you owe it to yourself to do so!

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a fun addition to the Hare Brained Schemes recent forays into the lore. The setting was interesting and the characters, for the most part, felt genuine and original. Unfortunately it suffers from similar issues to its predecessors and some entirely new problems arise as well.
The party members felt varied with some exceptions, Duncan Wu, your foster-brother, is a completely one demensional tool used as exposition into your own past, he hardly ever has anything to say that isn't directly related to telling you what your childhood was like. Rachter, the Russian Rigger, is an interesting concept, and has entertaining quips when you are out on runs, but talking to him at base, he will also only ever talk about one subject, and I feel like there wasn't enough variety in how to respond to his particular obssession.
In general HBS seems to have put a lot of effort into more character development, but I feel they went too far, especially in a game with so few actual missions. There is hours and hours of dialogue, every inane NPC feels the need to tell you their life story, as a completionist I found it frustrating because I wanted to see everything, but most of it was such drivel I felt the drive to just get it over with.
On top of the short number of missions, a big selling point of SRHK was the updated Matrix mechanics which I felt backfired rather badly. Hacking anything takes much longer now, several runs I took had me spending 70% of the time in the matrix. The new matrix is heavily stealth influenced, which can be infuriating to try to avoid sight lines in an isometric game. The hacking mini game was overly lengthy and generally felt like more bulk.
I often found myself feeling much less powerful in SRHK than I did in Returns or Dragonfall. I poured almost all of my points into rifles and decking, and neither really felt like they got any better than they started. Even at the end game, loaded with cyberware and the best equipment, combat still felt like the opening scenes, there was no feeling of progression, of your team rising to greater challenges.
That said though, it did have some fun moments and was worth the play through. It will never be considered a masterpiece of the genre, but if youre itching to run the shadows, it does the job and at least tries to shake things up a little, even if the results were luke warm.
