Blade Symphony is a 3d fighting game that ditches the classic "you're always locked onto your opponent" movement of most traditional 2d and 3d fighting games in favor of simply moving with the arrow keys/your controllers directional pad and aiming attacks with the mouse/your controllers analog sticks.
Though I can see that it seems to be shaping up to be a solid game, and I appreciate more experimental fighting games that don't necessarily stick to Street Fighter styled controls, I'm not quite fond of the "stance" system. Basically, instead of having light/medium/heavy attacks, you instead have to switch between 3 different stances which alter your entire moveset. 1 is "light/fast", 2 is "medium/medium" and 3 is "heavy/slow". Each of these stances is designed to be strong and weak against the other two stances in a classic rock/paper/scissors weapon triangle. While that's all well and good, I still feel that having to roll over the mouse wheel to select from 3 stances in the heat of combat in order to get the move you want feels clunky and convoluted. I would have much preferred just having light/medium/heavy buttons. I mean seriously, imagine if in Street Fighter you had to roll over a damn mouse wheel or reach over to the number keys on your keyboard and than do a movement sensitive input every time you wanted to throw a damn sweep as Ryu.
There are a few other nitpicks with the combat, though I assume these will be tweaked out and refined with time. At the moment blocking seems to be pretty useless, and since blocking sucks, throws also suck. The game is basically all about hitting buttons right now.
Anyway, as for content, the game has a small roster of characters at the moment (about 5 or so), but each of them has a huge variety of weapons to choose from which alter their movesets and abilities pretty heavily. The game also has 2 on 2 matches along with 1 on 1 matches and various lobby settings, so it's pretty decent for online play. Though the netcode is bad.
I like most of the music also. The aesthetic is pretty cool too, though Pure has way too much junk in the trunk and her random cyborg ninja fanservice feels really out of place IMO.
Seems like a solid game, and one I might return to from time to time, but I really don't like the convoluted design of the stance system. Personally I think Max Anarchy/Anarchy Reigns on Ps3/Xbox360 does pretty much the same thing much better, so I'd honestly recommend picking that up instead if you have either console.

Blade Symphony harkens back to the classic Jedi Knight series, focusing on 1 on 1 sword duels.  If you were a fan of lightsaber duels in those games, you'll feel right at home here.  For the uninitiated, this is a rather unorthodox and very unforgiving fighting game, with a steep learning curve.  You will struggle over the nuances of the controls.  You will lose a lot of duels.
However, once you can get past the initial bumpiness, you'll find that there's a lot of depth.  What seemed random at first actually requires quite a bit of technique and timing.  The veteran players can be very friendly, and will be more than happy to provide advice.  Some servers will even hold impromptu classes for players who ask.
As for the Early Access Beta, the game is adequately playable.  There is one character that is still a work in progress, but the other characters have fully realized movesets.  There aren't a lot of game modes, but when the focus is on 1v1, this isn't a big issue at this time.
Post-release edit:  The gameplay itself is much more refined after several fixes and balance changes.  Pure's moveset has filled out nicely.  This is still a lean, mean fighting game; perhaps not the most feature filled (for now), but it certainly isn't lacking in depth.  Jedi Knight/Academy fans will be chuffed.

Brilliant RTS with ever-present balance issues, plenty of options but startling little strategic diversity. Various in game factions  capture the essential doctrine of WW2 armies fairly well, but if you want to play higher ranked multiplayer, only 7 or so units per faction are viable at any given time.
Let's say you want to use the Jagdtiger, a super heavy late-war tank destroyer that can take on entire platoons of allied medium armour head-on at extreme range with a 127mm AT gun and win, sometimes without even taking meaningful damage.
Unfortunately for you, the Jagdtiger comes into play so late that you often win or lose before you can deploy it and it also costs a sum of resources equivalent to the rest of your force combined. Once you manage to call it in, it's hideously vulnerable to flanking, anything faster than a tortoise, infantry which it's completely helpless against, air attack, rocket artillery, conventional AT guns,.... et cetera and you end up losing it to a bunch of conscripts with AT grenades.
10/10 World War 2 realism. Would not deploy Wunderwaffe again.

A Story About My Uncle is a fairly straightforward first person platformer. The premise of the story is that you have wandered into your absent uncle’s house and find a teleporter that takes you to another world. Using the suit he left for you, you must find your uncle and make your way back home.
The central mechanics are quite simple; there’s no combat in this game, with the game being wholly devoted to platforming through 3D environments. Your abilities include a normal jump, a super jump, an energy grapple you shoot from your hand that can connect to most (but not all!) surfaces and pull you towards them while allowing you to swing after a fashion, and later on, a pair of rocket boosts which give you an abrupt, very large bit of acceleration in a certain direction (yes, as if with a rocket) when you try to double jump in midair.
These controls are quite simple, and the game fundamentally consists of using them to traverse environments. You start out only getting one grapple per jump through the air, but soon you end up with the ability to grapple up to three times before landing – and in the final area, refresh them mid-jump by draining glowing crystals on the walls.
Sadly, the lack of much variety in mechanics means that, in the end, a lot of puzzles ultimately feel fairly samey – there’s only so much you can do with a limited control set, and it feels like you’ve done it all by the end of the game, and probably more than that. A number of areas feel kind of samey, which isn’t helped by the graphics – while each area of the game has its own unique look, each individual level looks pretty similar internally.
This is kind of annoying later on in the game, when it becomes increasingly more difficult at times to see what exactly you’re supposed to be grappling onto – there’s a few points in the game where you have to do a bit of searching to figure out where you’re trying to go next, and it can be less than obvious. Combined with the game’s general aesthetic of “rocks floating in midair/stuck in the sides of a cave over bottomless pits”, the environment can start getting a bit confusing and very same-looking over time.
Really, that’s all there is to the game; there’s three or four characters, with decent but slightly off voiceovers that contain the odd grammatical error betraying the writer as a non-native English speaker (or just some poor proofreading), but in the end, I didn’t feel a strong connection to any of the characters. Without this, there’s just the platforming – and that wears thin after a while.
Overall, while the game has an okay aesthetic on the most basic of levels, in the end it ends up feeling too samey and there just isn’t anything else there to give it much oomph. It just is what it is, and what it is isn’t anything special. At the end, I was left walking away without feeling like I’d gained anything from the experience, or experienced anything really memorable. It just isn’t worth your time or money.

This third outing for the Shadowrun Returns team has just the same standard of high quality shown in the first two SRR games, but with more polish.

I've just finished the main campaign, and after playing through the older ones a while ago, this expansion is a really good refreshment. If you're a fan of turn based combat, this is a game for you. Sure, there is a TON of text to this game, and without any voice-overs this may be a turnoff for some, but i assure you that the story and characters in it are more than enough to keep you in your seat for hours, reading through the conversations. You have multiple options for completing given tasks, and as you go through the story you will notice that decisions you made previously actually matter, they shape the way story unfolds. You have almost complete freedom of how you're going to build your character, since the "karma" system is generous, and you don't actually need to "specialize" in any let's call it profession to finish the game, even though it's commonly better to build your character in one path.
Give this game a try, you won't regret it :)

While the story and pacing aren't as good as in Dragonfall Director's Cut - it's still a solid addition to the Shadowrun series.
Quests are varied, the RPG system is further improved, plot is good and once again avoids typical RPG cliches. All in all while not reaching the standards set by classic RPGs of 10-15 years ago - Shadowrun Hong Kong is still one of the best RPGs this year.

Harebrained Schemes once again captured the essence that emanated from the original Shadowrun games (SNES/Genesis). That is, by incorporating intrigue, cluelessness on your part as a Shadowrunner and a wide array of weapons.
The story is what you would expect when you think of Modern China blended with a game. It is creative and realistic (in terms of character dialogue). Though it lacked the same intensity from the first two games they released. However, the intrigue did keep you wondering what the heck was happening! As for the audio, they could not have made anything better then what they offered - they always do an upstanding job at that! The character creation is pretty straightforward.
- Very intriguing story. At first, you won't understand the intro, which is how it should be.
- Good gameplay, like in Dragonfall.
- Some of the Cyberware seem new (haven't seen some of them those before).
- As far as I know unlike the other games, you don't lose any AP by upgrading cyberware, which is a HUGE plus.
- As usual, you get the chance to obtain a stun gun. Very nice.
- Interesting characters with each their own perspective and way of dealing with things.
- The Matrix has a nice visual appeal to be certain. In some instance, it's like mixing Chinatown and the Matrix in one.
- Brute forcing the nodes in the Matrix was nicely added into the game.
- The added stealth element to the game makes it more interesting. It's not always about the fight!
- Vast Chinese lore, myths and legends seem to be present (at least other gamers say so, so I will trust them in this regard). In any event, the vast amount of it surely makes the game more intriguing.
- Very lengthy character backstories. I mean, VERY lengthy. It took me thirty minutes to talk to all of them after any mission. They won't shut up it seems, eh.
- Is0bel is a real nerd, which may add to your connection to the team (I'm a introvert like Is0bel, and I fully understand how she felt).
- Racter has this pretty awesome Drone with him.
- Gaichu has some awesome attacks plus different stances. Very cool.
- Gobbet can kill hostile spirits 'just like that' with a skill of hers.
- All in all, the characters have their own set of personalities and attacks. The varieties are  perfect.
- One of the things that bothers me excessively is the amount of characters that smoke. That is NOT necessary. In fact, it's quite disgusting. They kept throwing that at you over and over. Especially with your fixer and Racter.
- I noticed at times, there were scenes that were disgusting (I do NOT mean gruesome, bloody or anything of that nature).
- Most of the time, I could not know who I was hitting in the Matrix while using AOE programs. Most of the time, I did not know if I was hitting myself or even my own ESPs while trying to attack the enemy. The AOE overlay was too pale and I could never be sure where it was hovering over.
- They incorporated Islam in the game (in a negative way) during one of the character's backstory. NOT a fan of these types of things. Despite the briefness of it, it did ruin part of the gameplay by seeing a negative connotation to Islam in the game.
- There were no deckers you could face in the Matrix.
- As a decker, anytime you go in the Matrix, the programs and ESPs are never set to you. They are always in the inventory, which means you have to ALWAYS gear yourself up again.
- The re-vamped Matrix is not an improvement. The one from Dragonfall was way better.
- You NEVER have enough Nuyen. I was never able to hire mercs, because I only had enough to spend it on Cyberdecks, programs, ESPs, guns, jackets and meds.
- Way too much dialogue compared to the action.
- The ingame gliding (especially in the Matrix) should be replaced with actual running. Gliding makes me feel like a ghost.
- We should know what were are hitting in the Matrix while using AOE programs. Most of the time, I did not know if I was hitting myself or even my own ESPs while trying to attack the enemy. The AOE overlay was too pale and I could never be sure where it was hovering over.
- A rotational camera (which would only be optional for the player)
- Perhaps an option to make the enemy characters "redder", with an outside red glow (optional of course).
- Seeing more of Renraku, Ares, Shiawase, Saeder-Krupp and other groups like Novatech would be very promising.
- The ability to create your own personalized Cyberdeck. The looks, the feel, everything!
- More Nuyen (the current amount covers one of two things: weapons/jackets/cyberdecks and a limited amount of meds OR mercenaries.
- Having Jake Armitage and/or Joshua ingame as playable characters. That would be a massive plus.
- There should be actual Emporium shops - that would be so cool!
- Your character, as a decker, should always have his programs and ESPs equipped.
- Cyberdecks should have their own specific slot, as it's NOT a weapon.
- If each Shadowrunner in your team (both the permanent ones in your team and contract ones) could have a secondary set of slots, that would be great! Example: Let's take the items row which has multiple slots. Below this row should be a new row where the items placed there are placed by you (or grabbed on missions), and are permanent. So, if you place three medkits in these secondary slots, and they would be consumed, then those three slots would be empty the next mission out. If you completed a mission and you consumed one, then you would be able to use the remaining two in subsequent missions.
- The ability to see everything related to stats when dealing with weapons (whether trading, buying etc). Especially, when the other Shadowrunners from your team are not with you - that is, when you're in the city. It's hard to buy stuff when you can't see what they might need or if you don't know their stats. This includes you as well when buying a weapon/jacket/cyberdeck for yourself.
- There should not be any attempts at portraying any religion in a negative way.
- Any reference, imagery, notion or idea to smoking should be removed!
- The Matrix should be re-vamped. The new Matrix is NOT as good as in Dragonfall. The minigames, I found, were to a certain degree nerve-racking, and not very casual play friendly. They can be extrmeely stressful when you're trying to avoid an IP trace. Not something I enjoy at all. Perhaps give the option to the player to choose which version of the Matrix they want? If I have to deal with another Matrix like HKS, I will not play as decker, as I usually do. That would be very disappointing, but what else could I do?
- There should be deckers in the Matrix that you can face.
- Better character creation and ingame enemies (often times, the avatars do not look like the characters).
- Lastly, I wish that options ingame truly had an impact - your dialogue choices make practically no difference, except in a few instances where the outcomes isn't all that different anyhow.

Aside from its shortcomings, the game itself is decent. I wish that Harebrained Schemes will continue making Shadowrun games, and hopefully expand their work to encompass something even more brilliant.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong the third entry in the Shadowrun Returns franchise, following up on Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun Returns: Dragonfall. This title is stand alone and playing the previous games is not mandatory to enjoy it, though you will miss out on a few nods here and there. Players control a team of Shadowrunners - mercenaries performing illegal operations for anyone with enough cash - while trying to work through a complex and vibrant plot of family secrets, mystical danger and corporate espionage.
Fans of earlier entries in the series will find that the mechanics have received some much-needed polish: my own experiences noted hefty changes to the Shaman class and to decking in the Matrix. Combat feels mostly tight, and you seldom feel you have wasted your karma, no matter which skills you have invested in.
I don't want to discuss the plot very much, because that's the main reason why you play titles like this, but I consider it on par with Dragonfall's in terms of quality. I cannot gush enough about the characters - no other series comes to mind that has managed to produce so many well thought out and well-written individuals, both on the team and off. If background information  and dialogue are big sticking points for you, then the game will not disappoint.
The only real negative I can discuss for SR:HK is the frequency of bugs. Every patch fixes things further, but there's nothing more frustrating than eating a load of damage because the game decided to lag out and skip half of your characters' turns in combat. I see a big dip in the number of issues that people are having since release day, but in a game that can be sometimes unforgiving, it just takes that happening once to leave you raging.
Ultimately, I would say this is worth it at full price and a must buy if you can snag it during a seasonal sale. Play time for me clocked around 30 hours for one run through with full completion, so I absolutely got my money's worth. Highly suggested for fans of strategy RPGs and excellent writing.

Gonna be honest with you here. This is the best version so far. I have all three games, and I can say that, without a doubt, this is the best version so far. Not because it's the newest. Not because it's the shiniest. But because it adds so much to the previous two games that I found myself having to read the tutorials despite playing the previous two games for hours on end. If you've played the previous two games in this series, you will not be disappointed on a gameplay front, as they have added so much since they original game.
In short, among the weapons, new locations, new characters, and whatnot, they have made two major modifications to the core gameplay: Adept alterations and fundamental changes to the roles of the Decker class.
Before, the Adept was a somewhat servicable, if not very specialized, substitute for a melee Street Samurai. Now? Well, they're still a substitute for a melee Street Samurai, but they have added a new mechanic for the class that shakes up so much. Basically, what they have added are stances for the Adepts to adopt to alter their fighting styles, such as increased defense and dodge capabilities in exchange for reduced HP damage or just straight out AP damage, or increased damage in exchange for reduced dodge and defense. Basic stuff, nothing too special or out of the ordinary for most differing "stances" in other games, but now the Adept is more than just a guy who can swing twice per turn. Now they can actually stand a chance against guys with guns if they are caught off guard. Want to know the best part? I'm fairly certain that I'm leaving out at least 2 stances, because I specifically remember an NPC ingame talking about 5 different stances, and how each stance can counteract another based on its elemental leanings!
The Deckers, however, have had the biggest change to their core gameplay in that they are no longer just mages in another location. Now, they have basic stealth mechanics to avoid drawing the attention of enemy deckers and Black IC units to themselves, and the hacking is no longer just click and done. It now requires the player to solve a puzzle of "which sequence is correct?" The longer the player waits, the more symbols and their locations are revealed, and in order to successfully hack, you must find the correct sequence of symbols before the timer runs out, or else you raise the alarm bar by a certain number of points. It's much more tense and, frankly, more fun than the previous iteration of the Deckers. So, yes, I would recommend this game based on its gameplay changes alone. But is the story good? Well, I don't know yet. I haven't beaten the game yet. But I will edit this review when I do finish it. The characters in the game, however, I CAN vouch for in my current state of completion, and I will say that the characters are very well-written and fleshed out. The party member missions take place much earlier than Dragonfall, so I've had time to bond with them even quicker, and the quests, once you complete them, do not stop affecting them afterwards. I finished Is0bel's quest and she's STILL dealing with the baggage! I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of the previous two.

Short answer: Reccomended for completionists, peopel who love NG+, and achievement hunters. If you like to complete a game and put it away, your experience may be lacking.
This review is somewhat late, as I beat it several months ago. It only took me about 4-6 playthroughs if I remember right. I think I only unlocked 2 additional classes and barely any of the other content, as I was able to "win" through the luck of the RNG. I am someone who does not mind restarting games over and over due to dying and learning, but I can't say I like replaying a game once I've beat it.
One Way Heroics has fairly standard roguelike combat which I got the hang of fairly easily having played other games. The darkness adds an additional layer to this, almost making it like chess - you have to be able to plan your moves several steps ahead, taking into account each enemy's movement speed, movement patterns, item locations, and whether you might get trapped by the terrain. This can all be done fairly rapidly in most areas outside towns and dungeons. The game, being a rogelike, has a decent amount of teaching through experience and playthroughs.
The big big big gripe I have with the game, and is the primary reason I wish I could give a "mixed" rating? I managed to kill the dark lord before I think I should have been able to. I discovered one of the special artifact items and managed to fight him inside a town. Just a single artifact, my level wasn't that high. I truly expected him to be harder. Then I expected that to not be all and for the devs to pull a "Disc 1 final boss" on me. But no, the Big Bad of the game can be defeated by simply holeing up in an inn with a single artifact weapon and blowing all your items and special abilities.  I had no longer felt a real desire to play it afterwards.
However, this is my personal taste. While I find the idea of NG+ and completing a game many many times fairly dull (in most cases) for those people who DO like that sort of gameplay, this is a decent offering. I didn't encounter many, if any bugs in my playing, and the visuals are uniformly presented with nothing that seemed out of place. Worth the money for that kind of player, and having gotten it on sale and with the addition of trading cards I can't say it wasn't worth the 69 cents I paid for it, if not more.

Based on the theories, this game were, instead, supposed to be a DLC of Saints Row: The Third, but due to how the plot in the game flows, I believe making It a new game is somewhat a good idea.
The intro is too over long, being that It lowers the replay value due to that fact, since you may want to start a new character and jump right into action.
The Activities have 3 rankings, ranging from Bronze to Copper depending on how well you do it, finish It on Gold grade and gain the highest reward, and you can even repeat doing the activities to acquire the game money and exp.
The game Itself Is kind of fun, beside you need to unlock the possibilities this game has to offer, they even added some Boss fights in the game, you see them sometimes in the plot, or after reaching highest notoriety as possible, beside It is fun at the beggining to face the boss, after some time It starts to get boring facing the same boss, doing the same kill move and stuff.
The Mass Effect and Matrix parodies are also fun in the game, they even added the possibility of getting bald when leaving simulation, as seen in the movie, but no worry, entering and leaving simulation again fixes that, also, all outfits from Saints Row 3 and most outfits from Saints Row 2 are buyable from in-game stores, includding dlc outfits, pick your favorite.
And ofcourse, he's back, my favorite event, Professor Genki has returned with new maniacal events.
The game also adds a number of fun weapons to use, being that It is hard to pick which one is the funniest, but I believe the Singularity one is the most fun one, when It does not bugs out (When doing the mayhem It appears, leave the place the activity starts to make the Singularity blackhole be able to pull people and vehicles inside).
I believe that the major letdowns on the game, are the Super Powers, which are unlocked from the beggining, beside they are useful and fun to use, they are too op, making the game too easy most times... Why you need a car? If you can infinitelly sprint? Or why would you need a jet? Just use a abduction gun to send you higher and then glide your way to the destination. Also, after playing for longer, even the guns will turn to useless, since your character will be so op that
almost every enemy will be wiped out by your character super powers.
Another let down the game have, is that in the simulation, there seems to be nowhere safe for you to reduce your notoriety other than going to the ship, even more since the cribs are destroyed, and they removed the notoriety wipe from stores.
The game in some missions also have problems with higher resolutions, since It has the fps freak out in some cases, like the mission where the boss is driving a spaceship out the Alien's spaceship, and has to pass through the doors closing, If you are running the game with low fps, the doors will eventually crush your ship, failing the mission, to solve the issue would only be necessary to lower resolution. Such a bug is ridiculous If you think about it.
The game have also a number of coop activities, which I didn't had the chance of trying out, since none of my friends are playing the game currently, and neither looked in the server hub for open rooms to play, so I let them go.
Overall, the game Is fun If you want to pass the time and explode everything, If you want to try It out, be sure to take your mind of what you've seen on Saints Row 2 and Saints Row The Third, or else you will certainly give a not recommended to the game right on sight (Was going to do that at the intro areas, then decided to go ahead in the gameplay).

If you're looking for an alright single-player experience, this game is okay if fairly buggy [menus don't work sometimes, things break, data doesn't save very well]. The worst thing about it is that only the host's game saves, so up to 3 people will have no progress at all in the campaign or even with the characters they've been playing. I hope that this is just another bug for the pile, because it gives you the option to 'save' but it doesn't work.
They multiply the enemy count based on how many players there are, to ridiculous levels where there are clown cars of enemies as soon as you enter any screen.

There's nowhere near enough money to go around for 4 people to get any progress made at all.
Bug fixing needs to happen, and online play needs a closer look to understand the concept of 4-man multiplayer and what makes it fun [hint: not grinding money off hordes of guys for 2 hours just to get everyone started]

Honestly, the game completely lacks any and all substance. It's bland, forgettable, boring and tedious.
In the game, you play as an unnamed adventurer/trader, that sets forth to do one thing, become the Master Trader of the known universe/galaxy. One of the first missions is to find some chick that will give you a million credits on loan in order for you to buy a ship and start trading. You have a deadline when to get the million credits needed, and this formula repeats itself several times throughout the game, so much so that even the multiplayer is basically only that. Oh, and no one plays the multiplayer. In order to GET the million credits, you have to buy some commodities on Earth, and go to the Moon (which is just clicking a button) and selling your merchandise. Or you can do contracts. More on that later.
The trading system is very simple. You get to one of the merchants, you see the commodities they have for sale, and you buy it. There is a bar graph showcasing whether the market price for the item is declining or not, however the graph is pretty much nonsense, seeing as there's no trend whatsoever, and seems to be entirely, 100% random. To add to that, the trading is a pretty pathetic source of income, as even if you get lucky, you won't really earn a huge profit on anything you sell.
You can also find random commodities strewn throughout the worlds you find yourself, so there's no real reason to actually BUY commodities, as you'll find some semi-valuable stuff just laying on the floor in the map, free for the taking. Items range from wool to fetuses and radioactive metals and whatnot, and the "illegal" stuff is more valuable than the legitimate trading commodities. The game doesn't punish you for owning or selling illegal commodities, which was a wasted opportunity for some amusing gameplay as an actual smuggler. Shame.

The second source of money is through doing contracts or helping people out with arduous tasks. To get a contract, you have to go to the bar, where the barman will give you a target which you have to kill. This is where the game gets a slight instance of gameplay, by introducing an FPS arena, however, this falls flat as well, because the gunplay is so barebones it physically hurts to play through the FPS stages. The missions where you help people out aren't much better, as the case often is that you're simply collecting or buying X commodity and bringing it to some random dude or chick. Again, incredibly tedious.
Also, the game came out 2008 if I'm not wrong. I originally thought it came out around 1999, when Freelancer came out, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥2008????????????????????????????????
The music is obnoxious and not memorable in any way (read: elevator music), it features abysmal graphics, the little mechanics the game has are horribly unrefined, the economic system is non functioning, trading is next to useless unless you get some very rare, expensive commodities from missions, and the entire game feels like a chore.
Overall, I'd give it a 3/10, would not recommend unless you have literally nothing else to do in your life.

I genuinely don't understand all the negative reviews about this game.  The graphics are cutting edge for its time (even if the audio is cripplingly glitchy), the market mechanics are easy to understand and make sense, and the FPS element of the game is comparable to several others of its time, like Quake III: Arena - without the great multiplayer (which is the only thing about Quake III that actually *was* any good), and adding playing with commodity prices.   This game's multiplayer support was dismal, but as multiplayer was sort of an afterthought and not really what the game was about, I can forgive this.  I've played a lot of games where the single player campaign is good, and the multiplayer not so much.  Big deal.  Personally, I don't do a lot of multiplayer - meaning I don't live for it like other players, and my good review of a game doesn't depend on it having a good multiplayer mode, so it wasn't a major factor in my enjoyment of it.  When you design a game to be single player and add multiplayer support later in order to appease that crowd, it's always going to be lackluster at best.  Another thing others complained about was the price.  I got the game through Humble Bundle with a bunch of other titles for a very low price, so I don't really have a right to complain with the rest.  I'll be honest, by itself for 4.99 on Steam I probably would have never looked at it twice, but having got it in the bundle and trying it, I discovered that it's a decent game...though I honestly only kept playing it after I completed it in an attempt to get all the Steam achievements.  Difficulty isn't too severe - the market system is easy to figure out, and the FPS AI isn't particularly smart, though they do seem to have something approaching super-human aim (which is something that Quake III was also guilty of).  The challenges are actually fairly difficult to master, but the campaign is reasonably easy to defeat.  All this being said, I won't recommend the game - It's past its time.  I won't hate on it like others have - for its age, it's decent, but there's very little to attract my attention to it now.

This game is a lot of fun when the game is on. You're running along the stage, collecting clumbs of gold and other things to improve your score. I like the soundtrack a lot, and it is often syncronised for the moment you pick up gold. It is a nice touch. It also offers secret Retro levels and unlockable characters.
However, even though the gameplay is a lot of fun, it has two very frustrating things that destroy the fun for me. It is a terrible PC game. I want to be able to configurate my own keyboard controls the way it works best for me, and not be forced to use a specific way of playing. It offers three different way to control with keyboard, but they are all clumsy to play with. I want to be able to spread my buttons, and this game does not allow me to do that. But I am sure if you got a controller, you will have a much better time.
Even though you collect all the clumbs of gold and other collectibles on a level, you are not getting a perfect score unless you do a totally out of place minigame at the end of the level. Your character jumps into a cannon, a big target shows up, and you need to time it right and shoot yourself into the centrum of the target to receive the perfect score. If you miss, you are not getting a perfect score even though you collected everything, and you have to redo the entire level again to get to the mini game, and hopefully do better. I feel good about doing well on the level and have collected everything, but the mini game at the end is like a smack in your face. It is very demotivating to continue playing when it is like that.
Allow me to configurate my keyboard controls like any other average, PC game allows you to, and get rid of the out of place mini game at the end of every freaking level so I can get the perfect score I am supposed to get when I collect everything. When the game has been fixed, I will recommend it a lot. It really is a lot of fun.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is pretty rad! Playing this game is like going to your highschool reunion and realizing you are more amazing and more attractive than all of those d-bags. The game feels like that.
That being said. Go play it. I have sank WAY to much time into this, and after a few playthroughs, I can honestly say, Hairbrained Schemes nailed it again. They just keep getting better. My ONLY complaint is that the ending was not as good as Dragonfall, but it was still pretty damn good!

In short, Shadowrun Hong Kong can be described as the oriental PC-game edition of the cyberpunk fantasy world of the series, with core mechanic established in Shadowrun Returns, and general choice driven style of Dragonfall.

However, it is a pleasing surprise indeed that Hong Kong can not only stand on its own, it continues Harebrained Scheme’s journey of evolution and shows more polish, less bugs, and better writing than both earlier releases. Combat runs smoother than before, and is more engaging, introducing few nifty little new mechanics to the turn-based battle. Matrix is revamped for the better, offering more immersive experience of gliding through shadow world of information that runs at the very core of Shadowrun. From technical standpoint, it seems to run better and more reliably than earlier releases as well.

If you liked either of the earlier titles, I can safely vouch on the life of my firstborn that you will like this one too. For any newcomers to the franchise or the game series, this is, if not the ideal, so far the best entry point storywise to the world.
First, let me state that I will not shy away from occasional spoiler if review so demands. Secondly, the game reviewed is Deluxe Edition, which may or may not be reflected in the content. Thirdly, bulk of review is on the writing.

The first thing to highlight from this game is the quality of writing. It runs a much more self-contained narrative than its predecessors, thus rewarding it the “newbie friendly” seal offered to it a paragraph or so above this one. Where Returns was fairly inaccessible due to lore-heaviness that reminds me of titles such as Dragon Age:Origins and certain JRPG approaches that left me wanting a codex as a newly introduced participant in the events, Hong Kong has managed to strike a balance between lore and narrative: Even without knowing a thing about Flux state, Seattle, Tir, dragons, or Robert N. Charrette, you as a protagonist still have easily definable purpose (save yourself and your adopted father), complex relationship with your brother (slowly revealed in very natural dialogue and built by your decisions), and life as you make it in the city of Heoi and rest of Hong Kong while pursuing the said purpose.
Obviously a mammoth world spawning few DM core rule books will be reflected in any story set in it, but this time it is like a beautiful set piece draping around the narrative, further softened by intelligent references to modern day events and politics. This could have been a merely annoying wink aimed to stroke the egos of clammy neck-bearded armchair generals of game community, still weeping the loss of uniqueness as established by the first Fallout game, but instead they manage to serve as a pathway for original scifi thought-experiments aimed to describe possible futures of technology. While Shadowrun still stands with its chrome covered feet solely planted in contemporary sci-fantasy soil, it is small touches such as discussion of Euro Wars and Russian politics that distill the old school scifi into mix, elevating experience that could have been, completely legitimate, bare entertainment into something more.
The NPCs are more complex than seen before, relying, if not less, on stereotypes, different and by their own right interesting stereotypes. By giving character such as disgraced Red Samurai a personality that runs against the expected redemption arc, the game is playing player expectations resulting in refreshing take on the tropes of the industry. Not perhaps the most novel of ways, but much appreciated in its execution, which is both serious enough to not result in tiring fourth-wall breaking hipster winks, but not too serious. Same can be said about entire game, it avoids both pitfalls that could potentially ruin it: overbearing pathos and crippling self-awareness.
Final point about writing is a double edged sword: the interactions and reactions of the protagonist are more varied than before, allowing more free headcanon building than earlier. However, it is somewhat obvious it is just that, written (and mostly typo free) representation of how the player portrays their character inside their mind. I doubt most dialogue choices actually change anything in the game, merely the way I think about it. And even then, it is corralling the character into certain mold. For me this is enough, the illusion of choice is oftentimes as good as actual choice. However, keep in mind I say this having played 500 hours of Crusader Kings II with most elaborate narratives running inside my mind.
There is not much to say about actual gameplay, as it remains largely unchanged from Dragonfall. You point, you click, and move about in a beautiful handpainted isometric world. Your team has turns, enemy team has turns. Occasionally someone does damage. For me it is a plus, since I have enjoyed the fights since first installment. There are some novel elements, such as Gaichu’s sword styles or Koschei’s melee, but whether this is refreshing enough for those who want novelties, I cannot say. The battles do run more smoothly though, with less waiting and faster animation.
The major revamp of the game is that of Matrix, and despite resounding grumbling heard across interwebs, I argue it is an excellent revamp. You have to time yourself to glide through watcher IC occupied systems unseen, and use your memory and reflexes to hack gates to access information you need. For the first time, the Matrix provides some challenge and immersion.
As conclusion, Shadowrun: HK is a very good game. Due to its smart writing and integration of both game and real world lore I would hazard to say it is excellent specimen in its genre. The gameplay is familiar, but more polished, with one or two larger changes, for better. The game is as beautiful as the mechanic allows it to be, with excellent music. Setting is organic and interesting, and much more welcoming than earlier titles have had. However, certain gameplay issues, such as clunky inventory and illusion of choice, do remain in this one too. Yet it gives hope that the next title will continue the steady learning process and increase in quality Harebrained has shown throughout the series.

Mafia II is one of the greatest story ever told in a game to this day. It has to go down in history as one of the most mature, well written and acted stories ever. The characters are magnificent, and all have a distinct personality. It's such a shame that the original 180 side missions, explorable sicily, more weapons and cars were cut from the product we see today, but it's still amazing. The only dissapointing thing is the ending, but hopefully it gets resolved in the third installment.
Most of the time you'll be driving around the beautiful world of Empire Bay, however the fact there are no side missions makes it very empty. The wrest of the time you will be shooting the living crap out of everyone that stands in your way with a superb cover-based shooting system (It's nothing new, but it's great). This might get a bit boring, but you will want to get through it to watch the absolutely amazing cutscenes, and see how the main protagonist's story unfolds.
Buy this game if you're looking for a mature, and phenomenal story, and you dont mind a bit of cover-based shooting and driving in the 36 cars which are actually taken from the time period. It's great to see the character progress, and the city with it, but you'll probably only play this game for 11-15 hours the story offers.

I once fought a battle of annihilation against a foe for control over three bridges. The long back-and-forth struggle to seize a foothold beyond the river left the two southern crossings destroyed, and myself decidedly on the defensive.
Earlier, my bitter retreat across the middle span, fought just to buy my engineers enough time to demolish the traverse and delay my rival's advance, had cost me the bulk of my complement. Indeed, the brutal attrition reduced my forces to merely a pair of depleted rifleman squads and an antiaircraft half-track. The adversary quickly seized his opportunity, and readied an offensive to take the northern crossing. Anticipating that the Germans would act swiftly, I maneuvered my pitiful army in a desperate bid to delay the inevitable.
To serve as a screen for my sole remaining vehicle, I hastily positioned my undermanned troops behind a ruined wall for what I recognized to be the last firefight of the match. As they stared down the barrels of their weapons into the fog of war, they grasped that we had no hope of winning, but not a soul entertained any thought of retreat. Such was the mettle of men those days.
Out of the darkness rose a faint whine. My boys shifted nervously as the wail grew into a hellish crescendo that I knew all to well. On the far bank, a Tiger appeared on approach, her monstrous proportions dwarfing even the wrecked Shermans and Panzer IVs that her mudguards tossed aside. This infernal machine spearheaded a column of battle-hardened and well-equipped grenadiers, their eyes fixed on the defenceless bridgehead that so many of their Kameraden had fallen in vain to capture. Vengeance burned in their hearts, and the reckoning was soon upon us.
As the opposition charged toward my beleaguered defenders, the lines exchanged withering salvos. In a gesture of futility, I rolled my M15A1 forward, within range of the attackers, and pinned them in the mud of the riverbank. In response, my opponent ordered his mechanical beast to cross, planning to bring her fearsome 88mm gun to bear. Outrageously, my nemesis then called down a strafing run on my infantry, killing them to a man. How could such cruelty exist in a world where my soldiers had displayed such honor only moments before? I cursed bitterly as my GIs' bloody limbs rained through the billowing smoke and dust that shrouded the battlefield, and prepared to surrender.
Suddenly, to the astonishment of all, my AA half-track, in a burst of autocannon fire, downed the Stuka, and the flaming wreckage crashed into the weakened trestles, which gave way. The deck collapsed under the enormous weight of the tank, plunging the crew and the surrounding infantrymen to their watery graves. Only a handful of survivors remained, trapped and suppressed on the near bank, where my M15A1's machine guns made mincemeat of them.
I then rebuilt my forces, crossed the river, and vanquished the enemy.

Company of Heroes 2 is an absolute gem of the RTS world. It combines so many elements of different games and genres and brings them together in a masterful way. Sometimes it feels like imbalanced ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but then you realize that you just didn't understand a game mechanic, and then it becomes clear that you simply made the wrong decision. It is a game that punished bad choices and rewards tactical strategy very heavily. The beauty of this game is that it is different from the traditional RTS style of "Highest actions per minute (APM) = skill and victory". It abandons this way of thinking in favor of a more strategic approach. Your reflexes and memory are not what make you a good player, it is your strategy and decision making.
Strategy games should be about strategy, not reflexes.

This weird little game is an absolute delight.
You're a generic JRPG hero in a generic JRPG kingdom who has to keep moving east because a fog of darkness is coming in from the west and erasing everything it touches. The way this works in play is that every step you take causes the map to scroll to the right. It's a turn-based system like you see in most roguelikes, except instead of creeping around a dungeon at your leisure, you're trying to climb up the down escalator. Every now and then the evil wizard responsible for the death fog warps in and tries to kill you for a few dozen turns, but if you can get strong enough you can kill him and win the game.
Loot what you can as you go and just keep moving. You can duck into a dungeon in the hopes of finding a few treasure chests, but you run the risk of not being able to find an exit before the darkness swallows the building. It never stops being a challenge and you always have to think about what you're trying to do.
"Winning" by killing the bad guy is relatively easy. The REAL point of the game is to find secrets and alternate endings.

Now what can i say about this game? That it is worth the money. It is a small game with only one purpose for you. Go forth and kill stuff. But there is a twist to it. The World is ending and you are the legendary hero to venture out and try to get ahead of what is coming after you to kill you. And what is that right behind you? Pure Darkness.
This game leads in a certain direction and that one is Right. You go as far as you can get to meet at the end the Bad guy to stop the End of the World. But that is not an easy task. Even though this game is semi roguelike you wont have that much trouble with it like other roguelike games. Over the time of you playing you will die. But everytime you can transfer items into a little box that is between the dimensions. And as soon as you visit a new world you can decide if you want to take it with you or not. This makes the game a bit more enjoyable and easier for you. But in the end it depends on you how it ends.
The game brings you into a randomly generated world. Here will the Adventure begin and here you can do whatever you want. Go on and kill some bad guys. You are the Hero. Go into the Taverns and buy gear and let the people help you. Or just kill them and their guards. That is right. You are allowed to do everything you want. Kill, destroy and so on and so forth. But there is a nice twist to it. If you are the great Hero you are able to find people that want to help you defeating the bad guy. And since everyone trusts you they will not attack you when seeing you. If you do attack other people though the game will punish you. The word goes around very fast and in other inns or taverns the guards will recognize you for what you did and will try to kill you. But not only the guards will turn aggressive but also the other people.
So it is up to you what will happen in the game. At the very end it is the bad guy who you want to kill. But it depends on you how easy or hard this may be.

Factoid shotgun blast to the FACE:
This game is grindy, doesn't tell you where to go, or how to get there. It doesn't tell you what items do, or let you preview special moves before you buy them. The game is surprisingly tough, with enemies that will play the pack of wolves to your wounded moose. At the time of this review, there are also a handful of glitches that need to be addressed (though nothing that reached out and slapped the future controller from my hand).
If you're still reading:
Wonderful art in this game, combined with a great sense of humor. Experimenting and exploring is fun and rewarding (sorta rhymed?), and seeing your character come to life with amazing new moves as you progress is a joy. Lots of variety in the characters you can pick, with not only vastly different styles, but also functionalities--there's someone for everyone here (and you may just surprise yourself when it comes to your favorite. I picked Bruno, the Luchador, and I think he's great).
As for the actual combat, controls are nice and snappy, allowing for long and creative combos that only evolve as you grow your character. I will say, as a criticism, that for a few of the moves you can purchase, the instructions for pulling them off are too vague; one move for Bruno is listed as "J,P (after Jumping Drop Kick)." I tried every iteration of that description that I can imagine, and I still can't seem to make anything happen. This will hopefully be addressed in time, and it isn't a bad enough problem, to me, to warrant a thumbs down (INCOMING OLD MAN COMMENT: Back in the day, we had vague move lists in our illustrious, opulent instruction manuals all the time!)
Enemies in this game are as varied as the player characters, with different moves and A.I. that make you consider who's around you, when it's safe to attack, and what strategy you should use in a given moment. It's a game about being smart and controlling space, like any good beat-em-up aspires to be, instead of some brain-dead button masher.
Music and sound? While I was hoping to hear more remixes of the original RCR's tunes, what is present and new seems good enough, though not as catchy or memorable as what was in the old NES game (of course, the nostalgia is strong with this one, so opinions may vary). Sound effects are very reminiscent of the NES era--no complaints.
Here's what I'm gonna say:
If you're the kind of person who is used to the game design foibles of yesteryear--being pushed out of the proverbial nest into a world that wants to kill you--mitigated by a tutorial that doesn't really do anything to help in the long run, then you're going to dismiss the negatives of this game with a wave of the hand before seeking and appreciating all the good there is to be found (and there is a LOT of good!). And, if you like a good grind like I do, then this is the most fun you'll have farming for goodies and leveling up.
However, if you're the kind of person who wants instant gratification, thorough tutorials, move flow charts, a linear sense of progression, and you hate dying a lot in games, then you and I can never be friends.
Overall, I give it a buy it/10.

I gotta say, I really wanna like this game, I know there is something special here. But the game is criminally unbalanced, even just on story mode. It might not even be based on the difficulty techincially, it could just be left up to very poor design choices. Overwhelming enemies on single player alone, citizen that when damaged causes cops to appear (which can be reset when entering a hideout, but hey they aren't always near you when you need it), enemies that back away from you constantly and you have to have play cat and mouse just to catch them while other enemies take swings at you, long committed animations for wiffing grabble attempts which leave you painfully wide open, disgusting amount of time eatting pavement when knocked to the ground vulnerable for cheap hits from enemies, the list goes on. I know keeping the old school charm is a must, and it does beautifully might I add, but it should only of been aestheticlly, as the old gameplay that is clunky and unintuitive is no good anymore. And I'm not saying the money grind, or the amount of money that it takes to buy abilities, or when dying means losing half your money, those are fine to a point, but when really bad decisions get mixed in with these you get a very flawed and messy experience. There are challenging games, punishing games, by intentional, rational design, i.e Bloodborne, Bayonetta, Devil May Cry, etc. Those games have their own flaws but have overall challenge based around skill and learning the game, while River City Ransom: Underground is challenging and punsihing in an unrewarding way based on bad design. Hopefully, they will patch and rebalance the game if they can, which I hope they do, even balancing a couple of the issues listed would make for a better experience, but until then, buy at your own risk for a varied experience. If your an avid RCR fan, you should know what to expect to a certain degree, otherwise read up and be wary.

It's a welcome face lift to a familiar classic, combined with a unique cast of characters, each doling out pain with different and interesting fighting styles. Everything that made RCR great, such as the spas and food items that help buff stats to make you stronger, as well as classic lines like BARF! are present.
Granted, there IS room for improvement, as there are several issues with the game that I came across. For example, getting lost in the thrill of button mashing kind of screws you over, as there will be times when a dialogue or hint box will pop up for a second, and you won't have the time to stop mashing away, as any button press will confirm that you've already read the hint or tutorial message, even if you so much as push the d-pad or thumbstick in any direction, when you've never even took the time to read it.
Other than that, if you're a fan of beat-em-ups mixed with rpg elements, definitely give this game a go.

Ignore the reviews...people are angry because you cannot sync your regular account with your steam account. The game is utterly fantastic! 12 on 12 naval battles where fast twitch reflexes do not apply. If you stink at shooters like me but want to kill stuff, this is the game for you! It's all about positioning and developing good aim.
You can play as a destroyer, battleship, or cruiser and there are numerous countries. You can play them all. Despite being free, it is not pay to win even though there are premium ships there are far better ships you can earn with the credits you get from fighting. Premium ships are not the best ships in the game. People buy them because they give you a bonus to credits to get regular ships faster or sometimes just for historical reasons. but the best ships like the Bismarck, Fletcher or the Yamato are free. But the best ships are free if you grind them like the level 8 Bismarck or the level 9 Fletcher. You can sell your ships as you advance or get more port slots and keep them all. You can purchhase more slots or even win slots in challenges at times. You can add skins to your ships which makes them better and you win these too, although there are also premium ones.
Each day you get boxes after you earn enough credits and they can be full of goodies like free credits, signal flags, and even premium ships...that's right...the kind you normally have to pay for. Of course the odds are very low of getting a ship, but all the stuff you get is worthwhile.
There are campaigns and challenges in which you can earn other goodies which makes battles more interesting. One of your challenges may be to torpedo 10 ships over the course of a weekend followed by another challenge to sink 5 battleships. It gives you goals besides just fighting to win or grinding for the next ship. At higher levels the grind is significant, so I break it up by trying out new ships and countries when I get tired of the same ship. You also get captain skills and you can mold your captain to your play style. There are clans but I haven't tried those yet.
The battles can be epic! I was in my Konig (German Battleship) today and I rounded an island and saw another battleship (the Texas...a premium ship) quite close by. We were at about the same health level. We began dueling each other and I was winning. Then I started getting shot form behind. A destroyer had snuck up on me. He had very little health left due to a previous battle but was still dangerous. He unleashed his torpedoes and one hit me. I used a repair immediately since I was flooding, as my secondary guns, which I had improved with my captain skill credits started lighting into him. One of my secondarys caught him on fire and he sank several moments later! I continued to fight the Texas even though he now had more health than me due to the torpedo  that hit me. I hit him with He shells and started a fire. He had a repair ready and put it out much to my chagrin. I angled my ship straight towards him to give him less of a shot since I was really low on HP and his salvo only hit me once for minor damage. I shot my HE shells again and got really lucky starting two fires this time!!! He had just used his repair so this was critical because ho could not put them out. Even though he had more health than me, he started to turn away and I switched to AP shells. We were so close to each other...it was nerve wracking. i thought about ramming him which would sink us both, a kamikaze tactic if you think you may lose and a ship is close enough warrant it, but my secondarys were pummeling himso I decided to just fight it out and hope for the best. My guns were now up and I waited until he turned broadside to finish me off when I shot off my AP rounds and hit his citadel sinking him instantly!! It was glorious!!
I'm not a great player...I'm not even average... but I have great games like this one at least a few times in a long gaming session. And sometimes I get totally annihilated. But it's a blast either way. If you make a mistake and get sunk right away, you can leave the battle and still get credits so you can go back to port and get another ship and fight right away. You can even view your score afterwards on the ship that got sunk. It's so much fun! And when you get enough credits for your next ship, it feels so rewarding! You get free credits too and these can also get you ships. I use these to bypass ships I don't care for because there are some ships as you advance towards your goal that just plain suck.
Try this game out....you have nothing to lose...It can be played completely free!!! and once you get hooked and you will, you'll probably get a premium account because you'll be like me and want every ship in the game...lol! Don't get discouraged if you get sunk quickly or lose five or six battles in a row...it takes a little practice and teamwork and sometimes you just sail into a bad spot. You'll have good games and bad games...no big deal. But if you continue to play and learn how each class of ship works, you'll start to get better and better and it becomes even more fun! Take care my friends! Hope to see you in a glorious warship next to me in game sometime!!

This game is nihilist art. The Germans, not satisfied with their extensive library of ho-hum simulators and scat porn, have combined the two in a toilet management tycoon game that almost invariably becomes a titanic, never-ending struggle for toilet primacy - albeit solely in an unnamed German city. As people will never stop pooping, so will the Toilet Wars rage for eternity.
I mean, that's probably because the game's already simple mechanics are broken six ways from Sunday, but still.
One thing this game has going for it, apart from the 1997-era graphics, Google Translated text, and general shovelware aesthetic, is the number of victory conditions to choose from. I say this because picking the default condition, to achieve the highest rank of Toilet Tycoon, will most likely end up in defeat or stalemate. (The AI difficulty is hidden in the options menu and defaults to 'normal', for what that's worth.)
If a stalemate happens, you're in for a long period of spamming chance-based sabotage attacks at the AI's toilets. The hope is that their toilets will become filthy enough for the sanitation inspector to revoke their permit, allowing you to swoop in and buy the toilet stalls. The AI will try do the same to you. The fact that this sabotage consists of hiring goons for several thousand Euros each to smash or puke on the toilets (mainly puke), complete with sound effects, is just icing on the urinal cake.
Despite the oodles of money you and the AI will have from your turbo-charged solid emerald thrones with attached cup holders - that people incidentally don't mind paying for by the way - sabotage attacks and inspector visits can only be carried out once a turn. And since the sabotage always has a chance of failing, and since the inspector's mood fluctuates daily, it could always be for nothing.
The dominant player (did I mention there's only 2 players to a game?) is continually given free toilet items every turn from a bingo, and while it's only really helpful when players are initially building up, good rolls count for more than skill there. Random events can also turn the tide, although in practice the AI always eventually uses them to screw you in a stalemate. Research is also luck-based, which means even more wasted money.
This game is therefore like World War 1 by way of Dungeons & Dragons, with toilets, where fittingly enough you can only play as Germany. The Great Toilet War module for 5e. And this isn't even mentioning:
* the stupidly opaque and quite possibly broken rating system which the Toilet Tycoon victory condition revolves around,
* the fact that there's really nothing else to do once players are established other than re-enacting the Great War and questioning why this is even on Steam,
* the criminally small un-updated 640x480 resolution buttons that make actually
your toilets a chore,
* the fact that there's an entire fourth of the game world with substantially less traffic which means starting there is a death knell,
* the eternal mystery that is the "Pig of the Round",
* or the inane looping music that will drive you up the wall.
You'll enjoy seeing your numbers go up, of course, and bad game aficionados will obviously like this one too. But while most of the other victory conditions let the player win, in true nihilist fashion the game won't actually
, and thus the only real victory is pressing Quit.

A combination of almost-broken controls and unfair game mechanics kills this game's fun.
I thought the game's premise was intriguing, and not at all crappy.  I got this game (DRM free) in a Groupees Bundle earlier this year (2015).  It's a turn-based game where you compete against the CPU to try to own and equip the most profitable toilets.
It has two major problems.  One, your CPU opponent can send the sanitation board after you, and even if you cleaned your toilets 100% in your prior turn, they can cite you for having a terrible mess and divest you of that toilet and all its equipment.  Not fun, and doesn't feel fair.
Two, the icons to control the various functions of the game are so, so tiny, it's an exercise in tedium just to click the buttons.  And you have to click a lot of buttons to equip a new toilet, so the combination of these two flaws (losing your toilet and all its equipment, and the tedium of equipping a new one) kills this game.  Either alone might be tolerable.  Together they are infuriating, adding insult to injury.
I guess I played about 90 minutes before giving up on it.  It's definitely a turd.
I loaded this up and let it sit (no "sit" or "load" jokes, please) in order to accumulate playtime, just so I could warn you all away from this.  I see that the existing negative reviews aren't particularly informative.  I hope this one is more helpful.
Finally, I just want to say that it is obnoxious for Valve to require playtime (and not just ownership) of a game before reviewing.  It should be obvious by now that many people play games before they get released on Steam, and those people have legitimate opinions, too.  It's also obnoxious that they have yet to fix their review-posting bug whose only workaround is to post a one-word review and then edit it.

While Puzzle Agent 1 had quite a few simple puzzles, Puzzle Agent 2 is significantly simpler in its puzzle design and provides almost no challenge whatsoever. It is almost like a rehash of a lot of the easy puzzles from the first game.
In fact, this is my biggest gripe with the game: a lot of the puzzles feel like simple variations of the puzzles in Puzzle Agent 1. While this is not true for all the puzzles, I can't help but feel this is a lazy follow-up game.
A lot of the same characters and locations are re-used, and even the story becomes rushed and unfinished at the end. It *does* conclude - unlike Puzzle Agent 1 - however so much is either glossed over or ignored that it's just not the satisfying ending that you'd want.
Get Puzzle Agent 2 *only* if you have a burning desire to finish the story started in Puzzle Agent 1. Otherwise, I would recommend skipping it unless you can get both games together for cheap.

The plot was definitely improved since the first game, with deeper ties into Scoggins and new characters. Puzzles were also improved, with new puzzle types and concepts popping up around the game, preventing that repetitiveness feeling the first game got.

It's definitely worth $5, and it may even be worth $10 to you depending on how much you loved the first game and the series' story.
One note, though: This game has Steam achievements, but far more than the number of those visible. Each puzzle has a secret achievement and some events have their own secret achievements too. In addition, the "Puzzle Agent!" achievement is "bugged". The actual rank appears but the ingame requirements aren't correct - you must complete every puzzle with a score of 10/10 to unlock the achievement.

The controls are just horrible.  You have to spend a bunch of time practicing by yourself just to understand where your characters attacks are going to go, because they're completely unpredictable and nonsensical otherwise.  For example, your character might have an 8-hit combo for their 'Fast' combat stance, but even if you stand still and just hold down attack, only two of those attacks will actually place in front of you.  The others will have you rolling and cartwheeling around, attacking to the sides and stuff.  Now factor in that these attacks are modified by directional movement, and every character has different attack patterns for three different stances.  How the hell is the player supposed to get this under control?  Hit detection feels really strange on top of that, and the game gives you very little feedback to indicate what's happening.
As a result, fights feel like a bunch of spamming that has your characters flying all over the place, and you just hope that you're going to connect with something before the other person does.  Not a very satisfying combat system, and the combat system is the entire game.
I'm sure it could get interesting between people who have spent hundreds of hours memorizing the attack patterns of various character/weapon combinations, to have some chance of matching them effectively, but I'm definitely not the type who cares to do that.
I understand that it's early access, and I'll give it a chance when closer to a finished product.  Sadly, I'm not expecting much.  They need to deeply rework the basic functioning of their combat system to be playable, in my opinion.

Making a recommendation for Shadowrun HK is a pretty straightforward thing: Did you enjoy the previous Shadowruns by Harebrained? Then you'll most likely enjoy this one as well.
While it isn't as much of a clear case of a pure upgrade and improvement like with Dragonfall and the first official campaign SR:HK added enough small changes and toys so that you have some stuff to experiment with while keeping most of their tried and true formula intact. It uses the combat system of Dragonfall Director's Cut and also has the customizable perk systems for your fellow runners which was also introduced in Dragonfall DC which is a very nice addition.
Some of the completely new stuff include new spells, some changes to older spells, new more varied drones like sniper and auto fire variants, new decking rigs, a new cyber affinity skill for chrome and mostly more chrome itself, especially cyber weapons like cyber claws or a cyber leash.
The matrix segments also got overhauled, it offers more visual variations but the biggest change is that you can sneak around and crack firewalls with a minigame in order to avoid combat in the matrix almost completely if you wish. If you don't you can just let seekers spot you until defender drones spawn which makes the matrix pretty much play out like in the previous shadowruns. The sneaking in the matrix is frankly extremely clunky but the option to avoid fights is a very welcome one and even if you trigger the alarm the fights aren't as grindy/boring as in the previous games' matrix sections.
Another change which I really liked is that in general you have a lot more opportunities to use non combat skills and quick thinking to avoid a lot of fights, a lot more so than in previous instalments. Which is not only nice for roleplaying reasons but it also is very handy in situations where you would be kinda under-equipped and the fight pretty darn difficult.
The story/mission structure hasn't really changed, you eventually end up in an hub area from which you launch your missions, and you're mostly free to chose which mission to tackle next.
Your fellow Runners are a pretty interesting bunch again with entertaining/interesting dialogues between missions even though I have to say that some tended to be a bit less memorable than in Dragonfall. I feel that especially with Is0bel they could have done more - while her personal quest was very enjoyable the hub interactions with her felt rather bare bones. Props for the other companions though.
Another nice touch is that you get a chance to have a small conversation with each mercenary runner you can hire. Similar to what Dragonfall DC did with Lucky Strike just a bit less detailed but for all mercenary runners.
The plot itself is arguably more simple than Drgaonfall but personally I feel that Hong Kong has the best atmosphere of the Shadorun games yet which is saying something because I always enjoyed the setting and its atmosphere a lot. The music is spot on and helps to reinforce the atmosphere and the cutscenes and writing further cement it.
And the basic point remains that I very much enjoy the setting of Shadowrun, its cyberpunk and its bleak dystopian world and HK does a good job of bringing the setting to life yet again.
In conclusion it's easy to recomment Shadowrun HK to fans of the series, the only real flaws I can think of is that the pure plot is rather simple if that is very important too you - or that if you feel like you've grown bored of the previous games' formula then this game prolly doesn't add enough new things for you to to shake things up.
Otherwise I really enjoyed the game, especially that you have more dimplomatic/non-combat opportunities than ever. But most importantly for me I absolutely adored the atmosphere of the game and the mystery of it. It's gonna be interesting to see how a replay feels after the mystery has been lifted - I guess we'll see soon enough ;)

When you start playing Mafia 2, you might think that you are going to end up with money, cars, women, respect, freedom… What you will soon realize is that you get all of that, and more!!! You’ll go to prison, though only for a short while; it will teach you how to fight and survive and you will meet a man that will be like a father to you. All of it will end with the blood of your friends.
RESET, RESET, RESET...
You play as Vito Scaletta, a good guy just trying to find his way in life. Starting off in the 1940s you just get home from the war, not too anxious to get back to the fight. Your best friend Joe comes to your aid offering you a way out, if you decide to accept his help you could make it big. Or you could go back to the war, and die…
Ever play a game of tug-o-war? That is what this game feels like. You have nothing, you get some, you have nothing, you get some, you have nothing, you get some…
There is about 10 hours of gameplay in story mode, and most of that is spent driving, then you have over 2 hours of cutscenes (which are pretty good). Then of course you have the DLC. All in all, you will fork out about $20 for a day, or several depending on the amount of time you spend during a gaming session.
Though the game is a few years old now (2007), it is still a good one, and doesn’t make you feel like you’re playing an OLD game.

I tried to like it. I really tried. But there were just too many poor design decisions. So first I shall start with the most objective: The multiplayer is exceptionally poorly balanced to account for the commanders they want you to buy with real money (about $3 each). To unlock a commander you need 12,000 points. To have a chance at getting 500 points, or a random commander, or a vehicle skin you need to earn 6,000 experience. To get experience you need to play a multiplayer match or skirmish (1500xp for playing + 500xp for winning each) So to have that chance at obtaining 1/24th of a relevant commander you need to either win 3 matches or lose 4 matches. You see why this could be problematic? This means that to unlock ONE commander you need to play a minimum of between 72 and 96 matches. For every commander. For a game you paid money for.
"But supposing I don't want to use those fancy commanders, surely a strategy game would depend more on one's strategic ability?"
You'd think that wouldn't you? As it turns out the answer is 'no.' Now this part might vary for you as I am definitely not a good strategist however it became immediately apparent that of the two factions you are given in the vanilla game, The Soviets and the Wehrmacht Ostheer, the Russians are inferior in nearly every aspect. Theoretically they are supposed to dominate the early game which might have been true when this game first was released but now they merely dominate the morgue. The initial moments of the game usually involve sending out conscripts to get resources and to die from machine gun fire. To deal with the machine gun you either send a sniper team and have them die from wandering too close to said machine gun on account of not being able to see the gun due to the sight radius conveniently being barely outside the machine gun’s range, or you try to flank with conscripts and remember bolt action rifles are only slightly more effective than spitting in their face, or you send in a scout car with flamethrowers and have the basic german infantry fire a Panzerfaust at the apparently tin foil engine, or you grab a mortar and wait for them to die of old age while you announce your waste of manpower, or you ignore the one MG to try and cap everything else to find he used his engineers/grenadiers to cover all his other points with machine gun bunkers and kill you, or you can attempt to throw a Molotov and get shot because apparently the only guy who knows how to throw one was in absolute dire need of a nap and decided to take it right when you ordered him, alternatively finding out that its tiny area of effect damage over time merely tickles the now repositioned machine gun team. But eventually you figure something out and dislodge the MG to advance and run into Panzergranadiers which are superior to all of your infantry in every way. You don’t even get automatic weapons outside of commander specializations while these assault rifle wielding ubersoldatten can be upgraded with panzershreks and kill half your tanks in two hits. Meanwhile, it takes a dedicated Soviet anti tank gun 9+ shots to annoy a panther heavy tank. That’s not even mentioning the dlc factions.
I uhhh… should probably stop now. You get the idea. Its bad. Don’t get it.

The injustice of the enemy having everything they need to capture the somewhat stupid capture points is too much. You have to struggle to build a sizeable army to just capture one ! If you move too soon they walk all over you. If you wait you run out of time.Then there are the special conditions you are stuck with. They can have as many tanks as they wish.you can have none. On the subject of tanks you can have as many anti-tank guns as you can build but they never see a tank even when it is right next to them,and therefore are useless. If the enemy starts the other side of the battlefield from you why are they behind you on some missions ? In the few missions you do not have to capture victory points you can have some excellent battles without fear of running out of time. A good game but NOT by any means a great one.
