As it stands now, this game can't get a recommendation. There are too many problems.  If the problems are fixed, then I'd gladly recommend it.  I have a feeling that the critical problems will be fixed, otherwise it would mean that the project was a failure.
River City Ransom: Underground (RCR:U) is a 2-D side scrolling beat 'em up that presents itself as a sequel to the Nintendo game River City Ransom.  RCR:U offers online play and single-player play, the beat 'em up features management of character stats and abilities that are purchased with money you earn.  Your character also has a level that acts as a ceiling and threshold for your stats and abilities, your level is determined by your experience points, earned by defeating enemies.  When you defeat an enemy, it also spews out its lunch money, often exclaiming the funny BARF! from River City Ransom.  RCR:U has a good mechanical core for a beat 'em up however needs certain problems addressed.
Critical problems:
- If you play multiplayer and use your single-player save slot, the single-player save slot data is wiped of all the progress you had made alone.  If you wish to return that same save slot with your single player campaign after playing online, all your progress (money, items, stats, experience) is gone.  Unfortunately the only solution to this now is to have two separate saves, however the threat of losing all your progress has severely dampened the online play.  Last time I tried to play online there were only 3 games hosting.
- For the single player campaign that I completed, there were 2 crashes.  Both of which happened in the final stages, I won't mention specifics because it's spoiler free.  However it was frustrating to have a crash at the final boss.
- Pursuit scenes may have bosses/enemies that move too quickly to catch.  These scenes are required to complete the story, it would be helpful if the speed of the bosses/enemies were consistent.  Many players appear to succeed at these missions when the boss/enemy pauses before a ladder or door due what appears to be glitches. That's how it finally worked for me.  Pursuit scenes need to be more stable.
- After beating the final boss, you may not have 100% completion.  Now this doesn't sound bad on the surface, however after you beat the game you are stuck in a loop of watching the final cutscene and the credits.  You have no opportunity to complete the game to 100% and presumably unlock the new game+ option?   After beating the game without 100% completion it will also strangely recommends that you stay with the story level difficulty.  Either way, if completion matters to unlocking intended content, your original save should have been sufficient to complete your goal of 100%.
Although they are critical problems, it appears that these problems are resolvable.  If they are resolved, then I'll change up the review to a recommendation.

Presentation
Steam Sales are always a great way to buy more games than you'll ever be able to play, but between all the big purchases you will often find some random games to keep you busy when there's nothing else; Space Trader: Merchant Marine is exactly that kind of game, but unlike most small, indie games this one managed somehow to keep me around more than it should have, just because at its core, it's an addictive experience. The premise of the game is simple: you are a new trader trying to find your way in this business and since you don't own a ship yet you need to find someone who is willing to give you one. What follows is a simple story and you will see the little twists coming from miles away, but even with that in mind, the missing excitement of what's going to happen next isn't the thing that will keep you around. The campaign has only five chapters and once you understand the mechanics of the game you will have no problem making millions from trading food stamps, oil or even organs. This game simulates the stocks trades perfectly, following the same: buy low, sell high premise, and even though at first it may be hard to figure out how to make all those millions, once you get the idea, it will be only profit for you from that point on. There's no real reward for doing this except the fact that once you reach a goal you will advance to the next chapter and start all over, trading between different planets, but that little sense of advancement is what will keep you playing.
Rating: 5.5
Gameplay
The gameplay in Space Trader is pretty straight forward: you start on a planet and you have to buy commodities that will bring a profit and travel to another planet to sell them at a higher price, keeping a constant watch on the time limit that each mission has, calculating the profit per shipment and the travel time in order to choose the best option. Finding good deals is easy since those always have a gold star indicating that you should buy them, so eventually it becomes just a matter of having enough money in your pocket or enough cargo space, and your only enemy becomes the time as you carefully have to choose where to sell the stuff you just bought. You can make money by taking bounty missions from bartenders or by completing small tasks for different people, so it's always a good idea to talk with everybody because you might find out some interesting things or take on some missions that will give you some extra cash. The shooting mechanic feels old, but that's probably why it feels so addictive at the same time, as you will most likely instantly connect the dots between those shooting sequences and games like Doom, and even though all those bounty missions will get boring pretty soon as each map looks and feels the same and there are only two to three different types of enemies plus the target that you're supposed to assassinate, it is a good distraction from the boring buy and sell mechanic that the game generally delivers.
Rating: 6
Graphics
If you look at this game you will assume it was released in the early 2000's because it looks like it was made a generation ago; from the simple and stiff characters to the environments everything looks pretty bad and the repetitive level design doesn't help either. By the end of the game you will know every corner of each planet, you will start to love a certain section for how easy it is to complete a combat mission and you will hate another for how difficult it is.
Rating: 5
Audio
The sound in this game ain't exactly bad, but it's simply mediocre at best. The voice acting is horrible, but the soundtrack manages to save it sometimes, especially in the heat of a battle, but otherwise there is nothing that stands out, it simply gets boring as you will end up ignoring the other characters or laugh at how bad they sound no matter the serious, story essential thing they just said. There are intentional comic lines too, such as the robot that answers by saying WTF, but those only make the entire thing feel worse, as the game is undecided between trying to be serious and making fun of itself.
Rating: 5
Extras
After completing the main campaign you can also try the challenge mode that offers three extra missions that are pretty easy to complete and the only real challenge comes when you try to get the achievements, and if you're into that the game can get interesting and it has even some decent replay value as you can spend up to 18 hours struggling to complete everything. It's also supposed to have a multiplayer mode, which puts you and a friend in a race to get the most cash from those challenge missions, but after an hour of banging my head against the wall I couldn't figure out a way of making it work.
Rating: 5
Verdict
When a game is getting such a low score no one would actually recommend buying it, but in this case I'll make an exception: you should give it a try if it's on sale and you can get it for less than an euro, as for that amount of money it will keep you busy more than enough to justify the purchase. It is in no way a great game, one that you will remember after leaving it aside, but as long as you play it you will be entertained simply because it's so stupid it becomes like a good parody.
Rating Overall: 5.3

Ignore the reviews...people are angry because you cannot sync your regular account with your steam account. The game is utterly fantastic! 12 on 12 naval battles where fast twitch reflexes do not apply. If you stink at shooters like me but want to kill stuff, this is the game for you! It's all about positioning and developing good aim.
You can play as a destroyer, battleship, or cruiser and there are numerous countries. You can play them all. Despite being free, it is not pay to win even though there are premium ships there are far better ships you can earn with the credits you get from fighting. Premium ships are not the best ships in the game. People buy them because they give you a bonus to credits to get regular ships faster or sometimes just for historical reasons. but the best ships like the Bismarck, Fletcher or the Yamato are free. But the best ships are free if you grind them like the level 8 Bismarck or the level 9 Fletcher. You can sell your ships as you advance or get more port slots and keep them all. You can purchhase more slots or even win slots in challenges at times. You can add skins to your ships which makes them better and you win these too, although there are also premium ones.
Each day you get boxes after you earn enough credits and they can be full of goodies like free credits, signal flags, and even premium ships...that's right...the kind you normally have to pay for. Of course the odds are very low of getting a ship, but all the stuff you get is worthwhile.
There are campaigns and challenges in which you can earn other goodies which makes battles more interesting. One of your challenges may be to torpedo 10 ships over the course of a weekend followed by another challenge to sink 5 battleships. It gives you goals besides just fighting to win or grinding for the next ship. At higher levels the grind is significant, so I break it up by trying out new ships and countries when I get tired of the same ship. You also get captain skills and you can mold your captain to your play style. There are clans but I haven't tried those yet.
The battles can be epic! I was in my Konig (German Battleship) today and I rounded an island and saw another battleship (the Texas...a premium ship) quite close by. We were at about the same health level. We began dueling each other and I was winning. Then I started getting shot form behind. A destroyer had snuck up on me. He had very little health left due to a previous battle but was still dangerous. He unleashed his torpedoes and one hit me. I used a repair immediately since I was flooding, as my secondary guns, which I had improved with my captain skill credits started lighting into him. One of my secondarys caught him on fire and he sank several moments later! I continued to fight the Texas even though he now had more health than me due to the torpedo  that hit me. I hit him with He shells and started a fire. He had a repair ready and put it out much to my chagrin. I angled my ship straight towards him to give him less of a shot since I was really low on HP and his salvo only hit me once for minor damage. I shot my HE shells again and got really lucky starting two fires this time!!! He had just used his repair so this was critical because ho could not put them out. Even though he had more health than me, he started to turn away and I switched to AP shells. We were so close to each other...it was nerve wracking. i thought about ramming him which would sink us both, a kamikaze tactic if you think you may lose and a ship is close enough warrant it, but my secondarys were pummeling himso I decided to just fight it out and hope for the best. My guns were now up and I waited until he turned broadside to finish me off when I shot off my AP rounds and hit his citadel sinking him instantly!! It was glorious!!
I'm not a great player...I'm not even average... but I have great games like this one at least a few times in a long gaming session. And sometimes I get totally annihilated. But it's a blast either way. If you make a mistake and get sunk right away, you can leave the battle and still get credits so you can go back to port and get another ship and fight right away. You can even view your score afterwards on the ship that got sunk. It's so much fun! And when you get enough credits for your next ship, it feels so rewarding! You get free credits too and these can also get you ships. I use these to bypass ships I don't care for because there are some ships as you advance towards your goal that just plain suck.
Try this game out....you have nothing to lose...It can be played completely free!!! and once you get hooked and you will, you'll probably get a premium account because you'll be like me and want every ship in the game...lol! Don't get discouraged if you get sunk quickly or lose five or six battles in a row...it takes a little practice and teamwork and sometimes you just sail into a bad spot. You'll have good games and bad games...no big deal. But if you continue to play and learn how each class of ship works, you'll start to get better and better and it becomes even more fun! Take care my friends! Hope to see you in a glorious warship next to me in game sometime!!

Over the course of the last two weeks I've finally gotten around to playing Harebrained's Shadowrun Series and I fell in love with it.
The writing is ok, but the real strength lies in the NPCs and the way you get to explore their backgrounds in a very Bioware-esque fashion.
Hong Kong is probably my favourite of the bunch, because it really feels like the gameplay has been improved by a lot. I'm also a sucker for Chinese settings, so that helped as well.
That being said, the game is still a bit clunky and it feels unfinished at times.
There are many things that I'd like to see improved in the next iteration:
- Character Models: They have been improved by a bit, but they are still not good. Compared to the beautiful backgrounds, the characters stick out like a sore thumb when you zoom in on them. Also: we need a character creation screen with more customization options (height, stature, face, outfit etc.). The player character should feel unique and right now there is just not a lot you can do with it, aesthetically speaking. I spent hours editing my savegame and exploring the editor just to make my character look unique and cool.
- QA: While patches have been released very timely, we need better QA. Not just for bugs, also for typos. A game that relies so heavily on dialogues should not be littered with errors.
- More Weapons/Gadgets/Perks: Characters are too similar. More skills, weapon types & combat approaches. I really liked the non-lethal concept of Duncan's skillset - it would be great if Harebrained would expand on that and made NPC perks available to the player character. Hong Kong brought lots of new stuff in terms of Cyberweapons and Cyberware, which is a good tendency.
The game does have it's flaws, but I can definitely recommend it!

Disclaimer:  I was a Kickstarter backer for Shadowrun: Hong Kong.
I just finished the campaign and I believe it's easy to recommend Shadowrun: Hong Kong to both fans of Shadowrun and CRPGs alike.  Harebrained Schemes has been improving the gameplay, UI, combat and etc. with every new release they make and Hong Kong is easily the best in those regards.  I especially liked the upgrades to cybernetics even though I didn't use a cybernetic weapon myself.
Personally I thought the story in Dragonfall was better, but Hong Kong's story is still really good.  My main issue is how the main story is handled.  The story's main objective is left out for quite a long stretch (most of the game) until a series of missions at the end.  It reminds me a bit of Mass Effect 2, where most of the game is comprised of side missions you can either choose to take or ignore.  The side missions are all very well done, however, and so the game was still a blast to play through.  Dragonfall's narrative was just a bit better paced.
These games require a lot of reading and Hong Kong has the most text to read yet.  If this is a turn off then I'd suggest looking elsewhere.  But if walls of text do not scare you off then you're in for a great ride!
I just have these parting words for anyone about to purchase the game:
"Watch your back, shoot straight, conserve ammo, and never, ever, cut a deal with a dragon."

Choice is the name of the game of Shadowrun: Hong Kong, and while it rides that strength for most of the game, what you end up getting is a very inconsistent experience that has a lot of highs: but a lot of lows as well. Whether or not you'll be able to enjoy the game will be entirely based on who you are: are you a person who's willing to sacrifice consistency for high points, such as optional character's story telling and very indepth battling? Or will you have problem with the low points of missions that miss the mark completely and missing elements of narrative that tie things all together. In the end, I enjoyed my time with Shadowrun: Hong Kong, but the game will take a toll on you, and it's definitely going to cause a polar reaction out of people. Hello folks,
As you can see by the hours played I am not basing this on only a little time in the game. I also backed Shadowrun Returns and had about two hundred of hours on that game, beating it quite a few times. I have about one hundred hours on Dragonfall. I have played every video game based on shadowrun, including the FPS that other than races had little to do with Shadowrun. I picked up my first first edition books in June of 1990 from a little bookstore across from the docks in Port Angeles Washington. I own all the books, both role-playing materials and novels. I have run more games than I care to count and have been a fore-runner in the cries for more video games based on Shadowrun.
The first thing I am going to do is give rave reviews on the puzzle system for decking. It is interesting, provocative, and makes me feel as if I am achieving more than the original games afforded. I am looking forward to the evolution where a character can choose from a set of their own preferred visuals for the matrix, but I understand that incorporating those concepts are a long way off.
I also like the new system where I can initiate combat if I choose too. It incorporates stealth elements to a video game based on a role-playing game where the use of stealth is essential to succeed. This is very challenging for a Turn-Based Strategy (TBS) game to reproduce.
I like the TBS game style of play. I always have and always will. The character creation system is not far from the system in the game. I have concerns about the lack of cost correlation between race and points at creation. In the roleplaying game, you place points into the attributes before the racial changes take effect. It makes it worth it starting out to have an elf for the racial increases to quickness and charisma. I can tear apart any game based on a roleplaying game for the lack of ability to incorporate elements from the RPG correctly. It does not really degrade from the enjoyability of the game.
This game is fun with a great storyline. The amount of the information is large and if you are not a fan of reading text in the game you are going to have problems with this game. If you like a world rich with story and history, this game will make you very happy.
There are issues with glitches, but I only ran across one during my play through where it did not acknowledge my charisma correctly to afford me an opportunity in the tower. Glitches happen at release and take the time to resolve.
Good Hunting chummers!

I bought this game in a Humble Bundle package. It wasn't the game I wanted out of the bundle but I always install all the games just incase theres a hidden gem in there. I can happily say that this is a gem of a game.
Its very simple in its basic form. Jump gaps and objects. Duck under ledges and balls of death. Kick down barricades. Collect gold. Get highest score. Simple. But along with its nice art style and lovely music which if you haven't realised from the title of the game is linked into you collecting and jumping etc makes this a truely amazing fun game.
You will sit there for hours trying to beat friends scores. Not taking checkpoints to go for the challenge. Collecting all the Chests to get the unlocks. Theres a lot to this little game. Not only that it really is a challenge to play.

So all in all I would recommend this game all the day long. Yes it looks simple. Yes it plays simple. But there is a really big challenge infront of you if your up to it.
(You have been warned that this game is very addictive and falls into the "Oh just one more go" syndrome.)

This is a music game based on music that's not particularly interesting to listen to or "play" by kicking, jumping over and sliding under enemies (sometimes you do both at the same time).
Your contribution, however, that is to say: your accompaniment will always be in time, so there's that (unless you jump a bit too early/late). That's why you hated playing the recorder, the violin or whatever your parents, dear reader of Steam user reviews, forced upon you because they thought you were gifted (or could be brought to that state with the right amount of money).
It's payback time, it's video games.
The music has to be versatile (or reusable) enough to fit the themes of five distinct worlds of which only the first one is nice to look at; it works, I guess, but I hated having to hear the same stupid cadence at the end of a perfected stage. The arrangements are good, and it's surprisingly exhilarating to play syncopated drum kicks (by sliding and kicking) and phrasings (by collecting gold).
The progression is great, and yeah, this is where the game really shines, in my mind, it makes up for every shortcoming it might otherwise have. What you can (and will be asked to) do increases with every other level or so. There are always new mechanics to master and piece together in interesting ways, depending on your difficulty level and willingness to risk getting set back.
The humor is okay. The new art style is nice to look at (of which you'll see less and less as you progress, the worlds getting darker and darker, as I said earlier). The retro stages are better (and have different tunes depending on which world you encounter them in) than in the first game.
Oh, and you dance.

I'm really dissapointed by this game. There were a lot of cool ideas, QoL is better than the first, it looks crisper and should have been better in every way. The cover system is excellent, the tank combat is mostly fun, and its supposed to be all about spreading out, playing mobile and flanking.
In reality, its marred with frustrating problems. Tank combat usually isn't won by who has the better vehicles, who placed their mines better or who has their anti-tank guns in the right place, its one by whoever gets screwed over least by pathing. While blobbing is better than it was, the US and OKW are still absolutely insane at it. Flanking, the game's selling point, also tends to not work so well in 2v2 and up because the maps are narrow with strong defenses leading to MG and mortar lockdowns if you're lucky and British emplacement spam if you're not.
Faction design is also really bad. While the two starter factions are fairly well designed and could be balanced against eachother quite well with some changes, the DLC factions are terrible. The USF was supposed to be flexible, but they crutch entirely on 4 units and 2 Commanders. Said two commanders were designed to "fix" the USF's problems in a way where Relic could make money rather than actually doing the obvious solution. The rest of their commanders are terrible, but Relic has refused to fix them and has actively nerfed them further since launch.
OKW was supposed to be an offensive, Elite German faction; in reality, they're just as defensive as Whermacht and pay an arm and a leg for everything, including necessities. While they CAN be good if they hit late game, its extremely unlikely they'll get that far without call-in abuse or hunkering down, completely ruining the flanking, mobile game and turning the fight into an artillery spamfest.
The British were the nail in the coffin. Bofors and mortar pits can turn a fairly good game into a frustrating stalemate, especially since they both run themelves. Relic responded to critique by introducing a commander that makes hardy emplacements even tougher with teh added bonus of hands-free counterbattery and hands-free repairs. All 5 DLC commanders are significantly stronger than the stock ones, surprise.
But what finally got me was the meta abuse. When I first started playing, it was 5 minute T34s and the invincible Tiger Ace. Then it was the Elephant and ISU-152. Then it was Tiger/KT/T34/Easy8 call-in abuse and core infantry spam. Then it was KT/Volks/Ober doomblob for six months and so on. My point is, every time a problem is fixed, another takes its place. Its just a constant cycle of abuse that Relic continues to perpetuate with poorly thought out additions and changes. I'm just sick of it. If you want CoH2's style, go play CoH1 with a QoL patch, you'll like yourself more in the long run,

I backed this game on Kickstarter and was really excited for it to come out as I really loved the original game a lot.  Years later, with not much in the way of communication, they finally released it!  It looks very much like the original and has a lot of the same mechanics.
Right now there are some pretty heinous balance issues.  Playing solo is pretty rough as you can get mobbed pretty quick. And, of course, like the original you lose half your money when dying.  In fact, earning enough to buy more moves so you get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked less often is really, really grind-y.  Maybe if it scaled per human player it would be less so; perhaps four enemies max at one time.  Through grinding (horrible, horrible grinding) you can scrape enough together to buy moves on solo. I know some folks have really boring exploits to gain cash but that also drags down the fun of even playing the game.
The police mechanic, which is new, is kind of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥  Accidentally hit a citizen, parking meter, or break something?  Swarms of cops roll in.  They drop nothing and make the already unbalanced numbers of enemies even worse.  It was an interesting idea but really sucks in practice.
Right now the saves are also somewhat broken. I have lost levels, money, and moves for whatever reason.  It happens and can be fixed though so not a huge issue.  As I rarely buy new moves or acquire much money as I'm constantly being stomped into dust, and the levels are pretty pointless, it's not much of a problem.
Last gripe, the sound.  Old-school music and sound effects are heinous.  They sucked then and suck now.  They are pretty grating and I usually just turn them off, which is an easy fix.
Besides those fairly fixable complaints, the game is pretty solid.  Great atmosphere, beautiful pixel art, and very faithful to the original.  I'm really glad they got to make this game and, like I said, I was really excited for its release. Granted that excited dropped off pretty hard by the fifth hour of gameplay.  I hope they fix the issues though because it would be a great game.

Okay, take three. I've played for about six hours at the time of this writing.
RCRU is a beat-'em-up, which is a new genre for me. Aside from dabbling a bit in Golden Axe and its ilk when I was a kid, I really haven't played anything like this. I'm giving this as a disclaimer, because I'm approaching this game as a complete novice to the genre. I had read no press on this game, and had never even heard of its predecessors. Just bought it off the steampage because I had never seen anything like this before.
TL;DR
If you're new to the genre like me, this game's probably going to be more frustrating than fun. If you're experienced, you probably already know exactly what to expect and you'll love this game. It's raw around the edges and clearly unfinished, so keep that in mind when purchasing.
Pros
+ The animations and artwork are simply stellar. Everything is highly detailed, with smooth, cartoonish, awesomely fun animations for every attack. The enemies are also highly animated, with many damage frames depending on how you hit them. It's enormously satisfying to see the enemies react to your strikes appropriately.
+ The controls are tight and precise. The RPG elements are well designed and offer a satisfactory feeling of progression.
+ There's quite a few character options, and the ones I've tried all feel distinct from each other. I personally found Alex the most fun to play, and I think most people can find a character to suit their taste.
+ Once you unlock some combos and special moves, the combat is surprisingly fun, offering plenty of options for crowd control, grapples, tosses, and the like. It offers a great brawl feeling that I haven't seen in other games (possibly because this is common in this genre, I don't know).
Cons
- The game is clearly and painfully unfinished and unpolished. I'll offer specific details below, but it's abundantly clear that the developers either ran out of time or released early.
- There is a list of moves for each character. The descriptions of these moves are frequently wrong, occasionally missing, and do not tell you whether they have prerequisites or are part of a combo. You will grind up your cash painfully, buy a move, and be unable to use the move because you don't have a prerequisite you didn't know existed.
- Some moves do not work all the time, and some moves do not work some of the time. It's difficult to know whether these are bugged, because the moves are not described properly.
- You start with moves you cannot use, because they are part-way through a combo.
- You start with only the most basic, combo starting moves. Your enemies start with full combos.
- The difficulty curve is stupid, and nasty, and unpleasant. The game gets much, much easier the more you play. Your stats improve and you unlock combos, so it goes from a painful, sluggy grind to pleasant to play. Opposite of what you want for new players, in my humble opinion - difficulty should increase as your options for dealing with it increase.
- The enemies are psychic. Even at the beginning, they have perfect tracking. If you do a run-attack, they will dodge through you and hit you in the back of the head as you're still moving. If you run under their jump attacks, they will reverse in midair.
- Enemy AI changes depending on whether they're interested in fighting you at the moment. You will only be engaged by 1-2 enemies at a time, but which enemy is engaging you can change. If that changes, it is difficult to chase down any enemies not engaging you, and since all the enemies look alike you'll have trouble finishing off enemies in the confusion.
- There are some enemies that are not so much difficult to fight as they are unpleasant. There is a specific enemy you will encounter early on that will constantly moonwalk backwards unless you are blocking or facing away. It's incredibly frustrating to fight if there are no items to toss at them. They can actually outrun the slower characters gap-closers, too, so good luck with that.
- If you get knocked into the side of the map, you map transition, losing any money on the ground and any progress you made clearing out enemies. If you knock an enemy off the map or into the transition, you do not get loot (not sure if you get experience or not).
- The map is terrible. It does not do a good job of showing you where you are, or how to get somewhere, or where you need to go next. It's utterly pointless and I have no idea why it's in there.
- Screen transitions place you randomly onto the next screen. Enemies are frequently randomly placed next to you. They will attack you as you transition in, and result in a sucker punch.
- There are many multiplayer bugs. I haven't played MP, but people are enormously dissatisfied by this game so far due to progress loss and desync.

I came in with zero nostalgia for River City Ransom: Underground. I just thought it looked like a competent brawler with fun combos and diverse movesets for the different characters. I didn’t expect what it turned to be when I started playing it, a tragically flawed game crippled by poor design decisions. There are a tremendous amount of issues preventing this game from being the super fun brawler it can be. The list is long and I’m a pedantic person, so I’ll just pick a topic and start. Oh, and for reference, I chose Paul.
The game is painfully vague and doesn’t tell you things that you need to know. The tutorial windows pop up in the middle of combat during the intro and are closed with your attack buttons which meant plenty of accidental skipping for me. None of the items in the shops have any descriptions for their effects. I suppose they want you to experiment, but it’s also dumb that I can waste $40 in a shop and not seeing anything change when checking the stats screen. I don’t know what the items did for me. Also, the world map is not very useful in pointing out locations.
I spent a good chunk of time looking in the Community Hub for answers since I kept on becoming lost with where to go or how to trigger events. There’s an in-game clock where the short hand is minutes and the long hand is hours. Some bosses only appear during day or night which leads to plenty of time waiting around, shooting the breeze, until it’s finally time. The game will only sometimes point that out. The various moves you can purchase can have no real indication of how to activate them. It might just show a single button icon, but the reality of the situation is that those moves happen during a combo string that you must figure out on your own.
The cops are incredibly annoying in this game. Civilians love running into a fight, triggering a police response. The only way to shake the police is to clear the screen of all enemies (including the police) and hop into a dumpster. You can also go into a hideout and I think a subway ride will have the same effect. The police offer no experience or cash, making them irritating to fight in the beginning when you’re weak and poor.
The grinding is horrendous in this game. Progression is separate for each character, providing a huge disincentive to try out other characters at any time. Any money you earn on one person is separate from the others as is the inventory. You also lose half of your cash every time you die. To earn moves, you must purchase them. To earn stats, you must purchase food and consume them. It’s safer for money to be in the form of purchased food since dying on the way to the dojo means probably not being able to afford the techniques you want. This encourages just beefing up for a period until you can safely smash multiple screens worth of enemies, harvest their cash, and bring them to the dojo. It took me four hours just to have my first special move.
For a game that’s supposed to be a brawler, it sure loves making you not want to fight enemies. There are at least three “bosses” in the game that require you to chase them down. The first one isn’t so bad to catch up to and give a single smack. The next two have such a tight window that require very few movement errors and absolutely avoiding knockdown attacks or bumping into anything. These sections are incredibly frustrating and having to backtrack many screens after a failure does nothing for my fun meter. Let me reiterate, these bosses force you to avoid fighting enemies in a brawler.
I’ll list some of the smaller issues here: you can bump into the edges of the screen that transition into the next area, enemies will occasionally use a knockdown attack right after entering a new screen, screen transitions occur via proximity with no confirmation which allows enemies to knock you back into a previous screen (I’ve been knocked back into an elevator which took me back down to the floor below), you’re very weak in the beginning and have a boring starting moveset, and vertical movement is very slow.
Now here’s the last issue that finally killed all desire left to play the game further, the milk bottle quest. You must bring a bottle of milk back to a house for a lady to push the storyline forward. The bottle needs to be in pristine condition. If you bump into anything, it shatters. If you’re hit, it shatters. If you place it on the ground and anyone hits it, it shatters. I already had a lot of frustration and anger built up, but when I encountered this quest and saw the bottle hit the ground after being hit while in a subway train heading towards my destination, I felt nothing. I sat there in stunned silence during the three minutes it took for me to return to the location to pick up the milk. I could not believe this made it into a game. Three minutes just for the privilege to fail again and again which I did. I’m baffled by the inclusion of this quest.
RVR:U does not understand what makes a brawler fun. It does not understand what makes games in general fun. It constantly wastes your time with its terrible mechanics and makes a surprising amount of effort to either stop you from having all the cool moves or not letting you fight at all. To add insult to injury, the card drop rate doesn’t make any sense with only four card drops after eight hours of play. The game has eight cards to drop and it’s so reluctant to give them out.
The one saving grace of this RCR:U is its well-animated combat. When you get past all the barriers the game has you climb over, you can start executing cool looking combos and juggling enemies all day long. It’s satisfying, fun, and heartbreaking because I keep thinking about all the other characters I just don’t have the patience to raise. I just want to enjoy beating up goons, not finding a street to grind out money for ten minutes at a time. Still, once you have a powered-up character, you can start making it rain pain until you spill the milk on the train.
Finally, some tips for the newbies that decide to play: The sauna will give you +15 Stamina (Health) with each use, the sushi place which is on the same street as the sauna is a great place for buying stats (+3 STR and +3 AGI offerings), the time of day affects when some bosses appear, use your money on food if you think you’re going to die to minimize losses, dumpsters let you lose the cops, and die strategically to restore yourself to full health before making your way to a boss.
I can’t recommend this frustrating experience to anyone except CIA interrogators because it’s torture. As of right now, it’s not ready for purchase. You’ll need to stay updated on any patches that are released post-launch to see what issues the developers fix if you’re interested.

It pains me to say this, but this game is incredibly fatuiging and legit obnoxious to play. When the developers were making this, they never stopped to think if making a retro classic game to a fine point was fun at all, because this combines the best but also the absolute goddamn worst aspects of old retro games.
Grinding for money to slowly, slowly, slowly level up basic stats and BASIC COMBO MOVES just to do something other than mash buttons is arduous and tiring. Lack of autosave means you'll have to rush through areas to find a hideout when you just want to quit for the time being. The map system is beyond useless, offering almost no information about where anything is besides basic story points. NONE of the items you buy have any damn info, so you'll throw away hard earned money without knowing what the exact effects are for each. There's letting the player find out things for themselves, and then there's willfully obtuse game design that serves to waste your in-game money on random things. This is the latter.
It sucks because the graphics and presentation are absolutely fantastic, and there's a lot to like about the potential of combat. But all that goes down the drain with how hard you have to do busywork just to reach some kind of strong point with a character. If that isn't enough, you're constantly harassed with a horrid police invasion system that throws non-cash dropping swat team guys at you if you accidentally hit a bystander or parking meter in the midst of the chaos.
In time, maybe this game will get retuned so it's actually fun to play constantly. For now, there are just way too many incredibly annoying aspects to warrant recommending this.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong (SR:HK) is the third installment in Harebrained Schemes' (HBS) renewed series of Shadowrun games. Dragonfall (Director's Cut, obviously) was a vast improvement over Returns, and SR:HK has a lot to do live up to its predecessor. So, let's get started!
The game still runs on pretty much the same engine as the previous games. One major improvement (some dislike it, but I digress) made to SR:HK is the revamped Matrix (which I thoroughly hated in the previous games) with more emphasis towards stealth. You can now sneak around Watcher IC in real-time to avoid detection (Hooray!). However, I find that the pathfinding can be a bit of a nuisance which is what breaks this sneaky-beaky game mechanic for me. While playing through Matrix sequences, I sometimes found my Decker in detection range of the Watcher IC (marked by lighted tiles) only to reach the destination undetected. This is just a small imperfection which I hope will be fixed in the future. The new hacking minigame (to pass Blocker IC) can get boring after sometime due to its repetitive nature, and I think having more minigames will be much welcomed. My biggest gripe with the old Matrix was the *cough*
look and that has certainly been fixed in SR:HK. The new Matrix looks fantastic now. Overall, the new Matrix isn't perfect, but at least it's something different compared to the old (boring) Matrix.
SR:HK's main selling point is the story. This time,you have more influence over the outcome of the story and what happens along the way. This involves saving characters, killing them and negotiating with them (the usual stuff). The Gaichu mission itself has 3 different ways it can end. Although less grand than Dragonfall, SR:HK makes use of more interesting characters with unique personalities and background stories. They have much more to say than previous games, which is a major improvement from HBS. Also, short animations for the intro and ending (thanks, Kickstarter) add a little bit more flavour to the game. You get a few nods here and there to characters from the older games which is a nice touch. The game does however have typos here and there (which can get a tad annoying) but the devs are putting time into fixing them. Props to them. Also, there should be a mini campaign coming soon (thanks, Kickstarter) and that will definitely be worth a look.
Turn-based combat remains the same, except now you can choose to enter the sequence whenever there's enemies on screen. This is good to get your team in favourable positions before initiating the fight. Take note that if you are spotted or wander too close, the enemy makes the first move as in the previous games. Although an interesting mechanic, I find myself using it very rarely as it's either you talk your way past security, or they  attack you first. One thing that annoys me is that this mechanic is not present in the Matrix. It would be nice to be able to take out a few Watcher IC or use some programs instead of only being able to do it once detected. I suppose it was done to prevent constant spamming of Suppression programs because that would make the stealth sequences useless. Not much of a change here, which is good since I never had much of a problem with the combat system.
Overall, SR:HK makes for a great single player RPG-esque game. If you don't like reading or story-intense games (pfffffft), this is not for you. But if you enjoyed HBS' Shadowrun games so far, can appreciate good artwork, and love cyberpunk; this game is definitely worth your time (and nuyen).

This game is on the verge of greatness.  It's not quite yet there yet, but close.  I recommend getting it regardless, but I do have the following criticisms:
1.  The matrix should be a top down view, instead of the pseudo 3D like the rest to facilitate sneaking past the watcher IC's.  It's not that sneaking past them shouldn't be a challenge, but if it's going to be based on player skill, then vision shouldn't be blocked by 3D constructs, or by blacked out areas where the persona supposedly can't see.  The player is in the matrix, so should be able to see everything, because he/she basically sees the code that the matrix consists of, and understands it.
2.  The shadow runners follow too slowly, and sometimes not at all.  This coupled with the fact that a room that you walk into doesn't light up for you to see until several of them finally catch up to you can be annoying.  You should be able to see what's in a  room as soon as you set foot in it.
3. This game is basically an e-book with a couple of battles in it.  There aren't very many "side" missions, and they also don't pay very much.  You would expect by the end game to have acquired enough nuyen to be fully decked out or at least close to it but it's nowhere near like that.  If you are a rigger, you *might* be able to buy two of the best drones, if you don't spend any money for almost all of the missions except one.  I did exactly that; I had to save up about 10k nuyen and then I spent 8 of it on two drones, and the rest on an outfit... after having not spent anything for the majority of the game, and just going only with the equipment I started with.  Missions should pay double what they do now, especially if the player is actually to have the option of hiring extra shadow runners.
4.  I used Duncan's "subdue" on the plastic faced man because the mission stated that the goal was to subdue the plastic faced man after you shoot him with a device.  I shot him with the device, and then stunned with a baton, and then subdued with Duncan's ability and instantly failed the mission, because apparently the game counts strapping someone with zip ties as death.
5.  I had an intelligence of 7, and I was in a museum where there was an option to "look at books" on a bookshelf with a requirement of 3 intelligence, but was blacked out.  I met the requirement but it did not allow me to select it.
6.  Needs more customization.  I selected the character portrait with the dog faced tech mask, which I thought looked super cool.  Unfortunately, your character can never acquire an item like that.  Your portrait rarely looks like the actual in game character.  If the guy in your portrait has a top hat, you will not have a top hat.
By this point, it would seem I'm blasting the game, but I'm not.  All of these are improvements that could be added to the game that if they were, would make this game absolutely world class.  It is a great game and I highly recommend it, regardless of it's current flaws, and HBS is steadily patching the game, fixing bugs, and making improvements.  This is money well spent, and the story is top notch.
Wow, keep up the great work Harebrained Schemes

The guide to best enjoy LISA the Painful RPG:
LISA is a great game with a huge fault, if you want to take the most out of it, you have to avoid finding answers.
If you haven't played Lisa, I fully recommend making some time to emerge yourself in this gem. Dive in the game with the least knowledge as possible and avoid spoilers at all cost as they can ruin the experience!
LISA is a game focused on the idea of loss with strong atmosphere and narrative and simple gameplay about a man in a post apocalyptic world with no women.
The game can be played on normal mode or Pain mode, the second mode is the truest to the game's intentions, with limited saves it's harder to run away from loss and defeat, forcing the player to truly accept the consequences of the battles they've lost and the decisions they made.
This should be the best mode to play the game nevertheless if you want to enjoy LISA the most you should avoid that mode and the DLC at all costs. The biggest strength in LISA is it's suspense, the mystery, the fact that we don't really understand what's going on that makes it such a memorable experience! Obviously it's biggest fault is when it answers every question. Every extra in Pain mode, every secret place in the game that explains what is really happening in LISA's world will make the game considerably less interesting.
This means that if you play LISA only on normal mode, from beginning to end it will be an amazing and memorable experience filled with sadness, sarcasm and violence. Resist curiosity and don't search for answers and you'll have very fond memories of this game. Trust me.

Lisa is a 2D RPG set after an apocalyptic event that destroyed all the females. We play as a drug addict named Brad that stumbles across a baby one day and to his surprise it is a girl. Brad, along with two friends decide to raise and protect that baby which they name “Buddy” to keep her safe from the outside world. As you can imagine things eventually go wrong, she is kidnapped and you are off to save her. One of the first things you may notice is that the game is locked in a 4:3 ration annoyingly enough and there is no way to stretch it. This game has a very strange sense of humor and nearly everyone you meet is completely insane, making it so you never know who is going to try to murder or rob you and who is friendly. Along your journey you will meet a ton of potential party members and be able to take up to three with you at any one time.
Combat is a pretty normal ordeal that has you slugging it out in a turn based duel with your foes. You will be able to pick from skills, items or a chance to escape from battle. It is a pretty typical system with one of the few undue things about it being a 5 button input when you select to attack that allows you to pull off special moves. You can pull off these moves by clicking on the skill menu as well so it is pretty pointless. Brad is a junkie addicted to a drug called joy so if you don't take some every once in a while you will have a withdrawal effect in combat that seriously cripples his ability to fight. Winning a battle can grant you a multitude of items like cigarettes to heal poison and magazines which is the currency for the game. If you have ever played an RPG there is nothing really all that different here other than how insanely weird this game is and deciding how much you value yourself over those fighting by your side.
The world of Lisa is as cruel and violent as it is weird making you have to make some pretty difficult decisions such as losing an arm making you lose your sweet hadouken skill as well as making you weaker or sacrificing a friend in your stead. It sounds like a hard decision but the companions in this game are so numerous and outlandishly insane that you'll be missing their ultimately replaceable skill set more than anything. It's never an easy decision to make however and trying to resist your captors can lead to more disastrous results. Losing tons of your party members is nearly unavoidable since even during non-scripted events they can get kidnapped and murdered. If they fall in battle you can simply go rest in an inn or by a campfire to heal them. Resting by random campfires is as very risky gamble with someone possibly getting kidnapped, your party being poisoned by a random spider, your stuff can get stolen and much more I'm sure but at that point I'd sooner walk all the way back to the inn than find out what other nasty surprises lay in wait.
It is no doubt a very dark game that is masked by its weird “humor”. I'm hesitant to call it humor since very rarely is it funny and relies more on insane randomness that will have you wondering what “just happened?” from beginning to end. Nothing seems to make a lick of sense and you start questioning if it is real or if it's a hallucination in Brad's drug filled mind. In that regard Lisa does an excellent job as you will never have enough time to plant your feet on the ground and feel like you understand this world. It's not an easy game either, if you have been robbed of all your belongings don't expect it to pull back any punches, your decisions have consequences and even the snowmen want to kill you. Yes there are snowmen in the desert and that may be one of the least weird things about this title. To save the game you must find a crow and if you pick hard mode in the beginning of the game it will explode once used. Hard mode really should not be attempted your first time playing Lisa since it is difficult and unfair to begin with.
When not in combat you are free to explore the environments which are pretty open ended though you ultimately have to visit most locations nonetheless. There are no maps, the level design is really confusing and there are no reminders to what you are meant to do so it's best to make time for when you play Lisa as playing it a bit one day and a bit another day can easily get confusing. You can jump up small ledges and objects giving it a bit more variety than simply walking left or right. Rather early in the game you will unlock a bike that allows you to move much faster and jump from higher locations without taking damage. Be very careful though as there are endless pits all over the place and you can easily ride right into your doom if you are not paying attention. Riding a small red bike too fast was the lead cause of death for me in a world full of violent psychopaths as sad as that may sound.
This game only features few random battles in certain caves and in tall grass. You can grind for magazines and items though it will take a very long time as well as making it sting much worse when you get robbed again. Scattered around the world are stores, bars and vendors where you can exchange your magazines for their services. A risky thing to purchase is equipment for your party since they die off so rapidly, making them a potentially really bad investments no matter how much it may help you out in combat. Lisa is all about potential risk and rewards. The strange thing is that I've never felt I was having fun playing this game but for some reason felt compelled to keep going. It can be frustrating to be so helpless as you are repeatedly mugged, beaten and humiliated but it is a far more effective method of making you feel like the world is dangerous instead of simply being told it is, grind a bit and becoming the unstoppable king of the world like in most other RPGs these days. Sadly Brad's motivation of rescuing Buddy is something we the player most likely will not care about since she does not say a single thing before being kidnapped and all we had to base her character around is a short cutscene.
There is no voice acting and everything is told via text. Strangely enough the text is slightly cut off in the corners of the speech bubbles and while it's nothing gamebreaking it never stopped being annoying. Graphics are nothing special but it does its job decently to convey all the weird or disturbing things like mutants, someone's head being bashed in and random rave parties. The real star of the show here has got to be the great soundtrack. It is both weird and catchy enough to make you stay in an area for a bit longer just to listen to it. Lisa is not a title I'd recommend for those that like to feel in control or even understand what is going on while playing video games but for those that can enjoy a game that kicks them when they are down and can handle dark humor. As twisted as this game is it always has an almost surreal type of wackiness such as your childhood bully riding around on a small deer and proceeds to murder your friend or a random body building club with people bench pressing refrigerators. While not a fun game it is without a doubt a very strange and brutal experience that you will not likely find anywhere else.

If you are looking for multiplayer, particularly netplay, do not buy this game.
There are endless bugs between menus just not working/opening/causing crashes, to random interactibles not functioning (soda machines just do not dispense), and people getting stuck outside of the screen, etc etc etc.
Even if you can get over these bugs, the balance for 4 player is painfully off, the game spawns so many characters on every single screen (often in excess of 12 enemies in a single tiny space), that you can't keep track of yourself or your friends, and although I'm very glad for the wonderful art and character diversity, it makes the co-op a visual mess.
The movepool the game starts you off with after the prologue is flat out unreasonable. The luchador starts out without a grab move.
You read that correctly
Almost every starting character starts with no combos whatsoever, and moves are so overcosted that the game becomes a frustrating loop of grinding for a single move over and over. That brings me to the next major problem.
The moves aren't explained well at all. My friends and I all finally bought some moves, but couldn't figure out how to make a single one work. Half of them just replaced an old move but made the text yellow??? I understand wanting to emulate fighting game input displays but, well they don't.
In multiplayer co-op, only the host gets to keep save data. We all went to the hideout and saved, but unfortunately everyone but me (the host) had a blank save file at 0% in the prologue, and that was just insult to injury.
The police system (which I think is a pretty bad addition in singleplayer) is completely unforgivable in co-op. When there are 18 enemies on screen, and one bystander sprints through and gets tagged by a random punch, the screen is just even more of a cluttered mess.
OH! Money isn't shared by the way. The amount of money we were getting felt about correct if we *all* got each pick up, but as it was it became a huge grindy mess, which since you die sooooo easily in MP, is extremely painful (you lose half of your money if you die).
Just in case you're concerned I'm making this up or if you're a dev and want to see 4 people trying it and having a lot of problems for yourself, here is a link to the VOD of the stream.
Again, there's an amazing game buried in here, but the multiplayer is currently a bit of a buggy mess, and the balance makes it unplayable. As a massive RCR and Kunio-kun fan this hurts pretty bad, and I really hope the devs listen to feedback and make Multiplayer the great experience it should be.

So, overall, this is the game I have been loving since its Beta phase 3 or so ago. What needs to be said?
It's usually 12v12 PvP (unless you wish to play against bots, with a massive penalty on credit and exp income), each team consisting roughly of the same number of ships per class (Battleships, Cruisers, Destroyers), and the exact same number of carriers per team (most of the time 0). Your goal is to either sink all enemy vessels, gain 1000 points by destroying ships or holding onto cap zones, make the enemy team reach 0 points or have more points than the enemy team when the timer runs out.
You start out with rather crappy, old ships (from around 1900), and slowly work yourself to ships like the Bismarck, Iowa, Yamato and many more. On lower tiers (1-4), you will be placed against ships of up to 1 tier higher than you, after that (tiers 5-10) you'll face vessels with a difference of up to 2 tiers (example: A tier 7 ship might be placed as a "top tier", meaning it will get the chance to be among the strongest in the game, since they get the chance to fight ships of tier 5 and 6, as well as their own tier. On the other hand, they might be "bottom tier", which means they'll have to face tier 9 ships.) Personally, I think the low amount of "top tier" and hight amount of "bottom tier" ships per match is good: As a top tier, you'll feel really powerful, and as bottom tier, there's plenty of targets your own strength, so it's still fun for everyone.
When deciding which Branch of the Tech-Tree you want to go for, keep in mind, there's usually a theme to each branch:
Japanese Destroyers will be stealthy, with a very long torpedo firing range, but for the most part their main battery is crap. American Destroyers are the other way around, they have shorter range torps, but crazy good main battery.
American Battleships have among the best Anti-Air Defense available on any ships, but are rather vulnerable to enemy Battleship's main battery volley if they didn't angle their armor correctly. German Battleships are tougher, with better armor protection and great secondary batteries (which makes them excellent brawlers), at the expense of armor protection from above: Easy targets for dive bombers or plunging fire (When you shoot from a range so long, the shell will come down almost vertically). On the higher tiers, they also suffer from the Third Reich Gigantomania, meaning they're way to large for their own good. Those ships are basically swimming fortresses, but they're also about as agile as you'd a expect a fortress to be - which also makes them vulnerable to torpedoes.
TL;DR: Nations and their specific branches all have their own flavor which defines their role in contrast to the same class of ship from different nations.
If you're new to WoWs, I encourage you to have a go, once you get past those tiny cans on the lower tiers, there's a lot of fun to be had. I do have to, however, give negative feedback to Wargaming for not allowing to link your existing account with the steam version, which also why I can't recommend it to people who played it on the standalone and don't want to start anew. That said,  Wargaming said they wouldn't allow it, so I'm not surprised, but I still think it's a♥♥♥♥♥♥move.

Complaints about the lack of account migration and politics aside, this is a good game.  I've probably got a few hundred hours on it from before it was available on Steam.
Its got a uniquely slower, more strategic pace to it which I found to be quite enjoyable as an older gamer.  You have to analyze the flow of the battle and be thinking of where you need to be 5 minutes down the road.  You can't just zip over to the other side of the map in the higher tier maps so you have to be planning ahead.  This is particularly important playing as the big slow battleships.
I probably had the most fun during the early days playing Japanese destroyers like some stealthy ninja of the seas firing torps at battleships without ever being seen.  While the game doesn't have submarines, this is as close as you could get to it.  The game has changed a bit since then though and there are new mechanics like radar that have changed things on that front.
In the end, I found to grind to be more than I cared for without paying for premium, so I've mostly stopped playing it.  But I still might fire it up now and then and play with some other friends that play.  Considering I got 100's of hours of enjoyment out of this game without ever investing a dime, I'd say it was worth it.  If you are looking for a slower paced but still skill based shooter, give this game a shot.  Its free to play, so what have you got to lose?

I was reluctant to try this game out since the original BIT.TRIP Runner left a rather bad impression. But the folks at Gaijin Games knew about its high difficulty and decided to make sure their next Runner game won't suffer the same fate. They came through with Runner2. Runner2 basically had none of the problem that plagued Runner -- a checkpoint, a better and more gradual learning curve, and a much better level layout.
The checkpoint, while something that was sorely missing in Runner, is now present in Runner2.  However, the checkpoint is not a requirement but rather an option. A player can either use the checkpoint or skip it altogether, giving newbie players, veteran players, and hardcore players the option to choose. This is how checkpoints should be designed.
Another issue that was resolved in Runner2 is the high learning curve.  Compounded with the level design, Runner2 now eases the players into the game's mechanics by introducing new elements with a level design that is more gradual and less painful to the newcomers. I personally could not tolerate the high difficulty that is present in the first Runner game.  But Runner2 now makes it easier for me (even at its default difficulty setting) to get into the game and not be frustrated by it.  The level design has improved dramatically and makes playing the game a lot more enjoyable.
Overall, this game is many times better than its original -- not because it is visually better, but because it's designed better. Any newcomers should play this game first before attempting to tackle the original BIT.TRIP Runner, despite the story indicating this game came second.
Verdict: Buy it irregardless of price.

Blade symphony is a game pitting a drinking samurai, a fencer, a breakdancing yakuza and a sexy cyborg in swordfights with the choice of 5 swords. If you think this is awesome already, well you can go ahead and buy it. For the others, I'll shed some more light on how this game plays. Note that I won't go into graphics, nor the early access pasted on the front page.
So, the game is purely PvP. The training mode, at the time of writing, is just you in an empty room. Which isn't all that bad. You might want to practice here after the tutorial. Because you will lose a lot of times, before you get how to play the game. The advertisement isn't joking about this game being about precision and timing. There are still mindgames involved mind you, but they are all different, depending on the playstyle of whoever is fighting.
The fighting feels good. Even if they tell me one of the characters isn't quite finished, she still plays quite solidly. The sound assets do feel more squishy than meaty, but that's to be expected. IT's sword fighting, and the sounds work really well. And when you do hit, especially a hit with judgement, it just feels good. Flames from your sword, the opponent being knocked back quite a large distance... It just works. And the music just tops it all off.
Anyway, for those of you looking for a sword fighting game, if you remember bushido blade(note, never played it myself), then this game is just straight up your alley. Even if it isn't truly one hit kills, fights are still deadly enough to be a concern for the player you're facing off against.
But, I left something unsaid, didn't I? Well, the game seems easy enough to grasp, but is still tough to understand. You see, timing and precision comes with practice, and isn't easily gained. I lost a lot of fights before I grasped how it actually all fits together. But now, I'm doing pretty well. I still have my faults, but I play far more solidly than I did starting the game. So, if you don't mind being beat on at first for quite a large chunk of time(it could even happen 5-10 hours in, though Your Mileage May Vary).
But, there is another downside I have noticed... The tutorial doesn't explain everything. I don't remember if they explained that charged attacks can have different attacks, but I do remember not seeing the avoid commands in the game: Roll and step. Both are done with ctrl and shift, respectively. Incidentally, stepping can be done by double tapping the direction you wanna go.
despite that, I can definitely recommend this game, especially when you love going at it in PvP. The game just works very well.

If you're looking for a good FPS, this is NOT the game to run to. The controls are clunky, the weapons barely do anything at all to your enemies, the enemies to way too much damage to you, and unless you grind up to 1000 shields, you won't last ten seconds in the combat segments. The HUD isn't well thought-out either, using numbers instead of bars or icons for your health and shields, forcing you to take a crucial moment to read out your health and shields while the grunts pound them away. The graphics aren't appealing, either. The characters look only semi-realistic, fitting into the "Uncanny Valley" making them look actually really creepy, and the world models are too blocky and low-res to be serious-looking. The story just feels like an excuse plot, too. This game is definitely NOT worth the $4.99 normal price. If anything, 50 cents feels just about right for the little time and effort that was put into this game. Seriously, there must have been NO playtesting at all on this. The only thing I do like is the trading, and even then it's not enough to save this game. 2/10.

Let me start by explaining how much this game means to me personally:
As a kid, the original River City Ransom was the main way my dad and I spent any time together and had any sort of bonding. It was also my first video game ever anyways. Ever since I can remember, I've been playing the original one on the NES, the Wii port, and emulators on every computer and phone I have.
Having played all that time with all that meaning behind it, I can absolutely say that this game captures the spirit of the original game incredibly well while bringing a "modern-retro" feel, you could call it. It's a simple game with simple mechanics, in the vein of its predecessor. Screen to screen beat 'em up with recognizable gangs and entertaining text dialouge when you punch/kick the barf out of them.
It has the added bonus over the original of having more playable characters and modern comforts like savestates instead of the old save codes (but there is a nice nod to that at the beginning) and it even has online multiplayer.
Throw your $20 at Conatus like it's a lead pipe at a rival gang member.
Brings back the memories, no problems with multiplayer!  Some of the menus, need a little work.

Blade symphony has a simple to learn combat system, and a competitive, but honorable community. Simple courtesies like bowing before duels, and not interupting 1 on 1 fights are commonplace.
Each of the four characters (A samurai, a fencer, a ninja, and an acrobat) has three combat styles (fast, balanced, and strong) that you'll switch between mid-combo to confuse and outwit your opponents. Blade Symphony is a pure PVP multiplayer game where you challenge other players to see who has the superior swordsmanship. This game brings what most games failed to do.
Positive: Skill Based Combat. In this game you won't see some 80 lvl Swordmaster who will obliterate you with his mind. You won't see a man (or a woman) with Legendary sword of DESTRUCTION that will kill you even when you look at it. No Such Thing. And that is the best part. Player that just started playing has just as much chance of winning the game as the one that created the game. Only your skill matters nothing more. Every item, skin, mask or anything else is just cosmetic. You like big swords like in final fantasy? Here you go, buy that longsword for ingame money but don't expect it to be better or more damaging thatn the one you have right now.
Negative: This game is in early access stage, that means that there will be some problems. Like occasional lags, bugs and other annoying things. Currently there are only 4 classes and 5 weapon styles. Game doesn't have working AI for practice match (actually there is no AI for practice match). Matchmaking is non-existent. Some class balance issues. Automatic draw when time runs out etc.
Overall: I would give this game solid 8/10. Only 8 because it is still in early stage and lacks some crucial things. But it's not 6/10 because it has great potential and has innovative ideas of skill based combat. It is essentially what I look in games where wallet-warriors don't exist, or at least don't matter. Where every player plays at the best of his abbility. There are no sure-way fool-proof tactics to win the duel. This game will be a MUST BUY in a few months time. Right now it is good but mark my words, it will get exponentially better

With all the hubbub around another great recent sprite-based indie RPG, I keep recommending those that liked that one to try out LISA.
It's a post-apocalyptic tale of a father searching for his daughter in a hellscape full of twisted mutants and the worst of humanity that will play at your emotions and expectations, part absurdist, part horrifyingly real.
The battle system is unique, with a big emphasis on status effects and dialing in combos like a fighting game. While some of these techniques (anything involving tripping, oil+fire attacks) will turn most battles into a cakewalk, it's offset by the ridiculous brutality of many of the bosses.
However, the story and writing is the best part of the game. The creator toes a fine line between absurd, often crude or sardonic humour and extremely serious moments that will have you on the edge of your seat. Many times you will have to choose between two horrible decisions, and the consequences will impact the rest of your game. There are no happy endings in The Painful RPG and the game will always remind you of the awful choices you made.
A twisted and groovy soundtrack tops it all off. I am yet to find another game quite like LISA.

Hong Kong is very much a case of Shadowrun: More Of The Same
It's a game that leans very heavily on the writing in order to tell the story, which does a wonderful job of using the imagination to paint a picture of the world in which you inhabit. However, sometimes the writing intrudes on a good action sequence; when this happened I found myself skimming over the text quickly to get back crushing skulls, much to the detriment of the narrative.
The gameplay is rock solid, with abilities well balanced, giving a real sense of meaninful tactics and risk-reward mechanics. Many times I found myself gambling on a 50% one turn kill over a guaranteed two turn kill with less chance for harm to my party overall.
The story itself is another (rather trite) "end of the world boogeyman is coming to town, you are the chosen one, Neo" affair. Personally, I'm rather sick of these, they are predictable, worn-out, and not representative of general life in the Shadowrun universe. The story also makes the mistake of trying to force the player to care about a character through pure exposition. "This is your foster father, he's in some trouble, you should care because we tell you to." No, I'm sorry, I can't muster up a single care, there's no emotional connection there because the character I'm meant to care about is just a bit player whom I've never met.
The main benefit to this particular iteration of the shadowrun franchise will be what people are able to do with all the modding tools and all the new art assets. That said, at time of writing there are no major mods available in the workshop for Hong Kong. Give me a Shadowrun: Roguelike where I can just run the shadows until I retire or die please! Sprinkle on some minor story elements and you have game of the decade.
If you were a fan of the previous Shadowrun games, or you're a fan of solid tactical turn-based strategy then this game is worth picking up. If you're adverse to large amounts of reading, and sick of god-killer narratives then maybe skip over this one.

I want to like this game so much, but in the end I have to give it a thumbs down for one reason.
The ratio of reading static text boxes to _playing the game_ is just way too far out of whack.  I am 15 hours into the game and would be surprised if I have spent < 10 of those 15 hours reading essentially static text boxes of dialogue that have virtually no impact on the characters, world, or gameplay.
There's an old saying in the film and TV industry:  "Show. Don't Tell."  Essentially this is saying that it's incredibly lazy and boring to just sit there and explain the plot and character motivations to the viewer.  In film and TV (and games), you have the advantage of a medium that can _show_ the users what is going on, and let the viewers immerse themselves and figure out what to feel on their own--SO USE IT.  In games, I'd even go one step further and update the saying to be:  "Play.  Don't Tell _or_ Show."
Regardless, this game fails the "Show.  Don't Tell." rule worse than any game I've ever ever played.
The sad thing is that the writing is excellent in my opinion.  I would consider reading this if it were an actual novel.  But I bought this to be immersed in a _game_, not to spend countless hours reading to periodically get a 30 minute break to, you know, finally do something semi-interactive...

The idea seemed so great - a space trading game in which you fly around the galaxy and occasionally defend yourself from pirates in a first person shooter mode. That's what the description on the store page led me to believe. But after I bought the game, I found that the FPS screenshots are actually bounty hunting missions. I made it through the first few campaigns by buying the same "illicit" goods (which you're never confronted for selling as far as I can tell) and selling them at the Moon over and over. Heck, some flash games on Kongregate pull this general idea off better than this game did.
The graphics are nothing spectacular to look at, but it's an indie game from 2008, so I can't blame the developers for it, and same goes for the voice acting. The character models don't go as far as to move their mouths at all and the UI in the FPS mode make the Unreal Tournament and (original) Counter-Strike UIs look astoundingly progressive.
In other words, it isn't very good. It's fun at first, but quickly becomes extremely repetitive and annoying. It's definitely not worth $5, but may be worth the 49 cents if you don't mind having to see it in your Steam library for the rest of time.

I am not normally a fan of mobile ports to the PC but Sky to Fly really surprised me. It's kind of like a runner except it's mission based as opposed to endless and it has a story, though it's pretty threadbare and also poorly translated.
The game play is done with only two keys (with a third later on) and largely involves dodging things as you get from place to place to complete story and side missions. You collect two different forms of currency along the way, which can be used to acquire better crew members with different traits, as well as upgrade your ship. It's not complex or difficult in the slightest but it has a very relaxes, zen feel. The art style is superb and conveys the unique world of floating islands very nicely and it's accompanied with very nice, chill music. This isn't a game you play for challenge or a massive sense of accomplishment, it's just relaxing fun.
This is a game that clearly has free-to-play roots from mobile as some mechanics like timers are still in this (though made so fast, they're utterly pointless) but there are no in-game purchases whatsoever and you're given plenty of currency and can finish the entire 3-4 hour adventure in one sitting if you want. Many formerly free-to-play mobile games that port to PC either leave the microtransactions in or jack up the price to an absurd level to avoid them. Sky to Fly only costs $4 and has no microtransactions. For me, the experience was an absolute steal at that price.
If you want something challenging or "hardcore", you're not going to find that with Sky to Fly but as someone who does love hardcore games, this was a nice little diversion when I just wanted to check out and chill for a while. You can't go wrong for the price in my opinion.
