Finally, a Sonic Game worthy of the Blue Blur's legacy.  Classic Style 2D platforming combined with Modern 3D speed and action across reimagined levels from all across Sonic's history.  What else can I say?
So let's start with Classic Sonic.  He runs, jumps, spin dashes - you know, like what the classic Genesis games had him do.  Not much to improve upon here.
Next, Modern Sonic.  He runs, jumps, boosts, does mid-air tricks and always talks with attitude.  Again, like what you'd expect.
So how are each different?  Well, Classic Sonic definitely has the most changes, and not just the new 3D aesthetics.  His levels no longer have that feel of level exploration they used to.  Instead there are now multiple levels to run on in the levels similar to the multiple-paths aspects from modern Sonic Games.  It gives Classic Sonic the sense of speed that newer fans (like me) are more accustomed to, although Classic fans may be perturbed by this.  But there's still enough sense of exploration to appease their sensibilities so hopefully it evens out.
Modern Sonic has also undergone some changes.  The incorporation of 2D sections has continued to be improved upon since Sonic Unleashed with more emphasis on platforming.  In fact, in a weird twist, more exploration elements have been incorporated into the level design by having more and more paths to take over a single section.  It's like Classic Sonic has gone to Modern Sonic's levels and vise versa.  It's a welcome change that I hope SEGA continues to work on... what's that?  SEGA ditched this for planetoid physics?  Okay, so like the ARK levels from Sonic Adventure 2, that's fi... SUPER MARIO GALAXY RIPOFF?!!  GODAMMIT SEGA!
*Ahem* Moving on.
No Sonic game is complete without a kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack, and this one is no exception.  Modern remixes of classic tracks and reimagined modern tracks for classic levels are all glorious.  Even the menu and challenge levels contain remixed songs from the past.  If you don't get this game, at least get the soundtrack.
One added element to this game are purchasable power-ups at the shop.  They are bought with the (easily obtained) points you earn from beating levels.  They offer some variations, but I found that its appeal fades as I settle quickly into my preferred upgrades.
There are also challenges for each level and you need to pass one challenge from each level to access the boss.  At best, they are benign.  Then there are those pesky challenges that don't fit in with the game at all (that means YOU, Vector!).  And then there are challenges that are just awful - poorly executed twists on the solid gameplay that didn't even need to exist.  Yeah, screw the challenges.
And the last element I'll address are the boss fights and rival fights... they are awesome!  Metal Sonic, Shadow, and Silver - F***ING SILVER - are all really well done rival fights.  The boss fights are even more epic in scale (though maybe slightly tamer in intensity).  To say much else would spoil the experience.
This is the best Sonic game in a very long time.  The levels were well designed and the gameplay was very entertaining.  If only the challenges could have been better executed or eliminated in favor of more levels.  A Must-play for any fan.
Let's face it, after this game Dr. Eggman really needs a hug.  How many times has he been beat by Sonic now?  I've lost count, but it's been nothing but 25 years of constantly losing.  Please help me nominate him for "Villain Most In Need Of A Hug" award.  Undertale be damned.

Blade Symphony
To me, a solid sword fighting game that focuses on tactics was a breath of fresh air to me. Where you either charge in or bait your opponent into a false sense of security and superiority then you hit them with the cold, hard and unforgiving edge of reality via the blade you wield in your very capable hands.
You see that this game feels like other games but it still has its own identity.
Its not just some mindless hack and slash game. You gotta think, you gotta bait your opponent, you gotta find an opening before you strike or you could be on the receiving end of a painful and or deadly blow.
Its a fighting game that has you thinking about the next swing you make before you make it.
It forces you to be defensive when fighting a quick opponent and forces you to keep up momentum against a slower opponent. It punishes you with a swift and bitter defeat if you rush in too quick or too  carelessly. It gives you a quick win if you time your strikes just right and hit that massive tier 3 charge attack.
I love how Steam Workshop adds a variety of swords that you can use in combat as well as character personalization. You can actually wield an oversized pencil in combat. Think of how humiliating it would be for your opponent to lose to you. They wield badass swords, you wield a massive pencil and you dominate them. Just wow.

All in all this indie game is worth the money you put into it. If you still feel hesitant, pick it up during a sale. Beat up some swordsmen, customize your own and play. Download some new swords, practice those combos, charges and learn to parry.

Cheers

This is the third Shadowrun game coming from Harebrained Schemes, which crafted both Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun:Dragonfall. Shadowrun:Hong Kong takes place in a futuristic rendition of its namesake, where technology and magic co-exist alongside with several fantasy sub-human races.
This is a very narrative-driven RPG. The camera is locked in an isometric view with 3d characters running around in a mostly static 2D environment. The graphics are beautiful and lovingly crafted, while the excellent asian-themed musical scores set the mood for your 20~30-hour trek through Hong Kong. In all,  Hong Kong is a fascinating setting for a cyberpunk adventure.
General gameplay flow have you undertaking various tasks in Hong Kong while at the same time making progress on the main storyline. After every mission you will return to your base of operations, where you can purchase new equipment, talk to NPCs or check your computer for new missions. Talking to your party members after every mission will allow you to gain new insights into their personality and background, and eventually you'll be able to embark on their own personal quests.
Progression is made by mostly clicking on static icons which hover above static NPCS or objects of interest, which I can't help but feel is a missed opportunity. NPCS walking around would've made the beautiful but static environment seem more alive. The missions themselves are very well crafted. There are often multiple solutions to the same problem(although some of them are limited by your team composition and skills), highly increasing replayability and the sense that you're a true Shadowrunner, able to complete the missions in the way you see fitting. Combat is the same as the previous two games, which is a turn-based tactical affair not unlike x-com. There're a variety of skills and weapons at your disposal, understanding your team and making use of cover is key to winning the battles. The matrix system had been revamped from the previous two games. While the idea is good, the game's movement system isn't really suited for the stealth-based parts in the matrix(imagine trying to play Metal Gear with RTS controls) and the actual hacking itself could get repetitive after a few tries.
The true star of the game, however, is its writing. Very few RPGs can write at the level that Shadowrun:Hong Kong does and the writers had truly done a phenomenal job. There are sometimes so much dialogue between missions it felt like it slows down the pacing, but they're all very well written and if you love reading, you're in a for a treat.
Shadowrun:Hong Kong knows which audience it is catering to, and fans of the first two games are very likely to enjoy this one.
Pros:
+Writing is top-notch
+Hong Kong is an interesting setting
+Beautiful aesthetics
+Excellent music
+Memorable characters
+Strategic combat
Cons:
-Some overlooked bugs need to be fixed
-Some solutions are tied to skills rather than real decision-making
-Not much interactivity with the environment
-Movement system is not quite suited for stealth sections
Total reccomendation. Racter is a bro.

Before going to the pros & cons, let me just say: Get this game.
Let's start with the cons:
>The sneak feature/aspect of the Matrix could have been done better or removed entirely. The point & click controls of SRHK aren't well suited for the kind of navigation you need to do while sneaking. It ends up being more of a source of frustration than something that makes the gameplay more enjoyable.
>While I enjoy reading through a lot of the dialogue & description of events, sometimes the descriptions were excessive.
>There are still a fair amount of grammatical errors & formatting errors, especially as you near endgame.
> Inclredibly long loading times that sometimes end up with the game lagging.
>The economy in the game isn't sustainable; the profit from selling items is unbelievably small compared to buying them.
Pros:
>The graphics have definitely improved & the atmosphere of the game is much easier to get lost in.
>Spells & abilities are much more effective compared to the previous games & can actually make a difference in combat.
>The characters; more than your companions in runs, other characters in Heoi have their own stories & personalities that are varied, & interesting.
>There are a variety of missions that feel different from each other.
>While Dragonfall still had the better story imo, Hong Kong also has a solid story with decent pacing & a good amount of depth to leave you invested.
>The writing is superb as always, & despite being excessive in narration sometimes, the writing can still evoke a lot of emotions & is still full of wit & humor in the right places.
Admittedly, there are still a lot of cons but hopefully with more patches these issues will be addressed. If you aren't too picky & don't mind a few grammatical errors & formatting, some bugs (none of the ones I got were gamebreaking), and long loading times, then get this game now. Otherwise, wait for a sale. The experience overall has been worth it.

LISA is a game. A good game. A game that'll make you question whether it's morally right to trade porno mags for goods. To punch people in the face. To do what you think is right, but even then, you're not 100% sure.
It offers a wide variety of fun (or questionable) characters to assist Brad in his endeavours to find his daughter Buddy, all of which are memorable, and for some, even if they're weak as Hell, you'll still want them around.

I was craving for a good RPG Maker game and here it is.
LISA will make the player happy, laugh, but also disturbed and maybe even cry.
It has hilarious scenes, where you're sitting at your PC, grinning, chuckling and shaking your head, because it has such a sinister humor.
"A game about survival, sacrifice, and perverts..." it says. Trust me, it applies to what this game is. You are forced to make some difficult choices and you will see some unsettling scenes.
In the end that's what makes this game special and stand out.
But let's see how the other points are:
G r a p h i c s
I personally like the graphics. As you can see from the screenshots it's a RPG Maker game and not a realistic 3D game.
It's obviously inspired by Earthbound, the creators favourite game of all time, as he says so himself.
The graphics may look quite colourful and vibrant, but trust me, they don't clash with the the morbid story and occasions.
M u s i c
I absolutely adore the soundtrack! The composer did a good job. Fitting for every situation, battle and emotional moment and in my opinion very catchy.
S t o r y & S e t t i n g
The story follows Brad, who adopts a baby and raises it. She is the last female person in Olathe, the fictitious location we're playing in, which is based on a real city in Colorado. As she gets kidnapped, Brads journey to rescue her begins and with it the game. The setting is post-apocalyptic. Men have given up on themselves, take a drug called Joy and just try to survive this world in which moral and laws are abandoned.
While progressing, you're passing through three areas in which you have to do specific things to advance. The setting is well done and does the term "post-apocalyptic" justice, because you are consistently in danger.
You have to ask yourself: Should I rest here? Will something happen to my party? Will there be a difficult enemy? Will someone jump at me again? Will I have to sacrifice something or someone? What happens when I go down this rope?
The story itself is dark, depressing and emotional. It's not laid out obviously and you have to think a bit to understand and also explore the world to get specific informations or hints.
I also recommend playing the first game, which you can download for free
. Alternatively reading a bit in the
should help.
In the end, it just leaves nothing but a depressing feeling. The ending is just... Hell. Some people wrote that there's no catharsis and that it's nihilistic. It's true. LISA leaves you in your emotional wreck and doesn't give you anything to feel better.
G a m e p l a y
While progressing through said three areas seems to be a bit repeating, it's definitely not boring and still manages to provide huge variety- for example driving a bulldozer and driving over people and getting experience for it. Yay! LISA was very addicting for me and after I played through it the first time, I started it again, but in Pain Mode. I recommend playing it first in Normal Mode and then in Pain Mode. It's worth it, because it includes additional content.
The battles are on the one hand quite easy, but on the other hand there are many which will be difficult, especially boss battles and especially in Pain Mode. As I played I read a bit into a walkthrough here on Steam, which helps to understand the mechanics and your many followers better. The battles are strategic, not just because of that, but also because of the consistent dangers in the game you have to plan a lot.
Fighting is fun, due to a great variety of followers and their different attacks.
I found LISA to be extremely fun despite the sacrifices you have to make. (It's called "LISA: The Painful" for a reason.)
Minimal negative aspects are:
-That you can't skip the intro. I played the game three times to get all achievements and it would've been good if you could just skip it.
-You can die when falling off a cliff. In Normal Mode it's not such a problem, but if it happens in Pain Mode and you haven't saved for a while because the save points explode then it can be pretty annoying. But in the end it just adds to the atmosphere of having to be cautious and is not something I would remove.
C o n c l u s i o n
I love this game! If you like having a challenging, sometimes amusing but often dark and emotional experience then I absolutely recommend getting LISA!

Imagine Undertale, but everyone had depression and you had to kill your friends to continue playing. There are no good endings, and no bad endings, only this; would you sacrifice everything to continue looking for someone you love?
While it may not be as brutal as this, LISA tells the story of a broken man with a broken childhood, surviving solely on medication to forget his troubles. All women have gone extinct, leaving humanity to rot as the world slowly crumbles. All women, except the baby that fell into your hands. Once she goes missing, you vow to do whatever it takes to get her back, even if it means your life. And then, the game starts.
One of the only times in a video game where I laughed with utter amusement and choked up a little within 20 minutes of each other, it is truly an experience that can't be missed. From funny dialogue to memorable characters, this is the closest thing to a future cult classic I can think of.

Space Trader: Merchant Marine is a bipolar game.  On the one hand, it tries to capture gamer interest as a commodities trading game, where you would buy and sell different commodities seeking to make a profit.  Yet, the game developers seem to realize the major flaw with this game--it gets boring quickly.  So they made a hackneyed attempt to spruce it up by adding a bulky, vastly inferior First Person Shooter component with graphics that are reminiscent of Doom.  I think the developers should have focused solely on the trading aspect, because consumers do realize the commodity trading simulation is the major draw of this game, and certainly not the FPS aspect.
How would I improve the commodity trading aspect?  I would offer unlockable merchants when certain conditions are met (i.e. a million dollars worth of legit inventory, or x number of cargo holds added to your ship), or create another category of goods.  What about the trader's personal reputation? What if the trader's reputation changes over time, as he deals in certain types of goods, and that influences pricing of wares from the NPC merchants?  These are some simple ways to spice up the trading simulation, and I'm sure the game developers could implement these additions quite easily.
As it stands now, the game will capture your interest only until you get bored and tired of the commodity trading aspect.  How long will depend on personal tastes.

Hello everyone,
Most of you won't know me but I have been around the World of Warship community for a long, long time.  I have played the game since its early release back in 2014/2015 and have continued to come back to the game time and time again.  It has its flaws and drawbacks (most games do), but Wargaming is actively looking for community feedback for fixing the problems.
One thing to try to remember when playing, this is a FREE TO PLAY game.  You don't have to buy anything, and those that do spend money on things, most of the time being premium ships or cosmetic items, it does NOT make the game "pay to win." (Unlike other recent titles to have dropped *cough* EA *cough.*)
If you are interested in historical World War 1 and World War 2 naval vessels...or if you just like to blow things up, then this is a game to grab.  It's free, why not?  At least learn from your teammates and excel to Tier 5 ships before making the decision to no longer play the game.
I've easily 2000+ hours in the game and I have enjoyed every second of it, even when I lose.  The graphics are modern, there aren't a lot of bugs, and the ships are actual scaled models of REAL ships that once and do exist.  So yes, I recommend playing this game, at least TRYING it out.  But, as I stated earlier, level up to tier 5 or so before you decide whether you wish to continue playing.  You have nothing to lose but a few fun and frustrating hours of blowing other ships up.
One thing to note that is really important.  This game quite often has events and combat missions in honor of veterans and important naval battles (like the Battle of Guadalcanal), not just for the United States, but for pretty much all major nations.  It’s interesting to see how much the developers value the sacrifice that such a small percentage of the world’s population have given in service to their respective countries.  No matter where you are from, if you chose to volunteer and serve your country in peace or war, or were drafted during a war, then I honor and salute you as well.
I am not an official reviewer, nor do I necessarily agree with their Premium Shop prices, but I do thoroughly enjoy sailing around in this game. If I had to give this game an official review, it'd be about an 8/10.  There are a few drawbacks currently in the game surrounding the use of torpedoes and High-Yield Explosive (HE) rounds.  But I am sure the developers are working to find a fair and equal option to fix these issues.
In the meantime, Action Stations! (And God Save the Queen!)

If you liked BTR1, this game is likely to be for you, let's get that out of the way now. If you did not like BTR1 for difficulty reasons, maybe you'll like this! Levels have checkpoints now, but on the other hand, you've also got to do a lot more precision movement as the game goes on*, so... kinda wipes out the assistance the former gives you after a certain point.
Overall this is a good game! Again, if you played its predecessor, you know what you're getting into here. The problem is that it's a huge friggin' mess design-wise. If you're into challenging platforming, that's still here, it's true, but sometimes hitboxes are really unclear (and this is twice as bad with the DLC characters). If you were the sort of OCD completionist who loved the prior game's "perfect" scores, guess what: you now have 3x the content. The game ranks you on if you perfect EACH DIFFICULTY LEVEL. Irritated by buying the prior one later and finding the high score table locked up by perfect scores forever? Well guess what - this time you now have to spam a key to get the best scores while you're challenging the stage.
In fact, a huge amount of the problems I have with this game come down to "mash this button now!!!" or oddly-timed QTEs in the middle of what's generally a platformer**. If you miss an item, you see the item and you know where you screwed up. If you miss a button-press you don't get "too fast/too slow", and suddenly it's rage-inducing because YOU PRESSED THE KEY FOR CRYING OUT LOUD. The others are basically "learn the level or go screw" design - not only do some stages have multiple exits (kindly marked, however), a couple branch in multiple ways before converging at the end... and not always in ways that let each path get perfect scores. Having to replay a stage over and over just to HUNT for gold in an auto-scrolling game sucks. Having to replay a stage because you need to beat a level to go back and take a specific path in a prior level if you want to unlock a costume or character sucks***.
Again: this game is a mess, design-wise, but it's not a BAD game. Just... well, the kind of bitter pill pretty much every Bit.Trip game was, where it was JUST close enough to being excellent to make the flaws more jagged.
* It is entirely possible some of the "harder" moves aren't present on lower difficulty levels. (There are three: easy/normal/hard). I would not know about this, I've been going through on Hard.
** I am told that if you're not playing this on a keyboard, you have to spin joysticks in time with an obstacle instead on some of these. I don't know which seems more miserable.
*** This is not a joke. Every world has some items/paths locked behind keys, which only appear after you effectively finish a world and take a specific path to open "the Key Vault". Sometimes they will be locked behind "must have X/Y gold in this world to progress" gates, too! It's like a Rare collectathon in the middle of a pure platformer.

TL;DR: nostalgic, smooth-playing ARPG beat-'em up with a hint of Metroidvania. Goofy, and a lot of fun - if it looks like you'd enjoy it, you probably will!
(Disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter, and then promptly gave up on it ever coming out. Then it came out!)
* * *
When I was very young, I spent a lot of time playing River City Ransom. I didn't know to call it a "Co-Op Action-RPG Metroidvania-like Beat-'Em-Up," I just knew there really wasn't anything else like it.
And over the years, there still wasn't much that was like it.
The Bouncer tried, but was dreadful. Double Dragon Neon has some RPG elements, but is still a linear journey. Of all the things, Secret of Mana scratched the itch while being a phenomenal (albeit very differrent) game in its own right.
Open World games like Sleeping Dogs (also great) are probably the logical evolution of--and heir to--the game concept; but there really wasn't anything that felt like it was in the the same genre as that old NES game.
WELL, THERE IS NOW, AND I LIKE IT A GREAT DEAL, THANK YOU KINDLY.
This isn't nostalgia as it was, but rather how I remember it. RCR:U has smooth, combo-based fighting, responsive elegant controls (very different from the original, haha), a diverse cast of characters who each feel a little different, a wide array of envorinments and enemy types to keep the fights fresh, and a lot of other tweaks and details that lend it a feel both classic and modern at the same time.
And yes, when you beat people up, they turn into coins, which you can then use to buy Sushi, which will raise your stats.
I do wish there was a bit more customizability in the stats--they seem to have simplified it from the source material--and the game is definately designed as a co-op experience, which can leave single-player feeling like there's a little something missing; you definately want to do this with full-on 4-player co-op if you can.
Having said that, I'm playing it by myself, and enjoying the crap out of it.
I'll update this as time progresses, but I'm about 3 hours in, and VERY happy with my purchase.

A nice revival of the classic NES game. There is a lot to enjoy here, but the game itself has some poor design choices that hold it back.
+ It's River City Ransom! It took a long time but finally we got a game that actually feels like a real sequel (I know there are some Japanese Kunio-kun games that came after the original, but none of them felt like an actual sequel as much as this does)
+ Great pixel art that keep it true to the classic art style of the NES games, while upgrading the animation. I seriously want to give my special mention to the lead animator Bannon Rudis for amazing job with this.
+ Many playable characters, each with unique move set
+ Deeper fighting system than many other beat em ups, there are tons of moves and you can do impressive combos. This is one of the best fighting systems ever in a beat 'em up game, in my opinion!
+ Full of nostalgia for the fans, starting from the very first minute!
+ Has co-op and online play (I personally have not yet had the chance to try them but I hear the netcode is excellent)
+ The developers have been talking about a mod support coming later and how the fans can make their own characters. The details aren't clear yet, but this sounds great.
- Your characters start with very small amount of moves. To get more moves, you need to buy them, but you'll need both exp (levels) and money to do so. It means that the fighting can get very boring at the start when there is no variety and you can't really pull off any cool combos until much later. Also it will be very difficult to fight even the easiest enemies because you'll always be outnumbered and weak at the start. On the other hand, fighting the mooks may even get TOO easy after you get one special that you can spam.
- There is a move list where you can see what moves your character knows. The list is currently broken and literally has completely wrong information for many moves. I have to wonder why the heck these instructions went this wrong in the first place. It literally asks you to press punch when the actual move requires you to press kick button, weird. Needs to be fixed ASAP.
- Navigating the city can get confusing. There is a map, but it's not very useful when moving around.
- There are many enemies to fight IN EVERY SCREEN that is not a shop or a hideout. At least in the original game, the malls were neutral zones that had no enemies, giving you a chance to relax for a while and focus on shopping. But not here, you are always chased by like at least 5+ enemies and it might just get exhausting, as you are constantly outnumbered!
- I felt that the music is somewhat forgettable. I was also expecting to hear some remixes of the music from the original game.. but there are none.
- There are some features that I don't like, such as the wanted system. Many areas have civilians running around and you can easily accidentally punch them and then you'll get a wanted level, this is pretty much useless and frustrating feature in my opinion. There's also a day/night system that I see really no purpose for.
- There are a few scenes where you'll need to chase an enemy who is running away. It's not just disappointing that there is no boss fight, the chase itself can get frustrating because you need to be very quick or they'll get away, forcing you to restart the mission.
- I'm personally not a fan of the new character's designs
- I don't know if it's just me, but I felt that some characters simply have better move sets than others? I felt that Rudy, for example, has a very bad combo ability when compared to some others.
- The story, which was just bad and disappointing for me. This game's story takes place 25 years after the events of the original, but it's never really justified why (other than that it mirrors the real life difference between the two game releases). There are some familiar characters that return but their roles are often very disappointing, so don't expect too much!
- There are bugs, some that may even be game breaking
------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game took a long time to develop, and I can see that it was a big undertaking for a small team, and considering that, they still did an impressive job. But I can't but feel that they focused on some wrong things.
Even with some problems holding it back, this game is a fun and addictive beat em up for everyone who likes the genre. And if you are like me, someone who loved the original River City Ransom back in the days, this game is worth buying!
I really hope that the devs read the feedback from the fans, and at least try to fix some of these most common problems. There is a super fun game buried under some bad design choices.

TL:DR: Easily a must buy if you like turn based CRPGs, and a must buy if you like the shadowrun franchise.
Disclaimer: I have only played through the main campaign, so the campaign builder tools and what people have made with them are not included.
If you have played Returns and Dragonfall, Hong Kong is the next logical step in this games development. Notable in that the story is very well told, with some more nuanced approaches to missions as opposed to Dragonfall's tendency to have A or B endings to a mission. They also include several missions where giving up an obvious benefit or doing something right will benefit you later with allies. It still follows in Returns/Dragonfalls steps in including a rather major event that fits well into the history of shadowrun, without retconning anything. The prime runners you get are very likable, and the characters around town you talk to are fleshed out well enough that you don't mind talking to them after each run.
The major change in gameplay is the matrix runs, where they are now half-stealth and half combat. Mostly this comes down to avoiding obvious sight trails with careful movement, and unlocking doors with a rather clever and simple minigame. You can brute force still, but its obviously much harder and more dangerous. I got a bit frustrated with it at times, but I think it fits the hacking a bit better.
My only complaint is a relatively minor one, in that adepts are still restricted to melee. While obviously a CRPG will have a hard time adjusting to Shadowruns huge possibility tables, this still feels like something that would be easy to fix. Also any cyber-weapons in the game are melee, where it seems it would be easy to include a gun on the table as well.
If you haven't played the previous two: Play Dragonfall and this, not in any particular order (the stories don't connect). They are amazingly well done turn based CRPGs, with combat that is similar to X-com with hiding behind cover and action point based turns. Well crafted and unique missions make the twenty-ish hour campaign worth the price.

The bad news is that the game is very buggy, which for a third installement of a game title should not be the case. There are glaringly obvious bugs that can hinder or completely end your campaign. In my case, the main NPC dialog trees would get reset unless I played straight through. This meant I could not reach some of the storylines, such as the companions side-quests.
Other issues, like the wage slave agreeing to lend you a passkey to get in a door.. but not giving it to you. The new matrix engine being wonky with regard to healing and using suppression.. and a host of others.
Regardless, since the devs or community will fix these bugs, if you like Shadowrun.. pick this one up.... just make sure you check the forums regularly to see the status of the game-breaking bugs.

A very fun game for those who like to pick up and play games in short sessions, and for those who are fond of deep-rooted games that they can delve in for hours. OWH is a very interesting RPG that forces you to continually advance in your journey, as backtracking or lollygagging in the same area for too long will surely end in death. The game gives you fun classes to unlock and play, as well as neat and very useful perks to select for your character to help them along the way. The game does include permadeath to an extent, allowing you to save the game if need-be, but you are encouraged to start over upon death, as it allows you to level up characters and stats, unlock new classes, and transfer unique items through the dimensional chest. In this respect, this game isn't a hardcore Roguelike, but moreso a Roguelite, making death encouraging other than punishing. Add to this the great resource management system, the many stats and equipment you can find and upgrade on your quest, and you'll find a very fun game to kill a few minutes on, but at the same time, can easily cause you to sink countless hours into.

This game is mind-blowingly incredible. Depressing as hell so if you're not a very tough person maybe a game like Undertale is more up your alley, because that game rewards you for being a complete ♥♥♥♥♥. I kid, I kid (not really) but lemme get to my review. I'm a pretty disorganized person and I'm not going to give you a piece-by-piece critique of every part of this game so I'm just going to tell you how it makes me feel and you can judge for yourself how it sounds to you.
The story, first of all, I mean without the story what kind of game would there be? And the story here is one of a fat bald guy named Brad who
and finds a baby, moreover a female baby, which is very important as there are ostensibly no females left in the world. So he takes care of it for a while with his friends that he's been with since childhood, until one of them steals the baby and takes it to Rando, who is the "leader" of the wasteland, to "save the world". Cue wacky adventures! A cast of perplexing and unforgettable enemies await you (I'm not mentioning the companions because I feel like a LOT more work could've been put into making them memorable, they're really only good for combat. I never cared about them otherwise and sacrificed most of them to a certain mini game for a certain combat-focused follower) The enemies and various NPCs however were very unforgettable for me. You may have seen other reviews mention the disco suicide dude or the insane fast food mascot. They will definitely leave an impression on you, and probably not for the better. I found the main character to be pretty boring, though. He's completely focused on finding this chick and atoning for his previous sins, and doesn't have much of a personality otherwise. But this world will force you to make extremely tough decisions. No matter what you pick, you will lose something extremely important. I loved the story solely for the world he lived in, and love it I did.
Now the soundtrack. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have never bought a soundtrack for any game, ever, not even Undertale. I bought this one. Not gonna say any more, I'm going to let that speak for itself.
Combat is very nice. You get to mix and match a bunch of different abilities to the ones of your companions to work against your opponent's weaknesses or work toward your team's strengths. Brad has a nice system of tapping certain buttons in order to use certain moves, really makes you feel like you're doing a lot of the work. Don't use Joy, though. Unless you're doing a Painful run, then it doesn't really matter, and you will definitely need to be Joyful for that, especially if you want to beat the king of hell himself.
I can't really think of anything else that needs to be said. I'll update this review as I think of things, but for now this feels good to me. If you want a great story, if you want to immerse yourself in an uncaring, depressing, quirky world, get this game.
P.S: I know people like to compare this game to Undertale so i guess it's inevitable that I do so as well, though I won't do it as thoroughly as others will because I believe in judging a game solely on its own merits. But I did appreciate how this game doesn't really judge you that much for your decisions like Undertale. Undertale gives you a pat on the back for being a goody-two-shoes and tries to make you feel horrible for not playing that way, which really annoyed me. This game will not judge you. It will let you think about what you've done and it'll let you play the game with the consequences you've chosen for yourself, but it won't have some stupid♥♥♥♥♥skeleton judging you at the end, the only one who wil be able to judge you here is you.

When I first saw the game One Way Heroics it looked like something that could fill my spare time.
I decided to give it a shot for 3 bucks and this game blew me away.
This might sound like i am giving this game more credit than needed, but this has quickly turned into one of my favorite games to this date.
Of course the game has some flaws, but the good points of this game make it all. Let me give you a summary
This 2D Rogue-like RPG puts you in a world where the end is on it's way, and it is close! Every step that you make, every action that you do, will cause the end to draw closer and closer.
With dungeons, towns, npcs, monsters, holy items and companions spread all over the place, it quickly becomes a game where you have to think how much you can risk for opening that one chest that might give you a great item.
The first time you will complete the game will be in about your first hour of play ( getting to the end isn't that hard on the easiest difficulty) but with daily challenges, increased difficulty maps, secret endings (that i won't spoil) and a ton of classes to complete the game with. You will find yourself a new challenge almost every single day.
The game plays good, has controller support, has a good learning curve, and it makes you feel like a real hero when you accomplish something.
The cons?
Well if you don't like dying a lot, then this is not the game for you. One mistake or wrong decision can get you trapped and sometimes the game will be unfair to you.
Sometimes you will see the game paused with the message "loading map" which is a slight setback in pace.
Classes are a little bit unbalanced (in my opinion this only adds more challenge for those willing to take the risk)
Maybe if you are really looking for a complex story in a game this might be a let down. (You are the hero, save the day, thats about it)
But that is right about it for the Cons.
In short, while I only have 9 hours currently into the game, it feels like it has been minutes.
If you are looking for a cheap game that is worth the price, and that will consume your time like there is no tomorrow, you will not be disappointed with One Way Heroics.

This game is a fun Roguelike dungeon crawler where the entire world is your "dungeon". In this game the world is being engulfed by darkness and you have to outrun it while killing enemies, collecting treasure, and recruiting teammates along the way. Whats more is that each teammate has their own story you gradually learn as they travel with you as well as several alternate endings involving them. The goal of the game is to stop the darkness from spreading which you do by defeating the Dark Lord who appears after 400km (Walk in the park mode) or randomly set distances in every other mode. With Walk in the park (easy) mode the Dark Lord only spawns once but chases you indefinitely until either of you dies while with other modes the Dark Lord will despawn if he doesn't kill you within 3 hours game time (aprox 27 actions) and it's spawn timer will reset.
After each attempt win or loose, the dungeon crawler portion of the game kicks in. Your performance will be rated and you will get an amount of hero points based on how well you did. These hero points are used to purchase bonuses to make your future attempts easier such as new perks, more dimensional vault room, and new classes. After your performance is rated if you already have the vault unlocked you are free to move your most important items to the vault which can be withdrawn at the start of your next attempt. I'd also like to point out that this game is very informal both through your fairy companion who answers your questions and through the tips you get if you die which actually analyzes how you died
Overall it's a really fun game I like it

Long, long ago on a computer far away an enterprising game designer created a free program about the drug trade, and they called it 'DopeWars.'
A bit shorter time ago I had a palm III and I got a game with the same name as this one, but it was a more conservative port of DopeWars with a bit of ship management added in.
Now we have this latest entry into the 'trader' game pile, and I have to say I'm not exactly thrilled after nearly two hours of gameplay on just the first mission. This isn't to say that I don't see the potential, and I did have fun with the setup, but I noticed a few things that might be deal-breakers for those looking to just bounce around buying and selling.
Firstly, you seem to make more money doing the side-quest shooter arenas that are basically fights against bots, quake 3 style, complete with respawning weapons and pickups. For a game about trading this seems a bit off message, but easy enough to let it slide, since it does provide a break to the actual game and gives you extra funds and inventory for trade.
I think of it as something extra from what's on the tin.
Second, extra cargo spaces are treated as a commodity, which makes no sense to me. They even fluctuate in price between planets so you could feasably make profit selling the only part of your ship that you can upgrade. This plays into my even bigger point, which is this game could benefit greatly from just a bit more effort in the space travel side of things.
You go through this big setup as to the why and how of getting your ship, and the necessity of paying off the debt, but you never see this ship, nor any other. There is talk of space-pirates, but I doubt you really go into any sort of combat with them, unless it's another one of those bot-arena matches mentioned before. Plus it would be a great expense along with the cargo bays, something to use your money for. This calls back to the Space Trader from my palm iii days....maybe I'm just nostalgic.
Third, the first mission itself, and a particular side-mission forced on you by the same person, aren't clear on how to complete. I was given the task of amassing a debt-payment of considerable size, which was easy enough, and given a bot-match that I complete as well, but they remained in my 'news' tab till the mission failed, reloading just dumps me back to the start. This appears to be a bit broken, surely in this future space universe we're dropped into, especially one with banks, you'd be able to make installment payments to pay off your debt if the challenge were more long term.
As it stands, since the challenge has a short time frame, again it would make sense that the first thing you would be told to do after hitting the amount you owe in profit would be reminded that you have to pay it off, or at least told how you would go about satisfying the end condition. Maybe I'm just tired and it was blatantly obvious, I did write this up after basically struggling with it for two hours, and I haven't really looked into any guides or other solutions, but a game that presents itself so simplistically in places like this one shouldn't need a guide to finish the 'baby's first' challenge.
Cutting this short (yes short, I can keep going) I'm giving this game a tentative recommendation based upon its current price and availability in a sales package, since for this much you get what you can expect, a game where you trade between planets in space, with a bit of bot-shooting added in for flavor, but if you're just looking for a trader without the fluff and semi-broken, non-intuitive bits to slog through there are plenty of free alternatives.

River City Ransom: Underground is very obviously one of those games that try and bank on nostalgia by preserving the spirit of the original but does so with such clumsy hand and lack of understanding about what made RCR good that it's frankly kind of baffling.
Even outside the multitude bugs present in this release, ill-advised platforming, the absurd game-padding grind involved in learning movesets (ten of them!) fragmented into a million pieces and the legion of weird design decisions that range from useless GTA style wanted levels to a save system that's unusable most of the time; I think the "gangs" themselves are a good way to exemplify everything that's wrong with this title: See, back in the older games you'd enter an area and you would fight a gang of guys that wore the same colors. They all had different names and unique appearance to match (as unique as the technical limitations allowed at least) and fought in a way that gave each group a sort of personality. You had gangs that liked weapons, guys that liked to run in and deck you, guys that would throw a bunch of stuff or guys that would drop a lot of money and so on so forth.
It might have been basic AI preferences but then you have something like RCR:U in which gangs don't really exist outside of very small areas and the rest of the game is filled with a random blend of color-swapped and duplicate luchadores, greasers, nerds and stereotypical burglars trying to beat you up.
Charm has always been one of the franchise's biggest selling points. Everyone reading this has probably heard of the whole BARF! thing or might remember stuff like the sauna complete with humorous naked♥♥♥♥♥that even the trailer for RCR:U referenced. I'm sad to say that in the case of this game all that stuff is entirely window dressing: They are empty, soulless gestures amidst a legion of identical sprites mobbing you and much like the game's entire retro artstyle they are there because they were in the original, nothing more. This is no longer a story of school gangs duking it out against each other but an endless parade of references and unrelated wacky characters punching each other silly as they try to figure out a poorly written move list.
Avoid. Get it on a deep, deep discount if you absolutely must relive the game and cannot get hold of the GBA version.

(Text version below pros and cons)
Pros:

- True to the original.
- Improved combat system and AI, making the game less robotic than its original version.

Cons:
- Might feel really hard to the more casual gamers.

This is definitely THE beat em up you'Ve been looking for since the long forgotten NES era. The game's graphic are true to the original, the combat system feels fresh and deep while keeping the spirit from the original game. The game does start by introducing new players with a tutorial, but those may feel like the learning curve is really steep due to the game's difficulty. Just take your time, learn the basics (character's moves + attack/dodge pattern for different enemies) and you'll start enjoying the game. I'll put emphasis on the game's difficulty because it feels just like the average NES game from back in the days so, maybe those who hate a great challenge might want to think twice before buying. Once the introduction is done, the game lets you lose across a very vast world, so make sure to explore first so you get a good idea where to find the different shops and hideouts; those will be essential if you want to upgrade your characters fast and soften that difficulty a bit. I've run across a few bugs like boss events not triggering or access to the first dojo not being granted, but they are all fairly easy to avoid (in all cases I encountered, I was triggering events like using items at the exact same time as a boss or the last enemies was defeated). I would recommend evryone who misses the original River City Ransom (or any other beat em up from that era) to buy this!
EDIT: I must also add that the dev is indeed hard working to fix the game's issue because after being out for a few days, 2 updates have already been pushed.
TL;DR:
- Must buy to any fans of NES/SNES era beat em up games.
- Don't hesitate to think twice or get more informations before buying if you're more of a casual gamer or if great challenges aren't for you.

Wanted to like it. Really wanted to like it.
Couldn't like it.
Repetitive, grindy, needlessly obtuse. The cop mechanic is an absolutely baffling inclusion - civilians run around and if you hit them [even by accident] infinite waves of cops come looking for you. These cops are tough as old boots, take forever to kill and provide no money or benefits. There's a day/night cycle that probably seemed like a cute idea but is really just a pain in the fundament, that leaves you waiting around for time to pass.
All the cool moves you see the dudes busting out in the trailers? Good luck with that. The in-game move list just tells you buttons to press, with no clue as to context or timing. And you need to grind to unlock them. And you need to grind to make your character anything other than an anaemic pushover. And if you unlock anyone else you need to start grinding again. What moves a character starts with are a crapshoot - Glen, for example, starts with a fairly decent toolbox, whereas Bruno and Rudy are a nightmare to get past their initial uselessness. Criminally, the luchador doesn't have any grapple moves at first.
There's very little direction or instruction given to the player. Text dumps will pop up mid-fight, so you end up button mashing right past them accidentally and there's no way to see them again. There's a map with objectives on it, but it's totally unreadable. Sometimes key things will be explained at the bottom of the screen - where you're not looking because every single stage has around 8 enemies instantly trying to beat you up. Stores will offer you various products but give you no clue as to what you're about to buy. Extra moves for your characters are the same - and while something like "Ground Punches" is fairly self evident, things like "Viper Kiss" are a little harder to puzzle out. Have fun realising you've spent $22 in game dollars [around 15 minutes of grinding on mooks] on something contexual/useless!
Oh, and it's rough as guts. Crashes a lot, has frequent strange framerate hitches, is full of spelling errors and [in the move lists at least] the occasional flat out wrong item. Netcode is woeful, desyncs at the drop of a hat. Controller issues abound.
It's all just a shame. It's so close to being a good game. It's nicely presented and has excellent music. But it's not good. Don't buy it. Buy Mother Russia Bleeds instead.

About six hours of playing this game so far. The gameplay is quick to pick up on the basic characters and weapons. Gameplay seems like it has a good amount of depth to it. Depending on who you are playing and how you are playing them you have to decide on timing, positioning yourself, etc.
I wish the blocking mechanic was a little more robust. Currently I see no significant advantage to blocking instead of sidestepping. This might be something I am missing, but if there is a way to use blocking effectively it is not apparent. Sidestepping is very satisfying though once you start to get the hang of it. Being able to doge out of the way of an oncoming attack and positioning yourself in a place to take advantage of their openness is quite the visceral delight.
The characters have a wide range of styles to master. With my experience so far Ryoku the break-dancing fighter is the easiest to play. His sporadic moves cartwheel him around an opponent while dealing a surprising amount of damage. Button mashing with this character will carry you the furthest compared to other characters. Although you might have some problems when challenged by more experienced players.
The next tier of playing difficulty is filled by Phalanx and Judgement; a fencing style and Samurai style respectively. These characters depend on proper timing and positioning. Phalanx's quickness and small damage strikes are matched by Judgement's use of decisive powerful slashes.
By far the most difficult character to master is Pure. Her Wushu style is beautiful, but difficult to to land good strikes with. Most of her moves will deal less damage then I expected. I am not yet skilled enough to do well with her.
Adding another layer of depth to the game are weapon classes. Certain sword styles will grant you various benefits. Although initially promising I quickly found that certain characters perform best with their matching class of sword and therefore there is not much reason to use another. There are a few exceptions, but overall it seems as though you are locked to a specific sword type, which is a little disappointing.
With Blade Symphony you wont have to worry about memorizing complex button combinations. Its essential mechanics are easily learned, yet you will find the depth of combat is something not quickly mastered. The simple control scheme will enable you to always be searching for new ways to position yourself just out of the way of your opponent's strikes; yet just inside your range to exploit their open flanks. I have had lots of fun playing it and look forward to spending more time slashing, stabbing, dodging, and flipping my way to sword fighting mastery.

I still haven't played Shadowrun Returns, but I have played Dragonfall, and I can say that Dragonfall was quite an experience for me as RPG's go, with engaging, well-written characters and a fantastic plot.
Hong Kong definitely strives to meet the expectations it's predecessor has laid out for its fans, but after completing the main storyline, I feel as though it missed its mark, at least in terms of writing.
The characters, though interesting, didn't drag me into the world as well as Dragonfall's did, and for the most part didn't feel as fleshed out either.
As for gameplay, the new Matrix is a substantial upgrade from its previous iteration, a welcome change from what was essentially just the combat with a new paintjob, while the expanded Cyberware upgrades provide more leeway in tooling yourself up with chrome and steel, which I appreciated.
Overall, it's not bad. There are some new mechanics, and the game looks better, both of which are nice, but the writing isn't quite up to par with Dragonfall, which is definitely disappointing.
I suppose that about sums it up, actually.
I'm not angry or upset, just slightly disappointed.
However, Hong Kong still gets my recommendation.
It's a solid RPG with a lot of freedom to play how you want to, presented in a vibrant, beautiful setting, with a decent story behind it. The qualms I have with the writing are most likely present because the writing in Dragonfall spoiled me and set my expectations a little high.
So, make no mistake:
This is a good game.

Pros:

Cons:

-Storyline delivery was not particularly great

Note! Finished game at 3.0.5 version, so some points herein may not be accurate with upcoming patches.
Hong Kong is an interesting stab at the lore of eastern Runner hub. Typical to the setting, betrayal and intrique with nice eastern twists while you work out while people are out to kill you. Several interesting party members with well-fleshed personalities. Varied and interesting missions.
Now, as for the actual review. I was curious to see HBS's next scheme- certainly, Seattle has always been the heart and soul of the Shadowrun world, which often sadly leaves out the other interesting hubs and lore. Dragonfall gave us a nice glimpse at the Flux state and Berlin. Hong Kong delivers it's titular city, or at least, the less savory parts of it. But I savored them regardless.
Now, I'll try and keep my review as spoiler-free as possible, so expect certain amount of vagueness. After the initial tutorial level.
You're basically fresh outta prison, when you receive a call from your estranged step-father to meet him in HK. Keen on dusting off the Barren's crud from your boots, you fly off to adventure. Reunited with more than one estranged family member, you are soon embroiled in a plot involving your step-father's mysterious dissapearance and his captor's persistent attempts at having you killed. Welcome to HK.
The story unfolds pretty free-form from hereon in- you're allowed a choice of party members covering each base and skillset, as per usual, with some of them joining in on the ride later on. I found the starting party very affable and ended up having them on the team 90% of the time, if not for their obvious proficiency in getting things done, then for their dialogue and banter. For reference, I was playing a Rigger.
The missions provide a good number of choices between stealth and taking the thrillgang approach. I found myself talking my way in and out of trouble more than 'go loud', and found the game very accommodating to having your main as the Face of the party. Cheers to that.
There seem to be various skill checks of all sorts, and calls for Etiquettes almost constantly- maybe it was the smaller scope of the campaign as opposed to Dragonfall, but I definitely enjoyed having these options open, or at least, present.
As far as difficulty is concerned, I think the game was too easy by far. Then again, I've been playing Returns from the get-go, and maybe I've picked up a few tricks here and there, but I found most of the time I had no need for medkits nor revival kits. Maybe if I had been more combat-oriented rather than stealth-bluffing my way, things would've been different.
There's a lot of foreshadowing in the plot about the eventual Big Bad, but it turned out the final dungeon and the final encounters with the BBEG were almost too easy. Admittably, I had geared up with some of the strongest armour and weapons in the game, but I had expected a lot more fight out of this mysterous nemesis.
+ Interesting take on the eastern Runner Haven.
+ Good cast of characters, with the forerunning Gobbet and Is0bel standing out as the most memorable due to their personalities, conflicted pasts and mannerisms.
+ Fun side missions with unexpected twists.
+ Remixed OST with an oriental flair
+ New items to enrich your Running experience
+ Devs had taken time to make custom portraits for small Scene events, something I could appreciate.
+ I'm sure any and all UGC modders will appreciate the plethora of new assets for making our own adventures.
+ / - Quite short in length. Naturally, you'd want good things to last longer. :P
+ / - Redesigned Matrix. While I am a fan of the old, and was somewhat wary of the new system, I do admit it has it's perks. Much better stealthing. Although, being of a poor memory, I did not like how the new system plays out like a memory game now. Discovered passwords should be visible at code prompts, instead of having to rummage thru your Scene notes.
+ / - Reward choices at the end of certain missions. Loot or allies, loot or allies...
+ / - Varied levels of dialogue ranging from excellent and funny to downright bad. Main cast dialogue tends to be on the upper scale of things, but the writer(s) just didn't seem to flesh out any of the secondary or tertiary cast, save a few merchants.
+ / - There are no clear benefits for using Duncan's Ziptie ability. Although it's probably good karma to spare foes, the game does not particularly reward going out of your way in not killing combatants but neutralizing them instead.
- Personally, as much as I found the plot interesting, I did not like to be hammered into a certain role in terms of the story. Having that freedom taken from me sort of put a damper on the roleplaying experience. Felt like taking stage cues from the GM or storyteller most of the time.
- As the game currently stands, having the Laser Sniper rifle combined with an autoloader and Monofilament Whip turn you into a one-man army, as they are ludicrously overpowered. I even gave up using drones mid-way thru the game after I had purchased this fearsome combo.
- Lack of Polish. At 3.0.5, there were still numerous instances of missing or wrong dialogue, formatting errors in the dialogue itself, some anomalies with armour item losing it's AC, Stash lag and surprisingly long load times which may be attributed to the updated game engine, dunno. Hopefully fixed in the future.

SR:HK keeps most of the qualities of the previous games, largely following the standard set by Dragonfall both in terms of gameplay, characters and the quality of its writing. It improves on various aspects of the previous games, including richer graphics and deeper gameplay mechanics (with more varied cyberware, drones and magic as some examples), and well crafted missions. Unfortunately, the overall narrative feels a little weaker than Dragonfall's, and the early versions of the game (as completed on build 3.0.5) contain a lot of minor bugs, that while not game-breaking, can put a damper on the enjoyment.
Regardless: highly recommended for fans of the first two games, and already well worth a consideration for anyone looking for a solidly-written cRPG, especially if you're interested in the Shadowrun setting or cyberpunk in general. For everyone else, maybe wait for a few more bugfixes, the release of the mini-expansion and/or an eventual "Director's Cut".
===
I thoroughly enjoyed Shadowrun: Hong Kong, and feel perfectly content with backing HBS's Kickstarter: although (unfortunately) no great leaps forward were made compared to Dragonfall, Hong Kong once again manages to build and improve on various aspects of the previous games.
First the good.
SR:HK looks better than before, with more detailed environments, better lighting, and a very cohesive look. It's small improvements all around, but they add up to an aesthetically pleasing package. The visual upgrades to the Matrix also turned out rather nice. Combined with another good soundtrack and decent ambient sounds, Hong Kong may not necessarily feel
yet, but it certainly has character.
Strong writing and characters were Dragonfall's main claims to fame, and I feel Hong Kong kept to the same standards. Personal preferences may lead one to prefer DF or HK's setting and characters, and while certain characters are stronger than others, the overall writing quality remains high. Gobbet, Racter and Gaichu can compete with the better characters in DF, while Ambrose and Reliable Matthew's stories were just as good or better than most NPCs in Dragonfall. The Shadowlands BBS threads deserve a special mention too: there is some absolute
in there, well worth the extra reading.
When it comes to basic gameplay, Hong Kong does little to change the formula, but again various small improvements add up to a richer experience. More and better cyberware, including cyberweapons, more drones and variants (that actually look different!), more weapons, more spells... They open up a
more customization and strategic options. I'm looking forward to experimenting with different builds in the future, far more than I did in the previous games.
Gameplay-wise, the biggest changes were made to the Matrix, and they are a bit of a mixed bag. I personally enjoyed the changes for the most part: the ability to try to sneak around in the Matrix in real-time, with patrolling Watcher IC with sight cones and hacking Blocker IC to unlock data, is a welcome change from the "slower than meatspace fights until all IC is dead then move on and do the same" from the previous games... but the stealth gameplay itself can be frustratingly clumsy, and the hacking minigame(s) of "simon says" and "find the matching symbols" feel a bit tacked-on (although they look fitting enough).
To wrap up gameplay, the shadowruns themselves: most of the missions in the game are well-crafted and quite varied, with more options to complete runs (often completely) without resorting to violence.
Which brings me to what I consider Hong Kong's biggest weakness:
Unfortunately, as much as I enjoyed the missions, writing and characters on their own, the way HK ties it all together isn't quite as good. The overall narrative is just not as strong as it could have been, and the player's influence over the unfolding of the overall story is near-zero. Bad Stuff and Hellish Nightmares are going down, you have missing family members who may or may not be dead... and yet for most of the game there is little sense of urgency. You go around on various unrelated shadowruns, while one of the NPCs disappears to literally move the plot forward on their own once you've completed enough of them. As fun as the individual shadowruns may be, when it feels like they are merely a way to spend time while the game resolves the story
you... it doesn't make the main plotline feel all that relevant, to the characters OR the player. The fact the player character goes from "unexperienced outsider who no one really trusts" to "one of the most notorious shadowrunners around" in the span of a single run, also doesn't help in setting up much of a story arc. All in all, the main plotline is interesting enough, but the pacing and story
could have been a lot better.
Finally, there is the issue of bugs, which is perhaps the biggest disappointment. As mentioned in the short version of the review, build 3.0.5 of SR:HK still contains a good number of small bugs. I never encountered any game-breaking bugs myself, and most of the problems like spelling errors, faulty (or overly unclear) item descriptions don't do much to hinder enjoyment of the game. Other bugs lead to unfinished or broken conversation lines however, and another bug lead to one of the main characters (Is0bel) being completely unavailable in the epilogue, keeping me from finishing her storyline altogether. Harebrained Schemes have been rather active in putting out updates, however, so I have good hopes that a few updates from now, most of the frustrating bugs will have been squashed.
To sum it all up: Hong Kong is essentially "more of the same, but (mostly) better". Highly recommended for fans of the first two games, and already well worth a consideration for anyone looking for a solidly-written cRPG, especially if you're interested in the Shadowrun setting or cyberpunk in general. For everyone else, maybe wait for a few more bugfixes, the release of the mini-expansion and/or an eventual "Director's Cut".
In the meantime, I'll keep looking forward to "more and better"  Shadowrun games in the future.

I give a non-recommendation for two things, firstly, completely broken games, and secondly, games that I find mediocre and/or flawed, Sky To Fly: Faster Than Wind falls into the later. It’s a running game set in a steampunk universe, and while it’s in Early Access I feel the game has shown its original roots and developer intentions.
Review -

I’ll address the elephant in the room; yes it’s a mobile port. This is shown through the use of a premium currency and though it is obtainable in game it is extremely slow. Also the premium currency ships and crew members are superior to the ‘f2p’ options in every single way. It bares its ugly teeth when you have to wait 20 MINUTES! for a ship to recover its HP after a mission, but don’t worry, with some premium currency we’ll have ‘er up and runnin’ in no time!
Usual runner stuff applies, go through a level, pick up coins, dodge terrain and enemies, and use premium currency to give yourself a boost for that level. Unlike most running games though the controls are slow and stiff, and there is no feeling of speed. Your control options are either left or right and the use of an ‘active’ ability, this is less than your usual smart phone runner. Also the sense of difficulty is non-existent due to the slow gameplay and if you run into any difficulty it’s due to the limitation of the controls and generally poorly designed enemies, but if you do struggle you can spend that good ol’ premium currency and revive yourself!
Sky To Fly: Faster Than Wind is an example of a game that is extremely flawed for the PC space. While it may boasts great graphics and story mode for a smart phone game, this is the PC and the standards are different. The laziness shown through the keeping of premium currency and all the ‘features’ it entails is just something you can’t ignore, and turns something that could be a somewhat enjoyable experience sour.
Edit: The game is now fully released and none of the issues have been addressed. The points in the review still hold true.

Steam Sales are always a great way to buy more games than you'll ever be able to play, but between all the big purchases you will often find some random games to keep you busy when there's nothing else; Space Trader: Merchant Marine is exactly that kind of game, but unlike most small, indie games this one managed somehow to keep me around more than it should have, just because at its core, it's an addictive experience. The premise of the game is simple: you are a new trader trying to find your way in this business and since you don't own a ship yet you need to find someone who is willing to give you one. What follows is a simple story and you will see the little twists coming from miles away, but even with that in mind, the missing excitement of what's going to happen next isn't the thing that will keep you around. The campaign has only five chapters and once you understand the mechanics of the game you will have no problem making millions from trading food stamps, oil or even organs. This game simulates the stocks trades perfectly, following the same: buy low, sell high premise, and even though at first it may be hard to figure out how to make all those millions, once you get the idea, it will be only profit for you from that point on. There's no real reward for doing this except the fact that once you reach a goal you will advance to the next chapter and start all over, trading between different planets, but that little sense of advancement is what will keep you playing.
The gameplay in Space Trader is pretty straight forward: you start on a planet and you have to buy commodities that will bring a profit and travel to another planet to sell them at a higher price, keeping a constant watch on the time limit that each mission has, calculating the profit per shipment and the travel time in order to choose the best option. Finding good deals is easy since those always have a gold star indicating that you should buy them, so eventually it becomes just a matter of having enough money in your pocket or enough cargo space, and your only enemy becomes the time as you carefully have to choose where to sell the stuff you just bought. You can make money by taking bounty missions from bartenders or by completing small tasks for different people, so it's always a good idea to talk with everybody because you might find out some interesting things or take on some missions that will give you some extra cash. The shooting mechanic feels old, but that's probably why it feels so addictive at the same time, as you will most likely instantly connect the dots between those shooting sequences and games like Doom, and even though all those bounty missions will get boring pretty soon as each map looks and feels the same and there are only two to three different types of enemies plus the target that you're supposed to assassinate, it is a good distraction from the boring buy and sell mechanic that the game generally delivers.
If you look at this game you will assume it was released in the early 2000's because it looks like it was made a generation ago; from the simple and stiff characters to the environments everything looks pretty bad and the repetitive level design doesn't help either. By the end of the game you will know every corner of each planet, you will start to love a certain section for how easy it is to complete a combat mission and you will hate another for how difficult it is.
The sound in this game ain't exactly bad, but it's simply mediocre at best. The voice acting is horrible, but the soundtrack manages to save it sometimes, especially in the heat of a battle, but otherwise there is nothing that stands out, it simply gets boring as you will end up ignoring the other characters or laugh at how bad they sound no matter the serious, story essential thing they just said. There are intentional comic lines too, such as the robot that answers by saying WTF, but those only make the entire thing feel worse, as the game is undecided between trying to be serious and making fun of itself.
After completing the main campaign you can also try the challenge mode that offers three extra missions that are pretty easy to complete and the only real challenge comes when you try to get the achievements, and if you're into that the game can get interesting and it has even some decent replay value as you can spend up to 18 hours struggling to complete everything. It's also supposed to have a multiplayer mode, which puts you and a friend in a race to get the most cash from those challenge missions, but after an hour of banging my head against the wall I couldn't figure out a way of making it work.
When a game is getting such a low score no one would actually recommend buying it, but in this case I'll make an exception: you should give it a try if it's on sale and you can get it for less than an euro, as for that amount of money it will keep you busy more than enough to justify the purchase. It is in no way a great game, one that you will remember after leaving it aside, but as long as you play it you will be entertained simply because it's so stupid it becomes like a good parody.

Heart wrenching, wanna-kms type of♥♥♥♥♥♥that i absolutely love. HOWEVER if you plan on buying this game please play the first LISA, it's! So good!!! And free! But basically, this game has it all. The story is wonderful, there's humor and extreme depression, the tale of an abused man continuing the cycle of abuse. It's a very human story. Although it's ridiculous and takes some side character tropes to their extremes, the main cast and story are so human feeling. The world is an extreme, but honestly, probably not that far off to what a world of cis men would be like. Austin Jorgensen, the game's creator, put actual time into researching all-male institutions, and I think taking those real life examples and going off of that (and exaggerating a bit) really make the world feel like a true male dystopia.
A bit of spoilers for the game below, but very vague (you mostly should read if you don't intend on playing LISA the first):
The story is about a man who lived with his dad and younger sister. The dad was abusive to them both, and sexually abusive to the sister. She killed herself, and the main character, Brad, feels like it's his fault. He finds a baby girl and vows to take care of her, but he really..... well, a man with that kind of history, you can imagine what happens. That's the foundation of the story. It's very heartwrenching, and the story portrays these various themes very well. Jorgensen really, really gets it. The story of this game takes off from there, and anything more would be too big of a spoiler!

While this game boasts a very very nice open city, with a number of nice cars to drive around in, it is not actually an "open world game." It is completely linear, allowing very little freeroam - every time you go out on your own, you are pretty much gaming the system, and putting off going to the next checkpoint, while you explore the world a little.
But the story is good. It is a classic maffia story, with a fair share of clichés, but it feels different in a video game, than in a movie. You are actually participating in these clichés, instead of just watching them - they engage you a lot more. That doesn't mean, that you have any choice in the matter, you are just pushed along on the corridors (they don't always look like corridors, but the feeling doesn't go away). At least it is the fun kind of being pushd along, with nice action sequences, and entertaining cutscenes. It is like playing a gangster movie yourself.
Also, the music. The music is just absolutely amazing. Actually driving around the city listening to the radio is one of the best things you can do in this game. Shame it doesn't encourage that, or profit from the amazing art it has.
All in all, a fun game, very well worth the money, but there are a couple of BUTs.
1. Even tho' there is a big, very nice open city to walk and drive around, it is mostly empty and boring. It often looks gorgeous, but there is almost nothing to do in it. There's a couple of clothing shops, gun shops, car repair/mod garages and restaurants. The latter are useless, they only refill your health, but that regenerates anyway, so why bother? Car modding is interesting, but ultimately useless, since the game doesn't actually allow you to freeroam much (and there ain't much point to it either). Dur to that you won't care enough about your car to pimp it out properly.
2. Collectibles: the inclusion of actual Playboy magazines is an interesting idea. But a good lot of them are hidden away in areas that are only accessible within a particular mission, and even then, only in a particular part of that mission. Since you can't save wherever you want, if you miss a collectible, and finish the chapter, you'll have to start the whole chapter again, and replay it all. Bad game desing. Very bad.
