If you weren't the biggest fan of the original RUNNER's harsh difficulty swings, lack of checkpointing, and sometimes confusing visuals but actually thought the concept was pretty neat and fun, then I'd highly suggest giving RUNNER2 a go.  Everything about RUNNER2's gameplay feels as if it was developed in direct response to criticisms of the first game and is definitely more approachable and polished than before.  If you just straight up didn't like the original game however, this one isn't going to change your mind.
The setup is largely the same with the only chief differences being the spiffy and colorful new aesthetic and changes that make the game a bit easier to handle. If you were a fan of the original's retro visual style, you'll likely be disappointed with the more distinct cartoony look and sound of RUNNER2, but if you were a fan of the gameplay, you're still in for a treat.
The biggest and most requested change is that there are now optional mid-stage checkpoints, which can make learning stages a bit easier. It's up to you whether you want a score bonus or a safety net, so there's a nice little element of risk vs reward here. The difficulty curve is straight up perfect this time around, with really nice ramp ups in challenge where they need to be with some easier stages sprinkled throughout to keep the bloodpressure down. Stages feel more like complete songs now, each with a really nice build up and repetition of patterns and mechanics with really nice flourishes at the end.
RUNNER2 is also a much bigger game than the original, containing 125 stages (100 normal stages and 25 hidden retro warp zones), multiple characters to play as, tons of unlockable costumes, and some Super Mario World'ey alternate exits toat can open up different paths in each world. I certainly found a lot of enjoymen in wanting to unlock everything, but you don't really need that mentality to enjoy what the game has to offer.
Overall, RUNNER2 is simply a better game in every respect. The new visual designs may turn off some fans, but they don't affect the core gameplay which is still solid as hell.

As a veteran World of Tanks (WoT) player, I've been in clan wars, campaigns, tournaments, leagues, company battles, stronghold battles, team battles, and thousands of random battles... Needless to say, I've spent an overwhelming amount of time playing WoT, learning the complexities of an outwardly simple game that, at its core, has immense tactical depth. I've committed to learning the game mechanics and perfecting upon skills that often feel diminished by unfair metrics of balance and incompetent teammates. However, I'm here to talk about World of Warships (WoWS). Offering many of the same appeals of WoT, WoWS solves many of the former's issues. However, WoWS is (arguably) the exact same type of game albeit with a much more obvious level of complexity. Ultimately, WoWS is firing and maneuvering. Whereas WoT players sometimes found themselves hopelessly outmatched against higher tiered vehicles and tank types (heavy, medium, light and destroyers) mattered little to the metagame (camo and DPM), the different classes of warships (battleships, cruisers, destroyers and aircraft carriers) have significantly more distinctive playstyles. As a result, WoWS players will never feel incapable of affecting the outcome of a battle as WoWS rewards intelligent play in away WoT does not. Although a completely different game, WoWS will feel serendipitously familiar to WoT players who remember feeling excited at the prospect of a game with so much potential and opportunity for growth. I truly recommend that you give it a shot.

Pros: the game is campy in that good old-school NES way.  The dialogue is very basic so that can be a pro or a con depending on if you like story driven plot or not.  All and all, the controls are pretty smooth, albiet not as smooth as Skullgirls or Streets of Rage 2 (still the smoothest Beat- em- up EVER imo). Cons:  Biggest con so far:  Not all the moves work.  Provie's jup kick didn't work and Bruno can't seem to do anything after he grapples, which are HUGE bugs that need to be fixed, as it limis gameplay options and flexibility which, is like th crux of these types of games.  Not being able to change the control scheme is another one I personally have aproblem with because I have a not- typical xbox controller that i'd love to set to scott pilgrim or even street fighter settings, as this game was clearly made for classic xbox or steam control settings in mind.  Items and dojos seem kinda scarce and, while maybe it's a way to no overload the characters all at once to still provide some challenge, the lack of any visible buildup combined with the ease at which you can die in like the first level (the boss was surprisingly hard with Alex and Ryan having friendly fire on on TOP of having limited combat options; by the time i beat the boss I was like level 4 which seemed a tad high, but i was also playing on my own) leaves me wishing for the Scott Pilgrim style of play where you get rewarded with new moves and full life upon leveling (and that game is NOT easy, even with that)
All and all, i think RCRU will be an awesome game when they get the move bugs worked out, and you're welcome to try, it's still interesting to see even with what they got, but when I play a brawler, i wanna be able to brawl FULLY not mostly.

This is a game I have been waiting for since I was 9 years old and ran up my parents' rental bill at our local video store renting RCR on Nintendo to the point that I knew all of the gang members names, tag lines, color codes of the gangs, secrets, exploits, etc. Again playing it on emulators off an on for the last 20 odd years, always having a fondness and a great time. (even set up LMI Kamachi to do a VPN so that my friend and I could play co-op with an emulator :) ) My friend and I missed the backer window, however we all but stalked Conatus trying to find out when the release would be. When the day finally came and we got to play, the nostalgia was so immense.
Its an amazingly well animated game, and very true to form from the original. The graphics are much akin to something like Shovel Knight where it postures 8 bit but using modern tech to accomplish things that the original RCR couldn't. The music is a perfect timepiece of the era, and captures the "60's" vibe that the original had, and also the 90's rock tinge.  The characters are well thought out, diverse, and funny. The story line is very similar to any hero beat-em-up and is a loveletter to the original RCR. Multiplayer is jump-in, jump out, no direct host (meaning you won't get booted from progress or the game if the person who "hosted" leaves. Also you get to benefit from the leveling of the characters' your friend plays so your both helping to level up different characters together!
The gameplay design, and some aspects of the user interface, are lacking at times though. I'm sure some things are actually bugs and will be worked out but others seem like they are here to stay.
The text needs to be faster, and most of the text doesn't have any audio feedback, so you cannot tell when things are being read if you are paying attention to other things on screen. The wanted system feels a bit last minute or not fully fleshed out, and is relentless as innocent bystanders will run through a pack of baddies while you're in the middle of a combo, causing you to be wanted. Speaking of the combo system (although supposed to be a "discovery" based aspect), it is very, very vague. All malls are non-neutral and leave only the hideouts for any kind of respite, and are the only place you can go if you have a wanted level, or have to take a bio break or save. (NO AUTOSAVE?! :( )
Bugwise sometimes it won't let you into the options, friendly fire sometimes hurts you if you are in battle even when turned off, and sometimes weapons just drop or disappear when you are in menu. Sometimes the game allows you to go off screen to the next area, waiting for your co-op comrades to join you, and other times it will force everyone into the next area whethere they were ready to go or not. I'm sure there are others, and as I have only put in 3 solid hours of play before having to go to bed, noticing as many as I have is a sign that worries me a bit.
Overall, I love this game still. SO much love has been put into the design and execution, and I have no doubt Conatus will fix most things that are causing folks to give it a bad rap. I will be playing this nonstop each night with my buddy and/or buddies and we will have a great time, there is no doubt. Despite its fallbacks, this is the game I hoped it would be.

An absolutely amazing little game combining aspects of roguelikes, classic JRPGs, and even a little bit of action, all mixed into a nicely paced, well humoured game.
As with many games that it takes its roguelike elements from, the game has the capacity to simply drop you on your head and kill you off at the start, but the same randomness almost always results in a fun experience - if a little frustrating at times. On top of the charming little world that has been set up for you to heroically... walk... oneway... is an array of secrets and unlockables to make life a little bit easier, or prepare you for the next difficulty up - and make no mistake, you WILL need the help!
The ability to take items from your completed runs and keep them for your next budding adventurer is extremely helpful - playing without this function is extremely difficult, but rewarding!
A game with random elements cant help but occasionally turn evil on you as a player, but all things considered, this is an excellent little game that, unlike other RPGs, doesnt need a huge time investment - though you might find yourself spending that time anyway! Incredible value for money gives this a real thumbs up!

My main issues now after finishing the first run through of the story:
NO FREEROAM!!! Unbelievable how this can have been left out. I mean the city is not particularly immersive in the first place but there is NO option to explore outside the storyline. This is unforgiveable.
TOO EASY, even on the hardest setting there is little challenge. Only a few hours of play.
STORYLINE, just not well thought out. Its not believable. The character makes odd choices that just leave me scratching my head going "what an idiot" Its too hard to have any empathy for him.
VEHICLES. Not enough, and far too many that dont even fit in the time period! Its made clear to you at the start of the mission what day and year it is, then you walk outside and get into a car that doesn't exist for another half of a decade.
THE MAP. Its pretty limited. Its not big, and the landmarks kind of annoy me. If its supposed to be set in New York, then fine, make the map resemble it at least vaguely and dont stick things in it from other cities like L.A. If its not supposed to be New York, Then don't stick the Brooklyn Bridge and the Empire State building in the middle of it. It just seems to give the city a tiny bit of identity (which is pointless) when the rest doesnt live up to it. A generic North Eastern city would have been easier to accept, without the landmarks.
Theres a lot of small details that annoy me too. Controllers?. Didn't detect my G27, could't get it working. In this day and age this shouldn't even be an issue. You can't drop an empty weapon, for example during firefights you can find your self with a shotgun, 2 tommy guns, an MP40, a grease gun, a 45, a magnum, and a .38, half of them are out of ammo and you have to cycle back and forth through the menu vainly searching for something to shoot back with. Also unfortunately there is no first person driving view. Multiple camera angles but none from inside the cabin.
Mafia 2 might be worth a punt if you find it on sale, but £30 for the digital deluxe verion is daft. The little DLCs are a bit annoying too as they clutter up your garage with unwanted vehicles you cant get rid of.

So the third installment of the SR series is pretty good, but not as good as Dragonfall.
I will highlight two problems and two virtues.
Problems:
1) The writing is still solid, but at times it goes on too much.
In the mid game I felt like I was drowning in all the stories that NPCs had to tell. I would be sitting there for a solid hour listening to my party members and shopkeepers talking about their lives and all that. There's a whole lot of telling and not so much showing. I feel that if you'd just done two actual missions for party members rather than just one it would've fleshed things out a lot more smoothly.
Couple that with the fact that there are entire missions that you just talk your way through and this started to feel like a Choose Your Own Adventure game after a bit.
Also shopkeepers don't need elaborate backstories, don't waste time on that.
2) The game is pretty easy.
I played through the whole game on 'hard' difficulty and, outside of the first mission when I didn't have any equipment, never had trouble. The AI is just completely terrible and never offers a challenge. They walk through poison gas, they glitch and forget to do an attack and they never focus fire. And there's just never any curve ball that gives you that 'oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ moment like in Dragonfall. No Troll Cyborg hacking, no duels with other Deckers in the Matrix and no crazy duplicating satan fights.
I didn't expect XCom here, but I still pretty much beat the whole game without breaking a sweat.
Virtues:
1) The story and world are genuinely interesting.
After the travesty that was Shadowrun Chronicles, I'm quite relieved to find that this thing was back on track with a compelling story with interesting twists and turns. The game gives you a decent amount of room to develop your own character and her backstory, while also giving you the chance to have interesting relationships with people. I was pleased that the plethora of ways to complete each quest and felt I had built a character with real personality after some time.
2) There's a good diversity of missions.
You get to solve a murder mystery, infiltrate a convention and break down corporate offices. There's nothing quite as good as Glory's mission from Dragonfall, but there's good stuff here.
Overall: If you liked Dragonfall, you'll have something to like here, but it probably won't meet that gold standard.

It seems as though being passionate about art is quite a strong paradox.  You do art because you love it, because it's your passion, because you love to make things, because you're good at it, or any number of personal reasons.  Thing is, you're not validated or it's simply a waste of time if you don't reach enough of an audience, or you don't meet this or that standard, or you don't get into this prestigious school, or you don't make enough money, or you get too much negative criticism.
So, which one is it?  Do you make art for yourself, or for others?  Is it both?  Expression and art is not a product of survival.  Is "expressing yourself" really just a nice way to say you're trying to impress others with creativity?  Are you pushing your piece onto a broader platform to spread accessibility or to make money and gather attention?  Is exposing your vision to the world just a kind way to say you're trying to persuade people with your propaganda?  Would you create something if no one would ever see it?  Why are you so eager for anonymous individuals to see something you created out of supposed passion and love?  Are you a kind and insightful visionary trying to lift the minds and spirits of your audience, or are you a mere narcissist trying to get people to look at you for a few fleeting moments?  Does your commentary on another's work provide a whole new perspective and outlook, or are you piggybacking off of someone else's effort to sound cool and give yourself the capital to project an image of being a valid critic?  Is creating "for fun" a normal thing and an ends to an innocent mean because it brings you happiness, or is saying that a low-effort shield to prevent others from judging too harshly?
I dunno.

You kind of already know what you're getting into when you're considering buying this game. Yes it's a budget indie title probably made by one person, this is nowhere near mass effect level. Now keeping that in mind this is a good game.
For what it is it's very interesting, you have an alright trading and buying/selling system where you can walk around in a first person environment finding sellable materials and objects and you can sell them to random merchants who have their own independent prices. It sounds really boring but it's pretty easy and simple, buy low and sell high, there are stars next to amazing selling opportunities so it isn't super difficult.
So you buy and sell stuff to earn enough money to pay off debts, you can also earn money through hunting down bounties.
This is the coolest part of the game, you get to go into a Quake 3 Arena style FPS where you kill goons and lackeys until the bounty appears and you have to shoot him down, you have to pick up better weapons, health, shields, and sellable materials in this mode, it's a simple arena style FPS, but it's still fun.
This game is an alright budget indie experience, it is not worth $5.00, but for $0.50 it's fun enough that I would reccomend it.

The basic principle in this game is: buy low, sell high. Unfortunately there aren't that many things to buy and sell, but nevertheless the concept of trading and traveling between space stations is quite well implemented and works. This part is relatively easy, and once you get the hang of the game you'll see the numbers in your bank account grow exponentially. If you need some extra cash you can try your hand at bountyhunting, which teleports you to one of a series of FPS arenas where you get to shoot people. Very basic but enjoyable while it lasts.
The biggest annoyance I found in this game is the lack of a sandbox / open-ended mode. The game is divided up into missions, guiding you through the stages of development for your very own space trading enterprise, but after each mission you basically start over.
Other than that, this game is a lot of fun to play and although it won't be able to keep your attention forever (it can get a bit repetitive over time) it is a fun little game and a great timekiller if you have nothing to do for a couple of hours. The price is already fairly low, and if you can get this game in a sale like I did you basically just can't go wrong.

Part of a relatively recent wave of games called "Earthbound-likes", LISA: The Painful RPG is one of the best examples out there. A quirky and tremendously dark humor is present in most of the game, only interrupted by genuine heartwrenching and tragic moments. It gets you involved in the main character's choices, even if the player's impact is minimal. It's a game worth playing on those grounds alone.
As for gameplay, it has the usual trappings of the most classic jRPGs, but with a couple of in-combat systems to keep things fresh. It's rather difficult at the very beggining, but becomes much easier as you acquire other party members. There's plenty to choose from, all of them with their own advantages and disadvantages.
Since the game is a bit short, choosing different parties provides some replay value for challenge purposes or just to check how the characters work.
Finally I should also mention the music, which really helps the game's atmosphere.

I have to agree with the people that say it is nothing like the first Mafia game. That was epic. This is pretty lame. Sure, it looks a lot slicker and there are some nice touches to it like the vehicle physics and the shops (car and character customisation) but it could have been so much better and there are some glaring issues I just can't agree with.
My main issues now after finishing the first run through of the story:
NO FREEROAM!!! Unbelievable how this can have been left out. I mean the city is not particularly immersive in the first place but there is NO option to explore outside the storyline. This is unforgiveable.
TOO EASY, even on the hardest setting there is little challenge. Only a few hours of play.
STORYLINE, just not well thought out. Its not believable. The character makes odd choices that just leave me scratching my head going "what an idiot" Its too hard to have any empathy for him.
VEHICLES. Not enough, and far too many that dont even fit in the time period! Its made clear to you at the start of the mission what day and year it is, then you walk outside and get into a car that doesn't exist for another half of a decade.
THE MAP. Its pretty limited. Its not big, and the landmarks kind of annoy me. If its supposed to be set in New York, then fine, make the map resemble it at least vaguely and dont stick things in it from other cities like L.A. If its not supposed to be New York, Then don't stick the Brooklyn Bridge and the Empire State building in the middle of it. It just seems to give the city a tiny bit of identity (which is pointless) when the rest doesnt live up to it. A generic North Eastern city would have been easier to accept, without the landmarks.
Theres a lot of small details that annoy me too. Controllers?. Didn't detect my G27, could't get it working. In this day and age this shouldn't even be an issue. You can't drop an empty weapon, for example during firefights you can find your self with a shotgun, 2 tommy guns, an MP40, a grease gun, a 45, a magnum, and a .38, half of them are out of ammo and you have to cycle back and forth through the menu vainly searching for something to shoot back with. Also unfortunately there is no first person driving view. Multiple camera angles but none from inside the cabin.
Mafia 2 might be worth a punt if you find it on sale, but £30 for the digital deluxe verion is daft. The little DLCs are a bit annoying too as they clutter up your garage with unwanted vehicles you cant get rid of.

A slower paced FPS where you can succeed without having to have 3ms ping and godlike twitchy reaction times, because the games are much more about positioning, knowledge of game mechanics, and minimizing risks instead of running around corners and spraying as many bullets as possible in the hopes of getting that kill .0001 seconds faster.
Graphics wise it looks very beautiful imo, with lots of detail all over the ships. There's additionally mods out there to reskin basically everything. The sound design has been reworked a few times and each time it sounds even more immersive, from the guns, explosions and this is one of the few games that I still leave the original music tracks running even after all this time playing.
The learning curve is a bit rough, but also leaves you a fair amount of room to improve on even after a long time playing. A good player will on aveage perform better than the rest of the crowd, but don't expect to win 100% of the time or pull out some crazy 6v1 gamble, it's not that kind of game.
Premium time is well worth it for your $$, especially the longer time packages. Higher tier ships are more a strain on your credit income than on how much XP you've built up. Premium ships offer some interesting options, and usually reward you with a bit more than the average income on credits, plus some offer some unobtainable ways to play that no other ship line can give you, but nothing to the point of P2W, as you can always perform well in the majority of ships, even if they play very differently.
Pro tip for the new players: Turn INTO incoming Torpedoes, not away. You'll take less hits or even avoid them entirely.

Despite being a relatively new player of WoWS, I have enjoyed the game enough thus far to feel it worth starting up a new account on Steam. While I can appreciate that there is frustration about not being able to link existing accounts to your Steam profile, this review is based on the actual gameplay, and not an inflated sense of entitlement.
WoWS is an arcade-style naval battle sim in which you engage in naval warfare against other human players (and sometimes bots depending on which type of battle you select). As with any PvP multiplayer game, you can expect to see players both better - much better - and worse - much worse - than yourself. As such, there are times where you can expect to become incredibly frustrated, even more so because RNG is a bit of a thing.
On the other hand, rewards can come to those who wait, and who learn how to properly utilise their vessels. Rush through the tiers at your own risk. Keep in mind that WoWS is not a new game, and there are plenty of experienced players who will happily fire up their lower-tier ships in order to club some seals - and if you're new to the game, expect to get clubbed a lot. Try and learn from the experience :)
Despite the gorgeous graphics and detailed rendering of the ships, this game is not huge on realism, so keep that in mind when playing. It is, as I mentioned earlier, an arcade game.
Now go out there, and go shoot some ships. Give me a wave or a hi if you see me (preferrably before sinking my ship).
I'm far from an expert, but hit me up for advice, or alternatively (and the better option by far), hop on to Youtube and look up some of the excellent guides that have been posted by players of the game.
EDIT: NoZoupForYou has been posting guides here on Steam, so it'll be worth checking them out if you're a new player.

Fun follow-up to Shadowrun: Dragonfall. Hong Kong refines many of the elements present in Dragonfall. For example, there is a new stealth oriented matrix (still some combat involved) and more non-lethal options on missions.
Some pros:
- great dialogue especially with the Rachter and Gaichu companions
- combat is the same fun system as Dragonfall with a few tweaks
- more choices on how to complete missions
- some of the etiquettes are very useful (I hear others are almost useless - so a bit of a pro and con here)
Some cons:
- money is very rare, it is very difficult to completely kit out your own character (or any others). This is especially true if you play a decker like me and you want to buy guns, a deck, programs and cyberware.
- the game isn't as difficult as Dragonfall. I'm better at the game now, but it was much easier than Dragonfall. I didn't come close to dieing once (on hard) and rarely had to heal
- it seemed like the AI often made some questionable decisions, hopefully they will smarten it up through future patches
If you enjoyed Dragonfall, you will enjoy this. If you haven't played it I would start there and then play this one (and shadowrun returns eventually as well). The game took me 27 hours on hard. I completed all available missions.

Don't believe the hype YET. There is a TON of promise for this game, and i'm enjoying it right now, but in its current state, it is SEVERELY flawed. I guess the pressure to meet the Feb 27th Deadline was a bit much, as it was released with some serious bugs. Some flawed design choices as well, and when it comes to the little things it all adds up to a frustrating experience, especially since many fans have been waiting for years. $20 dollars is already more than most major indie productions, and it feels like a $8.99 game with the lack of polish and refinement.
EDIT: They've since updated that they are working on patching the issues, so there is hope.
EDITS for better explanation:
1) BIGGEST issue right now is the Multiplayer, with menus glitching out, saves not carrying over to single player, no chat function, and level breaking bugs. They are currently working on a patch right now, so we'll see.
2) Minor flaws in design choices like In-game text being true to the original, but without a way to "skip to the next line". It takes forever just to get through reading the effects of eating (when you hit any other button, it immediately cancels out the explanations). During the tutorial they teach you to hit a vending machine for drinks, only to never follow this up in-game. Considering you can get a wanted level for trashing public property, it woulda been a great design choice for risk-reward.
3) The "Wanted" System feels tacked on and has led to many a headache when civilians get caught in the crossfire or your surroundings start to get wrecked, by no fault of your own. What i don't get is why the cops don't also attack the gangs? They should be trying to break up the fights or hold them accountable for their destruction. Instead, they attack you even when a gang member breaks a table...
4) General community gripe is the lack of explanation for using new moves you just learned. The descriptions for each is ridiculously bare bones, with some moves mixed up with others and with erronous descriptions / instructions. This has been causing confusion as to what is a bug (missing moves), and what needs to be "discovered" in a combo chain. A LITTLE EXPLANATION IS NOT HAND-HOLDING, informing your players is part of gameplay design.
5) Some missions are severely bugged and game breaking. Not talking about having to do unexpected things, like climbing a fence to jump to the hidden side (though that was another puzzling and flawed game design choice). Sometimes Roxy updates your current objectives, sometimes not, characters that should be speaking freeze in place, others turn invisible or never show up but have their hit boxes still present ingame (arcade boss for one).
6) The dreaded Sewer Chase and Milk Mission. These are examples of out of place moments in game design. When you are given a driving game, you expect to drive, not suddenly be forced out of the car to do a fist fight sequence with driving controls... Same can be applied here and it's one of those outdated game design things that really break the immersion / game flow.
I could go on with more and more examples, but the general feeling thus far is the game needs a bit more polish, and a few design changes to make it more inline with a modern day revisit to a golden era game. For better or for worse it apes the original to a T. Some of the "worse" will drive you up the wall. Hopefully a patch comes soon addressing these issues, until then, this is going to have to get a thumbs down.

First off, I backed this on Kickstarter and am a huge RCR fan... seriously. I made a fan animation in Flash back in 2005 that hit the front page of Newgrounds back when I was in college.
JDPoZ vs ThoChan... look it up. :)
So, first off, it has a few changes made so far from the original. Some I like, some I don't.
------------------
==Like:
+ More buttons - don't have to tap punch and kick together to jump
+ More moves! AND you can BLOCK!
+ AWESOME animation. Has tons of weight and charm to it.
+ Enemies can actually get to you if you jump on walls :)
+ Expanded world
+ highly varied boss character types and move sets
+ Multiple characters with different fighting styles and moves.
==Dislike :
- Horrible early move set (for Lucha guy at least) after prelude initially. I literally grab enemies and NO button presses do anything. It makes me a sitting duck.
- after initial familiar RCR original "tutorial" section, the game does a poor job telling you whether or not you should attack fellow students, where the "classroom" you're supposed to head to is, etc.
- Too many enemies (and multiple gangs populating areas) early on. The original would only throw a couple of low level enemies at you in the beginning. And most of the time they'd run away. There was a balance to them. Immediately after the opening, the game throws enemies wearing skull clothes who fly and shoot green fireballs at you and "nerds" that throw ice spells that freeze you for seconds without letting you "break out" by button mashing or wiggling the stick (classic for beat-em-ups where the character would be trapped by an enemy). These early enemies seem (even if they aren't) WAAAY too strong and have way too versatile a move set for you to be facing early on. Same goes for the "greasers." Those knuckle slam hits seem to rip your health apart. These sorts of abilities seem like it would be better to have them start appearing later on. Maybe make a "high tier" version of these enemies that have those powers. The original game did this with different shirt colors.
- The same button to attack is the same button to immediately dismiss floating windows of text. Many times I would see a text box appear during a fight and it would immediately disappear as I was punching away. Might want to have a delay on input acceptance as those windows appear.
- Wish text would take up more than a line or two so you could get more info at once instead of having to wait for every line and then potentially forget what the previous one said.
- SFX. Is missing some of the original quality of the NES sounds
- Music. A bit generic. Wish they'd have grabbed Jake Kaufman / Virt for this one. Doesn't evoke the same as the original's music anywhere for me yet.
- I died a LOT... Like... a LOT lot. At the beginning I was really upset there weren't more "save areas." Why shouldn't a Mervs or Chicken Burger joint qualify as a save? And the map didn't make it very clear which area had the "hideout." Is it the arcade? It looks close. *pauses* NOPE. NO SAVE OPTION. Grrrr!
- HATE the cops. They smash into you in every area and seem to get mad at even the slightest bump into any property (which also gives no reward for risking being hurt by the cops - I'd like it if the coke machine dropped a few sodas if I hit them if the police are going to show up) And as you defeat them you get NO MONEY. They only get a stronger boss cop to show up AND the stupid news feed blocks a part of the lower screen. And even if you DIE they show up with you again. And the only way to get rid of them is to kill EVERYONE in an area AND there has to be a dumpster to hide in.
- UI design. Come on guys. Pass through iconography showing 8-bit versions of the controller detected. A green button with an S or P or K isn't very helpful. Especially because my controller has no buttons with those labels (even though I know they mean "Special" or "Punch" or "Kick" and not the button letter, this is not typically how player control guides are done).
What I HATED:
--confusing mission design with little to no explanation as to what the player was supposed to do. Most of the time the designers left you only vague notions where you had to make guesses to figure out where to go or what to get. I even went online to check out discussions only to find out how the "dog-tags" bit was supposed to work. I got the one set and went on base, only to find after reading online that I had to gather SIX DOGTAGS for some arbitrary reason.
--The chase scenes and the fetch-quest / escort mission for the milk. They were HORRIBLE designs. They make this game a "no" on my original "yes" recommendation.
==Nitpicks:
* Double tap to run doesn't "stick" like it did back on the NES. What I mean is, double tapping on the NES started a fast run that continued even if you let go of the direction. In this, you must continue to press the direction after the double tap or the character stops.
* Confused - why do old Ryan and Alex have red and blue hair? I mean I know the Nekketsu anime looking art that was always drawn changed their hair color, but most of the U.S. players know them all as just having black hair. Seems like a weird stylistic choice.
==What I wish they had:
+ Fast vertical run double tapping. Like I want to run up and down on the screen fast by double tapping those directions too.
+ Sometimes peaceful areas - especially malls. Sometimes the original RCR would have randomly peaceful zones with happy music and no enemies. Wish there was 2 RNGs for areas. Low chance for peaceful in normal streets and combat areas, and higher chance for peaceful in malls and shopping zones.
--------------------
As of right now, it still feels like a bit of an unbalanced fan game with a real lack of early-game balancing by a quality gameplay mechanics designer.
I am really disappointed. This series has incredible potential and I still think the best sequel now was the Gameboy Advance game.
TL;DR - Good art. GREAT animation. Forgettable music, mediocre sound design, unbalanced gameplay and really poor starting move set after tutorial. HORRIBLE HORRIBLE chase sequence and fetch-quest designs that will likely drive away any but the most dedicated RCR fans.

It's a damn shame that games like these will forever be overshadowed by games like Undertale, that got oodles of media attention. Hell, after the game was released and people were saying 'If you liked Undertale, you should play LISA! It's even better', people flocked to play this and the positive review percentage dropped like a lead balloon. These games are not similar, and people need to stop comparing the two. But I digress, on with the review.
In comparison to Undertale, which takes inspiration from the themes of Earthbound, LISA follows the source material much closer. LISA is a much more traditional, turn-based RPG where you play as a man called Brad, living in the barren world of Olathe as he finds the last girl left on earth, and swears to protect her with his life.
Story: 11/10. I'm not even joking, I don't think I can pop this thing any higher. When it comes to 'masterpieces' in video game storytelling, some either tell an epic tale with in-depth lore and feel, or some hit your emotions hard, and this is one of those games in which mixes a balance of lore and a deep, underlying meaning on the concept of masculinity.
Just please, don't spoil it for yourself, whatever you do. This is something that has to be played entirely blind.
Gameplay: 8/10 - Where some people say the gameplay behind LISA was repetitive and dull, I found the amount of creativity in the battle system incredibly engaging, and loved the use of story telling through subtle actions and notions done by the characters during certain battles.
Like many RPGs, LISA is your typical four-man party member turn-based game, recruiting party members with different roles to help your team. Where LISA differentiates from the rest, however, is how the combat is executed. There are lots of creative buffs and debuffs that you'd realistically think would occur in a world containing only men, such as depression, being drunk and even smelling pretty bad. Everything feels fresh and new, while keeping to a traditional RPG format, and that's something I can really appreciate with a battle system like this.
LISA's world is another thing that really helps the game stand out, as unlike most games that rely on a 3d perspective, LISA's overworld plays out like a 2d platformer, with certain areas being unreachable without certain items. This is used very well in a few gimmicky segments to help mix up the gameplay progression, but I won't be spoiling those here.
The game also comes bundled with a hard mode, entitled 'PAIN Mode', in which after using a save point, it cannot be used again, as well as the game in general being more difficult and having new encounters. This is really the mode that the game should be default to, in my opinion, as many of the game's features like the expendable party member roulette are seemingly meaningless in emotional value when you can simply savescum your way through it.
Presentation: 9/10 - Although the art style might be outdated, it stands out as being unique and different to other RPGs on the market, while still retaining that feeling of familiarity from its Earthbound inspiration. Every character looks and feels unique, with everyone having their own personality and traits.
Soundtrack: 10/10 - The composition work is truly a treat to behold with this one, with excellent use of leitmotifs and bizarre themes used throughout to further enforce that feeling of being alone in a strange place. It's exactly how I'd see a game like Earthbound's sountrack being made in the current era of games, and it really hits the feelings it needs to well. Not one song in the game is forgettable, and for that, I can praise the soundtrack with everything I have.
Aside from a few technical limitations due to RPG maker being what it is (Some slower load times in areas, which for how intensive the game should be, is abysmal to experience), the game is a must-play. People may complain about the gameplay, but you really only play RPGs for the story, right?
And it's not like you'd want to play it twice for how emotionally devastating the story is, anyway.
10/10 masterpiece, and I look forward to Austin Jorgensen's future endeavours.

Despite being a relatively new player of WoWS, I have enjoyed the game enough thus far to feel it worth starting up a new account on Steam. While I can appreciate that there is frustration about not being able to link existing accounts to your Steam profile, this review is based on the actual gameplay, and not an inflated sense of entitlement.
WoWS is an arcade-style naval battle sim in which you engage in naval warfare against other human players (and sometimes bots depending on which type of battle you select). As with any PvP multiplayer game, you can expect to see players both better - much better - and worse - much worse - than yourself. As such, there are times where you can expect to become incredibly frustrated, even more so because RNG is a bit of a thing.
On the other hand, rewards can come to those who wait, and who learn how to properly utilise their vessels. Rush through the tiers at your own risk. Keep in mind that WoWS is not a new game, and there are plenty of experienced players who will happily fire up their lower-tier ships in order to club some seals - and if you're new to the game, expect to get clubbed a lot. Try and learn from the experience :)
Despite the gorgeous graphics and detailed rendering of the ships, this game is not huge on realism, so keep that in mind when playing. It is, as I mentioned earlier, an arcade game.
Now go out there, and go shoot some ships. Give me a wave or a hi if you see me (preferrably before sinking my ship).
I'm far from an expert, but hit me up for advice, or alternatively (and the better option by far), hop on to Youtube and look up some of the excellent guides that have been posted by players of the game.
EDIT: NoZoupForYou has been posting guides here on Steam, so it'll be worth checking them out if you're a new player.

So, the developers wanted to divide Steam accounts (that give Valve a %) and non Steam accounts... They say is because of the game not being "cross platform" which is a lie, specially on PC when Steam can work as a launcher to launch the standalone game... So here is the thing
The game IS good, I do recommend it, however if you want to play with your old Wargaming account, here is what you need to do:
1. Download the game
2. Go to the directory it downloaded and delete steam_api.dll
3. Open the game (if you had the standalone version, move the preferences.xml file to the directory so you get the login and config automatically)
4. Log in and enjoy playing thru Steam
Here is the thing, doing this WILL NOT allow you to pay with Steam currency, so you got to buy stuffs with direct purchases inside the game; if they release achievements YOU WILL NOT be able to get them (you can always use SAM to unlock those achievements, keep in mind, it's not fair nor "legal", do it at your own risk)
So, why would you do this? You can do this to play your old account, while keeping the Steam overlay without any issue (adding the standalone version may cause some issues), have access to the community inside Steam, easier to have screenshots and share them, KEEP THE GAME UPDATED AUTOMATICALLY
If, in the future, they add Steam Trading cards, YOU WILL NOT, be able to get them, since this is a F2P game you need to spend money in their shop to get them... And because you can't, well...
It would be cool if the developers allowed us to log in with our old account and play with it like many other games do...

BIT.TRIP Runner 2 is a rhythm/platformer where you run along a path, collect gold, and avoid/defeat tons of obstacles along the way.
Much like the first BIT.TRIP Runner, I just couldn't enjoy this game despite my best efforts. The art is beautiful, and it's nice to see that Gaijin can make a beautiful, non-retro game. The music is wonderful as always. The gameplay, though... I normally really love music games of all sorts, but the gameplay is incredibly frustrating. The levels still go on way too long, and they're pretty hard, even near the beginning, which means that you will end up re-doing the same parts of the same levels over and over. I don't think the first Runner has a checkpoint system, and that is definitely a welcomed addition to Runner 2, but it's not enough. This game is certainly challenging, but for me, it wasn't a fun challenge at all.
The keyboard controls are baffling. You can use the arrow keys and space bar, which I highly recommend over what they tell you the controls are.
The BIT.TRIP series is a cool experiment in rhythm games, but Runner, for me, was a failed experiment and I don't know why that's the game that got a sequel. If you liked Runner, you'll love Runner 2, but I can't endorse this game for anyone else.

Some nice improvements over DF, like being able to manually enter combat mode, greatly exanded cyberware and improved inventory management. Decking has been improved as well, with stealth being a viable option now. Not a big fan of the hacking minigame, though it is entirely optional and can be bypassed in various ways.
Overall, I'd rate this slightly below Dragonfall DC. The main story wasn't as compelling in HK (particularly the ending), though the writing overall was about on par. If you enjoyed the previous games, you'll definitely enjoy HK.

Likes:
- Excellent writing - as in command of the language
- Interesting story with a Hong kong feel
- Sublime music
- Enjoyable characters, both runners and NPCs
- Well done cutscenes
- Revamped Matrix
Dislikes:
- Enemy AI is terrible
- Too few runs
- Shortage of nuyen
- Same classes and skills (with small changes) as previous Shadowrun games by Hairbrained
General:
As I finish Shadowrun: HK I am left wanting more. It's not a "Is that it?" moment as the final missions hold a sense of being epic, but rather I would have wanted to dive further into the city, continue leveling up my fellow runners and being able to test out more abilities. I think that's always a good stamp of approval. Yeah, some things aren't great, but overall it pales to the great ambience and interesting world.
Reflections:
My first or second run I picked was the one where a potential fellow shadowrunner could be recruited. However I didn't realize this was the case and chose another dialogue option fuelled by the prospect of getting to fight in anotherwise rather combat-less run. To my dismay I now read another review praising the story of that character. I like that the game isn't holding my hand, but that was a bit harsh.
I haven't encountered any bugs in my playthrough, atleast not to my knowledge. But that said, the enemy AI is dreadfully dull. Maybe it was in the other Shadowrun games by Hairbrained and I just didn't notice, but this time around I found myself irritated at a ranged enemy unit sitting in a clever cover position at the start of his action who promptly just runs out in the middle of open space and fires one shot at my tanky runner sitting behind heavy cover. Why not just remain seated and fire at my other, more squishy and already hurt, standing in a angle that allows for flanked attacks? This, and other very unwise choices by enemy NPCs keeps happening over and over again. On hard difficulty.
Conclusion:
For fans of Shadowrun this is a must get. For the rest ... get a package deal with all three Shadowrun games by Harebrained schemes. If it's not out yet it's bound to happen.

Fans of Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun: Dragonfall will feel right at home with this title. It's very much the next interation of the series, with very few changes to the mechnics, style, or story formula.

If you've played the other games and want more, or if you're new to the Shadowrun series and fancy a bit of a challenge, I definitely recommend it.

And thus another adventure ends. I'll admit, the series didn't glue to me until Dragonfall, interesting premise that Returns wasn't able to execute properly. After another Kickstarter, Hairbrained Studios come in to deliver a third journey to the dark deep magical and corrupt world of Shadowrun, this time, in the bustling ciy of Hong Kong. Hope you know how to speak cantonease.
So here's the the intro of the story: you're an ork, a human or whatever that was just released from a max security corp prison and have been summoned by your foster father to join him in Hong Kong, along with your foster brother. No doubt, nothing will inevitably hit the fan and everything will be alright. In fact, that's what happens, your father wanted to meet up with you and your brother so you can have a nice family reunion. Kind of anti climatic, but enjoyable and simple... ok that doesn't happen. Stuff does go south, rather a bit slowly, and the whole of Honk Kong's police force are looking for you and the party you met upon arrival. At least it's not the London bobbies. Even more, your farther is missing and nothing is making sense. Why were you attacked? Who attacked you? What's behind the fridge?
So from on there, the story preety much takes the same formula as of Dragonfall: peal out layers from the conspirancy surrounding you, take on varying missions that test you with hard choices, meet fantastic characters and do the Bioware thing where you help them in a Loyalty Mission. AMAZING MISSIONS, ranging from opening a pickle jar for a character to opening TWO pickle jars! I might add that the majority of the 47 hours spent in the game was me reading every line that the game presented me, the dialogue is more than spot on! Can't and couldn't stop reading it! I'm also glad that the game now features a more diverse race of a crewmen, not for the sake of race equality, just to get a more varying story.
I prefer a different location from Hong Kong, but it's nonetheless interesting and the asian background is also explained within the universe's rules and it's quite intriguing.
As for the combat and general gameplay, it's preety much the same as that of Dragonfall. Read it in my review of it here if you want to:
. You can now also ambush enemies and plan proper "door breach-in" situations. A point to be mentioned, there is no proper tutorial to tell you how its mechanics work. HOWEVER, there's a big change.
During the kickstarter, Harebrained promised a revamp of the Matrix areas. The Matrix areas are virtual network world realities. So imagine the internet in a futuristic tron-like world.... actually don't... I did find that the Matrix was quite shallow in previous games. Now, it's a bit of stealth and a bit of puzzle. So the stealth part comes in by figuring out patrol patterns of the guard programs and avoiding. The puzzle involves "Simon Says" interactions and figuring out the right code out of a certain selection. To be honest, this feels more like faffing about, rather than gameplay that makes sense with the rest of the game. It all feels out of tone with the rest of the game. You're reading calmly and performing long thought-out tactics in the combat, THEN PRESS 1,4,5,6,7,2,3 IN THE PRECISE ORDER OR YOU FAIL! DON'T BE CAUGHT BY THE LINE OF SIGHT! Get it? I didn't hate it, but I felt like it didn't belong in the game.
The game's end boss fight did improve imensly. Now, I'm gonna try to avoid spoilers, even though it's in the title of the game, but in Dragonfall
. Except during the battle it just sits there in front of you doing nothing. You can't even hurt it! Again, without spoiling, the final boss fight of Honk Kong not only makes you fight it but you can also dissuade it. I find it important of the implmentation of the latter because the whole point of the game is to understand the lore of the game and it the final battle, you get to use it as a weapon.
So the soundtrack is my biggest complain: it's too bland, unorginal and uninspiring. I get it that the studio needed to adapt the sounds to an asian background, but I miss the creative electronic sounds from Returns and Dragonfall. The latter had thematic music that associated with each crewnate. Quite a dissapointment. Aside from that, the game runs fine but there are various bugs to be fixed.
In conclusion, I'm very satisfied but I do feel like this formula might be getting a tad old. Either way, I felt quite satisfied from the unmonotonous game even though it was a tad long... I recommend it!

First off, I backed this on Kickstarter and am a huge RCR fan... seriously. I made a fan animation in Flash back in 2005 that hit the front page of Newgrounds back when I was in college.
JDPoZ vs ThoChan... look it up. :)
So, first off, it has a few changes made so far from the original. Some I like, some I don't.
------------------
==Like:
+ More buttons - don't have to tap punch and kick together to jump
+ More moves! AND you can BLOCK!
+ AWESOME animation. Has tons of weight and charm to it.
+ Enemies can actually get to you if you jump on walls :)
+ Expanded world
+ highly varied boss character types and move sets
+ Multiple characters with different fighting styles and moves.
==Dislike :
- Horrible early move set (for Lucha guy at least) after prelude initially. I literally grab enemies and NO button presses do anything. It makes me a sitting duck.
- after initial familiar RCR original "tutorial" section, the game does a poor job telling you whether or not you should attack fellow students, where the "classroom" you're supposed to head to is, etc.
- Too many enemies (and multiple gangs populating areas) early on. The original would only throw a couple of low level enemies at you in the beginning. And most of the time they'd run away. There was a balance to them. Immediately after the opening, the game throws enemies wearing skull clothes who fly and shoot green fireballs at you and "nerds" that throw ice spells that freeze you for seconds without letting you "break out" by button mashing or wiggling the stick (classic for beat-em-ups where the character would be trapped by an enemy). These early enemies seem (even if they aren't) WAAAY too strong and have way too versatile a move set for you to be facing early on. Same goes for the "greasers." Those knuckle slam hits seem to rip your health apart. These sorts of abilities seem like it would be better to have them start appearing later on. Maybe make a "high tier" version of these enemies that have those powers. The original game did this with different shirt colors.
- The same button to attack is the same button to immediately dismiss floating windows of text. Many times I would see a text box appear during a fight and it would immediately disappear as I was punching away. Might want to have a delay on input acceptance as those windows appear.
- Wish text would take up more than a line or two so you could get more info at once instead of having to wait for every line and then potentially forget what the previous one said.
- SFX. Is missing some of the original quality of the NES sounds
- Music. A bit generic. Wish they'd have grabbed Jake Kaufman / Virt for this one. Doesn't evoke the same as the original's music anywhere for me yet.
- I died a LOT... Like... a LOT lot. At the beginning I was really upset there weren't more "save areas." Why shouldn't a Mervs or Chicken Burger joint qualify as a save? And the map didn't make it very clear which area had the "hideout." Is it the arcade? It looks close. *pauses* NOPE. NO SAVE OPTION. Grrrr!
- HATE the cops. They smash into you in every area and seem to get mad at even the slightest bump into any property (which also gives no reward for risking being hurt by the cops - I'd like it if the coke machine dropped a few sodas if I hit them if the police are going to show up) And as you defeat them you get NO MONEY. They only get a stronger boss cop to show up AND the stupid news feed blocks a part of the lower screen. And even if you DIE they show up with you again. And the only way to get rid of them is to kill EVERYONE in an area AND there has to be a dumpster to hide in.
- UI design. Come on guys. Pass through iconography showing 8-bit versions of the controller detected. A green button with an S or P or K isn't very helpful. Especially because my controller has no buttons with those labels (even though I know they mean "Special" or "Punch" or "Kick" and not the button letter, this is not typically how player control guides are done).
What I HATED:
--confusing mission design with little to no explanation as to what the player was supposed to do. Most of the time the designers left you only vague notions where you had to make guesses to figure out where to go or what to get. I even went online to check out discussions only to find out how the "dog-tags" bit was supposed to work. I got the one set and went on base, only to find after reading online that I had to gather SIX DOGTAGS for some arbitrary reason.
--The chase scenes and the fetch-quest / escort mission for the milk. They were HORRIBLE designs. They make this game a "no" on my original "yes" recommendation.
==Nitpicks:
* Double tap to run doesn't "stick" like it did back on the NES. What I mean is, double tapping on the NES started a fast run that continued even if you let go of the direction. In this, you must continue to press the direction after the double tap or the character stops.
* Confused - why do old Ryan and Alex have red and blue hair? I mean I know the Nekketsu anime looking art that was always drawn changed their hair color, but most of the U.S. players know them all as just having black hair. Seems like a weird stylistic choice.
==What I wish they had:
+ Fast vertical run double tapping. Like I want to run up and down on the screen fast by double tapping those directions too.
+ Sometimes peaceful areas - especially malls. Sometimes the original RCR would have randomly peaceful zones with happy music and no enemies. Wish there was 2 RNGs for areas. Low chance for peaceful in normal streets and combat areas, and higher chance for peaceful in malls and shopping zones.
--------------------
As of right now, it still feels like a bit of an unbalanced fan game with a real lack of early-game balancing by a quality gameplay mechanics designer.
I am really disappointed. This series has incredible potential and I still think the best sequel now was the Gameboy Advance game.
TL;DR - Good art. GREAT animation. Forgettable music, mediocre sound design, unbalanced gameplay and really poor starting move set after tutorial. HORRIBLE HORRIBLE chase sequence and fetch-quest designs that will likely drive away any but the most dedicated RCR fans.

Problem has been resolved, adding a full review now:
Brawlers, my one true video game vice and weakness.  I am an absolute sucker for this long dead genre. When I found out about this one, it was well past it's KS backer faze, and given that I don't like backing Kickstarters (Personal opinion, I buy products, not promises) I was going to wait until it was done anyway.  I tried to convince myself to hold off, at least a month.
But given that it's a beloved remake/sequel of a game genre and game I absolutely loved when I was younger, this was a day one purchase for me,
However, I have a few question about the game decisions in RCRU.  Like, why do smashing enemies into each other with the various finishers or throws do no damage but knock them down?  You'd think that having a grown kid thrown at you hard enough to knock you down would hurt.  (Actually, it does.  To clarify, it's not that actually impact, it's the way you hit the ground, and how your body involuntary bends.  Yes, personal, anecdotal experience.)
This section is: Redeacted.  (It took a few levels, but the levels are starting to change visibly.)
Speaking of Grabs, which also links to issue no. 1, why does missing one have such a long cool down if they're not as effective at room clearing as they might otherwise should be?
And finally, why doesn't every character have a ground pound?  Why is it something you have to purchase at different level tiers?  (Doesn't help that Provies is busted, or if there's another prereq, like Alex's Roundhouse needing Crescent Kick first, before it triggers, the game doesn't say.)
Speaking of being unclear, can we get a listing as to what the stats do?  I've figured out Strength, Stamina, Willpower, Special and Weapon, but other than that, no clue as to what the others mean or help with,  Also, corrected tooltips would be nice.
There are good things about this game though.  I love the 'hidden' combo system, for example.  Some of the moves can be chained into others.  Alex has a couple I've found, which need certain skills unlocked/purchased but that's part of the fun.
The first I found needs to have Crescent Kick and Roundhouse, but if you hit Kick, Punch, Kick, Kick, you do a four hit chain as opposed to the basic three hit combo.  If you have Running K.O. unlocked, and hit Kick, Punch, Punch you finish off  with a standing version of the K.O.  Those are just two, there are a few more that I've found for the beginner six characters so far.  Which I'm pretty sure there many more to find.
The presentation is fine, the graphics are bright, popping, but without too much visual clutter.  The animations are smooth and feel impacting other than the odd throw design decision.
The audio is a bit hit and miss, though.  Some sounds are much louder than others, like Bruno's Poison Mist, or some of the Bomber Gang's attacks, which creates a loud spike whenever they go off.  Normalizing is all it needs though.
I like this game, and I'm sad I can't give it a better score in my head.  I give it a 6/10.  (With 5 being dead average, playable but not memorable.)  A fun brawler, that doesn't feel quite finished just yet.

Having played the game so far unto the end, I believe their are other paths I could explore in this, but I am content, as this game offeres technological innovations that demonstrate teh skill and tallent  of the creators, especially in my favorite scene, in the cover art, the gallery.  Where the use of a virtual camera showing the location of hidden objects, makes for a lovely transition, that a lot of games besides Portal and Portal 2 have failed to adapt into their games.

I feel it's worth playing, but if you come away feeling disapointed.  Wait a few years and play it again, I am confidednt with time you will enjoy the story being told, the heart break and love affair being told and for me a well rounded story :0)

Space Merchant is a game with an identity crisis. It is mainly a buy/sell stock market type video game of the future. It tries to incorporate first person shooter action as well.
If you're looking for a market based game where you trade commodities based on their profits, this is your game. There are interesting characters to trade with a quite a bit to do. The voice acting is simply a joke. One of the most annoying sounds I've ever heard in my life occurs when you walk up to civilians and they say "later" or whatever it is. Makes me cringe every time! The tutorial was quite lacking, although I understand there is a fine line between innundating/confusing players with too much detail and letting them actually play the game. So... LISA...
It's interesting to say the absolute least.
Leaves a sour taste in your mouth when you're done.
Makes you uncomfortable all the way through.
In general LISA is that game where what you feel can't be put easily into words, but I'll do my best here.
So LISA is a 2D RPG game that was made a while back, December 2014. It was actually made in RPG Maker 2003 which is a pretty good feat for how well this game is made. LISA tells the story of an aging man named Brad Armstrong in a world where nearly all women have suddenly vanished from existance after a mysterious event. Men now roam the plains of the earth, living life to the fullest as humanity slowly dies out. However most people have gone insane by this point. Brad grew up in an abusive home with his father Marty and his baby sister Lisa. You don't see much of her throughout the game however, but Marty occasionally shows his face in key moments. Now Brad is around the age of around 40-50 I would presume, and he lives with his three old friends, Rick, Cheeks, and Sticky. He's become an alchoholic and relies on a drug known as Joy to help rid memories of his past that resurface when he hasn't taken the drug in awhile. One day he runs across a little baby. He brings it back home to Rick, Cheeks and Sticky. They soon realize that this is a baby girl. The other three feel that they should take her to a Military group known as Rando's army, hoping for a reward, and feeling they would be more equipped to deal with the situation. Brad however, refuses that as an option and vows to take care of her, thinking her as his "Second Chance" to what we don't know he's referring to. He names her Buddy and raises her as his daughter and the game begins after an incedent that I will let you discover yourself.
The combat of this game is very Earthboundy, where you choose your move and just attack, leaving most up to chance. However you can type in the commands to certain special attacks to do more damage, rather than just letting the attack do itself. You can have up to three core party members to help you fight throughout the game which you can do the same with, and a massive amount of excess to bring in if needed. All these party members are quirky in their own way, but it soon dies off after you initially meet them.
The style of this game is quite interesting, I personally have never seen this type of gameplay in my experience, but the best way I can describe it is a 2D Earthbound-ish game. You walk right to proceed and left to go back, and into doors to check out new areas. There are small ledges that you can jump up and eventually you can become more manuverable with a bike. However one complaint was the instant death ledges that kill you and revert you to your last save point, which if on pain mode, can be a ♥♥♥♥♥. The music is also spot on with the tone it is trying to set. Very abnormal, creepy, awkward, and just completely strange.
Okay so down to the biggest part of this game, it's story. This story is a very depressing one, I caution those interested with easily depressed tendencies. LISA deals with some majorly uncomfortable and disturbing things, including Suicide, Murder, Canabalism, Drug use, Alchoholism, and it just goes on. (Decent Spoiler ->)
The ending is depressing, making you feel like, well as the description states, a broken man. You feel like a failure and it just gets worse once the credits roll.
Overall LISA was a strange journey and one that I'm glad, yet sad to have witnessed. It is something worth trying out no doubt but it was hard to go through. I can't fully put my words into how I feel about this game. However the best I can do is give it a 9/10, not for everyone, absolutely, but if it interests you and you are quite sure you can handle the moods it will set on you, give it a look and experience it yourself.

Lisa: The Painful, a review.
There will be spoilers. You have been warned.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Story: The game opens up in a playground where Bradley Armstrong and his 3 friends Rick, Sticky and Cheeks are getting beat up by a bully named Chris Colombo. Then, after Brad gets beat to♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bradley walks home. And you go home to see Marty Armstrong. Your abusive father who, upon seeing you, throws a beer bottle at you and tells you to go to your room, you do, and Brad starts crying. Then, the name of the game appears above the crying Brad. Flash forward many years. You take control of Bradley Armstrong, in a post-apocalyptic world in which, there are no more females. Therefore, the males can't reproduce and continue their species. And so Bradley and his 3 friends Rick, Sticky and Cheeks spend the last of their days drinking beer and taking/throwing away a new drug called "Joy". Until one day, after Bradley takes some Joy, He sees a baby of all things. He then takes it back to his friends Rick, Sticky and Cheeks, who are shocked and want to know if its a boy or a girl. It's a girl. Then, RIck suggests that they give it to the Rando army. Brad declines the offer and says the baby is his "Second chance". Then, there's a montage of Them building a room for the baby who he has named Buddy. Brad and the baby get older. Brad is now bald and the baby is now a young child. After the montage, Bradley is sitting out by a cliff, until he hears a man screaming for help and a dog barking. He goes to investigate and sees a sad looking man named Terry Hintz hiding in a tree. He tells Brad that there is a vicious animal attacking him and that Brad is the only one who can save him because he "Pulled his h-string" You then are pitted in a fight against a little dog named Cheeselegs. I'll talk about the combat in a moment. After the fight, Terry Hintz  joins your party. You and Terry walk back to Brad's house to see that the entire place has been searched and the girl gone. You and your team must go and rescue the last girl.
Gameplay: This game's combat isn't groundbreaking by any means. it's your standard turn-based RPG. the thing that the devs wanted to push most in this game is choices which affect your stats. Basically, you can choose to either give an arm or sacrifice all of your magazines (The games currency) and losing an arm will affect your stats.
Problems: The game was made in RPG maker, So the FPS drops at certain parts. Also, playing with a controler is...uncomfortable. Let me explain, with a keyboard, you press shift to get off your bike/run on a controller, you have to hold select to run./get off your bike. For me anyways. Combat gets pretty boring after awhile. And another big problem is the fact that cliffs are placed so close to where you see an item sometimes you just jump off a cliff and die.
Overall: It gets a solid 8.5/10 It's a good game. the FPS drops are frustrating. But they aren't that common. I usually just play with the keyboard to get over the controllers bizzare layout. It's humor is incredibly dark. Cliffs are everywhere. The game will make you hate yourself for your decisions. And story-wise, Brad is a little too selfish.

One Way Heroics might look like a cheap and generic jrpg made in rpg-maker but it's definitely not the case.
The game is a procedurally generated turn-based roguelike with many interesting features. One of the most noticable ones is that the game takes place on a world map, each move will take you one turn and the darkness on the left side of the screen will draw closer. Basically as you move and battle across the world, darkness will consume everything behind you. Be it an enemy, friendly npc, objects or the entire terrain. You have to avoid it at all costs. During your journey you can find various loot and treasures. From simple weapons and armors up to supplies and precious magic scrolls. The rpg mechanics are fairly generic, you defeat enemies and gain level points which can be spent later on cetain spots on the map. Although you still increase your stats normally by gaining experience. Various weapons and armors have different attributes. Scrolls and magic items might have special abilities, pretty much the usual roguelike stuff.
Combat is extremely simple and only requires you to attack the enemy by pressing one key, then a series of dice rolls will determine everything. It's not that engaging but yet very enjoyable mainly due to the smooth controls and fast pace of the game. Your character has certain special abilities though that require stamina points which are automatically generated as long as your energy is high enough. Energy is another ressource and acts mostly as a starvation meter. You lose energy with each term and depending on the terrain, you might lose even more. You refill your energy by consuming various food items.
Now let me explain the goal of the game and perhaps one of it's more compelling features. As soon as you start a new run, your goal is to defeat the Demon Lord which appears in 400km in the world map. During those 400km, you want to level up and get the most loot in order to prepare for the final encounter. But due to the darkness, time  management is vital and you have to carefully plan ahead your moves. Even if the combat is simple, there are many things to take into factor. For instance various terrain types can give you additional bonues/mali, some enemies are more resistant than others to various weapons. Furthermore with the spreading darkness, you really want to make the combat the most efficent as possible. Turning it into somewhat of a puzzle game. During your journey, you can also meet tons of charactets that have their own quests, some may join you on your journey. Others provide services or act as merchants. Finally there is a lot of variety and content in this game, there are tons of classes and things to unlock. Each generated map feels really unique and offers different challenges.
Also the game let's you save items that your next character can chose right at the start of a new run. So there is some progression in this game, furthermore you can spent a rare currency to save at certain points of the maps.
To conclude, there is a lot to talk about but this game is definitely a blast to play and offers something refreshing to the roguelike formula. It really conveys a sense of adventure.

FTL has earned a reputation as one of the great indie titles. Underneath the simple graphics, the gameplay is excellent and engaging.
Randomly generated locations and events each playthrough gives it great replayability. The moment-to-moment decisions of managing your crew, ship power allocation, weapons and upgrades, repairs and resource management along with an excellent array of weapons and tactics for use in combat (lasers, missiles, boarding actions, fire bombs, drones, cloaking device, the list goes on) keeps you engaged and every battle comes down to how well you use the tools at your disposal.
People who dislike FTL often state it relies too heavily on RNG and it comes down to luck only. RNG does indeed play a role, but the more you play, the better you get and the more you realise that your decisions and tactics affect the outcome far more than the random elements ever will. The random assignment of locations, events and enemies also gives the game great replayability as no two runs are ever the same.
It may seem like a tough, even unfair game at times, but FTL challenges you and forces you to learn, adapt and get better. Enjoyable gameplay, backed by a great soundtrack - definitely recommend.

I own and have completed Shadowrun Returns, Shadowrun: Dragonfall, and Shadowrun: Hong Kong, and I can say with confidence that Shadowrun: Hong Kong is, in my opinion, the best campaign out of the Shadowrun Returns franchise so far. The storyline is great, the NPCs are flavorful, and the gameplay is some of the best yet. Cyberware feels much improved, decking is far, far better than it was in the earlier two games, and the changes/upgrades to the body design of the characters is a welcome one, at least for me.
The only things I can really complain about are the (mostly annoying) bugs and the enormous amount of text errors. The former mostly includes load times steadily increasing as the game goes on and some minor hitching or freezing; I never encountered a CTD or game-breaking error. The latter is nit-picky, but literally the last half of the game has either missing or misplaced words every other text box or so. It really seems like they just used spellcheck and called it done, which is pretty disappointing for such a text-heavy and nicely-written game.
All-in-all, I would happily recommend this game to anyone who enjoys RPGs, the Shadowrun universe, or is simply in the mood for a good story with interesting characters.

For players who have never played WoWS before:  Try it! It's a very solid game and worthwhile as an arcadey naval game.
As far as I know, it's the only quality game in the genre of fullscale naval PVP ship-to-ship combat as of right now.  (Of course War Thunder, another f2p game, is going to add naval aspects within the next year, but we'll just have to see how that goes)
The game is free so you don't lose anything if you don't like it. As a free to play game, it does have ingame purchases and microtransactions, but none of them are necessary or forced.
These come in the forms of:
- Premium account, which just helps you grind through trees slightly faster than usual.
- Premium ships; which typically do NOT give you a competitive advantage.  They're often namesake ships, famous specific names or classes of ships.  For example, a premium ship I own off of the steam version is the USS Alabama.  Now while the South Dakota class battleship isn't currently ingame as standard.  Similarly designed fast battleship classes are, such as the North Carolina class (South Dakota predeccessor) and the Iowa class (South Dakota's successor), and they are standard trees, and having a South Dakota doesn't give me any advantage over either of those two classes.
Another example is a charity ship.  They have a bundle currently (as of November 14, 2017) on the shop to purchase the USS Texas, with a cosmetic ship camoflage of the Texas state flag.  Proceeds of this bundle go towards the Battleship Texas Foundation, for their efforts the keep the ship preserved, as the ship is having hull issues with flooding and leaks. The money raised goes towards keeping this beautiful piece of history preserved and protected.
Again, the premium ships are typically not better in any way, and the standard research tree ships are able to stand their own in their own regards, and of course they're optional purchases.
- Doubloons/Gold currency:  the ingame premium currency which could be bought and used to purchase certain premium vehicles, or premium account, convert to a large amount of ingame standard currency, or to convert to free XP which could be used to unlock a ship instantly, or substantially cut the amount of time needed to acquire, or to buy some cosmetic items.
None of these are like other publishers who choose to paywall stuff that should be a part of the base game. Wargaming are very proud of World of WarShips and they hope to see it flourish with a healthy playerbase, which I personally believe the game deserves.
My only issue with the steam client is not one that affects players new to the franchise looking to try it out, but rather those of us who have played off of steam.   There is currently no way to link your prior Wargaming account to your steam account, meaning your progress and premium vessels do not carry. It's like starting over from scratch.  Of course we still have our WG launcher accounts to play on, which is fine.  I personally was hoping to have the game on steam for screenshots and chat convenience, and the convenience of using the steam wallet for ingame purchases.  Personally I will likely stay on my non-steam version, but might play some on here as it could be fun using a different focus on a new playthrough/account.   But I still recommend new players to give it a try.
