Mafia II is still one of my favorite sandbox games.  It's not a perfect game by any means, but the action and story kept drawing me in.
Let me tell you the negative things I thought of the game first.  You have a massive city to explore with tons of little shops and distractions to keep your interest for a while.  However, I will say that the inhabitants of the world don't feel very "alive" to me.  Normal citizens only have a few actions they can go through depending on your interaction with them.  It won't take long to get exhaust all the different scenarios that can play out with basic NPCs.  Also, as I mentioned earlier, there are a ton of little shops and restaurants to be found, but you will notice most of the shops all have the same items in stock with very little variety from store to store.
The combat in this game is pretty basic shooter stuff.  You can take cover, shoot, rinse and repeat.  It's fun, but it's not really anything innovative.  I did like with the cover system that you were able to attach your character to a wall/blockade/whatever and then peek around the edges to take the perfect shot.  Once again, not innovative, but I've only seen that type of cover system in a few games.
The story in my opinion is where the game truly shines.  I loved the story.  It was interesting with interesting characters.  There weren't any real major twists in the story, but I was never bored with how things played out.  The voice acting for nearly every character in the game is some of the best I've seen in a video game....EVER.   The actors portrayed each scene so brilliantly.
So should you buy this game and give it a shot?  I have to say yes, however, I think gamers who aren't a fan of sandbox or heist/criminal-type games can avoid this one as it didn't bring anything revolutionary to the table for the genre.  If you are a fan of this genre or of the first Mafia game, I highly suggest giving this game a shot.  Hopefully you'll enjoy it as much I did.

OWH is a roguelike RPG in the shape of one of the old classics. Pick your hero and hack your way through one of the many worlds as you try to save it. You can influence your strengths and weaknesses by selecting different perks that'll allow you to increase your attack/health or other stats. A dimensional vault will allow you to carry on the items of your dead hero unto the next unlucky chap in line.
It also bears to mention that OWH has one of the most interesting takes on turn-based combat that I've seen for quite some time. While the game is technically "turn-based", everything happens in real time. Enemies will move as you move, attack as you attack and so forth. If you don't plan ahead, you'll likely find yourself stuck between 5 killer hounds.
Due to the random nature of the game, differences in the gameplay between the classes as well as the ability to have maps randomly generated for you, the replay value of this gem is off the charts. Oh, and the difficulty options will allow you to choose between having a quick 20 minute adventure, or an epic struggle for survival that might stretch on for hours.
With the risk of overselling a bit, One Way Heroics has gorgeous aesthetics, fun gameplay and a great soundtrack. I'd recommend this for anyone who enjoys roguelike games, or RPGs with a bit of a twist.

Shadowrun HK is an exceptional game and definitely worth the purchase. The big question though, is where would I rate it among the "greatest games of all time''. This is important since Shadowrun HK isn't just some random indie game, it is the successor of my 2nd favourite game of all time (Shadowrun Dragonfall).
In my opinion, what makes Shadowrun HK such an amazing game is that the game is most fun when a player makes mistakes. In many other games, players are forced to save-scum & reload or restart from a checkpoint after they have blundered. When I played Shadowrun HK, I stuffed up and instead of a ''mission failed'' cut screen, I was punished by having the computer unleash hordes of security forces at me. I was then forced to utilise combat tactics to resolve the situation.
What I found really extraordinary was that the developers actually found a way to improve the combat experience (over Dragonfall). The combat in Shadowrun HK is extraordinarily fun, and probably the most combat fun I had playing a single player game. The Laser prototype mission was especially incredible.
I was quite impressed by the characters in the game, especially the hillarious vampire. The party characters have all kinds of cool stuff. It's so fun using the grenade launcher or the robot dog. Dragonfall's characters were more interesting from a ''role-playing'' perspective, but Shadowrun HK's chracters are more interesting from a combat experience.
The decking aspect of the game has been redesigned as well. The graphics are better and there are essentially two ''mini-games''. As I like the ''normal game more'', for me - the less decking there is, the better. In my game, I used a decker for all missions - so I should try using her less in the future to see what happens.
Overall, my impression with Shadowrun HK is that it's around the same extraordinary quality as Shadowrun Dragonfall. It has essentially kept most of the brilliant gameplay aspects of Dragonfall and has even made some improvements - eg: the inventory system and combat mode.
That being said, I still feel Shadowrun Dragonfall Director's cut is the better game. The biggest difference between the two is the plot and the character stories. Most people who played Dragonfall never did see the utterly brilliant story (to completion) - because they never completed the game properly. In addition, Dragonfall's director's cut has some of the best parts/missions of the game. The storyline of Shadowrun HK is fine, but does not seem to be on the same extraordinary level. (Note I haven't played through the different endings yet though).
So in conclusion, Shadowrun HK is probably a top 5 game of all time for me. Shadowrun HK and Dragonfall are exemplary games that will probably go down in history as modern classics that would inspire lots of games in the future. It's a shift away from big-budget games with great graphics and technology  (but often uninspiring gameplay) - to games that can be played on a low-powered laptop, but are masterpieces in design - that are really fun to play !

So, after one complete playthrough, I can safely recommend this game.   It takes the positives from the first two Shadowrun games and fixes a lot of the annoyances like the poor inventory and party management that could make parts of the previous installments feel like a chore or an annoyance.
The UI is much cleaner than Dragonfall or Shadowrun Returns, and everything looks sharp.  They've even added a few cutscenes with voiceover via a sort of dynamic comic book presentation style.  The core of the game is still the same, though, so if you weren't into a grid based tactical RPG set in a cyberpunk world but with elves and dragons and other fantasy trappings the first two times, this game still won't change your mind.
PROS:
-The story is great.
-The characters are even better- not just your crew, but the NPCs are cool as well.
-While the story choices don't seem like they would drastically alter the way that everything unfolds, there are clearly a few things that would have ended differently if the PC had chosen to resolve certain situations differently.
-The music is decent and fits the setting well.
-Moderate replay value. I probably won't play it again right away, but it could be fun to create a completely different character and go through the story again in a few months when my memories of the story get a little fuzzy.
-Bug resolution has been quick.  The last patch seemed to address almost all of the ones that I had encountered.
-You have a modicum of control over your other teammates' skill progression and item loadout.  At various stages in the game, you will be prompted to choose one of two abilities for each of your regular runners.  These choices will affect how they should be played, sometimes in substantial ways.
-Matrix is WAAAAAY cooler this time around.  It was a slog in past games, but after a couple of hacks, you'll probably figure out how to skirt security in this game, making it more than a war of attrition where you have to kill every bit of security to advance.
CONS:
-While most of the bugs are fixed, I got no steam achievements.  I think this is probably due to Windows 10, and as I mentioned, HBS has been pretty diligent in fixing problems, so hopefully this will be resolved in the future.
-The game isn't terribly difficult.  This might be a pro for some players, and I was only on normal difficulty, but there wasn't really a point where I felt like I was about to get completely wiped out, especially at later levels when my team was all tricked out.  If you're a seasoned strategy RPG player, you should skip directly to the highest difficulty if you want a challenge.
-Some of the mission restrictions don't make sense intuitively.
Example: In one scenario, you have to subdue a target so that you can kidnap him from his condo.  To do so, you have to wait for three rounds while the special weapon knocks him out.  By this time, I'd unlocked Duncan's ability to zip tie an enemy to subdue him if they were unconscious.  When I did this, however, the game gave me  the death screen for killing the target.  There were a few situiations like this sprinkled throughout the game.  It didn't ruin my enjoyment since the game autosaves frequently enough that you're usually just a few minutes out from whenever you last made a huge mistake, but situations like that definitely ruin the flow in an otherwise awesome story.
-Wish there were more runners in your crew to choose from.  No one is the mage, so you'll have to fill that gap as the main character or do without.  You can hire others, but since there's no way to grind for extra cash, this will severely handicap your ability to buy new gear or spells.
-Summoner fetishes are too expensive as consumable items for Summoner to be a viable character build.
TL;DR:
This captures the Shadowrun experience in a fun and immersive setting.  Would definitely recommend to anyone that likes or is interested in Shadowrun or that enjoys strategy RPGs.

If you want an RPG with really good writing, fascinating story elements, and simple yet fun strategy mechanics, then this game is a must. I loved Dragonfall for those reasons (moreso the Director's Cut than the original), and Hong Kong improves on the formula even more. The characters are really engaging, the plot made me wonder what would happen next deep into the night (as I kept playing and avoiding sleep to find out what would happen next), and the RPG elements feel quite rewarding for those of us that love seeing skill stats go up and buying new equipment (and I do). Plus, avoiding spoilers, but the game also has horror elements, and it disturbed the hell out of me!
On a less formal note, I'm now on my second playthrough, so a few tips. One:
You aren't paid as generously as in Dragonfall, so you have to make your money last for the top-notch gear you want for your character. There's isn't enough money to spend on gear for your party members as well. Two:
At the very least you will need Gang. Personally I also chose Shadowrunner and Academic, but Socialite also seems very useful. Corporate also has its uses, but not for any problems that can't be solved in other ways, from what I've seen. Take your pick. Three:
This may be personal preference, but I played a cyberware-heavy Adept in my first game, and now playing a pistol Decker-Samurai for my second game. I find the latter a lot more fun. Plus, I'll be honest, it's also because I don't have to drag Is0bel everywhere for hacking; she's the character I find least interesting, so being a decker lets me bring someone more fun along, like Gaichu or Gobbet.
All in all, fabulous game, just as good if not better than Dragonfall, love it to pieces, really hope it does well enough to warrant another Shadowrun game.

To start out with, I shall give a basic synopsis of HK (no spoilers).
You recieve a mysterious message from an old aquaintence, asking you to meet him in Hong Kong, a Corporate-ruled metropolis, where the neon is bright, and the shadows are dark. You end up leading a group of mercenary criminals (Shadowrunners), each with their own talents and personalities. As you progress, you investigate the reason for the message calling you here, and even the city itself, which seems to be affecting everybody in a negetive manner.
Now, to the part where I tell you how this game is the bee's knees, and how it stands against the previous entries.
Lovely game, a real improvement from Dragonfall, much less Returns. HK goes deeper into Shadowrun lore, with the inclusion of the HMHVV and extensive references to events, including the Desert Wars, and the activity of dragons other than Loftwyr or the Feuershcwinge. The  Matrix is  improved, having more of a fluid motion aspect rather than a near-constant turn-based navigation like the previous enstallments. Many of the NPC's have custom portraits in the dialogue, lending more immersion to the experience. Speaking of dialogue, the dialogue is great. I mean, it was great in the last two, but i think that the dialogue in HK is *GREAT*. Each Character and NPC has a story (academic etiquitte if you want some more dialogue options with your team, especially Ractor), and your opinion of those characters change the more you interact with them (looking at you, Reliable Matthew, you beautiful SOB). Unfortunatly, there are some long-winded characters that aren't very memorable, i.e. the talismonger in the Five Elements (When talking to her, i just read the last couple of sentences and still got what she was saying). Thankfully, a majority of characters are more interesting and are well-worth talking to, not only for information, but also for the simple pleasure of it. Not only when interacting casually with characters is the dialogue spectacular. During missions, the dialogue between people is just as important as putting a hole-shaped hole in their head. When you hear, "We've eaten burritos tougher than you", it really makes you think about the bigger things, you know? Not to mention the ghost noodle machine, which made me contemplate human mortality and the transcending of our fragile bodies to become a part of something greater (seriously tho, ghost noodles super sp00k). As for the missions, the main story missions are good, but I always found myself wanting to finish as many miscellaneous runs as I could. I would actually argue thet the misc. runs are more enjoyable than the main ones, in particular the missions from your crew members. Nevertheless, HK is an excellent entry in this interesting series.

Having played this game for over a year i have seen some of the ups and a lot of the downs of this game. Since i have also been burned i feel a certain duty to  advise/warn new players on what to expect and then decied for them selfes whether or not to commit to this game (dont worry there wont be any WG/Steam integration rant).
I wont be focusing as much on the gameplay (not much to talk about it anyway) as i will be focusing on how Wargaming treats their game
Positive:
1. Gameplay
Very straightforward, you get put in a map with 8-12 players for each side and you fight to the death (or for the objective).
The ship types are (supposed to be) in a rock-paper-scissors formation
(Battleship(BB)->Cruiser(CL)->Destoryer(DD)->Battleship(BB)...)
Cariers(CV) are a bit of a special case since they can attack enemie ships without putting themselves in danger so they counter all of the other ships (as long as they arent found).
There are a few mechanics in the game that determine damage done to ships based on the weapon used and where it lands but i wont get into those details since there is a lot of them and thats not the point of this review.
You have the control point map
the attack/defend map

and the ''king of the hill'' map with mulltiple layers
(Most players consider the Standard and Epicenter maps bad as the promote passive play but it can be hard to understand unless you play)
Overall as a game, World of warships is very fun, but its the ''other things'' that causes me to  ultimately give this game a negetive review.
2. Content
There is a lot of content so there will almost always be something to unlock and even if you unlock everything there are differnet builds for ships, and there will almost always be a new line on the horizon.
Negative:
Some of the things i will talk about here wont affect you at the start (tier 1-4), but as you play more and more they will become more apparent and they can end up ruining the game for you.
1. Balance
This is definitely the weakest point of this game. WG doesnt understand their own game, they have been advised by pro players and comunity contributors (Flamuu, iChase, Notzer, Jingels and many more) how to fix the game, but they refuse to listen. Ships that are OP dont get nerfed (Conqueror T10 RN BB), ships that are underpowered dont get buffed (IJN DD, KM CL), Ships that are broken (CV interface and controls) dont get fixed.
It took WG almost a year to rebalance the USN carriers so they might be able to compete with the IJN carriers. (all they had to do was tweak the number of plane squads on the carriers).
2. Ship distribution
Because of the lack of balance there are way to many Battleships players in the game, because there is no line  to really counter them. The IJN DD  main arnaments are the torpedos which counter BB's, (because BB's have dificulties avoiding them) but the torpedoes in the IJN line (T8-10) are a joke you are better off using the USN and KM DD's which are gunboats and have more reliable torpedoes (because logic). The other DD lines (USN, KM, SN) are gun boats and arent the well equipped to take down BB's.
3. Premium content
Premium content isnt that bad in this game, even if you buy all the premium things that you possibly can, it's useless if you dont know how to use it properly (certain premium ships have there own unique play style). But lately most of the premium ships are just a copy/paste of the tech tree counter part. That wouldnt be so bad but for the last few months WG has increased the number of premium ships that have been released, while the regular content (maps, normal ships, balance) have taken a back seat.
4.Servers
EDIT (18.11.2017) I HAVE BEEN INFORMED BY SUB_OCTAVIAN THAT THE MISSIONS ON ALL SERVERS ARE NOW  EQUALISED
It is very imortant, your experience of the game will change based on which server you play.
If you play on the RU server you can expect to always have good missions (reasonable task with good rewards) and free content (flags, camos, consumables, xp)
If you play on the NA server you can expect simmilar things but not as many of them
If you play on the EU server you can go f*** yourselves. The missions are hard and unreasonable with pitiful rewards. Other servers almost alwasy have some missions going on, EU only has them on the weekends (They probably want us to spend more time with our families). In the past WG EU cut content from the EU server (they literally made a different patch and edited the patch notes video from RU), but after a backlash from the community the content was released in the EU as well (search Christmast convoy missions on YT). There is almost always some scandal going on in WG EU
5. Historical accuracy
When it comes to historical games i think that balance of the game should come before historical accuracy. However in this game there are neither. WG has lowered the positons of the weak spots of a USN T10 and T9 BB's (guess if a premium ships is in there) which has has made high tier battles againts them unenjoyable.
One important thing to note if you are a fan of naval history, there are alot of paper ships in the game (designed but never built/finished) so if you go into this game hoping to to see and play some legendary ships from ww2 you will be disappointed
6. Community driven
WG some times uses these words to justify certain changes in the game or if the community reacts poorly to something (lowered weak spots). You will find out that the only community driven things that get put in the game are the ones that make WG more money. most things the community is vocal about (nerf op ships, buff UP ships, fix broken stuff) fall on deaf ears.
7. Community contributors
Community contributors arent really respected by WG, to them they are more like advertisers. Their opinons on the pre released content tends to be ignored (Graf zeppelin) and WG just does their own thing. iChase,	who was a very good community contributor for over a year, was removed from the program for being critical of WG decisions and their staff.
Final words
I have covered the things i wanted to talk about the most, there are probably many more things, good and bad, about this game that i skipped so that the review isnt too long.
If you are a new player take note of what i said at the start of the negative points. This game is like day and night when comparing low tier battles (1-4) vs high tier battles (8-10). Dont let your fun at tier 1-4 fool you into thinking it will be like that at high tiers.
The problems arent with the game, so much as there are problems with the developer.WG doesnt listen to its community, balance doesnt exist, netiher do changes and money is the primary concern.
Having said all of this and giving this game a negative review, i still play this game a bit, i just dont enjoy it as much as i used to. In the past i did spend money on the game (~100EUR in 8 months, stopped about 5 months ago), however since there havent been any (good) changes in a long while i have decided to stop supporting WG.
Since i have played the game for so long i feel a certain commitment to it and i really want to see it improved and succeed so i can return to it and start regularly playing it again. The game was fun and sometimes it still is, but if i could turn back the clock and choose whether or not to play World of warships again, i would be writing a review for a different game.
PS: sorry for any typos or misspelling english isnt my first language.

Long story short, Blade Symphony is a fighting game and a good one at that.  But a review is a review, so I'll delve into it more.

Blade Symphony is a traditional fighting game except the main attraction of it is, as in the name, blades/swords.  Every match is a 2-out-of-3 match.  Your main weapon in this is a sword.  You can do the classic moves of any fighting game, such as grabbing, block-breacking, doing combos, etc.  Also, you do have a projectile, a smaller blade you could say.  But here is a main strength of the game: you cannot spam.  Instead, to throw you projectile, you have to charge the throw.  This is a good feature, especially for fighting game nuts like me since anybody who has played a fighting game online knows there are "annoying" experiances.  Not with Blade Symphony.
Anyways, you have three techniques to your disposal: heavy, balanced, and fast.  Balanced is as it emplies, balanced.  This means you get a good mixture of some speed and some power.  It's a fundamental skill for not just the beginning of your experiance, but with every match you get into and your future experiance.  Heavy is soley based on raw power, meaning you can completely deplete your opponents health in only a few hits.  The downside is that you are extremely slow and any medicore-timed hit can have the opposition racking up combos and defeating you quickly.  You'll have to know your opponents moves and have good timing to use this technique to your advantage.  And last but not least is fast.  Fast is all about speed. Get a quick combo then move out of range, then strike again.  You'll have to play smart, because the disadvantage is that you have low damage.  Naturally, fast can, in most correctly used situations, dominate somebody who is using heavy.  Make sure that if you're using heavy and your enemy is using fast, switch to fast or balanced.  There are also four different characters to use, though they all depend on the user and how they use them.  You can also download swords of the workshop, non of them being overpowered.
The key of every match is patcience and timing.  Wait for your opponent to get within range, then strike according to the situation and their placement on the field.  Blade Symphony is honestly a great sword fighting game that feels like you're actually in the heat of battle.  Use timing, the three techniques, and the character you are using's moveset and strike.  Picking up this game was a real treat, and hopefully it is for you.  Definetly recommended to anybody who has a few bucks on them.

I really want to adore this game. The core of something very good is there: combat and movement feels quite solid, the pixel art and animations are all nice. However, the game is full of strange, glaring flaws that make it impossible for me to recommend it in its current state.
In short, I'm finding the early game to be extremely poorly balanced and confusing. Once you've got a good selection of moves and you've learned to filter out the game's noise, it's entirely possible it turns into pure gold. The absolutely-missing-the-point nature of the multitude of problems I've run into don't give me a whole lot of hope, though. Here's a disorganized rundown of some things I consider flaws, I guess in the name of "feedback":
You don't start the game with enough moves. Bizarrely, the luchador begins with no grapple attacks, and after two hours of play all I've been able to find is a back grapple which is functionally worthless in single player. After having grapple attacks in the tutorial it feels horrible to grab enemies and have nothing at all to do with them. The movelist is illogically laid out and the dojo screens don't give you any feedback about what moves actually do.
The entire shop system is poorly implemented. After buying any kind of food you have to sit for ages and stare at the slowly scrolling text at the bottom of the screen telling you what the food actually did. If you press any button you cancel that text altogether. The first couple screens of the game proper have bizarre shops that serve no apparent function (why on earth am I adopting a cat???) other than to confuse a beginning player.
While it may be "true to the original" the text system in general is a mess. Massive amounts of meaningless noise flow through the text scroll at the bottom of the screen along with important, if vague, objective information. The text advances itself so you have no choice but to focus laser-like on any potentially valuable words lest you lose the thread completely. The "typing speed" option doesn't seem to change anything?
There's a GTA-style wanted system which is pointless and anti-fun. On many screens, civilians are constantly meandering in and out of the line of fire. It's too easy to accidentally hit one and summon cops who are worth no money and follow you across screens. Also pointless is the day-night cycle which has jarring transitions--well, no transitions at all really, the screen just changes in a single frame. You're locked out of shops and the like overnight, just because.
The curve of the "economy" feels broken. Early game it feels like it takes forever to save up for a single piece of food, but you really need to be spending your money on moves so the game is actually playable and fun.
Nearly every screen seems to have some foreground object that obscures your view for no good reason. Some kind of silhouette or outline would be nice in these ever-present situations.
There's a bunch of out-of-place background cameos that make the game feel like Retro City Rampage for modern indies. What are these even doing here?? Nobody's going to say "yo Castle Crashers are in the background? Sign me up!" This doesn't bother me that much but it just feels kind of trashy and it actively turns off some people.
Addendum after struggling through some more sessions:
Some of my issues with early game grind I now blame on character balance. Bruno and perhaps others are just objectively weaker than, say, Glen or Ryan. Bruno has at least two moves that simply do not work and has to struggle create worthwhile combos. So, the rate the game "gets going" is highly dependent on your character.
There are three un-fun and just grossly wrongheaded "boss fights" that involve chasing guys who don't fight back. Three of these, in a row. Apparently later there's an extremely unpopular quest involving carrying breakable milk across a bunch of screens. After spending enough time in RCRU to beat the original game multiple times over, I finally ran into some real, actually cool boss fights. There is no concept of pacing whatsoever.
Ultimately, what has caused me to quit in frustration more often than anything else is enemy AI. Nearly every basic enemy, more often than not, wants very badly to maintain a distance of about four character lengths; totally outside your reach but leaving you within the range of whatever charge or ranged attack they have. You spend way too much time chasing down enemies who just don't want to let you "beat 'em up."
I really just don't like this game at all. It's excessively padded out, the enemies aren't fun to fight for a myriad of reasons, and a lot of the game's "content" is pretty awful. "Sorry about the mess." - Han Solo!!

Bought this during the Steam autumn sale for €2.50 and what a bargain it was!
This is a first-person single player game where the aim is to make your way through obstacles using different kinds of leaps as well as your grappling device and rocket boots (you will get the rocket boots in Star Haven).
The game looks very nice visually with vivid colors and runs smoothly on normal computers; I believe you will not have a problem running it unless your computer's performance is ridiculously low.
The fact that there is no multiplayer may lead to people not buying it so if you really dislike playing alone don't get it.
However, when you grapple (at least at first) you feel like a total badass and as the obstacles become progressively more difficult you feel a certain satisfaction once overcoming them.
The achievements are fairly challenging and you will need to master the game in order to get them which is a fun challenge for those of you who are achievement hunters.
The gameplay lasted around 5 hours for me. I did not try to find collectables or interact with objects because I didn't know the game well enough so 5-6 hours is a good estimation of what the game should take at a reasonable pace.
Overall, this is definitely a fun game even though it's offline so as I said, if you only like playing with other people do not get this, but I recommend finding it on discount and buying it off Steam because it is definitely worth the €2.50 that you will pay!

TL;DR: LISA is one of my favorite RPG of all time.
Before I enter this review, I feel like I need to state that I never really liked earthbound. I love LISA because of it features, not because its like earthbound but (insert comment here). I will also try to avoid spoilers if possible.
Why do I love the game LISA? Well, theres several reasons why I love this game. I'll give a list of each feature and why it adds to the game's experience.
Well Written and Understandable Characters:
Unlike some games, I really could relate to the characters within the game. Their actions seem reasonable. For example, the main character, Brad, doesn't go out because he is destined to stop an evil force, but he heads out to fight a world of perverts to save someone who is close to him. Even the companions seem understandable, especially when it comes near end of the game, which leads me to the next feature I like.
Divserse and Complex Compainions:
Within the game, there are many compainions that you can recruit. Each with their own attack style and personality. It allows you to group certain compainions so that you can perform more damage. For example, you can find someone who can spit gasoline and combine that with fire based attacks for massive damage. My only complaint about this system is that once you recrute a compainion, they don't do much other than fight for you. I was expecting that a character could talk to you about a part of the story or even question your morals but sadly they don't.
The Story:
Probably the best feature, LISA's story is a gripping one. It uses a blend of dark humor and drama to create a great, quirky story. As stated before, each character seems to be rational. They don't act because they are destined to, but because they are just trying to survive just like you. The ending stuck with me because it tied the story in with the choices you made so well, which leds me to the next feature.
The Choice System:
In this game, your choices have real consequences. One unique thing about this system is your companions can die, as in straight up die. Their death can be cause in combat and out of it. This makes some moments within the game intense due how you can lose a party member. Not only are your party members affected by your actions, but so is the main character. For example, you can lose an arm, which will permanently affect your characters stats and animations. I felt that this added so much to the game because you can feel the stress and weight of having to make the hard decisions within the game, which many games fail to do.
While LISA is one of my favorite games, I have to point out some of its flaws.
Performance Issues:
When playing, I tend to notice issues when moving left to right. While it's hard to explain I'll try my best to do so. The screen tends to lag when moving left to right, which makes the movement feel clunky, rather than smooth. I believe that this could be due to the game running on RPG Maker but I have no evidence to prove so.
The Difficulty Curve:
This is probally my biggest complaint when it comes to LISA. Early game is very difficult. This is because there are sever instant death cliffs placed throughout the map and Brad and his party members are very week. Once you have a decent party, the game becomes a cake-walk, with occasional difficult moments. While I believe that this doesn't take too much out of the gameplay experience, I do wish that the game could be more challanging.
Overall, LISA is a great game and is one of my favorite RPGs of all time. I would definitly recommend it.
Sidenote: I would also recommend that you would check out the free RPG Maker game known as LISA: The First. This is made by the same developer who made this game and gives a little insight about the backstory of the LISA series.

One of the more overlooked games on Steam (probably because it was made in Wolf RPG Editor), this game was actually made by the creator of Wolf RPG Editor. In this game, you have to battle against the screen scrolling basically. If you get scrolled off the screen, you die. There are lots of interesting RPG elements at play here, such as different classes, leveling, skills, weapons, partners, and more. You can also save some items from your failed runs to use for the next run. The game is procedurally generated, and you can play worlds other people played by entering their world's seed. The game will also show you who was/is online on the same map you are. There are daily maps to explore and this game has a ton of depth you might not expect just looking at it. The expanded version is out on Playism and coming to Steam in the near future, but this version is well worth playing on its own.

Trials Evolution: Gold Edition is a game developed by RedLynx and published by Ubisoft
Trials set a standard for this generation of arcade style games. Although there are certain aspects you'd expect from this game that are missing; with its fast-paced gameplay, impressively realistic 2.5D visuals and its addictive quality
RedLynx open up the arcade genre to a new level of brilliance, showing other developers how to make a modern day arcade-style video game
The good things with Trails Evolution are, the physics engine in this game has the perfect balance of realism with an arcade-like edge
Trials matches excellent refreshed visuals with the classic 2.5D look to make another classics and Trials is crammed with hundreds of levels offering a decent amount of content for the player with community created levels add endless hours of fun on top of the offline single player content.
The limited bike and rider customisation is disappointing and gamers who aren't all that big on community content might get bored of the basic content
However, overall Trails Evolution: Gold Edition is a fun yet challenging arcade game!

It's with heavy heart, frustrated fingertips, and frankly, a bored-out mind, that I throw a thumbs down to Shadow Run Hong Kong.
What could have been an expected + close to an enjoyable trio, and a close-the loop of some prevailing earlier issues, quickly becomes a rush-felt, and less than immersive or impressive experience, one tht contains more gritty lows than highlights, and 1 where youre just plain readin 2 $&#*ing much (more later).
So where to begin w/ SRHK, this curious oddity of late August?
(DF:DC and HK SPOILERS)
1st, lets get a general thing with Shadowrun straight off the bat:
The aiming % system just ISN"T fun.
Sure, you miss a scurrying rat across the room with .45 pistol round, but what about the burly, great big lumbering troll scowling all up in your face when you're packing a 12 guage shotgun ready to release???? Look, it's anticlimatical when you miss over and over and over, due to something as insignificant as a few mere numbers of chance, especially when as with 80%, that chance should be considerably high. It makes one wonder why another solution was never considered, say one within a certain close range is *always* guaranteed a hit, but the further away the more difficult etc., less damage. In short, % are something that's always bugged the gameplay flow for me, and that goes for DMS, DF:DC, and even back on the days of SNES, it's just always been an issue. It may go well in pen and paper, and die, virtually, it's  a nussaince.
But onto some HK specifics:
Okay, I actually like the story. Qi? A nice touch. The story starts solid enough: Duncan is to-the-point, shadowruners die, you run. You're trying to erase your SINs... then after a while things get bogged down in Shadowrun NPC talk, and you find yourself just going through the routine.. Still, there's a very interesting overall situation and swing to what you're up against, it's just that it all never quite pans out. I don't really care for the old man you're looking into, (whats-his-name? Raymond?) Not cause I'm a heartless individual behind my computer screen, just that throughout the game, there's nothing to bounce back on and keep me involved that he exists and is a compelling character.I mean, really, what is there?
Duncan?
The guy drones on and on about life as kids, but never really *acts* Heck, I don't even see Raymonds face (or hear his voice again) until the very end of the game. It's dull, and the characters, including my team of unrealized eccentrics who yammer on for hours, don't make me care so much about them. When it comes to emotional attachment, they keep to their namesakes and they lurk in the shadows. you're left just passing missions and hoping the next one is way cooler than the one preceeding it.The game keeps you at a distance, rather than drawing you in too much, and that continues the entire game, leaving you with a mostly unemotionally satisfied experiecence. Still, at least Hong Kong *looks* nice.
Then there's the problem with the sub-narrative, or just the writing/dialogue/action events in general. ARGGGHHH!! Ahem, do you know what it's like for a completionalist gamer to finish a low active mission, return to the hub zone, and speak with NPC's and read the dialouge of characters you care #$*&*#$ about for over ONE BLOODY HOUR?!?! It is teeth-pullingly, dry-paint watchingly, agonizingly tedious thats what!!!! These NPCs don't support the main quest; they add nothing to it!!
Take the club owner family dad who wants to become a pirate again.
WHO THE HELL CARES?!?!
It doesn't make my life in the shadows any easier or add value to it or to the mission... Perhaps he's there just to add ambience to Hong Kong? Okay, look. I can SEE the area of Hong Kong is a $*#@ hole. I can use my imagination that it attracts pirates and that sort. There's no real need to spell it out, and certainly not over a tedious thirty minutes of family tension, and text bickering. If characters don't add anything to the plot (or contain no subplots of their own), why are they even there? If they're going to be of interest to you, they ought to tie in to the story with their own emotional arc. Otherwise, they should just sell you the guns, swords, and spellbooks, and tell you the boss is looking for you for the next task, and thats that. (The young girl at the magic shop started doing this after a while, much to ones haggard relief).
It's also of no help that almost all of Shadowrun is written in passive voice, and uses a ton of adverbs, so the action tends to bog down even more. Rather than just simply rely on the decrepit, slum visuals to communicate the job, the writing describes a great deal, getting caught up in every nuisance, and never quite hitting the main bits and then moving on. After a while, you tend to just skim the actions, read gist, and hope you haven't missed anything that'll cause you to loose an achievement or even get to play a mission.
The Matrix. Q) If you had some of $700,000, assigned to revamp the entire Matrix system, what would you do?
Apparently, besides the (excellent) visual upgrade, the result is to make "watcher" units, frustrating knit so close together you can barely pass comfortably, change the walking animation to an odd glide where at first you think your characters glitching, and include repetitive memorization and visual brain logic puzzles, some of which not every gamer may be able to pass with only a low kit Decker in tow; like the default provided. (Thank goodness I'm good enough at logic puzzles). The end result? A system revamp overhaul with *completely* nothing to write home about, and one that makes one wonder just what was so bad about the other suggestions put up for consideration that they weren't used.
The Matrix is probably the single biggest change letdown out there. Try conquering it with a low to average decker (Is0bel). It is frustrating as heck, and after a while, just to be sure you won't end up repeatinga watcher dodge and raising the alarm by 20 points, you'll opt to save like crazy whenever you pass a couple of the lamely placed enemies, cause, who knows? Next time you won't be so lucky...  Of course, it doesn't help that the aim system lacks: 90%+ should be guaranteed to hit, I miss 2 99%s in a row, at almost point blank range. Enemies turn: they hit me twice, BAM!! Force Jack out. $#&*!!!!

Still, SR:HK isn't all not all that bad.
Some perks: visually, it captures the now familiar disdain Shadowrun cyberpunk dysfunction. It's musical score is *sharply* on point, giving a delicious track of electronic and cyber with regional overtones, but never quite bogging down in a type of cheesy "futuristic Chinse sound" thing. Heck, the game's overall contextual situational story is interesting (as mentioned earlier). Up to a point, anyways. Some the missions are fun, though none stand out as stellar parts.
So, in conclusion, we have a game that has a good story and situation, but that never quite impacts with the mark, be this cause of bland characters who are barely emotionally invested with one another and their own worlds, a boggy mire of convoluted characterization, dialogue, and text, and some letdowns in bizarre upgrades in areas which really ought to hav come kickin'. Where does that leave us? With a pretty average title, nowhere near pushing the mark or the envelope and giving a bang for the buck.

I want to recommend this game, but I can’t. In its current state, it needs way too much work to be worth your time and money. [EDIT] I should mention that I've been playing the game since the closed beta, and have well over 2500 battles since the closed beta reset [/edit]
Let’s start with the good:
+Arcade battles allow for quick play, and make it constant action
+The gameplay itself is rather fun, and the progression through the lines gives you a sense of accomplishment and goals
+When a battle is well-balanced vertically and horizontally, the results make for a fun and engaging battle where while every team member counts, you can sway the battle in your favor by good play.
However, these positives are overshadowed by the glaring flaws in the game:
-Poor client optimization: I have a rather good computer, and the game constantly hangs and eats up an inordinate amount of power for comparatively mediocre graphics
-Steam is for new users only (while this is a minor complaint, it’s a giant middle finger to those who’ve played since closed beta and gets me to my last point)
-Ridiculous Price model puts “premium ships” around $25-$30 USD for a handful of pixels (and that is on the lower end)
-Premium accounts are about the only way to make your investment back at the highest tiers unless you have consistently great games (which you won’t)
-And why yes, premium ships are overpowered, making the game unbalanced
Which brings me to the ugly:
-	The aircraft carriers (CVs) are completely out of whack, ruin the rock-paper-scissors balancing, and that one ship can ruin the entire match (There is a reason why carriers revolutionized naval warfare, and the game promotes a pre-carrier battle with aircraft carriers). If you CV captain forgot his brain at home, you will likely get blown up by the enemy CV, as there is little you can do to defend against enemy planes.
-	Horizontal imbalance: ships from the same tier, but different nations are astoundingly out of whack.
-	The power creep is real, and recently released ships pound their predecessors into the water.
-	Vertical imbalance: You will get overmatched in a battle, up to two tiers. A tier V battleship cannot take a tier VII battleship on a tier VII map. You end up either slow and irrelevant or blown to bits in one of the faster ships.
-	Developer attitudes to player base are adversarial: they bully critical streamers into avoiding negative reviews, and are only remorseful when they are caught and the community backlash forces them to apologize. I’ve seen more customer cooperation from my internet provider and most US airlines.
While I really enjoy this game, I can’t support it in its current form with its current development team. At such a high cost for its premium content, the flaws should have been fixed a year ago. It has a great base mechanic, but not having the support it deserves drives players like me away. I hope to someday give it a good review, but that is not today.

Hello, random retard here to give you a review that no one cares about.
First thing I'd like to say is that it is possible to use world of warships on steam with an existing account which involves renaming the "steam_api.dll" to anything else, as far as I'm aware you still have to keep the .dll part but it allows you to login to the game with an already existing account.
So this brings about a solution to this problem that seems pretty simple to add. That's to have an option to play with your steam account or to log in with a pre existing account.
Now for a review of the actual game.
Pros:
- You get to play in a variety of warships around the ww2 era from a variety of nations. If you're into ships this game is probably going to be pretty appealing to you.
- Arcadey. The game is very arcadey in a lot of ways. this means that as long as you aren't too fussed about things such as historical accuracy and aren't looking for a warship simulator you'll find that the game has fairly fun gameplay.
- Balance (sort of). While this is very debatable the game is ultimately balanced enough that a large majority of the ships in the game are viable in some way.
- Good gameplay. The gameplay in world of warships largely rewards good play and punishes bad, while there are certainly a fair few exceptions it does mean that you'll generally find your results getting better as you play more and get better at the game.
Cons:
- Somewhat pay to win. Having premium ships in the game automatically means that unless the ships are straight up downgrades to their tech tree counterparts that there will always be some element of pay to win. At large premium ships are side grades to existing tech tree ships, however in a fair few cases it ends up being that the side grade results in a better ship than the tech tree counterpart. While this pay to win aspect is certainly there you generally don't feel you are at a straight up disadvantage when you're in a tech tree ship going up against a premium, mostly because they are still side grades and even if they do make for an overall stronger ship they still do lose things over their tech tree counterparts.
Along this there's also a pay to progress element which comes from premium ships, premium accounts and free xp conversion. Having premium and premium ships results in overall faster credit and xp gain and free xp conversion means that you can skip any ships that are weaker or you just don't want to play. While this doesn't have an effect on gameplay it does mean that you are losing out on getting ships faster if you don't spend money.
- RNG. This is a big point of frustration for a lot of people in world of warships. Almost the entire game is balanced around this and a lot of times it can be the difference between getting a kill and dying. Dispersion and fires are the main things which rng determines and it does take away from the skill of the game as you can have times where even if you play perfectly you can still lose out due to getting bad rng. Ultimately it isn't ideal to have but it is where a fair portion of the balancing in the game comes from.
- 2 tier spread. Once you get to tier 5 there is a 2 tier upward and one downwards and from tier 7 there is a 2 tier spread either way. This results in games where you can either be bottom tier, mid tier or top tier, When you aren't top tier it means that there are ships that are stronger than you and can do things you can't, this can result in some pretty sad situations where you simply can't have enough of an impact due to tier disadvantage. While this is the case you can always have an impact on the game though it is something that can make your experience of the game worse.
There's probably a fair bit I missed here but ultimately world of warships is a fairly good game. World of warships fills the role of an arcade warship game fairly well, and as long as you aren't put off by games having pay to win elements, large amounts of rng and matches that can involve you being a weaker ship in the match then you'll find that world of warships is an overall fun game that can keep you around for a very long time.

1:Make the minimap as big as possible

3: Save free exp for upgrading ships, not buying new ships
4: Look at guides on captain skills, don't just spec randomly

TL;DR: LISA is one of my favorite RPG of all time.
Before I enter this review, I feel like I need to state that I never really liked earthbound. I love LISA because of it features, not because its like earthbound but (insert comment here). I will also try to avoid spoilers if possible.
Why do I love the game LISA? Well, theres several reasons why I love this game. I'll give a list of each feature and why it adds to the game's experience.
Well Written and Understandable Characters:
Unlike some games, I really could relate to the characters within the game. Their actions seem reasonable. For example, the main character, Brad, doesn't go out because he is destined to stop an evil force, but he heads out to fight a world of perverts to save someone who is close to him. Even the companions seem understandable, especially when it comes near end of the game, which leads me to the next feature I like.
Divserse and Complex Compainions:
Within the game, there are many compainions that you can recruit. Each with their own attack style and personality. It allows you to group certain compainions so that you can perform more damage. For example, you can find someone who can spit gasoline and combine that with fire based attacks for massive damage. My only complaint about this system is that once you recrute a compainion, they don't do much other than fight for you. I was expecting that a character could talk to you about a part of the story or even question your morals but sadly they don't.
The Story:
Probably the best feature, LISA's story is a gripping one. It uses a blend of dark humor and drama to create a great, quirky story. As stated before, each character seems to be rational. They don't act because they are destined to, but because they are just trying to survive just like you. The ending stuck with me because it tied the story in with the choices you made so well, which leds me to the next feature.
The Choice System:
In this game, your choices have real consequences. One unique thing about this system is your companions can die, as in straight up die. Their death can be cause in combat and out of it. This makes some moments within the game intense due how you can lose a party member. Not only are your party members affected by your actions, but so is the main character. For example, you can lose an arm, which will permanently affect your characters stats and animations. I felt that this added so much to the game because you can feel the stress and weight of having to make the hard decisions within the game, which many games fail to do.
While LISA is one of my favorite games, I have to point out some of its flaws.
Performance Issues:
When playing, I tend to notice issues when moving left to right. While it's hard to explain I'll try my best to do so. The screen tends to lag when moving left to right, which makes the movement feel clunky, rather than smooth. I believe that this could be due to the game running on RPG Maker but I have no evidence to prove so.
The Difficulty Curve:
This is probally my biggest complaint when it comes to LISA. Early game is very difficult. This is because there are sever instant death cliffs placed throughout the map and Brad and his party members are very week. Once you have a decent party, the game becomes a cake-walk, with occasional difficult moments. While I believe that this doesn't take too much out of the gameplay experience, I do wish that the game could be more challanging.
Overall, LISA is a great game and is one of my favorite RPGs of all time. I would definitly recommend it.
Sidenote: I would also recommend that you would check out the free RPG Maker game known as LISA: The First. This is made by the same developer who made this game and gives a little insight about the backstory of the LISA series.

I am going to be honest, if you want to play this game as a free player don't waste your time. It is designed by Wargaming to be a miserable experience in order to encourage you to spend a little "here and there", and only snowballs from there. You will not find an honest positive review from a true free player. When pressed they will admit they occasionally spend some money on premium time.
The game is decent if you pay for premium time and a few premium ships, and is really good if you spend a fortune on premium time, gold doubloons, and some "pay to win" ships.
The Good:
The variety of historic ships is awesome. You can play as the Yamato, Hood, Bismarck and over a hundred others. The gameplay is really fun in the higher tiers due to extra features on high tier ships such as radar, heal, hydro search, spotter/fighter planes etc. Although you might expect fighting on a single plane (flat sea) boring, it absolutely is not. Ships have different firing ranges, spotting ranges, and firing arcs that allow you to strategically use mountains. Ship Commanders have a variety of different skills at your disposal and ships have different equipment that give a variety of bonuses. If you are willing to pay money the grind is not bad at all. However, if you want to play for free...
The Bad:
If you are a free player the grind will be miserable. A premium account gives a 50% bonus to xp and silver (xp includes commander xp). I'll give an example:
Take two equally skilled players, one with premium, one without. After 30 games in the same ship the premium player will have:
1)more powerful modules unlocked
2)more silver which will allow them to but more equipment and premium consumables.
3)a better trained commander which gives huge bonuses.
4)more progress in missions (and daily crates) requiring total xp or credits earned, giving that player more camos and bonus flags, which will further give an advantage.
If the paying player also buys premium ships, signal flags, camos, and doubloons, they will leave the free player in the dust. People may claim it is "pay to save time", which it is if your time is completely valueless to you. If you want to play for free against a player with similar skills in the same amount of time, you will get destroyed.
Premium ships cost as much as a single AAA title. There are players that sunk thousands into this game. The game is designed to convince you to spend a little, then a little more, then when you have some time and money in the game, to keep spending.
The Ugly:
There are some clear "pay to win" ships in this game. The Belfast, Kamikaze, Nikolai, and Black are a few that come to mind (there are more). A lot of these ships were removed from the game, so new players can't get them, but a lot existing players will still have them (like me). There are players on the WG forums and reddit gleefully awaiting the new Steam players in order to club them. I wouldn't doubt a lot of them left positive reviews here.
The RNG. There are times when a single hit can blow up your ship because reasons. I assume it is in the game to allow even terrible players to get a kill on a decent player.
Wargaming. Really a terrible company with terrible customer service. Look them up yourself.
TLDR:
If you have hundreds to waste on a single game, go for it. It’s a great game for whales. If you expect to play for free, avoid it like the plague.

I have about 5000 games under my belt over the two years I have played this game, and I have been here, quoting my good friend generaldort, "THROUGH BUFFS AND NERFS AND BUFFS AND NERFS AND BUFFS AND NERFS, AND IM STILL HERE ON THE BRIDGE OF A-" Okay maybe I got a bit out of hand there, but if I did not enjoy the game, would I still be here? It's got a bit of a learning curve, but you will see how you can alleviate that as a new player below.
As for the game itself, I find WoWS has a lot to offer.
A wide variety of customization: Modules, Captain Skills, Consumables, Bonus Flags, Camouflage, down to the very port your ships sit in, etc.
PvP as well as PvE Content is available.
Historical event missions, the ability to gain the legendary Isoroku Yamamoto is awesome! (I got my Steven Seagal when he was available, sorry new players!)
A wide range of gameplay and styles with all the current nations in-game. (My personal faves are the Akizuki and the HSF Harekaze. I hold 3rd in the world for HSF Harekaze damage in a single game!)
You could be a sneaky Destroyer, torpedoing without being seen.
You could be a cruiser, HE shells raining from mid-range, using your rudder shift to avoid shells.
You could be a Battleship, charging in, bristling with guns.
You could be an Aircraft Carrier, striking with aircraft from afar.
All of the nations give the player something new to do, and no nation is the same. Some may share similar qualities, but others will shine where one nation does not.

Destroyers: US Navy DDs (Jack of all trades, master of none)

Carriers: USN. I recommend the US CV line to newbies as it is less macro-intensive than the IJN CV line. If you have starcraft experience or any other RTS experience, go play the Japanese!

Alright look, despite some of the reviews ranting about not being able to merge or sync your original World of Warships account to Steam (i'm disappointed as well), that honestly does not detract away from the gameplay as well as the fact that you don't need to ditch your old account.
I've played this game since Closed Beta Testing which was over 2 years ago and even though I disagree heavily with the balancing of ships, the core gameplay keeps me coming back. They have a lot of issues with the balancing imho which is easily the game's worst aspect but even with "overpowered" ships, it's not an automatic "I win" button. You actually have to learn what is your ships' strength and weaknesses even in said "overpowered" ships. "Overpowered" ships to me are ships that clearly leaps and bounds ahead of the other ships at the same tier, and even with that, if the player driving that ship is not skillful, they can still be killed. It's when top tier players get into an overpowered ship, is when the ship is truly overpowered.
Premium/Real Money: I'll admit that I've spent a couple of hundreds in this game over the past two years. These "microtransactions" aren't that "micro" as some ships cost 40 dollars, while others cost 60+ dollars, the price of a fully fledged "triple A" game. There is no excuse for ships costing this much although I've justified it with the fact that I play this game a lot.
This game has its moments of frustration but for those moments when you outplay somebody or win the game single-handedly, those moments are worth playing for. The gameplay is honestly very polished and there are no ships that are "invincible," with the right amount of teamwork or focus-fire, that ship will eventually go down. There's always a satisfying feeling when you work together with a team to take down the enemy team in less than 10 minutes [games are 20 mins long and generally ~15 minutes is the average time for a game to end].
There are four classes to play, Aircraft carrier, Cruiser, Destroyer, and the Battleship. Each "class" are further divided into nations, the Japanese (IJN), the Americans (USN), the Germans (KM), the Russians(VMF), the British(HMS), and the French [no official prefix].
Aircraft Carrier (CV) - This "pseudo-rts" class is unlike the others, they have a top-down view of the map and launches aircraft in squadrons that you can control. Starting from t6, you can "Manual Aim" planes which allows you to set where the aircraft drops their payload. This is not a beginner friendly class and I heavily discourage you from playing this class as your "first" line.
Cruisers (CL and CA) - Cruisers are the most straight forward out of all the classes, they use their guns as their primary way of obtaining damage. Beware however that cruisers have a weak spot known as a "citadel" and this weak spot is aimed at by battleship players primarily in order to do devastating damage against you. For t1-t4, this is the most beginner-friendly class. I heavily reccomend playing the t1-t4 cruisers as your first class since the mechanics learned here apply to all classes besides CV.
Destroyers (DD) - Destroyers are the small lightly armored ships that are usually faster than the other two surface combat ships (BB and CA/CL) their primary method of attack at lower tiers are torpedoes, which are well, torpedoes. They are amazing at t2-t4 and this class is known to "seal-club" lower tiers. (Seal club is when you deliberately go to a lower tier and kill newbies). Destroyers are lightly armored and have the smallest HP pools in the game but gernerally have great concealment to make up for it. You will be "concealed" and outspot other classes. I reccomend playing destroyers as your "second" line or third as learning how to play destroyers will mean you will understand how to play against them.
Battleships (BB) - The big guns, easily one of the most popular classes in the game for a good reason. These big ships are the massive and the reload of their guns will easily be 25+ seconds. Beware however, that their guns at t3-t4 are insanely inaccurate. This class can repair damage and dish out damage and even though they have a citadel, the citadel is protected by armor unlike cruisers and as a result, most players consider this a beginner-friendly line due to how hard it is to be punished by another player outside of another battleship. This class gets stronger at t5+ and I would reccomend this as a third or possibly second class.
I don't mean for this review to be a mini-guide but I heavily reccomend watching a video guide on youtube after your first couple of games or so in order to learn how to play effectively. The subreddit /r/worldofwarships has a discord that you can ask your questions to and I will try to answer them if I'm online.
-ZomBry

Now I finished this game in less than an hour, and I’ll just say straight away there isn’t much to it. The developer says it is based on dreams, somehow I seem to be doubting that statement.
The game is flawed in many ways, but I am not basing my review upon this. So game mechanics, bugs and glitches aside, this review is only based upon what this game claims to be.
So let’s get started, first off the bat is the developer claiming that these awkward dimensions are based on dreams. I’m not sure of these are his or of others, but I doubt it all the same. For instance dreams aren’t short, I have never experienced a dream that was straightforward. But I have had dreams that were plain boring, so at least there is that.
Some of these levels are just walking from A to B, which can be accomplished by even avoiding interaction with the environment. Negating the entire point of the level. Other levels, are even more surprising by the fact that they actually have some interesting game mechanic, however the 5minute play-time is a constant disappointment.
Secondly, this game seems to be more… as if the developer uses this to defend the fact that he is allowed to make games. There is one level where the dev just keeps rambling on and on about why he makes games. Another level that has bad review posted all over. I keep wondering if this is how his so called dreams were.
And after thinking for about 15minutes, I don’t think there’s anything else to say about it. Other than something to the developer himself.
If you really feel like you should make games, if you really feel that this is your life’s dream. Than by all means keep doing what you do. Bad reviews serve their own purpose, if you feel assaulted by them then you really are in the wrong place. Mistakes are made so we don’t keep repeating them, we can only learn when we misstep. There’s no point in changing if we only do the right thing. My advice is, don’t throw this game away but just redo it. Put some more effort into and loose about 80% of everything else. Themes and transitions are important to know where you are and are going too. I’m really lost with the bull and the space level… Also, was there a level based on Mirror’s Edge? I don’t get it.

Sonic Generations is, without a doubt, the best Sonic game in years. The gameplay is great for both classic and modern Sonic, and the level design is some of the best I've seen since the 16-bit days. Classic Sonic plays pretty closely to the Genesis classics, with spindash and everything. Modern Sonic plays like an improved, refined version of the daytime gameplay from Sonic Unleashed, fortunately with more platforming and less boosting. The only glaring flaw that I can find in this game is that it's pretty short. The replay value is at least pretty high though; there are 90 additional missions to complete, and the levels are so fun that you'll want to play through them over and over again. Sonic Generations is awesome!

A Story About My Uncle is a rather pleasant first-person puzzle-platformer.
It takes you through a number of areas from water caverns, dark shadowy abysses, starry-skyed mountains and ice caves, all with a calm relaxed narration as the game is told by a father giving his daughter a bed-time story. It's very linear but what else do you expect from a puzzle-platformer in the end?
The game's mechanics themselves are quite well thought out, and you'll be effectively rope-swinging through the levels with boost jumps here and there as well. There are some collectibles strewn about the levls as well, but they aren't all that out of the way, and I didn't see a use for them. Perhaps I didn't find enough to get an alternate ending or something? Not sure.
The art-style and sound design also creates a calming and relaxed atmosphere without tension which also plays to the game's strengths, there were only a couple of times when I personally got frustrated with the game. Those were typically when the paths were not well sign-posted, or some of the game's mechanics were a little temperamental.

game was great, loved the story if you liked the storyline in mafia 1 you will enjoy this story too. The game's plot like is basically a mixture of the Godfather, and Goodfellas, you're a war hero, come back from the war and fall into a life of crime with your friend. The open world nature of this game is not the same as GTA, which to me is a good thing, there aren't a million half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥mini-games to play. Each section of the city feels different, China-town feels different than Little Italy. I'm not going to list any spoilers but I do feel like this plot is decent, the voice acting is pretty good for the most part, the in-car conversations are pretty humorous a lot of the time. The driving is a HUGE improvement over the first game, the cars feel like real cars would from the 40s that is spongey suspension and sluggish acceleration, this is not bad design, it's how the actual cars behaved back then. The map is actually displayed in the radar instead of the lame "map" that's in the first game.
The guns are all fun, though the pistols pretty much all seem the same power, even the magnum (and the magnum sound a little goofy, like a cartoon gun). There is an actual cover system in the game, and overall the fights are much improved over the first game. This is a great game, it's heavy on graphics card, so I recommend looking into mods on how to disable the physics of the clothing in the game.
Overall I've really enjoyed this game and don't understand why people are criticizing it for NOT being just a GTA clone, it's a game I honestly find more fun than GTA.

I'd go as far to say that Mafia II is one of the most original and well executed game I've played yet. Highly recommended

Real world Trials is nothing like this game. I doubt anybody know what "trials" is as a motorsport. That does not matter for this game. You have a bike and you need to complete courses within a time limit to get medals to advance through the game. Medals get you new tracks and bikes. You earn money but it has no point other than you can buy parts to make your bike look different. They do nothing for performance so you can ignore them if you want.
The game is fun. You get big air on some jumps. You can do back/forward flips all you want. It does nothing for your score but its fun and thats the point. There are some odd challenges like skiing on dirt, or trying to do a course with the throttle stuck wide open on your bike.
The game rewards your own gifted skills if your are skilled. You have complete control of your bike and rider and far as brakes and throttle. You dont turn in this game so cornering is out. Your rider has a huge effect on the bike balance. The rider can lift the front or rear wheels off the ground just by leaning forward or backwards. This is how you conquer the the challenges. This is my most serious complaint about the handling of the game. You control the rider with the left stick on your game pad. It is super sensitive. I wish I could slow that down like mouse sensitivity in other games. So when you move him up or back he yanks the bike a bunch. Like I said I am not in the top 10% of skilled people.
The game is fun. You crash a lot but you will make unbelievable saves that make you shout out loud. I got it cheap and played it a lot over the holidays but when I fired it up later on I just got frustrated.

I highly recommend this game to those who love naval action and history.  You can play the USS Iowa, or the Yamato.  Doesn’t get much better than that. And the ships are all beautifully rendered!  The game get's my vote.  If you are new to it, you will enjoy it.

Quick review from the short time I've played so far:
Love this true-to-the-original (in spirit at least) sequel to one of the best couch co-op brawlers in the history of videogames.  (Actually it was a series but I believe only 1 came out in the US, renamed RCR)
Anyway, the action is exactly how I remember it.  Cute, funny, and addictive.
My only criticism so far is that, when playing with 4 random strangers online, we had no way of communicating with each other.  There isn't a voice option, and there doesn't seem to be a way to type to each other.   However, jumping into a game with other players was easy.  Also, and this is perhaps bigger, we were sort of "stuck" in the highschool for the duration of time we played.  We unlocked a wrestler looking fellow and a chubby stoner grappler, then cops showed up to beat us down. But there was no notification of what we had to do.  We just wandered aimlessly from room to room, defeating enemies and clearing floors, then doing it again.  Then eventually just running from everyone and trying to go to rooms we hadn't been to.  It was frustrating and I wish the game provided some kind of simple indication of where we needed to go to progress, or a counter of how many enemies that needed defeating.
Overall, I would probably still be playing right now but I had to start making dinner.  Super fun, especially if you have some couch buddies or friends on steam with mics.   You can collect cash and level up, save to unlock moves, unlock new characters (and there appear to be A TON).. it's an SD Brawler throwback that's not to be missed.

God this game is garbage. First, the good. The game's concept is fantastic, the visuals are serviceable, and the game would be fantastically fun and hilarious IF. Now let's get the bad:
* Extremely unstable. The most unstable experience I've ever had. Crashes dozens of times a day, even if you turn off Uplay settings and play on lowest quality. Compatibility mode doesn't help. (I use Windows 10 and an i7-6700 but no dedicated GPU.) The shadows can completely break too and won't be fixed until you restart the game. Almost 100% of crashes happen inside menus; so if you give even half a damn, look into that, somebody.
* The button layout and UI combination is abysmal. The gas button is used heavily in menuing and you are constantly doing things you didn't mean to do and didn't know you could do because of the terrible buttons.
* The difficulty is so badly understood by the game that no matter what difficulty the game says the challenge is, it's a total crapshoot as to how difficult it actually is. In fact, getting gold in some events is nearly impossible, and the tournaments are so difficult that the lack of a "restart whole tournament" button is astounding. I'd bet a ton of money very little testing was done to see how difficult these challenges would be and what menu options would help lower the frustration. An Earthbound-inspired RPG that fails mechanically on many levels even with it's great writing. Areas are confusing. With crisscrossing paths, tons of bad backtracking that isn't enjoyable on any level, fast travel is poorly implemented as well. It grew repetitive, a lot of the time I was accidently riding off cliffs and dying.
I give it a plus for the fun battle system, but after a while, even that grew repetitive. It is simplistic, and eventually you simply use your strongest move just over and over for whatever character you have. There isn't much tailored for your specific situation or foe you are fighting.
Pacing is also very poor. In between these tedious and frustrating sections was a very small amount of compelling and great narrative that pushed me forward, but I no longer care to continue. I may read about it later, as the main characters were interesting but...
Companions are disposable. Very much so. I liked Brad. I wanted to know more about Lisa, and Buddy, but every companion just didn't matter in the least. The game gives a few choices a long the way, but when I care so little about these companions that are hardly fleshed out, and introduced haphazardly, these choices just have no effect on me.
I tried to enjoy this game, I wanted to quit much earlier, but seeing the reviews here made me at least want to try, and I played well past the mark where I considered stopping but I can't recommend this title. I may comeback to it and try again some day, but the narrative presented could not make up for such tedious, frustrating and often boring gameplay. If you are the sort of person who can completely disregard mechanics for narrative you may enjoy this title, but I could not.
