Have you seen that weird animated music video called "Truckers Delight"?, imagine a more gritty and less sexually explicit version of that combined with Mother 3, yes Mother 3 not Earthbound/Mother2, despite what other descriptions might tell you, other that the fact that there´s a lot of caves, the style, humor and gameplay is more reminescent of the third entry.
I have two pieces of advice for people who are unsure about trying this game:
1)THIS GAME IS NOTHING LIKE UNDERTALE, both games draw inspiration from the Mother series and involve choices, that´s about where the similarities end, the constant comparison between the two is just puzzling, especially considering they were released a year apart from each other, if you came to this game expecting another Undertale you are gonna get rekt son
2)A lot of people mention that the game is too crude and dark and that they wouldn´t recommend it to everyone for that reason, I say that as long as you can tolerate a bit of gore, a story that isn´t pure sugar and you don´t recoil at the mention of sexual abuse you will be fine; A more appropiate reason I wouldn´t recommend this game for everyone is because it will rub you the wrong way if you don´t tolerate unfairness or you are a perfectionist/completionist, you will end up savescumming the fun out of it.
I have three primary bad things to say about the game:
1) The combat is heavily unbalanced, you know how in most RPGs status effects are good for nothing?, this is the complete opposite, also the elemental damages are also all over the place, fire is way too OP and water is pretty much useless, a piece of advice I would like to give is for people to not use the Oil+Fire strategy, it makes the game way too easy to the point it will make combat seem like filler
2) Inns completely break the tension of having to rest, most of the time you will find yourself backtracking to them rather than risking resting at a fireplace
3)Joy is too scarce and it´s duration is too short, and while Brad, Carp and Buckets can do fine without it the other joy addicted characters are useless without it, severely limiting them as viable party members
For everythign else I think it´s an excellent game that I would recommend to anyone who likes weird games, it would be interesting to see more Yume Nikki fangames become their own thing

So, I really liked SR:HK -- a lot. And I'm recommending it because I overall felt very positively about the campaign itself, but at the same time, I'm not recommending it because I don't think you should play it immediately. I'm a huge fan of the series, so I've been waiting for this game since the Kickstarter was announced... and, of course, I played it immediately. This is something I slightly regret, because the game is *very* buggy: typos, repeating dialogue, skill checks that don't work, interactive objects glitching... if you've played Dragonfall, you've probably come across some of these problems, but I wish they'd been ironed out instead of made worse.
That said! The game underneath is great, I think. I'm not sure how it compares to Dragonfall in terms of length, but it feels similar, and it's definitely longer than Returns. I think Dragonfall's story built towards a satisfying climax perhaps more deftly than HK's did, but then it was telling a very different -- and arguably easier -- story. HK is interesting because it tells a PERSONAL story in the context of an impersonal situation; the conflict between family and shadowrunning is really interesting to explore, and Duncan is, in my opinion, the most well-written character Harebrained's ever created. I really loved uncovering the story between him and the PC.
... almost to the detriment of some other things. This might not be a fair criticism, but I found it a little harder to connect with HK's crew. I don't think it's because they're poorly-written by comparison to Dragonfall's (okay, Is0bel's kind of a discount Glory, but the others are better)... I think I'd just gotten invested in the family dynamic and the story of my character, and I didn't really feel like helping everyone through their individual problems. That said, the game is a little more forgiving of this than Dragonfall, which forced you to interrogate everyone in search of their inevitable tragic backstory: characters in Hong Kong tend to talk more freely, and even open up to you of their own volition after a reasonable amount of interaction. I preferred this because it relied less on my character playing therapist to all of Heoi (as I'd had to do for the Kreuzbasar in Dragonfall), but I also had less incentive to talk to people because my role wasn't so much "leader" as it was "peer"... hm. I don't know how to notch this one; it has pros and cons both.
The pacing of the main plot vs. the sideplots could be kind of rickety: lots of shadowrunning, main plot kind of starts and stops. I felt pretty okay with that given the relationship progression between missions, but I finished everyone's respective storylines a few missions before the actual endgame and that was kind of awkward. Jobs are fun, although not as challenging as Dragonfall's; in fact, many of them can be finished without firing a shot. I'm not sure how I feel about this because I really LIKED the massive fights in Dragonfall, but the formula of "stealth run -> reach objective -> something goes wrong -> fight your way out" made me feel like a poor runner. So-- I like the fact that you CAN do stealth runs now... but I'm hesitant to deliberately "go loud" just because I want a fight, because from a roleplay perspective a clean run is always preferable to a shootout... so I end up missing out on a lot of the combat. I'm not sure how to fix this, but at any rate there should be some larger levels.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong.
Easiest way to rate it? Halfway between Deadman's Switch and Dragonfall (Director's Cut).
Gameplay: In meatspace, basically the same. A few cosmetic changes here and there. In the matrix, quite different, sadly not for the best. New game mechanics force you to play frogger with "sentinel" programs. New mini-game to hack information nodes (mix between simon says and another memory game). Combat is about the same, some pretty new sprites for enemy programs. Overall, the Matrix changes make such sections boring and a "chore". The new mechanics grow stale extremely quickly and aren't immersive.
Graphics: Hong Kong brings a whole lot of new looks for Shadowrun. As you can imagine, the theme is very different from Seattle and Berlin. Though the engine is showing it's age. The Matrix looks much better now, though it's more a change in design than graphics.
Presentation: A handful of bugs. Some harmless, some bothersome and a few story-breaking (not game-breaking, I didn't suffer any crashes). The game plays well despite of this, perhaps the loading screens take a bit too long (specially if you have been alt-tabbing a lot).
Sound: Adecuate music, lots of ambience. Sound effects are (I believe) the same.
Items&Wares: There might be a lot of weapons but there's little variety in functionality. Better stats or a special ability, that's the most notable differences. A few new spells, a few new healing items and accesories but overall the same. When it comes to cyberware, things get a bit more interesting. Some new options to play around with.
Character Customization: The stat screen looks different (more stream-lined) but the core rules are the same. Same stats to raise than before and same skills to choose upon. In regards to how your character looks, the system remains extremely limited. Two new additions though. First, you are now allowed to choose your real name (first and surname) and cyberware (or bioware) got an overhaul. Now you have a wider variety of "spots" to choose for "chroming".
Story: And this is what it boils down to, isn't it? If you are like me you got this game for the story. So... how is it? In one word: Lacking. While miles ahead from DMS, Hong Kong's main story line is also miles behind Dragonfall. It's good, but it's just not Dragonfall good. It's "savior of the people" all over again. Repeating what we already saw in DMS and DF. This is the third game guys, come on, some variety would be welcome. In the characters department, HK is much closer to DF. You are presented with an interesting group of fellow runners all of which have their distinctive personality. They are good, entertaining and interesting, but just not as good as DF's cast. Some conversations were odd or felt stiff. Their personal missions where mostly way too simple or anticlimatic . There's a serious lack of innovation here. Again everyone is standing in their litttle spot in your safe-house, again they wait around doing nothing until you go to them... gone are the group meetings from DF where everyone was together interacting and being themselves. Here, the few group meetings that you'll have will be mostly cut-scenes with little interaction. I just feel that there could be so much more to these great characters. Side-characters (vendors and townspeople) are okay for the most part, but also below DF level. These people are also screaming for more content to be added to them.
So, overall... Do I recommend this game? Of course. This story is still worth playing through. Though I'm eager to know if they plan to do a Director's Cut for Hong Kong as well (it seriously need's one), and if it'll be free as was DF's.
Bottom line, or TL;DR, Shadowrun: Hong Kong's contributions to the series is a new Matrix gameplay which is hit and miss. Storywise it's below DF's level (substantially so) but way better than DMS (which was sub-par to be fair).
I haven't tried the editor (and I don't know if I will), but I KNOW there are a lot of very talented and dedicated people out there that are already producing content, so it won't be long before new modules (or adapted old ones) start popping up. UGC will extend the shelf-time of your game ten fold, which makes it worth buying for that alone.
EDIT - 02/08/16 After Extended Edition
Alright. Just finished the bonus campaign and here are my thoughts...
Overall, dissapointing.
I can't help but feel that this campaign (that took so long to release, not sure how long it took to make though... but it was promised a long time ago) is lackluster at best.
While the main story line is somewhat solid - and is imbued with a deeper "shadowrun" feeling than the original Hong Kong storyline - the execution is lazy.
What do we get?
1 Initital mostly scripted alley fight.
2 Main-story runs.
2 Side-story runs.
Very, very few new lines of dialogue with your teamates (a handful of which are bugged).
2 new hub areas, though both are completely underused.
---
I'd guess the developers decided to move your hub area to a new place just so they wouldn't have to write new dialogue for everyone in the original one.
I just don't see what the idea is. You created two new hub areas with new people to talk to, but those people have like 2 strings of dialogue. Basic setup at best, just flavor at worst. Second hub area had so much potential, yet you spend like 10 minutes in there at most. Get in, get quest, move to end of game.
Your team have few new things to say. I actually got my hopes up when I started. We have the noodle machine with Gobbet, we have the bird thing with Duncan and Izz... yet those things lead nowhere. They just stick there. Not to mention Izz kept repeating the bird event for some reason. What about those guards standing around? Two or three dialogue lines, also lead nowhere. Same thing with the vendors... What happened to the guy cooking the awful smelling food? I never got any more dialogue out of him and he disappeared in the second hub.
Oh, and everyone on the second hub... Wasted potential. Here we have a new set of characters with different motivations and stories to tell, a welcome change from being stuffed in that impound... All that setting... for what? 10 minutes of dialogue? Not even a mention of them in the epilogue.
And what the hell happened to the Ork that interrogates you at the beggining of the game? Does he ever show up again? 'cause I sure never saw a thing out of him during the entire campaign... it's like he banished.
You need to fine tune your AI, the Lily fight was a drekfest. I had two AAA corporations fighting each other on the street and it seemed more like a pillow fight than anything else. They kept throwing grenades at me though I kept throwing them back, they kept using silly cyberware powers that did no damage, the hired runner that I turned to my side hit someonen twice at most...
And what's with all the melee stun-baton wielding orcs? Here I am, shooting peeps with customized pistols and heavy weapons, Karma over 200 and you send orcs with stun batons against me? I think we already established that the team is full of badasses that pretty much killed a demi-god (as they say themselves)... Stun-batons ain't gonna cut it!
BBS messages were also pretty short... think they run out after the first mission... shame 'cause I love reading those.
---
But well. It's free, right? I just expected a LOT more. The Dragonfall - Director's Cut had so much content, so many improvements, so many new dialogues and quests... This Extended Edition frankly feels.... underwhelming.
Harebrained Studios... this is UGC quality, seriously. Step up your game. Shadowrun has so much potential, you have to keep upping the bar or at least keeping the same level of quality. It's clear here that a lot of people aren't content with the quality of HK. Just look at the UGC content for it and compare it with Dragonfall.
Still, I have faith in you and hope to see better camp

This game is actually itself a sufficient proof that the whole industry of computer gaming is a great invention... An incredibly deep and multi-aspectual simulation of development of a country... If you think it's biased, damn right it is! But if you saw my other game reviews and opinions, you'd know I'm more like a cold-blooded rascal when it comes to evaluating,,, but if I am to ever prove a non-humanless creature and show any positive emotions whatsoever, let it be for that game. Of course, if you are fan of deep strategies. However, Civ retains a pretty innocent, happy feel of playing in a huge sandbox full of toys... but if you are playing at hard levels, you'd better know damn well what use to make of yur toys before others come, take them and leave you hopelessly sobbing for mummy.
This is the pinnacle of the series, in which its follower, as well as spin-offs, are simply less complex, or less demanding. It truly shines at epic speed on natural, big maps, as it was seemingly its original shape and all elements click well togetehr in that kind of game... This absolutely means a real time devourer, but definitely a rewarding experience. Think of it like comparing trips; if you prefer "get to know that continent in a single weekend" king of experience, better look for other games. But if you are seeking an adventure of your life, get ready and go... If your family love you, they'll wait...
Admittedly, the game has a few flaws - AI is deadly dangerous and can be surprisingly ready to behave like humans, happily taking advantage of your every weakness - but sometimes it is predictable about its threshold of aggresion. Having learned that, you can often stay under the radar for enemy attacks, or stab great empires in the back when they cannot properly defend. - Some people also claim AI cheats - but to a great extent this is due to not knowing how the production potential of cities in the game can be fully used. Of course, at higher levels AI does get bonuses to production, but to a fairly reasonable extent (apart from the highest difficulty level, or at least I'm not good enough for it, or maybe that level is designed not for thet classical play style, but for those willing to create very specific scenarios, which could enable full exploitation of certain nations' perks). - The game also seeks to be pretty politically correct, which results in its excessive shyness in presentation of religious matters, or refusal to depict slavery... For an allegedly historical game, that is of course a serious reproach. However, it is still able to pretty well depict the general mechanisms ruling development of a country; it might seem that the omitted elements are in a way streamlined under the hood of more general phenomena, such as wars or cultural development, even if not openly presented under their true labels.
That game also feels in a way less realistic than, say Crusader Kings, where you are more or less a ruler with pretty many limitations. Here your society is not only puppets, but the huge scope of changes you can introduce, coupled with the time span the game covers, do not let you think "I would be a better king John if got in his shoes", The game does not shine in very short scenarios I believe. They are more like curios to me. You see, the game has such a general approach, that trying to use it to depict single years of actual history of particular countries is like doing brain surgery with road building tools... conceivable, but the results must be quite crude.
So all in all, in the games of Paradox you may seek depiction of challenges of a ruler, here - rather depiction of challenges which whole societies had to face on their way of development. So from a persepctive, you might dislike pretty many aspects... or wish them get even more developed, however than you might just as well play real-life politics, as it might take your entire life to play a single game... Anyway, the biggest asset of that outstanding production is that you truly need to be constantly balancing different aspects of your development, if you do not wish to stay behind. Typically, you seek to create anything-crushing armies. But firstly, not every country truly enables you to follow that path at all, and secondly, even if in your particular game you actually can, you still need to make reasonable breaks in your maniacal bloodbath to spend resources on exploration, establishment of money-providing trade, science, rearranging social policies... Excessive conquest typically creates a huge empire, but one which is so hopelessly behind technologically and financially, that a newly discovered neighbour will just puff you off the map without even truly focusing on you...
I could go on and on... But said enough, I hope, to evoke a sparkle of interest in the mind of any person with any taste in his or her soul for a diversified sandbox god-like simulator... To me, Civilization V is simply The Game.

Hindsight review:
Hear me out. Don't let my hours fool you. Despite having spent 80 hours pre-launch as a backer tester, I've spent most of my time in the Training Arena to study the game and figure out how I could improve it if the promised mod support does come through. I admit I was a little too hyped, and I let bias take over seeing how far they had come with my own eyes. I let the game settle now. Well, honestly I never felt comfortable recommending this to others because I knew there was some serious flaws, and the game needs some serious polish. I really had fun playing through the game, but some overall design decisions aren't going to change, which ruin my overall impression.
It's by no means a game that follows the simplistic beat-em-up formula. This is a game geared towards those into retro gaming or maybe wanting to look into hybrid mechanics. Not that the game is that complicated, but rules you need to worry about are never explained. You'd be spending a lot more effort trying to develop your character because you start off without basic combo strings to even knock someone down. Because of this it also becomes impossible to use untouched characters past a certain point. You have to beat the game to do that here. Better make a new save file if you want to bring friends in.
This game is also rather buggy. Some moves don't work properly, a couple of crashes, and even aesthetic errors. "Early Access" isn't too far off with how unpolished it is. You can play the game from start to finish, but there's a lot of dull spots that show how rushed the game is.
The story itself is a mess. Inexplicable love swap, enemies at every turn, chasing old bosses that becomes tedious if you fail because of enemies, and a villain that tries too hard to be secretive. Everything that drove the game forward was resolved before the ending, and narrative that drives the finale forward makes zero logical sense.
This game only has the aesthetic and mechanics of a traditional Kunio game. It tries to emulate the charm of RCR to only partial success. The lead guy's sense of humor is a little more cynical than goofy. I like the gameplay, although the experience really could have been better executed. Trying to mash a button at the start gives an unwelcoming thrust into the game's anti-infinite system. Combine that with the enemies' high health and you have something that drags on longer than the original.
This has been addressed by giving you a few more moves at the start, though this whole idea was just a lot better on paper than it was in practice. Having to buy your moveset becomes a chore, especially since trying to get the full experience requires you need to do it for everyone, and you won't know if you can buy the move until
you get the money.
Mechanically speaking, it's a very good game. Once you get the ball rolling you get to enjoy some of the depth the way it was intended to. The way the moves were laid out isn't beneficial for everybody; some you can't access until you beat the first act. There's also a few things the game never teaches you about, some of which you likely wouldn't get to utilize yourself playing through only Story.
The problem is that Underground tries to balance a game (in the wrong areas) that is inherently unbalanced. When has a Kunio game ever been balanced? Weapons are useless because of the anti-infinite system, and they swing slower to prevent infinites anyway. The designer's thoughts? You can throw as well. I admit weapons were busted in the original, but that didn't call for making them worthless. Don't get me started on what happens if you aren't positioned properly when you try to pick them up....
The game relies on its RPG system because each attack does one of three base amounts. Everybody starts off the same, meaning your strong guy will hit as hard as your speedy fighter until level 12 or so. The level system does stop you from buying through the game, however.
The prologue immediately shows how terrible the balance is. Many moves do the same amount of damage regardless of their speed or cost. Between characters this is where it gets really problematic. If characters started off higher or lower in where they deviate then we'd immediately see where they specialize as well as have better balance.
Arena Mode is kinda fun since you get to play as everybody. Keep in mind that while stats don't carry over, movesets do. This is where you get to see the mechanics shine the fullest; it's unbalanced. Sadly most of the NPCs are simply not designed with human hands in mind. Many boss special costs so high yet they don't even have a full moveset. That move they spam against you can't even be done twice when you use them. 2/3rds of my meter for 23 damage with a boss, while Glen can do 72 damage for that much. What could have been an interesting tangent to explore was instead crippled by trying to homogenize everything based on numbers.
My personal biggest complaint is the AI. It's a challenge, but the bosses are a pushover compared to the typical enemies you fight. I find myself on the defensive because mooks would move away or block my attacks, but bosses just eat damage. The AI knows how to dodge every move in the game, but it doesn't react to moves faster than a certain speed. This could be why bosses have limited movesets (although they were supposed to have moves to take on 4 players). Maybe it's because RCR's AI was primitive. What is a good game when it doesn't push its own rules for the finale? Many retro games did, but this game doesn't. As someone that admits their relative lack of skill in competitive fighting games, I stand by the belief this game isn't hard to learn mechanically.
If the AI would juggle you and the game teaches you how to break out, people would realize that despite being a beat-em-up there is some balance inside. It's not like Guilty Gear where you can only break a combo once every five minutes. All they do is pull a random move or string out of their pool and use it. No followups aside from hitting you on the ground. Players get the perception that juggles are OP, yet complain about BMD restricting them when the game never explains how it works.
What really turned me off is learning certain adjustments that are detrimental to the overall game are intentionally staying that way. Knocking people over with friendly fire off is something everybody brings up. Official word is that it will stay that way. There's also the game not fixing archaic problems like shop descriptions for the sake of being similar to the original game.
As a competitive enthusiast, it was a middle finger to me learning that you can't break juggles from behind anymore, and they didn't even tell us beta players. Trust me: setups and infinites exist to abuse this. Not that I really agreed with Bannon's conservative philosophy (not political, mind you) to begin with though. An anti-air throw that takes too long to even be used on reaction? Not even Abobo's AI uses that move! The fact it doesn't hit grounded people is reason enough to make it faster. It only works as a read, which is pretty much impossible when jumping lower is more beneficial.
Anyway... It's a fun game, but not the best game in the world as some people want to put it as. I'm a realist; not a pessimist. This game used to be worse but that's no excuse since it's released. Perhaps over time as it gets polished I'll gladly suggest this game to others. Just not right now.

It's a pretty cool. I wouln't reccomend it unless you can get it on sale or unless you really like endless runners.
Basically what's going on in this game is you play as a guy that is automatically running to the right for the whole game. And you have to react to what's coming up. Sometimes that means you have to collect things or jump over enemies, or slide underneath them. But it's all a bunch of timing challenges.
And it's pretty fun. There's a LOT of content in this game as well. And I really liked the art style.
The game also has this whole musical undertone too it all too. Basically everything you do makes a little musical sound, and the obstacles in the game are arranged in a way that it all plays in a musical rythmic sort of way. It's pretty neat, but it's nothing to get excited about either. It's cool.
My big problem with the game is that its rediculously hard and you have to restart from the beginning (or checkpoint) after each time you make a mistake. It really kills my flow. This is one of those games you really can get into a groove with. Because the game scrolls at an automatic pace, your dodging things, and everything comes together musically, and the atmosphere is light and exciting... and then you make one mistake and have to get reset alll the way back. The music stops and resets and it all just feels really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ when you hit something. Especially if you messed up by accident, or just barely clipped the edge of something. It's not the game's fault, but be warned before you buy this that there is a massive amount of trial and error going on here. Its really frustrating to me and it has stopped me a number of times from deciding to load up the game.
Altogether I am really enjoying the game. It's got good obstacles that are fun to dodge, good pacing so far, and it's definitly the best endless running type of game I've played.   I'd reccomend this game to almost anybody. If you like good games, this is one of them, but priced a bit high. Don't get it if you don't want a difficult game, or if you don't like trial and error type of gameplay.

A game with multiple personality disorder. Runner games are typically reserved for casual game players and the overall colorful lightheartedness supports this. On the other hand the game seems to target old-school platformers with it's unerring demands and retro sections. It also seems to target that weird audience that thought Rayman's Raving Rabbids was the FUNNIEST THING with the awkward backgrounds, adult innuendos, and a sassy dancing hamburger person.
As far as the gameplay goes it's serviceable for a runner, it basically boils down to a string of quick time events, but the levels are mostly ho-hum. The problem is there are a ton of levels with little variety and many sections get terribly repetitive. There are some levels, as well as boss battles, where you can see how everything could come together if really implemented well. Unfortunately the good ideas are watered down among so many levels, I would rather see half as many levels but more tightly defined and better designed.
A large part of the game is the challenge of collecting all of the gold pieces within a level. It's an interesting diversion but with the aforementioned staleness of the levels I really stopped caring about 100% completion. All the gold is used for is unlocks of further levels (didn't I say there were too many already?) Add in that the developers have added other ways to get you replay levels (hidden keys, missing the target at the end, achievements that reward you for completing a level on all 3 difficulties!?) and the repetition goes through the roof. If there were fewer well designed levels I would care more about my score, practicing to get it -just right-, but the motivation just isn't there to do it again and again 100 times over. Even the leaderboard isn't much of a motivator as many scores seem to have been gained through exploitation and you would never get close by playing the game as intended.
With the constant repetition of levels the soundtrack gets old FAST. I can only platform to soothing jazz with timed bleeps for so long. Each world has essentially one song with slight variants as you play, I found the fire world to be the most engaging but the rest to be forgettable or slightly irritating. Alas with a game so focused on the tie-in with the music I would have hoped for more variety and higher quality.
There are other nit-picks here and there (inescapable intro, you can't remap buttons, it often errors when looking for leaderboards) but at the end of the day the biggest issue I have is with flow. With rhythm games it's all about getting "in the zone," letting the music take you as you enjoy a grand musical adventure. Games like Beat Hazard, Rock Band, or Rez have this in spades; you are moving on instinct becoming one with the music. Sadly this game rarely offered those moments often jarring me out if I started to get into it. Whether it was from the camera zooming in or out at odd times, the overly busy backgrounds creating unnecessary distractions, or the "one hit you die" mechanic taking me back to the start of the level due to questionable collision boxes, the game just wouldn't *let me enjoy it*.
I really wanted to love this game but I've got to give it 1.5 out of 5 stars. There is a brilliant little soul hiding away somewhere in here but it is covered up by fluff and questionable design choices.

Okay.
Yes, it's an 'old' game from five years ago, so you can argue that the graphics shouldn't be expected to be cutting edge...but the modelling and textures and the like look considerably WORSE than Unreal - a game that came out _ten_years_before_ Space Trader: Merchant Marine.
I admit that I'm a fan of Elite-style games: a hybrid of space flight/combat and trading simulation - WC:Privateer, X: Beyond the Frontier, Freelancer, Frontier: Elite II, etc.
...this is NOT that type of hybrid, despite the implication of the title.
This game tries to weld FPS and trading together, and does NOT do a very good job with EITHER.
1) The trading is simplistic, static and easily exploited.
For each 'sector', there are a small handful of commodities, only a similar number of bases/trading hubs to buy and sell the same at, so you could probably chart out all the prices on a Post-It™ note...or even commit the best 'trading routes' to even a dodgy, old and  forgetful memory.
And you won't have to worry about breaking the economy with your efforts - apparently each base has such large demands and supplies of EVERY commodity that even a huge shipment moved by yourself has NO effect on prices on either end of your run.  Your only restriction to making money is finding the best profit margin, and the size of your cargo hold (& working capital).
...but hey; you don't even really need to worry about trading to get up these thinly-justified goals for earning - a) you can usually find piles of items just sitting in nooks and corners on the trading hub maps, which you can then sell to collectors for a decent starting stake, b) you can also pick up a considerable amount of cash from doing the bounty (aka FPS) missions - not always from the up-front wages of that, but from looting commodities from the 'hideout' of whatever low-life you're supposed to assassinate.
2) As others have said, the FPS is similarly unchallenging - the maps are limited in quantity and variety, the 'power ups' are uninspired (and ephemeral), and the opposing AI is laughable, resulting in no point in any gameplay strategy apart from sneaking quickly to a good vantage point and then sniping everyone just aimlessly standing around.
As such, you have two poor component-games, that barely feel like they should even belong together; the overall story is threadbare and challenges even the most credulous willing suspension of disbelief.
Normally, I have very low standards to play a game (gfx, music, v/o, story, etc.) but this game managed to sink below even those unchallenging requirements.
Do not even bother with this on a steam sale - the ONLY reasonable justification I could say for buying this game would be to bump up your XP from sheer quantity of game-ownership, and even then, a heavy discount would be necessary.
...but even so, I would under NO account EVER suggest you PLAY this 'game'...

Ever since I played the original Starflight, I've always had a soft spot for space trading type games. While Space Trader: Merchant Marine has a good trading foundation, it feels severely unpolished and overly repetitious. The game is essentially a hybrid shooter with trading elements. The gameplay is fun, but after the second chapter, you've pretty much done everything there is to do. I'd say most people will get bored with it after the first couple hours. The graphics are definitely dated, the limited voices are horribly comical, and the music does not fit the game at all. With another 6-12 months of polish, this game could have been decent. As it stands now, it is completely forgettable.

Space Trader Merchant Marine is that strange situation where two very different genres have been combined together in the hope of hitting that once in a lifetime combination that everybody agrees is pure genius, like Vampires and Teenagers, or Ninjas and Cheerleaders. Space Trader doesn't quite hit that special recipe however.
Space Trader is a combination of a numbers trading simulator and a first person shooter and by far and large the biggest problem is that playing the game you have trouble telling which of these two aspects feel the most tacked on.
The trading part of the game is simple enough. You travel between various planets in the solar system, each planet has a a few merchants each selling a few goods. You buy as much as your bank account and cargo space will allow and then travel to the next world. Space Trader has no real in game economy however and everything is decided by the almighty Random Number Generator. The challenge of choosing which products to buy is virtually non-existent as all items for sale lists how below normal market value they are next to their name. There is also a legal/non-legal system in place however it has no real effect in game making the actual buying and selling of products extremely dull and predictable.
You explore the various locations on foot, in a first person shooter aspect. The various trade hubs allow you run around a small area, collecting various sellable items littered about the place, trade with the local merchants and take on a number of missions. The missions mostly come down to "Bring X items", "Transport X items" or, the more common, shooter mission. The majority of the missions in the game, and perhaps one of the easiest ways to make money early on in the campaigns is the various bounty missions which are your basic FPS. You spawn in one of a few predetermined maps, kill a few henchmen and eventually a boss will spawn. All the while you can pick up loot that you can sell out in the proper game, and weapons, health and shields that'll help you on this mission only. The shooting is fairly poorly implemented, even for it's time. The weapons feel like pellet guns, the enemy AI is non-existent and the whole experience usually boils down to just sniping at enemies from around a corner.
The music throughout the game is a high speed techno beat that, while I am sure some of you will love it, made me play with the sound off after a few sessions. There is no voice-acting and very little ambiance. Even gun shots and hit sounds leave much to be desired. Graphically the game is nothing to write home about but not much below what you would expect from an indie title either.
All in all, Space Trader Merchant Marine is a game that tries to do two things and fails at doing either in an acceptable fashion. It's not a very good trading simulation and not a very good shooter. It doesn't sound or look very good and it doesn't feel very good. This is a game that can easily be skipped.

I about died when the cardboard box came out.
If you read enough reviews, it quickly becomes clear that this game is not for everyone.  If you showed up looking for a gritty open-world crime saga, you're going to be disappointed.  If you're on board with a spoof of gaming and sci-fi tropes (with Mass Effect 2 most squarely in the game's sights), you're probably going to have a good time.
As you add gray hairs, you're likely to have a better time, especially as you add gaming experience along with those gray hairs.  There's plenty of jokes here for a casual audience, but much will be lost on those that have not driven an Atari tank, played 8-bit side-scrolling beat-em-ups or stood in an open field west of a white house, with a boarded front door.
Long story short, for my money the biggest problem this game has is that inherited the map, mechanics and fanbase of a wildly different game.  If you're like me, you were somewhat underwhelmed with Saints Row 3 and appreciated this installment turning the insanity up to 11 while taking you back to your childhood.  But then again, I've actually beaten every single Infocom game as well as ME2, so I'm more or less the bullseye in the target audience.  YMMV.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong.
Easiest way to rate it? Halfway between Deadman's Switch and Dragonfall (Director's Cut).
Gameplay: In meatspace, basically the same. A few cosmetic changes here and there. In the matrix, quite different, sadly not for the best. New game mechanics force you to play frogger with "sentinel" programs. New mini-game to hack information nodes (mix between simon says and another memory game). Combat is about the same, some pretty new sprites for enemy programs. Overall, the Matrix changes make such sections boring and a "chore". The new mechanics grow stale extremely quickly and aren't immersive.
Graphics: Hong Kong brings a whole lot of new looks for Shadowrun. As you can imagine, the theme is very different from Seattle and Berlin. Though the engine is showing it's age. The Matrix looks much better now, though it's more a change in design than graphics.
Presentation: A handful of bugs. Some harmless, some bothersome and a few story-breaking (not game-breaking, I didn't suffer any crashes). The game plays well despite of this, perhaps the loading screens take a bit too long (specially if you have been alt-tabbing a lot).
Sound: Adecuate music, lots of ambience. Sound effects are (I believe) the same.
Items&Wares: There might be a lot of weapons but there's little variety in functionality. Better stats or a special ability, that's the most notable differences. A few new spells, a few new healing items and accesories but overall the same. When it comes to cyberware, things get a bit more interesting. Some new options to play around with.
Character Customization: The stat screen looks different (more stream-lined) but the core rules are the same. Same stats to raise than before and same skills to choose upon. In regards to how your character looks, the system remains extremely limited. Two new additions though. First, you are now allowed to choose your real name (first and surname) and cyberware (or bioware) got an overhaul. Now you have a wider variety of "spots" to choose for "chroming".
Story: And this is what it boils down to, isn't it? If you are like me you got this game for the story. So... how is it? In one word: Lacking. While miles ahead from DMS, Hong Kong's main story line is also miles behind Dragonfall. It's good, but it's just not Dragonfall good. It's "savior of the people" all over again. Repeating what we already saw in DMS and DF. This is the third game guys, come on, some variety would be welcome. In the characters department, HK is much closer to DF. You are presented with an interesting group of fellow runners all of which have their distinctive personality. They are good, entertaining and interesting, but just not as good as DF's cast. Some conversations were odd or felt stiff. Their personal missions where mostly way too simple or anticlimatic . There's a serious lack of innovation here. Again everyone is standing in their litttle spot in your safe-house, again they wait around doing nothing until you go to them... gone are the group meetings from DF where everyone was together interacting and being themselves. Here, the few group meetings that you'll have will be mostly cut-scenes with little interaction. I just feel that there could be so much more to these great characters. Side-characters (vendors and townspeople) are okay for the most part, but also below DF level. These people are also screaming for more content to be added to them.
So, overall... Do I recommend this game? Of course. This story is still worth playing through. Though I'm eager to know if they plan to do a Director's Cut for Hong Kong as well (it seriously need's one), and if it'll be free as was DF's.
Bottom line, or TL;DR, Shadowrun: Hong Kong's contributions to the series is a new Matrix gameplay which is hit and miss. Storywise it's below DF's level (substantially so) but way better than DMS (which was sub-par to be fair).
I haven't tried the editor (and I don't know if I will), but I KNOW there are a lot of very talented and dedicated people out there that are already producing content, so it won't be long before new modules (or adapted old ones) start popping up. UGC will extend the shelf-time of your game ten fold, which makes it worth buying for that alone.

Alright. Just finished the bonus campaign and here are my thoughts...
Overall, dissapointing.
I can't help but feel that this campaign (that took so long to release, not sure how long it took to make though... but it was promised a long time ago) is lackluster at best.
While the main story line is somewhat solid - and is imbued with a deeper "shadowrun" feeling than the original Hong Kong storyline - the execution is lazy.
What do we get?
1 Initital mostly scripted alley fight.
2 Main-story runs.
2 Side-story runs.
Very, very few new lines of dialogue with your teamates (a handful of which are bugged).
2 new hub areas, though both are completely underused.
---
I'd guess the developers decided to move your hub area to a new place just so they wouldn't have to write new dialogue for everyone in the original one.
I just don't see what the idea is. You created two new hub areas with new people to talk to, but those people have like 2 strings of dialogue. Basic setup at best, just flavor at worst. Second hub area had so much potential, yet you spend like 10 minutes in there at most. Get in, get quest, move to end of game.
Your team have few new things to say. I actually got my hopes up when I started. We have the noodle machine with Gobbet, we have the bird thing with Duncan and Izz... yet those things lead nowhere. They just stick there. Not to mention Izz kept repeating the bird event for some reason. What about those guards standing around? Two or three dialogue lines, also lead nowhere. Same thing with the vendors... What happened to the guy cooking the awful smelling food? I never got any more dialogue out of him and he disappeared in the second hub.
Oh, and everyone on the second hub... Wasted potential. Here we have a new set of characters with different motivations and stories to tell, a welcome change from being stuffed in that impound... All that setting... for what? 10 minutes of dialogue? Not even a mention of them in the epilogue.
And what the hell happened to the Ork that interrogates you at the beggining of the game? Does he ever show up again? 'cause I sure never saw a thing out of him during the entire campaign... it's like he banished.
You need to fine tune your AI, the Lily fight was a drekfest. I had two AAA corporations fighting each other on the street and it seemed more like a pillow fight than anything else. They kept throwing grenades at me though I kept throwing them back, they kept using silly cyberware powers that did no damage, the hired runner that I turned to my side hit someonen twice at most...
And what's with all the melee stun-baton wielding orcs? Here I am, shooting peeps with customized pistols and heavy weapons, Karma over 200 and you send orcs with stun batons against me? I think we already established that the team is full of badasses that pretty much killed a demi-god (as they say themselves)... Stun-batons ain't gonna cut it!
BBS messages were also pretty short... think they run out after the first mission... shame 'cause I love reading those.
---
But well. It's free, right? I just expected a LOT more. The Dragonfall - Director's Cut had so much content, so many improvements, so many new dialogues and quests... This Extended Edition frankly feels.... underwhelming.
Harebrained Studios... this is UGC quality, seriously. Step up your game. Shadowrun has so much potential, you have to keep upping the bar or at least keeping the same level of quality. It's clear here that a lot of people aren't content with the quality of HK. Just look at the UGC content for it and compare it with Dragonfall.
Still, I have faith in you and hope to see better camp

I'm a huge fan of the previous two Shadowrun games (particularly Dragonfall).  In fact, I was so excited about this game, I pre-purchased it (yeah, the only one of my 308 video games that I've pre-purchased).  The verdict:  Well, this game has the potential to be great.  But it's crippled by a few major issues.  I want to believe that these issues will be addressed by the studio/publisher so that I can happily change this rating to the glowing "thumbs up" that I've rated their previous two titles!  But, as it stands right now, this is the situation with this game:
First, the pros:
--Like the first two games ("Returns" and "Dragonfall") this game has a wonderful atmosphere/setting.
--Stat tree has been revised, for the better.
--Another good story.  The story is on par with "Returns", in my opinion.
--Some of the improvments to the Matrix are a plus, such as the aesthetics and the clearer distinction between white IC and black IC.  However, some of the changes were definitely NOT for the better (see below).
--Nice soundtrack.
And now, the cons:
--The game is loaded with bugs and flaws.  For example, the interactable objects in the environment work great...except when they don't work at all.
--There seems to be fewer interactables than in "Dragonfall".  Like "Returns", the environment seems like it's more for looks.
--The dialogue boxes are poorly proofread and don't always flow properly.  Sometimes a character will answer a question that wasn't asked.  Sometimes the same dialogue choice will appear twice among the list of choices.
--The story is really stingy with rewards.  I completed all the missions successfully, even making sure not to miss any of the optional objectives and I still finished the game with crappy mid-range gear and almost no cybernetics...and I barely afforded that.  The game does reward you with $5,000 nuyen during the epilogue when, of course, you have no use for the money (I thought that decision was rather lame.).  Half the fun is pulling off perfect runs so you can reap the rewards and build a powerful character.  However, the stingyness of the game with its story rewards could be viewed as a challege of mission completion on a frugal budget, and I guess that would be do-able if it wasn't for...
-- ...yup, another bug.  And this one is almost game breaking.  The inventory and trade system is badly glitched.  Often you'll buy equippment from vendors and they take your nuyen (in-game currency) and don't give you the merch!!!  Or, you get the merch but it disappears from your inventory shortly thereafter, never to appear again.  Even gear you already owned sometimes randomly disappears!  And this doesn't just happen when buying -- the same problem crops up when selling.  For example, I tried to sell a $1,000 smartlink shotgun to a vendor and the item disappeared...but I never got paid for the sale.  So, coupled with the stingy story rewards, the fact that this glitch constantly rips you off makes it almost impossible to properly equip your character by late game missions.
--Hacking in the Matrix is essentially a hyper-irritating, repetitve game of "Simon Says".  I mean, really?  That's the best they could come up with?!?  It's enough to offset the improvements they've made to decking in this installment.  The Watcher IC are annoying as well since line-of-sight often makes it difficult to determine their patrol routes.
--Items in game don't display their effects...or heck, I dunno, maybe they don't work at all.  For example, your character will don an armored vest but, according to your stats, you're not wearing it at all!  You don't gain the benefit of the expensive armor you just purchased.  Wow, isn't that nice?  That is only one example, but you get the idea.
Anyway, this game has the potential to be AWESOME, once it's heavily patched.  Until then, don't say I didn't warn you.

SR: Hong Kong is a gem of an RPG that’s (as of writing) still a few patches away from being a masterpiece.
Pros
It’s a visual delight that is leagues ahead of the previous games in *almost* every aspect of it’s presentation and finish. Between the great visual design and sharp writing, it truly feels like a cyber dystopian version of Hong Kong. There’s also surprising insight into Asian culture and conduct that most western games miss. The music is great but doesn’t feel as memorable as it did in previous games but definitely adds to every scene.
Every major character is interesting and memorable. I thought it would be hard to beat SR: Dragonfall on how much you learn to like your party members but SR: Hong Kong really exceeds expectations. One of the characters you start with, your adopted brother seemed like a pretty generic type of angry ex-cop. Over many conversations with him throughout the game, however, you effectively pick what your history and relationship with him and your adoptive father was. And as the ‘mutually agreed on history’ comes back into play throughout the game, you start to feel less like a person clicking through dialogue options and more like you’re in an improv play. The story, although nothing dramatically new, does things in interesting new ways and feels fresh and great.
The other aspects of the game are also well done and a marked improvement from previous games.
Cons
The story feels more personal than in most RPGs but it I wish there were a few more main story missions. By the time end game rolled around, it felt like there was a slight disconnect between the plot and the rest of the game. Which is not an accident, you’re hired as a shadowrunner while the NPCs run down leads on main plot but it still does feel a bit front and end heavy with the middle being completely unrelated stuff.
I love the changes to the matrix (hacking) sections but until the very last level, you don’t realise how lazy they got with the change. The matrix is simply the same throughout the game until you hack the big corporate servers in one of the last missions and suddenly, *this* matrix is vastly different. Gorgeous even. Why can’t each corporate matrix have it’s own visual identity? Surely breaking into the Ares research labs on a side mission should have this kind of effort as well. Seems like a lazy omission that is very unfortunate. Some people may also hate the new changes to the matrix but I’m not one of them.
Bugs, so many bugs. Nothing too dramatic but the game definitely needed a few more weeks of QA. They may have hotfixed the progress blocking bugs but a plethora of bugs remain ranging from:
- An NPC you spoke to for ages and used dialogue options to advance the story with: talk to them again and they have no memory of talking to you and all the dialogue options you had previously selected are missing. Progress isn’t stopped as the dialogue options all triggered stuff in the game it’s just weird and super immersion breaking. This happened MANY times but mostly in the last 25% of the campaign.
- 2 side-quest lines somehow resolved themselves as failures without me doing anything. One of these quests was both tied to an achievement and also glitched the relevant NPCs so there were 2 people where there should have been one (1 should exist in a mission success state and the other in a fail state, not both).
- The NPCs in club 88 and numerous NPCs in the epilogue all have a plethora of disappointing and immersion breaking dialogue bugs.
- During the final boss fight, there was… unusual behaviour among the NPCs. Instead of the character that was upgraded to throw back grenades doing that, a completely different party member was picking up projectiles and hurling them at friends. Very weird.
Overall this game is amazing but I did miss out on achievements and some good memories because of the bugs. If you’re a huge fan of the SR series then get it now, play it, and play it a second time after the bugs are gone (which I intend to do). If you’re on the fence and just looking for a good RPG, go play SR: Dragonfall while they patch out the bugs out of this one – but definitely revisit after patches. This game is fantastic.

Let me just start by establishing that shadowrun already has one of the richest fantasy universes in all of tabletop/rpg gaming. Their successful blend of cyberpunk, corporate espionage, and traditional fantasy elements gives it a lore vastly superior to most games. This game successfully builds on this creating once again an immersive setting which will hook you from the get go.
It features an epic story line which combines familiar elements from a known world setting to a dystopian future. A crew comprised of well fleshed out party members with their own motivations which sometimes tangle with your own and at other times branch out into over the top side missions. I also must commend the developers of the game on paying attention to details when it comes to your party members who will all have their own specific dialogue and interactions on each different mission. They also can turn out very different depending on your characters interactions with them. That's somewhere that I notice a lot of RPG's cheap out.
Your character has many diverse builds and can rely on hacking and charisma as much as combat prowess and magical ability. The best part remains the customizing of your body through cybernetically enhanced synthetic body parts. Nothing like getting rid of your pathetic normal eyeballs in favor of accuracy enhancing sniper cyborg eyes or getting rid of your soft humanoid skin in favor of a bullet proof carapace.
The combat is still very similar to Dragonfall and the original which is a good thing. Think X-com with a smaller budget its fast paced turn based tactics make it seem like a superhuman swat team basically going from floor to floor in gang ridden neighborhoods and evil corporate labs. On the downside the AI could use a few tweaks it sometimes does stupid things like go out of it's way to gain cover midway through it's turn when it will ultimately finish it's turn elsewhere, thus wasting valuable actions points. If you're familiar at all with the games I'd recommend playing it on hard to compensate for the AI lacking in the decision making department.
The new matrix(alternate world when hacking) feels a lot smoother and polished than in the previous iterations. It's more stealth based and differentiates better from regular combat. I'd recommend playing the game as a decker(hacker) because to get the most opportunities and rewards from the game you need a hacker on every single mission yet the hacker that joins your crew is depressingly boring while the rest of your crew are memorable and fun.
As a final note I'd like to tip my hat to harebrain schemes who basically have resurrected a dead franchise, produced three high quality affordable games from it. Games that always feel fresh and better than the previous one. All that on a crowdfunded budget which is a fraction of what bigger studios who most of the time make uninspired sequels with generic stories who don't interest anyone. 9/10
While it is fun game and the seem to have improved the game over all.

I thought Dragonfall was a step down from DMS due to it being longwinded.  The strategic element of this degenerates things even further.  I should not call it strategy...I should call it economic management.  You have 2 choices: 1) Specialize to the hilt and only partly play a role in your party or 2) Be so inept that you have to rely completely on your party.  Your fellow shadowrunners are far more powerful than you are so you are basically the face of your group rather than being a part of it.
The reason you must specialize is not the reason you might think either.  Most of the time it is because of Karma...not so this time.  This time there are 2 factors.  The first and biggest reason is money...there is just not enough for you to load out your character with better gear to make use of the skills you have if you try to split specialities.  Even as a specialist if you make a mistake choosing gear it could take you 2-3 runs just to correct that mistake.  The second is the badly scaled missions.  You are offered missions...but who knows if you are actually god enough to do them.  You either have an easy time of it or get your face ripped off and find yourself respecing and redoing content.  This is a save fest game.
The story is fragmented and does not really flow like the previous two.  It is open ended but so much so that you really don't have a focal point.  You are constantly pushed away from your RPG plot goal by NPCs who are dismissive and disgruntled.  Lots and lots of text to red through...a lot of which has nothing to with the main story or any missions, as well as plot lines that go nowhere.
Verdict: Buy on sale.  I am glad I did not kickstart this.  I think HBS should stick to the story telling and let somoene else deal with the rest of the games design.

This is an honest-to-god good Sonic game. I swear. Sega seems to have  remembered what makes Sonic fun - fast platforming, multiple paths through levels, not wandering around towns trying to find where to go - and made what may be the best 3D Sonic game yet. Better than 3D Blast, even.

The Sonic franchise has had its ups and downs...or rather it had a period of greatness and then nosedived into at best mediocrity at worst just plain terrible. After the disaster that was Sonic 2006, Sega finally showed signs of righting the ship with Unleashed (the daytime levels) and continued to improve on this with Colours but now finally Sonic Generations is what was previously thought impossible, a good Sonic game.
Unlike Sonic 4 which screwed up the 2D section and every 3D Sonic game which failed to translate the fun of the classics into 3D, Generations successfully manages to make both fun. The game isn't too long but quality over quantity, there's tonnes of fun that can be had in retrying levels for a better score and the game has tonnes of challenges so if you want more after the main story there's a bunch of challenges that for the most part are pretty fun.
Overall there's not much to say about Generations other than that it is the best Sonic game in years, if you've played the older titles to death and want a quality modern Sonic this is for you, if you not...what's wrong with you, go play Sonic 2 now!

If you read enough reviews, it quickly becomes clear that this game is not for everyone.  If you showed up looking for a gritty open-world crime saga, you're going to be disappointed.  If you're on board with a spoof of gaming and sci-fi tropes (with Mass Effect 2 most squarely in the game's sights), you're probably going to have a good time.
As you add gray hairs, you're likely to have a better time, especially as you add gaming experience along with those gray hairs.  There's plenty of jokes here for a casual audience, but much will be lost on those that have not driven an Atari tank, played 8-bit side-scrolling beat-em-ups or stood in an open field west of a white house, with a boarded front door.
Long story short, for my money the biggest problem this game has is that inherited the map, mechanics and fanbase of a wildly different game.  If you're like me, you were somewhat underwhelmed with Saints Row 3 and appreciated this installment turning the insanity up to 11 while taking you back to your childhood.  But then again, I've actually beaten every single Infocom game as well as ME2, so I'm more or less the bullseye in the target audience.  YMMV.

Gameplay: This plays a lot like Mystery Dungeon games, only instead of a dungeon, you get a rather linear strip of land. Luckily, the game spices things up by throwing in an instant-kill wave of darkness, which means you have to constantly move to the right while gaining enough exp and resources to survive. After you win or die, you get a chance to carry over Hero Points and a certain number of items to the next playthrough.
Each playthrough utilizes a seed (string of characters) that determines all the random NPCs, towns, obstacles, and everything else in the world map. Additionally, the game will also generate daily campaign dimensions with special conditions and challenges. This seed system gives you the choice of discovering new dimensions to keep the gameplay fresh or revisiting old dimensions that have favorable conditions for the various Steam achievements.
Story: At first, the plot seems fairly generic, since your mission is basically to find and kill an evil overlord to stop the darkness. However, once you play on higher difficulties, you get a chance to recruit NPCs, who all have interesting backstories and world building lore to tell you as you raise their affection. If you manage to set off all their flags, you will also get their endings along with an achievement.

Well... How to say that. It has been quite a few months that I rarely got into a game and played it more than 2 hours, except some like Borderlands 2, Minecraft, and some little other games.. And well, this game is a rare jewel in gaming industry, which I know I'll play a lot before stopping.
First, I got it as a present, so I didn't have to spend anything on it, but damn that was an awesome gift. As for the game itself, I first thought it would be a really repetitive thing where you always do the same thing with no fun... And it's an awesome game with lots of fun.
The first thing that hit me is that I will always want to play more. I'm not a fan of games where you have a limited amount of time to do something, but the darkness push you to go further in the game, and gives an incredible adrenaline boost.
Second thing is that I'm a great fan of Roleplay and such, and this game is just like urging my Roleplaying soul to put myself into my character. It just gives so many possibilities, you cannot avoid this game if you like Roleplaying as much as I do.
So, I guess I'll make kind of a summary:
Pros:
+ Very fun game, never gets boring
+ Graphics pretty decent
+ "Just one more turn"-kind of game
+ One playthrough is not that long until you find a save point/die, so you can play this when you're bored and have little time
+ My Roleplaying feti... I mean soul is pleased
+ It's quite funny sometimes as well
+ Your personal fairy that will ask you to bath because you stink
+ Great durability
Cons:
- Little character creation, only two appareances for each class and perks... Although the classes are all fun.
- The randomly created worlds can go from "you're fukken' lucky" to "lol ur doomd m8". I never screamed as much when I had to pass through a snow biome, then desert, then volcanic, and then snow again.
- Really frustating when you lose your game because you lacked one turn after achieving more than you ever did.
Conclusion:
Would I advice you to buy this game? Depends. If you don't want to play a game where you do quite the same thing over and over again, but in different situations, or if you want an easy-to-clear game, don't buy it. Otherwise, if you love RPGs and if you wanna get a game where Roleplay is highly encouraged, and if you have some patience, buy this game.

The real reason I'm leaving this review is because of the people ♥♥♥♥♥ing about UPlay. UPlay is a digital distribution and digital rights management platform. Exactly the same as Steam.
Here are my idling stats: Steam spawns about 5 helper processes. The two big ones use 100-150 Mb of RAM each. The main Steam client constatly hogs 1-20% of my CPU. Nothing ridiculous, but it's there. UPlay runs at 0% CPU, no matter what I'm running. It also uses about 90 Mb. For it's backup processes (3 of them), they each use about 30-50 MB of Ram, with no CPU drain. So addressing the comments about it's intrusiveness and instantly-♥♥♥♥-up-everything quality - what?
Another completely neutral point about UPlay - it's a DRM client, just like Steam. Unless you *only* get your games from Steam (if you are, stop), you realize how common it is for websites to sell keys that don't link to Steam. Hell I have several AAA titles that are on UPlay, not Steam. It won't stop me from getting games for pennies on the dollar.

Anyone who games on an iDevice or Android should be far too familiar with "Runner" style games by now. This one, I think, is actually tuned and polished enough to be well worth the time anyway. The melding of gameplay and music works perfectly as a sort of audio-visual mnemonic to help learn the more difficult sequences. The checkpoints are an incredibly welcome addition vs. something like Rayman Jungle Run, allowing you to perfect subsections at a time instead of having to do the entire level start to finish or sacrifice your Perfect. In my opinion it strikes an excellent balance, being challenging while never making you feel as if it's unfair or that you're wrestling with bad controls. So, in short, if you enjoy the genre you should love the stuffing out of this one.

My first thought as I started playing was 'ok, this looks really good', which held true until the last minute of the game. Gameplay essentially consists of jumping/grappling/boosting your way through a few levels while the main character narrates the story. The scenery, for the most part, is comprised either of colorful dreamscapes with floating mountains and cities, or else vast cavernous complexes riddled with bioluminescent life - and it all looks amazing. There's a soothing sort of awe in landing on a floating chunk of rock where a cushion-furnished gazebo happens to have been built. Who built it? Who spends time here? It's all very surreal. In fact, the space through which the player navigates is often littered with floating platforms and objects, odd-looking sculptures, sometimes entire villages, and the whole thing is so architectonically impractical that it could only belong in a dream, or a children's story and, well, the game works well on that level... dream or fable, it manages to endow the experience with a great deal of wonder.
The narrative takes the shape of a bedtime story which you (the grown-up version of the protagonist) tell your daughter about the time when you were a kid and went on an adventure, looking for your missing uncle. The voice acting is flawless, and there's a melancholic tone in it that makes you wonder about the unspoken details of the main character's relationship with his uncle, and the reality which inspired this hyper-imaginative tale.
I was really pleasantly surprised with this game. It's well-executed on almost every level and manages to convey a touching story with the support of simple and extremely fun gameplay. It may not be game-of-the-year material, but you know what? I wish there were more games like this.

Love it or hate it (and take a bullet to the brain) Shadowrun Returns is back with it's third standalone - Hong Kong. Shadowrun: Hong Kong is the new chapter in the cyperpunk-with-fantasy RPG series: a good story, great art style, interesting companions and lots of small improvements make this a great game which is sadly marred by some annoying bugs and glitches.
-great story, while not as long as Dragonfall this time things are more intimate as you look into the disappearance of your foster father while trying to uncover who ruined your life
-overall writing is really done well, there's tons of dialogues, ambiance descriptions and computer logs to read through
-the art style is really nice and really sells a believable bleak future: the graphics are also pretty detailed and crisp
-the companions you'll meet and recruit all have some deep and interesting backstories: they also all have very good skillsets making everyone useful in a run
-really nice soundtrack
-well-designed and varied missions, some of them can be completed without even firing a shot if you or your companions have the appropriate skills
-tons of skills for you to choose from allow you to create any character you want, even mixing different "classes"
-excellent length
-it can really get a bit TOO verbose at times with lots of details to read through and a few conversations that drag a bit
-some serious bugs still unpatched as of the last version (3.0.5) the worst being the "stuck in combat" one when you do not return to real time movement after killing all enemies in an area. I got this twice, the first time I had to go back to a previous save thus losing about 15 minutes since it was a big firefight with a matrix run occurring simultaneously. The second time it was towards the end of the game and I had to walk turn-by-turn until I finally entered a new area: I'm pretty sure this glitched an optional encounter that'd have taken place and prevented me from getting an extra companion for the end boss fight.
-dodgy framerate during a mission towards the end of the game (probably related to a bug aswell)
-loading times are quite long when entering a level, reloading a save or entering the skill screen
-a few difficulty spikes
-some typos here and there
Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a great and engaging RPG whose setting alone, with its mix of fantasy and sci-fi, makes it worth playing. I had alot of fun during missions since I'd experiment with my skills and try to complete objectives without drawing attention or using violence, said missions also had a good variety in their goals and level design: you also never know when something unexpected might happen turning a milk run into something more dangerous.
The story is really well-written, sports enough mistery and touches your character personally enough to make you want to uncover what and who is behind it: some more memorable moments can also be found in the few side missions offered by your companions (sadly not all of them have one).
The gameplay itself is also fun and flows well between exploring in real time and switching to a turn based system during combat: whenever a fight starts you'll have a plethora of different weapons, skills, spells and items to choose from depending on how you build your character and what companions you're bringing with you. The rewamped cyberspace also provides a good challenge and is an important part of the game.
I'm giving the game a positive review because it deserves it, but I caution prospective buyers to wait for a patch that solves the "stuck in combat" bug if possible: it's not gamebreaking per se but it'd make you lose quite a bit of playtime if you're not careful with saves and repeating difficult fights can get truly frustrating.

Dont get me wrong, this is an answome RTS ... because the original COH was too !
Seems like Sega just simplified the first game (there is less points to take and less buildings options, for example), and start to sell it in small pieces to justify the crapy DLC system.
Cons list:
- Lack of improviments considering the first game
- Even the graphics isnt evolved (and theres almost 10 years difference !)
- The standard game only allows to play with soviet and germans, and only one campaign and scenario pack. If you want to play the other 3 campaign and scenarios, you have to buy the DLCs. So the standard game is just about 20% of the total game content !
- The customisable comanders and skins should be a good improvment, but the loot system takes a lot of time just get one random item, so its almost impossible to get your desirable item without spending real money to direct buy it.
- And there is overpowered commanders ! You will need to buy them if you want to play truly competitive.
- Dumb AI, the veihcles doesnt obey properly, make strange movements, sometimes dont respond at all, and other times do the exatcly opost of what was told to do (example: turn the rear to enemy when you demand to turn the front).
- Why the loadings are so long ?
The new weather effects, what should be other improviment, isnt make a big impact. Just the foot soldiers start to freeze if they face a blizzard, and need to get to a warm place.
Conclusion: This game feels like just a expansion or remaster from the first, and you need to pay a full game price to get the limited standard game, who looks like a demo, and spent a lot more in DLCs to get full game experience. Sega ruined one of the bests RTS of all times to make more money with crappy DLCs politics and pay-to-win commanders system.
