LISA is a fantastic game.
I am a fan of video games that blend fun gameplay with a rock solid storyline and memorable characters.  2015 provided me with several of such games, games that I will always regard as some of my favorite games of all time.  The Witcher 3, Undertale, and......LISA. And I don't even know which of those great games I like best.
LISA is a game that grabbed me from the opening moments. It is the post apocolyptic journey of a troubled, drug addicted man on a quest to find his missing daughter, who is the only female in the world, and in the process tries to make sense of his life and redeem the mistakes he made in the past.  It sucked me right in with it's soundtrack that ranges from humorous and in your face to subdued and emotional.  The art style is fantastic. Each character looks different and unique, besides enemies, which, there is still a huge variety of.  Speaking of characters....THE CHARACTERS.  I can't say enough good things.  There is so much personality in this game, I can't believe it was made by one man. The characters often made me laugh out loud with what they said or did. You can recruit over 20 unique and hilarious people to join your party, each with different attacks and abilities.
The storyline is my favorite aspect of LISA. It progresses at the perfect pace, answering questions while presenting new ones about the world in which you live, the backstories of characters, and giving you BRUTAL moral dillemas to solve in your mind in the heat of the moment.  This is called the Painful RPG for a reason. You will cringe.  You will take your hands off your keyboard and mouse and sit back, and say, "Really? REALLY? I HAVE TO CHOOSE ONE OF THOSE OPTIONS?" It's brutal.  But this game is also very emotional and touching.  I felt so many different emotions playing through this beautiful and fun story...it left a truly lasting impression on me.  The world that Dingaling created here is deep and wide, full of lore and questions and answers for you to fine.
Now, pop some joy, put on your karate belt, and go find your missing daughter before.....

I've only played this game for an hour now, and I already made up my mind that this is my favorite party-based RPG. The story is fascinatingly dark, the combat is super-duper fun with the combo mechanics, the party members are very abundant from a sexually-expressive power ranger to a fish with legs named Harvey who just happens to be a lawyer, the enemies are creatively cool, the dark humor is very refreshing when living in a depressing world full of perverts, and the permadeath is a neat feature that makes you strategically think twice about how you take care of your party.
Overall, I give this game a 10/10 rating!

Story:
Lisa explores a very bleak and, in a way, post-apocalyptic barren wasteland devoid of the female species. It's a very dark game that deals heavily with mature themes of violence, loneliness and addiction. The player will be required to make tough and morally-grey choices within the gameplay itself, which lends very well to the overall experience of the game. Indeed, as you tranverse a broad and unforgivable landscape, LISA will seek to entice, terrify, and as well as excite you.
If you're into games with great stories that do not hesitate to delve into very mature themes, this is a game for you.
(Note that dark humor and comedic moments are also splattered across the gameplay, and seeks to enhance the user experience very well. You'll be letting out a kind of chuckle that you don't think you should, given the bleak circumstances.)
Premise of the Story:
You are Brad, a man who chances upon young female baby in a all-male barren landscape devoid of the female populace. You raise her, but she is taken away by other bad guys you begin to chase after. The story begins when you embark on a chase to get your child back.
Gameplay:
The game play ultilises simple movement keys: arrow keys and your escape button to open up your inventory. As an RPG, you can eventually pick up party members along your journey. Loyal to the format of an RPG, you can have a maximum of four characters to face battle each time, but can always switch (except for the main character) them out at a local bar. (In a sense all the characters you "collect" stay with you, but only a chosen four can surface in battle.)
It is not over complicated, and the game handles guiding the player through pretty well, at least in my opinion. There should be no worries as how to progress (if you pay attention enough, because what some NPCs say are very relevant clues to progressing).
Disclaimer: This is, of course, done in the 'Normal Mode' and not the insane one. I advise against going all out on your first try. Try the "Normal Mode" first.
Conclusion:
This is a bleak and yet surprisingsly witty game that engages. Its narrative is very intense and allows players to enter another world altogether. Enter Brad and delve deeply into mature themes like addiction, suicide, violence, loneliness, apathy... The world is no longer the same. Make choices that affect lives and limbs and cringe within your weakening heart for the heartache and regret you have to live with. Learn not to trust the hard way, while learning that in certain times trust, faith and perseverance may be all that is left of this barren world.
Are you ready for a journey of a lifetime?

*tl;dr:
This game is basically walking to the right side, while avoiding the darkness that keeps eating everything from the left side, with RPG elements and randomized world.*
-The game has different classes.
-Each world is different (randomized).
-The game has good difficulty modes (They are not too easy and not inhumanly hard)
-You level up your character, by gaining exp from creatures that spawn around the world or in dungeons.
-The game has multiple classes that you need to unlock. Each class has different strenghts and weaknesses.
-Each class levels different stats up faster. For example the sorcerer levels inteligents faster than the knight class.
-Story is scattered. You need to beat the game multiple times on different difficulties and with different characters, to find out more about the story.
-Great replay value if you like walking east every time.
Overall I'd say this is a good game for the completionists, who dont mind doing the same thing in a randomized world over and over again.
I wouldn't recommend buying this if you're not planning on spending hours unlocking the characters and the different endings or difficulties.
DLC EDIT:

-More items have been added and the spawn rate has been reworked so powerfull items are more rare
-More story has been added and the main story has been completed.
-Mini bosses have been added
-Random events have been added
-More terrain has been added
-More NPC's and shops/dungeons have been added
The DLC is a great addition to the game, the events, mini bosses and random loot will keep you busy during your runs, while the extra quests and companions will keep you coming back for more.

It's nothing particularly special, this game. It is goofy and fun. You get to ride bikes, but in special challenges there are also other modes of transportation like skis. There is a "main campaign" of sorts but there are also user made tracks. The gameplay is fast and it is easy to restart if you mess up.
After each run of a track, you get either a bronze, a silver or a gold medal, and the gold medals are usually relatively easy, so "winning" becomes a matter of setting the best time. However here is one problem: the leaderboards are lead by cheaters. You can watch their replays and see that they did not even finish their races, let alone set a record. Two questions immediately beg to be asked: 1. why have the developers not addressed this problem? and 2. What's the point of cheating like that? We can clearly see that you have not finished first but last. You have achieved nothing. Why would you want to prove to everybody that your are a loser?
Anyway, the music is good. Well, either you will actually like it or appreciate how stylish and silly it is. It's that teenage extreme sports music. The graphics are ok too. There is a lot of destruction going on around you and under you as you ride. The light bloom effect is quite annoying though.
All in all, a fun time. Just a shame about the leaderboards.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is the new chapter in the cyperpunk-with-fantasy RPG series: a good story, great art style, interesting companions and lots of small improvements make this a great game which is sadly marred by some annoying bugs and glitches.
-great story, while not as long as Dragonfall this time things are more intimate as you look into the disappearance of your foster father while trying to uncover who ruined your life
-overall writing is really done well, there's tons of dialogues, ambiance descriptions and computer logs to read through
-the art style is really nice and really sells a believable bleak future: the graphics are also pretty detailed and crisp
-the companions you'll meet and recruit all have some deep and interesting backstories: they also all have very good skillsets making everyone useful in a run
-really nice soundtrack
-well-designed and varied missions, some of them can be completed without even firing a shot if you or your companions have the appropriate skills
-tons of skills for you to choose from allow you to create any character you want, even mixing different "classes"
-excellent length
-it can really get a bit TOO verbose at times with lots of details to read through and a few conversations that drag a bit
-some serious bugs still unpatched as of the last version (3.0.5) the worst being the "stuck in combat" one when you do not return to real time movement after killing all enemies in an area. I got this twice, the first time I had to go back to a previous save thus losing about 15 minutes since it was a big firefight with a matrix run occurring simultaneously. The second time it was towards the end of the game and I had to walk turn-by-turn until I finally entered a new area: I'm pretty sure this glitched an optional encounter that'd have taken place and prevented me from getting an extra companion for the end boss fight.
-dodgy framerate during a mission towards the end of the game (probably related to a bug aswell)
-loading times are quite long when entering a level, reloading a save or entering the skill screen
-a few difficulty spikes
-some typos here and there
Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a great and engaging RPG whose setting alone, with its mix of fantasy and sci-fi, makes it worth playing. I had alot of fun during missions since I'd experiment with my skills and try to complete objectives without drawing attention or using violence, said missions also had a good variety in their goals and level design: you also never know when something unexpected might happen turning a milk run into something more dangerous.
The story is really well-written, sports enough mistery and touches your character personally enough to make you want to uncover what and who is behind it: some more memorable moments can also be found in the few side missions offered by your companions (sadly not all of them have one).
The gameplay itself is also fun and flows well between exploring in real time and switching to a turn based system during combat: whenever a fight starts you'll have a plethora of different weapons, skills, spells and items to choose from depending on how you build your character and what companions you're bringing with you. The rewamped cyberspace also provides a good challenge and is an important part of the game.
I'm giving the game a positive review because it deserves it, but I caution prospective buyers to wait for a patch that solves the "stuck in combat" bug if possible: it's not gamebreaking per se but it'd make you lose quite a bit of playtime if you're not careful with saves and repeating difficult fights can get truly frustrating.

So first of all the main difference is that decking and the matrix have had a huge overhaul. It runs on some completely new rules and features. Instead of fighting IC turn by turn, you have to play a stealth game where you slip past patrols of IC. If they see you, they keep doing system trace until you kill them. In order to get to data nodes, you also have to get past blocker IC. You can force your way past it, but it adds more system trace. Get too much system trace, and black IC will show up and kill you, so it's not an ideal soloution. Instead, you will have to play a mini simon says game and a matching symbols type thing.
These mini-games are extremely difficult and tedious. They aren't fun and I had no idea what the developers were thinking. It also takes you away from the game and your character, because suddenly you're not relying on your characters' skills, but rather your own skills. Obviously this is anti-thetical to the point of an RPG game. The old matrix system was fun and enjoyable, there was no need to change it. Also, you can't supress except for in combat. What?
Secondly, this game is way too easy. I played through the whole game on the hardest difficulty and easily tore through the combat encounters like they were kleenex. I only died twice, and I think one time it was an accident. The game is so easy that it provides no tactical challenge, and I was honestly losing interest about halfway through. It's twice as easy as Dragonfall, which is actually challenging and keeps you engaged.
Third, this game is unacceptably buggy. I would click an ability and some other ability would be selected, not the one I wanted. I had characters glitch out and be unavailable for dialouge, leading to me not being able to complete conversations, quests, or storylines. What an extreme buzzkill. I also had the screen CONSTANTLY freeze up on me when returning from missions. The bugs in this game are unbelievably frustrating and tedious, and honestly ruin the experience.
Fourth, I found that the diaoluge was extremely verbose. Characters re-hash the same point over and over again and the game tried too hard to be melodramatic. It get's old fast because you're sitting there thinking "Ok I get it, let's move on alreadly." The story really drags in a few places as well, taking too much time focusing on unimportant things or holding your hand.
Fifth, the game is way too short. It doesn't have that many missions at all, and some of the missions are quite short. The game feels artificially fleshed out with too much dialouge and melodrama to cover up the fact that the gameplay is sparse, which only makes it feel even MORE sparse.
Sixth, there was annoying thing where one of the main companions was hidden in a side quest, you can only get him if you do that side quest. Only, you don't know that ahead of time. So if you wait to do that mission, you won't have enough time with him to get to know his story and character. I feel bummed out over a huge loss like that, super lame.
Okay, there are a few good things though. Rigging has been improved dramatically. It sucked in the other games because drones are weak and there isn't that much variety. This game fixes that problem by adding new kinds of drones and makes them more bad♥♥♥♥♥ So that's a huge bonus if you like rigging.
They did add new magic as well, but at the same time they took away some of the spells from the previous games. So basically it's a wash. I don't get why they would do that, but oh well.
There is also a new skill tree, cyber affinity. Can't comment on that as I didn't try it.
Conclusion:
Hong Kong has a lot of the same elements that Dragonfall did, but in many ways it takes a step back. In fact it almost takes a step back in some minor way in every aspect. While there are inmprovements, there are underwhlemed by the negetive changes the developers made. At the core, it's still a good game with strong RPG elements. And it is a cheap game. So I give it thumbs up, but my official verdict is "mediocre".

A further improvement over Dragonfall. Shadowrun Returns was good, Dragonfall was better, but Hong Kong is by far superior. More options for character types, and more capability to play a character outside of the standard tropes. Damn well done, and I'll be backing whatever the hell next one they make!

: Harebrained Schemes
: Harebrained Schemes
: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
Since 2013, we have seen the re-emergence of a classic RPG IP: Shadowrun. Boasting some fantastic storytelling and art direction, Shadowrun has been very successful thus far. With Shadowrun: Hong Kong, we have a third, equally well done entry into the series. Being a fan of this series since the SNES title in 1993, as well as the tabletop game, you can imagine my elation each time they have announced a new Shadowrun title.
The title Shadowrun is taken from one of the setting's main premises – that corporate espionage runs rampant in the near-future of the setting. A shadowrun – a successful data theft or physical break-in at a rival corporation or organization – is one of the main tools employed by both corporate rivals and underworld figures. Shadowrunners are the mercenaries who take on these jobs. Let's dive into what you can expect as a Shadowrunner working in Hong Kong.
==========
This game has a lot to offer, and I will do my best to cover everything. I will probably forget *something*, so please forgive me!
Shadowrun: Hong Kong retains alot of the same mechanics and features as the previous two titles: You can create a character from 5 different races and 6 different character archetypes or classes. Human, Elves, Orks (yes, with a k), Dwarves, and Trolls are all available, with Street Samurai, Mage, Decker, Shaman, Rigger, and Physical Adept as professions. Each race has it's own perks and weaknesses, and each archetype has it's own strengths and downfalls. Street Samurai excel at physical combat and are typically heavily augmented with cyberware: cybernetic physical enhancements. Mages have access to a wide array of devastating spells, while Riggers can controls drones and vehicles from afar with them minds. Deckers access the Matrix with a datajack to search for an obtain important information, while Shamans commune with spirits to cast magic. Lastly, Physical Adepts are like Street Samurai, except that their melee attacks are magic-based, channelling them through their bodies.
Shadowrun uses a tactical turn-based battle system, using AP (action points) as a resource for all characters. Starting with 2 AP, all actions consume 1 or more AP to execute. Moving, reloading your guns (ammo is infinite!), casting spells, or using items all consume a set amount of AP. Once a character uses their AP, their turn is over and the next character gets to act. Being aware of yoru surroundings and using cover effective is one of the keys to survival many encounters. Cover offers several advantages, including higher dodge and higher defense against attacks.
Instead of the standard experience points system of many RPGs, Shadowrun uses a Karma system: completing objectives awards you with Karm points, which can be used to increase several stats and skills. Body, Quickness, Ranged, and Will are some examples, as well as weapon proficiencies such as Pistol, Shotgun, SMG, and Rifle. More points in each stat means more powerful skills and abilities. Certain character archetypes utilize certain stats, so make sure you invest your karma wisely!
The majority of the game is presented in text form, from the point of view of a storyteller/dungeonmaster. Dialogue takes place often, and you are given many choices for how to respond to certain situations during dialogue. Depending on how high some of your stats are, you will have different options during certain situations. For example, if you have a high intelligence stat, you might be able to hack a computer to access it, when you would otherwise be unable to. You also have a small handful of etiquettes to choose from, which allow you to respond to things in a certain style. Academic, Shadowrunner, and Street are a few examples.
==========
Hong Kong retains the same fantastic art direction of the previous games. During character creation, you are able to choose from dozens of highly detailed character portraits to represent your character. Environments are absolutely stunning and highly detailed. Character models are equally impressive and sharp. If you zoom in while in-game you can take a look at these detailed character models, which you are able to do at anytime. Even the loading screens feature some beautiful artwork, as well as a detailed description of the area you are heading to or a short summary of the most recent events.
==========
Hong Kong features alot of tracks with an Eastern influence, which works extremely well for the game's setting. The sound direction for this game is just as good as the art direction. Every track is designed to help immerse you into the story and every situation you encounter. Everything has a sound effect, including your gunshots, magic, even your footsteps (which can get annoying after awhile).
==========
Shadowrun: Hong Kong runs very well. I observed 60 FPS in most situations, with no lag, stuttering, massive frame drops, or random crashes. The game has no controller support that I noticed, and I wouldn't recommend it anyway. The entirely game is best played using just your mouse.
A feature added in Dragonfall makes a return here: the ability to save your game almost anywhere. The only notable exceptions are during dialogue or during battle.
==========
A worthy addition to the Shadowrun series of game, Hong Kong boasts enhanced features that originated in Dragonfall. An improved Shadowrun Editior allows for the creation of your own campaigns, utilizing the Steam Workshop to upload and share them with others.
If you are a fan of this IP, a fan of RPGs, or just a fan of great storytelling, Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a great game that deserves your attention.

Being a MASSIVE fan of the first Bit.Trip Runner on the Nintendo Wii I was heart broken that Runner 2 was coming only to the Wii U, 360, and PS3 which I will most likely never own. Thanks to the freedom of Steam I was able to play this game all the way through on my super modest Radeon HD4350 video card. Thank you Steam.
So Runner 2. Is it as good as the first installment? Well for me no. Some will be more attracted to Runner 2 simply because of the more modern graphic style vs. the first Runner's Retro 8-bit 3D graphics. The gameplay is still extremely tight as in the first Runner and the game is still extremely fun but there are a few things that keep this one from beating the first. First of all the music is also now more modernized and no longer has the chiptunes that I love so dear and the gameplay has been dumbed down quite a bit to allow for more accessability. Even on hard which adds alot more obstacles in your way Runner 2 is still not as challenging as the first game. Also there are check points in the middle of every level for pansies who whine about starting at the beginning if they screw up which can thankfully be skipped for a higher score. However there are checkpoints in every boss fight which makes them stupidly easy compared to the boss fights in the first Runner. I finished the game's larger 5 worlds in half the time it took me to finish 3 smaller worlds in the first Runner. That was kinda disappointing but grading this game based on it's own merit without comparing it to the first Runner, Runner 2 is still a first class title that should not be missed by fans of the old, or brand new fans. The music is still awesome, I still had a blast playing and highly recommend you play it too.

For a "what the hell, it's only $3" buy during the 2015 Steam Halloween sale, I found myself blown away by the deep, intricate storytelling of the LISA world. The premise of the story is intriguing enough — you're a dude searching for the only girl in a post-apocalyptic world of all men. But you'll miss the true "charm" of this story if you don't pay equal attention to the many, many side characters, countless variable events/outcomes, and just how fleshed out this messed-up world is. While most games play with the mechanism of player choices affecting gameplay, LISA brings it to the next level with some seriously twisted scenarios. But even after considerable deliberation, 9 out of 10 will make you feel like absolute pigeon poop. So many times I found myself jaw hanging open, in the spirit of either: 1. "Holy shiz, did that really just happen?!" 2. "What. The. EFF." or 3. "..." I can't stress this enough: Dingaling never, ever backs down from an opportunity to flip the bird at its audience.
My favorite activity during the game was collecting companions (many of them delectably weird, like Percy Monsoon, a deuce droppin' pervert) and discovering their equally ridonculous battle skills. But I don't discount the surprisingly vast — but hardly ever superfluous — world to explore, not to mention the crass-as-it-is-eloquent dialogue during both shorter conversations and elaborate cutscenes. Finally, I swear you'll never forget the damn music (Boyfriend, who only watched me play, will NOT stop singing the soundtrack, especially
).
In sum: If you're looking for feel-good, stress-relief, satisfaction-seeking sort of gameplay, this is not the game for you. If you're hankering for strong storytelling with a tongue-in-cheek 'tude, and some dark humor to soothe your agony along the way, take the plunge.

For people who like abstract stuff, I recommend to take a peek at this game.
In fact, I don't know if I like it or not, I loved the concept, it reminds me of a song I recorded where I played guitar for about 10 minutes only expressing my feelings on it, this game has this same "idea". For what I understand, the dev was trying to pass his feelings about life and a lot of things with this game.
I really like the music too, it's pretty good, raw and experimental.
The scenarios are awesome, I like them, and I think I understand the extremely dark parts.
And the feeling that you're actually dreaming is present, that's cool because itt's apparently the idea. You know those weird dreams you have and then wake up thinking "err, what..."? Yeah, this game is basically this.
But there's when I don't know if I like it or not, because the gameplay is kinda tedious and, how would I say, sometimes it "don't work" (I mean, for real, sometimes you pass through walls or jump straight through the platform, and the jump is bad btw). There's a part where it's kind of a platform, where you just have to jump from one platform to another, about 4 or 5 times, but that was a REAL pain, because when I pressed jump the guy didn't jump and fell, this happened like 10 times.
My problem is not the slow paced gameplay, but the lack of "content" in it. I mean, how would I like an abstract scene where you see something that looks like two friend's photo when you don't even know who they are, why it is there and you have not a single explanation about it? The dialogues are very hard to understand, too, specially if your room is not 100% silenced, because the sound of the voices are very muddy and most of the time, the music volume is way higher (I don't know if you can change the options, didn't look for it)
So, overall, I recommend this game if you like abstract stuff (or experimental and raw soundtrack, 'cause it's gold), otherwise stay away. You won't find great storyline, since you won't really fully understand it, as I said, it's not told very well (it's more of those internal jokes that you know there's a joke there, you know there's something funny about it, but you can't fully understand because you don't know exactly what it is about). You also won't find great gameplay or mechanics, since it's basically a walking simulator with some platforming parts that are not even that good.
As a game, it's pretty bad, but as an abstract work of art? Yeah, it's very good, you don't really have to understand 100% of it to like a work of art.

BIT.TRIP Runner2 is more of the same rhythm/platforming like that of its prequel, BIT.TRIP RUNNER.
No longer are the graphics and sound reminiscent of the 8-bit retro style (with exception of the Retro bonus levels), but fear not, this isn't necessarily a bad thing. The game looks and sounds much better, and Runner2's gameplay seems more forgiving than its predecessor. Levels now have checkpoints, which could be entirely avoided if one so desires. The bonus retro levels, once found, can be completed without having to go thru the main level again. And the difficulty isn't quiet as intense as in RUNNER although it still offers 3 difficulty settings. One of which being "Rather Hard" which could still be challenging to any RUNNER veteran.
Throughout some levels are hidden things like the Retro levels, additional characters, and keys & chests that unlock costumes. Those and aiming for Perfect+ in each of the 3 difficulties will have you replaying levels over and over again, easily spending much more time on this game than RUNNER.
Runner2 comes definitely recommended, more so than RUNNER.

A solid entry in Harebrained Schemes' "Shadowrun Returns" series of games; if you liked Dragonfall, you'll like Hong Kong.
Combat is still pretty terrible (and most of all, boring), but HBS has significantly improved the number of options you have to complete each mission, and the Matrix has been significantly changed - for better or for worse.

Games are rarely outstandingly well written - Hong Kong is one of those rare examples. Despite some typos, a few bugs that make speech checks impossible to pass even with the requisite skills and the odd reset on an NPC's storyline (Crafty magically forgetting I exist and acting like I'd never met her before was unusual,) the game is a joy to play from beginning to end.
Characters are very fleshed out and well realized, and the personal storylines for each one are very fun to play through. Any fan of the Shadowrun universe or well-crafted narratives will enjoy SR:HK.
Combat gameplay is basically how it was in Dragonfall though with a few usabiilty tweaks and some interesting new cyberware, chems and spells. Decking has been overhauled to be a much more interesting experience though.
That said, the game is not for everyone - if you hate reading (you will spend between 60-75% of the game just reading) then you should steer clear unless you are really interested in the gameplay.

Here's how good this game is. 99% of the time, I hate strategy games. I find them to be too rigid, too restrictive, and too... strategic? which is a weird criticism to give to a strategy game, I know, and Enemy definitely rewards careful strategy, but my problem with other strategy games is it feels like that's ALL it rewards. In Enemy, you can come up with some stupid, off the wall, hair brained strategies that shouldn't work at all, and it CAN work, and even if it doesn't, you'll have fun with it.
The key aspects to this, I think, are the physics-based environment which collapses into chunks when it takes damage, and the chaotic nature of it being randomly generated. I don't play this game well at all. I start off on the platformer world with stats put into throwing and endurance, every single time. I tend to lose really early on in the game, but I'm having fun the whole damn time.
One of my recent favorite moments in this game was when I was being attacked by anonymous gunmen who were setting the ground on fire around me. They set one of my party members, the princess, on fire. The princess specializes in throwing, so I ran over to the nearest enemy, picked them up, then ran back into the fire so he would die with me. The sacrifice wasn't worth it, as my last party member died shortly after. But the fact is that I had more fun with those few moments before losing than I ever have with any other strategy game. I want to see more strategy games that give you this much freedom to make bad decisions and have fun doing it.
Just be aware, however, that this game isn't free from bugs, but from my little experience so far, the developer is very open and receptive and is still working on polishing the game. I'd recommend this game regardless of whether or not it's on sale, please just play this game.

A brutally difficult game that combines the visual aesthetics of Minecraft with the tactical combat of the original X-Com. Default difficulty (which allows achievements) comes with ironman (lack of) saves, so beware!
The plot is short and to the point: the world has been taken over by four boss characters. It’s up to you to stop them.
You start with three characters: two random allies and you, a character who, aside from determining your starting world, and having a blank slate as far as skill points (you have 5 points to assign as you choose), is totally expendable – it’s entirely possible that by the time you get to the second (or even first!) boss that your party will not include any of the original three members.
You’re thrown into combat as soon as you leave your house, and depending on which world you started on (‘platformer’ world - which has giant mushrooms, green pipes, floating treasure boxes, and red brick walls - tends to be the hardest start, with the possibility of spawning living bombs who throw themselves at you, blowing huge chunks out of the area and killing pretty much anything unfortunate enough to be in the blast radius) you may well start losing characters just about immediately.
There are a number of different weapon classes which you can use: various melee weapons, pistols, rifles, bows, crossbows, spells and staffs (which throw out small bomb-like or inferno projectiles), and perhaps my favorite: brute strength, which allows you to rip out chunks of the game world and throw them at your enemies.
And here we come to one of the more fun aspects of ENEMY – the entire world is made up of little cubes, which can (and will) be destroyed in the course of your fighting. Walls will get holes in them, and will eventually buckle; trees will fall down in an explosion of leaf blocks. Trying to get into the boss castle, but the corridor outside the throne room is a deathtrap? Blow a hole in a back wall and go through that way, or if you can make your way up to the roof, toss a bomb and crush everything in a rain of bricks!
Both sounds and music are basic, but serve well enough.
Only two things come to mind as complaints: first that the interface doesn’t seem to have any way to automatically make sure that you hold enough APs in reserve to fire a shot during your interrupt; second is that the game can start to struggle if there are large amounts of bricks falling all at once, as can very well happen in town battles if you (and/or the enemy) use lots of bombs, fire, or staff weapons.
Well worth picking up if any of the above catches your interest.

This review is sans-DLC, but I did read up on the meat of the DLC to see what I was missing out on.
**Vague spoilers below read at your own risk**
I think LISA had a ton of promise. With the bizarrely crafted world and well crafted, unsettling imagery the story could have come back around really tackled some serious issues; instead it skirted around the subtexts of abuse/addiction in favor of a juvenile madmax-ish mutant... whatever. Just because everyone feels like this game is the best thing ever isn't important.
So why the positive review? Well, the game captured my interest the entire way before letting me down. The unacceptably large number of characters you amass is not justified given there are 5 parts of he game with so-called "grind spots". Each character is fun and unique but only a couple are really solid.
The world is huge and well-crafted. Each area looks great, the character/monster artwork is on another level (even with the rediculous pervy angle they approached the game with).  The music is also charming and unique but highly experimental.  It does fit the game.
Combat is OK. The way the characters land on the enemies with their own flare for each attack was my favorite part. When the main character loses limbs combat aptly changes for him which was a fine detail. Also it was funny watching him ride a bike that way.
This game, in my opinion, was crafted to confuse and disorient. Mission accomplished. Each sub-area has a bunch of doors, each going to other sub-areas and the player gets to stumble around trying to figure out where to go. It added a lot of time to an already lengthy RPG. The game is supposed to be thematically heavy but it could still be more... fun.  The entire game felt like a ♥♥♥♥ing chore to play.
While the first LISA game was about how abuse (be it sexual or physical) is inescapable and hanting. Even though it was over exaggerated and fantastic that game took place in reality.  I could see how that kind of trauma would scar a psyche.
This game is arguably about guilt, abuse, addiction and trying to project those problems on another person who doesn't want to be helped.  So the fact this game is literally taken play in the apocolyypse is ♥♥♥♥ing rediculous.  Had it come back to the poor kid and possible offered insight as to why he took his mental journey, well, at least I could buy into that. If this game is really post-apocalyptic it really screws itself over as that is just too dumb to get behind. Too wacky. Too "omg pervert mens is everywhere, shocking lol".
I did enjoy how the character's pre-apocolypse backgrounds/stories wove together by the end that much seemed deliberate but that was utilized the least of all the elements. The whole mutant angle was just dumb to me and didn't do the game any favors.
So, in short, great pixel graphics, music and bravery to approach heavy themes. Not so great handling of combat, length of game, story and themes.
Should you play it? It's weird enough to satisfy the curious just don't go in expectly anything that will make you glad you took the lengthy journey.

one of my favorite games of all time, this was a great game at launch, but after it got updated with the advanced edition, it simply became something else, much more fun and fair
this is a space exploration roguelike, you control a crew on a ship trying to flee from the rebels in order to alert the federation about a weakness in the rebel fleet
the game is mostly based around combat and decision making as you explore different sectors to reach your destination, the combat is in real time with the option to pause, when engaging an enemy ship you have to manage your crew, your systems, your power levels and aim your weaponry towards the different systems of an enemy ship in order to destroy it or kill their crew
the game takes place accross 8 different sectors and every time you die is back to the begining, each sector has a number of beacons you can visit, each beacon contains an event or a combat encouter, events have different outcomes depending on the decisions you take, usually its all chance, but most of the time you can avoid participating in the event and avoid a bad dice roll, however if you have certain crew members or systems in your ship you can turn many of these events towards a guaranteed win
the game is very entertaining and addicting, each time you play is a different campaign and there are 7 ships to unlock (plus the default one), and each ship has 3 or 2 variations so theres plenty of replay value, for 10 bucks you'll be hard pressed to find better bang for your buck

This is the Sonic game I've waited for since the little blue blur went 3D. Sonic 2 remains the top of the series for me, but this is the first Sonic game that felt true to the series in, what, 10 years now? Even Sonic's failed Episodic Sonic 4 didn't really do the mascot justice. The PC version could have been optimized a little more, since it's just a port, but pick this game up sometime. Tell SEGA they did something right with a method they're more likely to listen to. Sonic Adventure certainly had its fans, but can you imagine if this concept had been an early Dreamcast title to appease both sides of the fence? Ah, to go back in time. You know, like you do in Sonic Generations. Oh snap, I totally brought that right back around.

Generations brings an excellent mixture of the old and new Sonic without ruining either of them, however neither does it exactly copy the old Sonic or the new Sonic. Instead Generations gives a twist but at the same time giving you the same nostalgic feeling of playing the original Sonic back on the Master System or when Sonic was first brought into the 3D generation upon the Dreamcast.
Not only that but if for some reason you missed one or some of the previous games, Generations gives you an insight to what you have missed by bringing back those bosses and characters (The more commonly known) featured within them
Overall, no matter if you like the old or new Sonic, Generations gives some nostalgic and unique gameplay to Sonic, sadly you do get stuck with Tails talking to himself

Full disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter, and I backed it because I loved playing Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun: Dragonfall.
The game starts out with our hero, after you create him or her, getting off a boat to meet their childhood friend and foster brother in Hong Kong. You've been asked to go there by your foster father.
There are three battles before you even become a shadowrunner; one of them is avoidable, but yeah, there's a high probability of being killed first time out. There's even a Steam achievement for it.
The Shadowrun games involve a lot of reading. The writers seem to be more novelists than screenwriters, so they're really not concerned with anything seeming too much like a monologue. The balance between reading and playing is good, though. The reading lets you take a break from trying to shoot, fight, or magic your way out of the many encounters. Talking to your group is also encouraged, as some of them will give you missions. Some of the side characters you'll meet along the way will also help you in surprising ways.
In addition to the character quests, there are many hidden little things in the game that can be easily missed if you don't look around. There are other runners you can meet, more goodies to buy if you have the cash, and some entertaining characters.
There's also a heavier necessity for a decker, which seems to be why the decking virtual world has been given a major upgrade since the last game. It looks much better, and has a few more challenges to it. There are times in the game when a decker is absolutely necessary, and other times when a decker can help to avoid a battle, or even save everyone's lives.
Ultimately, though, the Shadowrun gameplay experience is looking very dated, especially after XCOM, and the upcoming XCOM2. Ideally, for the next Shadowrun game, I'd like to see more 3D, a rotatable map, and a lot more voice acting. Harebrained Schemes have improved their storytelling immensely since Shawrun Returns, but now it's time for them to improve the gameplay experience with some new technologies.

A deep and compelling story, exactly what you would expect from the nitty gritty world of Shadowrun. The devs learned a great deal from their first run in this world, and it shows.
First off, the combat of the game has changed very little from the previous Shadowrun. It didn't need to. It already provided what it needed and was robust enough, if breakable.
Where this game truly shines is the decisions you make, and the story you participate in. It. Is. INCREDIBLE. Unlike the original, you are not railroaded into combat and over-arching decisions. I am currently playing as a charismatic shaman with an acedmic and scholarly backgrounds, with the intent of smooth-talking through most of my problems. And I can!! And I've seen many options that other builds could explore but I could not, BUT! I've done 4 missions so far, and I've really only had 1-2 fights outside of the tutorial start. I've been able to bluff, lie, negotiate and silver-tongue my way to victory almost every time!
And the depth of the characters is just INCREDIBLE. I actually timed myself and I will spend an hour just running around talking to people. Everyone's got a story, everyone's got a background, and they all convey it in their own way. It is just obscenely great.
I can't comment on the Hong Kong in the game too much, because I know I'm only scratching the surface right now. Hopefully someone will remind me 300 hours in to finish up this review.

More.
That's the emphasis compared to the previous Shadowrun games by Harebrained. More art, more space, more writing (a *lot* more writing), more choice, more flavor, more everything.
Hong Kong as a setting in this cyberpunk Shadowrun game is fleshed out incredibly well - the mix of corporate power, corruption, and eastern magic flows together intimately. The characters are superb, the world is more open in terms of design and mission choice compared to previous Shadowrun games...
Here and now, this is the best Shadowrun game to date. And one of the best games I've played in my life. The story is tight, the characters superb, the mission design and choices offered for social, magic, or combat are very well done. Oh, and the Matrix is evolved considerably.

Fun rpg/strategy space game.  It's got a good amount of gaming diversity and detail w/o being overly complicated.  Very exact and yet simple control over your fleet in a turn based tactical battle scheme lets you maintain maximum control of your ships for near minimal effort.  Interface and game mechanics are very intuitive as well imo.
Only downside I have encountered is ease of use of the ui, mostly when trying to access ship menus.  What I've managed to do is click and drag the screen, and the ships near the middle of the screen open the menu.  As such I have difficulties in only opening a particular menu out of a group of closely packed ships since multiple will open up and all overlap each other.  I can still access everything in that state considering how the menus are transparent, it just takes a little more effort than it should.
Otherwise rotating shields or re-positioning the markers for movement as close to the ships as possible for slow movement/close turns can be a little finicky.  Have always managed thus far, just takes a little while to get it right.
Thus far I'd give this game a solid 8/10 for now.  Fix the UI stuffs and I'd say 9/10.     For 10/10.....   gotta play some more before I decide on that.  ;)

I was so impressed and entertained by the first few tutorial missions, I simply had to write this first-look review. Once I've really sunk my teeth into it, I'll update it to be more comprehensive.

I really enjoyed playing Enemy. It has its initial premise of course, but it does really well to incorporate the many different weapon types across medieval, modern, and futuristic lines. It also does well to allow the player to employ different strategies to get the job done.
Something I like a lot as well is that you can interact with the terrain or jump on enemies to damage them. Get someone with the Throwing skill to pick up a rock, a metal door, or chunk of wall and just throw it at the enemy. Additionally when you fire off a ranged weapon, watch as you cause pieces of the floor and wall to break off and fall away.
About the only thing I sort of dislike is some of the game's balancing. Lower Level characters seem to be extremely weak compared to Higher Level ones - which is to be expected, but it makes leveling a little too important and that leads to having to farm your character levels. Some enemies also seem to be outright more dangerous then others - going into the Plains for example you can expect to receive a lot of damage.
Part X-Com, Part Rogue-like, and in a world that is fully destructible, Enemy is a fairly unique game all things considered. Perhaps it may inspire other developers to incorporate some of its features. I fully recommend this game.
Only thing I should note is the price of the game - you might want to wait for it to come on sale first before buying it.

A strategically challenging turn-based game on a grid- but with fully 3d destructable environments. I had a blast playing it back when and, having thought of it out of the blue today, I decided to come back and say so!

Simplified XCom/JagAl-like game spiced with destruction. The idea revolves around the risk averse strategies, as any careless move will get your soldiers killed in 1-2 shots. You can't revive them and you can't load game (unless you backup the ..\Documents\enemy). The game saves automatically and you can only save in an inn, but you first need to find the city and get enough money to heal and save. It's not too hard to find new soldiers (squad of 6 max), but you will have to upgrade them from scratch. And their skills let you handle better weapons, first of all. And also run longer, have better accuracy, more health etc.
Metagame is travelling around the map. Environment is quite interesting and some squares have interesting stuff like cities with shops, castles with bosses etc. After clearing the square you can see all the loot in one screen which is very convenient.
Now on the secret sauce - destructible environment. It's not as satisfying as it was done in Silent Storm, but still refreshing. You can shoot through walls, sometimes you miss, but the block goes off and wounds the enemy. And there's a trait which let's you (or enemy) take a block or some bigger elements and through it for damage, which is useful as you won't have too many grenades along the way.
I think TBS fans should try Enemy, at least when discounted. But to put things into a perspective, Xenonauts with a similar price is still better.

Finally! A *high quality* turn-based tactics game with fully destructible (and throwable!) environments, with the added bonus that every casualty is at least as dire a consequence as in XCOM. And, better still, you can actually specialize in that very ability to pick up pieces of the environment and throwing them. Just, um, be careful about pulling blocks out of large structures, lest you risk discovering the excellet mechanics for attempting to extract yourself (some enemies may force you to learn). Oh! And you can level up your jumping ability to do longer, higher jumps, and even land on your enemies.
I could keep gushing, I really could. You won't regret this purchase one bit; you'll only regret any time not spent playing it.

Trials Evolution: Gold Edition is a 2.5D physics platformer that combines both Trials HD and Evolution into one package. You are tasked with getting across each level as quickly and with as little crashes as possible. Looking at some screenshots of the game you may think it is an action packed racing game but in reality it is about overcoming various obstacles in your path by using careful precision. Keeping your finger on the acceleration key will make it far more likely that you will crash in a spectacular fashion unless you are really skilled at the game. You can crash as many times as you like and still get a bronze medal as long as you cross the finish line but to unlock more levels to play you will need to go for gold or at least silver. The fewer times you crash and the quicker you get to the finish line, the bigger your reward will be. Aside from medals you will also be rewarded with cold hard cash which you can use to customize your rider and the bikes in your garage.
You will automatically unlock new bikes the further you get into the game and they all have different ways of handling. Some may be heavier and slower while others will be fast and very prone to flip over if not careful. Handling aside, each bike you unlock is a straight upgrade to the one you were using meaning that you are unlikely to use those bikes ever again. There is one bike called the Micro Donkey that is unlocked by completing any track without crashing or leaning though for the life of me I could not accomplish this so I have no clue as to how the bike is. Customizing your bike and rider is solely for aesthetic reasons and has no effect on gameplay. You can color each part of your bike individually, making it look like you painted your bike with whatever spray paint you could find in the dumpsters if you so desire. As for different parts there are very little to choose from so most bikes will look the same minus their colors. Same goes for the rider, not much clothes to pick from though you can color him however you please.
Starting off you may be wondering which of the two games you should start off with but it doesn't really matter as you will have to constantly switch between the two as they are tied into each other. Whatever medals you earn in either will count toward your total to unlocking newer, harder tracks so you will have to play through both game's easy tracks in order to unlock medium difficulty ones. You can use the same bikes, same rider and the gameplay is exactly the same so it is very seamless, making it feel like one giant game. With the combination of two already decently sized games you will have a ton of content in this edition of the game. Trails HD no longer has its original soundtrack unfortunately and instead shares Evolution's soundtrack for some reason. Evolution also has a setback in that its DLC is not available for the PC which is really unfortunate since they were very fun. This version is by no means awful but I would suggest getting them on the Xbox 360 if that option is available to you.
Port quality of this title is solid, ran well and I've experienced no glitches or crashes. Most people's issues seem to be with the added Uplay DRM. It runs far smoother than the 360 version especially when there are lots of explosions going on, which is a large portion of the time. It being a 2.5D game means that the explosions going off in the background can't harm you and are there to look cool. You can only move to the left and right of the screen though when you are sent hurling off your bike after a crash you can fly face first into objects that can't normally be interacted with. It is a small unimportant detail but it never gets old sending your poor rider spiraling off the course and directly into some explosives. There is no gore or blood, he will just ragdoll into objects while occasionally letting off a very goofy scream. Trials does not take itself seriously at all and it is always tongue in cheek about things such as the descriptions for the levels that are often times references to movies or other forms of entertainment.
It is goofy, it has respawn points littered seemingly every couple of feet and you can respawn as often as you want but Trials is by no means easy. It may start off as seemingly easy and boring but it will quickly kick off the training wheels, leaving you to fend for yourself as it giggles making you slowly drive your way over a row of highly explosive barrels. These insane, nonsensical things it puts you through is a huge part of its charm and in no time you will be riding through a WW2 battlefield, a floating island full of giant stone golems and a haunted castle to name only a few. You never know what to expect next since the theme of each level varies so greatly and so does the level design. Even after you think you have mastered the levels near the end of the game you will be able to earn a 4th platinum medal which require 0 faults and little time wasted. They are by no means necessary as by the time you unlock the ability to earn them you will have already unlocked all the levels, they are just there to add replay value and earn bragging rights.
After reaching the extreme difficulty tracks I'm just happy to get through a track and couldn't believe when I managed to get a silver medal on an extreme track even if I have played Trials since 2009. A neat feature incorporated into the game is the ability to view other player’s replays to see exactly how they got on the leaderboard and learn a few tricks from them. The community can even use the built in level editor to upload their created levels which are often time as good or better than the professionally made ones. It is a pretty powerful editor and I have seen the game turned into a First Person Shooter which was pretty mind blowing but honestly not that fun. There is tons of user created content to go through however the PC version has their own community that is separate from the Xbox version. That is really unfortunate since the Xbox version has been out much longer and has some amazing user created levels. Nonetheless what is here is typically pretty good and you will not be running low on tracks to play anytime soon.
Aside from your typical tracks you can play through a variety of “Skill Games” which massively change up the core gameplay with crazy ideas such as attaching a rocket booster to your bike, riding on ski gear or flying a UFO. They are very creative and a ton of fun to play through a few times though they lose their appeal quickly. If you are low on medals they can be a lifesaver since they are usually easier to get gold on and there are a ton of skill games to swift through. The other mode is a simple tournament that has you riding through a gauntlet of tracks in order to gain some medals. Each track has their own leader-boards where you can compete against friends and strangers as well as a feature where you can upload your playthrough of the level directly to Youtube. There is just so much content to the game that you'll likely be playing it for a long time if the gameplay is to your liking. A demo is available on the Steam store page which is rare for a PC game but much appreciated and allows you to see if this is your cup of tea before buying. If you have the option of buying these games on the Xbox 360 I would suggest getting them there as Trials HD would feature its original soundtrack and Trails Evolution has some really cool exclusive DLC for it. If not, Trials Evolution: Gold Edition is still jam packed with content and is a very unique, addicting game that everyone should give a shot.

Road to Ballhalla is a great, simple marble maze game with an awesome soundtrack, clean crisp visuals and a lot of challenge & variety. It's worth the full price if this is your type of game, with easily 15+ hours of content.
Anyway... This is such a little gem! Playing this you can tell a lot of love went into making it. I ran into no bugs or issues, and felt challenged from the start to towards the end. I could also see myself quite noticeably getting better as I went along. For each section there's a timed challenge that unlocks afterwards for each level, and the amount of small things you can do each try to improve your time- that you learnt while playing through each of the levels- is something to admire.
And the soundtrack! Albeit a bit repetitive- it fit perfectly. And the "rhythm" aspect of this game really shines through, with the world changing with the rather ambient song; helping you know when to move and when to avoid certain threats.
Prepare to get frustrated though! This game doesn't hold back, and if you're as bad as me; it's respawn after respawn after respawn. Which sucks because you can't earn all the marks for the level if you go over a certain amount (usually 5) and you can feel that pressure constantly looming over you.
Having said this, it is tough to think of actual cons for this game, as it IS simple in both concept and design. And what it has, it's done right. At a stretch I'd say at times the responsiveness or hitbox (of the ball) felt a bit off, but that'd be pushing it. If this seems like your type of game I don't see why you wouldn't like and enjoy it immensely.
...So why the 8/10 score? This game is great, and for the third time; simple. It's not going to blow your mind. What you see is what you get. I felt it lacked something to push it to a 9 or a 10, but this isn't my usual type of game/genre. So take that as you will.
...Or maybe I took 2 marks away because of some leftover saltyness from that damn narrator(?) tricking me so many godamn times. Yeah, don't trust the words. :(

Can simple rolling a ball game be interesting? Road to Ballhalla proves it can not only be interesting, entertaining but also... not so simple.
There are 20 levels in this game. Not much, as it seems. The aim of them all is to roll through them until reaching a hole in the end. There are orbs to collect in the meantime. And there are deadly traps and obstacles everywhere.
You stay too long on red. Die.
You accelerate on red. Die.
You hit blue. Die
Etc. Etc.
Many levels require to feel a music rhythm deeply, else... guess. Yes, you die.
It might be easy to pass if only you want to reach the end of a level. Or not. Depends on your skills. But if you try to reach all collectibles and die as little amout of time as possible, the game becomes difficult.
And it becomes even more difficult if you want to find all secrets.
There is also a time challenge mode for speedrunners that requires devilish skills to beat.
Every level has a different background music which changes accordingly to a place where, at the very moment, the player is. Its beats are easy to feel and follow. The music is very gentle. Soundtrack is well selected, therefore it is not tiresome even if you have to repeat same place over and over again.
Graphically the game might not look unique, but it looks truly fine. I like the idea of adding screen noise, which makes the levels look even sharper and realistic.
Summarizing:
Road to Ballhalla is lot of frustration, but even more entertainment.
Can I recommend this game? Yes, absolutely!

I loved playing the original version of this game, so trying out the Enhanced Edition of Little Big Adventure left me with mixed feelings about the game - it's still a very good title for its age, but I just wonder whether the improvements were worth it.
On the one hand, having achievements is nice, the user interface is very good and the ability to zoom out and have useful icons to let you know what to interact, are all quite nice touches that DotEmu put in. But I have issues with the fact that the control scheme they've chosen, one in which you use the mouse to move about instead of the keyboard, and removing the need for the player to switch behaviours, isn't exactly perfect; in some places, the scheme actually can frustrate you and be more of a hinderance with puzzles. The other issue I have is that the game has some slight bugs in it; one I have is that the game gives me an unexpected error everytime I quit it, which causes my computer to have to restart.
This game, therefore, is alright, especially with it packaged with the option of playing the original or the Enhanced Edition, but I think only fans of the series should take this on, as new players might have issues with it...

What can I say it's Little Big Adventure as you remember it but remastered and made to work on modern operating systems like Windows 10 and Windows 7. The graphics have been slightly improved and a few bugs from the original have been corrected and a couple fixes applied. The developer has done well enabling the game as a point and click/mouse game. Essentially Twinsen follows your mouse cursor now instead of having to hold a direction key on your keyboard or gamepad.
A few people have complained of bugs and things being broken due to the point and click system but I cannot see any problem. Being able to zoom in and out to view rooms and areas is a nice addition. Once you get used to pointing, clicking and Twinsen following the cursor which takes less than 5 minutes the game plays nicely. It still feels like the original and you can still sneak, run, fight and jump as you did before as you move around the gameworld.
Overall a good remake of a classic it's the same excellent story line and a must play at this price!
The game hasn't aged that well in terms of graphics and sounds but the improvements are alright but the story and gameplay make up for this. If you've never played Little Big Adventure it's basically an action adventure game in a semi open world... but don't expect anything as big as Skyrim this is a 1994 game after all.
Anyway game play wise you are Twinsen a member of one of several races on a planet under dictatorship from an evil bad guy (standard story no doubt). Without giving too much of the story away you must break out of prison and follow the story laid out. There is a set story line but you can semi explore certain areas and find secret places. There is no levelling or skill tree but you do have an inventory and acquire new items from time to time. The game mechanics have you dodging enemies, solving puzzles, sneaking around and doing things like jumping, fighting and finding the correct route out of an area along the way. You should get at least 4 to 6 hours gameplay out of LBA it's a very simple but playable story and isometric adventure.

If there was an inbetween option on steam, this would have it. This game is...interesting. Despite what the trailer implies, this is not a fun romp through a sugarcoated wonderland. This game is extremely brutal, and actually VERY dark tone-wise. Unlike XCOM2, there is no overarching grand strategy/research/construction metatgame here. Just a hero you create, two heros picked from a small pool, and a world that wants you f%cking dead.
In this game, you kill all the enemies in a region of the map, then move on to the next region, to again, kill everything to advance. Sometimes you will find towns, but everywhere there is a battle to be fought. This may sound repetive, but isn't. The battlefields are all procedurely generated, and are actually quite well designed at that.
There is no minimum to how many heros are in your squad. But, evertime you go to a new battlefield, it has a random chance of generating a new hero for your squad. The key word, though, is "new." On one hand, it is nice that the baddies on the squares on the map that you already beat don't respawn, but that also means they won't generate new heros, either. This becomes problamatic, since the areas get harder and harder the further you move from you spawn.You may simmply not have enough manpower to continue. This is compounded by how not only is their permadeath, but it is also absolutly compulsary, due to how the save function was built.
You may think to yourself, "Oh, so this is kind of like FTL?" No, not really. In FTL, with a bit of luck, you can make it halfway to two/thirds on your first try. But this game is so unforgiving, you will probably die in the first battle if you are not a vetran of tactics games.
You may think this is a bad game, but is not! It was just made for a very niche audience. If you want a tactics game that takes "easy to learn, difficult to master" to the upmost extreme, this is the game for you. Learning the basic mechanics is very quick. If you want to beat this game, however, prepare to spend a lot of time with it. It is made for a crowd who will pour in hundreds of hours to learn and eventually beat the complexities of the game. If you love tactics games (and I mean really, REALLY love tactics games) and want something you 'can sink you teath into for months or years, I highly recomend it. If you are just a begginer, or more casual, there are probably better way to spend your time and money.

Let's start with the obvious; This is a cute little voxel-based game, where your goal each level is to kill all the enemies, you know... Cliché stuff, and there is no problem with that. Let's get onto gameplay the game is a turn based strategy game, I've already mentioned your goal each level, but your overall goal is to kill the 4 main bosses. At the end of each fight you're sent to a map, you can select a square next to the one you're in, another fight will be initiated, you kill some skrubs, grab more loot, repeat. This game isn't very repetetive though, maps are randomly generated, and so are the levels, and to add to that, after making a character, you can select what genre they're in AND what they are within that genre, currently making 8 different paths for your character, why is this important? Depending on what you chose their will HEAVILY depend on what the map is generated to look like, the enemies you fight and the storyline... y'know... roleplay...
One of my favorite things about this game is the world around you, be careful, because the map itself is a weapon, break the stump of a tree? The whole thing is gonna fall and deal damage to anyone in its way!
To sum it up, I loved this game with it's satisfying destruction and turn based strategy that will leave you hoping that one of your units don't crack under the pressure!

I think the game is good. It's like Jagged Alliance meets Minecraft, with a bunch of old NES references thrown in.  I do have to warn anybody playing the game, that this game is HARD. LOTS of enemies will hurt you and you have very little healing. This forces you to be a lot more tactical than most games, so you can't just rush into the enemy with guns a blazing and hope to live for too long. You must use cunning, strategy, and tactics if you want to have a chance in this game.
You create one character at the beginning and are joined by 2 seemingly randomized characters. Some characters have guns or arrows, some are melee (having to get in close), some use bombs and explosives, and some attack by picking up things and throwing them. The game seems to favor the ones using guns, as melee characters are hard to get into the attack zone, throwing characters use too much time to find something then pick it up then throw it, and bombs are not plentiful to be very practical. This actually forces one to be a little more strategic than simply aim and fire so I think it works in the game's favor.
One thing the game doesn't mention, is that when you select your character, you can select what his environment and opponents will be (platformer based, horror based, fantasy based, etc). Also, each map is randomized, so you'll never get the same map twice (so you can't memorize maps and layouts).  Also, don't bother picking up items that you won't use, since nobody buys them from you. Though do take your fallen opponent's clothes if you don't like your own.
Despite this game being so difficult, it's still fun to play anyway and keeps me entertained, which is the purpose of a good video game, is it not? If you like challenge and tactical turn based strategy games, then you may want to give it a try. If you prefer to rush in with guns blazing to shoot a bunch of monsters, then this is not for you.

With its upbeat, mellow soundtrack and colorful visuals, Runner 2 is not only asthetically pleasing, but a well-crafted game. As an auto-runner, gameplay is fast-paced, demanding quick reflexes to avoid obstacles.
Runner 2 is significantly easier than its predecessor, Bit Trip, which was punishing from the very beginning and had a somewhat steep learning curve. Runner 2 does a great job gradually introducing new mechanics into the mix and the difficulty level can be easily adjusted to your play style. Checkpoints can also be skipped for the reward of extra points as well. The 3D graphics also allow for asthetics and camera angles that were not possible in the first game.
Gameplay does not seem to be repetitive, at least not yet. I have just started World 5 and I'm still enjoying the game. For those looking to 100% games, there's lots of replay value in collecting all the gold and achieving perfect on each level, as well as finding the secret retro stages and unlocking all the costumes and characters.
I can't think of any major flaws, but the color palette for World 4 is a bit strong. Trying to focus while staring at the bright red color scheme is a bit hard on the eyes.
Other than that, I highly reccommend Runner 2, especially if you're into platformers, rhythm games, or platorming rhythm games.

Right, let me preface this by saying that I did not go the extra mile in playing this game, so this review will only cover the base gameplay. Also, I got this via a Humble Bundle, and not full price, so do with that information what you will. Road to Ballhalla is a conceptually simple ball rolling game, in which you roll a ball through various obstacle courses with constantly changing rules. Clearly I think the game was worth my time, but let's look at the good and bad anyways.
The Good
- Fairly tight controls. The ball handles as you would expect, and there are few times in which the controls are the cause of a death.
- The gameplay itself is very varied, and new rules are added fairly often, keeping gameplay feeling new.
- The game is challenging at parts, but not to the point of tearing your hair out. It's a good game for people looking for a challenge without being frustrated.
- The humor scattered throughout the game is generally fairly funny, if not a bit lazy. It really does help add personality to what is, at the end of the day, a game about literally rolling a ball.
- For such a basic concept, a lot of heart and charm is put into the game.
- The music, is very nice, very good.
- There is plenty to do after the base game, and I would assume that it's fairly fun.
The Bad
- Look, at the end of the day, the concept is pretty bland, even if it gets changed up fairly frequently. You'll never need more than movement keys, and a sprint.
- Alot of the new features that you come across are one trick ponies. Some concepts only ever appear once in the base game. It would have been nice to see some more return more frequently.
- The game is not worth 15 bucks. It's pretty good, but the core game is fairly short, and you better be dedicated if you want to get your moneys worth.
Overview: Road to Ballhalla is a charming take on an old concept. Its constant switching of gameplay mechanics means that it feels relatively fresh throughout most of the game, and the difficulty level is set very well so as to cause challenge without frustration. It is hampered somewhat by a higher price, and basic concept as a whole, but if the game goes on sale for about 5 dollars, this games worth a visit.
Tl;dr: Buy this one on sale.

This game has good graphics, historically accurate AI players, and the ability to play online with friends for even more fun.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong suffers from murky storytelling and horrendous pacing. I'll forgive a poorly told story, but that story better be injected with fun. The game's pacing is what brings it down a notch.
After an exciting start, the game gets bogged down by two hours of exposition. After that, you move on to missions, a few which are interesting, but a majority of which are dialogue driven affairs. That brings up another problem. In Dragonfall, you could get a long way with three intellect and four charisma. In Hong Kong, you either invest a great deal into personality stats or find yourself getting into a lot of easily avoidable, dumb fights.
Unlike Dragonfall, there are no "big" missions. They're all  tiny side missions that are, for the most part, light on combat and extremely heavy on the dialogue. If you're a combat oriented character, this makes for an experience where your celebrated shadowrunner looks like a simple thug.
After each mission, you're expected to return to base and talk. Some of these talks are fun. Some conversations seem to go on and on, with characters speaking in circles. The tedium is interrupted every so often by unnecessary meetings with your boss, where you find out that you're no closer to finiding the answers that your looking for. In Dragonfall, you took jobs to pay for a final mission. In Hong Kong, you take jobs to pass the time between the first and final act.
Money and karma are an issue. Cybernetics don't just require essence and money, they require investment into a new skill tree. Do you get more karma per mission to invest in said trees? No, you only get 8 per mission. You'll receive less cash per mission. Now you may get more missions than in previous titles, but more missions means more medpacks and grenades. I remember being able to restock before every mission in Dragonfall, and getting a big enough payment before and during the final act to deck myself out. And one of your biggest cash outs isn't given until the very end of the game where it's no longer necessary.
On the plus side, combat is less tedious than the previous titles. Your party members seem to hit a lot more often in this installment, and you get more milage out of their abilities. The enemies' stats on the highest difficulty aren't as minmaxed as they are in Dragonfall, and your companions are statted out to be pretty effective in combat. If these improvements carried over to the matrix portions of the game, Hong Kong would have had the best matrix sequences out of the three games. But now the matrix sections involve puzzles and frogger segments. Fights where you have one character running the matrix, and the rest of the party fighting off security, become a bogged down nightmare.
*SLIGHT SPOILERS AHEAD
The driving force of the narrative is the mystery of why your foster father wanted you to come to Hong Kong, and what happened to him. Your relationship to him is revealed through dialogue with your brother, which always break down into him complaining about your current predicaments, and him realizing that he has daddy issues. Your between-missions chats become tiresome after a while. You'll receive missions from two of your crew mates early on, and if you don't do them right away, you'll be locked out of conversations with them for the majority of the game. If you complete their missions towards the end, you better be prepared to slog through long, out of place talks that should have been delivered between missions thoughout the earlier portion of the game. You will not appreciate Racter's "beat around the bush" style of speaking, right before you head off to start the final mission.
Where Dragonfall builds up to the final mission, Hong Kong brings it up abruptly, where you boss tells you "Hey, you can do the final mission now, but you better finnish your last three jobs". And the ending really feels tacked on and forced, as if it's supposed to follow the ending formulas of previous titles.  *END OF SPOILERS
Steam says I've spent 66 hours playing this game. I spent 20 of those hours asleep, having dosed off between missions. I probably spent 3 hours loading between screens, 18 hours in the main menu, and 15 hours reading dialogue.
