Mafia 2 is not what I consider to be an Open World Game. It has a big, beautiful map, and I felt that it was marketed as an open world game before release, but the gameplay and missions are very linear. Aside from robbing a few stores for pointless amounts of cash, or buying some new clothes, there is very little else to do outside the story missions. Do not expect this to be 1950's GTA.
However I found the story to be captivating, and is easily this game's biggest strength.
The gameplay is good. It's well built. Controls feel tight and responsive, and the character does what he's supposed to. But there isn't much depth, as most of the game is just gunfights and car chases, and I felt bored of the gameplay before I had completed all missions.
But what kept me going until the end was the story, and as soon as I'd finished the game I found myself wanting Mafia 3 as soon as possible, because I was that impressed with the story. It's well written, well paced and the voice acting is superb. Easily more entertaining than almost all movies that I've watched this year.
I highly recommend this game if you like a well told story.

Combat and movment can be changed by selecting one of the four 'moods', they alter the distance and angle of the attack which a magic throwing ball. how fast you move and how you interact with other things.

Extremely cool game with really satisfying tactical decisions. Reminds me of Jagged Alliance 2 without taking umpteen hours to get anywhere or start doing cool stuff, and without all of the fiddly economic management. Right from the jump, you'll be: accidentally bulldozing walls, knocking trees over onto enemies, starting uncontrollable fires that threaten to engulf everything you hold near and dear, and assessing every map for every exploitable tactic you can muster in an effort to keep your squad alive as the world starts scaling beyond what your six-person squad can honorably annihilate. The game gets tense as hell, as the intended play mode is essentially Iron Man mode in a world with dwindling resources. There's an easier mode with saves and less dwindling, but fie on that.
In a lot of ways, it's an ingeniously modernized X-Com 1/2 or JA2, in that it strips out all of the base-building and research and economic worrying, reinvests some of that into character leveling, simplifies the controls to what are actually necessary, adds genuinely destructible terrain and structures with good physics and fire modeling, and makes the time between booting the game for the first time and doing something fun about 2 minutes; and it does all this while still retaining the fundamental complexity of the squad tactics in X-Com/JA2.
An unkind reviewer would say it's JA2-lite, which is true in a sense, but I don't have a problem with that. I'm not trying to spend 200+ hours fomenting a revolution again; I'm just trying to sledgehammer someone into and through a wall.
Also, surprisingly good music, sfx and cryptic NPC dialogues.

Enemy is a charming game with solid mechanics.
Mashing up Super Mario, Zelda and X-Com sounds crazy enough to work, and here it does. Whether you're shooting, slashing, bombing or smashing Enemy seems to conistently hit the right notes. The art is all nostalgia. The music and sound is sparse but pleasant and unobtrusive. Destructible terrain, crazy boss fights and a simple yet effective character progression system make for memorable moments and emotional attachment to your ragtag band of heroes. I'm typically wary of inexpensive games made by one person but Enemy manages to deliver a surprising amount of content that all feels varied and well thought out.
The lack of a complex strategic layer keeps this title from being the proper second coming of UFO Defence or Jagged Alliance but any fan of squad based tactical RPG's owes it to themselves to at least download the demo. Hell, the first time you explode a building by jumping through the roof and onto an enemy is worth the asking price alone.
My main complaint is that a sequel seems unlikely.

This game has interesting potential. It's got roots in everything, all the classic hero type genres the 80's and early 90s could throw at you and a simple, fun atmosphere to play in. Visually it has a the voxel appeal of Minecraft, simple graphics no longer denote simple gameplay, so it's a decent aesthetic for the styles it's calling on, and it deals with the environments uniquely as massively destructable. Its learning curve is almost nil, you figure out your squad and motions and from there it's as simple as marching around, murderin' stuff. Depth is a bit of a missed op, it's in dev, but the game is so very direct, march, kill, equip, move along, making no strategic uses of the destructable environments, and strangely not including construction of any kind, stores do not exchange cash for loot, there are no power-ups per se, no squad combos, and frankly is missing a few awesome archetypes (such as a Dig-Dug class or Builders). Enemies are either completely impotent or outrageously overpowered, usually the ones with bombs are above and beyond, often performing insta-kills, otherwise most can be completely avoided by gaining the higher ground and shooting them down. Audially it's very mellow, this is a game that won't barrage you with noise, the soundtrack is restrained, very decent. I think with some time and possibly some modification this game could do quite well.

I fear I agree with the few negative reviewers.
The best thing about this game is its atmosphere, the sense of weirdness.
The story itself has lots of potential, but it is actually way too simple. There are some powerful characters that might have developed the story into something amazing. Alas, you only get to guess. Even after the ending you will not get many answers.
Then the mechanics are tedious and somewhat frustrating. Add here that I am not at all into turn-based combat style. Everything feels random and you get no sense of direction. There is no way of knowing what paths will continue the story or in which order you should explore them (to avoid spending hours in tedious back and forth).
And finding so many companions for your team was also not so enjoyable for me, specially given that you only get to use three of them at any given time.
In the end I admit I resorted to following a walkthrough (as guidance to follow the paths in the "correct" order mainly) so this may have detracted from my experience.
I guess I could say this: if you really are into turn-based RPGs and you are looking for a weird experience, give it a try. Otherwise, beware of the hype.

As a fan of small JRPGs such as Undertale, OFF, Wadanohara, etc, I had high hopes for LISA. I heard many great things about LISA and look at those reviews! Over two thousand positive reviews vs less than two hundred negative reviews?
I finished LISA (easy mode) once and just started LISA the Joyful. If I could summarise my feeling for this game in one word, it would be 'WHY!?!'
Don't get me wrong, I understand why people enjoyed the game. There are just too many terrible design decisions to recommend this game.
Let's first talk about the positive.
The game is excellently written. The game did a great job retaining my interest in the story, the world, and the characters. Players are given ample amount of information to understand the world, yet the writing doesn't hold your hand and respects your intelligence. I can't praise the game enough on the writing department. . .
The praise, however, ends there.
One of my biggest complaint is that I had no idea where to go constantly. I would backtrack to places I have visited multiple times because . . look at this.
or this.
Every entrance looks exactly the same! I would return to this game 3-4 days later and would be completely lost on places I went to, places I needed to go, or where the biker gang kidnapped my companion to. May be I am stupid . . but why couldn't developers put some sort of map in the game? Or any sort of indicator so that players do not get utterly lost? These kind of moments occurred frequently and really frustrated me.
Especially since many of the areas you need to use the rope and slowly descent down . . No you can't just jump off from the ledge from slightly high altitude because of fall damage. That is correct, a 2D turn-based RPG has fall damage. Not to mention, you will need to reload the game from save point if you accidently jump off to the pit. These kind of design decisions really made me scratch my head. Was it necessary for the game to force restart just because I accidently pressed arrowkey once more than I needed to?
Lastly, there are technical issues with this game. I don't know how this game could possibly drop frames and stutter in map transition in my new laptop. I am sorry, but this kind of game should have absolutely no problem running on toasters with screen!

This is a type of game that is hard to come by nowadays. Hell, any media like this is impossible to find it seems. It is what it is, it's very plain about that. It refuses to tell you what to feel. It does not coddle your feelings. It will ♥♥♥♥ you up, and you will enjoy every bit of it.
For me at least, where other story-rich games fall short is their utter dishonesty about humanity. This game tells a story that, with an adjustment of setting and situation of course, could be found in the real world. A story of perversion, of addiction, of violence, of insanity. It is relatable because of that. Undertale displays humanity through the mind of an immature 13-year-old: it is always good in the end, there is good in everyone, etc. And that is a blatant lie.
The atmosphere of the game is something I have never encountered before, the utter insanity of it was comforting, in a weird way. It did so well with so little that you can't help but smirk when finding a few select areas. The artstyle of the game contributed to this immensely, being uneasily cheery given the situation.
The story of the game is barebones, but impeccably done. Brad is, as stated by the game, a broken man. A childhood of abuse lay behind him, and the haunting visions of his past consume him. He looks for redemption, gives his body and life for it, and still he gets nothing. There is something to be learned in that.
The music was pretty damn good. It is something of a drug-laced version of rave music and just works so well with the overall direction of the game.
The gameplay is this games shortcoming, however, as it is an RPG-Maker game. If you have decent experience with computer gaming however those aren't that much of problems. The game itself is a bit clunky, the controls can really♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, especially in Pain mode. Nothing like spending an hour in game then losing it all after walking off of a cliff.
Overall, this is an EXCELLENT sophomore production from Dingaling, and even more impressive considering that this was made by one person. I give it a solid 9/10, and worth anyone's time if they have it to be spared.

I'm a good ways into the game, and I have a couple big complaints.
1. Feels like QA was non-existent. Scripts are poorly proofread and have tons of spelling or grammatical errors. At first I thought it was some idiosyncracy due to the fact that everyone is speaking Cantonese, but after a while the errors became more and more obvious and it became apparent that proofreading teams didn't do their jobs.
Additionally, programming leaves a lot to be desired. The fact that I have to wait 10 seconds to enter the matrix whenever Is0bel jacks in? What is up with that? Sometimes character models don't get their run animations and just ice skate around. I'm doing Racter's story mission at the Ares facility, and the poor AI programming I ran into there is what drove me to write this review. The other team of Shadowrunners has been naively programmed to simply run to the exit point and just stand there. They never leave the level or move out of the way. If you had someone left behind, they're stuck there and you either pray one of them moves out of the doorway for a turn to let you in or you restart the level from your last save (which is, unfortunately for me, back at the start of the mission). I'm not even to the end yet. Countless people I know have complained about even worse gameplay issues near the end of the game (portraits not switching, other strange behavior, unexplainable lag). I was going to continue with one run a day because of how long missions take, but at this point I'm too tired to continue the game at all if this is what I have to deal with.
2. Story is great, it's good. Story is what defines the Shadowrun games. Somehow, with Hong Kong, it feels like too much influence is put on dialogue in between missions with NPCs and side characters. I'm a completionist, so I try to talk to every NPC until they repeat dialogue, wasn't a problem in Dragonfall. For Hong Kong, it feels like every character gets their own sideplot, and it's a little too much. Talking to every NPC after a mission takes up to an hour, and I'm stuck in a Catch 22, either I speak with the NPCs and waste my time taking in details that may or may not matter, or I avoid them and possibly lose out on a side quest for nice gear/karma or some important story detail needed for an ending. All of them seem to speak with a heavy sense of foreshadowing, so a very fake sense of obligation is placed upon the player instead of genuine interest.
I'm hoping a Director's Cut will fix the programming issues, at the very least. I enjoyed Dragonfall a lot, and I saw a lot of elements from Dragonfall making their way to Hong Kong, and I think the setting and overall plot is interesting enough to warrant a thumbs up, poor programming and story pacing aside. The crew is more or less just as interesting as last game's crew (Gaichu, Racter, and Kindly Cheng are great). The game's heart is definitely in the right place, it's just implemented poorly.

A lot more Matrix action intertwined with regular charming through, or if you butched it an all out firefight with heavily armed security, while the clock is ticking. Manipulation of people and hardware to gain accsess to areas you are not supposed to be in and in the final act s*t hits the fan and you know what they say? Once s*it hits the fan, no one comes out clean. Those final missions felt like shadowrun, looked like shadowrun and quite franquly were what I was missing in the rest of the game. I will stick to my former statement, that the game has huge issues, is (at the moment) buggy to no end and lacks a proper pacing / story telling untill you reach the final chapter, but I will say that fans of the universe will love what is coming after they fought their way through the early / mid game.
It makes me wonder if those other runs where only implemented to get the game to a proper length, they sure feel like they were lacking love and attention (with some exceptions.)

Just wait until they patched it once or twice, so your vendors won't stop selling stuff to you, conversations won't get stuck or scripts crash.

Oh and one last thing, I don't care what anybody says; the hit chances in this game are beyond FUBAR. If you want to get the most enjoyment out of it, mentally swap the chances from "94% to hit" to "94% to miss" and you'll rage less. Trust me.

Better than Shadowrun Returns, not as good as Dragonfall. Definitely in-between. Combat-wise, it's not that different from the previous two installments save a few tweaks and the fact you can choose your allies' upgrades, which is a plus.
Like other reviewers have said, the story is a little wanting. At no point are you really drawn into the mystery the same way you were in Dragonfall. Everything kind of happens behind the scenes and it isn't until the very end that your characters figure out what the hell is going on. Compare this to Dragonfall where in learning about the history and the politics of the f-state, you slowly begin to figure out why things are the way they are. There's no deus ex machina, everything in Dragonfall is laid out at the start and you just sink deeper and deeper into the story. Unfortunately, this installment is not as well thought out storywise and in the end, you feel a little cheated.
When it comes to tone and atmosphere, it just doesn't feel as sinister as the flux state of Dragonfall. I think the traditional Chinese cultural references feel a little campy. Compared to Berlin, where very little traditional German culture is poking through, it seems strange that futuristic Hong Kong retains so many traditional Chinese values. Real, present day Hong Kong doesn't even act this Chinese.
On a side note, I understand this is based on a tabletop series and that this Chinese-ness is a staple of cyberpunk, but come on. It's 2015. People should look at actual Hong Kong today and extrapolate from there, the same way they did when conceputalizing the anarchy state of Berlin (which is a mashup of antifa with East Berlin).  Furthermore, many people in Hong Kong can speak English, don't you think a 2050 Hong Kong would have even more English speakers?
Despite these flaws, it has its strengths. Kindly Cheng is a memorable character. The new level up system for your allies is neat. This installment had a lot of potential and if they ever revisit it, I hope they focus more on the corporate espionnage angle/gang warfare. It was a much more interesting subplot than the main arc.

This is the ball rolling game I've been dreaming of.
Ball rollers are usually more miss than hit but the allure of the simple concept makes me try most despite the futility. But, finally, all my efforts culminated on the Road to Ballhalla! Controls are nuanced and tight. The campaign is a little short and sweet but timed challenges, "b-roll" bonus levels, and even a secret or two kept me entertained for nearly 10hrs. The difficulty picks up steadily throughout but also of note is the variety between the levels. This can lead to you finding a particular level that becomes your personal challenge. I know I had a hiccup or two. My only mark against would be the much heavier leaning on the rhythm in the majority of later levels. But that's just because like Navin R Johnson before me, I have no rhythm. I overcame it to be somebody and make it to Ballhalla though.
And that's all because Ballhalla is 100% fair. This is key. In any genre I find this to be of the utmost importance to having true difficulty. Fairness. You only die in Ballhalla because you made a mistake (aside from one or two encouraged joke deaths). You don't find secrets only because you don't understand the clue. The design is as clean as the controls here. I really appreciate when a game pulls off fair difficulty. It took perfectly executed simple gameplay and turned it into a true challenge that was beyond satisfying to destroy top to bottom.
If you've been rolling video game balls around since the 8bit days and its an itch that still needs scratching this is the one to get. If you want a good thumbstick challenge swoop this thing up. Or if you're reading reviews because your eyes got pulled in by the neon glow you might just want to consider buying it. Easy recommendation. Great fun.

Ballhalla is more than I expected it to be. The game is simplistic in theory, yet challenging and engaging in execution. It begins very easily, allowing you grasp the basics at a pace that I found to be exactly right. There are text instructions which guide you along the way, peppered with playful commentary from the developers. This kept the frustration of repetitive trials at bay as I made my attempts to both learn, and develop proficieny at getting the ball in the hole - trust me, it's not as easy as it sounds.
Speaking of sound, the entire idea behind the game is to follow the beat, to let the music guide you in order to tackle the trials which await you on your journey to the promised land of Ballhalla. Obviously this would be the case for a game with the "rhythm" tag, but it's worth noting that it is done particularly well in this instance.
Each stage gets progressively more difficult, augmenting new elements of gameplay to keep you interested, helping to avoid the common pitfall of tedium and staleness that plague so many other titles.
As you play each stage, you are benchmarked on two attributes - your ability to collect all the gold, as well as the number of times you fail. You are rewarded with tokens - up to eight (four from each category) - which allow you to unlock new areas, styles of ball, and the option to take on "Rush" mode for that world, which is a timed run of individual levels.
Thus far I haven't completed the game. I'm about to enter Ballhalla, but I can see there are still a good deal of things to be discovered, and that excites me.
If you like N++ (a game I've known since the early Internet days, when it was a flash game called N) then I have a feeling you will enjoy this game. It's very similar, only your ninja is a ball. Just pretend it's Samus.

Enemy is a turn based RPG with a few interesting differences.
First of all, you create your own character, then gather additional party members as you play, until you reach the maximum party size of 6. The characters are all based on common gaming characters - the action hero (good with guns) the wizard (focuses on staff weapons) and so on.
You move your characters, then the computer moves theirs. The goal is to kill all the enemies in the area, then move on. There are zone bosses to kill, and once you have defeated them all (there are currently 4) you win.
There are elements of roguelikes here too - permadeath for characters, and while the game autosaves fairly often, you can't save-scum and reload. Decisions are final.
What makes this special, for me, is the physics. Everything is destructable, and it is endlessly entertaining watching a stray shot bring down a tree that flattens an enemy, or making a tactful decision to blow up a buildings weak points in order to make it collapse in on the occupants. Fire spreads and degrades the materials it touches, and weakens them.
The AI is fairly basic, the challenge lies in being prepared for surprise attacks and not letting yourself be pinned into a situation you can't get out of. The game is pretty hard at first, but once you get the hang of it, and gather some extra party members, it gets easier... until you find yourself trying to kill an undead vampire lord with 6 allies of his own in a close-quarters battle-royale in a crumbling and fragile stone castle ...... and you've only got an explosive throwing lunatic as your available character.
I highly recommend it.

So, this one is a pretty interesting game, conceptually.  It has alot of things going for it.  It's a tactical squad strategy game, which reminds me alot of Silent Storm, actually.  And clearly takes some inspiration from the old Xcom games.
There's alot going on here; you've got randomly generated maps, a big worldmap to explore, towns to go to and buy stuff in, characters to recruit, and a wonderful destructible landscape.  It's very satisfying to watch things shatter when they are hit, and every individual brick or block or whatever is a seperate entity, and can collide with and injure characters.   There's tons of different weapons and items, an easy to use level-up-your-skills sort of thing, and of course permadeath.
But, there's one thing that, for me, absolutely grinds this all to a halt and keeps it from meeting, or even getting close, to it's potential, and that's the morale system, if that's the correct word.
Every character, friend or foe, has a stat representing their mind/morale/courage.  When enemy attacks are fired at your characters, they'll take a hit to this number... no matter if the attack misses or hits them.  When this drops to zero, they will flip the hell out, and either run around like utter morons (problem number 1) or go berserk.  The running around bit is a problem because it DOESNT MAKE ANY SENSE.  I understand the idea of representing a "fight or flight" response, and the urge to get the hell out of there to save yourself.   Too bad it's so poorly implemented though. Your characters wont run AWAY from the enemy; they'll simply run in totally random directions for awhile.  And I mean TOTALLY random.  They absolutely will end up standing 5 blocks away from 2 guys with shotguns and a ninja, or just stand in an open field with snipers everywhere, or.... you get the idea.  This makes no sense at all.  These guys, if they're going to panic, should run AWAY from the enemy.  You know, like people would actually do.  You run AWAY from the threat.  Not just zoom around in different directions followed by shoving your nose up the barrel of some guy's gun.  They can also go berserk instead, at which point they'll try a desperate attack against an enemy, and this one DOES actually work like it sounds, and so isnt much of a problem.
But then there's the way the whole thing is activated.  As I said, when attacked, your guys will get more and more scared.  But here's the thing:  they'll get freaked out EVEN IF IT MAKES NO SENSE.  If they're up against some guy who is so fantastically stupid that he's on the other side of the map, fires a gun DIRECTLY at a heavy object that's RIGHT in front of him, and thus hits it, your guys, who again are on the OTHER SIDE OF THE MAP, will stand there and go "HOLY EXPLODING COWS, BATMAN!!! That one almost hit me square in the forehead!  What a deadly sniper that guy is! I better get away!".  They will do this every.  Single.  Time.  And believe me, it gets really old, really fast.  You end up having to come up with somewhat odd tactics JUST to deal with something that is basically broken from the start.  Not a good thing, and for me, even though I wasnt exactly dying much, it just got so damn stupid that my interest just shattered.  Even if I won the map, I was like "That.... that was just so dumb.  I had to change my strategy because the bad guy pretty much shot himself in the foot a mile away, causing my idiot melee guy to run into the open and do a little dance for no reason!" and.... yeah.  I was just done at that point.   I love strategy games, normally.  But when they hit a point where logic just goes completely out the window, I just lose interest.
And that's pretty much what happened with this one.   Being totally honest, I dont think that mechanic is even necessary.  Particularly considering the theme behind the game.  Your guy isnt just some random idiot; he's clearly an adventurer, having already been on assorted game-ish quests, like being a horror game protagonist, to hopping over spikes and into pipes like Mario.  The pathetic reactions to.... basically everything.... just dont make sense in this context.   I can understand a mechanic like that being added to up the difficulty.  But there's SO many other ways to add extra challenge without having to resort to something like that, as so very many other games have proven already.
All in all, it's not a bad game, but just has some glaring flaws (as that's not the only odd issue it has) that for some players might ruin it entirely.  I strongly suggest watching some videos and lets' plays on the game before buying, to get a sense of how it works.
For now though, I cant entirely recommend it myself.  But your tastes may definitely differ from mine.  Again, it's not bad. But particularly when compared to so many other strategy games out there, it just doesnt quite hit the point where I can genuinely give it a positive score here.
Honestly, I'd rather give it a more neutral score, but Steam's overly simplistic system here doesnt allow me to say "Well, considering everything, I think this is a 6 out of 10, it's a decent game and you might like it but there's definitely some big issues". And I do still play it.  But since I cant just outright recommend the game and am suggesting that people watch some of it for awhile before buying, I'm not giving a thumbs up here.

This is a type of game that is hard to come by nowadays. Hell, any media like this is impossible to find it seems. It is what it is, it's very plain about that. It refuses to tell you what to feel. It does not coddle your feelings. It will ♥♥♥♥ you up, and you will enjoy every bit of it.
For me at least, where other story-rich games fall short is their utter dishonesty about humanity. This game tells a story that, with an adjustment of setting and situation of course, could be found in the real world. A story of perversion, of addiction, of violence, of insanity. It is relatable because of that. Undertale displays humanity through the mind of an immature 13-year-old: it is always good in the end, there is good in everyone, etc. And that is a blatant lie.
The atmosphere of the game is something I have never encountered before, the utter insanity of it was comforting, in a weird way. It did so well with so little that you can't help but smirk when finding a few select areas. The artstyle of the game contributed to this immensely, being uneasily cheery given the situation.
The story of the game is barebones, but impeccably done. Brad is, as stated by the game, a broken man. A childhood of abuse lay behind him, and the haunting visions of his past consume him. He looks for redemption, gives his body and life for it, and still he gets nothing. There is something to be learned in that.
The music was pretty damn good. It is something of a drug-laced version of rave music and just works so well with the overall direction of the game.
The gameplay is this games shortcoming, however, as it is an RPG-Maker game. If you have decent experience with computer gaming however those aren't that much of problems. The game itself is a bit clunky, the controls can really♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, especially in Pain mode. Nothing like spending an hour in game then losing it all after walking off of a cliff.
Overall, this is an EXCELLENT sophomore production from Dingaling, and even more impressive considering that this was made by one person. I give it a solid 9/10, and worth anyone's time if they have it to be spared.

Let's say you wanted to bring back the old, simple RPGs of the early 90s, like Dragon Warrior or Final Fantasy I. Plenty of people have done that, aped their style and failed. So you know you need to create a simple RPG, but you need to use all the gathered knowledge and experience of the past 20 years of RPGs to shake out what works, what doesn't, what's fun, what's not, what worked then that doesn't work now and what works now that wouldn't have worked then.
Congratulations, you've just created One Way Heroics: An early 90's style RPG informed by the knowledge of the past 20 years of RPGs!
The storyline is simple: Save the world. Classic, right?
Well, thing is, you're on a timeline. That's new.
It also makes it very difficult to explore everywhere and talk to everyone--two things you MUST DO in an RPG!
Ah, but the game is randomly generated, and you can re-visit a world by re-entering the seed (think something similar to old save codes). That's both new and old!
But there are save slots too, if you reach the classic save point. That's old.
When you die, you can transfer some of your experience and gear to your next playthrough. That's new!
So too is using some of that to unlock new classes and perks!
This revisiting, this ability to replay worlds and continue on after failure with an overarching metagame leads to another thing that works now which wouldn't have worked so well in an older RPG: The game can be run through and beaten in a couple of hours or less.
This game brings in some of the best aspects of casual games and hardcore games, of old RPGs and new RPGs, to make a great RPG you can put down and pick right back up on later. I honestly feel a little bad only paying 87 cents for it due to a sale, but the game is under 5 bucks normally... still a steal, considering it doesn't play like a $5 game!
If you like RPGs but no longer have time for them, this is the game for you.

All of the maps are re-designed and re-mastered fan favorite levels from all of Sonic's history. The story is mediocre, but when you play a Sonic game, you don't really play it for the story! This game is fast-paced, and even gives each Sonic(you play as two different types of Sonics...the older, shorter, chubbier and silent Sonic from classic Genesis days, and the modern smartass, loudmouth Sonic that does the third person levels) some special abilities that you can buy or earn by completing levels or achievements. Simply pick which power-ups or abilities you want each Sonic to have at his disposale during his levels, and use them when possible. This game is highly recommended for those who have enjoyed any Sonic game in the past!

I'm not really into Velocity 2X's gameplay, and have no intentions of completing it. Most of the time, I would give a negative review for such a game, but in this case of this game, I cannot, in good conscience, do so. Why? Well, the art style is aesthetically pleasing and crisp; the sort of thing that, while graphically outdated in years to come, will still look good thanks to its appealing design. It's the reason why someone might prefer the look of characters in Chrono Trigger to those in Final Fantasy VII, even though FFVII is graphically more advanced.
The gameplay involves the screen scrolling while you teleport your ship past solid matter to collect stuff, and dodging shots, while (eventually) dealing out damage yourself to anything you need to destroy. You will come across locks sealed in interior sections, where you will actually
, and run around in a surprisingly competent side-scrolling run to disengage the lock blocking your shift, before hopping back into your ship and proceeding further. At the end of several missions, you will eventually have a boss battle, and then you continue into new environments. It's not bad, but didn't hook me in.
The music in Velocity 2X is also pleasing to the ear, and while the controls felt a bit weird to me, you can remap them as you please, and despite being a screen-scrolling space game, there are story comics with fun drawn expressions for the lead character in between missions. The greatest compliment, in my opinion, that I could give this game, is that anyone could experience this game in its entirety, from start to finish. Is this an easy game? Oh goodness, no. Getting to the end of the game just takes some time and a little work, but progressing is not difficult. That means if you're terrible at games, I see no reason why you wouldn't be able to comlete Velocity 2X.
Now that said, the game has a scoring system, and for the super hardcore players who care about that sort of thing, this could be an outrageously difficult game. I find this lovely. It can be a relaxing game for some which they can enjoy, just wanting to complete the game, or a harrowing, rage-machine for folks who want a really hard challenge and are more concerned with a high score than simply "winning." The only people who lose out here are the people who don't believe other people should be able to enjoy games if they're not as skilled at video games, and I'm not concerned with the happiness of people who wish others ill for doing no wrong.
So in conclusion, I'm not into this game, but has great art style, sounds great, has story when most games wouldn't have bothered this much in the genre, and it should be possible to complete by some of the worst-skilled gamers, but still a great challenge to the score-seeking hardcore types. This game oozes with so much quality and one of the most cleverly designed difficulties I've ever seen. I suck at this game, and unlike most games, its actions didn't tell me to go fornicate myself because I didn't "git gud" enough to get further into it. Instead, it welcomed me with open arms, while simultaneously offering the same acceptance to gaming badasses who want a huge challenge. Thank you for that, Velocity 2X's devs.

Ahhh, one of the best games of my childhood, now on Steam.
Little Big Adventure (LBA) is an action adventure game, created by Frédérick Raynal (the same guy who created the original Alone in the Dark, in 1992). The gameplay is great. You can interact with the environment to look for items, talk to people, fight enemies (or even friends, if you so desire) with your fists or a magic ball that bounces around, etc. The game world is very lively; every NPC (and the game has hundreds of them) is voiced, and have at least a couple of lines to say to you. Oh, and the NPCs have their own agendas, which is quite nice to observe.
The game has a semi-linear progression. The maps are actually big, and you can explore every nook and cranny of them. And you have an entire planet to explore. Certain locations in the game are initially blocked from us until we progress in the story, but after a while, you can go almost anywhere.
The graphics where amazing in 1994, and even though are a bit dated, still look quite nice today, at least the backgrounds. Everything is colorful, with lots of little details scattered around. The characters aren't very detailed, since they are in (quite ugly) 3D, but are very well animated, at least. The sound department is great. While the voice acting is cringe-worthy, the sound effects remind me of a cartoon, and are very fun to hear, and the musics are great (in CD quality, BTW). Lastly, the storyline is simple to understand, but interesting enough to keep you in the game until the end.
This Steam version comes in two flavors: the Enhanced version (based on the mobile version) and the original one (bundled with a pre-configured Dosbox).
This Enhanced port changed a few things. While the original version used tank controls (like Resident Evil), and could be controlled with the keyboard, this version only uses the mouse (and a few keyboard keys to center the camera, open inventory, etc). At first, I was confused, but after 5 minutes, it felt quite good. Just click AND HOLD anywhere on the screen to move, double click and hold to run, click Twinsen and drag to jump or throw the magic ball, etc. It's a bit weird, but manageable. I would rather have the original controls as an option, and I hope DotEmu add them in the future, but the game IS playable as it is.
Not everything was changed for the worse, however. You now have a VERY GOOD zoom feature, and you can actually zoom out a lot, enabling you to see an entire area. Also, the new status bar is very helpful, and the save system that was broken on the original version was revamped.
Anyway, its good to have this game on Steam. I recommend for the fans, and for anyone that likes action adventure games with lots of exploration elements. ^^
And bonus points for DotEmu for bringing the original version as an option too. ^^

Thank you for listening to us DotEmu! This review has been revised due to post-release changes to alleviate some of my and others concerns.
It's fantastic to finally see the original Little Big Adventure on Steam! The "Enhanced Edition" now available on Steam contains a port of the mobile version along with the original emulated in DosBox. I really recommend getting this version not due to the mobile port, but rather due to the original bundled herein.
If you have never heard of this games series before and do not intend on playing the mobile port there isn't much more to say; stop reading now and get this gem! You won't regret it.
The intended main attraction of this "Enhanced Edition" is unmistakenly a port of the mobile version for Android/iOS and as of writing this retains the controls established for said port. Contrary to the original which is controlled by keyboard alone this Steam version can only be played using either mouse or a gamepad. While not being my preferred way of playing this game the mouse works mostly alright but detracts from the way I feel this game is meant to be experienced. Gamepad controls are severly underworked and bugged at this time, where control of the character is snapped at strange angles.
Showing evidence of misplaced priorities on part of the DotEmu team when porting this game from mobile to PC (read Steam), we can see that the main focus of this release has been a change of the aesthetics. I'm sorry to say but icons look like they've been made by a 12 year old trying out Photoshop for the first time and fails to retain the original feel of the game. The look of the menu have also been changed, having gone from the distinct LBA blue color we know and love to being gray and dull.
Now don't let the two paragraphs above get you down. This game is still fantastic and truely unique, it's a must for any gamer who may have missed it up until this point. Just don't play the "Enhanced Edition" at this point in time and instead launch the original version.
It's also well worth noting that all DosBox releases of LBA have issue in common with mistimed audio tracks (music) and poor midi quality out of the box. Just make a search for how to fix this on the forum here on Steam or on GOG and you should be home free.

This game has good controls with or without a gamepad, a steady difficulty curve and good introductions to new gameplay features, and probably other quality things I just haven't been able to get to yet. Not to mention loads of secrets, silly additions, and just pure entertainment*.
Edit 8/2/2017:   The rest of this review might have been written at 4:52 in the morning... that just shows you how much I liked this game. And also how persistent/patient I am. Anyway, here I am with all the rest of the achievements and the rest of my review. Most of the stuff I would say now is stuff I've already said about the actual content, so here are the interesting bits. Finding the secrets is challenging work, I did most of the work on my own. No, I did not look up the one about survival. Completing the game entirely by collecting all tokens and completing every Rush (speedrun) may take a while due to the annoying but fair difficulty, and doing so gives you a hint that some other secret exists. The really big Scavenger Hunt secret is fun to think about and complete, and is very well executed. The levels are good in length as well. That's about the rest of what I have to say, but just remember there are TONS of puns, secrets, and just amazing content along the entire road to Ballhalla and even after.
I definitely recommend this game, ESPECIALLY if it's on sale. Thank you Torched Hill and Tiny Build developers for this amazing game.   Edit: And thank you a lot for the amazing game, Kai. <3
P.S
*Entertainment includes but is not limited to: giggles, horrible/great puns, death, some frustration, speed-running, secrets, more giggles, more secrets, a bit more frustration, satisfaction.

Took me 45 hours to finish my first playthrough. Hell of a ride, I must say. I was hungry for more when I finished Dead Man's Switch and Dragonfall, now this was truly a feast. I must admit wasn't an absolute improvement over previous two installments, but I'm saying this only because the bar is already so high. Nonetheless I'd take another Shadowrun game over most other RPG titles anytime without a second thought.
Some people will complain that Hong Kong is way too text heavy, and while I'd agree that Dragonfall had a better pacing, having a better balance between passive reading times with action, it's still way better than having filler fights, fetch quests, crafting, grinding, farming and whatever other glorified ways to waste your time that plague many games of this genre. If that's your thing and you think Skyrim is the best example of an RPG out there just stay away, or better buy this game and leave it in your backlog lol. But if you value good story, high quality writing, a rich and atmospheric setting, interesting NPCs and party members, freedom to do things your way and see consequences to your choices (within a reason, of course) and adventures that start when you hit "new game" and get a complete and satisfying closure before you see the credits, this game has it all.
If you enjoyed  previous games for the reasons mentioned above, I don't have to tell you all this, I'll just say you're safe to buy this one. If you didn't play them, however, I'd recommend try them first, and while Dragonfall is quite an improvement over first campaign, Dead Man's Switch does a good job at introducing the Sixth World's setting to new players.

Third game in the series and, sadly, the worst of them all.
Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a buggy mess that should've had a few more bug passes before relase. The entire game is suffering from some weird memory leak that affects your gameplay and loading / saving times the more you play. The cursor / interaction marker is really weird. It either disappears and reappears a few moments later or it won't trigger the interactive item until you've clicked a few times. It's even worse than in Dragonfall which had a few minor issues with the cursor / interaction.
Lot of things in the game don't really make any sense. In one mission you can interact with a bookcase and with the proper main stats, you might spot secret things in it, but - here be spoilers:
Elf character with high Charisma rules all, once again. There's really no other reason to pick any other race.
Your companions are incredibly boring. They are just bland. There's no 'soul' to them. Out of all the companions you can have, only one is well fleshed out and interesting.
There is something really weird going on with hit chances. I've had several misses at 100% hit chance. Either the tooltip is wrong or the game calculates actual hit chance way differently than it's displaying.
Several areas of the game suffer from extreme memory leaks, bogging down and becoming sluggish. Certain rooms will also trap you in them, forcing you to cheat your way out of it via the console because you just can't leave even if the door is wide open. Prosperity Tower, I'm looking at you!
The amount of money you get from missions is appallingly low compared to how much upgrades and supplies cost.
The game is just ... bland! Everything that made Shadowrun: Dragonfall great seems to have been forgotten in this third iteration. While Shadowrun: Hong Kong is aesthetically pleasing, it's just about all it is.
As an old Pen and Paper RPG'er who ran Shadowrun like crazy back in the day, I cannot in good faith recommend this game. Until it either gets a massive overhaul to eliminate the bugs and memory leaks or is on sale, I would stay away from it.

After checking the baby's gender brad realizes he's come across the last girl in existence. One of his friends recommends that he give the baby up, but he decides to keep it and raise it as his own. The story of LISA is enigmatic and the humor is at times bizarre.  The level design is polished and there are plenty of secrets to find.  Since a fair amount of these secrets are bonus party members, completionists will end up with way more characters than they can use.
Expect to make some very difficult decisions, and for your actions to have some unintended consequences. One Way Heroics is a turn-based roguelike game. After the character creation and a bit of customisation you are dropped into a randomly generated world with death coming for you from the left side of the screen and adventure, loot and almost certain death waiting for you on the right. Every time you move, fight, use an object or talk, the world moves on: enemies act and the darkness comes a little bit closer, forcing you to plan your next moves well. Do you want to try going for that treasure chest? Kill that enemy? Explore that building? Maybe talk to a merchant somewhere else on the screen? You are very unlikely to be able to do everything. Luckily, you can generally move a bit faster than the darkness, so even if you let it come close, you will be able to outrun it for a bit again, provided you don't waste too much time for a bit. If you make it far enough, a boss will show up and you can win the game... or die trying.
Due to the random map generation, the difficulty of the game will vary greatly from cakewalk to trying to break a wall with your head. However, after each round you are allowed to buy new perks, unlock other classes or upgrade your dimensional vault, a storage that allows you to transfer things into your next round - great for storing that overpowered weapon you found right before darkness caught up to you.
Not a game you will end up sacrificing your social life to, but a great deal of fun to have in little bursts. It's quick to pick up, the rounds are short and refreshing, and afterwards you will still have a fair amount of the day left to spend on studying, working or even socialising if that's what floats your boat.

This game looks great and has so much potential, but it’s ultimately really disappointing. When I first encountered Velocity 2X, I thought that I was going to get something like The Guardian Legend on NES – an action/adventure epic mixed with a SHUMP game. The Guardian Legend is one of my favorite games, so I was excited. Unfortunately, Velocity 2X’s action and SHUMP sections are boring, repetitive, and not compelling at all.
The whole thing feels more like a time-wasting mobile game than a full-priced title (25 bucks Canadian, which is insane). The platforming sections are more like an endless runner type of game than the 2D platformer/Metroidvania sort of adventure that you may be expecting. You just rush through each stage, jumping over lava, gathering crystals, and avoiding obstacles/taking out enemies as fast as you can. The SHUMP sections are again very mobile-esque: quickly rush through the mission and be careful about getting caught on anything that might blow you up.
If the gameplay is shallow and repetitive, the controls don’t help very much. The teleportation mechanic is very poorly done in both game modes, and the entire process of dashing, sprinting, shooting, and teleporting during the platforming sections is really awkward and clunky. The game wants you to move quickly and accurately, but it never feels natural or pleasant.
Now, not everything about the game is bad. The graphics are very clean and sharp, and the art style is striking. I really like the character designs, and Kai Tana is an awesome heroine. I think that most people will find themselves drawn to the game because of the art and production quality, and I can't blame them - it looks great! The cinema scenes are pretty good and the writing is mostly brisk, funny, and enjoyable. The soundtrack is also quite decent, but the same song gets old after you’ve heard it a million times.
That's where the good stuff ends, though. Everything else about Velocity 2X is just undercooked at best. I can't believe how much they're charging for this. I know that the game has an attractive exterior and you might be tempted to try it out, but I would recommend steering clear of this one, even on sale...it just felt like a waste of my time.

The existing reviews sum up the basic mechanics nicely, so I'm just going to relate a few details that matter to me.
Don't be fooled by the friendly and colorful presentation. This game is serious tactical fun. There is zero handholding. You better get on your game fast son.
Merchants don't restock, there aren't that many of them and gold is precious. Since there's no rest-to-heal mechanic, temples or peace-loving hippies about, you have to hold on to those health packs. Occasionally you'll find one on an enemy. I think this is the tightest game for healing I've ever seen. I'm walking around with my team at 60% health because I can only heal one of them and I don't want to waste it. Tense.
I haven't even tried to take on one of the four bosses. I was creeping around the non-boss sectors trying to build up my team, but we got wiped. Noise counts. When you use grenades or shotguns, other enemies start showing up. If they have range weapons you could be in for a world of hurt.
Some great scenes:
Chucking a boulder at a skeleton and having him shatter over ten meters of space.
Guy's sniping at me from a house. Windows are too narrow to retaliate. Throw a grenade onto the roof, roof collapses and kills him.
Mobster in watchtower shooting at us, send my heavy in to take out one of the struts. Damn, it still stands on one strut! Still time to take out second strut. Tower falls over my guy, Buster Keaton style with him luckily standing in a gap.
Exploring a castle, I finally come to the throne room in the middle. Three guys. My heavy clubs a guy into a stone support beam (this was intentional). Beam shatters, enemy killed instantly. Other two guys throw down their weapons. "I surrender!"
pros
the game is straight up awesome
deeply satisfying turn-based combat
nice physics
much variety of enemies and environments
REAL CHALLENGE!
variety of enemy levels: sometimes they'll be stronger, sometimes they're much weaker
cons
enemies regularly get caught in their own area effect attacks (ie. Grenadier dropping a grenade at his feet to take out your melee guy right on top of him), OTOH their suicide tactics present an extra challenge

Quite a unique experience, and a very entreratining $17 (CAD) title. Hoping to see a little more variety in landscape generation, and a tutorial to explain all the camera controls better beforehand.
Even though I hate turn-based strategy games (because I generally suck at them), I love this one, and it is definately worth the money.

Being a HUGE Sonic fan, this is probably my number one favorite Sonics. Even over Sonic the Hedgehog 2.

The old Sonic titles on the Genesis are a staple of my childhood.  Growing up in a Nintendo household, it is the one franchise that made me want Sega's console.  Years later, when Sonic failed to find his place in 3D environments like his rival Mario, followed by a string of gimmicky garbage, I had all but given up on the hedgehog.  Fast forward to 2010 where my son, a newly indoctrinated Sonic fan due to the Sonic X DVDs his aunt bought him had persuaded me to buy him Sonic Colors on the Wii.  As I watched him play, I was fascinated my the new formula Sonic Team had applyed to this game.  A hybrid of 3D high speed reflex-based platforming and 2D precision platforming.  Sonic had finally found a home in the modern era of gaming.  Sonic Team has refined that formula to near perfection for my son's generation and was kind enough to painstakingly replicated the retro style of Sonic games of the past for my generation.  The end result is Sonic Generations, a Sonic game for all generations.

I will be the first to admit I am not the most "hardcore" gamer on the planet. Some may even call me a b***h, and I'm totally fine with that. This all means that when games become super hard I generally tend to turn them off and do something that doesn't make me want to smash my face into a concrete slab. This game however, is incrediably rewarding and keeps me drawn in. I have unlocked all the tracks in both sections of the game (Trials HD, and Evolution). I in no way would ever concider myself a "good" trials player. Look up videos of folks pulling off Extreme traks with 0 faults, and you will know what god looks like. The reason that this game doesn't get frustrating, is the amazing physics system. I have never once felt like the game cheated me out of landing a partifuclar obstacle. Everytime I fail I know it is my own fault and the only thing standing between me and the finsih line is skill, not luck. This brings me back again again and again. If I have 20 minutes before I head to class to play a game, this is almost always what I chose. I try my hardest to get a gold medal on whatever track I chose. If I suceed, I feel like like the worlds biggest bad a** all day. If I fail, I'm no frustrated, and all day I'm thinking about what I need to do different to reach my objective.
I love the fact that the online multiplayer allows you to use whatever bike and ride on whatever track you want (irregardless of weather or not you have unlocked that content in the single player.) This provided hours of enjoyment as me and my bestfriend tackled Extreme tracks knowing damn well we barely had the skill for Medium tracks. This system actually improved our skill quite rapidly and I'm all for it. I wish more games would allow players to access all content from the get go.
I've never written a review before, so excuse me if this was all rambling, but this has become one of my favorite games of all time and so I felt it was fitting to share my opinion!

Man, a little surprised at how much I ended up liking this one. It's a bit awkward to play at first because the developers wanted to take advantage of ALL THE BUTTONS, and the control scheme is maybe a bit of a convoluted mess, but muscle memory builds up the more you play it, I guess. I played on keyboard and I dunno if it'd be any easier on controller but I don't have one.
The game really emphasises speed and I really appreciate that because the mechanics are certainly designed for it; some of the levels in this game are kind of insane in how precise you have to be at the speed you're going, especially the later ones and pretty much all of the expansion levels. But it feels really damn good to nail the levels and get that perfect rating, even if it's ridiculously hard on a good number of levels; one of the hardest challenges I've faced in a while really, but the fact that I stuck with it only really hows how enjoyable the game is to play.
I do have a few issues with the game, though; the telepod throw is just a bad mechanic, first of all. It's awkward to aim and always breaks the pace of the game because you have to stop and try to wrestle with the controls to aim it and it's just aaaawkward. I also don't really like how the pickup suction works; it feels to me like once you start pulling it in you should already have it, but it's very easy to lose pickups by outrunning the suction and with how strict the requirements are for perfect, literally missing a single pickup is an automatic failure, which can be... a bit frustrating, yeah. Also don't like a few enemy types, especially the vokh guards when they start having waaayyy too much health. And there's a handful of levels that are far too long for their own good; it gets really stressful playing these long levels when they're 4, 5, 6, heck even 7 minutes long. There's not a ton of marathon levels thankfully but I'd prefer having none at all.
The game also looks pretty dang great visually and there's never any graphical confusion, everything stands out where it needs to. The soundtrack is... okay, but gets a bit old fast. The story's okay but a bit throwaway, but it's pretty clearly not the point so whatever.
This is definitely a game I can see myself replaying in the future and one of the better platformers on steam once you get past the initial awkwardness. Even considering picking up Velocity Ultra now since the shmup parts of this are plenty clever on their own. So yeah. Good game with a few roadbumps but on the whole pretty strong regardless.

Velocity 2x is the type of game you want to play on it.
If you want to see all the levels, it can be done with a small amount of effort. There's very little "challenge" to completing a level if you can use a controller.  If you die, the game is very forgiving.  You can't "lose" and you respawn and take another crack at it.  In fact anything you've already done including shooting an enemy, will be remembered, so you can plink away if you must (mostly on bosses).    If you miss an item and it goes off the screen, the game will (eventually) give you an ability to restore to any warp point you put down.  This includes the start of the level, which is always available.
So yeah... you can explore this game at your pace.
However if you want a REAL challenge. You can try to "perfect" levels.  To do that you need to collect all the friendly items, fly through the levels, run through a platforming level (usually), collect all the crystals, and get a perfect score (Which means destroy everything you can on most levels) and do it in a unforgiving time.  You have a small amount of extra time, but after the first few levels, this window is quite tight.  I believe I gave up around level 5.  It's possible to do mind you, but will take multiple play throughs of levels, and the last 10 levels might be near impossible to do so with out maps and fully thought out strategies.
However that level of perfection isn't required, if you want just an interesting shooter/platforming game, Velocity 2x is that.  If you want to prove you're the very best, Velocity 2x will give you that chance.  This is a game that found a way to be accessible but still contain a challenge for those players that want to excel.
The controls are tight enough to not become a frustration to the player, and this version appears to come with all the DLC which is a nice addition.   The graphics and gameplay are fun, and overall I'm more than happy to play this game.  I might return to try to get better, but I played all the levels and enjoyed them, I don't think I'll have the skills to get the perfect for every level.
The only thing to note is this is not like Megaman, or Castlevania, or Metroid.  Do not expect a adventure game.  This game is more like Super meat boy in progression, though no where near that challenge.
20 bucks might be a bit much for this game, but if you can get it for 10 it's worth the cash, and it is a fun game.   I'd recommend it.

I really wanted to love this game. The problem is, it's 2016 and it doesn't have the kind of controller mapping support you'd find in a 1990's game. The controller is hardcoded to one input layout.
That on its own wouldn't be so bad, but the running sections of the game require you to switch from face buttons to right analogue stick constantly. See, 360 shooting requires the right analogue stick. The face buttons each do very important things, like jump and teleport. The human thumb can't do both at the same time.
But it doesn't end there. The game rewards you for going fast, and sprinting is bound to both R buttons. The game doesn't let you sprint and 360 shoot at the same time; you start shooting, you stop sprinting. So why is the controller hardcoded to allow the player's hand to sprint and 360 shoot at the same time? Why didn't the devs move the critical face buttons to the shoulder buttons, and move sprint to a face button?
Devs, if you're going to make games like it's the Stone Age of Gaming, at least make the controls work with the human hand so we don't want to change the controls constantly as we play your game. You've ruined an otherwise great game by both being lazy input Nazis and chosing a One True Controller Layout that forces you to use a claw grip like Gollum. Do you want your players to develop mutant Gollum hands? Do you? Because that's what you did.

If you've played either of the other recent Shadowrun games from Harebrained Studios, then you basically know what to expect with this title. I can thoroughly recommend it to previous players, although I would say that, personally, I feel Dragonfall was the better game. And to interested parties who have never experienced a Shadowrun game before, I would say to go and try Dragonfall before trying Hong Kong: while I really enjoyed Hong Kong, I think a new player would get much more out of Dragonfall.
Shadowrun: Hong Kong plays like a rather standard tactical RPG. You create a main character, load him up with whatever stats you want (I prefer a gun-toting Bear Shaman, who can place barriers as personal cover to snipe from long distances, Haste himself to shoot up to two times more often per round, and use the Bear totem for the game's only AoE heal). You have a group of pre-determined party members, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. In addition, each mission provides you with a list of alternate Shadowrunners you can take instead of your standard party members, although why you would do this remains a mystery to me.
Said party members, I feel, are one of the ways Hong Kong falls flat compared to Dragonfall. Granted, several of Dragonfall's party members didn't have fleshed out stories until the Director's Cut update, but since it DOES have a Director's Cut update, that's what I have to compare Hong Kong to, and most of HK's party isn't as interesting comparatively. Duncan's story is hamstrung by the fact that it has to be tied into the main character's backstory; he doesn't have a defined history, you make up half of it as you go along, and that prevents him from being an interesting character in his own right. Gobbet's history is really only barely touched upon, and her personal mission, if you can refer to it as such, doesn't have much emotional weight (certainly not as much emotional weight as Glory's personal mission, and the comparison has to be made because of how similar the two are). is0bel is the most disappointing in this regard. Out of the entire cast she had the most potential to have an emotional effect on the player, but it's just squandered. Her personal mission happens before her storyline really even starts, killing any possibility of true connection or closure. Racter doesn't even really have his own mission, he simply requests to tag along on mission you already have, and his personal connection to the mission is barely there at all.
The story, however, makes up for the characters in many ways. The change in location to Hong Kong is welcome, given that both prior games had decidedly Western locations and aesthetics. Hong Kong brings with it a new subject in the form of qi, the lifeforce that drives much of Hong Kong's magic and forms a focal point for both the main story and several of the side missions. I was a little disappointed with how similar Heoi, the main city, was to the hub in Dragonfall. However, several of the characters are great. I especially liked Ambrose and Crafty Xu (fans of the series may be interested to note that Aljernon is NOT the proprietor of the magic shop in this title; I was never really a fan and much prefer Crafty Xu, personally). The main story fades into the background for large sections of the game while you run various jobs, which I felt was a little strange. Dragonfall set up the goal very early on, and every side job was a means to that end; while the missions were all disconnected, you knew why you were doing them and they all served a definite purpose to the main goal. In HK, you're basically just Shadowrunning because you have no other choice, and the missions you take have almost no bearing in any situation on the main story or your party's situation. And the ending is a major letdown, too.
Luckily, the gameplay is as good as ever, for the most part. There are tons of dialogue options available to the player (although this comes with its own negative, which I'll get into later), giving you the option to avoid several fights, if that's your prerogative. Many problems the game presents have several solutions; combat is always one of them, and often times it is a requirement, but not always. The difficulty curve is fair, keeping things entertaining with some level of difficulty, until about 75% of the way through the game where your party will simply power through everything if you've built it right. This is especially evident for the final boss fights, which were almost criminally easy.
However, the same targeting issues I've had with the series since Shadowrun Returns still haven't been fixed. Due to the game's isometric camera, it can be infuriatingly difficult at times to select the tile you're looking for. If the tile you want to move to is behind a crate and another character, you can spend a lot of time waving your mouse around trying to get the selector to acknowledge the tile and not the cover (or character) in front of it. I had really expected this to be fixed somehow by the third game. This wouldn't be as aggravating if the game had some way to reverse a command, but once your character moves you're stuck with whatever you've done; accidentally command your character to attack an enemy, when all you really wanted to do was move to the tile behind him, and you might find yourself unfairly down a Shadowrunner.
Another problem endemic to the series are the dialogue options. Earlier on I praised the game for giving you so many, but now I have to raise a gripe that I had with Returns and Dragonfall: the main character, in order to experience much of the dialog, is basically forced into leveling Charisma in order to get Etiquettes. Why is my main character FORCED into having Security etiquette if I want to use this speech option even though I have Duncan in the party? He's an ex-Lone Star, which is basically the police force; why can HE not bring up this rather obvious point? Why do I have to be the one to do it? Gobbett spends half of the game lording over you the fact that she's been Shadowrunning for years and you're a newbie; why do I have to choose this Shadowrunner Etiquette dialogue option while she's in the party? It's mind-boggling. Additionally, giving party members Etiquettes would add another layer of complexity into forming a party.
My next gripe is with the new decking mechanics. I understand why there was a call for a new format; decking in previous games was basically the exact same gameplay as the standard tactical combat (hide behind cover and shoot at enemies), and it shouldnt be. It should be different, and I applaud the decision and effort to shake it up. However, I feel the new mechanics are even worse. Decking is now, in large part, a stealth section; the decker moves around attempting to avoid entering the LoS of enemies; if one spots you, you enter combat, and if you're in combat long enough you set of a system alert (I'm simplifying it a little, but that's the gist). However, the game is NOT set up for stealth sections. They simply don't feel right. There's one "stealth" section in one side mission, and that is redeemed (SLIGHTLY) by the fact that you can enter turn-based mode and therefore have more control over character movement and cover; this option is missing while decking, and this combined with the floaty movement end up causing you to enter combat far more often than you probably should. I was so annoyed with the new decking mechanics that I simply avoided decking where possible.
I'll reiterate what I said in the opening: I really enjoyed HK. I enjoyed Dragonfall more, and I would point interested players to play that title first, but this is certainly a great game and, despite my gripes, I have no qualms recommending it.

One Way Heroics is a AMAZING RPG!
While theres not much o a story, One Way Heroics still is great in another aspects, from the fact that each level is randomly generated which gives you hard deciscions you have to make  in a way of a Telltale game. You start off talking to the Queen after creating your character, now first off playing it, there are instructions on how to control, but theres still no sense of starting & learning to make your way, it just drops you in without much to know, which is quite a minus for starting out. But prior to my last sentence, once you learn, it gets better, a lot better. After you learning the controls, first thing i did was die, why was that? i pondered for the few seconds til i made another game, then i understood, the game keeps scrolling to the right, everytime you do something, & it only stops when you use an ability which makes it stop for 3 turns, which unless you are fighting, or as it suggest when to use it, breaking through walls for which i will cover later, its not always that useful, less a emergency. (it also increases damage during this period)
As i said before, it scrolls constantly every turn, & thus this is were the hard choices come in. Your inventory weight is limited, meaning you can only carry so much, & at the start its not that big of an inventory, its allright, but you need to increase it early on by giving up your Levels at a goddess statue in a dungeon, there are several statues, but not in all dungeons, this idea right here is also very interesting, also at the statue you can increase specific skills (Strength, Intelligence, Agility Etc.), which once again, is very interesting & cool. But then theres "Where to go", as you roam there are towns you can pass by which of course you can buy equipment at, & at the same time, in towns (where scrolling does not stop, still gotta keep moving) & outside of towns, there a items you can find, there are a lotta good items you can get, but the problem where in lies with inventory space, if you don't have enough, then ya can't carry, or ya gotta trade it for something else. With limited amount of moves it can be hard to get through, or get to towns & dungeons, which can have major items, but depending on your previous moves, you may not be able to get through, but alas, there is hope. Breaking walls, literally you can beak through while hopped on coolade & 'splore dem dungeons or to get through the towns. (sorry you can't actually be hopped up on coolade) the last thing to mention, past all the things i said, this game can be long, & i mean long, do not expect a short game, the goal is to get to a certain distance & fight a appearing boss, but the distance to get to the boss, can be long, because it is randomized, & even if its at like, 250 distance, getting through 200 is long enough, & it doesn't end there, everytime you start a new quest is randomized, making it different everytime, thus far longer! You either have the decision to play a random generated world, on normal, or hard (Normals hard & long enough) or there are also different modes to playthrough, which i haven't even covered cause of the main game, damn its long!
One Way Heroics, is a constantly moving, tough decision making, level sacraficing, long tough RPG, & if you like those kind of games, its the right kind for you.
But alas here are the plus & minuses of it.
PLUSES
+Long, with several different modes & the normal game is randomly generated.
+Challenging, its really tough with the screen scrolling, & random hard enemys can pop up to kill ya instantly if your not prepared.
+Its an RPG, cmon, whoz dusn' like rpgs.
+Classes & traits, several different classes & traits to choose from & unlock as you slowly play through.
+Randomly Generated Worlds
+Several other different modes besides the story to play through
+Records Your Run, after making a run, it records the entire thing, which you can save & show others.
+A Universal Inventory, basically if yur current character dies, but you found such a cool item & ya wanna keep it, you can unlock universal inventory spaces, which can hold items for your next character.
MINUS
-Really doesn't teach you how to play, or whats happening so much at the beggining
-Customization, while its not a big deal, there would be a bit more if you could customize your character besides there being just a gender & class choice.

I absolutely love this game. I am enamoured by it, addicted to it, and appalled by it. I'm conflicted, because it is incredibly fun and incredibly flawed. It's fast-paced 1-on-1 sword fighting action that's neither realistic nor fantastical.
Before I say anything else, I will preface with this: you are buying into Early Access. This review is written pre-1.0 release. The game is inherently unfinished and has issues. I'm certain these will be addressed sooner or later.
Blade Symphony is a 3D directional fighter, taking cues from Soul Calibur, Jedi Knight Academy and GunZ. I've been told it's "like GunZ, without the guns." The (currently) four fighters have their own movesets and synergies with weapon types. It's up to the player to figure out the various stance chains (between Fast, Balanced, and Heavy), how to space them, and how to time them. Players will link these moves together, stabbing, slashing and bashing each other until one fighter loses. That's as simple as it gets.
If you're looking for a description of basic game mechanics, there are other reviews for that.
What I'm primarily writing about is where the game simultaneously fails and succeeds: its unintentional systems. These buried systems that new players will not be introduced to, and be simultaneously destroyed by, are my favourite and least favourite part of Blade Symphony. These tricks are similar to how K-Styling came to be in GunZ—happy accidents that came about as a flaw in the mechanics. Air canceling, animation canceling and gliding are some of the tricks and mechanic abuses that have become what is the current meta of "advanced play" in Blade Symphony. While many lower ranked players will play it straight, advanced players will frequently dominate arenas against players that do not know how to leverage these unintentional mechanics. Many newcomers will not have the patience to learn how to play against or adopt these strategies and will be put off. At the same time, it adds options and extra layers to a game that would otherwise be fairly simple.
This is where I'm conflicted. I love the community teaching aspect. I feel accomplished knowing how to beat cheese strategies, how to beat spam, and how to execute these exploits. At the same time, is it a good thing that a game relies on the crutches of unintentional design to succeed? Maybe. Maybe not.
I'm in love with the game. You might hate it. I support this game to the fullest, but be wary of what you're getting into. Blade Symphony is one of the best $15 I've spent in a while. It might be your worst.
All I know is that my adrenaline is pumping and I am having one hell of a time.

An improvement upon the already terrific original game in basically every way. Gaijin ditched the retro pixel-art look that had graced all their previous games in favor of improved, more modern visuals. While the old style definitely had some charm to it, the change is a very welcome one. The various backdrops are just beautiful. I've seen some people mention that the new art style can be too distracting, but so far it hasn't affected me negatively at all. The chiptune soundtrack is as catchy as ever and the game controls just perfectly; very responsive and accurate which makes getting into a good groove such a joy. I also like how Runner2 keeps the same basic rhythm-based gameplay from the original in tact while adding things like branching paths, cutscenes reminiscent of an old 50s serial, and a bunch of collectables to entice you to replay levels. It really does feel more like a full-featured game than the original.
There's also the addition of a checkpoint system and different difficulties to make the game more accessible to the novice/casual crowd. As someone who enjoyed the unrelenting nature of the original, I'm alright with this. Veterans can skip checkpoints entirely in favor of bonus points and bump the difficulty up from the onset to get the best challenge. It's a smart move by the developers and a win-win for everyone.
If you liked the original Bit.trip Runner, Runner2 is more of the same and then some. It's exactly what you'd want out of a sequel: It keeps the established gameplay in place while making some necessary and welcome improvements along the way. Even if you didn't like the original because of its difficulty, the more accessible nature could put Runner2 right up your alley. Absolutely recommended.
