Did you play BIT.TRIP RUNNER and think "Wow, this is really difficult. I hope the sequel is easier than this"? Conversely, did you play BIT.TRIP RUNNER and think "This is too easy. Please give me harder levels"? If you fell into either of these categories, then BIT.TRIP Runner2 is the game for you. If not, you probably didn't play BIT.TRIP RUNNER and you are missing out on a lot. You're probably wondering "But wait! How can a game be both easier and harder than its predecessor?" Good question. 10 points for you. We'll get to that later though. The original BTR was a 2D-8-bit-side-scrolling-obstacle-adventure game which incorporated rhythm-based platforming. Obscenely challenging, the game from Gaijin was played by a relatively small audience, but almost universally appreciated by its players. Cut to 2013, and its successor is released, in a more beautiful, elegant and dynamic form; Bit Trip Runner 2 (or BIT.TRIP Presents... Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien).
On the surface, a game is, basically, a set of graphics, sounds and controls. The better a game can balance and sustain these elements, the better it will be, fundamentally. In all of these areas, BTR2 shines; it differentiates from the last game in the graphics sphere, upgrading to a 2.5D look with fluid motion from the characters and beautiful environments which are illustrated in a style which is similar to that of comics. All of the animations are still reminiscent of the arcade style, but have been modernized with smooth textures and motion paths (although there are still 8-bit bonus levels, likely as a tribute to the rest of the Bit.Trip universe). In terms of audio, the soundtrack is where all of the Bit.Trip games shine; in BTR2, the chiptune style of previous games has been mostly abandoned, with a huge range of acoustic and electronic instruments being used. However, the drum tracks remain in the chiptune style, which characterizes the game as one with arcade influence, but (again) modernizes it. The controls of BTR2 are largely similar to the last Runner title; however, many players claim that it is much smoother with a gamepad. Personally, I prefer a keyboard, but it does seem that gamepad support is much more optimized for BTR2 than the original BTR.
You may recall earlier, when I mentioned the fact that BTR2 is both more difficult and easy than its predecessor. This is due to a couple of core game mechanic changes which have been incorporated in the newest installation in the series; for instance, there is now a checkpoint between the "Mega" and "Ultra" stages of each level (roughly halfway), which makes the game much less forgiving of late-level mistakes (a feature that was much desired by first time players of the infamous 1-11, or "Odyssey"). Furthermore, the courses themselves appear to be slightly easier. However, there are some features which make the game much more difficult; for a start, you are required to collect every gold bar on every level to advance to the next world, which was not compulsory in BTR. Furthermore, you are granted bonus points for jumping over checkpoints, so if you wish to compete in any way against your friends list (which has an integrated leaderboard that pops up at the beginning of each level), then taking the checkpoint is a poor decision. Finally, the inclusion of dancing adds an element of time management into the game, forcing you to try to suck as many points as possible out of this small animation, but not go for a millisecond too long and force an error, and the new obstacles which require you to jump and slide at the same time require much better timing than any other obstacle in the game.
In BTR2, you play as a character named Commander Video, whose apparent skill in consistently running, jumping, sliding, blocking and punching appears to have landed him within a hastily written story which somehow incorporates excessive obstacle courses into some sort of adventure. It is a captivating, heart-wrenching story which touches on themes of accepting the outsiders; the unwanted members of society. However, you're wasting your time if you play only as Commander Video, despite his well-written backstory and emotional struggles; there are a grand total of 8 playable characters, each one more interesting and enjoyable than the last. The greatest of these characters is Unkle Dill, a green alien who has various ridiculous costumes, such as a nerd outfit and a farmers' outfit, and appears to be under the influence of an extremely broad range of depressants at all times. If there was but one reason to play this game, it is Unkle Dill alone.
There are a hugely large amount of video game styles in this world, and in a medium of media which is largely dominated by military FPS titles and random fantasy RPGs, it is absolutely refreshing to play something as different and varied as the arcade/modern rhythm hybrid that is BTR2. Despite the reskin of the characters and environments and the new soundtrack style, the game manages to stay true to the Bit.Trip franchise to an extreme level. Furthermore, the beautiful graphics and encapsulating soundtrack make the unforgiving madness of the game much less frustrating than the barebones angerfest that was Bit.Trip Runner. The bottom line is, for a petty price of $15, the game is completely worth it, even just for something to look at. If even this is out of your budget, a Steam sale or Humble Bundle is bound to come along which will give you the game for pennies. Either way, it is an absolute must-own, and is one of the most enjoyable and interesting titles that have been released recently.
9/10

NOTE: When experiencing art, and especially when talking about art, each human being simply provides a unique perspective. Therefore, there can be no such thing as an "objective review". Anyone who claims otherwise is simply lying and is purposefully being deceptive.
So with that in mind, the following is simply a description of my subjective experiences with this game. It is arranged in broad categories in order to help the reader look at what they care about in games.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DOES IT WORK / BUGS / GLITCHES
------------------------------------
I play on Linux, and the game runs excellently without bugs or glitches almost all the time.
Sometimes, however, the game causes my PC to hang and gets stuck in a loop. This bug hasn't been fixed since I bought the game a few months ago, which I think is careless on the part of the developers.
Another consistent bug I have observed is errors in Leaderboard rankings at the start of each level. They often tell me that I am offline, while I simply am not.
Other than these rare or minor problems, I find the game to be a very well polished piece of software.
GRAPHICS / VISUAL ART
-------------------------
While this game is nothing groundbreaking in terms of graphics or visual effects, it has a very unique visual art style that might be described as cartoony and wacky.
As you proceed through the game, the visual art style, especially the environment, changes to match the progression of the game's minimal storyline. Not only does this keep things interesting, it is also successful in altering mood and affects you emotionally, providing context for the game to a small extent. Similar variation in the playable character's visuals are also a nice aspect of the game, which encouraged me to unlock as many of them as I could.
One major problem I had with this game's visual art style is that I found it difficult to concentrate with so many things happening on the screen. Some objects, when destroyed, fly all over the screen blocking your view. In a game where split second reactions to what is coming next is so important, this is frustrating and often irritating. This is especially true in the last level, where the visual art style is intentially pixelated while being 3D at the same time.
AUDIO ART STYLE
-------------------
This is one of the few games where music is actually a driving force in gameplay. The music helps in pacing, in making you move forward, in having fun and especially adds to the soothing effect the game has on you overall.
STORYTELLING
----------------
This game has a very minimal storyline which is essentially a placeholder to guide the player through the levels and gives a minor sense of purpose. This game isn't about a story.
GAMEPLAY / GAME DESIGN / IS IT FUN
----------------------------------------
Overall, I think this is the game's strongest point, and intentionally so. It succeeds in making you want to play it for long amounts of time, while wanting to finish all levels and complete challenges.
This is primarily due to the surprising amount of depth in the game's level design that constantly challenges you by trying to pull you out of your comfort zones. In some levels, you can almost hear the developers laughing in glee as you try to get past a particularly unnaturely placed obstacle which makes you learn new ways to react to it.
The way the game's obstacles sync up with the music and the overall "speed" of the game makes it a very pleasant experience. I often found myself wanting to play this game when I wanted to relax. This was surprising because the gameplay is the complete opposite of "relaxed".
VALUE FOR MONEY
--------------------
The amount of entertainment this game has provided me was well worth the price. I recommend it especially if you are looking for some simple gameplay-oriented entertainment.
VERDICT
---------
If you are looking for a gameplay-focused game with good design that challenges you and provides entertainment through visuals and music, I recommend this game highly.
If you are mainly looking for a story, this game doesn't have much to offer.
If you get bored/frustrated by timing-based gameplay requiring split-second reactions to lots of obstacles, this game can be very irritating.
On the other hand, if you get obsessive about completing levels and challenges, this is a great game for you.
Please note that this game does not play well with keyboards, and you need a controller to enjoy it to full extent.

This is a fantastically made game. It's a very good entry to the BIT.TRIP series and it's also a great example of how the sequels should look like. Even though this game is more of a spin-off to the original BIT.TRIP series, but that's a small detail. One thing must be said, if you didn't enjoy the first RUNNER, do not fret, as this game's difficulty curve is much more sane. The difficulty is controllable with three settings to choose which change the amount of obstacles in levels by quite a bit, unlike its precedessor, where it only removed gold bars on easy and enforced perfection on hard.
BIT.TRIP RUNNER 2's story takes place right after RUNNER 1 as Commander Video gets zapped into a different dimension while chasing after the vile Timbletot. All of the cutscenes that expose the plot to the player are narrated by one and only Charles Martinez, the legendary voice of Mario, as such they're done quite well both visually and in terms of voice acting, though they're not the main focus of the game.
The player's objective in BIT.TRIP RUNNER 2 is to guide the ever running Commander Videothrough quite a number of levels, 70 plus 25 secret levels. You can't stop the character in place whatsoever which is part of the challenge as you have to deal with obstacles thrown at you on the fly. Asides from such prude actions like jumping and kicking you can also dance which is a neat risk-reward action as when you dance, you can't do any other actions for half a second, but every time you do it, you get points. All of the levels, asides from the secret ones, have their own leaderboard and you can compare yourself to the world's finest and your friends which is a cool feature that makes you replay the levels trying to get the highest score. There's a tiny issue with this though, as the leaderboards from all the difficulties are combined. This causes a problem as on some levels you can get a much higher score by perfecting it on the hardest of difficulties while on others it's better to just choose 'easy' and dance through most of the level as there's a nigh negligible amount of obstacles.
I mentioned gold bars earlier but there's also more collectibles to find such as + thingies that look like the core from BIT.TRIP CORE that make your mode go up. You start every level at Hyper and ascend to Mega, Super, Ultra and finally Extra. The modes change a couple of things, first of all the music changes a bit every time from getting more instruments to a very mellow and melodic state on Extra. Secondly, the character will start getting some stars going from their back finishing on a cape on Extra, as Commander Video gets a 'Rainbow' cape which doesn't have the necessary seven colors but it's pretty in its own right. The least visible change is the scoring as the modes work as a multiplier system.
The game's difficulty is done in a very good way, some levels are not linear as you get to choose if you want to go the easier or the harder path and all of the levels have a checkpoint, that you can go through to do its job of becoming your new starting point when you slip up or you can jump over to get a hefty score bonus but at the risk of starting the level all over again if the player makes a mistake. The secret levels are much better done in terms of difficulty than in RUNNER 1 as they never use patterns that are either first shown in later levels or just plain don't appear outside of a singular secret level. Every single one of them tests what you should have learned by playing the regular game. Not to mention you have three tries as opposed to one and you can go back to it from the world map at any time.
The worlds are littered with gold bars which allow you to access some of the harder levels and possibly unlock Commander Video's friends or costumes. They don't bring any change to the gameplay, but they're there to enjoy the levels. Like I mentioned before, some of the levels are totally skippable as you only have to go down a path that's shown to you on the world's map. Every world has its own boss too, which are quite cleverly done as they never change the rules of the game but bring their ways of hindering your progress.
The graphics are quite stylish and very well done, although I can see why someone would just avoid the game due to its uniqueness. The backgrounds with their little details, the little faces on the stop signs which you have to kick, RUNNER 2' numerous details are quite amazing to look at if a bit hard considering the nature of the game, some of the details you might be able to see only by looking up videos from the game, as BIT.TRIP RUNNER 2 doesn't have a replay system. Some might complain about the animations as Commander Video instantly goes from running to sliding or kicking but I assume it's done in that way as to not confuse when you're in the necessary state to overcome the rapidly incoming obstacle. The secret levels themselves are done in a 16-bit style including the Commander Video that's known from the earlier games in the BIT.TRIP series.
The music is fantastic in this game which is not a surprise considering it's a BIT.TRIP game although it might get a bit repetitive to some people as there are two tracks per world that the game switches between so on 1-1 you'll get Track A, 1-2 gives you Track B and then Track A makes its return in 1-3, and so on. This is alleviated through the mode changes as you get more meat out of one track. The secret levels get their own tracks per world which are made in a retro way, just like their graphics.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game to the point where I would buy any DLC with new levels the moment it came out as I seriously would want more. Seriously though, if you're scared of this game because of RUNNER 1, try it out at someone else's place as the game unfortunately doesn't have a demo that I'm aware of.

LISA is a dark game.  It is a violent and perverted game.  It is a game that made me FEEL.
Very self-aware, LISA first appears to be an average rpg set in the post apocalypse with an above-average sense of humor.  As the game progresses, the humor gets darker and sometimes vanishes completely as you witness and are forced to partake in increasingly heinous actions.  With most games, I think I would be turned off by this.  With LISA, everything is important.  Everything is a little breadcrumb of world building.  Similar to Dark Souls, there is a pervasive mystery as to why the world is the way it is and you the player must make inferences based on items, npc locations etc.
The game is absolutely riddled with easter eggs and fun/worthwhile side missions.  There are a couple parts that can be a little frustrating but I think they are balanced by the sense of atmosphere they lend themselves to.  It all comes together in the end where LISA is slightly (thankfully) a bit more explicit that Dark Souls.
I highly recommend the DLC for 2 reasons: it fully completes the picture and it actually plays like a fairly different game.  Where the core game has a fairly fluid part structure and has as strong sense of exploration, the DLC feels a bit more like a survival and resource management type while having a new combat mechanic that shakes things up nicely.
On a final note, the soundtrack to this game...I can’t stop listening to it.  Not only have most of the songs become infused with the emotion from the game, they are good in their own right (and there are a couple easter eggs for the eagle-eyed consumer).  I cannot recommend this game enough but have the massive caveat that many people won’t be able to stomach many of the darker moments.
LISA, thank you for being one of those pieces of art that has indelibly imprinted itself on me in one of those ways that feels like it will influence me as a person.

The only thing this game has going for it is its story. The writing is actually pretty well done. It can successfully make you feel uneasy, scared, sad, and any other number of emotions. The dark humor is also well-written (for the most part).
Unfortunately, the good writing of the game are muddled with terrible, TERRIBLE design choices from a mechanics perspective. In my opinion, these aren't just mechanics that could be done better or aren't great; they are actively detrimental to the experience. The game is so far up its own♥♥♥♥♥♥in respects to the dynamic, unpredictable random events. When sleeping at a campfire (how you restore HP and SP in the game), various random events can happen. At first, these are harmless and even give the unnerving feeling that you are never quite safe in the game. One of the first instances of these campfire events comes when you wake up, and there is an insane man standing over you, staring at you. While this idea starts off pretty neat, it eventually degrades into pure RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ttery. I'll wake up at the campfire only to see that one of my party members has abandoned me (never to return), or has been captured by a group of hoodlums. Rather than recruit a new party member and spending an hour leveling him up, or going to retrieve him from the hoodlum base, it's a hell of a lot easier to just reload to the last checkpoint (sometimes a 10 minute loss) and try my luck with the terrible campfire roulette again. These unforgiving and time-wasting perma-loss mechanics also appear in the form of a "death" status effect (in which the party member is dead forever). This isn't "challenging", it's an incentive to reload your save and infuriate you further. Now I get this is supposed to be done to be a reflection of the game world and how unrelenting it is, but it's ♥♥♥♥ing tedious.
Traveling in this game is done from a 2-D, platformer-esque perspective. In reality, there's nothing platformer about it. You hold right or left and occasionally climb ropes the developer put there to break up the monotony. That's all there is. Now, I would be alright with this if there was some interesting music or setpieces to hold my attention while I hold the right arrow key. But there isn't. Environments aren't varied; tiles are reused with nothing more than a simple pallette swap or different shading. The music is either extremely repetitive (I'm talking what sounds to be 20 second loops), extremely grating on the ears, or nonexistent. So, the traveling in between points of interest is boring as♥♥♥♥♥♥ How does the developer account for this? Why, he makes it so that if you walk off the edge of a cliff, it's an instant game over! So just when my eyes are glazing over because I haven't done anything that can be considered a part of a game in over 15 minutes, a curveball is thrown my way when the platform I've been walking on drops off suddenly and I fall off. Nice.
As far as the battle system is concerned, it's Earthbound. Not bad, but nothing to write home about. You usually end up spamming the most powerful attack and/or one particular attack that causes tripping.
The game is also terrible at directing the player. The progression structure makes you go to three main areas, which is just a mountain composed of a lot of doors or crevices you enter (usually around 8). Which of these doors or crevices progress the story and which ones are setups for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ "ha ha, I made you waste 10 minutes of your time" jokes, you ask? The answer is: there's no way to know. You just try all the doors and after a couple of dead ends, you get your answer.
After my 20th time falling off a cliff and getting a game over, I just looked up the ending on youtube. It's a shame the rest of the game is so bad, because the story and ending are well done.

Since the update to the Extended Edition I noticed this:

Cons:

Old review:
As  a lover of both SR:R and SR:Dragonfall I simply refuse to recommend this piece of unfinished, glued-together, atrocities.
What is the reason?
Pros: Aesthetically pleasing, atmosphere is okay-ish, but lacking compared to either installment of the series. Most of the setting seems to consist of empty space, lots of running around from A to B, npcs lack that certain something in this game that made you feel for them (compassion, anger, disgust, etc.) in the other installments of HBS's shadowrun campaigns.
Some interesting characters, but far too few compared to Dragonfall.
Cool new Cyberware, new skills, awesome new spells, pretty sick unique weapons and for all the adept lovers out there: weapon foci and of course, revamped matrix, wow, am I tuned for this!
That's it!
Cons:
Almost everything.
Bugs over bugs, starting with missing equipment of followers (that you had to unlock via skillpoints!), over vanishing equipment (be it spells, weapons, or support items) up to mission breaking bugs.
Dialogues are ridiculously slow paced, arduous and options are rare and even if you find options, don't bother to try out different ones, as 90% of them will merit the same outcome, especially fun in the few final missions. Oh, and what is more, one cannot substitute the attributes of their followers in 50% of all cases. You need strength 5 for something? One of your team has it... Too bad, that does not count, joke's on you, logic! Obviously a character needs to be the leader to bash in a damn bookshelf. And whereas in the other shadowrun adventures of HBS it was perfectly normal to be able to reach an outcome via different means (skills, attributes, dialogue options, etiquettes, etc.) you will find in this piece of "art" you often enough can do stuff only if you have exactly ONE skill/attribute and that half of the options is (as aforementioned) simply placebo. Search the same shelf with the [INT 3: highlighted option], too bad, nothing special. Go medieval on it with STR 5, wow, secret tunnel, who would have guessed?
Combat system: where to start? Try hitting people with 50-65% and you will hit them significantly more often, as your team misses more often, the higher the chances to hit get. Half of your support spells does not do anything, if your shaman uses "Aim" to boost your teammember's accuracy, tadaaa, nothing changes.
Detail and Graphics: Nice, really.
Items/Gear: Half the stuff is linked wrongly or has no effect, e.g. Brain implant "NEXT" should give INT+1; Decking+1, guess what it does? Nothing.  Saeder Krupp Skillwires should give Quickness+1 AND Ranged Combat +1. You get the Quickness, Ranged Combat, however, seems to be a wrong label. Wow, am I glad I spent all my money on alpha-level cyberware which does nothing and/or less as is stated in the only game of the series in which you will find yourself chronically underpaid.
Magic: Even a maxed out mage (WP and Spellcasting, yes, been there, done that) sucks hard in terms of hitchances. Shamans? HAHAHA, that was a good one. Why? Spirits (your bread and butter signature abilities) which can be summoned from your surroundings will hardly EVER have a chance to hit greater than 55% to 65% with their spells. The ones you can summon via consumable (high-level!!!) charms rock the ground, however, as this game keeps you on edge in terms of what you can afford, I personally believe it is a real atrocity to ask the player to build a character around consumables, especially one as interesting as the shaman!
Decking: Again, you need to be a decker, as Is0bel (your "default" decker) has such ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ skills and programmes, that you are going to snuff it, pretty much 8/10 times you enter a room that has any IC higher than just trackers. The chances to hit suck even more in the matrix than in meatspace combat, you will find your decker missing ~40% of the time when the game tells you that you actually have a 99% (!) chance to hit. Neat. Oh, I almost forgot that in some missions, the option to jack into certain jack-points is MISSING if you do not have Is0bel on your team. Whiskey Tango Foxtrot!
Overall: They tried to re-create SR:Dragonfall and ended up gutting the series. This game has so many engine, item and mission bugs, I refuse to believe this is due to any other reason than blatant lazyness as the other two installments of this series are fine and even breathtakingly well done. Long story short, I backed this game on Kickstarter and got a copy, way cheaper than any of you buying it over steam, and I would refund this game immediately if I had not got it over the kickstarter campaign. Be smart, don't start, if you refuse to listen, caveat emptor!
What is left to say?
Hope; hope strongly that after some time, given the strong enthusiasm we saw so far from HBS, this game will also have a final "Director's Cut" version like SR:Dragonfall that makes this game awesome, as it should be and that proves me wrong when I say "Meh, this one stinks.".

Road to Ballhalla is a graphically polished ball rolling game using the Unreal 4 Engine. It combines colourful visuals with time based movement using music.
Pacing is done via the use of in game text giving plentiful tips and clues, as well as the snide remark breaking the 4th wall - the tone of which is a little grating, non politically correct and sometimes mildly insulting, and is a far cry from the serene and explorative ball rollers like Ballance, Marble Blast and Spectraball.
There is no major storyline, you are just shown new things like lasers and different coloured orbs and blocks, how to get past them and move onto more new things. As you progress you can unlock different colour balls and trails, but these are rather unimaginative. The completion objective is additive such that you cannot complete a level one time without falling, and another time just collect all the orbs, but you must do both together on one try to get the max number of yellow squares for the maximum of 8, nowhere is this explained and I found myself completing a level several times before I understood how it worked.
The soundtrack fits in with each level and is dynamic, different types of tone change as you move through. It seems to be all at the same tempo and does not change very much whether you are going through a fast or slow section or through the game. This makes it seem repetitive and almost forgettable, unlike the shatter soundtrack, which is also similar with constant tempo but done extremely well. Collecting orbs makes light tones too but not really in a way that adds to the overall soundtrack, in which it potentially could have done.
Damage indication is shown via a number in the bottom left, and if you are closer to 0 then there will be some audible warning too and slight red borders. It could have been done a better way in my opinion, e.g. a long bar or multiple blocks/'hearts' would be a better visual as you aren't really concentrating to much on it.
Level design has some experimentation with different coloured blocks, bullets, lasers, balls, level colours, timing, perspective and overall there is a good mixture of originality and uniqueness in level design. The levels can be fairly challenging but not overly so, although it could be frustrating for those who are not very good at these types of games. There isn't really much of a puzzle element - the hardest part may be pushing multiple buttons with timers in a certain order, or collecting blue orbs to unlock blue squares ala chips challenge. Other than that is just collecting and avoiding things whilst moving and jumping, no objects to push for example. Apart from the jumping, the game is almost entirely on a 2d plane.
What sets this game apart from others is the use of text, it can be seen also in the settings and menus as well as in game. It seems like the developer had far too much time to think of the amount of ways to be creative in the use of text as a means of driving the narrative. The personality is conflicting and bipolar, sometimes leading you straight into a trap, other times it will give you the obvious and only solution before you really had a chance to look at it, sometimes there will be cheap put downs. Mildly funny at first, but gets tiresome quickly. There are even different hints whether you are using a controller or keyboard. Unfortunately, occasionally I found it just too overwhelming, and I wish there was a way to turn it off. For example, one way the tips go overboard is in telling you what to do even though it is obvious, at times it should take you a few seconds to figure out but the text is already there on the screen telling you it might be a good idea to e.g. rotate your controller or monitor.
This breaks any chance of a puzzle element being a core part of the game, you are hand held throughout with annoying and witty remarks, which are completely unnecessary. It's like you're doing a sudoku puzzle, and the person next to you says: "by the way that number there is a 4, that number there is a 9, and you do know all the 3x3 boxes should include all the numbers 1-9, right?". It reduces the fun of solving it for yourself. Maybe they could have added a hint system where you only see these texts after pressing a button or over x tries or something.
As far as content is concerned the main game can be completed in 2 hours, and there is plenty of additional content, workshop integration, and level editor, so no complaints there.
Overall, probably worth trying if you're into these sorts of ball rolling games and have a couple hours spare, and a definitely recommend it at the nominal price of under a dollar in the first tier of the current Humble Bundle. However at the RRP of $15, I wouldn't recommend it as the experience is spoilt by the overzealous use and choice of text.

First couple of Saints Row game are quite dark that's full of blood, power and backstabbing fun. They are completly gangster game about turf war and revenge. Then come the third game that saints became celebrity and even though it's still turf war it's much less character death and more goofy fun.
In the third game there is a small part that if you have the right dlc you gain some super powers and that was a lot of fun.
Well guess what.. Super power goes though out this entire fourth game and this gangster game became a super hero game as you play the president of USA vs aliens.
Personally I don't have any problem of the game type transition as turf control mini-games are still the main focus of the game but a lot of negative review were from those changes.
Honestly.. Good enough graphics, Real Life event quotes everywhere, easter eggs everywhere, a throng of collection items, cleaverly designed minigame still make this game one that I have enjoyed very much.
Music effect are always strong point of saints row games and rock'n'roll are super enjoyable.
Bugs has always been a problem of saints row games and I ran into a few of them that abruptly froze the game in explosion animation that force me to restart the game. Luckly there is usually a pretty recent auto-save that could help me.
Achivements are tough as the collection and getting gold medal for every minigame is quite hard. Strangly I enjoy those minigame enough that I don't mind keep on trying. If you get this game and have problem of getting gold for some of the mini-game. Come back to it later after you upgrade your gun or upgrade your superpowers. It makes a lot difference.
Quite a few DLC related achivements too so hunters make sure you got them before starting to play this game.
8.5/10 for a very enjoyable wild ride. Not too heavy on the story but hey you got super powers!! (Death from Above!)

This game is outstanding and delivers the expected result with flying colors.  Be forewarned that this awesomeness comes with a fair bit of challenge and the game will not coddle you.  Every action you take has potential consequences and the permadeath of your characters means that one misstep could literally wipe you out.  This is not a bad thing (it's actually a good part of what makes the game so fun and engaging), but it's something you should be ready for.
Things to enjoy about this game:
* Procedurally generated content means no two games will ever be exactly the same
* Outstanding and highly challenging tactical combat
* Fully destructible environments present limitless tactical opportunities and exciting challenges
* Meaningful skills and character progression
* Very well-balanced gameplay
I would highly recommend this to anyone interested in challenging tactical combat simulations.  As cute as the graphics look, this game is not for the faint of heart.  The amount of satisfaction that is garnered from successful progression, however, is substantial and difficult to articulately quantify.

Bit.Trip Runner2 is a perfect game. The controls are perfect (I'm playing with a 360 controller). The visuals are perfect. The music is perfect. The gameplay is perfect. One can always have differing opinions when it comes to personal taste, so I'm sure Runner2 is not necessarily everybody's cup of tea. Still, looking at the game as objectively as possible it's clear that Gaijin Games put out a really exceptional product here. There's plenty to keep both casual gamers and achievement hunters coming back for more. Highly recommended!

This game really conveys the magical quality of music and platforming put together. The rhythm and the beat become one with the keystrokes, and it just feels like you're in sync with the level itself.

The Good: Charming graphics, catchy soundtrack, smooth controls, well paced level design, checkpoints make the game more forgiving, lots to unlock
The Bad: Not enough unlockable characters, a few levels were hampered with design flaws
8-bit style games are growing in popularity and Bit.Trip has been delivering excellent games for quite a while now. Runner was my favorite in the series but was relentlessly hard, even early on. Runner 2 fixes these issues by making levels more fluid and by adding a checkpoint halfway through. The game is mostly the same, but with added obstacles and better graphics.
The game plays roughly the same as the last one. Watch Commander Video and his pals run to the right while you jump kick and dance your way to the end of the level. Some added obstacles are a four-way diamond that you need to press the corresponding button when you get to each corner. Another obstacle is a loop-de-loop that you use the right analog stick to follow your character as he runs inside. Various obstacles are introduced as the game progresses and by the end you need to be quick and have all these memorized as soon as they pop up. I actually never felt overwhelmed by having to remember too many abilities, it felt just right. Levels have you ducking, jumping, using your shield to block flying blocks, kicking stop signs, and even kicking some in the air as well as while sliding. The abilities are timed to a catchy 8-bit soundtrack that is even better and richer than the last game. As you move along there are gold bars to collect as well as red plus blocks that add track to the music as you move along.
These elements are what everyone loved in the first game and they stayed in this one, but the game is just more forgiving. Honestly it was more fun because I never even got to the second level in the first game. Runner 2 features bosses at the end of each level that are pretty fun and very challenging. There’s a new path feature for levels that change the difficulty depending on which path you choose. Red and green arrows will point to which path is which, the red path usually has hidden chests that unlock costumes as well as Retro Cartridges. These 25 retro levels are actually in 8-bit like they were ripped straight from an NES game. Very charming and fun to play.
You are also scored by doing everything in the game. Dancing is one ability that adds 2,000 points with each move. I just found the whole game very addicting and couldn’t put the controller down. Rarely did I find a spot where I was stuck and even rarer were occasion where the game’s own design got in the way. I would fly by something so fast that I would die several times before realizing what was going on and what I had to do. The whole game is just super fun and challenging and very rewarding. If you get all the gold bars and the 4 red plus signs in the level you get to shoot yourself out of a cannon at a target to get a Perfect+ score. Very challenging but fun.
The graphics look amazing with each of the 5 levels being unique. My favorite was The Bit.Trip which was level 5. You can see other Bit.Trip games being played in the background as you run along. My biggest disappointment were the lack of extra characters. There are 5, but what about Super Meat Boy and other characters from the last game? I wanted more honestly. The PC version at least gets a little extra flair with depth of field and slightly better lighting effects. This is just one artistically stunning game.
Overall, Runner 2 keeps what everyone loved in the last game and adds a lot more depth and more layers of fun while being more forgiving. There are lots to collect and a ton of challenges to complete while you play. There are a few levels that were hampered by their own design flaws, and I just wish there were more unlockable characters.
--Score: 9/10

This game rocks. It is a fast paced runner game where the music really immerses you deeper in their universe. It is easy to pick up and play - and the game does a great job of introducing new moves and mechanics the deeper you get in the game. Bit Trip trains you well slowly and by the end of the game you feel like a pro!
Music! Every world and level has unique music - but what really stands out is every time you collect something - it feels like it is to the beat. The more you collect - the better the music and you end up having even more fun!
Frustration factor is ZERO, but that does not mean it isn't challenging. There are multiple difficulty levels so you can still feel challenged - but not once did I want to throw a controller because of wonky gameplay design or controls. It is a smooth experience from start to finish.
Length! There is 5 unique worlds with about 15-20 levels per world. You can unlock new characters and go into a few secret 8bit worlds. You will not be disappointed by the length of the game - and at no point does it begin to feel overly repetitive.
I highly recommend this game if you are looking for phenomenal music and stunning art. It is a running game with great controls. Jokes are peppered throughout the story and high production value shines in Gaijin Game's Bit.Trip Runner 2!

Taking every element from the preivous Runner titles, Runner2 offers an experience that flows wonderfully together. With over 100 levels, dozens of unlockables, lovely visuals and a wonderful soundtrack this game is a really delight to play.
The premise is simple: get from one end of the level to the other in a free-flowing smooth run. But this game is not for the people who have slow reactions times or get frustrated easily. It is hard, and quite unforgiving. Repetition is going to happening in this game, but because of the quick reload and charming music, it's hard to feel put out.
When you do get a great run going, it's fantastic. All the notes and melodies stiched together with your actions makes it a grand way to know you're doing well. Not to mention that it also helps timing your moments with the logical note progression.
Over the multiple different worlds, there are retro levels, multiple paths and different bosses to change things up, and the dastardly combinations of different moments makes you really appreciate the level design - which may appear simplistic at times - but it very finely tuned.
This game is great in short bursts for those that don't have much time, it's great for those wanting a challenge, and especially if you like the recognition for seamlessly stringing together your levels and actions. Everything about this game screams that the developer cared about making their game. From the cutscenes narrated by Charles Martinet (who also does the voice for Mario) right down to the charming animations and fluid movement.
This game is something you should seriously consider purchasing, playing, loving and then realising that you have to do the whole game on all three difficulties and then all the extras and then costumes and then...

BIT.TRIP Presents... Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien is the direct sequel of BIT.TRIP Runner. It has a lot in common with its predecessor, but it features different graphics. In addition to almost a hundred levels set across five different worlds, it also features retro levels which are reminiscent of the 8-bit era. Unfortunately, it only features singleplayer gameplay. In general, BIT.TRIP Presents... Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien is a great platformer for everybody and it stands as a welcome addition to the BIT.TRIP series.

NOTE: This game allows you to play as one of several vampire clans (essentially character classes), either as a man or woman, and as an ally of one of four factions in the endgame. My first and so far only playthrough was with a male Toreador who allied with the Camarilla, focusing on stealth and speech skills, playing only the main quest and WITHOUT any Unofficial Patches. This review is informed by those experiences.
In this game, you control a recently turned vampire from one of several vampire clans. Your task is to help the local vampire prince acquire an ancient artifact that some fear will bring about the end of the world. Along the way, you are courted by other factions: a group of Chinese vampires called the Kuei Jin, the rebellious Anarchs, and the aristocratic Camarilla, all with their own plans for the artifact.
I did enjoy the rich story of this game. Having never played the tabletop game, I can't say whether or not it captures the spirit of the original work, but I can say that it is one of the best examples of a modern-day vampire story I've seen. Each character you meet has a unique personality and values, and their goals in the game follow logically from these. The voice actors used their talents well in differentiating different characters, from the refined speech of the Camarilla to the coarser language of the Anarchs.
As for your character, this is one of the few role-playing games I've played where you can actually play a role to your tastes rather than just playing a single character of variable appearance. Each vampire clan gets unique gameplay and dialogue changes: the grotesque Nosferatus must travel through the sewers because their appearance threatens the "Masquerade," for example, and the Malkavians get various meta-dialogue options that, to an in-universe NPC, sound like mad ravings. This along with the game's multiple possible endings give the game excellent replay value, since each class can look tackle situations differently based on their strengths.
Unfortunately, I found gameplay somewhat lacking. While the stealth mechanics were okay (similar to the original Deus Ex, which was released around the time of this game), combat was poor. Maybe that was because my character wasn't combat-focused, but it is still frustrating when you hit a relatively weak enemy 5 times in a row and get 0 damage each time. I'm sure the Unofficial Patches fix some of the worst issues. Graphics were also less sophisticated than the screenshots show, but keep in mind the game's 10+ year age (and I always put games on the lowest graphics settings for performance reasons). There are also some typos and bugs which increase in frequency near the end, making the game seem unpolished and rushed out the door. The Unofficial Patches, based on what I've read, should fix these.
In summary: Good story. Great role-playing. Good graphics for the time. Mediocre combat. The Unofficial Patches should fix any bugs and improve your playing experience. I recommend this for fans of vampires, action RPGs, and games that tell a good story.

It also seems very counter intuitive when using the boost ability causes you to miss almost every shortcut because you're moving too fast, so you end up taking the longer path with more obstacles and you end up wasting more time than you saved by boosting.

The only thing this game has going for it is its story. The writing is actually pretty well done. It can successfully make you feel uneasy, scared, sad, and any other number of emotions. The dark humor is also well-written (for the most part).
Unfortunately, the good writing of the game are muddled with terrible, TERRIBLE design choices from a mechanics perspective. In my opinion, these aren't just mechanics that could be done better or aren't great; they are actively detrimental to the experience. The game is so far up its own♥♥♥♥♥♥in respects to the dynamic, unpredictable random events. When sleeping at a campfire (how you restore HP and SP in the game), various random events can happen. At first, these are harmless and even give the unnerving feeling that you are never quite safe in the game. One of the first instances of these campfire events comes when you wake up, and there is an insane man standing over you, staring at you. While this idea starts off pretty neat, it eventually degrades into pure RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ttery. I'll wake up at the campfire only to see that one of my party members has abandoned me (never to return), or has been captured by a group of hoodlums. Rather than recruit a new party member and spending an hour leveling him up, or going to retrieve him from the hoodlum base, it's a hell of a lot easier to just reload to the last checkpoint (sometimes a 10 minute loss) and try my luck with the terrible campfire roulette again. These unforgiving and time-wasting perma-loss mechanics also appear in the form of a "death" status effect (in which the party member is dead forever). This isn't "challenging", it's an incentive to reload your save and infuriate you further. Now I get this is supposed to be done to be a reflection of the game world and how unrelenting it is, but it's ♥♥♥♥ing tedious.
Traveling in this game is done from a 2-D, platformer-esque perspective. In reality, there's nothing platformer about it. You hold right or left and occasionally climb ropes the developer put there to break up the monotony. That's all there is. Now, I would be alright with this if there was some interesting music or setpieces to hold my attention while I hold the right arrow key. But there isn't. Environments aren't varied; tiles are reused with nothing more than a simple pallette swap or different shading. The music is either extremely repetitive (I'm talking what sounds to be 20 second loops), extremely grating on the ears, or nonexistent. So, the traveling in between points of interest is boring as♥♥♥♥♥♥ How does the developer account for this? Why, he makes it so that if you walk off the edge of a cliff, it's an instant game over! So just when my eyes are glazing over because I haven't done anything that can be considered a part of a game in over 15 minutes, a curveball is thrown my way when the platform I've been walking on drops off suddenly and I fall off. Nice.
As far as the battle system is concerned, it's Earthbound. Not bad, but nothing to write home about. You usually end up spamming the most powerful attack and/or one particular attack that causes tripping.
The game is also terrible at directing the player. The progression structure makes you go to three main areas, which is just a mountain composed of a lot of doors or crevices you enter (usually around 8). Which of these doors or crevices progress the story and which ones are setups for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ "ha ha, I made you waste 10 minutes of your time" jokes, you ask? The answer is: there's no way to know. You just try all the doors and after a couple of dead ends, you get your answer.
After my 20th time falling off a cliff and getting a game over, I just looked up the ending on youtube. It's a shame the rest of the game is so bad, because the story and ending are well done.

As a newcomer to the Blade Symphony scene, it is best to describe the first impressions as that is what most games hook you in with. That being said, Blade Symphony is not like most games - it is a special gem that is being developed as we speak and with time it shall be worth much more than it is now; this I am sure of.
Blade Symphony is a 3D sword-fighting games with an abundance of swords to use. It is a splice between arena based combat and arcade style fighting with a limited amount of characters to choose from but a large supply of weapons to pick. There are two servers included within the online component of the game (the 'chapters' for single player use are currently being expanded upon).
There is the 'Free For All' or 'FFA' server in which all players roam around the map to either make as many enemies as they want or challenge others to duels. A good addition to this is the lack of interference from other players during duels - while roaming you can see others duel and you cannot interfere with them. Not to say you can't fight without challenges - during FFA, you can potentially fight all other players on the map at once.
There is also the 'Duel' servers. These contain a series of fighting stages on a map that you scroll through and 'queue' for in an effort to fight. When a second player also signs up for the board you then duel them in a one on one battle. Who ever is hosting can change the dueling modes to support 2 v 2 battles - the possibilities are varied!
On the single player side, a nice little tutorial is in place that, for now, is the only major showcase for AI in the single-player portion. Although I have not played with bots, they also exist for certain servers.
Combat is varied depending on the character chosen. In a similar fashion to Mortal Kombat, Tekken and Street Fighter, you have a choice of your character that you use (and in FFA you can switch when outside of battle). There are four characters each with their own fighting style. Pure, Phalanx, Ryoku and Judgement have different playstyles involved as well. While combat is usually high-paced among the visually lighter characters, don't be alarmed when fights take a slower pace. The ability to make your character 'walk' is as useful as the ability to 'run' on walls and manuever yourself.
Find yourself fighting an impatient 'fast' stance fighter? Switch to a 'heavy' or 'balanced' stance and take it slower by walking. Of course, using the fighter's to their best ability is done by using their innate techniques. It's better to take a heavy stance with Judgement than it is with Ryoku - but the game doesn't penalize you for taking it your own way. Finding your own technique among the four characters is part of the heart and challenge to this game. Don't be thrown off by the achievement statistics for winning one round. If you have the will to learn and the luck, you'll win your first round in no time.
A major part of the combat system to note is the combo system. Labeled as a 'multi-hit' the more attacks you link together in one string of movement adds to the counter; not taking damage helps. As you hit more than once the amount of damage dished out is increased, depending on the weapon. Characters don't have a set value for multi-hits but, because of the different speeds and styles, all can give out a different amount of comboed moves. Ryoku is a character that relies on the multi-hits when using weaker weapons because it increases the amount of damage he can give out. Judgement, however, relies less on this system, but, when a player uses it, it still benefits him in the same way it would Ryoku - it increases the output of his attack. With the fast paced battle taking place, it's imperative to complete multi-hits as necessary to win faster and mitigate the risk of losing.
The character design is hard to pinpoint - take sci-fi, steampunk, Eastern and Western influences and mash them together. That's a less eloquent way to describe the over-arching character costumes in appearence. It is harder to simply into a system when you get far enough to customize your character (described further down).
It's important to note that with so many factors involved, choosing from four characters is far from a simple game of rock-paper-scissors. Outcomes are reciprocated of player skill - at rare times is it up to your luck. If you learn from your mistakes quickly, this unforgiving dueling game can really shine and help.
This game is rewarding but such rewards are slow and take time and effort to attain them. You can customize and adorn your  four cool characters by adorning them with masks and skins - for a price. While there are NO MICROTRANSACTIONS in this game (a +), the system at which you gain the monetary units ('notes') can be seen as slow and tedious. No doubt, it's one of the minors in this upcoming game and it shouldn't deter you at all. The slow gain of 'notes' only impede character design and weapon unlocking. It rewards those who play the longest - or rather, the more you play, the more it pays. That said, it's a good way of differentiating the new comers from the more experienced sword masters. And while you can unlock more weapons, masks and skins you do not lose or gain an overbearing advantage over others. As long as you have control, the basic set of weapons are as deadly as the most brazen.
Capes, as of now, are also unlocked by completing special and secret objectives as you play. No doubt another rewarding factor for this game.
The characters?
Pure is a refined and acrobatic character - think Wushu fighting. With agile swordsman ship and experienced user skill she can be deadly - if you find yourself in a 2 v 2 against two skilled Pure users, you are definitely at a disadvantage. Pure is an offensive character that is best played by switching stances rapidly and soundly. Don't let up on your opponent lest they get the drop on you. Loosening the pressure is recommended however to open up the dueler's defenses when they lack an opening.
Ryoku is agile, fast but unrefined - he's great for stringing combos together and less useful at hitting hard. For him you'll want to build up your combos instead of vying for a one-hit kill. The fast paced action of this game suits him as you'll find yourself overcome if you fought these guys in a 2 v 2. The Scimitar is a fan-favorite for the Ryoku user as it allows them to (cheaply) build up 'multi-hits' and dole out punishment in the boss way the character defines.
Unless you are:
Phalanx. This guy. This guy is one I dislike - in a good way. He's a very plyable fencer that can strike from afar but will deal the necessary damage up close. He's also useful for stringing combos up and whipping an enemy into shape. With an experience player using him, he'll no doubt be the true challenge to beat. Watch out for Phalanx. They'll get you when you least expect it.
Judgement is a heavy hitting samurai. His default character, adorned in armor, has no trouble signifying how hard his experienced hand will come down upon his unlucky opponent. While he isn't as agile and swift as the other three, his recommended katana is useful for beating down the other. It's best to chalk Judgement up as one of the simpler to use. His slower speed allows for an easier string of combos if necessary by the less experienced player. He is, however, not a dominant combo chainer, his being the smaller out of all of them. Bulky and sluggish are in no way to describe him however. He is no doubt a tank and can take out a hit as well as dish them out - high damage with low speed if you look at it in technical terms.
In the end, Blade Symphony is no doubt a game for those who like swords, arcade fighting-games and arena based combat.
It is not a game for those who enjoy first person visuals, puzzle solving, platformers or role-playing games. Fast combat is not for slow players!

I haven't completed the game, but well into Act 2 I've learned a few things about LISA.
This game enjoys wasting your time. The biggest symbolic example of this is
But more than this, it's a game that constantly dangles you at the end of a line over an open flame mocking you for being in a position of constant discomfort. Even the way saves work is an example of this, each one limited to a single use, each one up to two hours of slow walking and battling a gauntlet of enemies to get through. Sometimes it's difficult, sometimes it's frustrating, and sometimes it's downright HARROWING. Be prepared for a game that feels like it hates you.
There's no better example of this than the sacrifices. And the sacrifices here are ACTUAL sacrifices, putting peoples' lives on the line to keep your main character at full strength, forking over cash because a teammate was kidnapped in the middle of the night (hint: if you're not resting in a tent, you're not safe), and much, much, MUCH worse.
Then there's the issue with resource management. Fully healing is only possible at a few specific locations without risking your teammate being kidnapped, as mentioned before. Some resources are absolutely limited in supply. New team members often enter your party 5 levels behind you, which means leveling them up requires an investment of time you are just as likely to lose because of how rare save points are. And grinding seems to be something the game hangs over your head like the sword of Damocles. There are few ways to collect this game's currency other than grinding, but even the time spent grinding goes back to the game's real sense of threat in how willing it is to have you throw away hours of gameplay on a randomly overpowered enemy you didn't see coming.
Is the game fair? Well, no. On the one hand, you can avoid many fights simply by not straying off the main map. On the other hand, sometimes you're thrown into a situation with no way out other than to lose a lot of money and experience you had just spent gathering. Oh, and worse... much, much worse. This game will occasionally throw you into the world's worst RNG meat grinder just to make a point about your helplessness. And god help you if you think you're tough enough to fight back, sometimes the consequence is several times worse than just taking your beating and hobbling away blindsided and broken.
And yet, this game is pretty fantastic. It's... grotesque and heart-rending and there are moments in the story when you are horrified at what has transpired. It's perverse at one moment and then warm-hearted in the next for how it reflects on what remains of a sense of joy and community long after such things should have been forgotten.
I can't really recommend buying it unless you are absolutely willing to invest time you will never see rewarded except with disappointment. On the other hand, as the story unfolds, I'm delighted at the kind of cruel, misshapen world I've been witness to. The cruelty of the game's mechanics somehow fit the cruelty of the world, and while it's not an experience I would recommend to anyone, it is definitely an experience worth having.

The jist of this post: I can safely recommend this as a *solid* game, with warts. Those familiar with the other games will want this game primarily for the updated editor, which allows a multitude of new options via UGC. Note: the Matrix environment is different to all previous HB games.
-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-` START `-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-
This is the 3rd modern iteration of Shadowrun to come from Harebrained Studios (excluding the original 'Dragonfall', which was an add-on for SRR), and it's another on-rails extravaganza. However, a lot of extra features have gone into this experience that will ultimately bode well for people keen to create their own adventures, via UGC (User Generated Content).
Shadowrun has a rich tabletop history, which HB have tried to bring to us three times before (Shadowrun Returns, the SRR DLC, 'Dragonfall', and the stand alone Director's Cut version of 'Dragonfall'). Each time, new features emerged; each time there were several flaws (that said, each iteration was satisfactory; low replayability, however).
This game was made from a tabletop perspective: create your own stories, to share with others. It's a noble goal, but tabletop games are meant to be played *with* other people, not *by* 1 person alone. This is the critical failure of the Unity-engine based Shadowrun games, and it's something that can't be fixed due to the nature of the game (sandbox, no multiplayer).
You can not revisit areas. You are on rails. The story that plays out tends towards linear (due to the complexity involved in properly branching choices taken in-game). You are not allowed to grind karma and nuyen indefinitely to build your little super shadowrunner.
People play Shadowrun to build a character, and a story, and essentially live vicariously through their created avatar(s) in a universe that can be *imagined* by a group of players. These games are very static & limited; what you see is what you get.
An example of some of my gripes: despite some *very* gorgeous art assets, once you've in an area & have completed the mission, you leave and (90% of the time) you can't return to the area. Once the game is over, most UGC won't let you import your character over. Just like SRR, when
, you're like "Cool, what's next?". Game ends, go away. Just like that. That's not *Shadowrun*, dammit!
Back to the game...this game *currently* has numerous typos, bugged scripts, bugged enemy AI & corny/flat dialogue in parts. I'm sure these will be looked at & addressed. Conversely, it has expanded in-game options substantially (the kind that are utilized in the editor). Monofilament whips, fetishes, expanded cyberware, passive totems, a rejuvenated Matrix environment...this game has had a *lot* of love put into it.
The rejuvenated Matrix is a vast improvement if you come from a tabletop background. These sorts of people are familiar with the fickle nature of the dice roll. You might have great stats, but if you botch a roll you get slapped down. And vice versa; you could have bad stats and be in a bad situation and roll multiple crits. The element of luck is ever present. In the previous iteration of the Matrix, there was a random element but it was hidden in the code (% to miss/hit). You were limited by your stats in a very real way.
Not so in SR:HK. You can, with patience and skill, skate across the ICE like a pro, even if it's not reflected in your stats. In many situations, you can avoid combat altogether. The time-based memory puzzles add a subtle layer of complexity to hacking, but my personal gripe is that it's is *far* too easy & should be nerfed slightly according to stats. You can literally have Decking of 1, a crap cyberdeck & a datajack & be fine with the Matrix for the entire game. Dead serious. The changes are good IMO, as it allows skill and luck to affect Matrix play.
Overall, despite some flat character development for many of the characters (it's there, but it has a paper-thin veneer), the plot is compelling & exciting; I liked this just as much as Dragonfall. I find it hard to say which is superior as they are both solid. I guess Dragonfall nailed the Matrix better, whilst Hong Kong nails the mystical stuff better (that said, no Astral Plane again *dammit*).
I'm a big fan of the Shadowrun tabletop game & the Super Nintendo, Sega Genesis/Megadrive & Mega-CD game(s). I've backed, played & enjoyed the previous HareBrained Studios Shadowrun games. Would I buy another Shadowrun game if it is Unity-based? Yes, but *only* because I am a diehard. Also, if it was another Kickstarter, I would likely refrain from backing at a high tier.
The format has been thoroughly explored over several years; it just isn't a good enough framework for a *true* Shadowrun game. I'd wager money that if Harebrained made it clear from the start of their Kickstarter that it would be extremely similar fare to the previous game(s), they would have struggled to reach 100% backing of their funding target. People are *sick* to *death* of this limited engine. Yes, I understand that the ultimate goal of all the games is for people to create better runs via the editor (which is why Unity is being used in the first place), but the monumental amount of effort and talent need to make something close to the base campaign is *frightening*.
If Harebrained can get together and find the magical formula that can distill the tabletop experience into a static video game, that would be the cyberpunk holy grail. These Unity-based games simply give the scent of the 6th Age; a compelling scent, but a scent, nonetheless.
-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-` END `-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-`-

Shadowrun: Dragonfall was already a big improvement over the initial release of Shadowrun: Returns and settled many of the issues the initial game had. Shadowrun: Hong Kong delivers another great story as well as some minor, but nice improvements.
Like in Dragonfall you get a detailed backstory for each of your crew members and talking to them leads to optional missions, which help develop the characters and are good for a change of pace when compared to the other side missions.
Only a few of the side missions have to be completed in order to complete the campaign, but you're really selling yourself short if you don't do all of them and miss out on interesting sideplots.
Personally I like the changes this iteration brings to the matrix and while the minigames can get repetitive, it is a huge step up from the old matrix system, which was a bit of a weakpoint previously.
While other reviews talk about a lot of bugs, I only spotted minor ones usually related to one obscure branch of some sideplot - a side effect when there are tons of different branches to keep track of and many of the choices have some

I just finished the game (well last night) and my experience with it was kind of bland.  Generally speaking the game played almost like a Point-and-Click Interactive Story.  The game played a lot like its previous iterations, from a game design point of view, and the graphical upgrades to the Matrix are pretty neat but not as exciting, it feels like they didnt put too much effort on it as they should have.  The new puzzle system (for hacking) in the Matrix killed it for me, the whole simon-sez / Memory game wasn't well laid out and was boring.  In general the game was good... But not exciting good.
The story itself was interesting at some points but it felt more like the campaign someone back in my highschool days would coin up to play on a saturday afternoon.  It was good but not $30 - $20 good.  There were a lot of flaws in the writing, like I said it was very bland and forgettable and not well thought out specially at the beginning.  A good word to describe it would have been... Meh.
Whatever upgrade they did with the graphics engine is pretty neat.  The artwork in the game is pretty good, it feels almost like being on a painting.  If it were not for the artwork I don't think I would have been compelled to play the game so much if it wasnt because the graphics were that pretty.
The so-called Matrix update artwork-wise was really good, I liked the new representation of it.  I still think at Char-Gen you should be able to pick an avatar for your character instead of the floating generic one, as it doesnt make you feel part of the game just another random icon to be a part of.  The Gameplay in the Matrix was horrible.  I understand the need to put a mechanic for the "hacking" part of the game but playing Simon-Sez with the numbers is not it... Then that memory game to figure the codes was also pretty stupid and boring.  They should have randomized the mini-games in the Matrix at least...
The other thing was you couldn't upgrade in any way any of your companions, you can "Level" them but its very bland and un-intrusive and pretty insignificant, but you can't add cyber to them or change their weapons or spells.
The overall gameplay was pretty much the same as in the other games of the series.  But the whole interaction felt like a point-and-click story than an RPG and overall the game was too short.  By the time you got the cash to up your gear the game was over.  The game feels more like an expansion to the original game than anything else... Dragonfall had a much more bigger impact on me as a player than this game overall.  I was really expecting a lot more for the time the developers took to build this game.  It feels incomplete and rushed, from the sense that the story even with the side stories and the "team" stories were interesting, but it felt rushed.
I wish tha game had been longer, had some more depth and had a better story.  But Shadowrun is one of my favorite Cyberpunk pen and paper RPG, and until Cyberpunk 2077 hits the streets it is what it is...
As a conclusion, I think of this game as an expansion-DLC type.  I wish they re-made the previous games with the engine and graphic optimization they did on this game, and have them all under one engine... But I think the game could have been better, for the time they took to make it.  I think it was very cool they added the portraits of some of the backers in areas of the game, it was a nice touch of gratitude.
Overall the game is a 7/10 in my book.  The game took me about 26hrs of compressed time, with all the side stories, companion stories and fiddle-farting-around.  Started playing it Friday afternoon and finished it Sunday evening.
I am going to give it a couple of weeks, and play the game again as a streeet samurai rather than a decker to see other aspects of the game, but I dont think i am going to see a whole lot different than I have seen so far.

I played through Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun: Dragonfall, (and the updated director's cut), and I can safely say that if you liked even a little bit of either of those two games, you'll have a blast with Shadowrun: Hong Kong.
It's 4:30am and I finished the game, and as much as I'd love to write a full review, I'm too dang tired. So let's start with the good:
Improved Matrix: That's right runners! The Matrix is graphically updated, more challenging, and now includes hacking mini games!
Improved Combat: The biggest upgrade for me is that a rigger doesn't need a deck anymore, meaing you can carry a gun and 2 drones with you into battle if you've invested the Karma. That's like having two extra members to the team, plus being able to defend yourself properly. *Very* nice change, and makes riggers even more viable than previously.
Improved Mission Prep and Inventory Management: This was a HUGE improvement. Now swapping gear and items between compansions and party guests is much, much easier with newly designed mission screens, which include tabs for gear, spells, and items. You can see in a glance everyone's loadouts at once and drag and drop items from your stash to the appropriate party. Also, if you find an item in the field and you have space in your characters slots, you can take the item immediately, and either hang onto it or hand it immediately to another party member! That's a big improvement for harder modes when you may be running low on supplies and won't be able to access a stash!
Great Characters: The companion missions are back, and the companions this time around aren't nearly as stereotypical as they were in Dragonfall. Gone are the goth chick, angry chick, and drunk german, (whom I liked, but thought they were severely stereotyped), and now you have a cast that includes an adopted brother, rat shaman millenial, samurai ghoul, and more!
Engrossing Story/Cutscenes: They're sparsely used, but worth noting since the previous games didn't include cutscenes. The storyline this time around runs much like Dragonfall, so you'll get hooked early in, but have a lot of time to run other missions till the main storyline picks back up. Once it does though, you're in it to win it.
New Cyberware and Essence Cap: For me, this was HUGE. You have access to really great cyberware from early on in the game, including some really cool weapons, (laser whips, anyone?!) The essence cap can be increased to 8, (Up from 6 in previous games), meaning that you can judiciously load out a character. There's even a new branch of Karma that expands on your cyber effectiveness.
New Weapons: Flaming and Electric swords, Cyber Claws, and armor stripping shotguns. Oh my!
Better Companion Abilities: The Companion Level Upgrade system is back from Dragonfall: Director's Cut, except now I found the abilities to be downright amazing. For instance, both your samurai ghoul and your shaman can develop abilities that one-shot opponents who meet particular conditions. Having the right party member and planning ahead with their tree can make some fights incredibly rewarding when your forethought pays out in big nuyen.
On the downsides: The story takes a big detour for a good chunk of the game if you're a completionist who like side missions and companion missions. Also, there's not a lot of Nuyen (Cash) to be had in the game in comparison to Dragonfall, so some very judicious spending is in order.
If you've never played either of the first two games, I have good news. This is basically a standalone game, so you can just pick up and play, and learn as you go. It's a thought provoking RPG where strategy, cover, and character building are the key to having a great time. Also, if you're into cyberpunk, this game is for you!

Wow... where to start!
I've never been a massive fan of the old real time strategy, top down view, board-gamey, style of games. But Company of Heroes 2 caught me off guard! This is an absolutely fantastic game, that is FULL of content, with new updates being pumped out wherever possible.
I haven't done much of the single player campaigne, but I feel like this isn't the main feature of the game... what IS the main feature of the game (for me at least), is the multiplayer. I have had a good few games with my friends playing against AI, and having an absolute BLAST!
One time we were on a map (I'm sorry I've forgotten what it's called) that has three bridges going over a river, two of them are destroyable. And our tactic was to blow up the two destructible bridges, to force the enemy to the middle bridge. And we would have an ABSOLUTELY EPIC battle at the bridge! I nicknamed the map "The Battle of The Bridge" as a result. My best experience playing this game.
Graphically... not brilliant, but it's in top down view, not first person view or anything like that. Besides, I can sacrifice graphics over solid gameplay, which this game truly has!
It does bug me that if you buy the standard version of the game (which is pretty cheap!), you have to buy three of the nations/armies. You get the German Wermacht and the Soviets, with the standard game. And the other three you have to buy are the Royal Army, the Oberkommando (German Army Special Forces), and the U.S. Army. I strongly recommend getting all the armies in order to get the most enjoyment out of the game.
What I like about the different nations is that they have their own unique abilities, and bonuses. So America has all of its unit making facilities already built, you just need the manpower, fuel and munitions. The Oberkommando have their unit making facilities onboard supply half-tracks which you can place anywhere on the map. The dialogue for each nation is also quite a nice touch!
My only real problem with the game is... where's the Imperial Japanese Army?! I would LOVE to play on a tropical pacific jungle map, with the U.S. Army against the Imperial Japanese Army! I think that would be PHENOMINAL! It could be that they are working on adding Japan... because they put the British Army a while ago. (I really hope that's the case!)
Overall I recommend this game without a shadow of a doubt! An excellent game, that is worth the money, but play it for the multiplayer! It's SO much better than going up against AI on your own!

When I first started playing Lisa, I wasn't sure if I was going to like it. It seemed kind of "out there" and just didn't seem like something I'd be interested in. I'm glad that I decided to keep going after playing through the tutorial, because I became hooked very quickly after that point. What I initially expected to be a shallow experience turned out to be a surprisingly deep game.
The setting of the game is post-apocalyptic, which has been done time and time again, but the thing that makes Lisa interesting is that it takes the concept of a post-apocalypse and adds a twist to it that makes it pretty unique as far as game settings go. The entire world is seemingly devoid of women. As the story progressed and I began to learn more about the characters, I was hungry for more and I found myself unable to stop playing.
The story alone would've kept me going, but the combat is also surprisingly fun. There are a large variety of unique party compositions you can choose from, which gives the game great replay value. I'll definitely be playing it again to try out different combinations of characters.
Another aspect of the game that I found interesting, though I can understand why some would not like it, was the inclusion of perma-death. There are certain enemy abilities, though used rarely in most cases, that can and will permanently kill your companions. Terrible things can also happen to your party while you sleep, which to me makes the setting seem more dangerous and mysterious, adding to the grim atmosphere. It isn't often that I become immersed in games, but I did with this one.
If you like RPGs, definitely play this. Even if you aren't normally a fan of RPGs, I think this changes the formula up enough to be interesting to non-RPG fans as well. It's fairly short, so it doesn't drag on at all and there is minimal to no grinding.  It's a great game, and it definitely deserves more attention. Totally worth the price. Check it out!
