What can I say about this game.. Well.. It's an RPG above all else, the gameplay is nothing special, it's not boring but it could use some work too, this is a game you play for the story and atmosphere. It is no secret that there's a severe lacking of modern cyberpunk games and this game certainly delivers on that and gives you a very interesting dystopian future setting with a twist, it has elfs, dwarfs, orcs, mythical creatures and magic but in a modern/futuristic society.
From what I have gathered the Shadowrun Returns series (based on the PnP Shadowrun setting) tends to be a hit or miss with people, as a roleplayer and video game story enthusiast I personally love it! If you care more about story than gameplay elements I would recommend it to you as well.
As for Hong Kong specifically, I haven't finished it yet but I have put in 10 houres or so around the time im writing this review, I would say it rates somewhere in between the other two games.. The first Shadowrun: Returns game, well, it's no secret it was lacking and kind of short, I personally still loved it due to the setting and as an old Inphinity Engine games fan I get my hand on every similar style RPG I can find, you just can't match the roleplaying and immersion you get out of these type of games anywhere else. I am getting a little off track.. The sequal Dragonfall picked up ALOT of slack and was just purely an amazing ride, Hong Kong seems to be somewhere in between, definetely more polished than the original but so far lacking a bit of Oomph, keep in mind though this opinion is formed only 10 houres into the game, and there has been some interesting moments, this opinion might change by the time I have experienced more of the main story. One thing that I am confident will not change however is this; I recommend any RPG fan to play this game, if you are new to the series I would recommend playing the other installments first since there's really no visible technological upgrades between the sequals, only the story differs. At the very least do yourself a favor and pick up Dragonfall, the original might give you a sour first impression, I would still recommend getting it as long as you dont allow it to turn you off the sequals (they are better, much like how Baldurs Gate 2 was better than 1 but both were good).

A worthwhile successor to Dragonfall.  Buggy at times, SR:HK recreates the tabletop experience with a plot that loses coherence and drive somewhere in the middle before whipping everything back together for the finale like an actual game master would have happen -
.
The maps are much larger, but most of it is empty space populated with nice atmospheric setpieces.  Nice scenery does kind of wear thin after a while when you're criss-crossing the hub area to buy things or advance the little subplots the NPCs have.
The new Matrix gameplay emphasizes sneaking around and playing Simon/a memory game.  It was novel, but wore that novelty out quickly.
Despite it all, would still recommend the game if only for one run through.  The story is nice and all the little details and in-jokes are appreciated. In short, replayability doesn't look good to me on the effort/payoff scale.

Have you ever gotten a game for sale price and after playing it, you feel like you'd have been satisfied with the value even if you paid full price? For me, One Way Heroics is that, except I'd feel happy paying more than sale price.
One Way Heroics is a rouge-like game kinda like a Mystery Dungeon game, except you're not stuck in a dungeon and have a randomly generated world to explore. Except with one twist: There's Darkness to the left. And it endlessly creeps up on you. And if you fall in it, you're dead! So you're stuck going to the right. And there's monsters out there, too, so remain on guard! Of course, there's helpful stuff out there, too!
One Way Heroics is kinda tough at first, but it gets easier as you go along, unlock classes, and generally get an idea of what to do. And it's alright if you mess up after you got some cool item, because after you die or clear you game, you're allowed to put items into the Dimensional Vault, to use them on another run. You've got limited space, though, so until you're heroic enough to expand it, watch how you use it!
I had a lot of fun with this game, and I only spent 87 cents on it! So it's a definite recommendation from me.

Takong "Gotta Go Fast" to the ultimate level, OWH challenges you to be able to manage your time, as every turn removes one row of the map. Everything save talking to an ally takes up a turn. Despite the intimidating apperance, the game is actually rather simple once one gets a idea on how to play. The easy mode really helps new players, but harder difficulties give signifigantly better rewards, like partners. Special mention to the partners, they really can steal the show. Especially Panty, who challenges you to take time out of your adventure to gather money, which can take lots of time, and Freida, for her ending.
Pros:
Psudo-Online: Ghost of other players can give you items.
Companions: Good time.
Titles: Titles can boost/weaken an enemy or ally, conversations also change to match NPC's title.
Gamplay: Simple but fun.
Seed system: Self explanitory. However, every seed has a Hall of Fame list, showing everyone who ever beat the seed in order, and every seed you beat gets added to a list, allowing you to check the Hall of Fame to see changes.
Neutral:
Artstyle: VERY Simple. I personally like it. You may not.
Cons:
Padding: One ending involves going about 2000 miles/tiles/km. This gets EXETREMELY tiring, and prepare to resort to save-scumming your way to victory here.
Saving: Not every world has everything. When starting, I often used the seed "Shinryu" and never got save points. (Moral, don't use Shinryu).
Terrain: Minor complaint, but after a while, the biomes start to repeat over and over, with no randomly generated structures to set apart (I once got three empty plains in a row).
Overall: 9.5/10 Would auto-scroll again

I only usually write reviews for games I really like, and this is one of them, but the game is definitely not for everyone. The themes and events in this game can be extremely inappropriate at times. Some of them are optional (seducing pretty much any of your crew mates (male or female ;D), or killing people with a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat), but there are also some components that are part of the story. There are nude scenes that are mandatory in this game (blurred out but still nude), some BDSM kinky♥♥♥♥♥♥(nothing really graphic or disturbing) in the DLC and you can also choose to potentially stay nude pretty much for the rest of the game. However, IT IS ALL MEANT TO BE FUNNY. You can't play this game and take it too seriously, the entire point is for it all to be funny, so if you have your mind in the gutters all the time, you may enjoy this. Pretty much, the main concern here is that the humour is inappropriate and not everyone will find it funny. But there are just so many good things about this game that I feel like unless you REALLY hate that kind of stuff, you should play this anyway. The humour really worked for me, there aren't many games like this, so I enjoyed it.
Second, the movement is amazing. The example that I've been using is Arkham City. I admit, I haven't played it much, but it seemed as if the movement was pretty much limited to gliding slowly, and a lame grappling hook. Obviously, I didn't expect batman to fly, but it still seemed kind of boring to me. In this game, you FEEL like a super hero. You have 8 super powers, some of which are for mobility. These include super speed (run faster than a car), super jumps (like sky scraper high if you charge it for a couple seconds), and gliding (you can also mid-air dash). You can also charge your jumps while doing other things, so you can land and then instantly jump high again. This allows for really smooth travel across the map; jumping, flying, and dashing all over the place. And unlike GTA5, when you run around for no reason, there are actually a lot of useful collectibles placed around the map, as to not feel like you are wasting too much time. Also skyscrapers are more common, so you can jump from building to building like a real hero.
Another incredible thing about this game is the freedom. One big concern that people have about this game is that they say it is too easy, but I don't think it's always a bad thing. I'm not sure if I'm just bad at games or what, but it's not easy enough that you could afk in the middle of a few enemies and go to the washroom, the lower difficulty just allows you to have more freedom in the way you handle things. Plus, if I wanted to play harder games, there are plently of them out there, that doesn't mean every good game should be hard. There are so many ways to kill enemies, you can choose to just gun every enemy down with an SMG all game and be bored, but you have to ability to do things differently. For starters, you have your many abilities, many of which also have different element types that change the effect. You also have a LARGE variety of weapons available to use. The dubstep gun, for example, plays a song and damages enemies on every beat,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bats, basic guns, RPGs, alien guns, and much more. Sometimes, you can choose to go in spamming AOE abilities, or take everyone out using a sniper rifle, or get headshots only with a pistol, it's entirely up to you.
Now onto the cons, which there are a few of:
Like I talked about earlier, the relatively easier difficulty means some people may get bored, but I believe it just allows more room for different weapons.
I haven't played Saint's Row 3, so that might be part of the problem, but a lot of people say that a large portion of the map is copy pasted from SR3, so if you have played that game, maybe keep that in mind and buy this on sale. As someone who experienced the map here for the first time, however, I can safely say I loved it.
From what I've heard, the previous games actually had you use the cars and homies (you can call them in, since it is SUPPOSED to be a game about a streetgang, this game hardly adresses it though), however, if you are used to that, unfortunately the homies and cars are pretty much obsolete. There are some missions where you need them, but I don't think I ever called for a single car or homie of my own accord. Because of your super powers they are incredibly pointless, and so don't bother upgrading them. Do not expect this to be Saint's Row 4, think of it more like a seperate game in the same universe, because it is very different.
Not a con, but just another warning that it is violent, not too much so, but it is a shooter.
TL;DR is it's a great game, if you are fine with the idea of beating people with a tentacle weapon called "The Violator," then buy this and you'll have a blast.
P.S. you might want to get the "How the saints save christmas" and "Enter the dominatrix" DLCs, those two are the only ones with more quests - each DLC takes about an hour, so it is NOT a lot more gameplay. The other millions of DLCs are just clothes and a couple weapons so unless you get them in a pack, probably don't buy them separately. Although, buy The Rectifier as well if you have a spare dollar. ;)

The players who've been in love with Sonic for all the past 20 years have already bought this game, so I'll address everyone else.
If you used to like Sonic, but gave up on him when his move to 3D was handled badly, give this game a serious chance, because this one is handled well. Very well. The controls make sense, the camera behaves itself, and the plot stays simple--almost shockingly simple. You'll get to see great scenery from both the games you remember and the ones you skipped, and it all looks gorgeous.
If you're new to Sonic, this game will be a decent introduction. It shows the best of what he's capable of in 3D without any nonsense. You can swing by Sonic Retro to brush up on your history later. If you want to see his best, period, then go for Sonic 3 & Knuckles or the 2011 Sonic CD remake.
Sega is doing a much better job listening to their fans lately, and they're putting a lot more more effort into ensuring that Sonic looks polished and handles smoothly. Their work really paid off in Generations.

I was surprised to see this game get good critical reviews... a Sonic game hasn't been this well-received for a long time. Sonic Generations mixes classic Sonic gameplay with modern 3D Sonic gameplay. The first few levels come from the Genesis Sonic games, and playing them with a 3D perspecive is a really neat experience. The later levels come from the 3D games, and the levels still make sense and are still fun in 2D.
The controls work well enough (except one obnoxious menu), the level designs are really neat, the camera is mostly competent (some exceptions), and the music is awesome. The plot is stupid and short, but the enjoyable dialogue makes up for it. Thankfully, most of the dialogue is between the Sonics, Tails, and Eggman, which means that Amy, Cream, and Charmy barely speak. The game is very replayable.
If you feel some nostalgia for any Sonic game, you'll enjoy the loving tributes made in this game. Platformer fans should check it out.

Probably the best competitive melee combat game available at the moment, with a deep combo system that encourages mixing up your approach. I found earning cash to buy new pieces slow, and half the time it didn't even seem to give them to me (and this was not in FFA mode, which is not supposed to generate any cash). Luckily you are provided with every gameplay relevant item there is; the only things you're missing are skins. It also features Workshop support, giving you access to a variety of skins for free, and if you have the know-how to model a sword, you could put your own skins into the game.

As an Early Access game, and even as a game in general, is very good. Due to a great community, vital strategy, and in-depth elements that lead to precision play, makes for such an interesting game, and makes me play it almost every single day, sometimes for hours at a time. The potential that this game has is amazing and the learning curve is great for people who want a challenge, mainly for people who also like games like Demons' Souls and Dark Souls, one mistake could be the end of you, and it makes you think about it everytime.

You can live all your dreams of pointed and sharp weapons, from poking someone in the eye to cutting their shin. One of the best parts is that not all weapons are pointed and sharp, thanks to Steam Workshop integration. Overall great game, would recommended to anyone who's a fan of sword fights. i give it a good/10 much sword so indie (im sorry). also all the unlocks are cosmetic ok

The graphics have been shifted from 2D to a 3D setting, which actually makes this game a lot more distracting than its previous incarnation as things are going to be moving in the background a LOT.  The shift to3D models also means that there's shading on the characters, which means backgrounds and lighting does have an effect on whatever character you're playing on for a stage, so when a stage is red, it will be REALLY red.  That could be a problem for people with red-green colorblindness, but I think you could still see the outlines on completely red stages, although everything will be overlapped in grey.
The music in this game is amazing, and I really enjoy the variety of music per world, as each world has its own theme.  There's a large selection of characters (plus character DLC if you want more) to run with, although they're all incredibly weird looking, which makes you wonder what the developers were thinking when designing them.  Each character feels like they have different hitboxes, but I'm assuming it's all the same even though it feels differently based on how tall/wide a character is.
If you haven't played a bit.trip runner (or bit.trip game in general), this game is probably the most beginner-friendly game in the entire series.  The entire game mechanic is that you are always running, but the player is in control of dodging obstacles along the way via jumping or sliding or flying or many other things.  They have added checkpoints into the game (which are skippable for bonus points), as well as adding a dance option to gain bonus points while putting you at risk of getting slammed by a random object.  The leaderboards are fierce and competitive, and it will actually show you who the top 3 are in the stage you are on, or if you're replaying a stage, the people that are around your scoring range.
The biggest downside for me in this game was the achievements they had, as they added a bullseye mechanic at the end of every level.  Basically you used to only have to collect all the gold and powerups in each level without getting hit to get a perfect, which leads you to a retro stage, and perfecting that will net you a perfect+.  In this game, you need to land a bullseye in a flash game-esque minigame after perfecting a level, but you have to do this on all three difficulties (easy/medium/hard) to get something called a triple perfect to actually 100% this game (this means getting a perfect and a bullseye at the end of the level on every stage in the game, three times).  This may sound a lot easier than how it used to be, and it is, but it just makes achivement hunting a really tedious task when you already know how to play the game.
Something that really made me happy is that they seperated out retro stages, so you don't have to perfect the entire stage just to get a shot at doing the retro level again.  It's really easy to tell that they put in a lot of work into the retro stages, as it has its own music and own sprites as it goes back to the 2D environment.  The retro stages were a lot more fair (easier), and a lot more fun than bit.trip runner 1's retro stages, and there's quite a lot of them to the point where you'll probably need a guide to find them all.
I would highly recommend using a controller for this game, although I think the best way to get points on some levels is using keyboard only.  I personally find the controller feel more fun and comfortable, but whatever works for you!
Pick this game up if you're looking for a good entry-level game into the bit.trip series!

One of the best games I have ever played. Mafia II tell us a fascinating story of Vito Scaletta, bringing us to rarely used 1950s. The main city, Empire Bay, is perfectly organized, it is much smaller than the cities in GTA series, but each district is different and looks really nice. I could tell the same about the cars, I really enjoyed driving them and you drive here a lot. It is a shame, that there is no 'free ride' mode, I would love to drive without any mission 'on'.
You will also kill a lot of other bad guys using many weapons including the WWII guns and, of course, the immortal Tommy Gun. Hiding behind the covers and shooting is well developed and was a real fun to me. The only thing is that the game is quite difficult and the chechpoints are sometimes too far from each other, making me once to repeat almost 10 minutes long sequence.
There is one thing, that has no flaw. The story is absolutely amazing. I would say it is more realistic, than the story in the original Mafia, and I really wanted to know, how it ends. It begins well with a short scene during World War II and then it gets only better. What I really loved, were the dialogues and the broadcasts - letting you feel the atmosphere.
To sum up, the game has some small cons, however it is one of those games, you will never forget. 9/10!

Very undewhelming roguelike.  For several reasons.
First, there is no inventory system, so the classic roguelike gameplay element of picking up resources to take with you and making decisions on what you need most and when to save them vs use them is nonexistant.
Second, success is completely reliant on loot rng to find the correct enchants/resists on random items.  If you happen to not find the correct resist for a given quest, you will lose.  If the dungeon is being stingy and happens to not give you any food to restore hp, you lose.  If you get lucky and find all the OP stuff right away, you probably win.
And lastly, the whole 32 characters to unlock thing is a bit of a lie.  There are actually ~3 characters, warrior, archer, and mage.  There are 32 variants of those, not characters themselves.  Each character has a different weapon/armor/start stats, but they are the exact same otherwise. This system is actually a bit of a downer, many of the games quests are basically impossible with the starter classes, but become objectively easier once you unlock some strictly better variants.
And tbh, there are better roguelikes that have been in developement for decades, still going strong, that are free and better than this.  I typiccally love roguelikes, gave this one a fair shake, and found it to be far too shallow for my liking.

Let me first say i loved SR:R and DF, but for me this game is a hughe dissapointment.
Pros:
* Fine tuned overall game mechanics.
* A couple of interesting NPC.
Cons:
* Lots of reading and reading ...
... but the story just don't do it for me.
* Reading and reading --->hardly any action --->e x t r e m e l y slooooow paced.
* Nuyens are hard to get so prepare to use the same gun you start with if you for instance buy better armor or decking gear. This is not challenging, it's just boring.
* And no loot - really, what is this?
* Not enough side quests/not enough rewarding side quests due to the above.
* Most side quests goes like this: Take the tube to this building. Then speak with your party members for ten minutes. Then qlick on a few clickables, read lenghty uninteresting emails on computers and talk to some NPC:s in the right order. Then leave and collect your "reward".
* And yeah, they changed the Matrix, like many reviewers have been pointing out. While a bit repetative, I find the new Matrix in itself rather good. Unfortunately this game hardly has no battles in the real world. You just jack in, battle the security system and jack out. In the previous games you had to protect your decker and fend off against aggressive foes with your remaining party members, which added a layer of suspense to the decking mechanics.
I really tried to like this game, but can't recommend it. It's just not fun.

Unlike the other Shadow Run games, Hong Kong falls short on several avenues. In this iteration, only two of the five characters have their back stories flushed out, with personal missions garnering comparable intrigue to the main story line. That said, the main story line was not terribly interesting; however, the final chapter did have an appropriate climax and resolution.
The engagements in the Matrix have changed dramatically and you will either love or hate the change. Personally, some changes such as the password component associated with firewalls is an interesting addition. Also the ability to disconnect from interface at any time is a nice change. A less welcome change is the addition of the frogger sequence where you need to dodge the path of the security programs.
While the main story line and personal stories of some of the characters are lacking, the brief interactions you have with NPC's in the world are short but very interesting.
Mission and gear:
There don't seem to be very many missions. I think there were maybe 10 missions before the final chapter?
There are some additions in terms of weapons but, in my playthrough at least, there were no special armors with attribute/skill bonuses - only cosmetic differences.
Overall, the game, the story, and the changes are quite disappointing.
If you're desperate for a new shadow run game, I would save your money until the game goes on sale.

As a fan of the Pen and Paper version I absolutely love this game. If you are a fan of the lore and don't hate cRPGs, then this is money well spent. If you liked the first two games, then this is money well spent.
After my first playthrough I can say, that the game entertained me greatly all the way through, even though the story was kind of predictable after some point. Nonetheless engaging and the writing is excellent. So overall I love most about everything about this game, but there are some minor nitpicks.
Please bear in mind that I played on hard, if you're playing it on a lower difficulty your experience may vary.
The matrix got an overhaul. Even though I was one of the few that liked the matrix in the old games, I still think this is an improvement. However, there are some things that might put people off. Note that I have not yet played a PC decker, the experience may therefore vary.
It is way to easy. I played on hard and finished the game as a Face (max. Charisma, all etiquettes) with some cyberware and some rifle-skill in about 27 hours. There wer only very few parts of the game where I felt actually challenged. And I am someone who seldom finnishes a game, even less so on the hardest possibility. The most bothersome thing was the grenade-love of NPCs, and you can get past that quite easily with a nice little cyberarm. The only thing, that was remotely challenging was the matrix and that is most likely only because I had to use Is0bel, who is only okay at matrix combat.
I have now started another playthrough, where I changed to normal difficulty, just to check things out and because I wanted to build an even less optimized character (burn-out adept-cyberweapon-shaman-grenade girl). It is ridiculously easy...
Loading times are long. Really long, and tehy got progressively worse. I had up to 30 seconds of black space before a loading screen even appeared. And when you're reloading your quicksave over and over again, because Is0bel screwed up in the matrix, but you want to get it just perfect, then you're going to wait. A lot. I think I can attribute at least one hour of my playtime, only to loading screens.
One nitpick of mine is the fact, that when you start up a drone, the controlls automatically switch to the drone. I can't even remember how often I have tried to relocate Racter after activating Koshei and relocating Koshei instead. But that was also the problem in the previous games, so that's old news.
Well, I already said, that I actually love most all of this game, but there are some things that stand out.

I'm now a good ways into this great game and feel comfortable reviewing it as a strong 9/10 skillsofts. I wish to write this as a counter-argument to RPS' ridiculous review which said "It only adds scenery, not actual gameplay changes, tho people who like the shadowrun universe will undoubtedly love it." I usually agree almost totally with RPS reviews, but this one really took me aback because it seemed as tho the reviewer didn't even play the game. I may love the shadowrun universe and its tropes, but I'm no fanboy in the sense of sticking to a brand just because it is that brand. In fact, while the same engine has been used (with new anti-aliasing x8 support for a real graphical upgrade), the mechanics of the game finally feel well-fleshed-out and balanced. Some spoilers on gear you can obtain ahead.
Changed Mechanics/Added Gear/Balance:
-Skills that are balanced and make sense: finally, the skill tree doesn't feel like it's reinventing shadowrun mechanics as much. While still not incredibly true to the pen-and-paper game, the addition of "Cyberware Affinity" makes body worth investing in not only for the HP, and cool things occur like mages and adepts both benefit from willpower, so I made a mage-adept (in that order) for fun, tho usually the mage skills are my mainstay, the adept passives like higher movement speed and protection from magical or physical damage are incredibly useful even if I'm not using my magical sword of doom on this particular mission, hitting twice per round, and using the adept counterattack qi. This kind of thing makes you decide between spells/qi to put in your spell slots and tailor it to the mission parameters.
-Trade most objects (some are character-specific and "locked") between your chosen team and the stash. Allows you to buy weapons for your teammates if you so choose, tho see below.
-Main teammates level up system: As you level up, your teammates will too, allowing you to choose between two distinct abilities unique to that character per level. Their gear will also improve, particularly if you talk to them often.
-Cyberware overhaul. Ever wanted cyberware to actually be game-changing and have insanely cool special abilities? Well, that's in now. Cyberweapons, like the monofilament whip that hits up to 7 tiles away. Eyeballs that flash bright lights acting like flashbangs to enemies. Wired reflexes/Reflex Triggers that give you significant advantage.
-Totally reworked Matrix/Hacking minigame: The Matrix really comes to life in this game, and not just in the art. Now tracer drones patrol the matrix seeking to make the system more aware of your presence. "Blocker IC" walls can be overcome by forcing them (costs 50 system awareness), hacking them in a challenging memory-minigame that costs 20 awareness, or knowing the password and keying it in. The Matrix is insanely useful now, with cooler programs to choose from, and I keep my decker-teammate close at hand on every run, tho it's not strictly necessary.
-Foci/Fetishes/Totems: Focused spells available that mod the basic function of spells in cool ways... a strip armor spell that gives you back 1 AP if you hit, but does less armor stripping, for example. Fetish objects that increase your base stats when in your inventory (doesn't take up a spell slot tho). Shamans now get to choose which "totem" or animal-god they follow, which can alter their stats, or give really cool active and/or passive abilities.
-New Gun Choices: Not only are there guns like the grenade launcher, but things like the remington roomsweeper (a pistol that shoots like a shotgun), pistols that fire three-times in one shot, prototype laser-snipers, flechette (bleeding dmg) weapons, and more now exist and force you to carefully choose your own style of blastin' badguys.
-Very Good Story: I do kind of feel like SRR: Berlin had a better story overall still, but this Hong Kong Mystery really does keep you wondering. My main complaint here is that the writing seems a bit stilted in places, and lacks the gritty polish of SRR: Berlin. Still, tons of side-conversations to have with your fellow runners and a lot of fun.
What I'd like to see in the next SRR game:
-New engine: scrap isometric rending, I'm a bit tired of being stuck behind buildings and not being able to rotate the camera. I want more character model choices that are more detailed, and I want to zoom in the camera very closely to see all the diffent details of my gear and active/passive spell effects on my character.
-Open-world: A bit less linear of a world. Yes, mission order and even which missions you take are optional, but let's face it most people playing are going to want to get all the karma and nuyen they can and be completionists. While different dialogue options do really influence the outcomes of runs now, there should really be an open-world in the sense of just exploring and running into runs rather than the formulaic "back to base, take the train to another run, loading screen, rinse-repeat." The sega genesis shadowrun game was much more open-world, guys, and that was ages ago. Use too-difficult-for-lower-level-runner areas to pace the plot
All together, tho, this game is EASILY worth the very modest non-sale price that's currently $20 non-deluxe. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED for anyone looking for a great story and tactical turn-based XCOM-like combat with a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of customization and character progression thrown in for a true, gritty, futuristic sci-fi experience that we've all come to know as "Cyberpunk."

It's unfortunate and really unfair that there remains some latent connotation between "uncles" and various forms of child abuse. But there does exist this comedic trope and given that, you'd think the Devs could have come up with a better name for this game.
Point blank: this may be the worst title for a prefessionally produced video game I've ever seen.
The real shame of it is that the gap between how bad the title is and how good the actual game is can't be bridged. ASAMU, as I'll classily refer to it, is nothing less than a diamond in the rough. It's one of those games where all of the content in it is extremely polished. There are only a few worlds, but all of them are distinct and beautifully crafted.
Though some of the actual character animations are a little too cartoony for my taste, the overall design is brilliant. The game really succeeds in pushing a sense of wonder, that frankly, most games that even attempt fail miserably at. The gameplay feels fresh - and fair - even when it gets difficult. The achievements are pretty absurd, but the game itself has a great balance.
If I talk about this game in generalities it's because I think the best way to play this is not knowing a whole lot about what to expect - particularly the main action mechanics of the game.
You really have to treat yourself. Do yourself a favor Morty - load up this game and just start playing with no expectations.
It's worth it despite the God-awful title that will shame your Steam Status.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

Short version: I recommend despite not being a big fan of fighting games in general. That said, it might not keep you terribly entertained for any great lengths of time, but it has potential as long as more content is added by either the devs or by the community.
Long version:
Basically game plays similar to a fighting game. Two people, one arena, best out of three. The twist is in the combat system its self. Swords clash and deflect off each other, creating opening for light attacks and heavy stance attacks, when timed well, can do tonnes of damage to the people who dare give you an opening. Grabs, projectiles and charged attacks are thrown into the mixture as well to give you some more interesting options to play with.
To break it down there are four characters available in the game as it is now, each with their sword fighting style and speeds.
Sword lines project the path your sword is going to travel when you attack. To avoid taking damage from these attacks, you opponent can dart out of the way, roll to avoid the sword's path (yes, provided you can time it right, you can roll under a horizontal sword swing to avoid taking damage), block to take less damage or clash swords with an attack of their own.
That's just the basics of how the fights turn out. There are two types of server available as of now; Duel and Free For All.
The way duel servers work is quite neat. On each duel map, there are three different arenas to fight in. If all three are in use, you can queue up to join one of them and spectate the current dual as you wait. At any time, players in an arena and its queue can vote to make the arena they are in a 2v2. Free for all servers are quite different. Instead of the map being split up into three, all people are in one big space and can attack at random or challenge each other to private duels to avoid being interrupted by randomers.
As you fight, you gain a form of currency called 'notes'. These can be used to buy new swords, skins, capes and masks for your preferred characters. I'm interested to see how the workshop is integrated though. The workshop seemed to undermine the whole currency thing, letting you download free, visible-to-all swords. All the items off the workshop have been removed though, so they're probably addressing that now. The global ranking system is a neat idea too. With every win and loss (and apparently hit landed too) contributing to your rank which is on display and for everybody to see. Is a nice little touch to either give you a boost of confidence or a boot up the♥♥♥♥♥depending on whether you've been playing against a dev or not.
Speaking of which, the devs are friendly and very in-touch with the community. I've run into them a couple times in game, which I can't really say for anything else I've played.
Anyway, I would say this game is worth your money. It's a nice little idea, and I'm interested to see how the devs are gonna continue to add to this game.

Insanely good - I had concerns about latency or hit registration, all gone after the first minute: it *is* solid.
There's really a tactical dimension in the fights, so doing the wrong move at the wrong moment can be punishing if the enemy react properly to your error - but you can always come back into the fight after a nasty beating, if you manage to surprise your opponent.
Playing with the expectations of your adversary is central to the gameplay, which mean even the beginners have a chance to land a good hit or even a victory.
The game already has a "ranking" system, so if you're still learning you can stick to the other beginners - but even the veterans will adapt their playstyle to your level: I wasn't stomped or crushed by them, they simply enjoyed trying more risky moves.
When Chivarly duelling is bashing medieval weapons at each others (all in good fun), Blade Symphony is dancing around your opponent to land accurate strike on their sides, back and front (when unguarded), swinging your sword to counter their attacks.
Ever managed a successful dodge with the Man-at-Arms, to strike your target on his sides or back, as his heavy sword/axe/pole misses you by an inch ? Blade Symphony is that, taken to whole new level.

Edit: About 90% of the community is gone, there really isn't much here anymore. DO NOT PURCHASE.
With such an elegant fighting system Blade Symphony can bring out plenty of "fight for your life" moments where everything shifts into full gear leaving you wanting to experience more. A small but nice selection of character and sword classes Blade Symphony feels elegant and classy when dualing others.

The Bit.Trip games are all pretty polarizing. Runner seems to have the most notoriety of the series, probably because as a platformer it's theoretically the most accessible, yet in practice it's a complete exercise in masochism. Runner 2 (mostly) ditches the deeply ingrained faux-retro look of its predecessor, makes the bonus stage system less horrible, and adds functional difficulty settings and a midway point to each level to somewhat mitigate the frustration factor. If you weren't a fan of the original, though, I wouldn't expect this to change your mind.
Despite checkpoints the levels are still just as finicky, the game now utterly botches its tutorializing of the keyboard controls (protip: use the arrow keys and spacebar, not WASD and J), and regardless of which graphical style the game uses it still seems overly 'busy' and can be unnecessarily hard to focus on the elements that you have to to be able to play well.
In brief I'm really lukewarm on both games, but this one does have Charles Martinet voicing the narrator of the game's plot which is presented as a corny homage to old Saturday morning cartoons. So it's got that going for it.

Runner2 manages to fit in a lot of character, challenge, and humor, in an unlikely place.
Bit.Trip Runner was simply too hard for me. My sense of rhythm and eyesight are both pretty terrible, so it was too much for me. Runner2 improves upon the original in every way, though the art style might be harder for some to read.
Revolving around a constant runner of your choice, you have to enter a series of combinations that both make music and allow your runner to progress to the end of the level. It may sound simple enough, but the difficulty ramps up on its own, and the level of challenge can be controlled by the player. The levels rarely feel too long, and the check point can be a life saver.
Runner2 constantly gives incentives to keep you going, with humorous costumes and characters to unlock, leaderboards, retro levels, and great animation. The reverse merman and disco hamburger had me grinning even when I was stuck on the same section for an extended period.
Runner 2 is aesthetically pleasing with simple mechanics, great challenge, and lots of personality.

Very undewhelming roguelike.  For several reasons.
First, there is no inventory system, so the classic roguelike gameplay element of picking up resources to take with you and making decisions on what you need most and when to save them vs use them is nonexistant.
Second, success is completely reliant on loot rng to find the correct enchants/resists on random items.  If you happen to not find the correct resist for a given quest, you will lose.  If the dungeon is being stingy and happens to not give you any food to restore hp, you lose.  If you get lucky and find all the OP stuff right away, you probably win.
And lastly, the whole 32 characters to unlock thing is a bit of a lie.  There are actually ~3 characters, warrior, archer, and mage.  There are 32 variants of those, not characters themselves.  Each character has a different weapon/armor/start stats, but they are the exact same otherwise. This system is actually a bit of a downer, many of the games quests are basically impossible with the starter classes, but become objectively easier once you unlock some strictly better variants.
And tbh, there are better roguelikes that have been in developement for decades, still going strong, that are free and better than this.  I typiccally love roguelikes, gave this one a fair shake, and found it to be far too shallow for my liking.

LISA is a post-apocalyptic turn-based RPG with an 8-bit grindhouse aesthetic. Like any grindhouse movie, the violence, swearing, and uncomfortable sexual overtones that the game forces on you are gratuitous and handled without an ounce of nuance or subtlety.
Lets get the gameplay out of the way first. Bog-standard RPG combat with a pointless combo system that is incredibly tedious to play once you understand how it works (never explained, btw). Find the best combo and spam it. Go back and forth between big, empty levels where you do little more than climb up and down platforms for seemingly no reason than to extend the playtime of the game.
Completely lifeless level design through and through. After the "shock" of seeing mutilated bodies and blood splatters wears off (clock that at about 3 seconds) you'll find that you're just pressing on from screen to screen without really taking in any scenery...because there isn't any. It's just big brown screens with platforms and ropes, forever.
LISA prides itself on being challenging and forcing you to make hard choices with its "make a sacrifice or lose a party member" mechanic and the fact that resting in many spots will often incur a large penalty onto your party. These are the only cool things about the game, and I will give points for these interesting mechanics! That said, any "difficulty" in a turn-based RPG is always nullified by grinding, which LISA encourages you to do, relentlessly, with a propensity to throw you into an inescapable combat at a moment's notice - hope you're levelled up enough, or saved recently.
Back to the elephant in the room, though - the art direction/tone of the game. I'm sure there are people out there who play games like this and go, "♥♥♥♥ yeah! Finally, some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s make a real game that isn't afraid to show you some ♥♥♥♥ed-up♥♥♥♥♥♥like a guy's head getting bashed in with a baseball bat and jokes about♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥a little girl!" LISA caters explicitly to this demographic, and naturally comes with the token pretense of intellectualism. You know, the "ooh, this is humanity when society breaks down, man" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that makes people think they're experiencing something other than pure, animalistic carnage for the sake of carnage.
It's not that I'm even against that, in the right hands. You know who did this better? Hotline Miami. The aesthetic, the mood, the Heart of Darkness horror, all of it done loads better, in a game that was actually fun to play. If you want to drill into an NES sprite's skull, you can do that in both games - but Hotline Miami is a game first, and a snuff film second.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a turn-based action RPG. This game encourages you to spend a lot of time reading. There is no spoken dialogue, so a lot comes down to your own imagination. I know reading lots of text is not for everyone, but the dialogue in the game is well-written. If you allow yourself some time to follow the conversations between your character and the personas you encounter in a tumultuous, futuristic Hong Kong, the story
suck you in. The beautiful art style of the game really helps the story gain a foothold and the areas in which combat takes place seemlessly blend in with the surrounding environment. The music in this game is great and diverse, and in each different area of Hong Kong  you will hear various background noises that make the game come to life.
When you are not busy delving into the rich background stories of your fellow Shadowrunners inside your headquarters, you can embark on missions (so-called Shadow Runs) that you can select via your mission computer. Each Run consists of completing verious objectives, such as kidnapping a target or infiltrating a building. Each mission contains plenty of turn-based violence for you to enjoy. Tactically positioning your squad is a must, for the enemy will try to flank your Shadowrunners whenever possible; increasing the damage you and your squadmates take. Combat is fun, challenging and dynamic, and there are often multiple ways to deal with your opponents: Be it engaging them from afar with heavy (sniper)rifles while your melee fighters sneak in to finish the job, using mages and riggers to summon powerful spiritual and robotic allies to wreak havoc from multiple directions, or even by jacking into the matrix (lol) to cripple the enemy's infrastructure before taking the fight to them head-on. You decide how you want to play.
Even when you are not much into reading the story, the game's combat system is challenging and diverse enough to encourage multiple playthroughs. Having the ability to create a completely different character that you can heavily customize by spending points in different skill trees will make each playthrough significantly different from the last.
The only minor point of criticism I have is that the choices you make often only have a minor impact on the main storyline. In an RPG, I would expect the (dialogue) options you choose to have a little more impact on how the story unfolds.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game, provided you don't mind reading a lot of dialogue.

This is NOT A HORROR GAME! I wanted to put that sentence at the very top, not as a criticism, but just for anyone who might have been scrolling past this after having seen the bizarre "horror" tag attached to this game. That tag nearly put me off from playing to begin with, because I'm just not a horror fan. But I'm glad I did play, because only the second level is even remotely horror-related, and the rest of it is much more my kind of thing. Anyway, on with the review:
So first thing's first, when playing this you will find yourself very tempted to compare it to Davey Wreden's The Beginner's Guide. The overall "feel" of the game, as well as several of the individual levels, are reminiscent of The Beginner's Guide, and the developer's commentary name-checks Wreden twice. The game even borrows one piece from The Beginner's Guide's beautiful OST (the housecleaning song from TBG can be heard during the ladder-climbing sequence in this game.) There's even a "Beginner's Guide to..." book that can be seen on a shelf in the game.
However, despite the fact that this game practically begs to be compared to TBG, I reccommend you restrain yourself from doing so. While there are certain similarities, the two games are fundamentally different in what they're trying to do. TBG is a heavily narrative-driven game with a relatively more limited degree of abstractness, whose clearly defined surface-level story conceals deep layers of hidden meaning and symbolism. This game is pretty much the exact opposite of everything in that sentence. Not because it's an attempt to replicate TBG that failed, but because it's trying to do something else entirely. So let's judge it on its own terms.
If you fail to do so, you'll search for hidden meaning in every piece of abstract symbolism, and when you find none you'll be disappointed. You'll assume it's secretly trying to say much more than it's letting on, and you'll feel confused and underwhelmed when you can't find the deeper meaning. You'll expect it to build and crescendo into an emotionally devastating revalation at the end, and you'll be surprised when it actually ends in decidedly anti-climactic fashion. In other words, you'll judge this game far more harshly than you otherwise would if you simply accepted it for what it really is, and proceed from there.
Having played through the game twice and read the developer commentary, I am now reasonably confident that it actually is just a series of little mini-levels, strung together in no particular order, mostly inspired by dreams. The only thing that really consistently ties them together is the presence of a door in almost every level, and a more or less explicit autobiographical aspect to many of the levels.
However, this is essentially just a series of interesting little ideas, presented to you by a very young developer, and most of them are at least fairly enjoyable to look at or to think about. I particularly liked the fact that there was an unaknowledged hidden level, which (for me at least) could only be accessed by the level select screen, rather than being integrated into the flow of  the main experience.
One legit weakness this game does have - aside from just "Boo hoo, it's not as good as The Beginner's Guide!" - is that the three levels which were, in my opinion at least, head and shoulders above the rest, and without which this review would probably be more of a "meh" than a "recommended" - namely the countdown/ladder level, the sabotage level, and the "Time to get over her" level - were also the three levels which seemed... err... "most heavily dependent on external inspiration" would be a kind way to say it. They're still great levels, with brilliant ambience and competent execution, but I was a little sad that the game's three peaks were also the three bits which most closely resembled ideas and symbols from Davey Wreden's games. However, perhaps that's just a comment on my own personal prefrences, and other people found the more original and inventive levels to be the highlights.
However, all in all I would recommend this game for an enjoyable, reasonably well made, fairly interesting, and somewhat emotionally impactful 1hr abstract walking simulator. It competently hits the target it's aiming at, and that makes it a good game, regardless of whether you think it's not the most interesting target it could have picked to begin with. I mainly enjoyed it because you can definitely see the seed of something interesting in there, and I can't wait to see how that seed grows and evolves in this developer's future works.

Road to Ballhalla is a marble maze game.  The only goal in each level is to get your marble to the end of the track, while collecting as many things as possible.  Many obstacles will get in your way.  Some require pinpoint timing and twitch reflexes to overcome, and still others involve puzzle-solving or memorization.  Later on, time trials are introduced.
I was disappointed with this game.
I’m not really sure what the developers were thinking.  This game looks and feels very promising.  The game’s aesthetic is very appealing, with a decent soundtrack and a modern arcade feel to the art style.  Clearly a lot of effort went into perfecting the gameplay, as the controls are responsive and the ball handles well. I also really like how the music syncs with the things that kill you; lasers fire on and off to the beat; etc.
Ultimately, I consider this game a real sideways-thumb.  However, in the end, this isn’t a game I’d recommend.  First, it’s too damn hard.  It is a game that is designed to kill the player constantly, and you will die a lot.  While there is a checkpoint system, levels tend to have too few checkpoints, and you will be doing some of the same sections many times.  Additionally, upon completion of the level, you will be penalized for death in the form of a reduction of the amount of your awarded badges.  The game expects (and mocks you for) failure, but demands perfection.
In an attempt at humor, frequent tutorial messages appear.  Occasionally, these will lead you to your death through deliberate misinformation.  This would be fine if death were penalty-free; however, it is not.  If I want kazio deaths, I’ll go play Eryi’s Action instead.
My stopping point was a level midway through the second world, in which the camera angle would frequently change; with each change of the camera angle, the player controls are inverted in a new configuration.  Inverted controls are mighty frustrating and not really very fun, but I was progressing in the level.  However, on top of this, at a scripted point, the camera pans away from your ball to show the upcoming level segment, and waits for you to complete the remainder of the previous section while blind.  At this point, I put the game down.  Who thought either of these things would be a good idea?  It’s just not that fun.

The game is something I regularly recommend to people who are unfamiliar with WoD, but are interested in vampire stories that are more traditional, intriguing, and -not- like Twilight.  Many people in this category also might not have time or interest to find a VTM group to play with.
This is an incredible journey through the World of Darkness universe, and it takes the tabletop game mechanics and adapts them ridiculously well to a PC video game platform.  Sure there's no GM, but they do their absolute best to make the game as non-railroad as they can while still preserving the story and spirit of choice within the game.  The choices also -mean- something.  Some choices are better than others, some dumber, rather than a lot of games that just chalk it up to efficiency vs. morality with there being barely any functional differences between the two.  The wrong choice -could- get you the Final Death.

TL:DR Great vampire orientated RPG though given its almost unplayable in it's vanilla state, installing the unofficial patch is essential to get the most out of the game.
Full Version:
Vampire: The Masquerade, despite it's age, is a great RPG. Despite the vanilla game being in quite a poor state, there is an unofficial patch thats easy to install and fixes most of the bugs and glitches as well as allowing you to set the game to higher resolutions than the limited options in vanilla.
It may be a little extra work to be able to play it in a workable state but it is very worth it. You get to play a freshly sired vampire who finds themselves in modern day LA. You get to pick one of several vampire clans in the game, each with there own unique style and skills. The games story and lore is pretty good as well as the whole being a vampire thing. You can drink the blood of the people walking the streets to heal and top up your power meter, but get caught doing that or stuff like using powers or attacking people and you get a masquerade strike. The masquerade is like a law that prevents vampires from revealing their existance to humans and get 5 strikes and its game over. However if you dont drink blood you can lose control as you give into the beast. All this adds an extra layer of fun on top of doing the games many quests.
Other than the fact the vanilla version of this game is unfixed the only other let down for this game was the combat. You can use your fists, melee weapons, firearms or your powers in combat. While the powers are useful, the melee and shooting is quite poorly implemented and combat becomes kind of irritating after a while. It's a shame that its quite often forced on you as well, as while building a purely noncombat build is possible, it's not advisable at all.
Overall though Vampire: The Masquerade is well worth playing despite it's flaws. It's a really unique RPG. I'd strongly recommend installing the unofficial patch for it though.

If you just want a short, quick oppinion: BUY.
For the details:
This is a 3D duelling simulation. I could say sword fighting, but that just isn't justified. The core of the game consists of 1on1 (or 2on2) duels with a best of 3 rounds system. The rounds itself are limited to 90 seconds, but often they can end in less then 20. Means each duel takes ~1-5 minutes.
The fighting itself is fast-paced, takes a lot of timing and precision, but is NOT the buttonmashing combospamfest you would know from other 'fighting games' (Street Fighter, Tekken, Mortal combat).
Graphic, Sound and Atmosphere wise you can easily call the game 'beautiful', because that's exactly the asthetic direction it tries to follow. Far-Eastern bells accompany your idle periods and fierce, but 'background-ish' war tunes accompany the duels. The graphics and maps are definitely influenced by eastern sword fighting movies and fit well into the game.
However, one of the best selling points of the game: The community. As of now, it got a large boost by the recent launch, but is still comparatively small. However, opposed to most other games, the communityin Blade Symphony is a POSITIVE surprise. On my first day I ran into the #5 ranked player worldwide, who wiped the ground with me and then spent the next 2 hours teaching me the in's and out's of my character. And when he was done with that, he went on and trained the next newbie.
Blade Symphony puts a lot of emphasis on that 'beautiful, honorable, gracious' style of duelling, adding a vide variety of emotes, most notable the bow, which is by now common etiquette at the start of ALL duels... and always obeyed. I think it's the atmosphere of the game, the example given by the good players and the way duels are presented that make people actually value the respectful tone of the duels.
Of course I must now as well mention it's downsides:
Whilst the overall appearance is nice, the graphics aren't completely up to current engines anymore. As well, the animations are not all fully perfect and there ARE animation glitches. Movement along walls (yes, the game permits wallrunning) isn't exactly smooth either (and is really more of a gimmick then an actual gameplay element). The ragdolls are usually horribly amusing, too.
Effectively, I could say the whole negative point of the game is that it's a budget game made by an indie developer who has nowhere near as much ressources as an AAA title.
Overall, Blade Symphony is, in my oppinion, the single most detailed duelling (/sword fighting) games on the market and well worth both money and time, even more so since it actually comes at a budget price.
Rating: 9/10

This does not make the game unplayable or not fun, but it does make it short lived and boring after some time. First of all, the player must realize that Hack, Slash, Loot is totally item based. The hero does not level up or improve statistics by earning experience points. All alterations, positive and negative are dependent on items that you equip or interact with. Because of this deliberate design limitation, there is very little to be done in terms of experimenting with strategy. The player stumbles upon items, hovers over them, and compares the numerical statistics with the already equipped items, and then makes a decision on what to keep and what to leave behind. The potions, altars, and other items that the player is allowed to interact with are complete surprises, changing your attributes at random without giving the player a choice. The sound effects get annoying and distracting after a while and I feel are not a good match for the art style and setting, sounding out of place. I beat a few of the quests and picked up some of the rare relics, but after the third quest win, I had had enough. Winning the quests simply does not feel rewarding and fulfilling. It seems more like a chore or a painful test rather than anything else, but in the beginning, when you realize how to approach the game, it's fun for some hours. Learning the enemies' vulnerabilities and resistances can be fun at first, but the game quickly outstays its welcome and becomes boring and shallow.
Hack, Slash, Loot is okay.

It's one of very, very few RPG Maker games that are actually good. LISA sends you into a miserable world populated solely by men who have lost all hope for the future. Life is cheap, those who live long enough suffer horrible mutations, and your character will be made to suffer. Like many Earthbound-inspired games, there is much disturbing imagery within, with music designed to unsettle as well. Although the game isn't all that dialogue heavy compared to other RPGs, it does a great job of telling a story with its wide variety of original, clever and imaginative visuals. The characters are pretty deep, deep enough to warrant multiple playthroughs just to have a full understanding of why the last hour of the game played out as it did.
There's a lot of permanent consequence in this game, so beware. From my perspective I find it to be kind of annoying and save-scum bait, but honestly that aspect of the game just isn't made for me. The Russian Roulette portion did feel like the RNG constantly cheating me, though. I actually had to save scum once I lost 4 characters to the enemy's one...geesh.
Two things worth noting: You'll get a bit more out of the game if you play LISA: The First, which is a <60 minute free RPG Maker game, before playing this game. The other thing is the game can be annoyingly grindy -- but RPG Maker save files are pretty easy to hex edit. (just be aware that values are always the minimum byte width necessary to store said values, i.e. exp will be 1 if under 256, 2 if under 65536, or 3 [not 4!] if >= 65536)

Going in blind I didn't expect this game to grip me like it did, but Lisa is quite the addicting ride. It's weirdly and strongly reminiscent of Earthbound and from start to finish was unique, depressing, and profoundly disturbing. The Joyful dlc was just as wonderful, although definitely too short to really sate my thirst for more. If you're not easily offended and like a non-traditional rpg, PLAY LISA RIGHT NOW.

is a clear spiritual successor to Earthbound. It is built upon the the same foundation - deep rpg elements, quirky graphics, and self-referential humor. Yet Lisa's form is infinitely darker and nihilistic. This game earned my runner up for best games I played in 2015 for its ability to affect my emotions.
Lisa: The Painful takes place in a world without women. In this void, men have taken up male prostition, murder and thievery to slake their lusts. You play as a troubled man named Brad. The discovery of a lone swaddled babe marks the beginning of his conflict - Brad has found the last girl in the world. After promising to protect her with his life, he hides her in his house and takes care of her with a few close friends for many years.
From the moment I started the game, until the moment it ended, I felt completely absorbed into the world of Lisa. At points I even felt abused. This is truly a painful game and something I would not recommend to everyone.
Lisa: The Painful is a 2D sidescroller with an rpg focus. Throughout your journey you will need to recruit different party members with varying abilities and powers. The gameplay feels natural, fun and intuitive. The developer has given you plenty of tools to customize your party orientation in whatever way you feel is best. However, where the gameplay truly shines is in the choices you will make.

The graphics are simple, but used to effectively to create a powerful canvas of sorrow and despair. Blood is strewn around the world with a liberal hand and the entire visual is one of rampant destruction and anarchy. The style completely engrossed me. In addition, the musical score also complements the game perfectly. One of my favorite moments of the game is when I

Don't get me wrong, I love a lot of parts of this game. The atmosphere, the characters, the music, and just the historical aspect of things following the Second World War and into the '50s. Vito is an alright character, but his interactions with his family and friends prove he's a lot less interesting than you might imagine. It seems they put a lot more effort into the other characters. Vito is just sort of tagging along. Also regarding Vito: I've watched a few WWII movies, the "rough Italian" is done one-too many times. But onto the game itself, mechanically, this game is adequate. Driving is /alright/, gun mechanics are simple, but fun, and fisticuffs is easy, but satisfying. Onto the (big) negatives. The story, overall, is just lackluster. Your entire experience in WWII is just one mission, and a short one at that. Most missions consist of "Drive x around. Drop off x. Pick up y. Follow y's orders." And I guess that can be sort of fun at times, but overwhelmingly you turn into a taxi driver who occasionally sells untaxed cigarettes or chops cars for parts. But I kept feeling, myself, that the story was going to get better. When I realized that I was 90% through the game, I was kind of shocked. What had I done? Where was my sink for the $50,000 I made? I can't buy cars or houses. Weapons and clothes are dirt cheap. Modifying cars is kind of cool until you remember the driving system isn't very good. The game, as a whole, just feels very rushed mission-wise. It's a shame, really, because the first game was amazing, save for the first two-or-so missions, and even those weren't as boring as the ones in this game. Overall, buy this game if it's $5.00 or $7.50 at the most. It's certainly not worth full-price.

I'd like to preface this review by stating that this particular motorsport subgenre has been either ignored or given a pretty crappy treatment for decades. "Why" you ask? It’s simply not popular enough. The fan base has shrunk over the years and therefore, we go largely ignored because we aren’t the cash cow fans of NASCAR or Final Fantasy. So, developers mainly produce the same games year after year without really branching out most of the time. Once in a while we get an odd duck that’s out of the blue from companies like EA or Rockstar Games that just works and gets popular and is what we wanted. Most of the time though, us small track visiting, mug bog loving, tractor pulling, monster truck watchers get ignored. The last decent attempt at dirt track games that focused on small towns and even smaller tracks was from RatBag. Dirt Track Racing 2 was great, even included wheel support, but no monster trucks. The last monster truck game available on the market was some sort of variant of twisted metal featuring the trucks from the USHRA series (I believe). And let’s face it; Us mature rednecks prefer a purer response when we ask to crush cars from the safety of our homes.
In comes ODD Games with the Android port: Monster Truck Destruction. I feel it’s a solid entry into a subgenre that has been abused like a red-headed step child.
Upon my first play of this game, I admit, I had to use xpadder and some magic gamer dust to get this to work, but the patches came pretty quick and after a while, I didn’t need xpadder or any kind of trick to run it. It just works now. I find that there still are bugs, but none which make the game completely unplayable such as the tree disappearing in a drag mode. (Shut up and just hit restart, ya pansy.) There is another glitch in freestyle where it will miss tricks or fail to continuously add combos without a restart or two once in a while.
On to bigger and badder fish, the trucks. They did include some interesting entries like “Wild Thang”, “Snake Bite”, and “Bigfoot 5”. Scrolling through the list kind of makes you think the game was partially funded by the good folks at Big Foot, when you realize that there are 15 (possibly more) trucks that Big Foot owns. Kind makes me long for a customization option. I’m happy for now though, as most of the trucks feature different wheelbases, and weight distributions which heavily effect driving style. After you get through upgrading a few trucks and really delving in, you’ll find that the AI is kind of Odd. The will either go fine to the finish, or lose their line and go nuts, flip over and reset. As of this review (1/13/2017) This hasn’t been fixed. Either way, just keeping your truck in line is a task as they drive pretty well and require you to fight all of those horsepower, as you negotiate turns, avoid obstacles, and mash it when you see the line. I find that when the AI is acting fine, they provide a better challenge on later levels.
You will also notice that the upgrade system is a bit on the rudimentary side, as buying better parts does effect things like handling or acceleration independently of each other, all you’re really told is that the bar describing the truck’s “power” goes up with ever purchase of an upgrade. I feel like there is a lot of room to expand on this feature alone. A lot more parts could be added, maybe prices adjusted to a real world standard, and a true rating system for trucks before, during, and after upgrading would be a beautiful feature here. However, the fact that we even have this is a miracle if you consider what we’ve gotten in the past.
There are several modes of play including Single event, Career, and Online Multiplayer. Personally, I prefer career. It’s just fun to zone out and go nuts. In my opinion, the online piece needs an overhaul. People will routinely leave in the middle of a match and it’s generally just like a free-for-all. Single event is good for practicing a complex track you haven’t mastered yet and for setting a best time. I feel as though they can expand on this as well. In the 90’s, they did tug of war, mud bog, hill climb, water races, and so much more. We already have the groundwork, guys, we just need to build upward.
Is this game worth it? Yes, I’ve certainly gotten my 6 or 7 out of it and then some just mashing around in Bigfoot One and doing terrible things to it and the earth itself. No, the graphics aren’t perfect, no, the damage models aren’t perfect, the handling isn’t quite perfect, and there are certain things that need to be fixed but trust me, this game takes up very little Space on your drive, has a low price, and it isn’t half bad.
What can be done to make this perfect? Since ODD games seems to be a little…preoccupied at the moment, I feel as though the best move would be to turn this diamond in the rough over to the modding community and let them put the shinin’ rag to it. There are hundreds of talented modders out there who could give us something incredible from the mundane. (Just a thought, guys. -wink-)
In conclusion, buy this game. If you are any fan of monster trucks, 90’s monster trucks, 80’s monster trucks, monster truck racing, or freestyle, you won’t be disappointed. It has never failed to draw me back to it, despite it’s issues. Sort of like an ex that you can’t quite stop seeing but you don’t know why. I mean, they have their little issues, but overall they are a good person and one hell of a lay.
So, why not give a little for a monster truck booty call that ain’t so bad to chill with from time to time and the best entry in this subgenre in decades. After all, we have to make the best out of what we have. It’s not like big companies are knocking down our doors to give use great monster truck games.

Road to Ballhala is a platform game with some puzzle elements. In this game you control a ball and must reach a goal while avoiding obstacles. Overall it is a good game but requires a lot of patience.
+ Nice minimalistic graphics
+ Pleasant non distracting music
+ Very challenging
+ Easy to understand and control
- Snarky comments can be annoying
- Restart takes too much time (completionists may be annoyed with this)
- Small unnecesary annoyances can become big annoyances (e.g., restart requires pressing Enter instead of any key, menu does not loop when reaches top or bottom)
You control a ball that must be dropped into a hole. The objective is that simple. While you're at it you must avoid obstacles and you may get orbs in order to get a better score. Simple objective but hard game.
Patience is absolutely required for this game. Often you have to stop or slow down in order to avoid hazards. The game is also full of helpful but also snarky comments. If you don't have patience, stay out of this game. It is possible that you may rage quit quite a lot in this game.
There are some issues with this game. Restarting and respawing may be slow to some people. You cannot press any key to restart, it must be Enter. Respawning itself is fast enough but you have to remember you have to press Enter. Annoying at first but you do get used to it. The menu does not jump to bottom when there's nothing up and you press up. This is could be annoying when you want to quit the game while you're already frustrated from losing a particular level many times. Restarting ideally should be instantaneous but it takes more than I'd like, especially if you want 100% completion on every level. BTW as the developer of the game mentioned in the comment section you can press 'R' to restart. These small issues can get very annoying in a game that requires a lot of pacience.
Anyway apart from small issues it is a good game. I recommended if you like challenging games like I do.
In the first levels I had some issues with the overall speed of the ball and hazards but you eventually get used to it so I removed that particular issue because I don't think it's actually an issue at all when I got further in the game.
Clarified that the biggest issue is that restarting takes more time than I'd like to. This could be particularly true for completionists. Unfortunally many games suffer from this issue, especially fighting games.

Review of Company of Heroes 2
I am playing Company of Heroes 1 for several years now, so I will have to compare COH 2 with it - there is now way around it.
I bought the complete edition of COH2  last week on Steam Wintersale.
Big question: is it worth it? Especially if you already have COH1…
Let’s see:
I played the first mission of COH2 - Stalingrad - and a coop game through multiplayer.
So you could say this is a - First Impression Review - if you like.
- Menu:
What striked me first was the messy menu: buttons and info everywhere.
Too much on one screen for my liking.
- Complete edition ????
Thought I bought the complete edition….but it seems I have to buy a lot of extra’s in the build in store for some reason…WTF? Like skins and so on….I think those kind of things have to be free of charge or should be unlocked by playing the game as a bonus - FOR FREE! NOT STEELING MONEY FROM PLAYERS WHO ALREADY BOUGHT THE GAME!
- Graphic settings:
Very few - but enough to customize to your personal liking.
The autodetect feature is not very helpfull. Tuned everything down on my laptop on - low -.
But I could easily run the game on high after I customized the settings by hand myself.
- Streaming:
The game automaticly records everything you do. This causes a lot of fps drops.
It cannot be turned of in the menu at all! I had to edit some files myself to switch it of (just google - fps boost COH2 - and you will find a fix).
- FPS:
Sadly to say: this game is very poorly optimized. I can not see any difference of graphics quality between COH1 and 2, only that COH 1 runs smoothly on Ultra settings and COH 2 suffers huge fps drops even on medium settings.
Sometimes COH 1 looks even better - especially using mods (Europe at war and/or HD textures).
- Sound:
One word - GREAT ! No complaints there. Guns, vehices, voice acting, ambient noises are all well done. Escpecially when playing with a headset: bullets are flying from left to right and back again.
- Atmosphere:
The game sets the USSR mood very well I think. The - bit depressing - attitude of the Russian army is well played out. The desperation is dripping of your screen.
Sometimes you have to do stuff that could be considered war crimes, just to survive (no spoilers).
That dilemma is well set in this game and adds a lot tot he general feeling of the game.
- Modding/replayability:
The modding community is very much alive, so this game has lots of replayability in it.
- Muliplayer:
Lobby’s are abundant - so no worries there.
Tip: if you want to learn the basics of multiplayer : try coop with a fellow human player against CPU first.
From 5 different factions to choose from, replayability is not an issue here.
Verdict:
Like COH 1 a very good game, but I have to say: looking at the year of release COH 1 - for me - looks and runs much smoother on my rig ( Win10 - 64 bit - i5quadcore -Nvidia 710m - 8gb ram) - especially with the Europe at War mod installed.
I bought COH2 just to have my COH complete and it was on sale. Otherwise I would not have bought it. But I am glad I did:
Lots of new weapons, maps and units to explore - the atmosphere.
I would recommend to buy the game only when it is on sale. The standard retail price is way to high.
I think this version of the game (COH2) could easily been brought out as a mod or addon for the original game - that is also what I am reading of forums etc - and I have to agree.
If you do not have any of the games, I would suggest COH1 complete edition with mods (Europe at war - free download on Steam if you have COH 1).
Sorry COH2 -lovers.
But if you have COH 1, this game is a MUST HAVE to complete the saga!
You get A LOT OF GAMEPLAY for your money!
