Compared to other more well known mainsteam series, there probably aren't many vampire games in the world, and even if there are, there aren't many where the protagonist is one.
Bloodlines is also the first and so far one of the only titles to explore the concept of a vampiric society, where there are laws that must be obeyed in order to maintain the masquerade, a facade that allows vampires to live amongst humans without them realising it, lest the be wiped from the face of the earth forever.
These things make Bloodlines unique, and a classic. It's easily one of the best RPG games I've played over the years and still holds its own against newer games today in the same genre, despite using the Source engine and being released in 2004. So graphically it might not be up to snuff, although there are plenty of mods and addons out there that attempt to address these issues, as well as patches that fix a lot of the bugs that plagued the game.
Some have described Bloodlines as being similar to Deus Ex, and it is in more ones than one. Graphically dated, animation although nowhere near as bad is past its best, AI which can be kind of dumb at times, and combat which doesn't work particularly well. Technically very flawed, then.
But the writing in the game is top quality -- from dialogue to the overall story, it's all very immersive, atmospheric to the extreme, and it's what has kept me coming back to the game for years. It features replayability like few other games, as you can try different clans of vampire, all with different abilites, and you can go about completing quests in different manners, which will yield different results. And there are mods out there which add entirely new quests, new areas, characters, and clans to play as too. Bloodlines certainly has one of the most devoted communities out there, constantly seeking to breathe new life into this cult classic.
If I were to make a top 100 games to play before you die list, this would undoubtedly be somewhere very near the top. That much is certain.

There's plenty of excellent games that I would love to replay a couple of times, but for some reason going through the initial missions or prologues or tutorials tends to feel like a slog, and inevitably makes me stop playing and uninstall. It's just such an enjoyable experience - characters, writing, locations, music... It feels really, really cool to be a vampire in Bloodlines. It's far from being a perfect game, but it's easily one of my favorite RPGs.

This very ambitious game was far far ahead of its time, and it suffered because of it. It is buggy, broken and incomplete without a fan-made patch, and even then it's kind of difficult to get the game running properly, but when you do, therein lies a game that should've been released today, in one of the most fascinating universes I've ever experienced. VtM:B is a game that brings you into the massive World of Darkness universe and lets you experience bits and pieces of it's lore, vampire politics, and the sheer uniqueness of how it handles vampirism in the world. The story is great, the characters are well written, besides a few bad early 2000's tropes and choices in design, and it offers some good replayability just replaying as some of the different vampire clans you can choose from. I just hope that one day I see another great WoD game made that gets the treatment it deserves.
Word of advice: Don't play Malkavian or Nosferatu in the first go, they're far more enjoyable as a second or third run of the game

Sonic Team has ultimately achieved a pinnacle of perfection with Sonic Generations. Sonic Generations presents classic Sonic 2D gameplay paired together with modern 3D Sonic gameplay in a celebration of Sonic's history that captures Sonic's intense sense of speed and recreates a selection of the franchise's most memorable environments.
Each Act has been fully reimagined in vibrant and colorful palettes with branching paths and hidden areas that will have you blazing through each zone at impossible speeds leaving crumbling platforms, bridges, and columns collapsing in your wake. The soundtrack is a highlight of the game with tunes from previous Sonic games and some fantastic remixes.
The main game is relatively short but there are multiple challenge stages for each Act, many hidden collectibles, points that you can earn which allow you to buy skills that enhance Sonic's abilities, and a competitive Online mode. This is the game Sonic fans have been waiting for!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

Hack, Slash, Loot: Not, Very, Good
There have been multiple occasions wherein I have tried to play Hack, Slash, Loot. Both times didn’t last very long… As you can tell by my total play time of an hour. I’m just gonna be straight and say I don’t like this game. But the fact that I’m reviewing it after an hour should be more than enough evidence of that.
The main issues I have with Hack, Slash, Loot stem from the fact that it is based entirely around luck, it’s rather shallow, and frankly it’s just unengaging. Also I wanted to play it more, but it’s now continuously crashing; thus preventing me from even giving the game another chance. It’s almost as if the game knows I’m not fond of it and it’s hiding from further examination!
Crashing aside Hack, Slash, Loot definitely has some cool ideas, but the game’s execution could definitely have used some work. When the game launches, after you’ve taken about five minutes to parse the UI, you can pick from a rather large selection of quests-- these are essentially the game’s ‘campaigns’; and four character classes. The game’s various quests are really just a set of parameters on the random dungeon generation. Apparently the dungeons span multiple floors and also contain bosses but I’ve never lived long enough to see one…
This is because the game pits you off against a nearly unending horde of monsters that do far too much damage, have way too much health, and almost comically out number you. Plus healing items are few and far between due to the random nature of the game’s loot. In the hour I’ve played I’ve probably run through thirty or forty dungeons.
Let that sink in.
My longest run was probably 20 minutes, and I still never made it past the first floor. Hell, I’ve died in the room that I spawned in.
Fighting hordes of powerful enemies can definitely be fun, other games prove this. But Hack, Slash, Loot’s reliance on luck permeates into the combat as well. Even with a 60% chance to hit I find myself missing the majority of my shots. A fight with a single monster can take upwards of ten turns or more, which are spent watching your character and the monster haplessly flail at one another only occasionally connecting. Once you finally land a hit and damage to the monster you have to hope that you roll well... or you’ll find yourself dealing almost no damage, making the fight take even longer.
There’s nothing like missing ten attacks only to land one and deal 2 damage.
The best way I can describe this game is that it feels like a Pen and Paper RPG, like Pathfinder… But without any of the systems that actually allow you to do the cool stuff.
There are no modifiers that help your dice rolls, or give you an edge. It’s just raw randomness.
Most of the time you simply rely on luck, and hope that the five orcs breathing down your neck miss more than you do. Or that you get a good weapon that can deal decent damage. But that only happened to me once, and then I promptly died.
This game definitely has potential. And it’s clearly there under the layers of randomness… But  as it stands Hack, Slash, Loot isn’t worth your time.

I feel that, after Choice Provisions made the BIT.TRIP experience as what they wanted it to be, they could make the ideas in the games as what they *should* be. RUNNER is the game that needed a sequel the most: It was loved by Nintendo fans, and hated by SPUF users, and worked the best in line with an actual game. Designed with the PC in mind, it's a breath of fresh air like no other. Pretty much the only thing that remains from the original is the gameplay. The map system, difficulty settings, secret paths, and virtual "new car smell" (new car... paint?) make this so much of a better game than the original, you'd be hard pressed not to want to see Commander.Video go on entirely new adventures of the ilk. It has the voice of Mario, too.
There is one major flaw to this game, however; one that renders this entire exercise doomed by unfortunate heavy matter baggage. That is, this game is almost unplayable without using a controller. The first RUNNER had it completely fine using keyboard controls, so I don't have any idea why they needed to change them for the sequel. Therein the problem lies with having both hands uncomfortably bunched up in one part of the device, which makes pressing the keys seem so wierd when you should be able to re-map the arrow keys to jump and such.
Okay, so maybe it's not that bad, but still, the point remains that even the guy that beat Super Meat Boy at 106% with a keyboard couldn't tolerate this. This was the game that got me an Xbox 360 controller (thankfully it was a birthday present, so I didn't have to pay),  and after just a few minutes of play I could tell that this game was designed, like many others, with a gamepad in mind. So, this is great, but you should be cautious of the leaps and bounds you might have to make if you want to get into it.
A big improvement from the first game.

Future Legend picks up beautifully where the original Bit Trip Runner leaves off. It has you playing as CommanderVideo, jumping, blocking and springjumping his way across 5 different worlds to escape back to his crew.
The game expands wonderfully on the original, with different playable characters, costumes, challenges, bonuses, dance combos, the lot. It looks better, it controls better and it feels better.
Nor does the game ramp up towards the end arbitrarily, but instead puts difficulty into the game thematically.
Really super fun, completed each level on hardest difficulty within 7 hours. Check this game out!

Just as Dragonfall improved upon Shadowrun Returns, Hong Kong improves upon Dragonfall.  While the changes are often subtle, they make a big impact.
Runs are unique affairs, and rely as much on infiltration as they do combat.  Decking is no longer re-skinned combat, and is now real-time infiltration and mini-puzzles.  Shaman summons seem to be balanced better, and new totems add passive benefits.  Dialogue choices are more subtle and varied.
More importantly, I snuck a ghoul into a party filled with socialites by claiming he was the new star of an upcoming trid show about a cannibal chef.  Said ghoul was not amused.
10/10 will continue to drag Gaichu into uncomfortable situations.

This is going to be less concrete than the reviews I usually do, mostly a stream of conciousness thing, Maybe in reflection of the fact that the game is very here-and-there and doesn't really bother framing a complete picture.
I believe that SR:HK is the most "complete" Shadowrun game made since the Genesis title, in terms of adjusting the player to the unique setting. With scenarios like burning SINs, talk of essence, the infected being treated as a marginalized group rather than monsters, the unsteady march of Matrix tech, toxic shamans, geomancy metamagics and so on, the game really does go all in on the setting. Fans of the series will be pleased to know that the writing doesn't assume that the player is completely clueless about all this, though new blood might be a bit overwhelmed. Holistically, this is easily the most ambitious Shadowrun videogame to date. After finishing the game, I do commend the efforts of the design team, but I'm 100% sure they bit off more than they can chew.
Let's start off with how the game has changed since Dragonfall. There' a new "Cybernetic Compatability' skill, tied to Body, which is about as weird and unneccesary as it sounds. Cyberware is oddly not that much different from Dragonfall despite the extra attention given in the statistic system, although there are now cyberweapons, which is great. Etiquettes, which were unlocked in the past 2 games for every 2 points you put into Charisma, are now much more useful, likely a direct response to the widespread criticism of the imbalances between etiquettes in the other games. Some small changes exist across the weapon classes, such as small buffs to SMGs and small nerfs to ARs. The Matrix has been completely redesigned, now existing as a crude but easy-to-understand minigame where you evade matrix perception from White IC to keep your alarm state low while you "hack" (using simon-says like password crackers) through datastores. In keeping with the artistic redesign of the Matrix, the art team went all-out and really made a vast improvement over Dragonfall's visuals.
That's about as far as it goes. Combat is fundamentally the same, with the same enemy AI protocols being used since Shadowrun Returns, with, what I believe to be no effort whatsoever gone towards environmental design focused on their strengths. In Dragonfall, the AI was quite bad, but effort was given to make suit of their strengths, like positioning cover so that the enemy had the cover advantage and giving most of them grenades so that they can flush you out of cover and punish you for crowding. In Hong Kong, it seems that the design team focused more on what enemies would "realitically have to work with", which, since you are Shadowrunners and don't operate in conditions where you know you're going to have a tough time, is barely anything. There is no longer a Very Hard difficulty, and even on Hard, the combat is laughably easy because the cards are clearly stacked in your favor.
It might seem odd for me to say that this is both the most ambitious SR title yet and a game that made no effort whatsoever to improve the core mechanic of the game, but I think it's a matter of the design team's philosophy. I believe that HareBrained Studios considered the lackluster combat to be a "neccessary sacrifice" so that they could focus on the rest of the game without finetuning the core gameplay mechanic. HareBrained seem to subscribe to a Biowarian philosophy, where the "technical in-between" of the game does not matter as long as they deliver an immersive interactive experience. And, well...they're better than Bioware at it? But much like the metaplot of the tabletop game, any interest I would have in this story and it's characters mostly comes from the relationship between the characters and the setting. There's such a strained attempt at pathos that it becomes embarassing after a while. I realize that opinions are opinions, and that just because I didn't feel attached to SR:HK's companions doesn't mean others didn't either, but even compared to Dragonfall, who had a companion who's entire personality was "I ♥♥♥♥ up a lot", there's a real disconnect between what the player wants and how the companions deliver information.
It's like this: Is0bel is cool because she is a dwarven decker with a freaking grenade launcher. Gobbet is cool because she's a rat shaman who likes weird food. Duncan is cool because he's an ex-cop ork who can literally handcuff extra-dimensional beings. All these characters are
cool from a first impression, you don't have to jab me with poor attempts at pathos to make me like them. Gobbet is probably the worst example with this, you have to sit through three different "It was the summer of 83'" style talks with very little (and very forced) room for player input to even get a glimpse of her personal mission, and THEN you have to talk to her AGAIN just to here her say "I need some more time". The companions do this thing where they "emotionally process" things which basically amunts to them not bothering to tell you the whole story until you get 4/5ths of the way through the game in a rather stilted progression. Duncan, mother of god, is nothing
"emotional processing", his entire character is built around the idea that he "can't deal", and you don't even get a cool mission out of it. Look, I signed up to be a Shadowrunner, not a therapist, and I'm not saying you can't have a character that's traumatically driven and also likeable, because the game even accomplishes that with a different character, Gaichu. Gaichu is how you're
to write past-driven characters, in that his past pushes him in a direction that coincides with what you need him to do, instead of awkwardly meshing with it. It's too bad his dialogues have apparently not been proofread at all and sometimes he assumes things have happened that have not happened yet, and vice versa. Richter might be the best companion solely for the fact that his dialogue is straight and to the point and not buggy.
Speaking of which, this game, at least at the time I'm writing this review, is incredibly buggy. I normally don't even mention bugs and performance issues in reviews unless they're very pronounced, and my god are they pronounced here. Dialogue options are greyed out for no reason, dialogue "plays" out of order or fails to trigger at all, companion upgrades don't work, objectives don't work, and I softlocked the game twice during two different missions and had to restart. This is not even getting into the huge amount of typos or failures of logical sequiter, let alone incidents of truly suicidal AI behavior.
My consumer review is this: If you love Shadowrun, get Dragonfall, and if you like it, get this. If you've never heard of or are iffy on Shadowrun, get Dragonfall, and then MAYBE, if the bugs are all fixed, get this on sale. Overall this is about what you'd expect from a $20 game.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a continuation of the Harebrained Schemes series of stories taking place in the Shadowrun universe. The predecessor, Dragonfall (Directors' Cut) was a gem in RPG-gaming and improved upon the original success. In spite of being a rather small developer, HBS has had some success in this series of games which is the reason why this is their third kickstarted game.
Shadowrun: Hong Kong starts on a story arc which is separate from the previous games, so you do not have to play those to get into this series, however if you are unfamiliar with this games series there are some precautions you should have to consider:
1. The game has a lot of text in it
2. While story-driven, there is no way to play it without entering many firefights and combat situations
3. It has bugs
The first point is definitely something to consider for the modern gamer, almost all dialogue is written text without speech, just like in the old days of gaming. The advantage of course being that there are a lot of dialogue and interaction in the game which immerses you, with well-written sequences that create a lot of atmosphere. If you like to read, then this will be a pleasant experience - but if you don't have the patience for it, the game will be frustrating.
The second point is rather frustrating for a role player, while you will meet characters that are prone to combat that will aid you, there simply is no easy way to say this: You will have to fight. If you don't like combat, Shadowrun isn't for you. Shadowrunners are essentially mercenaries hired to do mostly combat runs. You will be able to gain advantages through dialogue and hacking and such, but there is no way to complete this game without long tactical combat scenes.
And to the last, third, and possibly MOST aggravating issue with the game, its bugs. HBS has made three games and all of them suffer from similar bugs. Some of which completely block you off from doing certain areas because there is a problem with some trigger, or because of a general "combat won't end"-bug. On top of this there are glitches where certain weapons won't show, and it looks like your character is shooting an air rifle (á la air guitar) and other things (like noxious clouds being immensely overpowered in the final chapter of the game). In some cases you can't do anything but reload the game and take a different route, in other cases you can try and press escape, and resume the game, click wildly, press tab, and sometimes you will be able to get back to "normality". This is a rather huge caveat though, HBS has many bugs from the original game still in their code. This is simply sloppy. I backed the game, and now am hesitant to do it again due to lack of playtesting and bugfixing.
Shadowrun: Hong Kong is still a very much enjoyable RPG-experience that gives you many decisions and options that tread the grey areas of morality and sometimes delving into complete chaos and amorality. The storyline is well written without going cliché on you, and manages to surprise you at times. For the prize, it is a very enjoyable game, but in spite of playing it through the weekend I felt it was short, and that interesting characters could have had more development, and that some scenarios could have been fleshed out more - add the bugs on top of this and it is a flawed gem, but still a gem indeed.

Once you tap the 9 or 10 numbers (that increase the number you have to memorize several times), you get a more interesting mini game to finish it. If you didn't, this one won't make you a fan suddenly.

In my opinion, Lisa is more about the setting than gameplay itself. The game is not player-friendly whatsoever as you'll get lost several times as you go through the game. But doing so you'll interact with different groups of characters and their personal conflicts. Is nothing groundbreaking as the story is pretty basic, but the characters are good enough to work together the whole story. Playing Lisa: The First (is free) might also provide some context about the protagonist behavior.
As i said before this is not player-friendly, and that's probably my main problem with the game. I am not asking for spoonfeeding gameplay, but with several random outcomes where party members you worked hard to power up might suddenly become unavailable for the rest of the playthrough can feel quite a bitter move. This RNG nightmare might make a big challenge for players, but i personally didn't like it as the next step you take you can either face a boss with instakills or find a moral choice leading you to several resets.
Lisa: The Joyful however doesn't take this approach as is a very short epilogue of the whole story. But while the game starts difficult with a small party and inventory, as soon you get a healing skill the game becomes repetitive since you can safely beat every enemy using the same tactic.
If you want a very dark game Lisa is a solid choice and will make you keep going with all its struggles. And/Or if you're the opposite of me and want a 'nuzlocke' RPG where your party is at one step of crumbling this might be your cup of tea.

This is one game designers should notice. Why? Because it goes so very, very far with so little.
-interaction of elements: take notice how the checkpoints, the blue "keys" and the teleporters work: all their characteristics will be used in different ways in later levels
-level design: with just a handful of elements to roll through, how different can levels be? Well...very different
-humour: I've just tried shiftlings, a game that attempts comedy at every corner, but that just didn't grab me. This game's designer is smart, know what the gamer is attempting to do and messes with that in just the right way. I probably never laughed as much with a game as with this, and I've played games like portal and the monkey island series. The great part is that perhaps because of the minimalistic style, the entire game becomes a part. From the "you don't like my carefully selected default settings?" over the many puns to even entire parts of the level ("here's what these elements will lead you to" <you pass a HUGE♥♥♥♥♥HARDCORE level> ...and then that never is a level in the first place).
-variety: there may not be as many levels as professional reviewers would want, but no level is alike (or easy, for that matter)
I would mention the clean interface, responsive controls and the very decent music, but these are but a standard level of "it's good". Not to sound diminishing (ey! it has good music, clean interface and responsive controls!), but there are more games out there that feature this. The things I mention above are the thing really worth noting where this game stands out above many others.

The great thing about a having a sequel that reuses an easily customizable RPG engine is that the developers can concentrate entirely on writing and quest content, which are generally the strongest parts of the genre. I've played Shadowrun Returns before this and it's easy to see how immersion and character building has greatly improved thanks to this increased focus on storytelling.
Each of your main companions have interesting and varied backgrounds, can have detailed conversations with you after every mission you take, and eventually grow as individuals as the story progresses. My favorite is Racter- a reserved, pragmatic rigger who can be pressed into revealing having such extremist views on the future of humanity that he could have easily filled in as a sympathetic supervillain in another game. Seeing my relationships with these characters grow and learning about their history was one of the biggest draws for me to keep progressing. Ironically, you also have the option to ignore these character stories entirely and focus entirely on missions- don't do this or you will miss a great deal of the game's content! This is a game for slow enjoyment, not rushing around mowing down enemies as quickly as possible.
However, people who do like Shadowrun's mishmash of magic and gunplay will find plenty to enjoy here. Gone are the long, grueling combat gauntlets and gimmicky boss fights of Shadowrun Returns, mainly replaced by short but intense firefights centered around interesting environmental pieces. The vast majority of combat in the game can be entirely avoided, and since your companions are more than capable of standing up to enemies at any point in the game you can feel free to upgrade your main character entirely into diplomatic/non-combat skills if you so choose. Or if you want to effortlessly kill everyone, be an Elf and invest all your Karma points into Quickness and Ranged Weapons. Seriously, no amount of reality warping magic and techological wizardry can match an ungodly accurate guy with an assault rifle.
I really liked all the creative ways the player can infiltrate corporations and trick NPCs during quests. However I think the game drops the ball a bit here by making combat much easier than it ever was in Returns or most other RPGs. Enemies tend to rarely be much of a threat except in huge numbers, and you generally can get away with mindlessly charging an enemy's defensive position instead of trying to intelligently make use of the environment. Compare this to a game like Wasteland 2 where trying to rush down a sniper will get your characters killed in a hurry. Sure, this isn't supposed to be a combat focused game, but it takes out a lot of the reward in trying to outsmart and avoid a group of guards when I can easily just mow them down without any consequence.
Overall this is a fun RPG with great quests and characters that suffers from being way too easy in terms of combat and a lack of replayability. If you're the type of player who enjoys reading a lot of dialogue and finding creative solutions to quests you will probably enjoy this game quite a bit.

Did you like BIT.TRIP RUNNER? Or at least the general gameplay of it? (The autorunning, jumping ducking, collecting gold, things like that.) But hated how the difficulty curve was all over the place, that a lot of the levels were really long, and had absolutely no checkpoints? And having to perfect a stage in order to get one try at a bonus stage that was trickier than the stage itself? Well don't worry, because Runner 2 fixes a lot of problems that the first game had!
Runner 2, is a really fun game. And it's clear that the developers had a ton of fun making it. (Or were on a ton of drugs.) Charles Martinet (I'm pretty sure you know who he's well known for voicing. If not, get out of that rock you're under) is the narrator for the game's cutscenes and menus, and it's very charming to hear his narration over the whimsical lines in this game. The game itself is a lot more forgiving than Runner was. For one thing, there's checkpoints, which makes Runner 2 a lot more forgiving than Runner. Don't worry, for those of you that got far enough in Runner to know what I'm about to talk about, there's nothing like Odyssey or The Gauntlet in this game. Gaijin Games finally learned what a difficulty curve was, and the game doesn't have any huge spikes in difficulty. And the game has a difficulty selection, which actually does something meaningful in this game such as removing or adding obstacles, unlike Runner, which either removed the optional gold, or forced you to collect them. And if checkpoints aren't your thing, you can also jump over them in order to skip them, which gives you a huge point bonus and lets you make the game as difficult or as easy as you want, which makes it really accessible.
Gaijin Games didn't fully learn their lesson about game design stupidity though. While you don't have to go through a bonus stage anymore by perfecting a level, you have to do a cannon shooting minigame, and if you mess up, you'll have to redo the stage if you want to get a Perfect +, which can get really annoying if the stage you went through was a tough one. Better than going through a bonus stage to get that though. Bonus stages are their own thing in this game, they're a lot fewer in number, and are nowhere near as tricky as the retro stages in Runner. Also you have 3 attempts to go through the stage, and can retry immediately if you happen to lose all 3 lives.
The gameplay has a lot of the elements from Runner, plus a few new moves, such as jumping and ducking at the same time, or ducking and kicking at the same time which can cause you to do a bunch of crazy maneuvers in some levels. There's also obstacles which can't hurt you, but give you a lot of points if you do them right. There's also dancing, which does nothing but lock you into a dance animation for 2 seconds, but gives you some points for doing so. Unfortunately means that you have to spam the dance button at every opportunity in order to get a high score, and adds a layer of frustration to the game if you're the kind of person who likes score attacking.
Unfortunately, one of the game's biggest problems are it's visuals. They're not bad, they're really good looking. Too good looking, to the point where in some levels, it can get hard to see your character and the obstacles ahead, which can cause you to make a mistake and force a restart. It 's pretty frustrating when that happens, and it gets really bad in the last 2 worlds. Also if you're into really hard games, Runner 2, even at max difficulty and skipping all the checkpoints never gets as hard as any of the other BIT.TRIP games. Of course for most people, this would be a good thing, as they were difficult games by just being ridiculous and having an unreasonable difficulty curve.
In short, this game is really good and much better than BIT.TRIP RUNNER was, and you should go and get it.

A humorous yet depressing post apocalyptic RPG about surviving a world completely void of woman, filled with perverts and weirdo's, this a sequel to the very lesser known RPG Maker game, "Lisa The First." You take control of Brad Armstrong who stumbles upon a female baby named "Buddy", who is the last hope for this humanity. Being the last female on Olathe, Brad wants to protect her from harm's way. As she grows older, her curious mind lets loose after years of being sheltered, and she inevitably gets captured. Brad set's out to save his adopted daughter, while the Painful journey begins.
Living up to it's name, Lisa "The Painful", is a game all about sacrifice. Being an Earthbound inspired RPG, the humorous tone is very apparent. Lisa crosses boundaries that not many other games have crossed, some moments you'll laugh, but some you'll be gravely upset with.  There are a lot of instances where you don't know what to think, along with sometimes being outright disturbed. I believe this is one thing I really enjoyed about Lisa, it really crossed those boundaries that too many games shy away from these days. It's important to note the sacrifice in this game that I mentioned earlier, you'll have the choice of sacrificing limbs, killing off party members, or maybe ditching all your items. These can end up being legitimately difficult decisions that will affect the gameplay no matter what choice you choose.
What seperates Lisa from other RPG Maker games, is that it's set on a 2D plane. You'll eventually obtain a bicycle which will make for faster transportation. You could call it "Metroidvania" in the sense where you'll have to backtrack to some areas with your newely accquired items, though it's a lot less complicated, with each crossroad consisting of 4-6 areas you'll be able to visit, making it easier to backtrack to areas without it being a hassle. It's also important to note how Lisa always gives you this feeling of being unsafe. Sleeping at campfires overnight can cause negative effects the next day, such as being poisoned. With over 30 recruitable party members comes with a price, some can leave you over night while resting, and some can end up getting captured. The battle system is your typical RPG stuff, although with few neat things added in. For one, Brad can string together combo's while bursting a special move (that drains MP), to finish it off. Secondly, your "TP" meter, which raises the more you get hit or deal damage. This allows you to perform some deadly special moves. Last thing that shoud be noted here is that unlike most RPG's, Lisa REALLY encourages exploration rather than grinding for you to level up which I think is a really good approach.
Lisa's soundtrack really is... something else. I can't go too in-depth on it, without saying it's really undescribeable, yet still really awesome and very worth checking out.
Of course there are a couple negative points that should be addressed. Being able to save and load constantly can sometimes draw away from "The Painful" feeling of the game. If the game forced you to save after sleeping overnight, or making a crucial sacrifice, this definitely would have lived up to it's name a little more. I'm aware the "pain" difficulty allows you to only save once at every save point, but it doesn't change the fact you can still load to prevent some of these. Sometimes text boxes can't even fit the whole text, it's not a huge deal, but it's really strange when I see a bit of text cut off.
I'm aware I've left out few important details such as "joy", and who exactly "Lisa" is. But I can't recommend this enough to anyone whose a fan of "comedic" RPG's. Be wary though, Lisa make's damn well sure to poke fun at you for some decisions and not hold back on making you feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥all while being really unsettling. It's important to note, Lisa eventually got a DLC sequel titled "Lisa The Joyful". While it lacks the charm of "The Painful", it's still very worth buying in the complete package. Any RPG fan who wants to see an interesting approach on the genre should definitely pick this up, especially while the complete package is still on sale.

This game is brilliant, absolutely fantastic.

Road to Ballhalla is a simple top-down arcade-style game. You control a ball, and your goal is to navigate your way through 20 levels, collecting little sparks (the game’s collectable) and avoiding dying as you go.
The game is very simple – there isn’t even a jump button. You can simply move in any direction, or speed up your rolling in a sort of dash move. The dash move makes it so you die instantly if you take damage, rather than simply… well, taking damage. This makes it risky to use at times, so it must be used judiciously.
The levels themselves present virtually all of the game’s mechanics. Each level has its own set of unique mechanics, and only a relatively small number of them recur – and those which do generally show up no more than twice, save for the most simple of things (jump pads, laser beams, switches, bullets, damaging patches of ground, ground sections which kill you unless you have picked up blue “keys” to roll over them with, which each deactivate one such spot).
However, the game still has a pretty broad variety of levels. One level sees you constantly phasing in and out of reality, allowing you to pass through/over deadly ground without being harmed. Another has the ball “hiccupping”, launching the ball in the direction of travel through the air every time, allowing you to clear gaps which you could not otherwise clear. Another level has a rhythmic bouncing which keeps sending you up in the air, a much more controllable thing than the hiccups – but you have to do much finer manipulation with it. That level also has a laser beam from the sky that damages you for 10% of your health every few seconds, limiting the time you can spend boosting as well as forcing you to get through the level within a short period of time (and avoid taking other damage). Other levels distort the view of the camera, require you to solve puzzles, require you to bounce over pits using launch pads, use a gigantic ball which keeps trying to crush you to deactivate lasers and trigger switches, and a variety of other mechanics.
The game feels like it is of the right length; if it was longer, it would probably get repetitive. But at 20 (fairly difficult) levels, it feels just about right. For added challenges, you can speed run the levels, which unlocks additional skins for your balls as well as various secrets. There’s also a scavenger hunt which requires you to use clues from the scavenger hunt area and then go into the various levels and hunt down secret areas, activating purple portals which give you directions so you can solve a puzzle where you’re running your ball over invisible blocks.
The game also has a narrator of sorts. The narrator doesn’t talk, but he leaves messages in the levels for you. Some of the messages change as you progress through the levels; others appear when you meet certain conditions. The narrator not only explains mechanics (often in a roundabout way), they also taunt the player, crack jokes, make endless ball puns (indeed, virtually every name in the game is based around ball puns of one kind or another), and sometimes try and get the player to kill themselves (including in one level where a new deadly mechanic is introduced and the narrator tempts the player into killing themselves repeatedly by making false claims about how it works).
The game has tons of checkpoints, so getting through the levels is not an impossible task even for a fairly mediocre player. However, if you want to get all the secrets, you’re going to need to collect every collectable spark in every level, and do it without dying – as well as speed run the levels. These optional challenges are much more, well, challenging, and combined with the secret areas from the treasure hunt provide a second, higher level of challenge for the player who wants to do more than merely progress.
All in all, beating the game is likely to only take a few hours, but 100%ing it is likely to take 12 hours or so.
If you’re looking for a fairly simple but challenging arcade-style top-down navigation game, this is actually pretty decent. The graphics are clean, there’s a bit of humor in it, and the gameplay is challenging but generally enjoyable.
Just be aware that this is a very simple game which is very mechanically oriented – there is no real story, just a series of well-designed mechanical challenges.

"Mafia" was a stone cold PC gaming classic. It was one of the first open world sandbox games and was the most matural and fleshed out of it's time, nothing short of a classic mobster movie.
Mafia II takes this and pushes it into the next generation. The game may seem slightly dated now for an open world sandbox game, but for it's tone and content, it absolutely works. Not only is it's time period and content extremely rare in gaming, so is it's story telling.
If anything struck me about this game it's that there is DISTINCT progression! You start off in Italy WWII while learning game mechanics, then it's 1940's america during the holiday season and all the cars are distinct. Then what I didn't expect is you eventually go on to an even later time period and it feels amazing.
All in all Mafia II is a distinct and memorable experience that is worth your time if you enjoy story and sandbox gameplay, don't pass this up!

I'm disappointed. Don't get me wrong, i still like the game and if you're familliar with its predecessors and enjoyed them, then you'll like this game too - but maybe with the same sense of 'if only' that i have after wading through it.

The art is pleasing but the text side of the game (not necessarily the story itself) is like some socially inept bore at a party who pins you to the wall with tedious rhetoric only he finds interesting and has no comprehension of actual conversation. There's so much useless text in this game that my eyes glazed over far too quickly, and i generally like text heavy games. For mood, theme and function (and it was the lack of the last that was particularly notable) presented in text, Baldur's Gate or Planescape Torment this is not. Hong Kong's predecessors were tight and slick in their text use and storytelling while Hong Kong just isn't, it becomes a laborious 'click through' that swamps the better features of what could have been the best iteration of Shadowrun by Harebrained yet.
Ultimately, its the editing of the game that is flawed, not the game itself. What a shame. Still, at least it /has/ a good plot and two dimensional characters in gaming are always better than the conventional one. I also think that this game will be much more palatable on a tablet rather than hunched in front of a desktop. Something i think proved true of the other two games too, so maybe wait for that... If you liked Dragonfall, then this game is for you.
I've fallen out of favor with ranking games on a 1-10 scale, so lemme just give the good points short and sweet:
This is a turn based RPG in the Shadowrun universe, and the second standalone expansion. You do not need to play the original or the previous installment to understand this one (though a cursory knowledge of the Shadowrun setting helps.)
If you like BioWare games, especially the classes like Baldur's Gate, get this game ASAP.
If you like cyberpunk and RPGs, you'll like this game.
If you're a fan of later versions of the Shadowrun setting, since this uses an earlier version of rules as its base (and changes those to fit the PC platform) you MAY be put off due to how different it is.
It also doesn't have the deepest of combat systems (your party members aren't COMPLETELY customizable, for example) but it's no shallow pool either.
While the characters are quite interesting, they also don't gel quite as much as Dragonfall's cast did. Interestingly, YOUR character actually has a history beyond "knew a guy" this time around. This may not sit well with some people who prefer to project their own stories on their characters.
Shadowrun is a rather unique setting. Honestly this game is about even with Dragonfall in terms of quality, so don't be afraid to pick it up if you liked Dragonfall.

Tl;dr: This series is just getting better and better.
Shadowrun is an isometric RPG set in a dystopian cyberpunk future. This is the 3rd game in the series by Harebrained Schemes and also the best. No knowledge of the previous games is needed to play this one.
In Shadowrun: Hong Kong, you follow your main character (which you create) and his/her childhood friend to Hong Kong as a request from your childhood father figure. When you arrive, you're ambushed by the police and forced underground to attempt to clear your names of a mythical crime and locate the man who brought you to Hong Kong.
What defines this series has always been the writing. You care about this story. You care about the characters. That's really hard to pull off so well and consistently in a video game. You *want* to spend time talking to your partners between missions and learn their backstories. You sympathize with everyone, even your main protagonist. By the end of Dragonfall I missed those characters and thought about them long after the story ended. This is a marvel in modern gaming.
As for the gameplay, it's another rock-solid progression in the series. Great and fluid and fun tactical combat that doesn't feel slow, a highly detailed world to explore, great characters and missions... there's really nothing to not like about this game.
I just can't recommend this series enough.

This game was made on the very first version of the Source Engine. It is riddled with bugs, barely even runs without the Fan-Patch fixing things up, and feels very rushed in its final quarter.
So why can't I stay away from this game?
Because it has a very unique, interesting and brilliantly executed setting. It's one of the few vampire-themed games that actually bothers to go into "Vampire Politics" without getting bogged down by big unskippable chunks of exposition. And lore-wise - which is based on the popular World Of Darkness Pen & Paper RPG - it explains you just enough out of the gate that you know the basic structure of the world but can still be intriqued and surprised by the things that bump in the night you'll come across.
You play as a new Vampire fledgling just after you've been turned. In exchange for sparing your life (since creating new "children" without permission is punishable by final death for both parent and child - as your Sire unfortunately gets to experience) the current ruling faction decides to employ you as an errand boy / girl in Santa Monica.
As you soon find out, L.A.'s secret nightlife is in a state of a calm before the storm. A rare, potentially devastating artifact is on its way to the city and each of the factions wrestling for control wants a piece of it and soon you'll have to decide who deserves your loyalty the most.
But that's not even mentioning the things that go bump in the night you'll come across in the various sidequests. While you don't get to see much of the other World Of Darkness denizens, keeping it (mostly) limited to Vampires and anything adjecient gives the game some focus. But you're still going to be surprised what can even scare an immortal creature of the night.
This is one of my favorite games of all time but please, if you pick this one up, go do yourself a favor and search the web for the fanpatch. They have done a tremendous job of not only keeping the game alive, but they've also restored some of the content the devs had to cut. If you're willing to put that little effort into it, I promise you you'll have a great time with this!

Simple is not always good. A game needs to offer its players enough options to form strategies against whatever challenges are posed. Otherwise, you're just playing a glorified slot machine. I don't think the folks behind Hack, Slash, Loot understood this because they made a dungeon crawler that has classes with no skills and loot with no inventory.
The game dumps you straight into a cluttered, pixellated menu where you pick your class and your quest, and then get dumped into a crowded, nondescript dungeon. The perspective is a weirdly squished 2D where tiles are twice as wide as they are long, which crams the otherwise pleasant character sprites too close together. As you navigate the random floors and rooms, you'll find items like weapons, armor, potions, and scrolls laying around. Gear can only be swapped with what you already have, with the stat change shown in the corner when you mouse over items. Similarly, consumables are used the moment you pick them up, and their purpose is obfuscated in an annoyingly Nethacky way so you don't know what they'll do for sure until you use them.
These are all corner cases for those times that you're not beset by monsters. HSL is packed to the brim with things that want to kill you, while offering absolutely no tactical options for killing them back besides funnel them through a doorway. While this isn't terribly different from many old-school roguelikes, the distinct lack of healing items or reliable gear upgrades is. Everything appears to be randomized in the extreme, and with no inventory, there's no way to store potions or food until you actually need it. There's not even a guarantee any will appear, because I've definitely had runs end on the first floor because literally no healing options were offered.
Imagine playing Diablo without skills, potions, or inventory, and you get a very basic idea of how flawed HSL is. Streamlined roguelikes are an excellent idea because many of the classics go way too far in their complexity, but this completely overshoots the mark in the opposite direction. Nothing you do in this game will effect whether or not you win, and there's not even any sort of overarching progression system to make losing worthwhile. With all the clever, interesting roguelikes on Steam now, Hack, Slash, Loot is better left forgotten.

Road to Balhalla is a nice ball rolling game with some rhytm game elements.
The controls are precise (I played on a keyboard) and the core gameplay is quite enjoyable. You navigate your ball through the levels collecting as many as orbs as possible. At the end of the level your performance is rated based on both the number of orbs collected and the number of times you had to restart from a checkpoint. After finishing each chapter you also unlock the levels for time trial mode.
The soundtrack is an important part of the game too. Many of the traps are triggered based on the tempo of the music, so playing with the music enabled is crucial. Personally I wasn't a big fan of the music style, but the mechanic certainly adds another interesting layer to gameplay.
My main complaint with the game is the lack of content. The campaign feels rather short and more official levels would have been welcome. On a positive note the game does include a level editor and Steam Workshop support.
Despite its faults Road to Balhalla is rather easy to recommend. The price feels a touch high for the amount of content you get, however, so it might be best to wait for a sale.
The good:
- Tight controls
- Well-designed levels (with a few exceptions)
- Nice humor
- Rhytm game elements are a clever addition
The bad:
- Feels a little overpriced for the amount of content
- Not a big fan of the chosen music style

Don't let this game catch you off-guard. You might look at Road to Ballhalla and think it's a shallow game with a simple mechanic - roll the ball through a series of obstacles and get to the end. You would only be partially right. This game will surprise you with its humor, its refreshing mechanics that always seem to add a fun and interesting spin on the gameplay, and its fair yet challenging difficulty.
Its controls are tight and responsive so that your deaths never feel like a result of unfair physics.
The soundtrack is a masterpiece of downtempo electronica that provides the basis for the gameplay. Every level shuffles its defenses right along with the tempo of the music, giving you a rhythmic foray through the stage. The levels are choreographed in such a way that a perfect playthrough often feels as though you're dancing through it.
Road to Ballhalla is a game that capitalizes on everything it sets out to do. Its basic yet beautiful art style, intelligent gameplay, and groovy melodies come together to make a seriously fun game. Reccommended to anyone who enjoys a good precision-controlled puzzle platformer.

Road to Ballhalla feels like if you took some of the concepts of the arcade classic Marble Madness, kept it largely 2D and gave is kind of a snarky attitude. It's a puzzle game that will test your reflexes and your patience but also feels oh so rewarding when you master it.
You'll have to navigate a ball through increasingly complex levels with more and more mechanics introduced as you go. In every level, there are orbs to pick up that will contribute to your final score. You are also graded on how many times you die in a level. You can just brute force your way to the end if you want but getting the highest number of stars for both orb collection and lack of deaths is paramount, especially as you'll need to have earned a certain number to progress to later levels. I'm not always the biggest fan of roping off content this way but since you can just plough through a level, it makes it easy to practice. While Road to Ballhalla isn't easy, it does get easier quickly with patience.
The campaign isn't super lengthy but it will certainly take a while to earn all the stars. There is also a separate mode that challenges you to beat levels as fast as possible and rewards you accordingly, unlocking more bonus content. There is also Steam Workshop support, allowing you to both create and play other levels. Some of them are positively mind bending.
Visually, Road to Ballhalla is simplistic but also pretty. It also has a great, largely chill soundtrack that also syncs to elements of the levels and becomes a key mechanic. The game has a purposefully dickish attitude and will mock you as you go. Some might find this annoying but it made me chuckle sometimes too.
Road to Ballhalla is a puzzle game specifically targeted as people who will like this kind of puzzle. It demands good reflexes, control and patience. If you liked Marble Madness back in the day, this is worth giving a look to.

is a puzzle platformer developed by Torched Hill and published by tinyBuild.
The game itself doesn't have a story, but throughout your experience you will find some writings that will either help you out by pointing out traps, or trick you intro trying something that will lead to your death. This way, you start not trusting them anymore, making for a very fun imaginary dialogue between player and developer.
The game is very, very colorful: each level is vibrant and it feels alive. The level design is top notch, and I never had problems with the perspective.
You play as a rotating ball who can only move and speed up, and your goal is very simple: get to the end of the level and try to die as little as possible and to collect yellow dots. What makes the gameplay fun and constantly changing are the traps, switches to activate, big rolling balls to avoid, leaps of faith to surpass, hidden passages, and many more...
Honestly, the game gets pretty insane later on in the game, but it always manages to be enjoyable and fresh, which is something very rare nowadays.
Each level is very challenging, but rarely frustrating, mainly because there are plenty of checkpoints that you can use.
The soundtrack is hugely important here, since some traps activate and deactivate by following the rythm of the music that is playing in the background, so playing with the music on is a must if you want to avoid dying more times than you normally would.
There are a few secrets, and once you finish an area you can play Rush mode, which is a Speedrun of the previously played levels. The achievements require you to unlock 100% in the game.
Overall, this is easily the best puzzle game I have played so far this year because of its fun gameplay and smart use of the soundtrack. Highly recommended at full price.

Ball or marble gliding games have been popular ever since Marble Madness became a smash hit in the 1980's. Many developers have tried to emulate the high-quality gameplay and mind engaging levels that  marked the title. Almost as many have failed in their attempt to capture that classic feeling. Hence, I am always hopeful that the next one will be great but quietly pessimistic. Developer Torched Hill is the latest challenger with their Road to Ballhalla. The title is appropriate not only for the game itself but as a description of the journey brave developers have taken to contend with Marble Madness.
Intellectual innovation is of undeniable importance in the video games industry. When a title has been made of such a high stature newcomers have to provide something new in order to better the title. Unfortunately, it seems like this is something that developers often do not realize or understand. Some developers have a belief that if they put a fresh coat of paint on top of the classic design that that will suffice. What ends up happening, however, is that gamers are delivered a product that disappoints. Hence why hugely popular games such as World of Warcraft have survived wave after wave of clones.
Thankfully, it doesn't take long to realize the innovation in Road to Ballhalla. I've never come across a game that successfully incorporates rhythm-driven gameplay into a genre entry quite like this game does. The developers have done a marvelous job in this aspect and deserve recognition. In some ways, it reminds me of Crypt of the NecroDancer in that it combined one genre with rhythm gameplay effectively. It seems like it may have been a source of inspiration.
The developers further understood that in order to have a successful title with their ideology that they had to have a great soundtrack. It is for this very reason that they hired Nicholas Singer, an Emmy-nominated composer. The soundtrack is as vibrant and alive as the futuristic styled graphics which are also of an exceptional quality. In a very nice touch, the sound effects are adjusted to the music.
Consequently, I recommend that if you own a headset that you play with it on and the volume turned up. It will enable you to immerse yourself fully into the intended experience.
If you enjoy a healthy dose of humor in your video games then you're in for a treat. The game is as full of puns and witticisms as it is balls. This is very good because it adds to the presentation value of the game dramatically. The constant flood of comedy gives the game a quirky and fun-filled personality that similar games just do not have. This, on top of the stellar gameplay, is one of the reasons why Road to Ballhalla is one of the best games in the genre that I have played.
There are two basic modes of play within the game. First, there are the standard levels or 'trials.' When you complete a trial you are awarded tokens. The more tokens that you unlock the better you have performed. Performance is graded not only on how many lives you lost but on how many shiny orbs you managed to pick up on your journey throughout the trial. The less you die and the more you collect the better you grade. In order to progress to the next set of trials you must collect a certain number of tokens.
Secondly, once you have successfully completed each of the trials a timed mode unlocks. This mode incorporates the Steam leaderboard system enabling competitive players to set the fastest times on each of the levels that you have previously completed.
As well as Steam leaderboard integration the game currently has a set of 18 Steam achievements. The developers are also working on Steam workshop capabilities. As a result, the only thing lacking - and not announced - are the addition of Steam trading cards.
As a big fan of Marble Madness, a game that I still return to from time to time, Road to Ballhalla had to be of outstanding quality to win me over. It was able to do so thanks to its excellent presentation and fun gameplay. Of course, the humor played a significant part in it too. I am almost ashamed to claim that the game had me slowing down at several points because I didn't want to miss anything. Consequently, this is an easy recommendation.

VtM - Bloodlines is a timeless classic that holds up even more than a decade after its release. If you are thinking about checking it out for the first time or reliving this great expirience, here are some reasons to do so:
1. Plot: there is just not much to tell without putting in some spoilers, but the jist of things is rather obvious even from the game cover. You become a vampire in a modern (sorta) LA and start to adapt to your new community. The world itself is very detailed, as it is based on a long-lived pen and paper RPG setting called World of Darkness. However, instead of filling every second of gameplay with pointless exposition, like some modern RPG do, in this game all the intricacies of the vampire society are gradually fed to you through, honestly, really well written dialogue. And every dialogue in itself is quite a treat, since the characters are thoroughly thought out and make the story all the more natural and driven. The plot is unlinear, giving you five different endings, which is not exactly a lot, but not as little as three endings in all of which a protagonist dies (you know which game I mean). With all of its twists and turns, the story is sure to be memorable enough.
2. Gameplay: this game combines the features of FPS, RPG, slasher and stealth action in a perfect way. It is not overly original concept, but it is rarely done so well. If you liked how "new vegas" allowed you to choose between talking, creeping, shooting, hacking or punching your way out of every situation, you are going to love this game, as it rewards unorthodox thinking, giving you better bonuses for picking less obvious routes and just generally puting in a little extra effort (and also, unlike fallout, includes blood magic). It features an open world, which, to be honest, is a little small, but very well made, uncluding continous side quest, some of which last almost through entire gameplay. It also has some replay value, as there are two clans (classes), for which general gameplay and dialogue vary greatly. So, all those years after, it is still a fun game to play.
3. Design: So, this game came out in early 2000s, so don't go setting the plank to high, ok? It was absolutely gorgeous for its time, which is why it took whole minutes for locations to load. It used to be utterly annoying, but well worth it. On a modern PC it is barely noticeable, at least, but when compared to modern graphics it definitly takes a hit. Don't get me wrong, the visual design is spectacular, some locations are borderline genius and all the character's appearances are some of the most thought out i've seen in videogames. But, let's face it, the game is old, so it might give out a little "minecrafty" vibe. The audio, on the other hand, is as brilliant as ever. All the voice actors are involved and suit their characters, and I am still listening to "Lacuna coil", which was used at some scenes.
So, what's not to like? A few things, actually, but they are not related to the gaming process. First of all, if you are going to run it on windows 8 or later, you might run into some difficulties. I didn't but the reports are plentiful. There are also some patches easily found through the community, but if you are not ready to spend, like, ten extra minutes to setup one of the greates RPGs of all time, there's allways a refund. The other thing is that it is a little short. It gives out some solid 50 hours of gameplay, more or less, but if you are looking to disappear into game for no less than 200h, i might recommend morrowind (or TF, pick your poison).

This feels like the most watered-down rogue-like experience ever. There's definitely a very good randomly-generated element to it, with randomly generated maps, enemy placements, loot, etc. What kills it for me, however, is the fact that there is barely anything to do in terms of combat -- there are three damage types (magic, melee, ranged), but the magic and ranged attacks play out identically in that they both have ranged attacks compared to melee's 1-tile range. In essence, it feels like the only reason there are ranged and magic damage types is so that the randomly generated loot isn't a coin flip to see if it's relevant to you or not.
I haven't seen anything resembling skills or abilities (though there are evidently artifacts that you can unlock once you beat a small campaign, allowing for better starting stats), so combat is literally just rolling the dice to see who hits and who doesn't with no room for any other options. As a result, playing with line of sight to minimize the amount of ranged attacks that can hit you during combat is the closest thing to tactics you'd have to employ. Inevitably, at many points in the game, you'll just spend many turns clicking on the same tile down a bottleneck, which is about as degenerate of an experience as I can imagine. Given how wild the RNG can be with the combat, sometimes even this much planning is not enough to do well, as enemies can hit devastatingly hard and your character's ~60% to hit does not perform as consistently as it would have you believe.
If you want a fantasy dice-rolling simulator, look no further. If you wanted something interactive or exciting, there are many better options out there.

Another fantastic Shadowrun campaign~! I'd just like to take a moment to compare Shadowrun: Hong Kong, to it's predecessor, Shadowrun: Dragonfall.
Feels more organic and less blocky. Limitations on the Karma screen are more apparent. It is now possible to do a number of simple things that you couldn't before, like equip teammates, distribute acquired items, and swap equipped items with one another.
Not only with members of the team like Duncan Wu (with whom dialogue choices reveal your history together) but with characterizing some of the other Random NPC shadowrunners you can choose to hire. Note that I'm not saying that the characters are better this time around (that's a matter of personal preference), the game just does a better job presenting them.
A few motion-comic sequences penctuate key moments of the plot. Not that many though (I think there were three or four).
Diffrent approaches to combat are more balanced than before. With additional skills and a dedicated merchant, playing a Physical Adept is actually viable this time around. Body has found a derived skill in Cyberware Affinity, which grants additional options to Street Samurai. Mages get a few new tricks like Blood Magic which are kinda OP, but for the most part the balance is welcoming. New items and drugs provide additional options, and are more important than before because...
IN my honest opinion, both the original  Shadowrun Returns, and Shadowrun:Dragonfall were too easy. Shadowrun: Hong Kong, on it's highest difficulty, is more challenging, and I welcome it.
This last one won't matter to most people, but the Shadowrun Editor has gained some new options with this game, like Ambient Sounds and Ley Line control.
So you click to move, which normally would be fine, except that your squad does a pretty unpredictable job of following you. Sometimes they're right behind you like they should be, other times they inexplicably end up a half mile behind you for no reason, so that when combat suddenly engages 'cause an enemy you didn't see ambushes you, your team needs to waste several turns getting in position. The clunky movement is worsened by the fact that Hong Kong adss STEALTH missions. Thankfully, these aren't instant-fail like some other games, but EVERY time you enter cyberspace, and even for some missions in meatspace, you'll have to fight against the movement system to remain undetected.
Loads take much longer in Hong Kong than they did in Dragonfall. This might not be an issue if there weren't so many damn loading screens in Shadowrun. In any case expect to be doing a lot of waiting around. At least the load screens have text.
This is a problem that Shadowrun: Hong Kong shares with the others, but whereas both previous entries have community-made campaigns availble for them (some pretty damn good ones too, like
) Time will tell if Hong Kong gets the same kind of support.
This one's still getting worked on, but there are a lot of bugs here that I just didn't see in Dragonfall. Dialogue boxes often have the wrong portraits attatched to them, missions sometimes crash, and NPC conversation trees don't always advance. It may get fixed later, but as of posting it's still an issue.
Okay, so only hardcore nerds will have a problem with this one, but I think it was a huge missed oppurtunity to explore some of the lore of Shadowrun and of China. But little to no mention is made of the other countries that China's split into (except a brief news report about Sichuan), Lung (the Great Dragon of China) never makes an appearance, and neither does his rival/apprentice, the Japance dragon Ryumyo, even though one of your squadmates is one of his Red Samurai. Overall, just a bit of an annoyance.
Again, unless you're bilingual like me, you probably won't catch it, but some of the translated phrases are pretty bad. Especially hillarious is when they literally translated "傻瓜" as "Stupid Melon." And this one bad guy's name in particular, “千牙" is WAY too literal.
Don't let the Cons list deter you though, Shadowrun: Hong Kong is an AMAZING game, and if you ever had any love for isometric games, turn-based strategy, or Shadowrun itself, you owe it to yourself to play it.

So you will have to take use of the turn-based system to plan a strategy. But! Is there enough time for a rigid strategy as the world is swallowed up behind you? (each turn) -That is for you to adapt to as you discover this ever changing landscape.
-Good-
About the turn-based system, keep in mind it goes as fast as you want it to. You can run just as in any overview-2d game. But when you stop, everything else stops. This makes it both exhilarating but calming at the same time to me!
Want to compete with other players? You can play the very same world (not simultaneously) and check leaderboards for whom performed the best in a variety of aspects such as leveling and treasure hunting etc-.
And lest forget the character art, they have a charming manga-illustration kind of look which takes me back Final Fantasy IV.
-Cons-
Not a variety of tile texture- Since you'll find yourself writing a story to complement the lack of complete story, a larger variety of landscapes to inspire our minds would be nice. Also weather and lightning effects would be welcome.
No simultaneous multiplayer (just leaderboards). If the creators got an idea for how to implement multiplayer but still hold this fast-paced turn-based system, i could potentially see how that'd make for a sequel with great promise! But that's just me. (^^)

I was given a copy of this game to review.
This is a game that will challenge you. But it’s so fun you don’t even mind. It’s hard, but it’s also super fun. I found myself laughing more than I ever have while playing a puzzle game. Road to Ballhalla is an amazing experience I quickly found myself falling in love with.
First off you need to take a second and appreciate all of the ball puns and jokes the developer Torched Hill has crammed not only into the game, but also the promotion material. It makes my inner 12 year old very happy. What is even better is the humor injected into the game. I’m going to try not to spoil much of it here for you, but the developer has a grand ol’ time screwing with the player. I found myself laughing quite a bit as I played through. It’s even fun when I go back and replay the game. It’s even more fun when you put someone you know in front of it and watch them play.
Road to Ballhalla perspectiveRoad to Ballhalla is a puzzle/platform game where you must guide a ball through tons of devious stages designed not only to challenge you, but also to make you laugh. Road to Ballhalla is a wonderful experience at its best and frustratingly brilliant at its worst.
Next up is the beautiful art design. I mean wow, this is a great looking game! Levels pop! I know that term gets thrown around a lot these days in reviews, but Road to Ballhalla’s levels are really nice! This game is enjoyable enough with just its masterfully crafted gameplay and level design. The fact that the developer went out of their way after nailing the game design to make the game look this beautiful is great. I’ve found myself admiring every stage. Later stages will really force you to pay attention and take it all in as you deal with ever changing visuals. Simple camera changes had me holding my breath as I tried to get through seemingly simple paths.
The obvious comparison to make with Road to Ballhalla is to the classic game Marble Maddness. Well, I can say as someone who liked/loathed that game – Road to Ballhalla is the evolution fans have wanted. I feel I cannot overstate just how great this game is. It nailed every aspect of what makes a game like this great: Tight controls feel just about right for a rolling ball, wickedly smart and devious level design, mindbogglingly great music and lots of replay.
Road to Ballhalla is a fun experience that is totally worth the full price of admission. I can go on and on, but really it’s nothing but love and praise for this masterpiece.

Road to Ballhalla takes the ball-rolling frustration simulator to a whole new sarcastic level with tight controls, interesting puzzles and a steep difficulty curve.
Full review:
Text:
The game is a nice mix of clean gameplay and cool graphics, where the simple controls are exploited to the fullest to bring complex and deep puzzles to the player with a nice variety of levels and mechanics that shake the thing up quite a bit.
The PC PC controls are pretty bad, with both no mouse control in the menu's and weird audio levels in the options, and with no advanced graphics it's preset or bust. This doesnt make it an ugly game, but it does mean that unless you like what you get, you're out of luck.
The game also does not shy away from being hard, so unless you enjoy the physics puzzler ganre, this might not be the game for you, but for me personally, as someone that generally does not like puzzle games, the varied mix of mechanics and puzzle elements coupled with the variety of sarcastic jokes and notes in the game, does keep it special.
The game also splits Speedrunning and score attacks, which is a smart move.
The game doesn't pretend to be more than it is: It's about rolling a ball to the end of a level and surviving the puzzles. And it does that with charm, control and good execution.

A great example of a game that knows what it is, and complements its core design with smart design decisions along the way. Puzzle action fans will love the level design here, as it does a great job of keeping a good pace of introducing new mechanics and keep the gameplay fresh. The game is right in terms of difficulty, allowing for speed runners to really challenge themselves, while allowing “regular” players to take some time and try to work their way systematically. The controls complement the gameplay rather well, and the sound and music enhance the gameplay in the right ways. The biggest disappointment that the game has is maybe its lack of content: but that will be helped by the forthcoming steam workshop integration and capabilities. But rather then quantity, Road to Ballhalla focused on Quality, and it shows in a lot of elements here. In the end, it's not going to blow you away in any element, but it rewards you with solid gameplay.

When you look at Road to Ballhalla it looks like you basic marble rolling game. It should since that it was it is. Road to Ballhalla is a marble rolling game. Road to Ballhalla is one of if not the best marble rolling game I have ever played though.
Road to Ballhalla is a great marble rolling game for three reasons. First the controls are simple and tight. When you die in the game it is your fault and not because of the controls. Second the game has great level design. Care and thought were put into the levels. The game does a great job coming up with unique ways to use the different mechanics and obstacles to make each level feel unique. Finally the game is surprisingly funny. Who would have thought a marble rolling game would actually be funny. Road to Ballhalla is genuinely funny as the "narrator" tries to trick you and taunts you when you fail.
Road to Ballhalla is not a perfect game though. The biggest problem is the game is pretty short. If you aren't into time trials or 100% levels, the game will only last around three to four hours. The game is adding Steam Workshop support though so hopefully the community can add a lot of interesting levels to the game. The other slight issue I had with the game is that it is kind of on the easy side.
If you don't like marble rolling games, Road to Ballhalla is not going to be for you. If you like marble rolling games though I think you will really enjoy Road to Ballhalla.
