I find FTL to be a good game, but not as great as everyone seems to claim.  It is certainly unique, but it demands far too many replays that all turn out to be very similar.  The different ships help add some variety, but even that can't make up for the frequency that events recur.  My advice for new players: feel free to look up strategy on crew, weapons, and the flagship, but NEVER look up the outcomes for the events.  Once you learn all the events, the game loses a huge amount of replay value.
I played through the game on Easy three times, always getting to the final sector to die against the Flagship.  The game provided no feedback along the way to indicate that I was unprepared for the final fight, so these losses were quite frustrating.  I ended up watching some tutorials, which provided good information for the weapon type you should have against the Flagship and an appropriate strategy for destroying it.  After watching those, I finally beat the game!
Links:

The initial steep learning curve is really off-putting, but once you know the strategy the game becomes too easy.  Thankfully, the game offers several different ships to use, each with 3 different layouts, so you can certainly find a happy middle ground between too difficult and too easy.  You can also select from 3 different difficulty levels.  These mainly affect how the enemy ships will attack and how much scrap (money) you collect.
I found that I rapidly learned how to deal with each event, so I knew choice to make each time the event repeated. (Once you know a certain choice causes you to lose 4 hull or a random crew member, you're unlikely to make that choice again.)  Luck really isn't as big of a factor in the game as you initially expect, except for determining whether or not you encounter the events that give you free upgrades and weapons.  That is not to say that luck isn't involved.  You'll certainly still need luck on your side, because several unlucky events in a row can cripple your ship or crew.

Welp time for another Shadowrun game. And this one I pre-ordered and have been waiting awhile to play, so here goes.
STORY: This is probably the 2nd best story out of The Shadowrun Returns Series (Next to the 1st being the best and Dragonfall being my least favorite imo.)
You start off in Hong Kong, getting a message from your foster father to head back so you can help him with an issue hes having involving some big megacorporations (which by the way practically own Hong Kong) you are not only dragged into the mystery but so is your foster brother and two other shadowrunners. Its up to you to figure out what happened to your foster father and maybe become a shadowrunner during the crossfire?
The story is really REALLY great, I just absolutly loved the characters, even though they have no voices, just reading their lines just gives me an impact.
Also there was really creepy final boss I encountered in the game, and it got more creepier by the 2/3rd time I faced it.
There are multiple endings to this game, and the one I chosen was really good, but I know it wasn't the only ending so more replayability there. 9.5/10
GRAPHICS: I want to say that the graphics here are mostly still the same, though I will admit the characters have been improved upon slightly a bit.
Still Its nice to see some areas that are inspired by real life Hong Kong and other cool art pieces and characters. 8.5/10
GAMEPLAY: Again everything is mostly the same, but the combat UI is changed a bit to resemble the 1st ones unlike dragonfall.
The upgrading is changed slightly as you can now use cybernetics along with it like upgrading to lvl 1 cyberarm and further and further by your body lvling system.
The team lvling is still the same but its still good.
Everything is slightly the same but slightly different too but its still awesome. 9/10
VERDICT: Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a great 3rd installment in the Shadowrun Returns Series.
It doesn't really changed much, but its still a great turn-based RPG, has a great story, and lots of replayability. 9/10
TLDR:
PROS: Great story, good turn-based combat, lots of replayability, slightly improved character models.
CONS: Really didn't changed much combat UI wise
Buying Price: Full-price

I find myself continually impressed by Harebrained. As I haven’t played the table-top / P&P Shadowrun, I can only speak to the game itself. (TL;DR: Skip to last sentence)
The Shadowrun Returns series have brought me back to enjoying overhead sprite based games. Since the early Fallout games, I’ve never found RPGs with this style to be particularly engaging.
As the latest iteration of the Shadowrun Returns games, Hong Kong provides a lot of polish and features that were missing while improving upon the foundation that was already pruned from the previous two games. This is not to say it is perfect, but I’ll touch on that in a bit.
The characters you run with are quite interesting. I’d say that they kept a lot of the improvements from Returns to Dragonfall in this new game. How do these characters compete with Dragonfall’s? The conclusion I come to here is that your perception of this depends upon your personality. I’d say it was an improvement (especially since there are more character to get to know), but perhaps some may find them slightly less engaging than before.
New skills have been added that, I felt, increased the immersion. They allowed for greater specialization and seem to level the field for greater viability between classes. On that note, cyberware as a whole has seen a massive facelift which made me very excited.
The matrix has been revamped and personally, I love it. I have heard the complaints concerning the difficulty of some tasks within the matrix, but I found the difficulty refreshing and overcoming it equally satisfying. It is worth mentioning that it doesn’t seem to be common knowledge that you can skip pieces of these puzzles by hitting the “next” button. While it increases the challenge of the following section, I usually found that final section easier than the rest of the “memory test” combined.
The story and atmosphere are, once again, to die for. For me, this is the real appeal of these games and Hong Kong is absolutely no exception. If magic seems a stretch in a cyberpunk universe, I promise, these games make it feel right at home in the dark, seedy, grimy world of dystopian cyberpunk. Further, I would strongly assert that the addition of magic adds significantly to the universe. Its addition makes the universe feel that much more uncontrollable (yet very tightly controlled), dark, and dangerous.
I won’t try to tell you that the game is flawless. There are certainly bugs and problems--I haven’t experienced nearly as many as some and I beat the game before the first major patch was announced so I don’t believe they are as prolific as some claim--but many of these have been patched out.
*Edit: On my second playthrough, I have noticed quite a few more bugs. Most of them have no effect on gameplay.
The biggest complaint I can offer you (which is a meagre gripe in comparison to the game’s merits) is that it is text based instead of being voice acted. For its predecessors, I didn’t see this as a flaw in the slightest because the dialogue was either minimal or very engaging. In this game, while the dialogue retains its very interesting dialogue, there is simply so much of it that I sometimes found it difficult to want to speak to many of the NPCs and simply gave priority to the ones who I found interesting. As a counter to my own complain though, I do like that I didn’t spend all my time talking to every single NPC in the small little village of a home as that felt closer to real life. So, ultimately, I’m conflicted on the matter.
*Edit: Aside from this, the loading times are quite sad. I moved the game from my secondary hard-drive to my SSDs and it's still an issue. This is really the only thing about the game that I find unnacceptable.
In the end, I can say this: if you liked the original Fallout games, if you like cyberpunk themed stories or games, or if you like RPGs, you really ought to pick these games up. I’d be a bit surprised if you didn’t enjoy them.

If you liked Shadowrun Dragonfall, you'll love Hong Kong. If not, then you won't enjoy this game. It shares the same pros and the same cons, but is a marked improvement overall.
The combat system is largely improved, while still being an underwhelming copy of XCOM's. Your companions now have attacks to stun and quickly dispatch stunned enemies. You have at least one close combat specialist who won't win any damage contest, but a successful hit will deny the victim's cover, allowing your ranged attackers to deal critical hits, and since by the end of the campaign you will have close to a 100% chance to do a critical should you hit, this is a pretty sizeable bonus.
The cyberware and bioware options are improved, if pricy. And no refunds.
Armors give an armor rating and nothing else, in the same tier there is no difference between the armor sold by the guns vendor and the mage styled one. For weapons however, you have finally some very nice options for melee characters, unique weapons, cyberweapons, etc.
The matrix system is completely revamped, thematically spot on and, for me at least a chore. While still being an improvement compared to Dragonfall.
The writing, for the dialogues in particular, leaves nothing to be desired. The companions, except one annoying decker dwarf, are all top notch, interact more with one another, and one in particular makes for some hilarious moments.
The music and artistic design are very immersive and efficient, the asian theme is fully incorporated in the visuals, sounds and story.
If sufficiently optimized, your character will wreck everything and everyone, even on the highest difficulty level, but your companions will have issues hitting. This is especially jarring if you take Is0bel for the decking, as her incompetence will heavily get on your nerves.
The game is too short. Fully finishing the game in the highest difficulty level takes 25 hours and it's still too horribly short. You will want more and more and more. This is how addictive this game is.

If you like roguelikes Hack, Slash, Loot is a brilliantly simple one. No inventory management, if you can equip it you have to choose what your taking with you then and there, and if you can use it you have to use it where you find it or leave it. There is a bit of permanence in the form of unlockable characters (unlocked by getting a certain number of wins or deaths) and Relics you can find and then start new games with. While levels are randomized in typical roguelike fashion there are 6 quests that offer distinctly different flavors.
If you're having a bit of trouble at first here's a hint: die until you unlock the Amazon, then play the Mask of the Boy King mission, keeping your starting weapon (until the boss, who's resistant to it). Don't open Tombs but open everything else you see and bottleneck monsters in doors. If you can kill the boy king the burial mask he drops is a relic you can use on all further runs. :)

Hack, Slash, Loot is a game that I got as part of a bundle, that I dearly wish had never been redeemed. Its presence, forever a taint on my library.
Avoid this game, for this game is precision crafted to avoid literally everything good about roguelikes ever. Hack, Slash, Loot is such a bad roguelike that it can be considered the anti-roguelike, the embodiment of all the bad parts of roguelikes with none of the good whatsoever.
The game lacks any sort of mechanical depth whatsoever. Everything boils down to boring, static numbers. Where a better roguelike would have classes that play differently, different skills perhaps, equipment preferences and the like, the ability to use magic perhaps, this game has none of those things. And I'm not saying that a roguelike has to have those things, you understand. I'm saying that most fantasy roguelikes would have those things, for instance Dungeons of Dredmor and Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup. Even within the "Roguelite" games, you'd have characters with a vastly different playstyle resulting from different skillsets, stats and starting equipment, like in The Binding of Isaac, Risk of Rain, Nuclear Throne, Ziggurat, the list goes on.
Hack, Slash, Loot instead has classes that boil down to melee and ranged, no resting to regain your health, no skills, no mana. Your character is simply a walking sheet of stats, bolstered by your equipment that are nothing but stats. This creates no interesting gameplay choices, either you find something that has better stats than your current equipment, or you don't. There is no strategy, there is no way to build your character, there is no game to be enjoyed here.
This creates a game that is nothing but dice rolls upon dice rolls, with little to no player input involved. There is no feeling of accomplishment if you get further than you previously did, there is no anguish when you die. You cannot self reflect on a defeat that was entirely out of your control, you cannot ask yourself what you could've done better.
The beauty of a roguelike is its nigh infinite replayability, the ways you can experiment with builds, the magic of discovery as you find something that works, figure out the tricks of the game, and get further everytime. The excitement when you turn a bad run around after an item that perfectly synergizes with your current character appears, or the opposite, where you make it far, even perhaps to the final level, before dying. Lamenting that you would've won if you had the right items. And what about the times when you pull through a bad run? That is the core of the roguelike experience that Hack, Slash, Loot ultimately fails to capture.
In conclusion, Hack, Slash, Loot is a thoroughly incompetent roguelike that tries to distill the experience, but what you instead get is a shallow game with no identity, no soul. It is a bad game, it is a bad roguelike, and you should avoid it like the plague.

First things first, like nearly everyone has said I do recommend you play Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines with the unofficial patch. I have not tried playing without the patch but I still came across one or two bugs in the later stages of the game (thankfully nothing game-breaking) with the patch, so I don't even want to imagine what state the base game is in.
Right, onto the review. This game... it... you see... um... Ok, I don't know what I can really say that hasn't already been said by many other people. This game is praised by many and I think it fully deserves all it receives. The world is great, the characters are interesting and the story is engaging. The gameplay is simple but there's still a sense of strategy to what you're doing, normally I don't like playing these kind of games with a keyboard rather than a controller but this control scheme feels extremely natural and is easy to get used to. And the presentation is amazing, yeah some of the graphics are outdated but there's still a definitive style that gives everything a sense of charm, and the detail in the facial animations for many of the characters really brings them to life. VTMB also has a brilliant soundtrack, with songs that I had stuck in my head even when I wasn't playing and a cast of very talented voice actors who fully get into their roles. The writing is really clever and downright funny at points (the Abbott and Costello reference really caught me off guard) which only served to make me even more eager to continue the story. And while there are a lot of fetch quests, combat sections and exploration quests each mission you're given still feels different, I rarely found myself getting bored or wishing I could skip sections of the game.
But the best part is the choice. You have SOOOOOOO much choice right from the character creation screen and that choice is reflected during gameplay. For a long time I've been looking for an RPG that offers more social options, not just in initial character conversations but in missions themselves, and I feel like I got that with VTMB. I played a female Ventrue with a focus on Dominate, Seduction and Persuasion. Throughout my playthrough I found so many ways to completely avoid combat or fetch quests altogether just through talking to the right character or having the right social stats, and it was absolutely amazing to be able to do that. It didn't take away all of the combat or puzzles (in fact I got so obsessed with my social skills there were a couple of sections early on that I was severely under-leveled to do anything but scrape through) but it gave me new options and interactions for certain missions that was wonderful to experience. Once it was over I was already itching to start again, and I am really looking forward to my next playthrough (currently debating between Tremere, Malkavian and Nosferatu) and seeing what else I can discover.
VTMB is a fantastic game that you should play if you like RPGs and Vampires. I really want another game like this, either from the same developers/universe or something completely new using this gameplay template, because I've never experienced this kind of choice in a game before. After doing some searching for similar games it does appear that VTMB is one of a kind in terms of the scale of choices and options available to the player (if anyone has any recommendations for similar games please let me know) but, in a way, that just makes it more special. I'm on the VTMB bandwagon and I'm not getting off anytime soon.

I find FTL to be a good game, but not as great as everyone seems to claim.  It is certainly unique, but it demands far too many replays that all turn out to be very similar.  The different ships help add some variety, but even that can't make up for the frequency that events recur.  My advice for new players: feel free to look up strategy on crew, weapons, and the flagship, but NEVER look up the outcomes for the events.  Once you learn all the events, the game loses a huge amount of replay value.
I played through the game on Easy three times, always getting to the final sector to die against the Flagship.  The game provided no feedback along the way to indicate that I was unprepared for the final fight, so these losses were quite frustrating.  I ended up watching some tutorials, which provided good information for the weapon type you should have against the Flagship and an appropriate strategy for destroying it.  After watching those, I finally beat the game!

The initial steep learning curve is really off-putting, but once you know the strategy the game becomes too easy.  Thankfully, the game offers several different ships to use, each with 3 different layouts, so you can certainly find a happy middle ground between too difficult and too easy.  You can also select from 3 different difficulty levels.  These mainly affect how the enemy ships will attack and how much scrap (money) you collect.
I found that I rapidly learned how to deal with each event, so I knew choice to make each time the event repeated. (Once you know a certain choice causes you to lose 4 hull or a random crew member, you're unlikely to make that choice again.)  Luck really isn't as big of a factor in the game as you initially expect, except for determining whether or not you encounter the events that give you free upgrades and weapons.  That is not to say that luck isn't involved.  You'll certainly still need luck on your side, because several unlucky events in a row can cripple your ship or crew.

Hack, Slash, Loot, or "HSL", looks charming at first with it's retro-style pixel art... until you realize that the gameplay is even more primitive. It is not an understatement to say that everything in this game either comes down to little more than random chance and comparing numbers.
Combat is completely limited to clicking on an enemy until they die. That's it. No special moves, no abilities, no changing gear, nothing. Sure, depending on your weapon you either use melee, ranged or magic attacks, but unless you're fighting near a weapon drop you can't change on the fly, plus your character will usually specialize in one type so there' very little reason to change unless you get VERY skewed consumable drops (more on that later). At best you can try to bottleneck enemies in doorways or tight coriidors to fight them one by one, or run away and hope you find something useful before you get surrounded, but that barely qualifies as "strategy". And even then, you still have to hope that RNGesus is smiling down upon you.
The item system is almost as primitive. Most of the time, it feels less like you are trying to decide which weapon or piece of armor to equip, and more like you're just comparing numbers (although special damage types such as the stunning Lighting do make things a little more interesting) As for consumables, you never know if a potion or w/e will help and/or hinder you, meaning once again it's entirely up to luck rather than any sort of choice or strategy if it help you.
Oh, and there's no save system. At all.
All in all, this game had a lot of potential, but instead the gameplay is comparable to banging your head against a wall while comparing helmets and popping pills that "might" make it hurt less. What this game needed was something, ANYTHING that might have made the gameplay more complex than dice rolling: Abilities/items to use in a pinch, swapping around weapons, etc etc: anything that would make success less dependant on how lucky you are.
If you're at all thinking of picking up this title anyway, I highly recommend buying another game called One-Way Heroics instead, which in a nutshell is practically like this game with the improvements I just suggested, and at only somewhat more than half the price.

I have to be honest, I believed the story of Mafia II to be an incredibly strong point, one that epitomizes the "all that glitters is not gold" aspect of the American Dream. However, at critical points, I felt that the story failed to deliver a decisive enough blow to make up for the (what I found to be) shortcomings. For example:
[SPOILER ALERT]
-The death of Henry at the hands of the triads felt brutal, but not brutal enough to inspire the emotion I believe it wanted to incite. Sure, you certainly felt for Henry, but did you really feel that savage anger that makes you empathize with Vito and Joe?
-The killing of Tommy Angelo was particularly infuriating to me, since the protagonist of the first game was killed and given less screen time than the men who serve you coffees at Empire Bay's many fine dining establishments. I certainly didn't expect an entire chapter devoted to him, but I felt that the effort toward his death was minimal.
-And finally, the death of Joe Barbaro at the end of the game. Perhaps the most frustrating death in the entire game, I was not moved at all at the death of "my best friend". Why? Because it was sledgehammered into the final resolution of the game. Much could have been done to inspire sadness and regret in the player (ex. Vito visiting Joe's grave in an epilogue or leaving Empire Bay after apologizing to Joe in spirit), but it ultimately fell short at a point where I feel the game could have ended on a fantastic note.
[END OF SPOILERS]
These critical points of the story were depleted before they even gave battle, and didn't make up for the gameplay elements I found pointlessly dull. Driving, for instance, was both laborious and more of a chore than an entertaining pasttime; crashes are deadly (a tribute to realism, I must admit), police decide to arrest for running red lights but not for brutal traffic negligence at times, and the narrow roads don't allow for much experimentation. Coupled with the fact that you must drive in the majority of the missions (once again, needlessly), it leaves a sour taste in my mouth. How do you write an objective review for a game that you spent hundreds of hours playing couch coop on while you were a teenager? You can't.
Star Wars Battlefront II is an absolutely fantastic game. While the game is incredibly outdated, the mod support for the PC version allows updated visuals, improved weapon sounds, maps, factions, and even character models. Mod your game and you have a competent shooter that rivals many of the modern ones that dominate the market. The amount of content is incredible with multiple game modes, classes, weapons, and 16 (I think) maps for the vanilla version, though mods literally extend the amount of maps to the hundreds.
There is no comparing this game to EA's crappy version: one is a masterpiece made for Star Wars/third-person shooter fans, while the other is a Battlefield clone that ships with little content and features a horrendous community. I recommend everyone skip that dud.
The shooting mechanics still hold up and the modding process is easy, which is half of what makes the game a blast today. Get a couple of friends and try it out; you won't regret it.

Fun, almost addictive game. The gameplay is simple: start on a random or previously seeded map, keep going right and don't get consumed by the darkness on the left.
Unlike most rogue-likes, this doesn't have a real permadeath as it lets you hold items at the end of an adventure in a space-limited vault as well as unlock different stat boosts and classes to start with. This means no matter how many times you die, you're still keeping progress and, provided you don't mess up, can go further after each adventure. You can also save at certain points, by buying and using certain items and by giving up 5 experience levels so it's all a lot more forgiving.
It does however get ridiculously hard near 400km (on the *easier* mode) when the demon lord arrives and I haven't played enough to pass it yet but it's possible, I just didn't use the right skills. Which is one of the main points about this game: failure is on your part as the game gives you enough to survive. It's nice looking at the quick replays and just seeing where you can optimise.
Other positives: Great music, simple SNES-era JRPG sprites. The badge looks pretty nice too. There's also some event maps with special restrictions to keep up the replay value. And it's cheap!

Vampire is an old game by todays standards, and easily clunky at parts. Attempting to look at this game without rose-tinted nostalgia glasses, it's a game with several flaws and a dated engine.
However! What this game does well, is atmosphere, writing and characters. And those things are incredibly important for any game wishing to tell a story.
Yes, this game manages to scare. Yes, this game manages to make you care about several of the people you meet, and yes, this game manages to drag you in, identify with the character you play, and keep you invested.
I realize that by now this games graphics will put off a lot of people who needs more realistic animations, but if any of the following points sounds like something you'd enjoy, i wholeheartedly recommend giving this game a try:
- Character Sheet: You pick every step of the way exactly how you want to develop your characters abilities, whether you enjoy improving your social skills, basic stats or combat strength.
- Multiple sollutions: Almost every situation in the game can be solved with either sneaking, social skills or raw force (guns blazing). You can play the game pretty much as you please, and enjoy the feeling of succeeding in the way you chose.
- Side Quests: Yes you can rush through the main story if you so please, but the large amount of sidequests allowing you to explore the lore and the people that make up the cast, allows you to really dive into the game world.
In the end, it all comes down to personal taste, and there will probably be as many people who doesn't like the game, as people who does. But for the ones it does appeal to, this is a gem you'll be glad not to have missed.

Dear potential customer, if you are reading this, I have one humble request. If you are interested in this game, don't watch the video on the store page. Seriously, go in blind. I knew very little about the game, and boy was I shocked by the experience. I'm kind of scratching my head as to why Daedelic felt the need to spoil the premise of the game in the first 30 seconds of their trailer.
The game itself is a spiritual successor to "Edna and Harvey: The Breakout". You don't need to play that one first, but characters and locations from the first game are used in this one. Unlike the Breakout, it's a massive improvement in quality, stability, and overall gameplay. A few of the puzzles are a bit mind bending, but nothing too difficult or confusing. It's a lot easier than the first game.
The game uses the "Monkey Island"-style formula, cutting the game into easily digestible chapters for you to puzzle through. It introduces an odd system of restrictions halfway through the game that add extra constraints to your ability to solve the game's puzzles. This system doesn't feel fully realized, and feels more tacked on to the experience. I will give them credit for trying something new, though.
The biggest thing the game has going for it is its atmosphere. It has a thin coat of innocence over what is an astoundingly dark game. I mean dark as in subject matter. The game gets pretty grim. This is why I warned above. Go in completely blind if you are looking to be unsettled or shocked. The first act is front-loaded with this style of humor.
The characters are fairly one note and flat, but I don't feel like that really detracts completely from the whole experience. There are so many point-and click adventure games that have heroes who are loveable goofs with a penchant for inventiveness and luck. In their adventures, they somehow manage to get by relatively unscathed, despite being pathological kleptomaniacs and daredevils. Here, it's interesting to see the more "hazardous" side of this archetype being explored, when normally it gets glossed over.
All in all, it's a decent point-and-click.

"Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes" is a point-and-click-adventure in the classic 90's sense. However it is not specifically trying to be a retro game, instead simply adhering to the tried and true formulae of robust game play, clever puzzle design and an engaging story to tie it all together.
It's set within the "Edna-verse" of studio Deadalic which currently encompasses this game and its predecessor "Edna & Harvey: The Breakout". However no prior knowledge of the other game or the setting is required. It is a fully standalone title that fits neetly within the greater picture of the world it shares with The Breakout.
With handdrawn sprites, backgrounds and animations it immediately emanates an aura of a playful cartoon or comic relying on its cute characters to do cute stuff for its emotional connection to the audience.
First you might be surprised by some of the more odd actions and events involving the otherwise unsuspecting and innocent characters. But soon enough the player realizes the game is using its backdrop of a little girl daydreaming about a bit of escapism to delve into themes such as emotional trauma and even mental disorder. Before you know it you will be talking to dead people, running from percieved government agents and gleefully sending children, elderly and otherwise innocent people to their deaths. Don't worry, though. It's all just a dream ... or is it?
Luckily this never completely tips over to outright shock or horror but continuously builds up suspension to a finale that might leave some people confused or unsatisfied but in my opinion was the perfect close to a narrative that never committed too much to rationality by giving you all the answers.
To tell more would mean to spoil some of the best experiences in the game. To put it simply: this is a solid title that improves greatly on its predecessor in terms of technical execution, narrative cohesion and puzzle logic, as one would expect from a sort-of-sequel. The game will surprise you, grip you and probably leave you wih a mixed feeling in your guts after it ended, but in a good way.
Tl;dr: If you like adventure games and don't insist on them being a strictly comedic string of set pieces then this will be worth your time.

I've played a decent amount of early access games, and I think this is probably the single worst offender as far as feeling so unfinished that it barley qualifies as a game. It has several faults that are forgivable on their own, but they stack up together to be incredibly frustrating and made me decide this game wasn't worth my time.
1) Terrible localization.
Probably will be fixed eventually, but the English localization is full of spelling and grammar mistakes to the point of most dialogue being pretty much incoherent.
2) Terrible tutorial
The only tutorial is a manual-style still image you can access when you pause the game that throws a textbook of information at you all at once, even though at the start you cannot do most things it talks about. There is no sort of interactive tutorial that introduces new mechanics over time. You are thrust into the game with only the pause menu tutorial (which, remember back to the localization makes absolutley no sense in some parts). Even during the various levels, the only way that your "helpers" interact with you is by saying things like "We have to harvest an energy!" and then going away until you accidently complete the level.
3) Terribly opaque
Even with the poorly translated menu tutorial, the information this game gives you is incomplete in almost every facet. There are 4 colored attacks that both monsters and your characters have and they are based off of.... something probably. It is difficult to discern what actually makes each color whatever value it is, and during the real-time sections of the game, it is hard to tell if the upgrades you have bought for different colors even do anything, or what any of the values are.
And, most offensively
4) Terrible gameplay
You don't really do anything. You just aimlessly click different colored attacks until something happens, something being the level ends.
I really wanted to like this game as I am a fairly active member on the SCP wiki, but it just plain and simple is not a good videogame. Maybe someday the developer will turn this into a real videogame, but as of now I would not recommend it to anyone as it is so unfinished that they should not be selling it.

I write this with a bit of a warning; the game is NOT easy.

So why play it?
You like a challenge. You want something that's "Gauntlet" without being Gauntlet.
It's frustrating as hell, and that's what makes it fun.

The game in a nutshell:
*Miss*
*Miss*
*Miss*
**Dead**
Buy a couple of dice. It will be cheaper and WAY more fun than this game.
And the chances of getting a desired number on said dice are accurate, as oppossed to this game's RNG.
RNG (random number generator) is an important part in roguelikes. It's not, however, the ONLY meaningful part.
This is the game's worst sin. it's completely random. In good roguelikes, there's a lot of strategy and thought. Randomness can screw you up, but usually, a good player can turn the tides.
Not in hack, slash, loot. Frankly it's like someone saw the success of rogue-lites and jumped the wagon without actual knowledge of what makes a roguelike/lite a good game.
Protip: it's NOT randomness what makes a roguelike good. Randomness is just one of the ingredients.

If you don't need the shiniest graphics, even in 2017 this is one of the most complete gaming experiences and one of the best Star Wars games you can get.
I played countless hours on the original Xbox and didn't even touch the multiplayer back then.
Even though it has been patched for Steam multiplayer, a move for which I compliment the devs for, games still seem hard to find but even in singleplayer I'm amazed at how much is at offer here and how well it holds up.
Even without nostalgia goggles, it plays absolutely fine and with the command line
set in the Steam launch options, it runs natively on widescreen, some misaligned menus aside.
My favorite part is the Conquest mode, which plays like a turn-based boardgame, intertwined with lots of shooting when battles ensue.
A great, simple addition that gives battles some context and meaning and is an ideal campaign experience to pursue in your lunch-break. Or, you know... binge it until the galaxy is yours.
Yeah, the AI isn't great, but I must admit when playing conquest particullarly, it can feel pretty great to have tons of kills to your name after you single handedly turned the tide of battle or stand victorious after facing of against the last dozens of enemies alone, which to me almost makes it feel like a FPS-Dynastie Warriors hybrid where you are the secret weapon of your faction.
It features:
- Fun gameplay in large-scale battles in the Star Wars universe.
- Space battles including boarding and infiltrating enemy ships.
- Going rampage as a hero against hordes of enemies.
- An actual campaign.
- Conquest mode.
- 16 maps for land and 6 maps for space combat.
- No Lootboxes or DLC-Packs.
- No CoD style progression system.
- Modding possibilities.
- Dedicated servers.
- Not a single Midi-Chlorian in sight.
It's dirt cheap on sales or in bundles, so give it a shot and travel back to a time when games could still be packed to the brink with content without slicing it up and selling it separately to you.

Awkward Dimensions is a game I'd rather call and experience rather than a game.
As a game, its often incoherent and unclear, but eventually "solving" the levels just happens, almost like a dream.
As an experience, it tells a brief story in each level with their own themes in an interesting albeit bizarre way.
I can easily see how one can jump to the idea how this is pretentious and drama filled, but the main idea of the dream and levels in this experience are things that happen to everyone, and the ideas portrayed in this experience are those of not only of what every person faces like conflicts of love, but also the notions of the fear of failure and unacknowledgement as a content creator.
This is not a game for everyone, but it is something I would recommend to those who face similar problems in life especially those who are the artists, the musicians, game developers, and ingeneral the creators who are dealing with the fear of failure, the self doubt, and the harsh internal critic they deal with every day.
If there is anything I recommend while playing, play with the developer's commentary on, since another theme behind this game is how works, such as a game, are taken at face value and the creator is just another faceless being. Turning on the commentary lets you hear what the developer wants you to know about each level and establish them as a human being and not some indie dev #495 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out a shovelware game to make a quick buck.

It features:
- Fun gameplay in large-scale battles in the Star Wars universe.
- Space battles including boarding and infiltrating enemy ships.
- Going rampage as a hero against hordes of enemies.
- An actual campaign.
- Conquest mode.
- 16 maps for land and 6 maps for space combat.
- No Lootboxes or DLC-Packs.
- No CoD style progression system.
- Modding possibilities.
- Dedicated servers.
- Not a single Midi-Chlorian in sight.
It's dirt cheap on sales or in bundles, so give it a shot and travel back to a time when games could still be packed to the brink with content without slicing it up and selling it separately to you.

So I normally don't review games while they are in early access, but this game seems to be for some reason really obscure even though its really interesting game. Anyway, yeah, Its SCP style game about managing monsters. Goal is to gather energy by interacting with monsters until energy quota for the day is reached. Its not a tycoon game, you don't build facilities or anything, though you do select which departments you upgrade next. Game is trial & error in fun way, before you interact with abnormality you don't know how they react to one of four different methods until you try it out so there is chance for some abnormalities to just kill your employeers if you picked wrong option, but since you can retry each day as much as you want its on softer end of rogue-lites meaning you aren't punished harshly. Real difficulty of game comes when you have gathered up enough abnormalities for their different rules and effects start to combo in really horrific ways making management harder. I also think that strongest class of abnormalities disable pausing option meaning you have to be really fast thinker if they breach the containment. On first playthrough, its possible you end up gathering really hard to deal with abnormalities and thats fine, if you start game over you keep encyclopedia entries and e.g.o. equipment so you know which abnormalities to avoid picking next playthrough.
That said, game mechanics can be bit of obscure and I think there is severe need of tooltips. Like I had no idea that white damage type can be used to heal panicked agents <_<

LISA: The Painful RPG certainly lives up to its title... in a good way. I don't think I've felt this attached to a story in a video game (or just about any medium, for that matter) for a long time.
+ The game has a unique sense of dark humor to contrast the emotionally tolling story. The humor is unexpected, cruel, and memorable. If you enjoy a more twisted kind of joke, you'll really enjoy the comedy this game has to offer.
+ The story is amazing. Without spoiling anything, it is something that will make you feel just about every emotion possible. It also challenges ideas of both games and life in general. Scenarios will make you question aspects of life and will test your sense of morality.
+ It has an interesting style of music. It's not something I'd recommend to everyone, but I personally enjoyed it. If I had to compare it to something else, there are a few tracks that remind me of Hotline Miami's soundtrack.
- The gameplay is pretty typical for an RPG. The few elements added into LISA that make it different than most RPGs can be seen as a hinderance. For example, there are parts of the game in which you can permanently lose a party member. This makes the game more challenging, but some people can view this as challenging for all the wrong reasons, especially when you are forced into one scenario where you have to risk party members' lives. There's also a good amount of backtracking, which can get rather tedious.
- The game is quite depressing. With a title like LISA: The Painful RPG, this is probably expected, but still. Don't get this game if you do not want to go through some emotional turmoil. I myself view this as one of LISA's positive aspects, but I can see why people will view this point negatively.
If you like dark humor and emotionally impacting stories, then you'll enjoy this game. But, this game is not for the faint of heart, so keep that in mind.

Having completed S:HK, I figure it was time to share Wot I Think about the game.
Game Length: About 12-13 hours and that included every mission I found but one.
It's easy to start this review. If someone liked the other games, they'll probably like this one. It has the same music style. Same art style. Same character leveling. Same skills. Same gameplay. It's basically the same game with a different story. As such, you could easily call this a new DLC adventure of Shadowrun: Dragonfall. So that's the basic recommendation - if you like the others, you should buy this. I did and I enjoyed it. Somewhat...and that's the kicker.
I'm not nearly as happy with this game as with the past games and I know why:
Empty
Derivative
Disjointed
PCs and NPCs
The Matrix
Empty: Tthe maps appear to be bigger. They're lovingly created and visually appealing. I've always loved the art style in this game. But they often feel empty and underutilized. There's very little compelling content that rewards you from straying the least little bit from your course. There are no quests off the beaten path, no interesing rabbit holes to fall down into.
Derivative: The game and story are entirely derivative. It's impossible to play this and not feel like you've played this before multiple times. FAs I said above, it's bascially the same game with a different story. But even the story isn't all that different - you run into a problem, watch someone get killed in the opening adventure, end up working for a broker who feeds you jobs, interact with the same computer terminal, do the jobs and finally advance the story. It's Dragonfall's premise all over again.
Disjointed: Unlike Dragonfall, where the above quest-system made great sense, this is a wasted opporutunity. Instead of nibbling around the main plot line by facing some weird incidents to build tension towards the final climax, you're off on entirely unrelated missions that aren't all that interesting. As I said, this made sense in Dragonfall because you had to make bank to advance the plot line. Here, they're just something to do for a while. So the plot is very disjointed. You go to the Walled City early and then never again until the final battle. The plot about dear old Dad isn't all that interesting and doesn't even make all that much sen sense. The denouement attempts to explain it, but by that time it's far too late. Missing Dad is just a plot device and an illogical one at that. So the missions and the mission structure are a massively WASTED opportunity to bring a more cohesive adventure to the story.
PCs and NPCs: The ghoul was a nice touch. The others...forgettable. Your brother? Annoying. The NPCs here really took a step back and weren't all that interesting. And there's still no control of their leveling. The specials are an attempt to give you some control, but frankly they're not all that great or that useful. I'd much rather have the ability to shape my party the way I saw fit. And it didn't help that my character - a sword-wielding street Samurai - happened to be the same exact type as the only interesting NPC out there. As for the player character, I didn't see how any of their responses would have changed the story much if at all (with the exception of keeping the vampire girl alive). In short, the PC doesn't matter except to be the wall that everything bounces off. When will HBS learn that the best stories often have the PC to go through a journey and not just move through the story without impactng it?
The Matrix: The gameplay in the matrix is still incredibly annoying. Even more this time with their "Simon Says" hacking game and the overall detection meter. It's not fun and it's not interesting at all. It sucks. I finally started using the deathray cheat to make it through these parts. And at times you simply can not avoid it. It's terrible and HBS should entirely dump the systems and start over there because they're making it worse, not better.
Again, it's not that it's a bad game. I'll give it a thumbs up review. But as for Kickstarting the next one in this series or buying it at full price? I'd have to see some genuine advancement in gameplay, strategy and story telling before ponying up dough again because I feel like I'm playing the same game over and over again - especially when this version isn't as good as the last one.
Verdict: A tepid thumbs up. Very tepid.

Awhile ago, HBS releases Shadowrun Returns, something of a love-letter to the RPG aspects of Shadowrun.  It featured Jake Armitage of the SNES game, allowed you to do some fun stuff with rigging (robo-puppetry), featured functional decking (hacking), and in general got the atmosphere of the Shadowrun setting right, but was a little awkward in terms of writing towards the endgame.
Soon after, Shadowrun: Dragonfall comes out, and more importantly, it's director's cut (as a free upgrade if you owned Dragonfall already).  This made for a near perfect modern cRPG, in my opinion; between the writing, the plot, the music, the character growth, and mechanics, it was an all around stellar title.
Now we come to their third Shadowrun RPG, Shadowrun: Hong Kong.  I've little to say about this that I haven't just said about Dragonfall, but let me say that all in all, it feels like a much better game mechanically, if with a slightly weaker story and better level and character design.  I'm not sure if it was my just being too enthralled by  the damn thing, but it felt much shorter than the thirty hours that I played it for to the end.  It greatly improves on its weaker mechanics present in the past two games, even if the hacking minigame is a little tedious.  I would have to say my only significant complaints are that the music feels tacked on, maybe even limp or ill-fitting in places, and that there seemed to be a dearth of equipment to be found in the field (unless you're into sniper rifles).
All in all a fantastic title.

Negatives:
1. Far too much emphasis on driving, not enough on the actual missions. Simply put, there's not enough required weapons use.
2. The game holds back the full weapons inventory for to long and places you in missions where you are either not allowed to use your weapons as you wish or they are taken away from you and not returned, leaving you to have to recollect your inventory. Further, they could add more weapons to the game, as well as beef up the gun store inventory.
3.  When you upgrade the cars of your associates they fail to remain upgraded.
4. Having to take associates cars when you'd prefer to take your own upgraded car.
5. No big scores. No bank heists. No armored car robberies. In short, more could have been done in terms of possible missions, stuff that could have been really fun. Additionally, your character is always seems to be short of cash (again, no big scores), which is a drag when it comes to upgrading cars and buying weapons. It would have been great if the player could hit a bank or armored car whenever they needed money. It would also make for some great random, player initated, missions.
6. It would be great if there were more things in the game to buy or earn.
7. Not knowing where you are in the poster (hunt) count is a drag. It would be nice if the game allowed you to know how many were left.
8. The inability to save the game at certain points. It would be nice to just cut to the missions as opposed to always have to jump through the hoops to get to the destination.
9. The constant driving home just to get back, to drive somewhere else to get some information, so that you can now drive somewhere else to do the mission. It's pointless.
10. Pointless missions: A mission to drive to a 'Cat House' only to leave to dump a body and then go home, is not a mission. It's a waste of time. It's boring.
11. The police are not aggressive enough and the numbers that will come at you at any one given time, even when you hang around after committing a crime, shooting at them and trying to do battle with them, are very limited. Only a few will show up and then they'll stop. It would have been great if you could draw the police out and have hundreds of them come at you.
12. The inability to access roofs, buildings, homes and business, anything you wish, is a drag. It would have been a lot of fun to have been able to break into a house or something to evade the police, citizens or fellow gangsters, and then have battles all over the city - inside or outside. To the point, if you can break into a car, why not everything?
13. A family tree of criminals, a who's who wall to follow along would have been nice.
14. A car dealership with cars would have been nice. Some place where you could go and steal anything. Also, when you steal a vehicle, any vehicle, it would have been nice to be able to keep it. Simply put, all things should fit in the garage.
15. Store owners should be tougher to kill. They should certainly have a staff. Perhaps give the gun store hours and then give the player the ability to break into them during off hours. The cops, citizens, or store owner could stand a chance to intervene and the building could be alarmed as well.
16. It would be nice if the raido had more songs.

This is a long, roughly 80 hour course in learning how to draw the human figure from your mind, Mr. Phoenix covers a surprisingly large amount of material which includes the skeletol and muscular system. I have gone through this entire course, and I can say with confidence it has definitely improved my drawing abilities, especially with the human figure directly from my mind!
I would suggest to Mr. Phoenix to slow down a bit from time to time in any future tutorials he does, however that is nothing a quick pause to the video cannot fix. It's understandable why he is fast, as he is a proffesional artist of many years.
I would recommend this course to anyone who has a goal of learning to draw the human figure directly from imagination. I would also like to recommend a book:
Freehand figure drawing for illustrators by David H. Ross.
This book will also be good as Mr. Ross covers some things Mr. Phoenix did not. I would still recommend this course, as it is easier to follow along and see how Mr. Phoenix draws, which is the advantage with these videos as opposed to learning from a book.
Thank you Mr. Phoenix for a wonderful 80 hours of helping me improve my drawing ability!

I have watched most of the free video content, and while it could have been useful to a beginner, it teaches a lot of erroneous things, such as dividing too much a head in "halves" in a "perfect" square. The head is a box but of a rectangular shape, not a square, and those with life study experience will also tell you that measuring with halves only work for so much, because you always find people who don't fit that category.
To be honest, I wouldn't even give one cent to someone who can't even confidently draw a single straight line without darkening it by drawing it over, which is extremely wrong not to do as a "professional". If this person truly had clients such as Disney and Lucas Art like his website states, this kind of work would need to go fast, and he would have gained the confidence to draw a nice, clean line or an ellipse without so much as a flinch. This is why people like Scott Robertson are much better than him and his 40 bucks video library.
I usually recommend that anyone tries and sticks to a website called drawabox. This helps to do things even the author of this video isn't able to do, such as:
- a clean, straight line drawn with confidence and improve line quality
- an ellipse of any angle and rotation, up to a perfect circle
- a methodic and mechanic way to learn information
- perspective down to a level where it is no longer needed to be drawn for the growing artist
- a community centered about improving themselves and willing to help others
And it is 100% free.
Combine that with books from Loomis, Bridgman, vlippu's videos on New master's academy($35 per month for an entire video library of deciated and masterful artists), life studies, and proko's free videos, and you will have a better understanding of everything that person is not teaching you, more naturally, than being fed erroneous information from the wrong people.

BIT.TRIP Presents... Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien (Runner2 for short) is an auto scrolling rhythm based platformer (or what I like to call it). I naturally love rhythm games and spend way too much time playing them but this is less of a rhythm game and more of a platformer.
Content:
There are tons of levels and each level has 3 difficulty levels, so if you have the patience to beat each level three times on different difficulty levels, the game has lots of replay value. Add on the collectables and leaderboards and you could spend lots of time in this game. It took me around 10 hours to finish it at first on Rather Hard (hardest difficulty) and almost triple that time to get Triple Perfect+ on each level (which you can achieve by completing each difficulty perfectly on said level) so I personally got tons out of this game. Let’s not forget the 20 hidden stages and hidden costumes too!
Graphics and Performance:
The graphics are very appealing and are a step up to the first six games in the BIT.TRIP series. If you have a weakish computer, you shouldn't have much of a problem running this game @ 60fps, just make sure to turn the depth of field off. Unfortunately that (and resolution) is the only graphics setting you can change.
Sound + Music:
As expected from a rhythm game, the music is some of the best (in my opinion) of what I've heard from a rhythm game. The developers even got the voice actor of Mario (Charles Martinet) to do the narration!
Controls:
Finally, the controls are great and responsive on the 360 controller and all the actions are where it should be. Even though I (and the game for that matter) highly recommend using a controller, the keyboard configuration is great and does the job properly once you get used to it.
Final Thoughts:
If you are a rhythm and/or platformer fan, I highly recommend you pick this game up. With lots of content, appealing graphics and an amazing soundtrack, the $15 asking price is a solid price. If you want, you can get the optional $3 DLC that adds characters like Atlas, Razputin and Dr. Fetus who of which all look great, but these are just characters, no extra levels or abilities.
This game is amazing. Buy it. Play it. This game makes the world a better place.

I have tried to find a single reason why anyone enjoys FTL. And I can't find it. After 30 hours of not winning a video game, you get tired. This game is really just not fun.
Let's start with the event system. One of the main issues with the event system is a lack of random chances. The same thing happens every time. Instead of "explore astroid field, 30 percent chance of success." You get "lose five HP everytime you click this option."
Furthermore, the lack of random events suck the game dry of replayableity. After 30 hours of gameplay I have seen every single event. Which makes the "die die again" model that FTL is trying to achieve insufferable.
It should also be noted that every single random event is fairly awful. There are a couple of good events that don't lead to your ship simply getting blown to bits for a huge ton of HP. But odds are that you'll get a constant stream of negative events.
Next, we should move onto the shops. Effectively, you will get the same list of weapons in every single store ever created. You only seem to ever get Lasers, Beams, Missles and/or Bombs, and drones. That sounds pretty diverse and it sounds like the weapon depth is great. Well just to give you an idea, beams are completely useless in this game. Because they don't pierce shields and are only useful at the early stages of the game. So you only have two choices, Lasers or Missles. Of which, you will quickly run out of missles.
It should be noted that I might be wrong. But so far, the shop RNG has been completely awful throughout the game. And has left me to assume that these are the only weapons in existence.
Moving onto fighting. Boarding Drones are basically broken in this game. If you destory a boarding drone, the enemy can simply pop out another in literally two seconds. If you're lucky, you can break the drone bay in time. Of course ion drones are even more unbalanced. An ion drone has the ability to walk around, zapping all your rooms and crew every five seconds. Again, no point in destorying the ion drone because another one will be sent shortly in a micro second.
Of course, odds are that you will need at least a minium of level two shields. Unfortunately, upgrading the shields costs scrap and a huge chunk of your scrap wallet that could be used to buy weapons. So either you end up in a situation where you have no guns to fire at the enemy expect for your puny burst laser. Or you end up in a situation where you have no shields and make a glass cannon.
And overall, this game has a lack of depth. It really doesn't have much in the way of depth. It feels like you're always getting the same weapons and shops over and over again. With the same events and overall, it's just boring.
Engine upgrades are a cheap alterative to shields. Seems like a good idea right? 25 percent envasion should logically equal "every forth laser misses." You would be quite wrong. As volley after volley of laser hits you on the nose. Missles will constantly blow you up. Of course, when you fire your own weapons, either the lasers and/or missles miss the enemy. Or the lasers get "resisted." Whatever that means since this game does not have a tutorial.

Moving onto replayability. Literally every sector feels like the first sector. Sure the music changes slightly. You get different ships in each sector. But overall, it's not really all that different to the first sector. Again making the whole "die die" again feel like nothing more then a massive headache.
Because you will fly through the same sectors. Fight the exact same enemies with virtually little difference from the first batch of ships. Then you'll die, fight another identical batch of ships in virtually the same sectors. Until you literally want to pull your hair out of your skull. The word's "repetitive" can not even come close to describing this game.
On the brightside, the game's graphics are simply amazing. Despite the lack of ALT-Tabing. If you want to enable alt-tabing, you'll have to hack the config.ini in order to allow boarderless windowed mode. The audio itself is amazing. The OST is worth every dollar I spent.
Overall: 6/10
Graphics: 9/10
Sound: 10/10
Replayability: 3/10
Depth: 4/10
Overall, I just can't recommand it. Simply because the game loses it's fun. Sure, for the first twenty hours, you might have a bit of fun. Then you just get to the point where the game loses it's luster. Eventally, you will get tired of the die die again model. Because it's boring. Games like Binding of Issac execute the die die die again model in such a way that you always get new powers, new unlocks. New characters every time. But this game refuses to reward the player for continuing to play it. Which limits the replayablity.
There's a reason this game is rated "Overwhelmingly Positive". If it looks interesting, get it, and try to stay alive as you randomly explore the galaxy. It's that simple.

FTL: Faster Than Light. A gloriously simple, yet complex game. This is a top-down rogue-like that simulates the experiences of managing a crew on your own spaceship in a futuristic setting. It was initially released on the 14th of September back in 2012 and is currently on sale for £6.99 or $9.99 on Steam.
Chances are, if you’re into Sci-Fi, Strategy or Rogue-likes and you play on Steam. Then you’ve seen or heard of this game. It was also massively popularised by YouTubers such as Nerd3 and TotalBiscuit. And if you haven't, then you're actually missing out on quite a lot. The premise of the game, is that you control a crew of different races in different ships as you try to flee from the ongoing Rebellion and complete your mission for the Galactic Federation.
One of the most notable things about the game is it's easily recognisable Indie and Pixely design which seems to give an Arcade or Retro feel without limiting the game to such a style entirely. However the design still feels exclusively (and entirely) it's own, although their is a definite feel of inspiration from games such as Spelunky, X-Com and the classic board game of Battleships.
One of my favourite additions to the game would have to be it’s free expansion pack: “FTL:AE (Advanced Edition)”. This added a whole new series of Ship Classes, weapons, events, augments and a whole new race.
If you do intend to play this game, then be warned: If you find yourself enjoying this game, then you will soon find it incredibly addicting and infuriating, terrifying and heart-breaking. However one of the biggest falls to this game is how quickly the use of RNG becomes an annoying sensation of "Copy and Paste" and the repetitive feelness of the same scenarios occurring time after time.
In Summary;
This game is a must get. Even if you aren’t a fan of rogue-likes or micro-managing in games, I would still recommend this. The gameplay is innovative and the design is immersive in it’s own 2D way. The variety of mod's and achievements/unlockables also make this game so replayable that at times, it almost becomes second-nature. It's only downsides are it's difficult gameplay and at times it's repetitiveness...
Pro's:
- Detailed & Beautiful Pixel Graphics
- Beautiful Soundtrack (2 Hours Long)
- Unique Gameplay
- Variety in Freedom of Choice
- Good Modding Community
Con's:
- Repetitive Gameplay
- Insane Difficulty Curves
- Overly Addictive & Infuriating
9.5/10

Okay. This is going to be really hard for me to write, so stick with me on this.
LISA is a heavy RPG with comedic moments littered throughout it. This might seem really bad, but trust me, this works. The story follows a man named Brad, a drug addict who lives in an apocolyptic world with his three best friends. One small thing about this world is that there are no women whatsoever. However, on a walk home one day, Brad finds a baby on the ground. A female baby. Things move on, and you are suddenly on a journey to go find your kid.
Choice is super prominent in this game, and you will be faced with many hard choices. Even the smallest of choice can actually effect your ending of the game. It can range from losing all of your items or having your teammate killed, to an arm or your teammate. These choices have a lot of weight to them, so it would be wise to think them over.
The combat in this game is quite something. Your party faces off against the other team in a screen similar to those of Final Fantasy, with each party member having health and either a SP or a TP bar. SP is filled already and you can use this to use your special attacks. TP is used for certain other characters and raises as you deal damage and take damage. TP is also used for special attacks. You also have the normal option of attacking. Certain characters have the ability to use combos which will then link to their SP or their TP attacks, via WASD input, when they use attack. Each character also has a guard and then the ability to use items. Certain characters also have healing abilities and SP restoration abilities, so don't worry to hard about having no items at certain times. There are also many different status effects, but don't worry. Those are explained at the start of the game. Just make sure to pay attention to the tips that a certain Hinster leaves out.
In the end, I think that LISA is one of the best games that I have played. Many people compare it to Undertale, and honestly... I think this beats Undertale. Undertale stays happy throughout the story. LISA knocks you down. It reminds you that you are supposed to be sad, and it makes sure you stay sad. I didn't feel that many feelings from Undertale, compared to LISA, and I am a guy who cried when I played Super Pokemon Mystery Dungeon. The attack styles are completely different though, and the graphics. Plus the premise and the dialouge, so in the end, it is unfair to really judge these two games against eachother.
TL;DR
LISA is an emotional rollercoaster that I had so much fun playing and beating. I bought the DLC and had a blast with that too. The game is also rather replayable. In the end, I reccommend it highly.

While I didn't like the game, I know why its great. But for me, menu-based combat is a complete snore- an archaic system used free up precious information and pad time in order to add more text and values to the game. But in the process results in a weird fraction of game world and the “action”. Concepts that make perfect sense in the battle world don't always cross into the game world and vice-versa. The action also tends to be simple or boils down to value checks- do you have high enough numbers? Good you may pass. No? You better waste more time fighting the same enemy before you come to this boss. Games today, even those made by individuals or small companies, have lot of technical room to play in and as such just shouldn't use this kind of disjointed system to tell a story.
But LISA is great because of its theme: sacrifice and a faulty protagonist. Few games tackle it, fewer do it right or roll with it through the whole game. Your actions have mechanical and game world consequences. That takes balls to develop. Games can take a long time to develop and can be babied by their design team. Not here.
You play as Brad- a man who has stumbled upon the last female in the entire human race and you gotta make some tough choices. That's all I'm going to give you, cause it spins out of control from there. It's also humorous and strange- which is good, cause a post apocalyptic world is a downer.
You can actually like menu-based combat or can stand it, give LISA a go. If you can't stomach it, you can always watch some videos of LISA and skip the droning combat parts- preferably with no commentary. Or you can always read about it. If you haven't played menu-base Japanese role playing games, do not start with LISA. You'll have a skewed vision of what to expect. Furthermore, LISA is made specifically to rub up against the norms associated with the genre. Get familiar with JRPG games from 80's and 90's like Chrono Trigger, the Final Fantasy series, the Dragon Warrior series, the Breath of Fire series, and so on.

Lobotomy Corporation is the first offering of Korean studio Project Moon (not to be confused with Type Moon), and it has to be said, if they can consistently keep up this kind of quality, they have a bright future ahead of them.
Lobotomy Corporation is a resource-management game, with your chief resource being employees. Failure to keep your employees in good health, both physical and mental, results in death, panic and general nastiness, but the best way to ensure that you complete the goal of each day (achieving at least a certain number of P.E. Boxes) is to put your employees into situations likely to result in damage, physical or mental or both. As a result, after a certain point, without proper management, your facility is likely to end up having all its employees dying, all manner of horrifying monsters invading and/or breaking loose, and general chaos occuring, which, as anyone who's played Dwarf Fortress knows, is immense fun for all involved (except possibly the employees).
The reason that your employees are going to be put into dangerous situations is the central concept of the game - Abnormalities. Abnormalities are monstrous entities, some of which seem to have humanity's destruction as a priority. Most of the captive ones seem content to stay in their cells - or at least, they do provided that they aren't messed around with. Unfortunately, this messing around with them is essential to completing the goal for the day, as many Abnomalities, when interacted with, generate Enkephalin - a possibly magical substance which, according to in-game lore, can be processed to generate enormous quantities of energy.
The sheer complexity of handling the numerous different Abnormalities, all of which have differing effects and restrictions upon interactions, should make this a good pick for anyone who's played and enjoyed other resource- and time-management games.
While Project Moon are still actively building the game, and I strongly suspect will continue to do so for a considerable length of time, I feel like their attention to detail and clear desire to release a quality product make them a team to watch.

Company of Heroes 2 (CoH2) is a Real-Time Strategy game based in the perodic time of the second world war. CoH2 is seen as a cop-off of the first title (Comapny of Heroes) as the game lacked content and focus on the national faction of the USSR or Soviet Union. The campaign itself isn't an amazingly one told, with the game holding your hand throughout the story but the main point of an RTS isn't the story but the competetive online match between players. CoH2 over the years have realease downloadable and standalone content like the United State Force, the SS Oberkommando plus the recent addition of the British Forces. Online PvP is a battle of balance as many see a certain factions as more power than others but it comes down to the response of an individual and their decision making. Perfect for people who vaulve risk-reward situations. CoH2 acted as a filling for a void during the downtime of game production.

In retrospect, this game was never actually that great. It controls terribly, and the game is unbalanced as hell in terms of class choice. Each team essentially has the same classes, but there are a couple of classes that might as well not exist as they are nearly useless - such as the engineer - theoretically useful for fixing healing and ammo droids and parts of the battleship, but in practice not very good, especially with their terrible gun.
The gunplay is... so bad. It's some of the worst gunplay I've ever experienced, actually. There's no feeling of weight in the guns, they all feel like peashooters that give no real feedback. Character movement is so fast that hitting an enemy is a matter of spamming bullets in their general direction. There's not a lot of skill here. Do you want to win? Get a vehicle. You'll get at least a dozen kills before you're destroyed, and that's if the enemies are spamming rockets at you like there's no tomorrow. I once got in a tank and got around 40 kills before someone took me out. And god forbid if you're against a hero class. There's no fighting them.
As I said, character movement is fast, but it doesn't feel like YOU are fast. It feels like everyone else is fast, and you're just slipping and sliding around the ground. Its terrible.
And of course, multiplayer is revived without the use of an external program now. Sounds good in theory. But the servers are all Peer to Peer, so most matches are extremely laggy, which makes the character movement even worse, and enemies even harder to hit. Whats worse, the server browser is a piece of total garbage. If you fail to connect to the server, which is often, you will likely be forced to restart the game entirely to try again, as the server browser will be broken. Rinse, repeat. Lets just hope that the ONE server with over 6 people is the one you can successfully connect to.
There is no reason to buy or play this game. The space battles are bad. The gunplay is bad. The balancing is bad. The multiplayer is bad. The movement is bad. This game has no redeeming qualities besides maybe looking real nice underneath your nostalgia goggles, which, I'll admit, did help for a little bit. But not for long.

A very addictive free to play beat'em up which plays like a more varied version of One Finger Death Punch in that you can't move but rather it's your enemies that move towards you. The difference here is that in Iron Snout, you can jump and there are enemies that will come at you in the air, on the ground, or sometimes sliding on the ground. The interactions between the available weapons and the enemies results in dynamic situations which can be highly amusing or very frustrating. The core gameplay is that of a survival mode in which you have 10 health to take out as many wolves as you can. The wolves spawn more frequently as time goes by. There are 3 leaderboards to compete on, best fight (highest number of wolves killed in a single run), total (highest total wolf kills), best combo (longest combo). There are some reports of bugs with achievements but I myself didn't face any issues.
Ultimately it comes down to whether you can say no to 'bacon-flavored combat' ?

LISA can be compared to another other RPGs, but that isn't terribly fair to it. LISA is a game about sacrifice in an insane world filled with less than pleasant things. Nobody's really the good guy or the bad guy, death is everywhere and the only real constant, and things may not be getting any better no matter what you do.
So just ride with it, do what you think should be done, try to stay true to something and have it be your choice. Even if it's a terribly sucky choice that you have absolutely no control over and will end badly. Because that's what LISA's all about. Choices, but often forced by those who really should have made better ones earlier.
Gameplay-wise, LISA is a turn-based quirky game filled with humor both surreal and pitch black. Lots of replay value in the many many party members you have allowing you to take different folks through the game where necessary to make different choices from your last run. If you choose to experience every possible route. Though that said there aren't many huge differences from each route, and despite the ethical feelings these choices can lead to, ultimately they're just different kinds of sacrifices that don't lead to some kind of end all golden ending. It plays well and is super challenging, forcing you to adapt quickly and not focus on just grinding things out but instead exploring as much as you can while confronting the insane denizens around you and probably killing them all horribly in the process.
Strongly recommended unless you have a weak stomach, this is a game that will stomp all over you even if you're ready for it. The title screen is of the titual character Lisa already dead and hanging, it's just going to get worse from there. Much much worse.

Just 10-15 minutes into the game, before you really get into the gameplay, and the storytelling is already more powerful and gripping than even the story in most AAA games.  And this is something that came out of RPGMaker.
The story is funny, haunting, depressing, hilarious, and fear-inducing all at the same time.  Decisions you make could cost you a party member, or even an arm.  Then you run into a situation that makes you laugh your♥♥♥♥♥off.  You want to play this game until 3 in the morning, but you end up staying awake even longer thinking about what you just saw.
The game is difficult.  It requires a lot of old skool strategy to get past the encounters, and you shouldn't expect a lot of situations where you can get repeat battles for XP farming.  (They exist, but you have to find them.)  Even resting in the wrong areas has a chance of hurting your party.  Keep multiple save points, as there are plenty of "points of no return" you may want to re-explore.
Widdly 2 Diddly's soundtrack is bizarre and goofy, but really enjoyable and fits the game extremely well.  There is a lot of music in this game, too.  So much so that there isn't really a universal battle theme for each encounter.  It's varied enough that you'll never get bored, and you'll have something awesome to listen to as you fight a big boss.
