So I don't normally write reviews but I felt the need to say something this time around.  Let me start by saying I do recommend giving this game a go, though not for the reasons you might think.
As a hobby developer myself who has unity in the past for similar projects it was definitly interesting to see how someone else acomplished similar ideas.  Mechanically it was a lot of fun to run around in and try and decipher some of the game design tricks the dev used.
My problems are with the actual content of the game.  A dream-state game with disembodied doors is lazy.  I have seen it far too many times (one of which was something I made in highschool myself).  It is a way to have several ideas and design choices without having to come up with a narrative reason for the change other than "uh its a dream" or "uh its limbo" or whatever.  I don't know if the dev reads all of the reviews (I know I wouldn't) but in case you do, or for some reason you get to mine:  Keep doing what you love.  But don't put so much of yourself in it.  This was very avant garde.  And while games have the potential to be art pieces, this feels almost like it tries too hard to be an art piece.
This kind of game is great for practice when it comes to developing games but it is more theraputic for the developer and not actually meant to be played.  If you ever do another one of these, give it to close friends, family.  Maybe post it on a smaller site like gamejolt or something.  But I would avoid putting this kind of stuff on steam.
So if you are game dev I recommend this game, but only so you can see what works and what doesn't.  Things like the ladder and the video are far too long the player will get bored easily.  But the self-destructing room was a neat little puzzle.  (although took me a few tries because the audio is a bit clippy and the audio is essential to figuring out what to do).  So yeah, if you are developing games or thinking about it give it a try.  But keep in mind this interactive art piece is nowhere near perfect.

Honestly, this is probably the best RTS of all time. The quantity of DLC is pretty shameful but honestly each of the expansions (Brits, Western Front, and Ardennes) are all really great. Most of the in-game purchases don't bother me. They're mostly skins and coats of paints which frankly no one should be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about. They've updated the game to allow for players to purchase commanders with in game currency but it takes a lot of grinding.
Shoddy in-game purchases aside and a lackluster campaign aside (get Ardennes Assault for a good campaign), this game is absolutely great. The cover based combat mechanics means that, unlike in other RTS games, managing the units you have is far more important than pumping out as many units as possible. The factions all play quite differently and while the balancing still isn't perfect Relic has been tuning it continuosly and its balanced quite well at this point. The commander system offers you different ways of playing each faction and the winter mechanics offer a unique change of pace.
Overall this game is a 10/10 for me and anyone who likes RTS games should pick it up.
Also Relic release a Japan or Italy DLC, Germans are cool and all but we really don't need three German factions.

I really, really wanted to like this game.  A grappling based first person platformer is an awesome idea, unfortunately A Story About My Uncle fails at implementing it.  It gets a lot right, but unfortunately the platforming itself is finicky and boring.
Positives:
Interesting story - If you like short but engaging stories, this has a basic but enjoyable thread pulling you forwards with a satisfying resolution.
Beautiful - A lot of great vistas and areas to look at, really great art design.
Negatives:
Easy, boring platforming - The grappling mechanic works well, but everything else about the physics fails.  Most deaths will be due to sliding off or getting stuck on random objects, or unclear grappling surfaces.  The actual levels are extremely easy once you figure out what will glitch out and avoid it.
Really odd voice acting - The voice actors are clearly skilled, but English is definitely not their native language, which results in really odd intonations and pronunciations.  I would actually prefer they spoke in their native language and had subtitles, the very odd voice acting continually brought me out of the story.
Short - I was actually happy to get it over with when finished due to the poor physics, but even then, the game is very short.  I would recommend only buying it on sale.
I didn't hate this game, it had a lot of things going for it, unfortunately the core mechanic just doesn't work and hence I cannot recommend it.

A great addition to the Shadowrun Returns franchise. So far the storyline and NPC's have been engaging and entertaining. The new Matrix set up was a bit to get used to at first but it looks great and works well once you get the hang of it. Over all I give it a big thumbs up.

First of:
Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a really good cRPG and it takes all the good stuff of the previous titles and builds upon that.
Your crew is cool, the characters are well made. I, for example, never considered hiring mercenary runners, because I very quickly learned to appreciate Gobbet and Is0bel.
The artstyle is once again on point, the portraits are fitting and the score definetly fits in.
HB also did a good job on building your home district, Heoi. It catches the flair of a cyberpunky/scifiesque chinatown slum, but you still get to feel at home there.
The gameplay is not too different from Dragonfall, but I already liked it back then. If you are into isometric RPGs with turn-based combat, you will feel comfortable here and love the huge amount of possibilities this game offers.
The story. It's not a bad story. I got pretty absorbed.
But it is really straightforward imo. You have the main continuing main quest which progresses really fast and aside from that, only a few runs. The game felt a lot shorter than Dragonfall. Also I miss gimmicks like the Schockwellenreiter or missions in which your crew is personally involved. You do not get that here (or I was too stupid to notice , but then again, I noticed in Dragonfall, where that was really well made).
You also do not get to make as many impactful decisions or if you do, they do not feel impactful and I have overlooked them.
So, this review is a mess, but summing things up:
Pro
-Story itself is nice
-Nice character, level and gameplay design
-Artstyle and score
-Well concepted runs
Cons
-Feels a bit empty (feel like DF had more runs, also no gimmicks like Schockwellenreiter or that secret dragon guy who always messed with you)
-No really impactful decisions. It's like an action movie, you have your mission and with the exception of one or two cases, you just gonna stick to it. Of course you have freedom of how to achieve your goal, but you cannot change your goal.
-Minor Bugs
Final Statement:
I had a blast with Shadowrun: Hong Kong. But it felt more like an Addon to me than Dragonfall did.
A rerun with a different character might change that opinion, but I am not too hopeful about it.
(Also what exactly was the Deluxe Edition Content?)

Alright, I tried to like this game, I really did. Normally I can get some enjoyment out of rogue-like or rogue-lite games. Hard games are fine. Games like Demon's Souls or Dark Souls? Great fun. But Dark Souls has a design philosophy that makes sense. If you die, it's your own fault. You're punished for your own failures. But this game? It's basically just a coin flip that determines whether you win a fight or not. You're punished for things you have no control over.
I think the biggest point of failure is the lack of a maximum health stat. Sure health is there, but the problem is it is finite, and can only be replenished by picking up a random enchantment from a scroll or potion or what have you. And keep in mind that it's random whether or not you find a scroll and random again whether or not this scroll will heal you. It could even be detrimental and hurt you instead. Basically if you get unlucky and take too much damage in combat? You're hooped. You have no chance. The point of health in most games is to give you a chance to survive even if you get unlucky.
There's additional classes that you can unlock, but the game is so entranced with being obtuse that it doesn't tell you at all how to unlock them. I unlocked one somehow and the game didn't even inform me that I had. I only found out when I returned to the main menu and found another class just sitting there.

In retrospect, this game was never actually that great. It controls terribly, and the game is unbalanced as hell in terms of class choice. Each team essentially has the same classes, but there are a couple of classes that might as well not exist as they are nearly useless - such as the engineer - theoretically useful for fixing healing and ammo droids and parts of the battleship, but in practice not very good, especially with their terrible gun.
The gunplay is... so bad. It's some of the worst gunplay I've ever experienced, actually. There's no feeling of weight in the guns, they all feel like peashooters that give no real feedback. Character movement is so fast that hitting an enemy is a matter of spamming bullets in their general direction. There's not a lot of skill here. Do you want to win? Get a vehicle. You'll get at least a dozen kills before you're destroyed, and that's if the enemies are spamming rockets at you like there's no tomorrow. I once got in a tank and got around 40 kills before someone took me out. And god forbid if you're against a hero class. There's no fighting them.
As I said, character movement is fast, but it doesn't feel like YOU are fast. It feels like everyone else is fast, and you're just slipping and sliding around the ground. Its terrible.
And of course, multiplayer is revived without the use of an external program now. Sounds good in theory. But the servers are all Peer to Peer, so most matches are extremely laggy, which makes the character movement even worse, and enemies even harder to hit. Whats worse, the server browser is a piece of total garbage. If you fail to connect to the server, which is often, you will likely be forced to restart the game entirely to try again, as the server browser will be broken. Rinse, repeat. Lets just hope that the ONE server with over 6 people is the one you can successfully connect to.
There is no reason to buy or play this game. The space battles are bad. The gunplay is bad. The balancing is bad. The multiplayer is bad. The movement is bad. This game has no redeeming qualities besides maybe looking real nice underneath your nostalgia goggles, which, I'll admit, did help for a little bit. But not for long.

TL;DR: Incredibly addicting little beat 'em up. Need to waste a couple of minutes? Play
! It's
You're the Kung Fu Pig, the very pinnacle of self-defense. Instead of running away when murder-crazy cartoon wolves come at you, you punch them.
Gameplay is very simple, yet challenging: arrow keys (or ASDW) left and right are attacks (the faster you hit buttons the faster you hit baddies), up is jump and down is crouch or dive. Wolves come at you at steady pace, few at first but then several at the same time and your task is to beat them all up before they kill you.
Various kinds of wolves carry items that can all be used against them. Butcher knives, hats and baskets can be thrown, and punching a wolf towards a rocket wolf explodes the whole bunch! Someone throws a knife at you that you can either deflect back with weapons or even grab and throw back to their face. The combo potential is great and fun to explore.
The challenge is the fact you can't move around. When two rockets are circling around and a wolf with a pongo stick is coming from one direction and a chainsaw dude and knife thrower from another, it's a feat to escape unharmed if they all come to the middle at the same time. In those situations you wish you could go and beat one side of enemies before the rest come at you.
Actually the whole game is seen in few minutes, when you've seen all the seven enemy types and fought against a small horde of them at the same time. Still, it's addicting and fun to keep going for the highscores. 100% completion (achievement-wise) however takes roughly 5 hours because of a couple grindy cheevos.
It's polished and technically works great, assuming you can get over the cartoon graphics and the casual mobile vibe. It's very alt+tab-friendly so I found it convenient to play it at the same time as playing a clicker game in another window.
Rather miraculously it is totally free. I think it says something about the game that I wouldn't have minded paying a couple of bucks to play this.

A brave little game from a small, passionate team of creative individuals. Currently (11/11/2017) a bit of a diamond in the rough:
First off, progress can be very shaky at first, though there are gameplay systems in place to let you preserve things like knowledge, individual creature energy supplies and equipment, even if you have to restart from the beginning or five in-game days back. There's also a daily checkpoint which works differently but is better if you want to avoid losing employees and their equipped items if things go wrong, as well as being able to restart on the current day.
Some of the monsters and abnormalities are less fair than others. Notably, one will literally kill your entire staff if you so much as click on its room, and eventually crash the game if you keep clicking. Fortunately you will likely have the option to go back to a previous checkpoint and... well, not choose that one! Besides that and a few other bad eggs (I'm looking at you, keyhole murder machine that freaks out unless you move the camera away while researching it... how counter-intuitive is that? At least give us some kind of clue!) there are many that are dangerous but manageable with the right approach, which can be deduced through experimentation and the assignment of competent (or more rarely, incompetent) agents of your company. This, I feel, is where the game shines best: The dangerous but not impossible energy-monsters.
I did eventually start to feel a bit invested in my staff members, having spent enough time honing their skills and kept them alive through careful job assignments and tactical positioning during each crisis, and there is a certain curious charm to the kooky, gloomy, possibly-a-worrying-metaphor-for-a-certain-kind-of-asian-business plot, and the various characters who convey it.
Graphics are a bit... Newgroundsy, I think. But that isn't necessarily a bad thing. Someone obviously put a lot of effort into the backgrounds, the fairly large variety of monsters and their various states and weird influences over their environment, and the assortment of hair styles and facial features which -while, again, somewhat cartoonish- is still kind of better than it is in a lot of triple-A RPGs I've played. Just the fact that there are proper ponytails, pigtails, long hair, short hair, bangs, whatever kind of hair you like, just about, and later in the game you can easily afford to customize each new employee if you so choose. Even before you earn the points to customize each person, you can just keep rolling the dice for new appearances until you find one you like the look of.
All in all, I feel this is a game that deserves more success than it has apparently had thus far. It is a creepy, spooky, gory game, make no mistake, a game about facing some pretty freaky terrors... but if that sounds like fun to you, I heartily recommend giving it a try!^^

The game keeps improving, the new UI is visually fantastic, I like that we have more interactions with the team we manage, and the reward system from working with Abnormalities in the form of weapons and armour is an added bonus. There's a few things to keep in mind, however. Firstly, the game is still very much unfinished. There are a lot of tweaks, bugs, and off translations floating about. Secondly, if you have no interest in world building and stories like the SCP Foundation archives, you're probably not going to enjoy this game.
The whole point of stories like these are to study, learn about, and prevent containment breach. As you discover how to handle them and what they do, Agents are going to die. Employees are going to go insane. You're going to fail as you learn and retry. That is the point. That's why your archives you uncover maintain regardless of your save state, and the game will get easier to progress as you learn. Sure, it's frustrating when your favourite Agent dies, but that's one of the weights of sending them in to manage deadly anomalies for the greater good of mankind. They are sacrifices to better your understanding in order to prevent more deaths in the future.
However, it's very frustrating when your employees die to bugs and sub-optimal handling in the game. But that comes with the Early Access package. I've lost a lot of Agents to issues of toggling them in and out of combat ineffectively and problems with targeting them through other objects to get them to move. But it keeps getting better with the updates since I first started playing it.
Another big thing to note is this game is Korean. The small dev team seem to be handling all of the english translations themselves as ESL, which inherently causes some weirdness sometimes for native speakers. But it's not unreadable, far from it in fact, and they constantly take fan input for spelling and grammar corrections in the Discussion forums. Personally, I'm not too concerned with the translation quality at this stage of development because dialogue and translation tweaks are usually reserved for the polishing stage.
TL;DR: The game, including its translation, are raw and incomplete. It is shaping up to be a great SCP-style game, but if you're not interested in the management side of SCP stories, or wading through unfinished features, non-fluid dialogue, and game breaking bugs, then you should either wait for it to be complete or Lobotomy Corp. might not be for you.

I really want to recommend this game. I do. But I can't, because this game is a mess. It's a mess, because the game doesn't know what it really wants to be. A horror game? A management sim? A visual novel? A roguelike? It has no idea. The ideas in the game are fine, but it's the mechanics that destroy it, because it's trying to be too many different things and succeeds at being none of them. None of the mechanics are explained either; none of the things that would help the player grasp what they're supposed to do are revealed. There's no tooltips or signs for how anything is meant to function; it just happens and you're left wondering why it's all there.
The game keeps everything after a restart like it's a roguelike, has cut scenes like it's a visual novel, has the design of a management sim, and does none of them right. Its entire advancement system is based around days, not actions the player takes, meaning there's no way to actually do everything right and succeed, which makes the game pointless. It actively penalizes the player for trying to do things correctly. You both need to grind to acquire equipment, but then grinding also kills your people which causes them to lose their equipment, which means that it's all pointless. Time advancing is the only way that you can get upgrade points, but they're so small you'll run out of people and be unable to continue. You'll decide to forgo grinding and just complete the daily energy requirement, only to rapidly end up with new tiers you weren't prepared for with woefully unprepared people that die instantly and can't interact with the new abnormalities that are presented. With upgrade points being set, the game apparently wants you to follow a formula, yet the rng of what abnormalities you get and what happens day by day means that the game wants it to be a roguelike, yet the systems do not mesh.
This game reaks of not having a clear vision for what it wants to be. It's like ten designers all got together and made different games, and shoved them all together, and the result is a mess that is nearly impossible to play. It's a cool idea, but a cool idea does not make up for terrible mechanics. and unless the game decides what kind of game it wants to be, it's going to remain a mess.

As a game, on the other hand, it is clumsy and confusing. The controls are clunky and most levels left me confused about what I was meant to do. The graphics were shaky (on my admittedly low-powered laptop), which, combined with the overuse of darkness, often obscured vital gameplay things. Overall, there were too many ideas and not enough effort put into making each one playable. The third installment of the Shadowrun Returns franchise, Hong Kong again captures the feel of the setting exceptionally well. The mechanics have been adjusted (mages have been rightfully nerfed and decking runs very differently now), and that's OK. The studio is making adjustments based upon how people have responded to the previous games. If Hong Kong suffers from anything (aside from numerous text bugs) it is that as the third game, its story formula is starting to feel stale. Where the story is still good, it is following the same pattern as before. That and copious extraneous text has actually left me bored and skipping text that I wouldn't have in an earlier game.
Also, decking needs to go. I really wasn't a fan of it in table top. It meant the GM dealt with one character exclusively while everyone else waited around. The computer game doesn't suffere from that. Instead it suffers from it being equal measures boring and frustrating. Sometimes there's just a dialog choice to hack an interface. This is wonderful because it moves the plot along and makes you feel like your karma (copious karma in this case) was well spent. A five to ten minute aside that climaxes in a ten key version of Simon just makes me want to skip decking altogether. And since decking is both so specialized and not a regular occurance, you are discouraged from playing that sort of a character rather than a straight combat monkey.
At the end of the day, if you like the Shadowrun world or you just like this style of game, then Shadowrun: Hong Kong is totally for you. If not, skip it.

What is FTL?
FTL is an rougelike game, in which you fly your spaceship across the galaxy, to reach the Fedaration base.
The galaxy is randomly generated each run, and so are the events, so 2 playthroughs are never the same.
How does it play?
This game plays amazing, it's quick to learn, hard to master.
The first sectors may be easy but as you progress you will need to adapt your tactics around new weapons and tougher enemies. Weapon types are simple, going from Lasers, Missles, Beams, Bombs, and Ion Weapons. While I won't get into those types, let it be known that the types are all diffirent and have advantages and weaknesses.
How hard is it?
Hard. The difficulty settings say Easy, Medium, Hard, but it's more like Medium, Hard, Hardest
You will die. A LOT. Dying is part of the game. It's going to happen a lot, mainly when you haven't learned the game mechanics yet. Thanks to the random generated nature of enemies (excluding certain events and the final boss) any fight can kill you if you're not prepared.
How do I get more ships?
Unlock quests. Some are easier, like the ship that requires you to make sector 5/8 which can even be done on the first run, and the one that needs you to beat the game on any difficulty, anything other than those have their own unlock quests with their own requierments. However, beating the game with the previous ship will unlock the next one.
Overall Rating: 9/10

Let's get right down to it.
Pros:
Balanced class system.
There are several different classes that you can play as, each with its own special weapons and items, suited for unique roles and play styles. Because of this, each class is balanced, having just as many strengths as it does weaknesses. There is no single class that is good at everything, only classes that are specialized for specific roles.
Map variety.
From the cramped starship interior of the Tantive IV, to the wide open ice plains of Hoth. From the dense jungles of Felucia, to the elegant Jedi temple on Coruscant. There are a plethora of different maps, each offering a unique game experience.
No unlockable content.
This game was made in the time before DLC. But back then, and still today, a lot of games had content that is locked until you reach a certain point or achieve a certain goal. Not this game. all classes, maps, and game modes are available as soon as you download.
Great storyline.
this game's campaign mode features jurnal entries from a clone trooper serving in the 501st legion. Although it isn't canon, it provides some insight on what many clones may have thought and felt during and after their many battles.
Great AI.
As the game has had no online multiplayer support for years, (until recently, that is. it was readded on Oct 3 2017) all you had to do was single player. Which isn't as bad as it sounds. The AI players in the game are actually formidable opponents, and trusty teammates While they aren't as unpredictable or resourceful as human opponents, they are in no way pushovers. They aim properly, they use simple, but effective tactics, they actually play the objective, and a team of them could possibly beat an entire team of actual people.
It's Star Wars.
Enough said.
Cons:
Lack of game modes.
This isn't to big of an issue for me, but for others it may be. There aren't very many games to be played here. Every map has conquest, which is a dominaton type game mode, and most have a form of CTF, either 1 flag or 2 flag. However, there isn't much more than that. There are a few other modes, but they are all limited to certain maps. Personally, I feel that the variety of maps makes up for this, while you are still working towards the same objective, different maps force you to go about it differently. But some would consider this a con, so I'm mentioning it.
Old game.
pretty much everything else that's negative can be summed up by the above. There's never going to be any new content, because it's an old game. The graphics aren't anything special, because it's an old game. Any glitches and bugs you find (although I haven't found any) will never be fixed, because it's an old game.
Conclusion:
Star wars battlefront II  (classic) is a fantastic game that any star wars fan will love. Even if you aren't a star wars fan, but are into shooter games in general, this is a great one to try. Hours of fun and unique gameplay on single player, and even more now that multiplayer support has been readded.

Another brilliant platformer, the connection between the music and gameplay makes it very addicting and encourages you to complete the level. It's a bit easier than BIT.TRIP RUNNER (at least on normal difficulty), which might make it more accessible for most players and makes it a lot more fun to play for longer sessions. Oh, and the graphical style blows the first game out of the water, although that can make it a bit harder to see your character and the obstacles sometimes...

On paper this game sounds fantastic, basically a game based on the series of 'creepy pasta' (or short horror fiction) based around the world of the SCP foundation. Basically the Men in Black who capture and detain eldritch horrors that could alter if not destroy humanity. Only in this case, you use them to produce power....somehow.
Logic failure aside, the SCP stories are all based around the cruel and creepy way these abominations operate. Everything from an apartment that absorbs people to create new furniture, to a creepy golem that will kill you if you look away from it or even blink. Even the horrors of....a rock that will change your sex if you touch it? In any case, horrors and oddities abound in the SCP universe, and Lobotomy seeks to imitate the weird and unusual in managing a facility that exploits these abominations for literal power.
But that is where things start to break down. First off, there is no obvious tutorial or even tooltips to how to play the game. You get a monster, and then have to send a generic worker to do one of four actions to produce power. It seems some monsters produce more with certain actions, but this is very inconsistent. But successful interactions allows you to build weapons and armor tailored to that monster or give you more insight in how it operates....but by the time you unlock all of that you already know pretty much what you are doing with said monster.
Which is the second complaint. While it should be obvious that these monsters are dangerous and you shouldn't get attached to your generic workers....some of them are seemingly unusable. In my first couple of tries I came across two that just seemed to be good ways of getting rid of workers I don't like. One was a grandmother looking monster that just killed workers for entering her room. The second was a bunch of spider beings that killed one worker by the time I finished a session with them.
Which leads to my biggest overall complaint....it's either boring or you miss out on the fun. The former being that the majority of the time you are just clicking rooms and sending workers with nothing really happening other then confusing lines like 'purging humanity' or 'only faithful can hear the whispers' popping up as your worker does it's job. On the flip side the real (sadistic) fun is when things go wrong such as when workers go crazy, monsters escape, workers get killed by said monsters, or you seem to get invaded by horrors for some reason. But...it's so easy to miss these things happening.
Far to many times I would be directing workers only to find that one of them comes up as dead, and looking into rooms shows a corpse. How did they die? Was it a cool death? I don't know because I neither could see it happen or got any sort signal that such thing was happening. Because you spend so much time just fast forwarding time because most of said time is just sending workers to do their job.
The long and short of it is, this is a horror game that is more a horror on how boring it makes the concept of running a jail to exploit monsters be. It may be an early access, but unless they can make the horror as much fun as they imply in the trailer I would suggest going to read up on the SCP universe over buying this game. SCP is more fun, creepy, and free.

(Day 7.  It's all over except for the crying.  It's been so broken for so many days that I can't properly remember where it first went wrong anymore.  I missed something, but I can no longer remember what at this point.  All this death is my fault, and I can't stop making it worse.  Five agents dead in one instant, snapped up by a giant angler fish plant hiding under the floor plating that I can't even tell if we ever restrained properly, or if it wanted to come inside and allowed us to bring it here.  It was loose and the only thing I could do was to somehow finish the day.  The only hallway open was to the robot.  I knew what it meant for the agent chosen.  My last woman standing, SooYung went to her death with her head held high, proud to save the human race with her sacrifice.  She still screamed though...they all do.  I should have made myself watch, but I just couldnt.  If I had watched, maybe it wouldnt have made any difference to her. But now anytime I close my eyes I hear that scream.  What am I becoming...)  <---dramatization of my last game session.  Don't laugh at me, thats what it felt like.
So I like this game a lot now.  It creates some amazing stories, and never fails to keep me interested.  There's an obvious thematic comparison to Cabin in the Woods to be made here, but it stops at the barest bones concept; the secret government facility full 'o monsters.  That concept is one hell of a playground.
My original complaint of bad translation still stands.  The confusion and odd language is present and plentiful, but frankly...I no longer care.  The manual is a critical must read, and its a bit of a long read.  But the writing on it is so delightful and interesting, it goes pretty quick and I'm already considering re-reading it just for fun.  Once the manual is coupled with an already promised tutorial, I'm sure this will be a solid hit like FTL was.  If they continue to clean up their translation, which I've noticed a difference in already, my main issue will evaporate.
The vibe is unforgiving, but it actually isnt so hard to be successful.  It's just complicated.  Once you go from a place of doing well to doing poorly (ha!) in the space of a single mistake, you can usually still recover, or at least limp across the finish line for the day.  That gameplay dynamic is MUCH more interesting than just responding in a predictable manner to every single event for success.  This game is surprisingly fun.

If you follow my reviews you may recall that I was particularly non-plussed with the characters in A New Beginning, another title from Daedalic Entertainment. Despite being on a mission to save the world they were venomous, illogical, boorish, and downright abusive to each other. I got a few hours into it before the cacophony of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s wore me down, and I checked out of the game with great confidence that I had seen the worst characters the adventure genre had to offer. It was then, however, that Edna & Harvey poked their misshapen heads in and asked me to hold their beer.
Edna & Harvey follows the adventures of... Lilli, actually. She's a weird-looking Q-tip of a girl locked away in a convent run by a raging misanthrope of a headmistress. The doofy announcer is more than happy to tell us all about how Lilli is the nicest, sweetest, bestest little girl in the world who just happens to be misunderstood by her cruel guardian, and by everyone else for that matter. And sure enough she's practically mute and extremely accommodating in her interactions with the others residing at the convent, her dear friend Edna (there she is!) included. At least, she is at first.
You're probably not here to listen to me ramble vaguely about the game, so let's cut to the quick. I warn you that what follows are mild spoilers for part 1 of the game, but it's very important you understand what you're potentially getting into here. One of the first puzzles has you nearly drown a fellow child in a well and drop a beehive on him. Granted, he's a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥leading up to this so I thought it was darkly funny, if a little mean. The last leg of the puzzle, however, has Lilli feed him to termites. They eat him offscreen, leaving a pile of viscera that some random♥♥♥♥♥gnome comes and paints pink.
Within 15 minutes of starting the game, you murder one of the kids at the convent. It's goofy and indirect, so I thought it was weird but not alarming. It got alarming when Lilli locked another kid in the basement boiler with a bomb. From there, part 1 is just a pure killing spree, crushing children under statues and planks, chucking them off cliffs, and driving them to suicide. I'm not kidding about that last one, you seriously ruin this girl's rep with the headmistress and the last time you see her alive she's bawling her eyes out, minutes before taking a swing from the rafters neck-first.
Like... what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on in this game? Who on God's green Earth sits down and decides "Y'know what would be a fun game? Murdering children!"? Lilli's massacre is obviously played for laughs, with the bizarre gnomes covering up the carnage with goopy pink paint and the narrator talking it all down as misunderstandings. The stupid ♥♥♥♥ing narrator is another brick in this twisted wall, playing up Lilli's innocence and ignorance in one breath, then revealing her dark fantasies and murderous intent in the next. He's an unreliable narrator not because he's hiding some secret, but because whoever wrote his awful lines must have the attention span of a gerbil and kept ping-ponging the jokes all over the place.
I've dwelt plenty on the detestable plot beats of the game because seriously, ♥♥♥♥ that filth, but the puzzles are really no better. The cartoonish airs of the aesthetic extend to the puzzle logic, requiring you to cut things with nails, unscrew things with hair clips, and at one point remove a bolt with a balloon. You're going to spend a lot of time trying random things on other things just to keep up with the fever-dream reasoning, which is going to make the big setpiece puzzles that much worse. One of the first requires you to collect nine items from around the convent, talk to people about what emotions they represent, then listen to an old guy's insane ramblings and create a logic matrix out of those items. It's confusing, it's laborious, and it's boring, all things your core gameplay should never be.
Between the aggressively old-school puzzles and incredibly distasteful story, I can't imagine who this game was made for. It's the same problem I had with A New Beginning... maybe Daedalic is losing something in the translation from their mother tongue, but that can't possibly account for playing bloody child murder for laughs. A more logical conclusion, now that I've played two of their games, is that Daedalic is a passable game company haunted by a psychotic writer who has no idea how humans relate or function. And that's my charitable assumption, because I have rarely been so put off a game as I have here.

Overall Rating 6.5/10
The Good
The game is populated with wacky comical characters at every turn, so much so that you will never have a case of déjà vu. Not to mention the premise of the game began super interestingly. This all fits well with the theme, which is refreshingly light-hearted despite the story. Major areas in the game are unique and well executed throughout. The great music and art do certainly add to it as well. The gameplay itself was quite standard with a little bit of extra. Solutions to puzzles were often creatively bizarre with unexpected outcomes. Mini games, while few, were always fun, challenging and different.
The Bad
The conclusion was terribly anticlimactic. While it had a good start, the taste of the plot quickly became stale as the conflict nor the antagonists can be taken seriously, and there was never any significant character growth. There were also a significant number of minor plot holes and unattended questions at the end. Close to no characters were able to display complex emotions or personality. Gameplay felt a little clunky in some sections—minor bugs certainly didn’t help it either. Some problems leave you confused as the solutions were unintuitive. A key mechanic also was a bit forced and did not contribute much. While there are a few great voices, most voice acting felt a bit off and unpolished. The dialogue transition was too quick too.
The End
My overall rating for Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes is a 6.5/10. This game has so much potential to be something more on every level but it failed to capitalise at every turn as well.

If you've enjoyed the very excellent Shadowrun Returns series, then you perhaps already planned to get Hong Kong. However, if you're simply curious, then you should know this game is excellent. Of course, this really depends on how much you like the first two games. If you greatly enjoyed them, you will most certainly enjoy this one. Mind you, there are no major steps forward for the game, Much is the same. Character creation, the interface, combat, etc. are all pretty much the same. But as they say, if it isn't broken, don't fix it. And the Shadowrun Returns series has been an excellent series of turn based RPGs. What we get here is a new, well written, and exciting story. As the name implies, the setting this time is Hong Kong. You play as a ex-con from Seattle who has just recieved an urgent message from someone who could basically be called your foster father. Not having seen him in ten years, the message is cryptic, but the circumstances surrounding what is happening in Hong Kong even more so. After meeting an old friend/brother, another person you haven't seen in ten years, you are immediately thrust into a situation that forces you to relinquish your identity and essentially become a shadowrunner. Like the previous game, this is another mystery to solve, filled with side missions, interesting characters, and new environments to explore.
In addition, there has been a key, and very welcome, change to the Matrix element of the game. No longer do you simply enter the Matrix and fight off enemies when they show themselves. You are now free to roam the Matrix, lest you get caught by internal security and then have to fight them off as usual. Every encounter with an IC in the Matrix loads a certain amount of tracing percentage that, when filled, will lead to you being attacked by enemies. You can avoid this happening by not getting caught by enemy IC. In addition, there are new puzzle elements that you must solve in order to hack into certain nodes. Failing these puzzles will add percentages to your trace time. These additions make Matrix running more exciting and add variety to gameplay. If there was any weakness to the previous games, it was the dull Matrix running segments, but HBS listened to the fan base and improved this factor.
As I've stated, this game doesn't take any massive steps forward, but that is really more of a relief than anything. Shadowrun Returns has always been a fun series to play, with it being more about exploration, narrative, and character than trying to experiment with gameplay. So, it succeeds in presenting an excellent new environment to explore, and characters that move away from being the brooding silent types. At the same time, it keeps the very excellent gameplay we have come to love.

Vastly improved character progression system adds up to the replay value, you can now customize your fellow runners and edit their loadout.
The side dialogs and the sub-plots are as good as alway. A good improvement over the past chapters is that now you won't have to wait until the ending sequence to reap what you sow, often times there will be immediate consequences to your actions although of course the main turning points of your adventure will still leave some loose ends to hear about after the final battle.
The combat, while challenging at times, leaves a lot of room for the player to experiment around. During my playthrough i ran most missions with 3 characters and Simon Rigfield, my main character, crouching against a wall as far away from the action as possible. I wanted to save up skill points for later but doing so i was stuck with one useless char, yet the game was flexible enough for me to make it to the last mission and mind you i was also playing on the hard setting.
Hacking is the aspect of the game i feel has improved the most, you can sneak around countermeasure programs to avoid fighting them, the awarness levels rise everytime you engage enemies in combat and to download paydata and other valuable informations you have to clear puzzles.
If i had to say one thing i didn't like that would be the usual etiquette unfairness: some etiquettes kept popping up almost every mission while some others i have only seen used once in the entire game.
All in all If you are a fan of the lore, if you like turn based combat or if you are simply curious about sci-fi rpgs Shadowrun: Honk Kong is definitely the game for you.

With as much written content as a novel, branching storylines intimately linked to your character choices, and a real tabletop feel where intrigue and negotiation can supplant the need for bloodshed; Shadowrun: Hong Kong is the commensurate single player RPG experience.  It is best suited for avid readers who love video games, and for gamers who love interactive fiction.  The tactical combat, the freedom of character creation, and the a-la-carte missions should appeal to the more goal-oriented RPG fans among us.  But if you don't like to read, you'll find the game (and its predecessors) to be a bit of a turn-off (even though they are a much better read than basically every other RPG these days).  For me, the game's writing and art are on par with Dragonfall, and its gameplay has been dramatically enhanced.
The Writing:
S:HK's writing is its single greatest feature.  The narrative voice and descriptiveness of the prose is unlike any you'll read in a modern game.   Even so-called indie titles whose primary content is text--housed in a minimalist frame--cannot compete with the evocative style of the narration.  Each intro scene paints a vivid picture in a concise few paragraphs.  At no point does the game talk down to its player, who is quickly immersed in the language and style of the setting with little primer.  Those familiar with the first two games may earn more from the reading experience: The lingo and dialogue of the Shadowrun universe are unique and endearing.  It is not "Star Trek"-style technobabble; it all makes sense in this dark, urban fantasy.
A few grammatical errors here and there don't detract much from the experience, by my reckoning, and occur on the order of once per hour or two.  When you write an entire novel's worth of exposition without a highly-trained editorial staff, this is to be expected (and it will probably be tidied up in an update).
The Art:
The game's art style is baroque and daunting to the senses.  It is cluttered and claustrophobic, because it needs to be.  The models and character portraits stand out like beacons.  Something always seems to be hiding in the margins, lurking in the alleys.  Visual information is at a surplus--amalgamating into a chaotic whole--with blurry text scrawled on signs, arcane graffiti on every wall, and the unsettling sharpness of corporate billboards hanging overhead.  Those familiar with the series should take note of the Matrix's new visuals: Parallax foreground elements and yawning crystalline chasms give cyberspace a needed sense of openness and vertigo.  It juxtaposes well with the oppressive disorder of "meatspace".  The new assets for use in Hong Kong and its Walled City are perfect: Bold reds and yellows pour forth from the neon calligraphy-shapes of the East Asian sprawl.
The Music & Audio:
The music works well within the setting.  Combat cues are good, mounting highs and lows help steer the narrative, and the pace and length of the tracks works well during dialogue scenes.  The leitmotifs present in Dragonfall make a return, with a distinctly Asian flair.  The battle themes are all new and sound amazing: Not too gut-churning for a turn-based game.  Just enough tension to keep you anticipating your next action.  Other audio cues are rare, but make nice additions.  The ambient sounds of gambling, the squaking of comm links, the trickling of rain, and the susurrus of a crowd help to immerse the player in each type of scene.
The Plot & Themes:
The plot of the game is a tightly woven and intricate work, with nuanced and imperfect characters, drenched in a thousand shades of moralistic gray.  The Shadowrun universe benefits from this sort of storytelling.  Shadowrunners, after all, exist entirely in the margins: The margins between bad and worse, the margins between metahumanity and poverty, the marginality of magical individualism in a society that fears the imperative of individuality.  The game has more plot diversions than Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall.  Your characters' Strength, Charisma, Intelligence and other skills play a big role during dialogue scenes, where combat can be entirely avoided (or engaged with greater advantage) based on how you built your character and the choices you make.
Magic users have entirely different characters they consort with during gameplay, as do techies and weapon specialists.  Bringing different people along for a run will dramatically impact what you can do during that mission, as well as the conversations that take place.  The game is more in-your-face than Dragonfall in a lot of ways.  More profane for sure (lots of♥♥♥♥♥♥and ♥♥♥♥ to be had), grimier and more gory (with both visual and narrative horrors that work well to frame a scene), and more fantastical in its enviroments.
There are several "missable" NPCs.  If you play your cards right, you can get them on your team to use during runs.  They have an enormous amount of dialogue and a diverse repertory of skills.
The Gameplay:
For those new to the series, the XCOM-style gameplay can be a bit clunky at first.  It definitely takes a bit of learning.  Having played the first two games (Dragonall numerous times), I play on Hard and combat can take a few retries.  The chance to hit an enemy is similar to a tabletop RPG (sometimes only 50% or less), which may take some PC gamers by surprise.  You need to use cover, you need to plan ahead, and you can't just use all your actions to attack.  Tactics are key.  A diverse set of abilties are key.  Crowd control is a rare commodity, and you should make sure you have a little bit in your party.  Fast-acting magi are needed to heal allies on the fly.  The occasional spirit/drone must be summoned, to tank damage for the party.
In Hong Kong more than its predecessors, combat roles are better defined and more vital--for this reason, there are NPCs around to help fill out the roster.  The NPCs' level-ups are quick and unobtrusive.  You make a simple choice for each character as you advance through the game.  No two NPC combatants are alike, and each allows you to try something new.  This is important because you can only really build one character of your own.  Getting to try out sorcery, summoning and conjuring, the firepower of a street samurai, the talents of a melee warrior, and the augmentations of a cybered-up decker/soldier provides a well-rounded experience for players who only intend to do one play-through.
All of these combat necessities are counterbalanced with the non-combat necessities of the run.  Do you need a decker to infiltrate?  Will this infiltration help you avoid combat, thus compensating for the loss of firepower?  The game is built upon big, important choices and the same run can go in two or three different directions, depending on your roster of shadowrunners.
The Matrix has been beefed up.  Stealth elements are now in play, requiring you to wait and advance in order to avoid getting "traced" by enemy programs.  If you get traced too many times, the IC shows up and you've got to fight your way out of the system.
The Verdict:
If you played Shadowrun Returns or Dragonfall and liked either one even a lil' bit, get the game.  It's just as good as Dragonfall on each axis of comparison, if not better.  If you aren't sure you'll like a Shadowrun game, get whichever one is the cheapest and give it a try first.  Bear in mind, this one will be a more fleshed-out experience altogether.  If you like interactive fiction, tabletop games, or old school RPGs where your choices matter; this game will inspire nostalgia for something that may have never existed.  It's just got a great feel.
All in all, I'm loving this game, and Harebrained Studios keeps putting out better and better stuff.  Keep your eyes peeled for more of their work.

What is FTL?
FTL is an rougelike game, in which you fly your spaceship across the galaxy, to reach the Fedaration base.
The galaxy is randomly generated each run, and so are the events, so 2 playthroughs are never the same.
How does it play?
This game plays amazing, it's quick to learn, hard to master.
The first sectors may be easy but as you progress you will need to adapt your tactics around new weapons and tougher enemies. Weapon types are simple, going from Lasers, Missles, Beams, Bombs, and Ion Weapons. While I won't get into those types, let it be known that the types are all diffirent and have advantages and weaknesses.
How hard is it?
Hard. The difficulty settings say Easy, Medium, Hard, but it's more like Medium, Hard, Hardest
You will die. A LOT. Dying is part of the game. It's going to happen a lot, mainly when you haven't learned the game mechanics yet. Thanks to the random generated nature of enemies (excluding certain events and the final boss) any fight can kill you if you're not prepared.
How do I get more ships?
Unlock quests. Some are easier, like the ship that requires you to make sector 5/8 which can even be done on the first run, and the one that needs you to beat the game on any difficulty, anything other than those have their own unlock quests with their own requierments. However, beating the game with the previous ship will unlock the next one.
Overall Rating: 9/10

But the game quickly becomes very self indulgent and egotistical. I appreciate that the developer has made this as a form of catharsis...but it just comes across as whiny. I particularly didn't like climbing the ladder and watching the developer throw stuff around a stage for what seemed liked half an hour. Yeah, you got turned down for college. Thousands of people do, but most of them don't feel that they should expect others to sit down and watch your attempts at drama.
What exactly do you expect to happen? Are you hoping that people are going to go "Wow...he's actually really good! They must have been crazy to turn him down!"? That might have been possible...if you hadn't made it so transparent. If instead you had simply shown us that you're a talented developer by making a small, well crafted game, then it might have worked. But no, you actively shout in our faces "IT'S NOT FAIR! IT'S NOT FAIR! IT'S NOT FAIR!" as if that will have the result you want. Sorry, but it makes you look like an unhinged petulant teenager throwing a hissy fit because they JUST DON'T REALISE YOUR GENIUS...or something.

Still quite early on, but as things stand this is, if anything, even superior to Dragonfall. Of particular note is the huge number of etiquette/skill dependent dialogue options. These etiquettes were rarely used in Dragonfall, but almost every conversation in HK seems to feature multiple special options.  The Matrix has also been revamped, with gameplay there now allowing you to try and stealth your way through systems - a very welcome change.
The new crew are well written and engaging - I was skeptical that they could match DF's party, but they've managed superbly. Gobbet is lots of fun, and the brotherly camaraderie with Wu is something you don't often see in RPGs which are usually bogged down in melodrama and brooding.
The art and design are all lavish, the environments sprawling and a delight to explore (DF might seem rather drab and cramped in retrospect), and missions so far are offering many varied options for completion ranging from fighting, talking, or simply bypassing threats through manipulation of the environment.
There are one or two bugs - a few conversations which seem to be misfiring, saying you screwed up a run when you didn't (no actual gameplay impact here), but I'm sure these will be ironed out quickly. Beyond that I don't have a bad word to say.
I you've played the previous SRR games you know what you're in for - but this experience is honed and refined almost to perfection (I would appreciate more meatspace stealth, but I believe even that is in this game later on). If you're new to SR this is a fine point to jump into the series. Highly recommended.

Firstly, this game is not as awful as people say. It's not unwinnable, I certainly managed to win it. I stopped playing the game because it became too easy for me, but that's because I have a lot of good gear (due to winning the game) and knowledge about the game after playing for 80 hours. I was very persistent and I learned more every time I died.
I must be one of the few people who really enjoyed this game. I greatly enjoyed the challenge and tried to get just a little further each time, before finally making it. Roguelike perma-death games that reward you for trying and trying are quite hilarious.
This game only lets you have a small amount of gear, but the gear is vital. The combination of gear lets you take less (or more) damage from certain types of damage, as well as improving your ability to hurt stuff.
There's a ton of luck involved, but a lot of skill. As I played more and more, I realised which classes worked well on which levels. I worked out when to fully explore certain areas with certain classes and when to rush to the next area.
Some people won't like this game because of the graphics, and that's certainly one downside. Others won't like this game because it's repetitive and because you only have the ability to only carry a small amount of loot.
I loved the game because of the challenge of the game, the complex simplicity of the gear management, and the huge amount of enjoyment I got when I started winning games.

Hack, Slash, Loot is a nice little turn based dungeon crawler.
The maps and the loot and monsters therein are always randomly generated, which at the beginning can be quite frustrating as you have a steep learning curve as to how this game exactly "
" Since you start out with rather weak characters (you unlock new ones by dying in/failing a quest) the game seems rather frustrating. But don't let that ruin your experience as you advance you'll unlock new characters and get to the fun/challenge of the game rather quickly and more easily.
completely bypasses difficult and complex skill and stat systems for a rather basic approach. You have 2 stats per weapon class (Attack Chance/Attack Damage) a defense skill and health. In addition to the stats there's an "elemental system." You can either cause, resist or have a vulnerability to one of the 7 damage types; silvered, fire, lightening, poison, divine, necrotic and psychic. And that's it.
If you start the game up you'll first decide with which kind of character you want to play (32 in total once all are unlocked. You unlock new ones every N^2 deaths) you'll then decide what quest you want to approach (there are currently 6) and what artifacts to take with you (once you found any).
Depending on these choices you also set the difficulty for your game. Melee characters are hard to play with (since they need to get close first), ranged characters have a medium difficulty (since they can shoot from afar) and wizards are easier to play with (since their shots penetrate armor if the enemy hasn't got an enchantement against it). Depending on their starting elements or enchantements they also add or substract from the difficulty, based on which quest you are approaching. It'd, for example, be quite foolish to try and attempt the "They Dwell beneath" Quest, wherein you go out to hunt down 5 dragons in a mountain, with a starting character or artifact that makes you vulnerable towards fire damage.
Artifacts are found in specific encounters throughout the game or by finishing certain quests. Artifacts stay with you and can be selected as starting gear making your life significantly easier.
With all this in mind the games actual
is rather simple but shines in one particular aspect: choice. In every quest there are 5 levels with certain enemies of certain quantities but they are nonetheless of the same kind. With this in mind the biggest challenge of the game is to take or not to take risks. As the "Loot" aspect in the title of the game suggests it makes you think rather hard on what to use and what not to use; "Are you taking this shield with you that makes you less likely to hit enemies and makes you vulnerable to psychic damage but gives you a steady defense stat that'll continually help you out whenever you are hit and in addition makes you resistant to poison?" or "Do I drink this potion which name doesn't suggest neither positive nor negative effects that could heal my low health but also make me vulnerable towards the current enemies most common element and therefor kill me?" are examples of the most common and frequent choices in the game.
A lot of other people think this game is "
" to them but it really isn't. It is true that a lot of luck and chance is involved in the game, however this feeling of "unfairness" will usually go away once you've understood the game and beaten it once or twice. While it is based on chance and luck a lot you'll, as it is always the case with luck and chance, on >average< succeed quite steadily. That's what odds are all about. If you get into the game a bit statements will quickly go from:"Stupid game always spawns too many enemies and no good loot," to:"Maybe I should've taken that other helm with me instead and risk being poisened so that I'd have received less normal damage by upping my defence."
Some words about
: The graphics usually don't exceed the 10x10 Pixel boundary per sprite or background element so don't expect too much even though it features fantastic and distinctive design within this limitation and the sound is really nice. This is actually the only thing that bugs me: The music doesn't consecutively play throughout the game but rather plays one soundloop on occasion. Starting a quest? Soundtrack 1 loops once. As you descend the enemies get harder and harder, and they get more cheap with their attack powers, such as poison that can take off half your health over time, fire attacks that can also destroy your equipment, and lighting attacks that can chain stun-lock you.
There is also no leveling system, you gain (and loose) attributes from equipment, which is further modified scrolls, potions, and altars.  The loot in general is also very boring and uninteresting, and you will often see the same equipment you didn't want over and over again.  The best part is that to unlock extra characters, the game expects you to die over and over again.  You start with 3 out of 32 characters unlocked.
I cannot recommend this game on any level.

I recommend this game with a bit of a warning. It can be fun, but only if you're extremely patient and don't mind having your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you every ten minutes or less.
It's a simple enough premise. Choose your mission. Choose your character. Go through the dungeon floors to try and complete your mission. Die. Try again. It's your typical roguelike in that regard. However, there is one thing that really makes this game more difficult than other roguelike dungeon crawlers such as Legend of Dungeon or even The Binding of Isaac (I know it's a bit of an odd comparison). The hit rate system in this game is seriously flawed. Your hit rate automatically starts out at roughly 60% regardless of what character you start with. You can deal a fair amount of damage and kill enemies in one hit, which is nice. Yet, you only hit them a fraction of the time and you can find yourself exchanging blows with a single enemy for two or three minutes until one of you dies. If you're surrounded by multiple enemies, odds are, you're going to die because you have such a small chance of killing them all before they've managed to kill you.
Luck based elements in roguelike games are not unheard of. Quite the opposite. They're a crucial part of the genre. However, when it becomes TOO luck based, it becomes a problem. Random level, enemy and item generation is a good idea. Random hit rates however are not. It makes completing a single floor almost impossible, let alone a whole mission. If you're patient enough to actually sit through countless runs of this game to beat a mission, then this is the game for you. However, if you do not like the idea of huge maps with a flawed probability driven combat system, then I would recommend other roguelike titles first.

By this point, we all know what a roguelike is, even if the exact distinctions have become muddled. Perhaps many of you play roguelikes fanatically. I am not talking games like Binding of Isaac or FTL. I am talking ADOM, Nethack, Dungeon Crawl, those sorts.
Those of you who do play those games may feel at times that their greatest strengths, their vast complexity and length, can often become overbearing and intimidating. By the end of any roguelike, the game becomes exhaustive. You've been at that game for days just for that one playthrough. And how many times did you have to die just to learn every special situation, and figure out every monster along the way to victory? These games require a lot of cognitive overhead and rote memorization.
Doesn't it seem counterintuitive that I write a gripe about roguelikes in a recommendation for a roguelike? Yes, sure, but this is exactly what One Way Heroics tries to shy away from. It is a true roguelike, but it shies away from the issues I stated before. It plays fast and simple. You could expect to complete a full game within a few hours, and it provides enough of a challenge that it isn't a pushover for it. The wall of death to your left also rids you of the tedium of stashes and grinding.
Your perspective of the game may be different from mine, but this is the most important aspect to me. This is how I sum up the game and why I play it.
I play roguelikes for their nuanced and complex gameplay.
I play One Way Heroics for its simplicity and short length per playthrough.

Is this supposed to be a free alternative to The Beginner's Guide? Because both were equally as boring to play as they were a big ego-stroke fest for both game designers. I mean, it's your own method of expressing yourself, but there's a reason they let you negatively review free games/mods here on Steam. I'm literally convinced the developer played The Beginner's Guide and then started this game the same day.
Gameplay-wise, it's a walk and look at stuff simulator with one actual interesting moment involving paintings. The controls feel like I'm playing Rock of Ages in first person or something. Walking into a portal sometimes works right away, sometimes takes a bit, and makes me feel like the game glitched or something. Graphically the game is okay, but a lot of areas are buggy. Also - it's not fun to play at all. I've watched movies more interactive than this.
The narrative being pushed is a silly one. This game (if you can call it that) would have been much better as something like LSD Simulator rather than some Stanley Parable-esque cry for attention. If making video games is that difficult and you can't deal with the pressure, then go do something else and stop crying in your own games.
We get it, making video games is hard. If it's that much of a trouble, and if you're having all this internal struggle, why not go get another job? And if you made this for funsies, that kind of undermines the whole point, no? Maybe I just don't "get" art, if you could call this "art". This was free and all that, but I still wouldn't say it's worth the time it took to download it.

I've never played the first one, so I have no thoughts on this game as a sequel. However, I will say it's a fun and humorous (very dark humor at that) short play.
Graphics: Edna and Harvey has a very simplistic art style, and at first may feel a bit too simplistic for a point and click adventure game. However the art style does fit in and I found myself quickly getting used to it in a few minutes. But compared to most Daedalic games, this one is still down on graphics.
Voice Acting: The voice acting is great and really brings out the characters in fitting ways. But while the characters are colorfully brought to life, don't expect much for emotional voice acting, as that's not really part of this game's theme to begin with.
Gameplay: Pretty much what you'll expect from a point and click adventure game. Functions work fine, not too many bugs, and it does have skippable tutorials and puzzles (if you're just playing for story). And the rules list ends up being an excuse to click stuff more rather than play as a full feature, but the idea is entertaining.
Music: The soundtrack in this game is... ok. The main theme song is definetly great, but the dragged on opening sequence and the credits playing it twice overwelcome it's stay. And if you take a long time finishing the first chapter, the instrumental theme will ring in your head for days. The soundtrack itself isn't bad, but the direction could use some work.
Length: Very short. If you have a guide or just catch on to all the objectives fast, you'll easily be done within 4 or 5 hours. But I will say those hours are filled well, and nothing feels like it drags on too long (unless you get stuck or lost). When you do finish it, it won't feel like it was only 5 hours, but it won't feel long either.
Story: The story isn't very deep, and whenever the plot tries to throw in a twist, it feels it's parodying itself. I won't spoil the twists or anything, but the laughs and unexpected moments are pretty much what you'll be expecting from it. It's cute, funny, colorful, but not deep.
Price: My advice is to buy this one when a bundle is on sale. Anywhere around 5$ is well worth it, or higher if you really enjoy Daedalic games. I just really advise the bundle sales as they'll give you other titles to play as well for less money than any of them alone.
Overall, I do reccomend this game if it's your cup of tea. It'll brighten your day, but not be one your games of the year.

This is a well made game, absolutely. It is fun to play and engrossing. Charming in its way. But at the end of five hours of playing it, I cannot stand this game.
Why?
This game is based on random rolls and nothing else once you get into the heart of its mechanics. Imagine playing a card came where there may or may not be a full deck, or a deck with extra cards, that's how this game works. You can plan and strategize all you want, but if the RNG isn't going to give you what is required to win, you will not win. This casino win/lose factor ruins the game for me since it creates situations where it is impossible to win.  You gamble that your strategy will work and depending on how the cards are dealt it may or may not, and if you change strategy it may be too little too late, because again, the cards might not be dealt in a way that it pays off.  When you put in game timer to boot, it's no different than playing a slot machine.
This results in playthroughs that are impossible to win from the start; no amount of adaptation will win the day. Pick a strategy play it until the RNG aligns and you will win. That's it. Casino-strategy. You're playing a slot machine. You're playing odds.  The game acknowledges this by "rewarding" the player with unlocks for continually playing it over and over again. If this were the days of arcade games this would be the perfect product.
Predetermined gameplay. Abortive gameplay. No thanks. Not for me. Definitely for others though and I'm not knocking that. : ) If you're the type of person who is upset by investing time in something just to find it was all for naught no matter what you did from the start, avoid this one. Only the facade of strategy here.

Shadowrun Hong Kong, a game I helped to Kickstart after thoroughly enjoying both Shadowrun Returns and the incredibly good Dragonfall campaign.
Currently I'm some fifteen hours in and this is like living up to the Dragonfall experience all over again, the same core elements are there. The storytelling and the writing, an interesting locale and of course the companions who all have their own stories and backgrounds.
The runs themselves are much the same, with different solutions and variables playing out, you can go in loud or you can try and play things out quietly. You can be the 'good' guy or the bad guy, whichever you prefer.
Everything else is more or less the same or improved. Some new gear for all sorts of classes, I'm sure adepts will find the new weapon additions interesting. And as for cyberware, well.. hand razors, spurs and even monofilament whips are in, street samurais rejoice? Graphics are updated, backgrounds and the environments are still amazing.
And while I'm sure there's all sort of needs for fixes and such, I haven't encountered anything game-breaking or bothersome so far, in fact, I think it's a more solid piece of work than the original Dragonfall release which did suffer from some bugs.
The biggest complaint I have is that.. well.. the game will eventually end.. and I want more. I just want more! :p
I hope Harebrained Schemes will push out an expansion/add-on/possible directors cut version again in future.. and Ihope they'll keep working on the Shadowrun title, because they know how to treat the franchise.
So, a solid yes on recommendation. If you enjoyed Shadowrun Returns or Dragonfall, this game is definitely for you!

TL&DR: Fan of the previous shadowrun games? y: buy this game, n: buy the older (cheaper) versions to see if you like it, the core mechanics have not chagned., nor the graphics.
What a story. It's right up there with the previous versions. Top notch writing, the music blending perfectly with the portrayed atmosphere. The game really makes you think about the choices you have your characters making to the point of actually feeling bad for some of the choices you're forced to make.
The atmosphere is amazing, parts of the game are really terrifying if you keep up with the reading and have the in-game sound on.
It's not all sunshine and rainbows though. It took me exactly 13.9 hours on focusing on the main story line to finish this game. So it's pretty short. I've not gone out of my way to rush the game so it's definitively on the short side for those who are experienced shadow runners.
I've also got mixed feelings about the innovations, or lack thereof, in SRHK. I understand that on some level the creators want to stay true to the previous versions, and not break much with what is obviously a winning formula. There's nothing wrong with that. But I do feel that there is too little iterative improvement in this version. I mean that while it's ok to leave the game's fundamentals as they are, it's not ok to have them stagnate and age. I would have very much liked to see more quantitative improvements: more spells, more guns, more enemies, more effects, more locations, etc.
None of these improvements would have impeded or changed the series' main draw and mechanics.
All in all this is a top notch game in my option. But I hope that the next story will have some definitive expansion in terms of scope and quantity of content.

Short and sweet thoughts: more of what I loved and wanted from previous SR:R titles, with progressive, albeit baby steps, towards improving the team system. Truly another labor of love and care that exceeds mere expansion status, while still not yet radically improving upon the existing formula to make a next-level product. Detractors of previous SR:R titles won't likely find enough reason to give Hong Kong a shot; fans of the methodology behind Dragonfall - Director's Cut 's collective design goals will find plenty to keep them happy for the duration. Prepare for heavy reading.
EDIT: I simply -must- also mention that, as of 8-21-15, there are an alarming number of odd gramatical errors at numerous points of character dialogue, from duplicate words, to incorrect plural usage to entirely wrong words all together. Fortunately, not to the extent of wrecking immersion, plot understanding or game functionality, but for as experienced and seasoned a writing team as can be found at Harebrained Studios, these flubs are cropping up more frequently than I would personally be comfortable with seeing, coming from a professional game development studio and writing team.

This is a refreshing taste of Shadowrun after the bland  gruel served up by Cliffhanger and Shadowrun Chronicles.

I recommend this game with a bit of a warning. It can be fun, but only if you're extremely patient and don't mind having your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you every ten minutes or less.
It's a simple enough premise. Choose your mission. Choose your character. Go through the dungeon floors to try and complete your mission. Die. Try again. It's your typical roguelike in that regard. However, there is one thing that really makes this game more difficult than other roguelike dungeon crawlers such as Legend of Dungeon or even The Binding of Isaac (I know it's a bit of an odd comparison). The hit rate system in this game is seriously flawed. Your hit rate automatically starts out at roughly 60% regardless of what character you start with. You can deal a fair amount of damage and kill enemies in one hit, which is nice. Yet, you only hit them a fraction of the time and you can find yourself exchanging blows with a single enemy for two or three minutes until one of you dies. If you're surrounded by multiple enemies, odds are, you're going to die because you have such a small chance of killing them all before they've managed to kill you.
Luck based elements in roguelike games are not unheard of. Quite the opposite. They're a crucial part of the genre. However, when it becomes TOO luck based, it becomes a problem. Random level, enemy and item generation is a good idea. Random hit rates however are not. It makes completing a single floor almost impossible, let alone a whole mission. If you're patient enough to actually sit through countless runs of this game to beat a mission, then this is the game for you. However, if you do not like the idea of huge maps with a flawed probability driven combat system, then I would recommend other roguelike titles first.

I really want to like this game.  I mean--really.  It could have been so good.
But, the movement-combat mechanism, combined with the rogue-like randomness, makes it an exericise in frustration.  The "mechanic", in this case, is how your character attacks and moves.  I've played the old ASCII rogue-like game "ADOM", and it has exactly this same mechanism; you'd think that the developers could have come up with something other than a mechanism identical to one that's been in place for the last 20+ years.  This mechanism, lIke most similar games, functions where each attack or movement takes roughly equal "turns", for both you and your opponents.  This means that you will get into situations where you can't out-run your opponents, reducing the combat to simply a matter of "trading shots."
Unfortunately, depending on your class selection, you will be "trading shots" either a lot, or all the time, which means a unfortunate roll of the dice will effectively (or definitively) end your run.  This mechanism, in combiation with the lack of any RPG elements to provide value to "wasted" runs, means this becomes a glorified dice roller.
You're better off playing any number of better rogue-like games.  I recommend Binding of Isaac or Rogue Legacy.
