Hack, Slash, Loot has almost no redeeming qualities.  Seriously.  The pixel art looks cool and retro for a couple of minutes but there is no variation on the blue tileset.  What you see in the screenshots, that's it.  Blue.
There is no strategy to it, you cannot avoid monsters once you've seen them and combat is random.  That means you're playing a dice simulator and hoping to roll only winning numbers.  There is nothing more, you can't hide, you can't change from melee to ranged fighting you have no inventory and can't heal after fights.  You can't even run away because evey character moves at the exact same speed.
Gameplay-wise there are just two tyes of enemy.  Those that do random damage from a distance and those that do random damage up close.  Again that's it.  There's no space for depth of play, roll a dice and hope.
The strange view angle sometimes makes it difficult to tell if you're standing next to something or one square away from it and also sometimes hides cupboards behind walls.  A minor gripe but gvien Hack, Slash, Loot does nothing right it all adds up to a pretty terrible experience.
Lastly - and for me the most frustrating - is the 'animation'.  One character moves at a time, if there are 8 serfs around you and a bunch of demons then you've got to wait for each one to do their little bobbing movement.  Similarly with ranged combat, if you're firing at an archer on the other side of the map it degenerates into a very slow game of ping-poing as the arrow crosses the screeon one way and then crosses the screen the other.
Play 'Doom the Roguelike' instead.  It's free and it's awesome.  Hack, Slash, Loot is neither.

The way the sequel is set up is both refreshing and disappointing. Unfortunately, the game doesn't revolve around Edna this time but we get a whole new protagonist instead: Lilli, a friend of Edna's. The girls are in a convent that's run by a very harsh Mother Superior. When this hag of a woman decides to bring doctor Marcel to the convent to help her discipline the children, Edna knows it's time to get out of there. First, she needs to erase all traces of her stay at the convent but she's afraid to be spotted by Marcel, so it's up to Lilli to peform the series of tasks for her. This turns out to be just the beginning of a wacky adventure for Lilli that will take her to places far beyond the convent's walls...
Harvey's role stays about the same: he takes you into an alternate world where you learn things that will help you in the 'real' world. But since you don't carry Harvey around with you this time, he plays a smaller role than he did in
.
The story of
makes no sense whatsoever. Ok, so Lilli doesn't see everything as it is (no spoiler, you find that out during the first scene after the tutorial) and her mind changes blood and gore to something cute and pretty. But why does nobody else see those horrible things, neither? The ending of the story makes even less sense and in retrospect it creates many plot holes the size of Jupiter.
But ah well, it doesn't matter much, really. The fun of the game is in the adventure itself: advancing the story by exploring the vibrant game world and interacting with its colourful inhabitants. And
is a lot of fun to play.
The graphics are still basic and cartoonish, but they're a lot less crude and more detailed than
's graphics.
The music is nice but it sounds a lot more melancholic this time. The snappy, jazzy theme music of
for piano and drums is replaced with a slow, sad tune for the harmonica in
. Most of the other music is slow and broody, too. This may seem a bit depressing, but it complements the sad overall mood of the game perfectly.
is not a happy story, after all.
The quality of the supporting cast's voice acting ranges between good and very good. With one exception: it's great to hear Jocasta Gottlieb reprise her role as Edna. Which only rubs salt in the wound of not having Edna as the main character in this game.
Lilli's voice acting is... non-existent, really. Lilli doesn't talk. Well, the game tries to have you believe she never gets the chance to talk. You see, she makes sounds like 'uh-huh' or starts a conversation with "I..." or "Do..." and people immediately interrupt her, saying things like "Let me guess, you want to...", "Don't tell me, you need..." or "You're probably wondering...". As this happens every time, for the entire game, it gets old quickly. And that made me miss Edna even more as a protagonist: fully voiced, she would spew wacky comments on everything the game threw at her.
compensates Lilli's virtual muteness by having a narrator talk about everything that happens on the screen. Although this mechanic allows the developers to have the 'grown-up' narrator make humorous comments about things that poor, naive Lilli doesn't understand, it creates a bit of a distance between the player and the game's protagonist.
is challenging but not very difficult. Only twice did I come close to looking up a walkthrough, when trying the most absurd solution turned out to be the solution for both problems. An example:
This makes no sense but before resulting to a walkthrough, you will try it out of desperation. In that particular case, the developers even underline that the solution doesn't really make sense as the narrator says: "What Lili now did was actually void of all logic and she could already hear uproar of the online reviewers but she did it anyway".
I did look up a guide for the 'pizza puzzle', a puzzle revolving around colour blindness. Turns out the instructions you're given to solve the puzzle are completely wrong. The game tells you that each of the people involved "mixes up two colours" when it should have been "they can't see any item in either of those two colours". Huge difference, of course. I can only assume this is a problem that results from the game's translation from German to English.
So besides that one instance, I never had to use a walkthrough, which means the logical problems and the puzzles presented in
are not frustratingly hard and  -with only one or two exceptions- pretty logical, while always presenting a challenge. Well, that's the recipe for a fun point & click adventure game, so
passes as far as I'm concerned.
has 8 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 4 while running the game.
Now, about the Steam Achievements... oh boy! If there were an equivalent of the Raspberry Awards for games, Daedalic Entertainment should get the award for 'least fun achievements in a game ever'. The achievements scream "We can't be bothered!": they are boring and uninspired, and they are just copypasted from one game to the next.
There are 12 unmissable achievements that are either story-bound or awarded for solving the puzzles. Those are fine. But most of the remaining 17 achievements, which are missable, require you to perform a number of actions 10 or more times. This means skipping through the same conversation each time or sitting through some animations each time.
And then, the icing on the achievements cake: perform an action 99 times by clicking a button! Each of those 99 times, you need to skip through some conversation
wait for some animations to finish.
Now, that's an improvement, really. In
, you have to click some buttons 400 times to get two achievements and in
it takes 500 mouse clicks for one achievement. But the animation takes longer this time, so in the end you'll waste about as much time getting this mind-numbingly boring 'achievement' done.
Also, exactly like in
, there's an achievement for skipping all the puzzles again. How can that be called an achievement? That's the equivalent of giving a medal to wartime deserters!
Adding some missable Steam Achievements to your game can be a great thing when they add optional extra 'quests', challenges and depth to the game, and at least a bit of extra fun for the player. If they add neither of those things, it shows you can't be bothered. Well, then DON'T! Stick to the unmissable achievements, which is fine for a point & click adventure game. It's certainly preferable to adding chores instead of achievements, and to rewarding players for not playing.

FTL is a game that possesses incredible pace and an incredibly difficult yet rewarding gameplay. It can take some time to learn how to really thrive within gameplay, but it really does get satisfying as you go. There's a significant amount of strategy and thinking that go behind it all. Gameplay definitely encourages replayability. My only qualm with the gameplay is that there is a fair amount of luck and getting the right things at the right time involved. Sometimes you may get incredibly lucky with the amount of materials you have to work with, sometimes you get off rather unlucky and die within the first five-ten minutes of playing a game. However, I would say that given enough practice, it becomes easier to work around bad starts.
In regards to polish and style, it's all well done. Whether or not pixel art and chiptune-esque music are your thing, it is definitely and consistently well developed within FTL. The backgrounds don't necessarily fit the pixel based artstyle, but to be frank, I find that nitpicking at that point. Every other part of the game's style very much makes up for it.
Overall, I recommend giving FTL a shot, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who's a fan of fast paced strategy with a lot on the line. It's well worth the price, and I would recommend buying the soundtrack as well. The developers here certainly deserve it.

This is a well made game, absolutely. It is fun to play and engrossing. Charming in its way. But at the end of five hours of playing it, I cannot stand this game.
Why?
This game is based on random rolls and nothing else once you get into the heart of its mechanics. Imagine playing a card came where there may or may not be a full deck, or a deck with extra cards, that's how this game works. You can plan and strategize all you want, but if the RNG isn't going to give you what is required to win, you will not win. This casino win/lose factor ruins the game for me since it creates situations where it is impossible to win.  You gamble that your strategy will work and depending on how the cards are dealt it may or may not, and if you change strategy it may be too little too late, because again, the cards might not be dealt in a way that it pays off.  When you put in game timer to boot, it's no different than playing a slot machine.
This results in playthroughs that are impossible to win from the start; no amount of adaptation will win the day. Pick a strategy play it until the RNG aligns and you will win. That's it. Casino-strategy. You're playing a slot machine. You're playing odds.  The game acknowledges this by "rewarding" the player with unlocks for continually playing it over and over again. If this were the days of arcade games this would be the perfect product.

Definitely for others though and I'm not knocking that. : ) If you're the type of person who is upset by investing time in something just to find it was all for naught no matter what you did from the start, avoid this one. Only the facade of strategy here.

I'm probably most qualified to speak on the topic of writing, characterization, and the sociological and cultural elements of the setting.
The writing itself is, I feel, the best in the industry at this time, including games such as Thomas was Alone and even entirely text based experiences.  Not only is this accomplished in staggering volume, as there are likely hundreds if not thousands of pages of text that the player may not even encounter during a given playthorugh, but also in quality.  I strongly feel that the manner in which the game is written is more satisfying than cutscenes or even voice acting toting the same lines.  Most character's speak simply, or in their own, distinct, vernacular, and yet the simple yet highly literary english utilized by the writers conveys every emotion to near perfection.
On the topic of the characters in Hong Kong, as in Dragonfall, the writers seem to have internalized one of the primary themes of shadowrun: induviduality.  Living as outlaws in a varyingly dystopian corporate society affords those in the shadows the opportunity to be unique, ideosyncratic, and memorable.  Beyond the shadows, the general populace is factory farmed, homogenous office workers.  Every character has a reason they're in the shadows, and no two characters have the same one.  The greatest share of the characterization is left to the player to uncover by interacting with their team and community between missions, adding again the intense feeling of community found in Dragonfall.
The Shadowrun setting can be a bit dense at the best of times, Hong Kong is unique even within that setting.  What the player must understand is the concept of post-modernism in Shadowrun.  The world is cyclical the past and future, as determined by the changing of the "worlds,"  are one in the same.  Hong Kong carries cultural elements that seem exagerated or out of place at times, but this is an element of world building in Shadowrun. The syntax of the names is a good example of this.
The awakening of Magic in the setting empowers cultural practices and beleifs.  Amerind culture in North America and Feng Shui in Hong Kong.  This does not establish that any one of these philosophies is truly the universal backbone of the universe, but takes a rather pluralistic approach, as there are multiple, paralell paths to gaining "magic."
On a concluding note Kowloon walled city was a real place in the former British region of the Chinese mainland, if I recall, it no longer exists.
Even if you are a veteran of the setting, Hong Kong will demand a listening ear to truly experience the game, I would recommend that anyone reading this piece offer that ear.

UFHO2 Is a very nice (now) free2play puzzle game developed by a small italian indie software house. How can I describe it? It kind of reminds me of a chess game, but ignoring the entire setting consisting of funny aliens going around in space and meeting other species to confront, you will have to move your tiny character along the "game field" with a limited number of moves before your turn ends, and the purpose is to reach and grab more crystal than the adversary. Most of the times you will play 1v1, but in some missions you will play 1v2, 2v2 or worse! The peculiar part of this game, besides the funny alien voices, is the game field made of hexagon checks which link to each other by limited sides, hence you can move from check to check only if they are facing by the riht sides. If they're not you can rotate them, but this will decrease your available moves per turn.
This sound simple and almost boring but the real challenge lies in the fact that You can turn every check in the field but your adversary can do this as well, and considering that the AI is quite clever the game will quickly turn into a prediction game, where you must value all the possible moves from the adversary and make his path longer or more difficult so he has to waste moves to make a quick path while you reach your goals.
That's all. Along the game you will find other powerups and things like that, but the game is actually this and nothing more, yet it entertains you with AIs more and more challenging.
Oh, I almost forgot. The game uses Unity, but it works fine as the game has a very simple design, hence it can run on many systems without pretending so much from your HW.

Lisa: The Painful is crazy. It sets the player in the shoes of one Brad Armstrong in his morbid, fairly depressing voyage through a world of men. Runner 2 is the follow-up to the first Bit.Trip Runner game. I think it's best described as a rhythm/melody game on rails.  Your character will automatically run and it's up to you to jump, slide, kick, dance, block (et cetera) your way to the finish line while collecting as much gold as you can (which can be used to open up new levels).
The game will create sounds based on your actions and it's very satisfying to hear a song in its entire glory. You're allowed to miss a beat, but if you hit an object you'll be taken back to the beginning or the last checkpoint.
Bit.Trip Runner 2 improves on almost every aspect of the previous game; the graphics are now 3D, there are many more moves, multiple ways to finish a level, a bit of a story, items/unlockables to collect and it even looks like it's more accessible (ie, easier; this might not please everyone however).
If you enjoyed the first one, this one is a must have.

This game is not worth the time or money spent to play it.
There is absolutely no progression in the game save for what you find. There is no leveling, there is only loot. Of course, to get such loot you need to find it, off enemies, or out of barrels and chests. But, good luck surviving long enough to actually get it! In this game you have absolutely no passive regeneration. HP has to be restored through use of items and only through that.
In terms of mechanics, there's moving, attacking, and looting. Moving is really the one part I can't complain about, since well, you move just fine. Attacking is either ranged or melee, but regardless of range you will spend most of combat missing. You will miss much more than you ever hit. Now, with looting, there's one large thing that stands out: you don't have an inventory. You only have what you currently have equiped, and that's all. Want to save that potion for later? Nope, you have to use it now! This also means that looting devolves solely into: "is this better or worse than what I have right now?" And potions are only for chugging on sight.
Generally speaking, a game such as this has some sort of scaling difficulty. Either the lower/higher the floor, the more difficult things get. Or you find something like Risk of Rain, where the longer you spend in game, the more difficult it gets. This game? There is no difficulty. There is only the RNG. Add to the fact that the floors are absolutely tiny, and I hope you like get swarmed if you're unlucky.
This game is overly random and gives you no tools with which to determine your fate. This game is simply an overpriced RNG that looks like a rogue-like. Look elsewhere for a good rogue-like.

Company of Heroes II (COH2) is very similar to COH1 and the Dawn of War II series. I highly recommend all of them. COH2 has a single player campaign, multiplayer (with or without AI) matches and more. In the Single Player campaign, through 15 missions, you play as the Soviets against the Germans during World War II and get cutscenes and play out key historical encouters. The game is categorized as an RTS with an isometric view. Base building is very minimal. Expect to build only a dozen buildings troughout the entire campaign. But you can pause the game at any point and give - and queue - your orders to any of your units. That makes the game extremely enjoyable if like me, you like to play battles mostly on pause! You can't build turrets or defenses and you can't increase your production capacity with additional buildings. Instead the game focuses on just your units. You call in units which arrive from specific points on the map. Units level up as they kill enemy units. Also units can be upgraded and have many abilities which add variety to combat. The game uses the Essence engine, which shows you as you move your units and shows you if they are in heavy, light or no cover at all. Cover affects how well protected and hard to hit your units are. So you will control Russian troops, tanks, jeeps, half-tracks and various specialised infantry units. You can call in Global abilities such as airstrikes and "free" reinforcements. The game lets you capture weapons and even tanks from the enemy. I've had a lot of fun capturing Panzer 4s and turning them back against my enemies.
So overall, I bought this game as part of a pack containing various DLCs and one or two expansions and I don't regret my purchase at all. COH2 lived up to my expectations and delivers a solid bug-free, RTS that continues on the success of COH1. A must if you like WWII, military units, realism and strategy.

This might be my subjective opinion, but as a diehard fan of the predecessor CoH2 felt clumsy and just not enjoyable in some way or another.

I spent most of these 2000 hours climbing up the ranked game ladder (I was pretty good in the end tbh - in the top 100 as brits and as germans in 2v2 and top 500 as brits in 1v1), which ment the original release of CoH2 with no "real" competetive gamemode and neither a ladder was frustrating for me(The default game mode got a ladder later on, but the ladder was pretty dull only listing the guys with the most total wins (no matter how many games they needed for this amount) rather than any real skill). I also encouraged Relic and the Esl to take steps in real competative tournaments (Starcraft, Lol, etc. got immense tournaments with huge price pools, so why not this game, too (which is way better than sc2 in my eyes)) Sadly Relic, being bought by SEGA had not the money to get a competitive Series rolling, so the ESL CoH2 league was disbanded after 3 small tournaments.
The second point, why I do not like this game might also be very subjective, but I really didn't like the new graphics. I said to myself "you are new to this game and you played coh1 pretty long so you are just not used to the new graphics" so I decided to play the game for 'at least' 100 hours, before judgeing its graphics, but I still was as displeased as before. Now even though I just told you, that i would hate the graphics, I nevertheless must admit that the game looks better, newer and more detailed, than its predecessor, though, but there are two mayor issues I never got over. The first issue are the tanks. Compared to CoH1 they just look odd in their surroundings, way to polished, thick outlines and a wibbly-wobbly movement that gave me the feeling, that they were some kind of plastic tanks and worse of all their projectiles did look like glowing red dots rather then real tank shells. The second issue I blamed on the new graphics, was that the game became far less responding due to all this visual effects. I do not talk about framedrops or something, but if my Infatry troops got caught into artillery fire I easily lost focus and realized first after the dust of the bombardment lifted, that I had lost several squads.
Now lets calm down the negativity a bit. Even if it has to take quite a few hits here, CoH2 is a excellent game, CoH1 just was a perfect game. I would also love to recommend Men of War to you folks, if you are looking for a simular game, but the community of this game is as dead as the community of CoH1, and despite it provided me with a lot of fun during the singleplayer missions, I never got warm in the multiplayer and was utterly destroyed without any clue what was happening.
But so much for that, lets continue about CoH2:
There are a lot of positive aspects, I just must metion when talking about this game, like true sight, one of the most beautiful things I've ever seen in my whole life. No kidding. I really wish I could like that game just for this game mechanic. Instead of just having a circle around your unit, your vision is limited by objects and terrain. There are some other games with simular game mechanics, but including this to Company of Heroes made this game sooooooo much better. And it also made Sound more important, because you can actually hear enemy vehicles now before you can see them not that sound wasn't pretty important in the predecessor, too. Damn Nebelwerfer-Trucks. Glad you could determine their position by tracking their incredible loud launch-sound).
I also already mentioned the new Graphics-stile, which just is more up to date, despite I dislike that the game lost its fitting but depressing shades of grey, which made its predecessor feel like a actual 'dirty' war game.
Another great feature are blizzards and the possibilty to just drown an eney assault in a icy lake by breaking the ice on it.
Well, Relic has already proven, that they can make great real time strategy games and I trusted them - them alone - so much, that I bought the Preorder, but as THQ began to crumble, poor little Relic needed someone to feed them and this someone was - sadly - SEGA. Well, SEGA at first doesn't seem to be the worst for this job, as they already own a studio producing great Strategy games (Creative Assembly) and while new Total War games tend to be released faster and faster with less (and less bugfree) content, more dlcs and less positive reviews (Rome 2 was mostly negative the time SEGA bought Relic), it sure seemed like a good investment to buy in another renowed game studio.
Their first step was to call back all promises Relic made while still under THQ like that all Pre-Oder Buyers would get a season pass (and thus all addons for free). Needlessly to say that I couldn't get back my 60 Bucks anymore. Now don't get me wrong: I neither blame this game nor relic on this. I do not even blame SEGA (they would've lost profit on a promise they never made), but it still sucked. I ended up with getting the Theatre of War DLC and some Tank-skins for my preoder.
Now SEGA wouldn't be SEGA if they stopped ruining my day by taking away my season pass. On top of having to pay for every new Addon I also had to pay for every ♥♥♥♥ing 5€-commander they released. For many of you this might not be a big deal. And at first it really looks like this. Why do I complain about a 5€-Commander in one of SEGAs game, while I silently pay the double to play a new faction in a Total War game. Well, the difference is, that Rome, Shogun, Atilla or whatever CA ever created are mostly SINGLEPLAYER games, while CoH2 is made for MULTIPLAYER purposes. And hell, these commanders were OP when they were released. (The Tiger Ace commander was so strong on release, that you could win with your tiger ace alone) Sure, these commanders got nerfed a few weeks after they were released (and any of these rich kids already owned them) until they were as strong as any commander in the base game. Now being beaten by someone who spent 5€ more on a title you already paid 60€, really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me on. I wouldn't be as mad if there had been ANY chance to test a new commander BEFORE getting owned by it on the field, but you either learned its strenghts and weaknesses by buying it or by losing over and over again until you figured it out yourself.
Wow, I never knew there was a restriction for review length.
Lets keep my last point short: In the beginning the game was terribly balanced. You either waited hours to find a game or played as a faction, which was so underpowered, that it was more ore less an insta-loss.
Well, thanks to anyone who made it so far.
TL:DR CoH2 is really a awesome game, but based on my expierience with the Beta/Launch-Version of the game, I cannot give it a positive rating.

Drenched in irony, its absurd and dark humour is often spot on and easily one of the game's best feature, if only also at times too obvious. A properly cast narrator delivers most lines and almost feels like the main character in lieu of a fully detailed protagonist.
It touches on slightly disturbing subjects in a facetious manner, jovially poking fun at anything and everything. However, the overall story and tone are a lot more sinister than the kiddy graphics would let you believe, with a lot of implied but not graphic violence.
Unfortunately, the game is off to a slow start during most of the first chapter, beginning with a very long intro where absolutely nothing happens. For the first few hours, the player must endure some completely detestable characters, a few with insupportable voices (Doris!), and mundane puzzles with inexplicably cheap UI.
An important game changer occurs about halfway through and only then does the game really get interesting, with the addition of an innovative concept that enforces restrictions on Lilli's behaviour. The player must then visit alternate realities to banish demons and regain free will over these mental blocks.
A very good soundtrack is wasted by the repetitiveness of the one song replaying constantly within each major area, accompanied by poor sound effects and improper timing in between dialogues that cause some lines to feel delivered in a rush.
Minimal animations do little to add life to the washed out hand-drawn backgrounds. Despite some good scenes, it's difficult to fully appreciate this unaccomplished art direction.
Strangely, the game is not chiefly about Edna or Harvey and is clearly not meant as a direct sequel to The Breakout*, although it does make innumerable references to it and is set in the same world. Edna is at best a recurring secondary character, while Harvey plays an increasingly significant role later on.
Instead, the game centers around Lilli, a peculiarly mute schoolgirl with a comically growing list of issues. She never speaks a word, which is sort of endearing initially and is key to the overall narrative, but also gets repetitive.
The game does have a few interesting puzzles of varying levels of difficulty. I especially appreciated how dialogues give the player exactly the right guidance, sometimes outright laying out solutions in a subtle and funny way.
I finally began to warm up to the game during chapter 2 (out of 3), which brings a lot more diversity with its dream-like variations of the real world, but there were too many things I disliked to fully recommend it.

Shadowrun Returns was a good game, rough at the edges, but offered a great plot; interesting characters and lots of fan-service.
Dragonfall was better in every way; more indepth mechanics, better art-work, music and alot more polish on the core-gamelay, all in all a 100% improvement.
Shadowrun Hong Kong follwos right on, making hefty jumps in quality over Dragonfall; grafics have been improved alot, soundtrack is fantastic as always (better quality yet), there`s even more art-work everywhere, the whole immersion works even better than in SR:R and SR:D, combat, char-building, and lots of other gameplay aspects have again been worked on a lot; also the save-everywhere-feature is now part of the core SR-mechanic.
lots of new stuff has been added, from dragon-lines, to new passive-totems, new spells, etc. ; there`s voice-work now also.
But first and foremost these games live on their story, conversations, the setting and characters -> Hong Kong delivers perfectly...even better than it`s predecessors; you will get soaked in Shadowrun-immersion, the story starts of quite fast unlike in Dragonfall and bores you rarely;
all in all again a must buy for crpg-fans and a massive step foreward for the franchise; at that rate one can only what Harebrained will do for future titels.

Updated now that I've finished the game.
Extremely similar to Dragonfall. It's not deviated strongly from the formula established by the previous game - you have a hub area and you go on runs while waiting for the plot to move forward, getting to know NPCs and team members during the down time. Not necessarily a bad thing, though I do wish they would've mixed things up a little bit with the format. The story does rely a bit too much on telling rather than showing (we're often told that conditions inside the Kowloon Walled City are real bad, but we see precious little of that, for example), and the game does not have an antagonist as interesting and well-characterized as the previous game's.
The writing is all around great, as expected, and the gameplay is likewise solid. All the same, it feels like it's retreading old ground - beyond a few minor improvements to interface and the gameplay, it does nothing new - the structure of the plot is similar in that your central goal is revealed early on and much of the game is spent doing other things before you can pursue it. Unlike in Dragonfall, you're not actively working towards a goal, but rather passing the time until plot-related events crop up automatically, which I felt was an unwelcome change, as it deemphasized the player character's role as principal actor, though this is a bit of a minor quibble.
Furthermore, there seem to be less impactful choices to be made than in Dragonfall, and there's less of Dragonfall's bits of cleverness, like the metacommentary on RPG dialogue conventions that was Eiger's throwing back your empty compliments at you. Some things did leave me guessing - a character I thought to be a minor NPC turned out to be regularly recurring character who hated my guts, and I'm unsure whether this was because of my conduct towards him or whether it was pre-determined by the writers. If it was indeed the former case, I suppose I'd have to be quite impressed - nonetheless, regardless of how he feels about you, that entire subplot amounts to exactly nothing by the end.
Overall though, I'd call this game an excellent work that nonetheless fails to reach the heights of its predecessor's glory. If you liked Dragonfall, you'll definitely enjoy this a great deal.

I have to say, this game is surprisingly addicting. It's WAY more addicting than it should be. It's actually fairly difficult as well, though mostly because certain attacks do more damage to your pig, which I think isn't really fair. All attacks should simply take off one slice of bacon from your meter, but that's just what I think. Anyways, it's very fast paced and once the enemies start coming more rapidly and frequently, you are forced to pull off much faster and much more ridiculous combos, of which look pretty cool. There are a few improvements I would like to see to this game to make it a bit better, and maybe give you an actual reason to keep playing. For one, I think an upgrades system could be well integrated into this game. For example, kills give you money, and then with that money you buy upgrades for your pig such as new attacks, combos take longer to dissapear, dual weilding weapons, attacks do more damage, triple jump, stuff like that. A few gamemodes, perhaps could work well. I want to see one that starts you off, as if you were at level 1000. Since the game gets progessively more chaotic and crazy as you kill more wolves, for example, at around 20 it's fairly chill, but begins getting pretty ridiculous at, say, 100. It should start you off immediately at a really high number, and maybe you have less health. Y'know, like a hard/cruel mode. It would let you see a lot of really cool combos, since there would be wolves coming from literally everywhere. So all in all, this is a surprisingly fun game, and it's free, so there's really no reason NOT to download it.

Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes is the sequel to Edna & Harvey: The Breakout, and is set some time after the first installment (I think that especially in the beginning of the game there is some uncertainty about that).
It is defenitely a spiritual sequel to the first game, but not its continuation, as there are some main differences:
First of all: You play neither Edna nor Harvey. Both characters appear in the story, but you don't get to see too much of them.
Second: While the main voice acting was done by Edna and Harvey in The Breakout, you now have a sarcastic narrator who comments on basically everything you do or try to do.
Third: This game is a lot bloodier than the first one. There is few explicit imagery, but a lot of violence is implied.
All these changes are not negative in my mind, but I wanted to mention them.
Of course there are many similarities as well: The optical style is the same, the story is in parts absolutely absurd, only topped by the absurdity of some of the riddles, and there are fourth wall breaks.
I would defenitely recommend this game, I loved it. Just don't expect Edna & Harvey 2.
Edit for Achievement Hunters: The Achievements are mostly stupid. Half of them imply doing the same thing over and over again, which is nothing but time-consuming.

I was hardly a fan for Point & Click because 1. I prefer more complex gameplay 2. I prefer more complex plot. Yet this game is good on both, and more. I strongly recommend it.
- Gameplay:
The gameplay is still P&C here, so you just click your mouse around, but personally the difficulty is really good - nothing insane, but hard enough that you actually need to think and explore. The simple gameplay also makes the plot more ironic - all this dark plot only requires some clicks.
- Plot:
As many have suggested the game is really dark. REAL dark. There's no "normal" character so far and the relation between people is really fked up. It is very unique.
- Atmosphere:
The cartoon graphics, the cheerful music, the simple control... EVERYTHING adds up to the dark atmosphere. I feel very emphatic with the main character because of the way the story is told and, like said, the casual setup of the game just makes it even more ironic. I'm so impressed with the things one can do in P&C.
- Achievement:
Now many people say that the achievements are breaking their mouse and they are not wrong. However I appreciate the role these achievements play in character building a lot. How do you know that a girl is diligent and a bit eerie? Well, she rakes the leaves back and forth for nothing for 50 times! (Of course, you are gonna be the one actually clicking on the leaves for 50 times...)
Most of the achievements don't contribute to the gameplay in any way - like, you really don't have to talk to this character 10 times to proceed - but they are NOT random. They are beautifully designed.

Warning: minor spoilers within.
I've only played an hour or two so far, so here's a provisional review.
There are few games which get Hong Kong right. Sleeping Dogs knocked it right out of the park with sheer authenticity, and Shadowrun: Hong Kong has managed to translate Hong Kong effectively into the Shadowrun Universe. Feng shui is an actual thing, there's the typical Chinese obsession with the number 8 everywhere (Club 88, 8 members in the Council) and there are accurate references to how the Hong Kong Triads work. I love it.
Karma levelling system has been given a more coherent UI, and even though most of the combat system is still the same as Dragonfall and Returns, the revamp to the Decking sequences is praiseworthy. Movement in the decking cyberspace is real-time and your avatar gets to evade the roaming ICE Metal Gear-style, which is a huge improvement. The turn-based combat kicks in only when you've been detected.
There's plenty more to be looked at, but based on what I've seen so far? 10/10. Harebrained have once again delivered an excellent game.

Like SR: Returns and Dragonfall, Shadowrun: Hong Kong is another gem for those on the lookout for a more traditional roleplaying experience.
Beautiful enviroments, a good (if somewhat cliche) story and multiple-choice options for convesations, that don't sound completly unbelievable, make for a great experience right for the start.

Shadowrun Returns is what got me into Shadowrun as a whole. Just gonna throw that out here.
So, is this game good? Well, after binging through eight solid hours of it on launch day my opinion is that of my new favorite shaman after we did a run involving a museum heist, the walking dead, and ancient magic tomes: "That. Was. AWESOME!"
For those of you who haven't played the other two games in the series; Shadowrun Returns and S.R: Dragonfall... NO! BAD GAMER! GO PLAY THEM! GO DO IT RIGHT NOW OR I'M GETTING MY BEATING STICK!
For those of you who are fans already, this game met all it's kickstarter goals and, as promised, they pulled out every stop and completely redid many aspects of the game... so here's whats new:
Graphics: The graphics look MUCH sharper and more detailed in this than in the previous two games. The difference is akin to going from one generation of game systems to the next really. The animation is a lot smoother, the spell effects have been redesigned, the elementals that shaman summon look different (though that might just be the Chinese setting), and so on.
Story: I'm going to wager that I've gotten about a third or so through the story, but so far it's a HUGE improvement over even Dragonfall's lofty heights. Fully voiced cutscenes, a lot more dynamic action in the story itself, and so on. Right at the start, within the first ten minutes, you're leading your foster brother and two shadowrunners through a hail of corp police gunfire to safety after watching your brother's partner and two of the shadowrunner's teammates get a surprise headache via a high powered sniper rifle... and thats all I'm going to say. The series has always had amazing writing and this game has taken it up even higher than it was before.
Combat: They changed around the UI a lot in this one, but I'm liking it so far. There's new weapons to find and use, new tactics, lots of new spells for mages and shaman to use... but here's the big one for me.
I'm an IT major in the real world (or meatspace if you prefer), currently going to college to earn a degree in Network Security. So when I play Shadowrun games I might dabble a bit as a mage, or toy with the idea of being a shaman, but when it comes right down to it... I'm a decker... which brings me to one of the biggest changes.
Decking: Decking has been -completely- redone. Its not just 'you're doing the same thing as before, but in a computer now!' like it was in the previous two games. Here's bullet points with the changes:
- Stealth matters! When you first jack into the matrix you aren't immediately going to be set upon by White and Black IC like you would before. Instead there's little security scanners floating around that you can sneak past. Even if they spot you they don't immediately attack, instead you start building up a meter called 'trace' as they try to track down where you're jacked in from. If you're good enough at decking you can take them out before the meter fills... but if it does then the security programs activate and you'd better have some ESPs and a decent deck because you're in for a fight then!
- Blocking programs. To get to the ever-so-important nodes in the matrix you have to remove security walls. Now, if the trace has already gone out then this is fairly straightforward. You blast the things apart with your code and your programs as per usual. However, if you manage to sneak all the way up to them now you can, instead, hack the gates to remove them. You do this by basically playing Simon with the number pad on your keyboard. You get a few seconds (dependent on your Deck) to match the sequences of numbers in a security test pattern. Match several in a row and your deck will begin a brute force password hack against the system. A row of symbols will begin to spin above a series of other symbols, the password to get past the block. Use the remaining time on your hacking attempt to match up the correct patterns and the wall comes crashing down! Be careful however, get it wrong and you get a whole bunch of Trace dumped on you at once, perhaps even enough to get security protocols on your digital♥♥♥♥♥
- New decks, new programs, new ESPs. Yep, its not the four standard decks anymore. There's new ones that do less damage and give you less max IP in exchange for an extended hacking time for the aforementioned blocking programs, for those confident in their stealth. At the same time you can go with ones that have more power but aren't as subtle if you just wanna break some IC. The new programs are useful too. There's programs that'll boost a decker's speed so they can dodge around security scanners, that'll slow down the timer on a hacking attempt, and more.
- Graphic overhaul. I'm just gonna say it. The matrix looks GORGEOUS now. It really does look like the inside of a computer program. Your decker's avatar dashes through the 'air' rather than running, the IC and ESPs are all sleek and shiny, and it's a joy just to look at. One Way Heroics is a very addictive rogue like game, but instead of lasting for hours or days rounds are 5-20 min runs in which you'll be trying to out run the ever present Darkness consuming the left of your screen while gaining enough gear and lv's to defeat the Demon Lord. This makes for an intreasting dynamic as you try to balence exploration, monster slaying, cheast looting, and even buying and saving. For every action you take the darkness creeps a little closer. Luckily after each run you'll earn points towards buying classes (you start with two of the 8 available), Perks (you start with 3 slots and only stat perks available, you can buy skill perks and will aquire 2 more slots as you buy perks), and most importently Dimensional Vault spaces (Which allows you to carry over your best/favorite gear and items).
OWH is a little light on the story but compared to a lot of rogue-likes it's on par or above. Features a party system you can take advantage of (As long as you have charisma and don't abandon the appropriate npcs to the darkness). A fair amount of gear which can hold up to 10 enchantments meaning a huge variation of what can be found/made. A MASSIVE random map generator (seriously this things HUGE you can create a world by typing in nearly anything). An online mode where you can compare your success to others and even find player ghosts which will grant you half a lv's worth of exp and a random item said character possesed. There's also multiple difficulties ranging from the very very short Walk in the Park  to the slightly more demanding Massive Odeisy, online scoring and 44 acheivements to collect.
Now I paid full price and I'm an old school gamer so I can honestly say I've blown a lot more then the measily cost for this wonderful game in an arcade and I'm getting a ton of fun out of it, it's worth the buy!
We don't often see console-style roguelikes - ones that handle well with a controller and are generally accessible - especially on the PC. One Way Heroics is one such roguelike.

To be perfectly honest, I didn't expect that much for the $3.50 full price of the game.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The number of hours of gameplay to price has proven to be a solid purchase.
I do not wish to oversell.  This is a solid game.  It has both pros and cons.  However, at this price point, it's a very high return on price.
The Pros are that it's a 2d sidescrolling, roguelike, fantasy style game that contains elements of progression post rogue-like death.  The unique aspect of the game is that the world is constantly scrolling to the right, and that if the hero is trapped on the far left of the screen, it's game over.  The game offers a few classes, with more unlocked as you continue to play through, and the ability to carry forward items (how many items can be expanded as well).  It's a typical 2d fantasy style throwback game.
The Cons of this game is the seemingly random difficulty at times.  Experiencing impossible creatures right outside the starting castle, and random event demons that you can't avoid.  This can be painful if you're trying to clear with a particular class and have dedicated some game clearing items towards your hero!  As mentioned in other reviews, there's also random map loading, which can hurt continuity of the game, but is overall relatively minor.
With all of this in mind, I believe buyers will experience a good playtime/cost ratio with this game.

This game has a great plot and aesthetic (it's seriously a goldmine for screenshot collectors) and the grappling mechanic was fun and responsive. There was significant variety to the different chapters, from tight dark caverns to wide-open floating cities and it stayed fun all the way till the near-end. Much like Psychonauts though, this game suffers from Meat Circus Syndrome and the difficulty goes vertical in a way that feels not so much deliberately challenging, but moreso "this wasn't playtested". Apparently the game was patched to make the penultimate section of the chapter a bit easier, but the game should've been patched to remove the entire chapter outright since every minute of it is irritating beyond belief. The last chapter is super janky and disorienting in a way where you're never quite sure where to go, or which way you came from, or even if you passed the last section in a manner that was intended. It's pure trial and error aggravation at the very end of a primarily narrative game, and it hurts the overall product and takes away the punch of the ending, much like the afformentioned Meat Circus or Xen in Half Life.
Still, much like Psychonauts and Half Life are bonafide classics despite their obnoxious endgames, ASAMU is too for the same reasons. Definitely great, but the 11th hour difficulty spike holds it back from perfection - worth a fiver, but not full price.

LISA is a masterpiece of video game storytelling and maybe the strongest piece of evidence I've ever seen in favor of the argument that video games ARE an art form.
LISA blends a fantastic sense of goofiness and humor with an incredibly dark storyline, the likes of which are not often seen in video games at all.
You WILL get wrapped up in this world and its characters. One minute you'll laugh hysterically, the next you'll be in total shock of the depravity and darkness of the plot.
LISA is a game that handles some extremely serious subject matter but doesn't take itself too seriously.
The gameplay is satisfying, if repetitive but that isn't what LISA is about. You have never experienced a story in a video game like this.
If you or someone you know claim to be a fan of strong narratives in video games but you haven't played LISA, you are WRONG.

An emotionally powerful game. What starts as an emotional story quickly becomes a quirky RPG. You will laugh your♥♥♥♥♥off. You will probably tear up at least three different times. You WILL be uncomfortable, uneasy, and horrified at many points. You will grow to love and hate everything in this game.
The mechanics of the game are somewhat simple, and it sometimes plays like a medium-to-fast paced platformer at different points. The RPG dynamic is done rather well, and once you gather a few party members you'll find yourself a reliably badass team who you never want to let go. Each has its own story, even if some are a little shallow at times.
The story, well... it's almost entirely perfect. Never has a game made me feel so many emotions at once, aside from Undertale (which I also reccommend just as much.) As I said before. It's 200% worth going through the entire game.
The only problem I have with this game is walking off of cliffs by accident. If you walk off of a cliff; and there are many in the game; you get a Game Over. It's silly. But get used to it... and the only other issue I have is Pain Mode. Sure, it unlocks a bonus part at the end which is AWESOME, but it's horrifyingly difficult. You know how there's hubs where you have a save point since there's a trillion tasks to do in the same area before you move on? Yeah, well, in Pain Mode, all save points can only be used once. Let that sink in. Oh, and also, many encounters are changed and made hella more difficult.
All in all, LISA: The Painful is an extremely awesome game. The RPG system is done well, exploration feels gratifying, the atmosphere is extremely immersive, and the story is worth your times hundreds of hours over. On sale or not, BUY THIS GAME. You won't regret it.
P.S. For bonus points, either play or just read through the plot of LISA: The First. It's a Yumme-Nikki type exploration game which gives some insight into a few of the scenes, but not entirely worth the hours owing to the short story.

Breaking it down:
Bad:
-It was clearly made up to a point and then told to ship which means that the freeroam was cut back (no sidequests, messing around, gambling etc) and the ending is like hitting a brick wall (although maybe that was their plan?)
-Freeroam is only avalible before or after a mission...which is also during a mission.  If you want total freeroam I would suggest the DLCs.
-Some plotpoints remove your weapons and clothing, thus is can be a pain to build up a nice arsenal only to have to collect them all over again.
Good:
- The story is fantastic.  One of the early missions has you trying out what it would be like to just be an average worker on a dock.  After moving four boxes it becomes clear that this isn't worth it.  Low pay for painful work.  It gives the player a motivation why they would join Vito as a mobster.
- The characters.  This is the weakest point of 99% of GTA's characters.  They are all awful and jerks to you.  Why am I even talking to these people?  In Mafia II it's hard not to like Joe, even when he's making a fool of himself.  And Leo Galante is like a father figure to you, leading you on a path to the mob.
- The vehicles, while slow and heavy, are classic to the period.  Most can be modded in garages and, unlike GTA, will return to your garage if they explode.  All of them have excellent levels of damage and even layers of dirt if you drive them enough or go down dirt roads.
- Great visuals, even if this game is a few years old now.
- Other fun stuff: The shotgun is just as loud and deadly as it should be.  Cops pay attention to basic driving so no speeding around them!  You can also fill up your gas (although most likely you will blow up or find a new car before then).
While I haven't played Joe's Adventure, I did play a far amount of Jimmy's Vendetta.  Its basically a collection of side missions with only a bit of story to bring you along.  It does make freeroam feel like it should.  Nothing's better than leading a cop car through a department store.
I originally pirated the game, and even after beating it I had to buy it.  It's well worth it.  The only downside is that there are only weak rumors of a Mafia III.  If Mafia III could be just like Mafia II but with a bit more time to work on freeroam, I would be there.
Not convinced?  The demo features a portion of the map that can be freeroamed for, I believe, 15 minutes before you start the mission.  It has most of the features of the main game like buying different clothes, guns, and a few of the cars in the game.

Despite the line above giving you a bit of a hint, I thought it worth mentioning that despite Steam saying that “Edna & Harvey: The Breakout” was released after “Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes”, this is infact wrong and resulted in me playing the two in the wrong order. This game is the sequel. They follow each other very loosely in terms of story but I think playing them in order would be more enjoyable.
First of all, compared to the previous game, there was a big improvement between the two. You can really tell that Daedalic Entertainment had the means to step their game up. There was a bit of a time gap between the two and it shows.
Better resolution, nicer and more detailed graphics, a more intuitive point and click system and a generally more polished and bug-free game are just a few things that have gotten better with the sequel.
I played through both of these games recently and I have to admit that this was one of those games that I just didn’t mesh with the best. As people who play point and click games often will know, they can vary in terms of how logical the item combinations/puzzles will be. The best case scenarios for point and clicks is that all the puzzles and combinations just make sense to you, you don’t get stuck and sail through the game with no problems. Unfortunately I got a teeny tiny bit majorly stuck on this game at one point. It was a bit frustrating because the game then suddenly came to a grinding holt. Fortunately for me, my boyfriend ended up sitting with me for the rest of the game and we managed to figure it all out together.
In that sense, point and click games can be quite good for a single player game that you can playthrough with someone. But on my own, it was a bit annoying.
With that aside though, I enjoyed the story. It was longer (at least it felt like it) than “The Breakout”, with several different chapters and settings for you to explore. The game even takes on an interesting mechanic after the first chapter that really peeked my interest and opened up new puzzle ideas within the game. You face “restrictions”, which are put in place so that you can not do certain things, and are forced to overcome these restrictions by entering an alternate reality, a manifestation of our shy school girl Lilli’s mind. You have to work your way around these in order to progress and it’s an interesting puzzle mechanic to work with.
The puzzles are interesting and fun, although difficult at times. There was a few that I was quite impressed with the creativity of. It’s always nice to see fresh ideas in point and click games, rather than the usual old puzzles.
This game tends to have a dark theme, they include subjects such as mental illness, murder and questionable therapies yet the vibrant, cartoon-ish graphics and upbeat narrator mask those themes. Instead you get this slightly twisted comedy which makes for quite a unique point and click game.
Lastly, the achievements.
Unlike the previous, I encountered no bugs in this game and did not have any real trouble with any of the achievements. There are a lot of missable ones, but I would advise that you keep different saves as you go along. It makes it a lot easier to go back for any achievements that you missed. It’s an easy 100% overall I would say.
All in all, I enjoyed this game and I think I enjoyed it a lot more than it’s predecessor. It’s a great add on to the franchise and another great Daedalic game. I would definitely recommend that you play them in their proper order but both are worth adding to any point and click collection.
TL;DR : Despite what Steam says, “Edna & Harvey: The Breakout” is the first game and “Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes” is the second. A big improvement from “The Breakout” as there’s better resolution, nicer and more detailed graphics, a more intuitive point and click system and it generally being a more polished and bug-free game. There is an interesting story, a unique mechanic after chapter 1, fun puzzles and a dark comedic theme which makes it a little more unique to other point and clicks. Easy 100% worth adding to any point and click collection.

To start the review off, let me enlighten the dim-witted.
Just because a game is free does not mean that it's immune to criticism. Giving a free game a negative review is not mean, bullying or something to be shunned.
The game, if you can ignore all the negatives(which I shall not) is, in some places, a visually beautiful game. It contains a great soundtrack.
Some levels are very beautiful, some levels are thought-provoking.
Some levels are sad, some are frightening and some are quite relaxing.
Certainly a weird game, I don't think
is the correct word.
But that looks all good and well, doesn't it?
Yes, on the surface it does. But the actual game isn't quite what it's advertised as.
Note that I said
levels are very beautiful.
The screenshots used to represent the game on the Store page are quite obviously photo-shopped and tinkered with to make them look better than they actually are.
The graphics are not something to brag about, they're quite choppy.
I've seen far better graphics in other games using the same engine,
The sound-effects are terrible, some sound-effects are horribly loud and deafening.
No options menu except for the standard Unity options in the Unity launcher.
Lacks sound sliders, lacks a slider for cursor speed.
Lacks any real graphics slider, Unity only offers 1 over-all graphic slider.
The game lacks loading screens.
The way you transition from level to level is by walking into a door at the end of the level, but there is no loading screen so your left wondering if it is loading the next level or not.
The gameplay is mostly walking, with minor interaction. But that's quite abundantly clear.
The game just feels unfinished.
I wished more time was spent on it before it was released to flesh some stuff out and create an actual options menu, implement loading screens. Fix the sound levels etc...
The game is free. There is nothing binding the developer to release it at a specific date.
5/10.
Great premise behind it, not enough work put into it.
Keep on doing your art.

There's not a lot game-changing elements, only minor tweaks. The core gameplay was never particularly great nor broken so I'm not suggesting it warranted an overhaul (Shadowrun was always clunky on pencil and paper anyway). Some substantial new elements like sub races or gear customization would have been nice.
I got a great package out of Kickstarter. And people who played neither Shadowrun nor Dragonfall will get a steal for their money. But if you somehow missed the Kickstarter (shame on you!) and played Dragonfall, I'm not sure if there's enough progression from there to warrant the price of a full game. Well I do still think it's great value but the competition is great.
Hope it's not the end of the franchise though. Sure hope there are more cities to come!

Shadowrun Hong Kong: Early review
so an hour or so playing the introductory level of the game, i find myself enthralled by the sequel that HBS made. like dead man's switch and dragonfall, you jumped off right away into a vortex of mystery. no "once upon a time" slow start, s*** is going down, and you're in the point of no return right when you click the "NEW GAME" button. if you played the previous game, you're in for a familiar, yet new experience. THE UI is revamped and the graphics are more polished, yet the same core mechanics as its predecessor.
story:
as i said, the mystery sucks you right away, and the writing is incredibly sharp, with a lot of description text, great dialogue and various kind of responses to ensure top role-playing experience. i haven't gotten far yet, but i can say the intro wants me to know more, delve deeper into it. the characters are so far really great, useful in combat and have intriguing personality. yet, this is all i can say for now.
gameplay and mechanics:
pretty much the same as before. your skills are governed by stats, you have several classes to pick to (including custom class) and the combat is X-COM enemy unknow-esque turn based combat. nothing stood out too much yet, but really entertaining on its own.
graphics and music:
like it's predecessor, this game has 3D character sprites over beautifully, detailed hand drawn 2D background. what i noticed is animation, effects, 3D models and textures are vastly improved over the first 2 games. they are not state of the art level graphics, but quite pleasant to look at. the 2D background resolution is noticeably higher and you can zoom in much further than previous games.
the music still live up to this game's older siblings. ambient, and atmospheric tunes that fit the grim, cyberpunk dystopia that shadowrun series are set. combined with the graphics, i can say the game provide top-notch atmosphere and immersion.
flaws:
with all of that good points, nothing is perfect, and so is this game. i've noticed the revamped UI, especially the skill page is a step down from previous games. the description of stats and skills are put above the clunky looking spreadsheet, and it's kinda sore to look at. so far it's the most galring flaw of this game, but all things considered, i think shadowrun hong kong is a worthy successor of the shadowrun franchise. good job for HBS and their hard work for reviving this unique RPG.
this review will be updated as i play trough the game further.

For fans of SR:R and SR:DF wondering if this new installment is good/bad/worth buying now:
TL;DR . . . YES.
So far, Harebrained Schemes seems to have capitalized on Dragonfall's gameplay improvements while improving certain frustrations. Decking has been overhauled both visually and in terms of gameplay. It adds a stealth element that lends a much-needed element of unpredictability. Outside the matrix, you can play with new skills and weapons and sweet gadgets. The Karma system is now more UI friendly. (Still wish they didn't use the word "Intelligence" for tech skills - I resent the notion that my wiseass shaman elf is not intelligent just because she doesn't know how to deck.) They seem to have removed the Street etiquette as well, which makes sense with Hong Kong's narrative and frees more charismatic players to dabble in etiquettes they might not have tried before. (In Dragonfall, the distinctions between Street, Shadowrunner, and Gang etiquettes always seemed a bit tenuous to me.)
But is the story as interesting as Dragonfall? Yep. Maybe more. I need to finish it first - and I feel compelled to finish it. The narrative is high-strung with urgency. It seems to rely on the same framework as Dragonfall (go on missions to raise money in order to find Missing Person X and uncover mystery along the way), but this is forgivable. If it ain't broke . . .
My final comment: The art team on this one deserves praise and hugs and cookies sent to the office. Their work has improved since Dragonfall. The city of Hong Kong drips with atmosphere and character, and visual environments seem to correspond more convincingly with the game's narrative descriptions. (The same goes for the character models themselves. A gripe I had about Dragonfall was that character models tended to look nothing like their avatars.)
Kudos, Harebrainers. Take a well-deserved soykaf break.

If you liked Dragonfall you'll enjoy this.  It's the same game with a few tweaks.  That's not a bad thing.  Great visual appeal, good writing, tight mechanics, sweet tunes and awesome replayability is what makes this series special.  Some of the good with the bad below.  EDIT:  I have double the time in now and there are a ton of bugs.  Bad/lazy programming bugs.  You'll want to wait for the first major update before picking this up.
Get your reading glasses out early because the first hour of the game (at least) is textual back story and getting-to-know-you dialogue.  They probably would have been better served by breaking up the sheer volume of text by spreading some of the dialogue more evenly over the game.
I personally love the look of the game but wish you could zoom in further to better admire the models/backgrounds.  There's so much great detail it begs to be seen up close but it keeps you at a teasing distance.  There's also something up with their high stepping run animations.  It looks comical at this point in time which I can't imagine is intentional.  The taller the character model the more hilarity ensues.  Male Elf is a riot.
The skill interface is more visually appealing but less functional as you can only review one primary attribute and its related subs at a time.  This makes getting a sense of your character's present and future skill progression more challenging as they're not in an easy to read format that can be viewed holistically while spending karma points.  You're stuck toggling back and forth between stats which isn't ideal.  Admittedly, the super long list from the earlier games wasn't perfect either.
The matrix portion of the game is visually improved (cleaner) with some added pseudo-steallth and alarm mechanics.  A step up in my opinion.
I appreciate good writing and you find some of that here, however it's unpolished in the sense that I found a mountain of spelling and grammatical errors in the first few hours of reading.  Seeing the game is text driven you'd think they'd go over it with a fine tooth comb...but they didn't.  This probably bothers me more than it will others.  I'm harsh with this sort of thing because quite frankly there's no excuse as it's 100% preventable.  Having said that, it's still good writing and I could feel and taste the gritiness of SR:HK.
Back to it.  I hope I've only scratched the surface.  Again, if you like cyberpunk settings, RPG's and/or turn based combat you'll enjoy this series.  It's well crafted overall and will most likely continue to pump out and support more content over the years to come.

This is a really nice game!
Not groundbreaking, but it manages to convey childlike wonder with its story and mechanics that I don't see too often.
It's a first person platformer, with a great sense of scale that, fortunately, works more in its favour than its detriment.
There were some sections where it was hard to judge distances, due to the huge scale, but it wasn't a problem, most of the time. And when it was, it didn't get too frustrating.
As the title suggesting, the game is about a story about the narrator's uncle, to his daughter.
It's a rather simple minded adventure through a mystical world with frog people and a grappling hook that almost makes you fly.
There are some darker overtones spread around the game for those interested (it requires attention to the environmental objects and also simple decryption), but the main game really did feel like an adventure.
A big help is the amount of freedom that the game gives you in your movement. It's not too challenging, most of the time, but it allows for some additional difficulty if you want to find the secrets.
One game I hadn't though about in a while is Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers. This game reminded me of it, for great reasons! As I mentioned before, these two are the 2 of the few games I remember giving me this childlike wonder, making me want to explore all of these caves or suspicious paths. It's great!
It also looks really good, and while short, the few sections it has you go through look very unique!
One gripe I have with the game is the achievements. They're all very "completionist" oriented, which I don't really think fits in a game like this. They should have guided the player to look for the small details, instead of focusing on the "100%", which, in my opinion, puts players in a more systematic search for the required items, instead of actually exploring, if that makes sense? The objects stop being objects and start being an abstraction to get "achievement points", and you stop paying attention to how they fit into the overall experience.
If you don't mind short games, definitely give this one a shot! Won't change your world, but I truly enjoyed playing it.
Just strolling through the game and seeing the world they created is worth doing.

I never hated/loved a game as much as FLT. You are in control of a spaceship as part of the Federation which, apparently, is close to losing the war against a Rebel Army. Your goal is to travel for 8 sectors, upgrading as much as you can your spaceship while doing so and finally defeating the Rebel Flagship.
The sectors are randomly generateed. Once entered one you have to reach the exit by jumping from beacon to beacon. Each one may have some random event which may vary from helping some people to fight against enemy ships. By doing this you may earn enough scrap to upgrade the energy of your ship and make it more powerfull. You can also spend scrap in some store in order to buy fuel, repair your ship, recruit more crew and buy more powerups for your ship.
You can choose your ship before start. Initially there would be only one but you may unlock other ships by doing different task, usually deafeated the game with specific ship. Every one of them have different room and crew and it required the player to learn the right strategy to use it. This also increase the challenge, because HELL IF THIS GAME IS NOT CHALLENGING NORMALLY!
The fighting mechanic is turn-based-ish. You have to aim the part of the enemy ship you want to hit and wait for the weapon to load and repeat the procedure till you win. Or lose. Which will occour. A lot.
Yeah it is important to talk about the difficulty. It is exagerrated and mostly based on the game random generator, especially while exploring. In later stage you may fight ships which weapon always charged, also very precise and apparently very skillfull to dodge everything. Most of the time I didn't understand what was wrong, if I was playing wrongly or not. This is right on the border between "challenging" and "unfair".
Some people may say that you have to "git gud", it's trial and error and so on. The problem is that, since everytime you die you start for begin, there is no way to retry. Everytime the game resets and therefore you will find different events and encounters. The number of time you will ragequit is unthinkable.
On the other hand, the game mechanics and the "choose your adventure" type of game made this game highly playable and enjoyable. Most of the time you feel like part of the game's universe and you feel like continuing to play till you reach the end.
I can't give a score though because part of me want to give it a 8/10 for the gameplay but the unforgiving difficulty is really a big thing and sometimes I think it is quite exagerrated. Buy it knowing you will cry

This is actually a really good game. They've managed to upgrade the original a lot. The graphic style is great and the controls are great (after you get used to the default j-k-s-d-w scheme). The levels are all rather short which is a good time.
It's one of those game where you keep saying to yourself, "Ahh, ok, just one more level, and then I'll stop."... but you won't!

This is one of those games where you sit down to finish a level before sleeping for the night. You start it up, and begin playing. All of a sudden, you wake up to blinding sunlight, and find yourself 20 more levels in, and also an hour late to work.
Why is it so addicting? It has a brilliant art style, which I would compare  to watercolors. The gameplay is addicting and meaningful, despite the fact that you really only have to press 4 keys the entire time. Sound effects and the narrator are high quality and easy to listen to. Cutscenes are done very well, with several refrences and funny moments, however it doesn't have quite as many serious ones. Due to this, the game has a very lighthearted and cartoony feel, which matches the asthetic quite well. My only complaint here (and really, for the whole game) is the way the background scrolls; it makes me a bit nauseous and sometimes I lose my coordination, but the detail in the background itself more than makes up for that.
It has what I believe is 6 reskins for each of the characters, along with 100+ levels. That alone is plenty to keep you coming back for more of hte game, but a global and friends-list only highscore board makes you want to redo levels over and over until you get all the collectibles and gold. On top of that, there is a minigame that activates at the end, but only if you collect everything in the level. This is yet another way to fail getting 100%, as accidentally firing too early or too late can ruin the perfect run you just had in the hardest level in the game and crush your dreams of being on the top of the leaderboard.
In addition, for those who preferred the retro feel of the original, there are certain points in quite a few levels where you can drop into a box that reveals a retro styled map. Charming Mario style jump noises and a traditional 3 hearts system for this mode make it a solid addition in my opinion. Another new system that affects fans of the original may be the checkpoints. I feel that Gaijin handled this perfectly, giving the newbies and casuals (me) some leverage in terms of screwing up. On the other hand, they gave the good players and vets satisfaction by giving them points if they skip the checkpoint. In fact, the checkpoints can even turn into obstacles for players who intend to get perfect runs, since missing the jump over them results in using it whether you want to or not.
To top it all off, the soundtrack that builds in layers brings even more incentive to do as well on the level as you can, since the gold pieces add to the music. I have already experienced playing just so I could hear the end of the track.
To summarize it all: Bit. Trip Presents Runner 2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien is a loveable, addicting platformer that is an improvement in every way to the original. The stellar soundtrack, voice acting, animations, and character adds up to make this a great gaming experience for a casual gamer who has never touched a platformer, and just as much so for a speedrunning veteran who has been doing this for years. Definitely a great buy for $15. I highly recommend it.

Breaking it down:
Bad:
-It was clearly made up to a point and then told to ship which means that the freeroam was cut back (no sidequests, messing around, gambling etc) and the ending is like hitting a brick wall (although maybe that was their plan?)
-Freeroam is only avalible before or after a mission...which is also during a mission.  If you want total freeroam I would suggest the DLCs.
-Some plotpoints remove your weapons and clothing, thus is can be a pain to build up a nice arsenal only to have to collect them all over again.
Good:
- The story is fantastic.  One of the early missions has you trying out what it would be like to just be an average worker on a dock.  After moving four boxes it becomes clear that this isn't worth it.  Low pay for painful work.  It gives the player a motivation why they would join Vito as a mobster.
- The characters.  This is the weakest point of 99% of GTA's characters.  They are all awful and jerks to you.  Why am I even talking to these people?  In Mafia II it's hard not to like Joe, even when he's making a fool of himself.  And Leo Galante is like a father figure to you, leading you on a path to the mob.
- The vehicles, while slow and heavy, are classic to the period.  Most can be modded in garages and, unlike GTA, will return to your garage if they explode.  All of them have excellent levels of damage and even layers of dirt if you drive them enough or go down dirt roads.
- Great visuals, even if this game is a few years old now.
- Other fun stuff: The shotgun is just as loud and deadly as it should be.  Cops pay attention to basic driving so no speeding around them!  You can also fill up your gas (although most likely you will blow up or find a new car before then).
While I haven't played Joe's Adventure, I did play a far amount of Jimmy's Vendetta.  Its basically a collection of side missions with only a bit of story to bring you along.  It does make freeroam feel like it should.  Nothing's better than leading a cop car through a department store.
I originally pirated the game, and even after beating it I had to buy it.  It's well worth it.  The only downside is that there are only weak rumors of a Mafia III.  If Mafia III could be just like Mafia II but with a bit more time to work on freeroam, I would be there.
Not convinced?  The demo features a portion of the map that can be freeroamed for, I believe, 15 minutes before you start the mission.  It has most of the features of the main game like buying different clothes, guns, and a few of the cars in the game.
