Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines is action RPG released in in 2004 by Troika Games.
**My review is based on retail CD-ROM version which I bought in 2004 and completed on multiple playthrough (without unofficial patch). Although, I didn’t cover all vampire clans, it’s still one of best RPG experience despite of technical issues.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines inspired by Tabletop role-playing game like the World of Darkness. Set in Los Angeles where vampires, werewolves, and other creatures are no longer myths. Rule of masquerade set the wall between humans and vampires. You are one of them; spend time in endless night from the complex alley in Santa Monica to Asian distract in Chinatown and reveal the true secret of dark society.
---------------------------------------------------------
At the beginning of the game, you will introduced by biography and allowed to choose between 7 different vampire clans; The Brujah (fierce warriors), The Gangrel (animalistic loners), The Malkavian (mentally insane), The Nosferatu (disfigured sneaky), The Toreador (socializable artist), The Tremere (mage and warlock), The Ventrue (classy rulers). Each clan affects how you perceived the world. The clan offers set of unique disciplines (vampire powers) and passive skills that can completely change your progression, dialogue, and perspective. For example; the classy Ventrue can’t feed animal blood which is a contrast to the Nosferatu crawling in the sewer to the objective and can’t freely roam on street like other clans. The Malkavian will face twisted dialogues; question you what is real answer or your hallucination.
Moreover, you spend point on attributes and abilities which affect the effectiveness of each task (unarmed, hacking, persuasion, perception, stealth, etc.) which greatly support your accessibility or additional choice for conversation and combat approach.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines has same set of linear main story quest, but it won’t hold your hand to progress in specific way. The quest design allows multiple approaches which can end up to full stealth or non-lethal. If the situation went wrong, the game still offer you a decent combat system. A bit flimsy, but still fast-pace and fun from unarmed to range gunplay with association of some disciplines. Stealth can be bit tricky in term of enemy line of sight, but reward you with satisfied finishing move.
The side quest has its own story and adds a bit of world background or support the role of NPCs. Leading you to unique location with engaging story and objective (haunted house, mysterious serial killer, clan conflicts). They are memorable and very entertain when you revisit with different approach.
You gain experience points from completed quest, it’s balanced design that emphasize the main goal regardless of your play style. Some quests also reward special item or regain Masquerade point (it depletes if you break the appearance and violate human which result hunt and death.).
Some choices can affect Humanity point which can result losing your character control. So, choose wisely.
---------------------------------------------------------
The strongest point of VTM: Bloodlines is the dialogue. Most of them are extraordinary well written, natural, bit comical, and filled with clever lines without distinct black and white choice like some modern RPGs. Make you think twice and keep your engagement.
Every NPC has their own personality represented by supporting voice and animation. You could sense their moment from intense feeling to amusing humor. They are part of the world not just static NPC with bare bone quest. With based design of Source engine, it’s well executed to deliver facial animation, gesture, and top-notch voice acting by various talented actors.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines fulfills the atmosphere with amazing soundtracks. Synthpop, Techno Dark, and other memorable songs by real bands. Ambient soundtracks give you some vibes of classic horror, dark movie depend on each location you visit.
The combat sound provide satisfied feedback (melee impact, firearm sound), although it’s sometimes unsync with animation.
---------------------------------------------------------
The major flaw of VTM: Bloodlines is technical problems when it was released (probably rushed by Activision for marketing purpose). Some players addressed different game breaking bugs, glitches, and poor enemy AI. In original version, I was forced to use console command to bypass most quest glitches. The end game is quite forced to use range weapons which give you hard time if you had spent all point to melee combat. Bloodlines also suffer from graphical issue due to unoptimized Source Engine compared to Half-Life 2 released in same date.
Fortunately, the community delivers unofficial patches to fix most critical issues and still update to this day including several mods to improve every aspect and balance the gameplay to its best.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines is underrated gem but it’s somehow overshadowed by several issues on release. With deeper inspection; it still represents one of best well-crafted world and dialogue that emphasize the best RPG experience. It features high amounts of replayability which you revisit the world of vampires for different clan and choices. A classic and highly recommend for RPG fans with latest unofficial patch installed, worth even it’s on full price.

(This review is absolutely full of spoilers. If you want to play it without spoilers, do not read this review)
This is a game about dreams, specifically those of the developer, Steven Harmon. "Dreams", in this context, however, extends to a more figurative sense than pictures in your head as you sleep. This game is effectively a look inside the head of the developer, seeing not only the fanciful reveries he experiences when he shuts his eyes, but also the various aspirations, joys and disappointments he has experienced. Given the personal nature of this work, it is difficult to avoid criticising the individual without overreaching into a personal attack. Before I say my critique of the work, I will indicate that I feel this is the product of a talented individual who, in all likelihood, has a great deal of promise in the future, as I am of the understanding he is fairly young and new to the game design industry.
That said, it comes across that the developer confounds, like many developing artists, self-obsessed oversharing and actual poignant displays of artistry. He makes the unfortunate mistake of "telling" us what we are seeing rather than merely showing us. The dreamy vistas of the various levels are lamentably undercut by insistence upon narrowly specific personal examination. It can be compared to "The Beginner's Guide", in this way, however, Wreden crafted a narrative wherein the actual level of personal anecdote involved is left ambiguous, and it remains focused on a very specific relationship and the conflicted emotions and interests involved. Harmon's work is extremely scatterbrained, failing to draw us to any massive climax or epiphany, which is essential considering the emotional and personal nature of the project.
The level design is also, at times, quite meandering and unintuitive. Any doubt that this is largely a product of vanity dissipates when one reads the developer commentary, wherein he spells out plainly the personal connections he has to each of the levels. In said commentary, the developer makes some fairly irksome remarks regarding level design. In one such comment, the developer flippantly dismisses a glaring bug in the level "Noise", remarking "Meh, you can reset." This is the same developer who later is heard in the game making a breathy, somewhat quixotic, rant about why the University of Southern California should accept him because of the tireless passion he puts into game design. I personally became a bit miffed when the developer expressed a strange anger towards players who skipped a level about his self-loathing, indicating "If they won't give me their time, I won't give them my time". Unfortunately, it is not the burden of the player to draw themselves into your work for you. I did not intitially skip that level because I lack compassion for you and your personal struggles; I did so because it appeared unsolveable. In exchange for reaching the culmination of this level, I was permitted the license to ascend a ladder at a crawling pace while watching what appeared to be a rather overperformed live-action re-enactment of a nervous breakdown. In "Two Steps Forward", the dev tries to make us feel his pain in development by creating what is probably the most needlessly frustrating level I have ever played. He justifies this by saying it is a rule of theatre to never "bore" the audience, but somehow frustrating them is not out of the question. Which is seriously contrary to everything I understand, as a consumer, about game development as well as not particularly clever. "Oh, it's making me go back. This is dumb. Alright, I'm out, what's next?"
There are shades of brilliance in the design of certain levels that does bear mentioning to offset the faults, however. The "Frame" level has quite a wonderful element of the levels (one in color and one in monochrome) being stacked on top of one another, as it one is resorting to memories and images of the past to resolve a dilemma of the now. The rushing feeling of escaping authority in "Curfew" by running away from the lighted sentries and finding one's own path is highly reminiscent of youthful skirting of societal/parental restrictions. I agree that the Running of the Bulls is a barbaric, foolish ceremony and that it has greater implications of how "No One Wins" in a zero-sum game. The campground level with its silly, childhood joke is actually made far more impacting by the commentary, when the developer, in an uncharacteristically stoic manner, presents without comment that the level is dedicated to someone who lived only fourteen years of life. There are the hints of subtle, wrenching experiences within this work.
Many have commented on the love levels, and, again, I will not lower myself to commit a personal attack or demean anyone's experiences. However, I will state that it fails to elevate the subject beyond a mere mundane experience in one's personal life that hardly merits mention. It is a universal experience, but the lack of powerful images and emotive sights makes it fail to grasp me in to feel I can relate. "Emily Is Away", by comparison, manages to make my own heart sink through nothing but text. In the last few moments, you feel the protagonist's pain as he tries to open up and have an in-depth conversation with his friend, but he censors himself, in an odd admission she has already slipped away from him. The small talk at the end underscores the massive elephant in the room that will go unmentioned and trample their relationship to nothing. From what I observe in Harmon's work, by contrast, no arc is shown of the dev's relationship, no gripping scenes or images, nothing.
The comment in "Sabotage" that he was showing us the anxiety he experienced in his junior year of high school further indicates a lack of self-awareness regarding the audience. The level itself is fine enough symbolically, but the aforementioned scene wherein he sits before a test and a board relating to him why he falls short of USC's admissions standards fail to convey to me any strong emotions. It fails to emotionally tie in to a universal feeling of having "fallen short" and feeling as though one's hopes for the future are dashed, as a result. It merely comes across as disappointment with the "unfairness" of admissions standards which...um, I was playing a video game, correct?
Any artist will have to be sensitive and vulnerable in order to produce lasting, worthwhile works. This, however, seems like a pretty clear example of someone who lacks the self-awareness to graciously balance out a very personal work. I am unsure of how to take the use of Steam reviews at the end of the game, but it comes across as somewhat passive-aggressive. I feel this game is worthwhile, if only because it gives a great deal of insight into the mind of the creator. However, the insights are not always the most positive. With time and experience, I feel the developer could end up being a very great one, and I do recommend the game, as it is free. But, bear in mind, the dimensions can indeed be quite awkward and these are "[Steven's] dreams".

What can I say? I'm a sucker for the Shadowrun lore and setting. So, my opinion might be kinda biased.
But with that out of the way, the game, to me, feels amazing - as others have said before me, if you liked SRR and Dragonfall, this is absolutely a must have. The story, at least as far as I've gotten into it, is on par with Dragonfall, along with interesting supporting characters and personal stories. The enviroments feel much more alive and vibrant with the new setting, getting in an even more colorful, exotic enviroment.
Loving the serie, I can't say much of the story, since despite the time I played I'm still pretty much at the start, but the writing is very good. And I could already see some interesting puzzles and hints to make your life easier on at least one run. Just a little hint, don't dismiss poetry slams.
There's comedy, there's intrigue, there's a mistery that I hope to solve, and there's characters I love.
The new Matrix is a really good step forward from the old interactions, in all aspects: artstyle, musical score and expecially mechanics. Not to mention some glimpses of other places as well, but I won't go much further discussing them, I'm still not sure how much they've been implemented.
The game isn't devoid of problems, obviously.
The artstyle is amazing, but the models do seem a bit dated, and despite that in opening/closing the menus I've seen some weird loading times or framerate issues. Nothing major, and with the nature of the game definitely not a dealbreaker in any way, but still something to keep in mind.
The animations, expecially the running one, still feels slightly off, BUT, spell, lightning and other visual effects HAVE definitely been improved.
Alas, I do have some gripes with the new Matrix system: mostly, on the controls. While the addition of free matrix movement and the new system are really amazing, point-and-click controls in my opinion don't meld really well with the nature of the minigame (For those of you who played Dragonfall, the AZT tower first room is a good reference to have an idea), and the camera sometimes works as much against you as the IC that you encounter.
IN SHORT:
Pros:
-Looking nicer and quite slick, with a lot more modelwork and with some snazzy effects here and there.
-Voice acting in some parts and animated cutscenes!
-Interesting characters and story
-New Matrix system!
-Lots of new stuff and mechanics, like spells, augmentations, different spirits etc.
Cons:
-Still some really really minor framerate issues in navigation/opening menus/etc.
-Matrix system is nice, but with some control and camera issues.
-Some animations look slightly off.
IN SHORT:
If you liked SRR and Dragonfall, this is an absolute yes. More of what you love, with some extra cherries on top.
If you are new to the serie and curious about the setting, this is a good chapter and it's self contained (as Dragonfall was self contained from Dead Man Switch.) Pick it up and give it a whirl, but be warned you might find the first games somewhat less enjoyable after getting used to the new mechanics and stuff.
If you don't like CRPG's, lots of text, and a slower, more methodical approach, or you didn't like the first two games, then chances are you won't like this.
See you in the shadows!
~Jariel.

I am only 4 hours in but I'm already enjoying Shadowrun: Hong Kong far more than the original Shadowrun Returns. The UI is much cleaner and usable. The addition of free party members with interesting backstories is very welcome - they actually feel like they have personalities and I want to keep them alive and take them on runs with me whenever possible. The story is much more engaging from the start and I really like how you can craft your own backstory through dialogue options with Duncan - your foster brother. The matrix runs are much more interesting and have puzzle, sort of platforming and stealth elements. There is a much bigger diversity of sidequest runs that do not directly impact the main quest, and those for the most part are enjoyable. I also really liked the support for a street monk subclass, I'm definitely going to be playing one the second time through! The final positive note is the music (har har). I love the new soundtrack, it's very moody and often fits the theme of a particular run perfectly - it reminds me of Deus Ex and Vampire: Requiem soundtracks a lot.
On the negative side there still isn't a great diversity of gear (rifle, better rifle, even better rifle, cyberdeck, better cyberdeck, and so on), there isn't a whole lot of new gear or spells either, although I like the look of some of the new drones. A lot of art assets are recycled (sometimes bizzarely so - what is a Berlin parking booth doing in Hong Kong?), but overall the game looks crisp.
Tl;dr If you liked Shadowrun Returns, you will love Shadowrun HK. It is better in every way. If you haven't played Shadowrun Returns, I highly recommend playing Shadowrun HK instead.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is the third standalone game in Harebrained Schemes’ critically-acclaimed Shadowrun cRPG series. From early on with the first edition ruleset when I played the paper and dice version with friends, to the SNES version to today's offerings I have always been keen on the hybrid, genre smashing world of Shadowrun. One part Cyberpunk and one part Fantasy.
With several decades of both table-top roleplaying books and novels to pull from HBS has taken many of the important elements and injected them into this series of games. SR:HK promises a revamped matrix (something my Decker is keen to jump into!), better 'maps'/lanscapes, improved choice and more interesting non-player characters.
The world is controlled by massive mega-corporations who do battle with one another by using 'Shadow Runners' as their illegal proxies.  Much of the time in the Sixth Wolrd (another name for the Shadowrun Universe) the strings are ultimately being pulled by a powerful entity such as a Dragon and thus the term - Never Deal With A Dragon which was lifted from the title of a SR novel. At the beginning of this tale we recieve a message from our past, urgin us to travel to Hong Kong. What will be waiting there for us? My guess, trouble, what else?
So far I am enjoying my time with Shadowrun HK. The NPC interactions can get a little wordy but pacing seems solid and the story ramps up quickly. Circumstances are not what they seem and the story unfolds in comfortable layers. If you enjoy Cyberpunk, tactical RPGs and games like XCOM, then this is likely a game you want to check out!

Got this on sale a while back for less than a dollar. Still trying to beat it. Worth even more than its original price.
Graphics: Old-school graphics, which can be a boon or curse depending on your tastes. Art style for the characters is anime-style, and I kinda like the sketch style for the PC portrait.
Sound and Music: the music is pretty good( especially in snow terrain), though one track seems to cut out a little when it loops. The Music does fit the mood really well every time, though. Sound effects are nothing special.
Story: Being a rogue-lite, the story isn't all deep and engrossing as the heavier hitters, but has some interesting twists.
Characters: Pretty likable, actually. The way they develop as you go on your journey is great and while they're not totally original, they're awesome nonetheless. ( and the endings can get pretty touching.)
Gameplay: If you're dipping your feet in the rogue genre, this would be a great place to start. The Ransom aspect is there( provided you don't make perfect world by abusing the world naming system) and death is permanent, but you can reload from saves, provided you have the crystals or luck, the awakening skill helps save your♥♥♥♥♥if things don't go as planned, and the Vault helps with later playthroughs. The idea of using levels as potential stat boosters is great. There's a variety of classes, each with their own playstyle(defense, long-range, offense, charisma, etc.), though you'll have to earn a few before you get them. I love the simple idea of the side-scrolling aspect; it leads to some very tense moments( especially when in dungeons or near mountains.)And the little touches, like the NPC dialog, the varying levels for enemies, the differeing difficulties, the replays,  and even the multiplayer aspects( no co-op, but there is a way they can help... and you can show how awesome you are when you clear a world.)
All in all, if you can live with the old-school graphics, the relative lack of multiplayer and the rogue-liteness, you'll find a game that is well worth or even more than the price. ( and also, keep an eye on a sequel, which is in developement at the time of this writing.)

Buy it. I am really moved by the plot, once you are smart enough to see through the veil and get to the deeper part of the characters and their backstories and the future you want to create for them.
Let's start with the pros:
Maps related;
- Enough rogue like elements to keep players who wants new experience every time interested (create random world/enter different map codes)
- Rogue-like features frustrates you? Don't worry, you get to stay on the same map and die as many times as you want if it pleases you. In another word, this game will provide you the opportunity to get a good learning curve, and the elements to make your future gameplay easier or more challenging, totally by your choice (such as using pre-saved items from last playthrough/death or not doing that and just hop right into a new world)
- Maps aren't just 'different', they have different characteristics, coming with different perks and extra challenge. Pick according to your own liking/style (some of them are pre-sets with description, no worry of getting confused!)
In another word, a great deal of variety for gameplay experience and control on difficulties, pick as you desired or just go random!.
Gameplay;
- Interesting game mechanics; More than 'move and attack'. Different classes have totally different play style (aside from knight and swordman, the 2 starting classes. Tho not having the same stats and starting items already meant a great deal of deaths and exploring for new players until they got lucky or unlock other classes). Strategies are based around classes more than how skillful you are. Also, you are at risk every moment. Move to the right or be annihilated!
- Challenging; this is a game that you will die quite a lot in it. Is it unfair tho? Like, deliberately making the game overly punishing or clunky to play? No, nothing of those. "How to win" is something that needs to be learned in this game. Game difficulty scales according to how far you traveled, so no 'getting to level 99 and 1 shot the boss'. Try that and you will get one shot by a skeleton instead.
Plot:
- IT HAS DEPTH. Esp consider the different worlds you play in and as a result, having different play route/traveling experience. Without trying to get all the NPCS, it took me 3 clears to fully understand the story of this game, which left me almost in tears when I finally 'know'. All the npcs have more personality than you do :0)
Music:
- I like them. That small ense of sadness coming from them fits very well with the atmosphere and the plot of the game.
There is so much heart in this game that this sales is totally not doing it justice!
Ok, as for the cons:
One may complain about it being 'too short' i guess. As much as I liked it, I am a bit disappointed when I see that I have only 13.4 hours on it... well, there's only that much it can offer I suppose. That keeps it concise tho! I am just sad that it ended so soon hm...
Game can be a bit too punishing/unfair at times :0) like, a wrong map for new players whatnot.... that is compensated by allowing players to try different maps, preset or no. Also there are lots of sharing/walkthroughs online, just try google. Seriously tho, just because it's pixiled which may or may not remind you of FF/dragon quest, doesn't mean "One Way Heroic" is as easy when you first started; just move, encounter, level up and kick♥♥♥♥♥ Doesn't work like that, and it will be your♥♥♥♥♥that is kicked.
No other complaints really, you'll find the game quite fair once you actually start playing it.
For any RPG fan that doesn't mind a challenge, 10/10 must buy, esp consider its low price. You'll find it worth it, the creators deserve the respect.
Extra points if you're into oldschool RPG music and characters development.... no, just the NPCs, you are as uninteresting as you ever are.

I never hated/loved a game as much as FLT. You are in control of a spaceship as part of the Federation which, apparently, is close to losing the war against a Rebel Army. Your goal is to travel for 8 sectors, upgrading as much as you can your spaceship while doing so and finally defeating the Rebel Flagship.
The sectors are randomly generateed. Once entered one you have to reach the exit by jumping from beacon to beacon. Each one may have some random event which may vary from helping some people to fight against enemy ships. By doing this you may earn enough scrap to upgrade the energy of your ship and make it more powerfull. You can also spend scrap in some store in order to buy fuel, repair your ship, recruit more crew and buy more powerups for your ship.
You can choose your ship before start. Initially there would be only one but you may unlock other ships by doing different task, usually deafeated the game with specific ship. Every one of them have different room and crew and it required the player to learn the right strategy to use it. This also increase the challenge, because HELL IF THIS GAME IS NOT CHALLENGING NORMALLY!
The fighting mechanic is turn-based-ish. You have to aim the part of the enemy ship you want to hit and wait for the weapon to load and repeat the procedure till you win. Or lose. Which will occour. A lot.
Yeah it is important to talk about the difficulty. It is exagerrated and mostly based on the game random generator, especially while exploring. In later stage you may fight ships which weapon always charged, also very precise and apparently very skillfull to dodge everything. Most of the time I didn't understand what was wrong, if I was playing wrongly or not. This is right on the border between "challenging" and "unfair".
Some people may say that you have to "git gud", it's trial and error and so on. The problem is that, since everytime you die you start for begin, there is no way to retry. Everytime the game resets and therefore you will find different events and encounters. The number of time you will ragequit is unthinkable.
On the other hand, the game mechanics and the "choose your adventure" type of game made this game highly playable and enjoyable. Most of the time you feel like part of the game's universe and you feel like continuing to play till you reach the end.
I can't give a score though because part of me want to give it a 8/10 for the gameplay but the unforgiving difficulty is really a big thing and sometimes I think it is quite exagerrated. Buy it knowing you will cry

LISA is a side-scrolling RPG in the vein of Earthound that tells the story of Brad Armstrong, resident martial arts master and unholy beater of♥♥♥♥♥ as he attempts to locate and rescue his adopted daughter, buddy, all the while struggling with drug addiction, an army of perverts and an economy that's based on stacks of porn. Over the course of your mission you'll be joined by an off-beat group of wierdos  who will help you in your mission or be total liabilities that you keep around because the only alternative is to let their annoyingly endearing selves be kidnapped or murdered. Combat in this game is very much in the vein of standard 90's RPG's wherein groups of dudes line up and take turns wearing each others faces like flesh-mittens, using martial or legal jargon to bewilder and curb-stomp each other into the grave. Some characters (like Brad, Rage Ironhead, etc.) have the ability to use the WASD keys to lock-in moves and get additional hits in before using more... This is, without a doubt, the best game I have ever played. Now, that is my subjective opinion, but this game beat out Paper Mario, Xenogears, and Undertale in my heart and I never thought a game could do that. LISA has changed my entire being in a seriously profound way, I could write a thesis on it (actually, that's not a bad idea). Very existential, even somewhat meta in nature.
A work of staggering brilliance in an astonishingly honest narrative.
However, don't play this game if you absolutely hate
1. RPGs.
2. Watching child abuse
3. Talking about depression, suicide, sadism, addiction, and other parts of the dark side of humanity.
That being said, I'd even reccomend this to people that dislike RPGs. Even if you dislike the format, the gameplay is fun and interesting enough that you'll probably be quite surprised.
The DLC is an amazing expansion and I hope that it isn't the last we see of LISA, though with the DLC the game is flawless.

There are probably better adventure games to be playing (hint: Edna and Harvey: The Breakout). If you played the first game and need to sate your thirst for more of Edna's adventures (like me) this game is barely passable.
Edna does play a role in this game, but only as a sidelined, watered down version of the wickedly clever and funny girl from the first game. Our main character in this game is Lilly, whose only vocalisations are monosyllabic grunts and moans. The game and item interaction narrations are done by a generic, movie-trailer type voice.
The humor in this game was a huge step down from The Breakout. Most quips follow the formula of "[Violent, disturbed, or psychotic action/thought here]... But GOOD little girls wouldn't think/do that, right?" Gone are the unique lines for combining random items, or trying to use items on the environment here. Instead, the same lines are repeated over and over.
Even the characters in Harvey's New Eyes are a huge disappointment. I will always remember the great interactions I had with the NPCs in The Breakout. The hilarious conversations, and all the personality that shone through (Edna's water impressions vs. Bladder, the iron bladdered security guard is a conversation that may never be topped). In Harvey's New Eyes, NPCs are reduced to item recepticles. You interact with characters only to give/take something from them, then they fade into the background.
Even the puzzles in Harvey's New Eyes were a downgrade from The Breakout. New Eyes feels a lot like the last portion of the Breakout, which in my opinion was the weakest part. Very linear progression through the levels and barriers that prevent you from backtracking. The logic puzzles were interesting, but simple and unrewarding.
I played this game out of a sense of duty, to follow the tale of Edna and Harvey as far as it would take me. But I probably would have had fun playing through The Breakout a second time. This is a very average adventure game that looks even worse next to its predecessor.

Edna and Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes is an investigation in the consequences of protecting children from violence through the censorship of violence. Graphic scenes in the game are literally covered up by paint, and the primary protagonist is unable to see them. She is hypnotically prevented from accomplishing goals through strict rules ("I must not play with fire").
Through this, Daedelic offers a critique of overprotective modes of parenting by having you actually play as this child. It does this successfully, through the use of satire and extremely clever game mechanics.
There's a lot more. An assessment over how some of the rules and regulations in place for children and people who require mental help aren't there to actually help those individuals but to insulate society from them. Edna and the playable character are "deliquents", and as such cannot be allowed any agency.
There's also some really clever juxtaposition of what the "player sees" and what the "character sees". You're never quite sure what's through the eyes of the protagonist, and what's reality in the gameplay space due to the cartoonish art style.
I just really enjoyed this game. I think it's smart, funny and fun. However, as with any Daedelic game, it's best to try out the first half hour and see if the satire is your speed. If you're not a fan of this sort of satire, you likely won't find the game fun. Also, if you don't want to see even cartoonish depictions or implications of violence towards children, then you're better off skipping this game. I will note that there is nothing graphic or gratuitous,because the results of the violence are "painted over".
If this is your speed, enjoy. This game was a pleasure for me to play.

In all fairness, Hack, Slash, Loot (HSL) is a decent rogue-like. Realistically, how would any human fare trying to kill a dungeon full of ogres, undead skeletons or parasitic demons that burst out of his fallen comrades? The answer: he'd probably die long before reaching his goal.
HSL's main feature is arguably the starting character choice and the initial artifact they can bring with them (in case they have unlocked it). You start out with 3 mostly crap characters and then you unlock more through either
successfully clearing a session or
dying a certain number of times until the next unlock threshold. For most people, their first few unlocks may be the death based ones.
An "interesting" design choice was the strengths/weaknesses of elements in the game. To sum it up, every element has a chance of doing some effect. If you're strong against the effect, you take half the damage and never suffer from the effect of that element; if you're weak, however, you take double damage and the chance of being applied the element's effect is increased. This comes with some very nasty consequences, such as being poisoned for a bad evasion roll or having a random piece of your equipment destroyed by fire. It gets even worse when you figure out that holy and dark elements' effect is applied when you kill something and that both give you health, increased accuracy (aka hit enemies more often) or even increased damage: the game is practically forcing you to find and stick to a holy/dark weapon combo of melee, ranged or magic varieties, since randomly finding a potion and carelessly using it without knowing what its affix might do is bound to either screw all you've worked for or not heal you when you'd really want some health.
HSL also starts handing you characters that are arguably better for specific dungeons or have gameplay variability to help you find your niche. One particular character has intrinsically magic resistance, for instance: you'd definitely want to bring him to at least two of the dungeons for that reason alone. But on the other hand, every character is more or less gimped in some way, and the arguable best stat to stock upon is armour (which, unfortunately, is more likely to come from your randomly dropped equipment than it is from being boosted from a potion) because it is applied BEFORE strengths and weaknesses come into play.
As for the artifacts, the undeniably best all-around one is the Mask of SomeMummyGuy (name forgotten, not the actual name), the goal from the crypt dungeon and forever unlocked once obtained. There is no real reason not to bring it with you either, since it boasts an incredible amount of armour and reasonable stat boosts for your offensive ability. Compare to the Butcher's Knife, which makes you walk twice a turn but does such an insignificant amount of damage that you'll be seeing the numbers 1 or 2 popping out when you attack something, or the Necronomicon, which if you aren't a melee character or don't have holy or dark weapons means you will also be hitting a lot less for the "benefit" of being able to pass through walls (which may sound nice, but on most of the dungeons it simply means that if you don't clear a room FAST the monsters are going to start opening doors EVERYWHERE and the entire level is going to make a never-ending conga line to beat you up).
Also keep in mind, my worst gripe with HSL isn't about the gameplay but the accuracy of targetting itself, a game mechanic. As you may see from the screenshots, tiles are rectangular: they are wider than taller by a ratio of aproximately 2. And when you want to click on something, you HAVE to click on their bottom half, because otherwise you'd be targetting the tile above it. It also doesn't help that targetting a tile to move that is far away AFTER having seen a threat doesn't cancel the order to move unless you click again or are hit by a monster, and if you are trying to attack from a range that will mean you will most certainly get hit before you realize that you are moving instead of attacking, and that in itself will usually get you killed since ranged characters tend not to have the best survival up close.
But, as I said on the opening line, HSL is a decent rogue-like. Not too deep about it nor very long-lasting, but if you like rogue-likes you may enjoy it. Should you buy HSL? Maybe. Maybe on a 75% discount. I still hate the inefficient targetting system and how hard it is to move long stretches of the dungeon when you're on the last rooms to find the stairs, pixel-clicking on the map or hitting the wrong tile. If you think you can handle it go for it; don't bother otherwise.

Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines is action RPG released in in 2004 by Troika Games.
**My review is based on retail CD-ROM version which I bought in 2004 and completed on multiple playthrough (without unofficial patch). Although, I didn’t cover all vampire clans, it’s still one of best RPG experience despite of technical issues.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines inspired by Tabletop role-playing game like the World of Darkness. Set in Los Angeles where vampires, werewolves, and other creatures are no longer myths. Rule of masquerade set the wall between humans and vampires. You are one of them; spend time in endless night from the complex alley in Santa Monica to Asian distract in Chinatown and reveal the true secret of dark society.
---------------------------------------------------------
At the beginning of the game, you will introduced by biography and allowed to choose between 7 different vampire clans; The Brujah (fierce warriors), The Gangrel (animalistic loners), The Malkavian (mentally insane), The Nosferatu (disfigured sneaky), The Toreador (socializable artist), The Tremere (mage and warlock), The Ventrue (classy rulers). Each clan affects how you perceived the world. The clan offers set of unique disciplines (vampire powers) and passive skills that can completely change your progression, dialogue, and perspective. For example; the classy Ventrue can’t feed animal blood which is a contrast to the Nosferatu crawling in the sewer to the objective and can’t freely roam on street like other clans. The Malkavian will face twisted dialogues; question you what is real answer or your hallucination.
Moreover, you spend point on attributes and abilities which affect the effectiveness of each task (unarmed, hacking, persuasion, perception, stealth, etc.) which greatly support your accessibility or additional choice for conversation and combat approach.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines has same set of linear main story quest, but it won’t hold your hand to progress in specific way. The quest design allows multiple approaches which can end up to full stealth or non-lethal. If the situation went wrong, the game still offer you a decent combat system. A bit flimsy, but still fast-pace and fun from unarmed to range gunplay with association of some disciplines. Stealth can be bit tricky in term of enemy line of sight, but reward you with satisfied finishing move.
The side quest has its own story and adds a bit of world background or support the role of NPCs. Leading you to unique location with engaging story and objective (haunted house, mysterious serial killer, clan conflicts). They are memorable and very entertain when you revisit with different approach.
You gain experience points from completed quest, it’s balanced design that emphasize the main goal regardless of your play style. Some quests also reward special item or regain Masquerade point (it depletes if you break the appearance and violate human which result hunt and death.).
Some choices can affect Humanity point which can result losing your character control. So, choose wisely.
---------------------------------------------------------
The strongest point of VTM: Bloodlines is the dialogue. Most of them are extraordinary well written, natural, bit comical, and filled with clever lines without distinct black and white choice like some modern RPGs. Make you think twice and keep your engagement.
Every NPC has their own personality represented by supporting voice and animation. You could sense their moment from intense feeling to amusing humor. They are part of the world not just static NPC with bare bone quest. With based design of Source engine, it’s well executed to deliver facial animation, gesture, and top-notch voice acting by various talented actors.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines fulfills the atmosphere with amazing soundtracks. Synthpop, Techno Dark, and other memorable songs by real bands. Ambient soundtracks give you some vibes of classic horror, dark movie depend on each location you visit.
The combat sound provide satisfied feedback (melee impact, firearm sound), although it’s sometimes unsync with animation.
---------------------------------------------------------
The major flaw of VTM: Bloodlines is technical problems when it was released (probably rushed by Activision for marketing purpose). Some players addressed different game breaking bugs, glitches, and poor enemy AI. In original version, I was forced to use console command to bypass most quest glitches. The end game is quite forced to use range weapons which give you hard time if you had spent all point to melee combat. Bloodlines also suffer from graphical issue due to unoptimized Source Engine compared to Half-Life 2 released in same date.
Fortunately, the community delivers unofficial patches to fix most critical issues and still update to this day including several mods to improve every aspect and balance the gameplay to its best.
---------------------------------------------------------
VTM: Bloodlines is underrated gem but it’s somehow overshadowed by several issues on release. With deeper inspection; it still represents one of best well-crafted world and dialogue that emphasize the best RPG experience. It features high amounts of replayability which you revisit the world of vampires for different clan and choices. A classic and highly recommend for RPG fans with latest unofficial patch installed, worth even it’s on full price.
If you're willing to take the time to make this game playable, then you will not regret the time you spent applying that patch.

One of the truly great action-RPGs of its time, and one that still holds up fairly well today. It's got a few flaws - it's a little exploitative at times, with more Vampire-strippers than it really needs, and the RPG element fall by the wayside in favour of pure action in the last third - but it's still more than worth looking into. If nothing else, the gothic-modern setting is a welcome relief from endless fantasy medieval worlds, the voice acting is excellent, and the story has more than enough twists and turns to keep you interesting. And the combat's a lot of fun, as you drain mortals dry to power your vampire powers, and turn rival vampires to dust.
I do advise tracking down the unofficial patches; they solve a lot of little glitches, and depending on your hardware, may be necessary to get the game to run at all; the game uses an early version of the Source engine, which is a little finicky on modern hardware.

I believe a lot of people feel compelled to leave a good review because they either felt strong emotions towards some in-game moments, or because they'd be directly going against the creator's self expression. I don't think feeling strong emotions necessarily makes this a good game, and I think it's fair to leave a negative review if the creator's message is bland and incredibly cliché.
Disclaimer: The controls are sticky, and there's some serious need for loading screens instead of just waiting around with no idea if the next level is loading.
I played through the game twice, first in regular mode, and then with developer commentary, reading what I hope are all of the commentary nodes that explain how/why certain things in the level are the way they are.
I enjoyed my first playthrough more than the second, as I was trying to figure out the deeper meaning behind each scene and how they all tied together. My second playthrough answered those questions for me: there is no meaning, aside from the surface message. 'Here are a collection of teen angst moments/dreams/memories that I want to share with you through not-entirely-literal imagery.'
The commentary mode was disappointing, since I was looking forward to uncovering some cool secrets about the game I had just played through, but there was only two or three nodes for every level. I understand that developer commentary is not something you see very often, but it seems to me that, for this type of game, you need to go all out and get into the little details about each level (which of course isn't possible, because I don't think there was that much thought put into each level). At least that's what I would have wanted to see.
Despite the disappointingly superficial narrative and the general lack of cohesion of the game, I did enjoy a few key moments, like the breakup level where I got shivers when walking outside and seeing the chat log in the air, or when I grabbed the picture frame in the gallery level and I felt like I was granted access to a hidden reality. But those moments were too few and far apart for me to recommend this game, despite it being free.
I, personally, wouldn't feel comfortable letting such a large public see a product that I feel is lacking, incomplete, or perhaps under-developed. I don't want to♥♥♥♥♥♥on the creator's self-expression, and I encourage them to continue making what they want to make, but it feels like the developer is still in the early stages of discovering themselves, and the whole experience just feels awkward (appropriate game title).
If you are the type of person to enjoy learning about others through their (somewhat superficial) art, I suppose this could interest you. But aside from a few rare moments, I don't feel like I got a lot out of it.

Like FTL, but as a medieval RPG.
This game has a deceptive level of depth to it, especially for such a cheap game. What makes this roguelike different from most other roguelikes and yet similiar to FTL, is that there is an advancing wave of darkness that forces the screen to scroll to the right. If you fall into the darkness? You die, and thus you need to keep moving to the right to survive, hence the name of the game. You would think that something like that would leave very little room for story, and in a way you are correct. But there is actually a bit more plot than it appears on first glance and you will need multiple playthroughs to fully understand what is going on.
The gameplay is mostly based around exploring, killing enemies and finding items while staying ahead of the scrolling wave. You need to find items to recover your energy, health and stamina, while also looking for weapons, armor, and enchantments. During this time the Demon Lord will occasionally pop in to try to kill you, and you either have to run from him, using whatever status effect items you have to slow him down, or finish him then and there. This sounds very simple on paper, but in practice it's actually a quite expansive resource and time management game, and you often need to plan your movements carefully to avoid getting killed by the scrolling darkness.
There are also a number of interesting NPCs, but sadly they very rarely appear. Each one has their own backstory, personaliy quirks, and even an associated ending. To mix things up even more, there is a random prefix system that can sometimes spawn either an enemy or an NPC with a stat changing prefix such as "stiff-necked", with some of them even changing the character's dialog, often in hilarious ways.
Like most roguelikes this game has a lot of replay value, but here it's even more enforced by the fact that you can "vault" items at the end of a playthrough so you can get them at the start of another playthrough. Combined with the various classes, starting perks, and random world generation, you will likely end up with quite a bit of variety right at the start of your various runs through the game.
There is even a limited online play component, in that you can start on a world where other players have played and see their ghosts where they have died. At the end of a run you will also see leaderboards listed all the other players who have played on that world.
Unfortunately this game isn't perfect, which is to be expected with it's nearly non-existant price. The stats aren't very balanced, with some like intelligence being less useful than the others, and charm in particular is almost useless given that it's mainly used for recruiting companions, who, as said before are extremely rare. I also noticed that bows seem a bit underpowered since they can't combo like melee weapons and often you can just throw things for similiar damage. Hopefully the upcoming expansion polishes the game up a bit, but even with the few issues this game has, it's worth far more than it's listed price at the moment.

This is a 2D Point & Click adventure game developed by Daedelic who also did the well-known Deponia series.
You play as Lilli, a sweet young convent school girl with a best friend called Edna and a stuffed toy rabbit called Harvey. The game follows Lilli's adventures on her many quests to help (and rescue) Edna. Alas, despite her best intentions, she leaves a swathe of violent death and destruction in her wake which is doused in neon pink paint by potato-shaped gnomes and described in a running commentary by a relaxed, cheerful narrator. Many a chuckle is had at Lilli's unfortunate incidents.
Daedelic titles are undoubtedly the Gold Standard of Point & Clickers and this is no exception. It's like experiencing a full-length interactive Hollywood blockbuster in cartoon form. Everything about it oozes professional quality from every pore.
the cartoons are beautifully drawn, as good if not better than the ones on TV although they don't have full movement, not even in the cutscenes. This didn't bother me at all and doesn't take anything away from the immersion. The only minor complaint I have is that the screen resolution only goes to 1920x1080 so I had black bars on my 1920x1200 screen.
an accordion plays a fantastic, melancholy theme tune in the background often but not constantly. Individual scenes have their own tunes and sounds to fit the mood and storyline. All sounds are highly polished and a treat to the ears. I never once considered switching to my own music.
there are so many characters in the game - I counted 20 voice actors in the credits!! - and every one of them has something interesting to say. It's possible to skip all dialogs with a mouse click but I never once felt tempted to do that, unless I'd already heard it before. I can't say that about any other game I've ever played. Lilli herself never utters a word (except in one of the endings!) she just makes little squeaks and sighs in response to the characters she's talking to, which all adds to her naive, innocent appearance.
the dark humour and exciting chain of events really captivated me and the character development rivals most of the real movies I've seen lately. Citing a Rolf Harris concert as a safe place for young girls to go is an example of the near-the-knuckle humour that has resulted in some of the negative reviews, so you need to be aware of what you're getting into before buying. This is definitely not a game for kids despite its friendly-looking cartoon graphics.
There are puzzles throughout the game. Puzzlers are my favourite genre. I've played many and consider myself quite good at them. The puzzles in this game are HARD logic and riddle tasks. Thankfully you're not forced to play any of them, they all have Skip options and I'm not ashamed to admit that I skipped half of them. I'll probably go back later and do them for the achievements though.
Most of the time I generally had a good idea what to do next by following the characters' dialogs, but there were so many areas and items to click that I inevitably found myself at a dead end sometimes, unable to find a new thing to click to progress the story. Some of the required actions are just bizarre, for example who would think to use a credit card on a tin opener? It's also easy to find yourself trying to complete a particular task blissfully unaware that it's impossible if you've failed to properly complete a previous one. At the time I often thought I'd run into a glitch but it always turned out to be my own stupidity.
At these junctures, with the narrator's sarcastic comments about my ineptitude ringing in my ears, I had to consult a guide to get through the blockage. The trouble is, once I'd sampled the guide I found it quite "more-ish". Here's a demonstration of my relationship with the guide for this game:
While in the grip of The Guide I found myself blindly following the instructions without paying enough attention to the blossoming storyline and cutscenes, depriving myself of the very reason I was playing.
If you buy this game I urge you not to fall into the same trap that I did.
Several months earlier I tried the demo version. It was full of glitches and I soon ended up permanently trapped inside the cellar stove, unable to play any further. I was worried that the full version might be the same since it starts with exactly the same content as the demo, but I'm happy to report that it runs smoothly and I found not a single glitch throughout the entire game - including the stove glitch which I double-checked! I played it mostly on Linux but copied my save file over to play on Windows a couple of times.
You might be thinking twice about spending so much on a Point & Click game but rest assured it's well worth it, even at full price, as long as you enjoy dark humour. It took me only 14 hours due to my horrific Guide addiction but would have taken longer under normal circumstances. There's also replay value to chase achievements.
Don't make the mistake of comparing the price of this against other P&C games, this is the Rolls Royce of Clickers.

I played this game back when it came out in 2004. It is a huge reason why I love RPGs today. This is a great cult classic, and well worth a playthrough, whether for pure nostalgia or as a first playthrough.
That being said, these are my observations and criticisms:
* At the time when the game released the visuals felt gritty and dark. They were perfect for the game and really added to the mood and feel
* The soundtrack is great. There are songs that I found through this game that I still listen to now (Lecher ♥♥♥♥♥, Cain, etc)
* Malkavians. Enough said.
* All the different classes were fun to play through and offered unique dialogue.
* The main storyline was fun and really pulled me in.
* Vampires. I've never played another game that really took such a dynamic and enjoyable approach to vampirism and vampiric society. I'd love to experience something of this calibre (or higher) again.
* The characters. I still remember a lot of the characters vividly. They were very memorable and fun to interact with.
* Bugs. All the bugs. Sometimes the game is unplayable and you have to have multiple save files or you might get stuck.
* Not very open-world. This probably wasn't a goal of the game, but it did feel like you were severely limited in what you could do.
* Not as fun to play over a decade later because it hasn't necessarily aged well.
That being said, this game will always hold a special place in my heart. <3 Worth a try, especially if you love vampires and RPGs.

As it is I simply do not think that a publisher, or a developer for that matter, should make any money off of a game that relies so heavily on an unofficial update to make it into a playable experience unless the price of that game were very low to refelect the quality and effort achieved by the "official" participants.

Where the game really shines is it's beautiful atmosphere and worldbuilding. The developers at Troika were genuinely fond of the TTRPG, and the game is absolutely oozing with that passion of theirs. The story is very well written and characters in it feel very much alive. Playing this game I really felt like I was experiencing a living, breathing world around me. It felt like the world had a real history and dynamics to it, instead of being rendered on my screen five minutes ago.
The game is very true to the VTM lore, and the handling of said lore is very well done. Bits of information are given to you throughout your journey, often between lines of dialogue, and never shoved in your face. You are left with a picture of this world that is very clear but still incomplete enough to leave you wondering. This is the kind of game that makes you want to read wiki pages.
And, even though I complained about the lack of diplomatic solutions, I have to say there's no greater satisfaction than seeing your character grow from a confused weakling to an unstoppable killing machine howling for bloody vengeance.
It's not a perfect game, not by a stretch. But it's a great RPG classic and there's a fare chance that you'll fall in love with it just as I did.

Okay, I hear a lot of how bad this game is, and how unfair it is. I am going to give my honest thoughts about the game, and help people understand the game.
First off, the graphic they look like they're from "Realm of the Mad God" and "Legends of Yore". That's because it is. Sure people can say that's a downside, but it could also be a plus side. Seeing how it's simple and easy to know the enemy you're trying to fight. Another thing is how the fog is. At times, you can see something, but not be able to shoot it with your bow or staff.
The soundtrack has seven tracks. No joke. I got the soundtrack from the Humble Bundle I got the game from, and it is good when you first hear it, it can be a pain hearing the same few tracks more than needed. But, the game does have one track that does help. When the track plays, that means there's five or more enemies in the room.
Okay, now, let's talk the gameplay. If you want to know, yes. It is a rogue-like game. The levels are randomly made as you play through the game. However, the game doesn't have one solid story like "The Binding of Isaac" did. This game has quite a few different stories that you can pick from, each with how to go through and manage the game. One story has a ton of tombs that you can look at for items, with another one with being a tower that a giant wizard use to live. They all mostly look the game, but little touches make it seem different.
Now, the buttom of the screen is everything, and I mean everything. Your settings, your stats, your map, your bloodtype, everything. You move around with the mouse, and you do everything with the mouse. You might be able to play this with a touchscreen, but I'm not to sure. Along with picking your story you want to play through, you can pick which character to play with. Each one is different and unique. You can unlock more if you do some tasks, like dying twenty times (I'm not kidding). Some characters work best with some stories because of the items you can get in the story.
Combat is what might make a lot of people mad. Whenever you move a space, all rendered enemies will also move a space. So, think of it as a game of chess, planning out where to move and when to strike your opponents. To actually deal damage on your opponent is as simple as clicking on them. If you have a melee weapon, you have to be next to them, if your have a ranged or staff weapon, you can be as far away as you can (but, still visible on screen). If you hover your mouse over the enemy, you can see their stats on the right side of the menu on the buttom of the screen.
To be honest, I wish I remembered how the stats work and how you can calculate your damage output. It is a pain when you start, but if you get this game, I recommend using Amazon (unlocked by dying twenty times), and using her on the story "Mask of the Boy King". This game isn't for everybody, but if you like rogue-like games, you might like this. However, I recommend getting it on sale or in a Humble Bundle, it isn't worth the full price. But, one last note, you can run this 8MB game on anything. I bet you can run it on a Raspberry Pi, I seriously think you can. But, with that said, I do like it. It is a game to play when you're waiting for updates to finish.

Hack, Slash, Loot lacks the depth of even the most basic Roguelikes, and brings nothing interesting to the table other than immediatley dropping you into a new game when you inevitably die. Unfortunately the game also makes other things immediate that probably shouldn't be, such as exiting your game. On multiple occasions I've hit the Escape key, forgetting that HSL doesn't have a seperate settings window, only to have it immediately and without warning, quit my current game.
As much as I like to see commercial roguelikes succeed, HSL is not an example of a roguelike that I'd like to see prosper. If you want to spend some money, go support Dungeons of Dredmore instead.

Hack, Slash, Loot has been described as a roguelike, it looks like a roguelike, but it completely misses the mark in terms of gameplay. There is no resource management, there seems to be no risk in using potions and scrolls; they all buff. Every entity seems to move at the same speed, which is not inherently bad, but limits the tactical landscape. There is very little thought involved while playing this.
In terms of playability, perspective can get the better of you if you are not careful around enemies. Sometimes an enemy is visible, but can not be targeted with a ranged attack, which seems strange at times. Otherwise, the simple gameplay leads to simple controls making it very accessible.
What was done well: the starting classes feel very different from each other in play. Allies intelligently stay out of your way in travel, but in combat situations they may block your path to the enemies and get themselves killed. Enemies stay out of reach generally, unless they have companions, which is interesting.
All in all, if you are looking for a casual turn-based dungeon crawler you may enjoy this. If you are looking for a thought-provoking roguelike then pass on this.
The game runs on Wine, so if it's something you're interested in, you have the option to play it.

If RNG rogue-likes are your thing, look no further than Hack, Slash, Loot. Level layout and enemy generation both perfectly balance the procedural generation of a rogue-like with the intentionality of a well-designed level. Unfortunately, other randomized elements are less-than-perfect. With a peculiarly inverted difficulty curve, players will find the greatest initial challenge is persevering through the 25+ deaths required to unlock the first character truly capable of rewarding a player's skill with success. Each successive character is more powerful than the last, and although some strategy is necessary in combining character classes with various artifact 'loadouts,' most of the later unlocked characters make previous ones obsolete. Similarly, choosing wisely from the loot at the player's disposal requires careful consideration, but the randomness of enchantments and loot mean that a session typically ends in either frustrating defeat or unsatisfying triumph.
On the spectrum of skill vs chance, Hack, Slash, Loot is just a bit more random than most players will find rewarding. Nevertheless, there is a wealth of unlockables that may keep a determined gamer occupied for many hours. For its unique interface and enjoyable retro stylings, the game is commendable, but overall it comes off as a quirky experiment that doesn't quite make the cut.

I gotta be strait forward with my biases with this game. I want it to succeed. I want it to be a great representation of all of the titles it draws inspiration from. As of now in early access it doesn't quite make it.
Basic Concepts: It's all about making the monsters to generate power. They only do this while they are happy. What makes them happy? You don't know. That's the point of the game, you are trying to find out more about these creatures so you can better handle them in the future. It is a game about worker management and researching creatures on your own. If you try to look up how to perfectly manage the creatures you may very easily ruin the game for yourself.
Pros:
1.) Diverse and interesting monster themeing. If this game does anything right then its that you really get the feel of being an SCP researcher.
2.) The agents you choose matter a ton. Monsters will react differently based on your agents traits and skills.
Cons:
1.) Hard As Bawlz. While you're still figuring things out your turnover rate for your agents will be insane. I haven't played a ton of this game so I don't know if it actually goes down. Basically if your monsters are unhappy some of them will start attacking anyone who comes into their cell, or cause facility wide effects that will destroy everything you love.
2.) As I said I don't know this game front to back, but It seems like with certain dangerous creatures that they may just randomly kill off your agents who come into their containment area. You could have ordered the agent to do something that that monster loves, but that's still not enough to keep them from murdering them half way through. The action also counts as incomplete in that case and you have to redo the action in the hope that the next guy won't be killed.
3.) Expect many failures. While it sort of goes with the theme that a lot of people are going to die figuring this stuff out, your entire work force will be killed off fairly often. I have yet to reach a checkpoint as well so every time I fail I have to start from the beggining of the game. While this means I get to know the basic monsters fairly well, things go so wrong so fast that its hard to figure things out the first time around.
Overall - If the sound of being an SCP researcher sounds fun to you, and you don't mind a high learnig curve, you'll probably enjoy this game. Unless you've watched a video and are absolutely sure that this is something you would like I'd wait until it has had a little more development.

Hey kids, do you like the SCP Foundation?
Do you think you can be a better moral compass while keeping the world safe, while also making money off the eldritch horrors that exist within the corners of the world?
Do you like magical girls?
If so, then this is the game for you!
…..In a few months! Yes even though I really like this game, as time of writing, you’re only permitted up to level 19 or so at the moment. Which while you have access to a very colorful arrangement of abnormalities to deal with, the game feels like it still needs development time.
But first, the good and the bad.
The good:
-The concept- Very fresh and interesting. To the best of my Knowledge this is really the first game like this where you try and keep horrors managed while also keeping the sanity of your staff paramount. Art style looks a bit odd with things looking both cartoonish for the people, yet also having the monsters look equally cartoonish and disturbing. It’s a good match and somehow works.
-Failure ever looms- The difficulty has a pretty good curve at the beginning with more simple monsters to deal with while teaching you the basics. You even get to retain the knowledge you accumulated about anomalies between saves. But even WITH this knowledge, a slight error or oversight can still mean DISASTER. Send the wrong type of person to deal with some shoes, suddenly you have a mad killer on the loose. Don’t tend to that crying baby? Watch most of your staff lose their minds. And god help you if you don’t pay attention to that magical girl…. The point is though even with this difficulty, the game still operates strong and with a decent checkpoint system (you go back to the start of the facility “week” for lack of a better term (Every 5 days), it doesn’t set you back too much for your failures, spectacular they may be.
-Rouge Like attributes- While the facility might change the monsters sure do. While some areas like the first area may be fixed, other areas you unlock have completely different monster load outs based on a pool. You might get a doomsday button one time or Girl staring at a wall another time. With the promice of even more monsters adding to the pool, the replay value continues to spike.
-The story- Sparse though it is, further on you learn some interesting tid bits about Lobotomy Corp that further questions your mysterious employers. Who are they, what is their real purpose, and what does it have to do with you? Well that’s where the bad comes in….
The Bad:
-Still in development- Ok this is the poison pill you have to swallow for early access but it’s worth mentioning.  The game isn’t finished and at level 19 you’re pretty much capped with the promise of things to come.  You don’t have access to a ton of monsters at the moment and again, the story just abruptly stops as it is just about to get very interesting. Its painful but you might want to wait for a while before getting this, even though the game really is quite good.
- Upgrade/money system- This was recently implemented in the January update, but its really something that needs tweaking. At least in the story mode there isn’t nearly enough points to go around between staff and upgrades and anything interesting. Roguelikes are my favorite type of game. Since the old days of Rogue and Hack, indie developers from all over have taken the basic ideas of roguelike games (procedurally developed worlds, blistering difficulty and permadeath, for example) and ran with it.
One Way Heroics literally "runs with it" by providing a game that forces you to keep running forward until you reach your destination: your final battle with the Demon Lord threatening the world. The parts of the world you leave behind are gradually consumed by a darkness that will devour you, too, if you wait too long or try to backtrack. So, in order to survive your encounter with the Demon Lord, you have to prepare yourself by gathering items and equipment and gaining levels on the way.
Replayability is high due to the fact you can use Hero Points gained from a previous playthrough to help your next incarnation succeed better or faster than before. There's the Dimensional Vault, where you can leave your best items behind for the next play-through. You can also unlock new advantages or even new classes, for greater variety and strategy. You may also choose to run through the same world next time, rather than generating a new one, meaning that you can remember where towns, dungeons, merchants and particularly dangerous enemies are on the map, and approach or flee from them accordingly.
The game itself is a short one, which is good for those of us busy folks who want gaming in small bites. You can sit and finish a play-through in less than an hour. But there are multiple worlds (including multiplayer ones hosted online) and modes if you get bored of the standard game. I suspect there is more depth and content in this game than I have begun to scratch the surface of, because it requires many playthroughs to get to.
Would definitely play again (and again)!

Fun and unique interpretation of the Japanese RPG game type. On paper, the concept sounds forced and confusing, but the game plays intuitively after only a few lives. Most importantly, there is a great design sense that unifies the game as a whole. Each class encourages its own gameplay style, and character customization, through an unlock system, is flexible without being overwhelming. An inter-game treasure chest, like that in Shiren / Mystery Dungeon, allows players not used to roguelikes accumulate treasure without being able to horde it. Well worth the price: a game that is rewarding whether you invest hours into it or simply play it as a coffee-break roguelike.

I've changed from a No to a Yes, but the Yes is provisional: you have to know what you're getting into.
First, the RNG can be brutal and you will just run into situations where you will get crushed, and you'll have to start a "new game". The "new game" is in quotes because you do maintain any unlocked ship types, achievements, etc. So watch how you can unlock new ships and do that and don't care that you get cruched before the Last Stand.
Second, it is frustrating to feel like you've finally gotten the crew and weapons you want and then, BAM, you get slaughtered and have to go back to the Hanger and start again. If you can deal that that, per the first point, you'll like the game.
Third, you can't run from a fight that you can tell up front you're not going to do well in. BUT if you can survive long enough for your FTL to charge, then you can jump out. Though perhaps out of the frying pan and into the fire. Still, better than an endless stalemate or outright losing.
Fourth, you will have to defeat the boss ship in the Last Stand at some point. To unlock the third kind of ship, that's the only option.
Given you can deal with an RNG ruining your run, you should like the game.

An extremely minimalist Rogue-like which initially may seem like it involves little more than dice rolling and therefore unavoidable death.  However, once you unlock a few characters and start to learn how to manipulate the odds in your favour, the game really begins to open up.
The other nice touch is that all the achievements are possible to get just by playing the game normally and you can easily set up the odd one or two that you missed along the way.
My only complaint is that you start the game with three relatively dull vanilla characters which might put off new players that  may otherwise be unaware of fun unlockables such as the Ninja, Pirate or Scout.

I strongly recommend you avoid this rogue-like. Since I can't really think of any pros that this game contributes to the genre, I'm just going to talk about the flaws.
This game is BRUTAL. I know rogue-likes are supposed to have you constantly die over and over but at least you make progress and learn a little more about the game each time you play through. However, I don't feel this way at all when playing this game. Well okay, I learned one thing.
This game practically eliminates 1/3 of your class choices. By attacking with warrior-like classes, you're guaranteed to miss most of your attacks and die within 3 minutes. With ranged classes, you, for whatever reason, have a higher accuracy and don't run as high a risk of getting hit, even with your health being low.
Speaking of which, it's almost impossible to get back any health you lose. In other games you find potions to restore your health and your armor is actually an important statistic. However, in this game, the potions are extremely rare, they don't always give you health (and the ones I've found give less than 10 HP), and with as much armor as I could find, I was still taking FIFTEEN damage from an enemy on the first floor of the game! Also, you start off with either 20, 30, or 40 HP, so...
Speaking of the floors in this game, the chances of completing a floor, or even moving on to the next floor, are low, really low. These floors are massive, and while that may not be the worst thing, there's no inventory system, and consider the flaws I've mentioned before. I've gotten to the second floor ONCE out of all my playthroughs, and naturally I lasted no more than a  minute. My luck, huh?
Speaking of luck, the biggest problem is the randomized generation this game has. I'm not thrilled with starting a game, having two enemies appear in front of me, me missing my attacks, and dieing without making A SINGLE MOVE. Also, like I said before with the damage, I don't find it really fair that an enemy on the first floor could whittle down a chunk of my health before even going through more than five rooms.
As long as you can deal with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that is UPlay, this is a fun game.

Overall a great, great game.
Yes, it's buggy as ♥♥♥♥, and needs to be patched up before it can be played at all. And yes, it's kind of dull that a lot of missions are either "go to this building and slaughter people/things" or "go to this building and sneak past people/things". There is no diplomatic approach to most issues, which is a shame. A character that's unwilling to bust a lot of heads is simply unavailable here.
Where the game really shines is it's beautiful atmosphere and worldbuilding. The developers at Troika were genuinely fond of the TTRPG, and the game is absolutely oozing with that passion of theirs. The story is very well written and characters in it feel very much alive. Playing this game I really felt like I was experiencing a living, breathing world around me. It felt like the world had a real history and dynamics to it, instead of being rendered on my screen five minutes ago.
The game is very true to the VTM lore, and the handling of said lore is very well done. Bits of information are given to you throughout your journey, often between lines of dialogue, and never shoved in your face. You are left with a picture of this world that is very clear but still incomplete enough to leave you wondering. This is the kind of game that makes you want to read wiki pages.
And, even though I complained about the lack of diplomatic solutions, I have to say there's no greater satisfaction than seeing your character grow from a confused weakling to an unstoppable killing machine howling for bloody vengeance.
It's not a perfect game, not by a stretch. But it's a great RPG classic and there's a fare chance that you'll fall in love with it just as I did.
Once you get past the 15mb error(Easy thing to fix with an unofficial Patch from patches-scrolls) It's quite a really good game Worth the money.
