One Way Heroics is like potato chips: you eat one, and you can't help but go for another.
For those moments where a player wants to pop open an RPG, but doesn't quite want to start a 40 hour time investment, OWH is perfect; simple combat, roguelike gameplay, and varied challenge levels depending on one's mood. Whether for a 20 minute stroll or an epic 2-hour odyssey with perma-death waiting around every corner, this game aims to suit itself to multiple tastes.
Finishing a game, whether winning or losing, awards points used to boost one's future playthroughs (with wins awarding more). Whether it be unlocking new perks or opening new slots in the Dimensional Vault to transfer items from one playthrough to the next, every run feels like it progresses the player. That being said, while there are technically save areas, losing concludes the run and records the player's performance right there - no going back to try and get more points, but it will allow you to conclude a run 'just for funsies'. Maniac Mode, the game's 'hardcore' setting also prevents players from importing items from previous games, though depositing new items is still possible. Save points and dimensional vaults make the game friendly for casual runs, but the true hero wins on Maniac Mode with no takesies backsies (the greatest scores are only counted upon no deaths).
More than that, the game is also surprisingly colorful. Dialogue and narrative is sparse, but sweet and entertaining. Furthermore, there are hidden secrets everywhere: the various characters you meet may have hidden dialogue, items may have unexpected purposes, and the non-restrictive nature of weapons gives a lot of freedom in designing 'builds'. There are even secret ways to win - it is recommended you do not go in with a guide, and simple explore yourself, as reading the wiki ruins a lot of the surprises this game has to offer (don't even look up those secret ways to win).
This reviewer's only criticism is that, after clocking a couple dozen hours, I'm ready for more! The weapons do resemble each other a bit too much, there's a hard limit on the available spells/abilities, dungeons resemble each other, and the charming character dialogues do eventually run dry.
For $3.50, this game was absolutely and totally worth it. It's creative, it's original, it's got high replayability, it suits people looking for various challenge levels, and it deserves to be recognized for what it is: a small but great roguelike RPG.
A minor edit to this review, a newer 'edition' has come out called Mystery Chronicles: One Way Heroics; however, despite slightly higher quality sprites, it manages to be inferior to One Way Heroics and One Way Heroics+. If you want the proper experience, it's here.

Pros:
1. Randomly generated world

3. Good graphics
4. Great music
5. Game controls work well whether you use an old controller (such as a Logitech f310 gamepad) or a keyboard.
6. Rewards system after the end of each run
Cons:
1. The options menu can be limited. I did have a problem with it at first but I got over it.
2. Can be hard to read everything that is in small text on the screen. I hooked up my laptop to my TV with an HDMI cable while playing One Way Heroics and even though it helped somewhat with what I was doing it could be improved on.
3. Very simplistic. For some it may be boring because of how simple the game it is, but for others like me it's fine since it's not at all complicated.
Summary:
Overall this is a very well done game. If you only have a few dollars for Steam, I would recommend giving this game a shot. Some people may not enjoy this game and other people will, but as for me I enjoyed it.

Man, I really wanted to like this game. I like the concept, the loot, and the randomess of where enemies are in the dugeons. However, this game suffers from one major flaw (which makes up the entirety of the game).
The combat is simply atrotious. The hit detection is all over the place. Depth perception is a huge issue as you can't really tell if your weapon will hit the enemy or not. Despite looking like a low grade game, Dungeons & Darkness isn't all that bad for a dungeon crawler.
The gameplay is somewhat remniscent of King's Field and Shadow Tower (games From Software made before they gained acclaimed for the Souls series) in that you're simply one person in a dungeon with nothing but monsters for company. Combat also harkens back to King's Field in that one fights in a first person perspective, each attack requiring stamina if one wanted to fight back against the various orcs, skeletons, and other assorted creatures of the dungeon.
The graphics do look somewhat mediocre since the game makes use of Unity assets but that can be excused due to being an indie game that wants to focus on being dungeon crawler.
Animations for enemies are rather simplistic, the skeletons being rather funny due to how they move compared to other fenemies.
I recommend this game for those that want to play something that is remniscent of King's Field, I also recommend it to those that want a simple dungeon romp at a decent price.
I do not recommend this for those that are expecting anything more than a simple first person dungeon crawler.

On the whole, I've enjoyed playing this game.  It's a cheap, fairly bare-bones dungeon crawler, with okay graphics.  Combat is fine, though repetitive - advance with shield raised, block enemy attacks, then counter attack and kill.  The charging of spells is okay, though some spells can't be cast unless there's an enemy in range (and if it doesn't know you're there, don't bother casting, just stab it in the back).
Two things would really improve it though - the addition of a map, and making the default sensitivity lower.  The controls are just so twitchy unless you turn the sensitivity down a lot.
A shop to buy new gear would be nice, but not needed, and some of the key prompts are wrong (controller prompts on the status screen when using mouse/keyboard for example).

So, only played about an hour; It was bad enough for me to realize this will *never* have it's problems fixed, which are really bad.
I enjoy the Dungeon Crawl aspect, the First-Person aspect, the simple equipment layout. All that is good.
It's the implementation of combat and in-town tasks.
In-town tasks are completely all text based and really lose you. None of the information feels relevant to what you're about to do. Simply; walk through dungeon until you find the item/complete the quest.  So, the long-winded story with clear signs that english isn't their first language, gets very boring (so, just click like crazy to get through these annoying segments).
The combat... you stop to do a normal swing. It's horrible. When you left click, your screen locks and movement locks and are forced to wait the animation, while everything else moves. Charging for spells or alt-attacks allows  you to move around. However, when you release the attack you are locked up for the attack animation. Which is way too slow.
I like the spell system; Old DnD style of memorized spells. That gets a thumbs up. The charging feature to cast spells is okay and feels well done.
You auto-pick up items from the mobs. Which initially is a moment of 'oh cool' but eventually I found myself desperately clicking at the bodies.
The world is very amateurish in quality. It feels like you're playing an alpha build of an indie game. The notable issues is like constantly leaks through walls, probably because they're so simply build. It basically looks like maps I built for Counter-Strike 1.6. It was dissapointly bad design.
With all that said; I'm not going to refund the game and hopes this will encourage the developers to hone their craft.

My favorite game is LSD. Although I usually refrain from comparing one game to another, I couldn't help but be reminded of it at the first one or two levels. Then it went way south.
Graphics:
The graphics are lovely, they're very dream like, as they are intended to be. It is apparent that a lot care was given to the asset choices/creation to maintain the dream like feel for so long.
Audio:
The first bit with the chicken was funny. Other than that the voices seemed out of place and I couldn't bring myself to care about what the voice was saying.
Cool Features:
If you explore long enough you'll see that there are invisible triggers that make pictures appear, that's pretty cool. I assume they are the developer and people important to him.
Overall:
The game was made by a caricature of an artist. If I had to put together a stereotypical artist personality, I'd probably end up with the developer. He had a brilliant thing going and ruined it for me by the constant 'woe is me' thread that was present throughout most of the game. The end especially had me rolling my eyes when he is talking to what I assume are the people at the college he applied to and made the game for. I appreciate emotional aspects in games, but didn't enjoy the way it was done here one bit. That is subjective though.
I enjoyed the first few levels, before it got too sappy and preachy. The concept was very nice and the trigger/picture feature was creative. I enjoyed the atmosphere of most of the levels. The assets were perfect for a dream like state. It reminded me of my favorite game for a few minutes, which was pleasant.
I would only recommend this game to someone who enjoys artistic games or people who develop games themselves, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone else. The game also has virtually no replayability, as it is linear and there is not a lot to explore.
I sincerely hope the developer continues to make games as I would love to see what he does in the future. If he drops the starving artistic hipster element to his games I would gladly play again.

Closing word: Only get if you're a glutton for punishment and don't mind dying hundreds of times before you complete even one quest.

This Game is honestly a bit of a dissapointment (probably more so if you got it for full price, I got it from a humble bundle). It looks like it should be a nice game, and while it does have its charm, but just not enough to make up for its flaws.
PROS:
-A number of artifacts, once you find one, you can choose to start with that artifact in any future game.
-A nice weapon/armor material system, silver weapons disarm foes, gold weapons give you stat bonuses occasionally, psychic weapons causes stat drain, among other things
-A couple of nice references to other (better) games in the form of some artifacts and uncommon rooms (such as an Aperture test chamber and I'm pretty sure I saw the castle crashers knights once)
-Despite not having an inventory (kind of a good thing, to be honest-it leads to less of the hoarding mentality many RPGs end up with) it does have a secondary weapon slot, and you can switch between the two easily, which I thought was a nice little feature.
CONS:
-Melee is awful-seriously, there's almost no reason to use it.
-combat is dull and repetetive (there's literally nothing beyond 'attack' and 'move')
-more than one or two friendly NPCs completely bog down the pace of the game
-Unlocking more characters seems to be completely random
-Death is frequent, not because the game is hard, but because healing is almost exclusively availible from random potions/scrolls/food (and the occasional vampiric weapon) and there's no garauntee you'll find anything that actually works well with your main combat stat. also poison is effectively incurable-if you can't survive until it passes on its own, you're dead.
While the game is flawed, it's still somewhat enjoyable if you stay away from the melee characters and the Battle for Stormrise quest. Playing as a Pixie Mage wearing plate armor and using a gun to shoot weapons out of your enemies hands is hard not to enjoy.

They should just rename this game to "Miss, Miss, Die", because that's the only thing that ever happens. This game is, in my opinion, a misunderstanding of the roguelike genre. The point and basic design behind classic roguelikes is that it's tough but fair - every decision matters and every situation is or should be winnable with good enough tactics. This game, however, is essentially just a slot machine with a cute fantasy theme and nice sprite graphics. Whether you win or die is entirely up to the randomization engine.
Will you survive and beat the quest? Depends on what loot you randomly find! There's no other way to level up, so it's all down to the loot. Will you survive the next fight? Depends on if your character suddenly feels like missing ten bloody times in a row! Essentially, your character in this game is the most useless warrior in existance. They can't even hit a mountain with a homing missile! Fights are tense, indeed, but not because the game is cleverly designed; simply because your useless character will just spend the entire fight missing their attacks.
Death in this game never, ever feels like it's your fault, because there is nothing you could've done. There is no room for strategy and enemies just come rushing at you, eating away at your health while your mentally disabled warrior keeps missing and missing. This game has very nice spritework, is nicely programmed and is generally well-crafted, but it is absolutely not fun or rewarding in any way. If you want to play some games of chance and see how lucky you are, hit up a casino instead.

I enjoy reading the old SCP archives, and the trailer sold me with it's light tone and art style. It's a good idea for a game, but this game doesn't quite deliver on the concept. The thrill of engaging with the unknown comes from discovery, but this game is more about maintenance. The interface is painfully unpolished, with critical info displayed in tiny text boxes, and recorded in a clunky log of mostly redundant records. The AI character acting as your adjutant spouts incessant reminders to pay non-specific attention to monsters' constantly deteriorating condition. This concept seems to be better suited to puzzle mechanics- a contemplative approach.

I actually liked this game quite a bit, though taking the fact I was a huge fan of SCP Containment Breech and the SCP franchise. This could be a bit of a bias but the game plays different from mose games I have been accustomed to. This in itself is a good thing and a bad thing about the game. As many before me had stated, this game is a lot of trial and error. Having to figure out that your guys could supress other agents was key information that was left out while other bits and pieces were similarly obscure ways of figuring out important game mechanics. I know this is due to being early access but this is a major warning. One UI problem I had was no clear way of examing all of my agents at a glance so I could tell who was doing what and there was no way to cancel their mission before the agent got there.
Another problem I had was there wasn't a whole lot of management outside of having your guys work with the abnormalities and observing them. There wasn't a whole lot of containing or progressing with them to the point where you could have your guys perform tests and such on them for bonus or negative effects. There is much that could be expanded upon here such as having specialized cells for the monsters or one could develop protocals to deal with said monster. One other Idea I had off the top of my head is perhaps being able to adjust what the agent is carrying, maybe have a few guys that carry around a tazer that is better at containing insane people running around your facility with a small chance to stun or pepper spray which would have a chance to stun any biologigcal abnomality or person with little physical damage. One thing that annoyed me was the regular people working in the facility will go mad and run around but there is no way to suppress or contain them so they sometimes attack my people or others.
One other large topic I would like to touch on is the story itself where the progression kind of halts in the middle of the creature. It feels imcomplete to cut off a monster at the end where you kind of file it away and don't care about it as much. Maybe the system should be more like a Sheet where each time an agent that fills in a important piece of critical information can placing it into a binder of where you can refer to all abnormatilies at a glance instead of having to dig through the UI.
One thing is certain that the game has a lot of room to grow which that makes me the most excited since the developers could take this even further and make it into a game that will have people coming back to it for more SCP type fun. With that eing said I hope the developers release the mod support so people could mod in their own monsters to make it feel like the 2000+ SCP we all know and love.

I feel like I can recommend this game again.  Early on it became a favorite of mine.  I even wrote a guide early on.  Then, they introduced some patches which just made the game horrible to play.  In particular there were some mechanics introduced which punished the player for pausing the game and trying to play strategically while simultaneously making the facility bigger.  They also brought in a bunch of abnormalities which were almost impossible to keep contained, or at least were incredibly tedious to do so.
The devs did a major re-design of the game, and now it feels very different.  When they first did it, the game seemed extremely hard, and I didn't enjoy it, but I went back to trying it periodically since they had fixed the biggest problems.  The chief thing here is that the game no longer punishes you for playing strategically, and there are no longer abnormalities which require a combination of incredibly precise timing and luck to keep contained.
I find now that the game works again.  I still sort of prefer the earliest versions of the game, but what it is right now is leaps and bounds better than when I soured on the game originally.  It still feels like it needs work, but it is getting to be fun to play again.
In some ways the game has even improved over the original I used to love.  You can now move employees around manually allowing for more strategic combat.  There are a lot of interesting abnormalities which didn't exist before.
So, I am switching back to recommending the game.  It isn't a favorite like it once was, but I find that I can enjoy it again.

Part roguelike, part JRPG, One Way Heroics is an hybrid game that should please many people.
The game tasks you to keep moving forward (from left to right) in a world that is randomly generated, to become stronger and stronger, until you're finally able to save the world by defeating the Evil Lord responsible for the Darkness invading from the left.
But contrary to pure roguelikes, a failure doesn't mean you lose everything : when you finish a game (regardless of whether it was a success or not), you can save some items from your inventory into a "Dimensional Vault". The vault allow your next heroes to grab the items from them, and thus start a new game with powerful equipments right from the start. With this system, you can soon have starting heroes that are extremely powerful.
Moreover, since this is an hybrid JRPG, there is a lot more story in this game than there is in a typical roguelike. During each of your travels, you may find some new locations or characters, and this will help you better understand what is exactly happening to the world, as well as unlocking new places, storylines and endings. This helps alleviates one of the problems of roguelikes which is that they sometimes feel like you're doing the same thing over and over again.
The gameplay itself is nice, with many items, skills, and classes that allow for different approaches to combat. It's turn-based, with positioning being an important part of the combat system. If you're lucky, you might later be able to expand your party, and have companions help you on your quests, which add more tactical options. Once again, this is a nice difference to classic roguelikes where you're usually all alone all the time.
Another good point for the game is that it should please a large number of RPG or roguelike fans. It has 4 different difficulty levels and you also have the option to turn off the Dimensional Vault as you wish. This mean that casual players will enjoy being able to finish the game on Easy and Normal, while Roguelike veterans will get the challenge they are looking for by playing harder difficulties, without the help of the vault.
On the whole, I really enjoy One Way Heroics. It offers me some interesting challenges, but somehow, it also feel like a relaxing game, because you're all alone in the vast open country (contrary to many roguelikes who prefer claustrophobic dungeons). It's a very nice game to both unwind, and also get my brain working hard, depending on which difficulty i play on. And i keep coming back to it, because there is a lot of secrets that i have yet to find and classes i have yet to finish the game with.

A fast-paced, unique and quirky "rogue-lite." One Way Heroics does away with the traditional floor-by-floor navigation of the genre in favor of a love it or hate it gimmick where the screen continiously scrolls to the right with certain death awaiting you if you fail to outrun the approaching darkness! The result is a frantic scramble for survival with the clock ticking down to your inevitable clash with the Demon King.
Far less lengthy than your average roguelike, OWH is designed to be played (and cleared) many times with a plethora of unlockables, performance evaluations and limited online capabilities providing incentive to keep coming back for more even after you've trounced the Demon King.
What OWH lacks in complexity, it makes up for with a host of novel features atypical of the roguelike genre as well as being surprisingly easy to pick up. Presentation is great too with pleasant music and charming SNES-era graphics as well as a responsive and smooth (but also cluttered) UI.
Concerning flaws: There aren't many as long as you're not expecting a traditional roguelike! As mentioned before, the UI can come off a bit cluttered. Luck/RNG plays a tremendous role in your success as usual for the genre and it can be difficult to impossible to mitigate a bad hand that you've been dealt. The forced march style of gameplay definitely will not appeal to everyone and the cutesy-weird anime style might be a deal breaker to some.
If you want to play a proper strategy game, don't look further.

This is not the prettiest game you'll find on Steam. It's not the fastest or most fluid. The translation is a little off in places (for example, the 'yes' and 'no' buttons in the store are in kanji). Even so, I still cannot recommend this game enough. Maybe it's because King's Field held a place in my heart during the PSX era, I dunno, but this game really feels a lot like it, and as far as I'm concerned that's high praise. In short, if you enjoy medieval dungeon crawls, if you like collecting loot, if you just enjoy smacking goblins in the face with a sword from a first person view, you will enjoy this game.

It's important to note that this game is not about to be winning any awards for it's graphics, musical score or story. But that's not why we play dungeon crawl games, now is it?
The gameplay mechanics are smooth, though the menu button was an odd choice. Once you know that the ESC button does nothing, and that the pause/inventory button is the "i" button, you're golden.
Graphics-wise, the game is nothing to write home about. The textures and lighting are quite nice, but monsters are barely a step above what you would find on the N64.
The musical score is hardly memorable, but unlike a lot of dungeon crawlers I've played it doesn't work to set you on edge. Personally I much prefer the relaxed nature of the background music.
There's actually more story than I expected going in, but the story was clearly written entirely with the intention to give you an excuse to dive into a dungeon to find treasure and kill monsters. That's fine, that's why we want this game, right?
Put simply:
Do not buy this game if you cannot stand older graphics.
Do not buy this game if you need heart-pounding action music.
Do not buy this game is you want a videogame storybook.
DO buy this game if you like diving into dank places in search of treasure.
DO buy this game if you enjoy slashing monsters to bits.

Dungeons and Darkness:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

All daredevils are looking for exciting sites full of challenges.  If you are one of these people who are seeking quests, treasures and fighting daring foe, do not look further! This world is full of dungeons and enemies, but mostly full of goodies! This is the place to explore . . . this is “Dungeons and Darkness!”
Dungeons and Darkness is a First Person/Action/ Adventure game where you are exploring daring dungeons. First, you will have to decide which class you are going to be. Will you be a Knight, a Fighter, a Mage or a Rogue? After choosing your character class, it will be time to select the difficulty. Normal is probably the best for new players, and hard for experienced dungeon hunters!
Shortly afterwards, you will be looking at the town market. From here, five tabs will be available to you:  the tavern, dungeon, inn, collector and tool shop. To find quests, talk to people in the tavern. The Inn is where you can upgrade your skill, save your game and also furnish your room with items you either find in the dungeons or purchase at the tool shop. The interesting thing is that whatever you add to this room will give you additional skills points. The tool shop is where you can purchase helpful items (health potions, furniture’s and more).
The tavern is where you are going to seek and accept quests. After accepting, just click on the dungeon tab and the fun will begin! As you move into the dungeon, you will quickly realise that  there is no map to show you where to go. Follow the blue torches and they will lead you to your objective. Through the dungeons, you will encounter orcs, sand slims, dragons, Skeletons, Zombies and other foe. In your first dungeon, you will be equipped with a standard sword and shield. As you go through the dungeons, you will find treasure chests which will hold interesting items, such as armours, new weapons (melee and range), potions and more. However, some chests will give you a bit of a fight and will show you some nasty teeth! It caught me by surprise a few times. Some chests will have a riddle for you to figure out before it opens itself. You will have access to magic, traps and great weapons to achieve each of your quests!
When you have successfully completed your quest, open your inventory and click “return to town” to collect your reward.
The fighting can be a bit awkward at first but it is easy to master. I really like the combination of hitting an enemy with a shield to stun him first, and then slashing him with a might sword - just spectacular! I think the animation, especially the enemies coming towards you, could have been better. However, this game is truly enjoyable!
The graphics are good,  and in terms of controls, I would strongly recommend using the mouse and keyboard. You can use a gamepad if you wish.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Plenty of weapons and items to loot
-	Good graphics
-	Different types of enemies
-	Good dungeons
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No map available
-	Animations could have been better
Do you enjoy exploring, defeating enemies and looting treasures in dungeons? Dungeons and Darkness should definitely have its place in your game library!
7/10

Despite its charmingly minimalist presentation, Hack, Slash, Loot takes simplicity a bit too far, resulting in a game where player choice carries exceedingly little weight against the overwhelming tides of chance.
Presented as a simplification of the Roguelike genre, Hack, Slash, Loot endeavors to be a casual, bite-sized dose of turn-based dungeon crawling goodness. Toning things down from more classical entries to the series like NetHack or the more recent Dungeons of Dredmor, players are relieved of such responsibilities as developing character skills, managing an inventory, or generally deciding what action to take at any given time, provided those actions might have been anything other than moving in a particular cardinal direction or performing a generic attack on an enemy.
The final product is a game where painstakingly small decisions such as what equipment you've chosen to pick up and wear will be most input the player has on each adventure's outcome, and even then, it won't quite measure up to the significance of what items and enemies the game decided to spawn in the first place.
Ultimately, the prognosis for each freshly-rolled adventurer is about the same as in any other hardcore roguelike- anything but the most carefully chosen actions will invariably end in your character's death, and odds are the right choices will still probably see you winding up dead sooner or later anyway. The difference between the two is that in a deeper Roguelike experience, you will likely have had more than a few memorable close calls where gambling on an unconventional action pays off in a few minutes of continued survival, or enjoyed the unique experience of mixing and matching talents to come up with a wholly one-of-a-kind adventurer whose inevitable death was a mere period a the end of an entirely unexpected story. In contrast, Hack, Slash, Loot will take every bit as much persistence and consideration to advance in, while completely failing to pay off in any sort of fun factor beyond trading genericized blows with enemies and crossing your fingers that the sword you found in the previous room will give you enough of a numerical advantage to be the last man standing.
To put it simply, Hack, Slash, Loot mistakes simplified graphics and gameplay for a pleasingly simplified gaming experience, while instead only succeeding in creating a dreadfully boring one that actively resists being played in a remotely engaging way compared to the sorts of games it seeks to emulate.
The final nail in the coffin is the pricetag, which at the time of this review exceeds vastly more playable and equally casual-friendly Steam roguelikes such as Dungeons of Dredmor and Tales of Maj'eyal, either of which is perfectly content to kill you every bit as quickly, while affording a comparatively staggering array of options with which to actually enjoy your brief life.
The bottom line is that fans of the genre and newcomers alike will do well to look elsewhere. Hack, Slash, Loot may be charming to look at, but there's barely a game here to play, and it just isn't worth the time.

UPDATE:  So far so good!
OK so i am very much a completionist--thus i am reading and talking to anyone and everyone in game so my progress might be a little slow.
So far though?  AMAZING!  If you love Shadowrun, then you have come to the right place.  As the games go (Shadowrun Returns or Dragonfall) This is the obvious evolution.  All the polish you saw in the directors cut of Dragonfall is here and it shines like a new set of chrome arms.
The story is engaging, each character--from your fellow runners to random people you chat with on teh streats has their own personality.  It really makes the world feel alive.
As gameplay elements go, the Matrix has been redesigned.  Even with modern hacking--the goal is to avoid/supress the defenses of the system you are hacking.  This element was completely absent in previous iterations of the Matrix (SRR and DF)
This new matrix is totally awsome--you could jsut run in there and fight through---but with a little skill you can avoid it altogether!  On top of that, there are new hacking mini-games that add some flavor to trying to get that paydata.  overall i am very impressed--kinda wish i rolled a decker now.
Anyways, the game continues--I just got 3 jobs and am about to head off
See you in the shadows, chummers!  more to come as i get through it...
UPDATE:  ok--been playing for many hours now and i can safely say that the game is great.  As stated before, the writing is top notch---and it really shines through in every character you meet.  I find myself wanting MORE from each character--they each have thier own backstory that really tugs your interest.
Also, the game time i have?  I haven't even made it through the first 3 "side" missions you get.  And no i haven't just left the game open.  There have been a few re-loads (matrix runs are much more challenging when you get caught...) but a lot of the time is spent just reading--there is SO much lore in this game and each of your fellow runners seems to have a full range of dialogue to flesh it out.
So to sum up--if you like Shadowrun and/or old school RPG's (i guess the official term is cRPG?) then this is the game for you.

In LISA, you have no choice but to play a battered man on the brink of sanity and follow the dark and twisted passages of your rotting, disheveled mind coming to grips with a disgusting future that leads you to make horrible, unavoidable decisions.
If you want a memorable, uncomfortable experience that will leave you delighted and disturbed at the same time, play this game. It was clearly made with by someone with love and dedication to the player's experience... or maybe an A.I. just got ahold of Earthbound and Videodrome.

Too expensive and too weird - and not in a flattering kind of way.
While this game is very fresh and has certainly never been done before, I questioned nearly every design decision in it. I did refund simply because it is in no-way-shape-or-form worth the high asking price right now.
Ok, so how do I start explaining this. First off, it is *not* a roguelike. Not even close. It is also *not* a management simulator.  You don't place rooms or mess with the structure at all. You don't manage anything in the traditional sense. The core gameplay involves starting with an unknown monster ('abnormality') and uncovering information about it, and most importantly, what icon to click ('management style') to get it to give you energy. Rinse and repeat for every monster. The information you find out never goes away between games. I suppose that part is what they tout as permadeath, but really it just means there are no continues.
+By all means, it is a fresh new idea.
-English translation is laughable (no seriously, I lol'd several times); in fact the poor translation makes things quite confusing too.
-I think the game is too confusing for its own good. Above I said this isn't a mangement sim - you don't really even need graphics.
You can't click most of them, and you certainly don't place anything. The same end-means mechanic could have been accomplished by much simpler means. I could go on and on.
-In the end, I figured out 'how to play', but you will spend a good bit of time pouring over the help file. Between the poor translation and non-intuitive gameplay, things are just confusing. I mean, you are trying to 'get energy' from monsters by doing weird stuff. The monsters could be a naked lady, a pair of shoes, or even an old lady. Too weird.
-The AI text in-between levels seems meaningless, and could just be left out.
-Why-oh-why do they space out the functional rooms (ie. monster rooms) so far apart?? It's insane. Did nobody playtest this? So, you have to have the screen waayyyy zoomed out to see two rooms, and therefore you have to squint to read any text, and can barely make out what is going on in the room. This gives me the impression that it doesn't matter what is really going on in the rooms. FYI I play from the couch on a large tv.
-Twenty dollars is an insane asking price.
Too weird and rough around the edges for the high asking price.

Think a mix of Lab of the Dead ( A game where you experiment on zombies to get reactions out of them) Fallout Shelter (The Base layout that is) and the character visual design of Don't Starve.
The game has a LOT of fun ideas in it. You are the manager at the Lobotomy Corp, which extracts energy from 'abnormalities' by putting them in a certain kind of mood. The trouble is, the abnormalities range from helpful to your staff if treated right, to...game ending horrors.
The most enjoyable part of the game is discovering what each of the abnormalities do. From the Shoes to the Teddy Bear to even the cross skull (god I love that one), it is a sickening thrill to send in an agent to see if they get killed...if they are lucky. SCP Foundation and Cabin in the Woods inspired the developers, but they have managed to create characters that feel fresh and interesting. Beauty and The Beast is one that makes me feel rather sad and disgusted.
However, an issue I have with the game is how unsure of itself it is. In that the idea that your motivation is...collecting energy instead of trying to figure out what these things are. Lab of the Dead had a convincing motivation (you are trying to figure out how the zombies work to develop a vaccine/cure), and SCP Foundation it is more about protecting both the abnormalities as well as the world in general. Now, a cynical game about collecting energy from abnormalities is fine, It's that it's too vague about the application of said energy or even what is outside of the base. If the game was kind of like X-Com where you send agents out to collect Abnormaltiies, that would be an incredible way to justify the use of energy as well as give the player an incentive to learn more about the world.
It also feels unfinished in a way that doesn't make a $20.00 price point seem justifiable. The game doesn't loop music in a natural way, the sprites tend to run and bump into each other, there are a lot of grammer mistakes as well as just...it feels more like a flash game on Newsgrounds.
Would I reccomend this game: NOT YET.
Give this game more time to actually justify the 20.00 price. If you feel that you want to keep the game a mystery, then you should wait till it is released. Otherwise, it is a game that needs a clear motivation for the player and a way to use Energy.

Heavily focused on storyline and action packed game with great attention to detail, which you do not want to miss on.
What can you expect from Mafia II? Beautifully crafted city to experience, '40-50s atmosphere delivered by music, clothing, guns, cars and rest of the visuals overall, well done driving mechanics, where every car handles differently along with the same feeling when it comes to shooting from a variety of guns.
There are so many tiny details, which make the experience even more rewarding, like: driving on a red light can trigger nerby police patrols to start a chase after you, if you drive car long enough it can run out of fuel, no more "every car is open and ready to go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" or packing two magazines of bullets into enemies, before they fall down. It's really easy to immerse into the world.
Strongest point of the game is without a doubt - its plot. Without spoilering anything - life in a family isn't as colorful as one would expect. One day you are rich and without any worries about tommorow, when suddenly you are left out on a street the next day. Story of Vito Scaletta goes through all of the shades, from white to black and all the way around again. You need to remember that being a member of the family has its own set of rules and responsibilities, and all in all - it's like walking on rope. Remember, everything is just a buisness.
Great cutscenes with beautifuly animated characters supports told story strongly.
I can't really put a finger on anything to be honest. If I've really wanted to find any flaws - that would be probably enemies' AI, who sometimes acted really out of place (like running straight on you for no reason), but for the most of the time it wasn't a case.
One thing I would wish for (even though whole package was complete) were moments where you had to make a certain choice. During the game there were more than a few moments which could be resolved by an ablity to decide about their outcome - choosing one or the other way to deal out with the problem at hand. Would call it a perfect game then.
My verdict? This comes as close to a 10/10 as it gets, but since some minor things could be improved 9.5/10 for overall experience.
P.S. Oh, did I mention the collectibles? Gotta find them all Playboy magazines!

I can't say this game is bad, but I can't say it's very fun.
The biggest problem this game has is its simplicity, in that there is no strategy to the game. Combat is just "click the enemy until it dies", and it becomes aggravating when enemies are swarming you and you can only deal with one at a time because all you have is just one attack and nothing else, no special abilities or anything, and it's also aggravating how often you miss even with high accuracy. There's a lot of characters to unlock, but there really isn't much of a point to picking anyone because there's virtually nothing to make each character special, save for cosmetics. The only real exception to this is the Amazon, since she starts with a weapon that can boost stats or health when you score kills, and I guarantee anyone who played this game never really used anyone other than the Amazon once they unlocked her.
As for the gameplay itself, once again the game's simplicity is what ruins the experience. There's no inventory or skill/magic/whatever system, which contributes to the lack of strategy (no having to strategize what items you want to keep, what skills you want to learn, etc.), and you end up praying the game is kind enough to give you some way to heal because you will constantly die. I understand that as a roguelike, this game is meant to be challenging, but when you literally begin the game surrounded by enemies and die just like that...well, that's not a challenge, is it? And unlike other roguelikes, where you would be motivated to keep trying, to see if you can get further, this game gives you no such motivation. There's nothing to make you keep playing this game, nothing to make you want to see how it ends. It just feels tedious and boring and not fun, and if a game fails to be fun, it has failed at what it has set out to do.
In conclusion, Hack Slash Loot isn't a fun game. It's boring, tedious, and in my opinion doesn't understand what makes roguelikes work. If you want a fun modern roguelike, I suggest Dungeons of Dredmor, The Binding of Isaac, Teleglitch, and Sword of the Stars: The Pit, as each are entertaining and fun in their own way. Don't bother playing this game.

The core of a roguelike is to slowly understand a world and its rules so that you may perform better and achieve greater successes, getting further and learning even more. Hack, Slash, Loot teaches you nothing about the little there is to learn and throws you into scenarios where nothing can be done or improved upon almost every single time.
The solutions are so simple - yet every single moment you'll suffer the pain of knowing anything that could solve it, make this game actually enjoyable, was simply not implemented. On top of that, the assets used are mostly recycled, and whatever was made from scratch is absolutely simple, yet confusingly "introduced".
Very disappointing.

The developers' primary language isn't English, this game was originally demo'd in Korean so there are going to be some slight grammatical errors here and there. They aren't severe enough to really detract from the game though.
Lobotomy Corp is best described as a management / simulation game with perma-death. You're assigned as the administrator of a facility hosting
Abnormalities. Lobotomy Corp has developed technology to harvest "energy" from these Abnormalities as a saving grace for humanity. Sounds easy right? Well, not really.
Every Abnormality is unique and has its own fully fleshed out character. But, just like SCPs, Abnormalities can wreak havoc given the chance. As the administrator, not only is it your job to keep these Abnormalities happy, but it's also your job to keep your employees safe. Easier said than done, every employee comes with an array of stats that will detail how effectively and efficiently they can perform their job; whether their job be feeding an Abnormality or caving the head in of one of their fellow employees.
The game itself doesn't give you much to go on in determining exactly how to handle Abnormalities which does make the game a tad more difficult (i.e. what exactly having an employee perform a "consesus" with an Abnormality actually does). There's also several mechanics in the game that are left unexplained and up to the player to figure out. It's a bit intuitive and there's a bit of a learning curve.
Progression for story mode is divided into "days" with each day becoming progressively harder as new challenges continue to be added for the administrator to handle. At the start of each day you're allotted a number of employees who you can assign to each section of the facility to perform tasks for the abnormalities in that area. This adds an element of strategy to the game as the player is forced to divvy up exactly who he wants where to match the preferences of the Abnormalities, etc.
To actually complete a day, players are required to (at least in the early days) harvest a specific amount of energy from the Abnormalities in the facility. This is done by keeping all of the abnormalities in a good mood. Likewise, abnormalities in a terrible mood will also detract energy from the gauge, along with going berserk on the employees.
The game is fairly straightforward with a slight undertone of complexity which makes for a very interesting game overall. To add, the story also presents itself through the administrator's accompanying AI who drafts notes and details logs about ongoing events throughout the facility.
I'd definitely recommend buying this game if you're interested in management / simulation games. I haven't had any performance issues though that's likely because the game is a smaller management game produced in Unity.
I'd also highly encourage fans of SCP to check the game out.

I wish I knew what my actual playtime is on this one, but because I've been launching the patched .exe outside of Steam, it hasn't kept track.  I'd say 20-30 hours for my first full playthrough.
You can read all about this games developement woes, and the very talented people who worked on it somewhere else.  Suffice it to say this game was pushed to the shelves in an unfinished but playable state, right before Troika Games went out of business.  Fortunately the game gained enough of a following to establish a good modding community. If you're going to play it, the first thing you need to do is read the configuration guides, and
Once you have it running without issues, there's further mods that finish and restore large amounts of cut content, as well as graphics mods that make the game look much better.
Video games can never truly recreate the amount of freedom players have in the old table-top, pen and paper RPGs, but every once in a while, a CRPG comes along that captures the appeal and world-building that keeps people playing those old games.  This is one of them.  Prior knowledge of White Wolf's World of Darkness setting is not required to enjoy the game.
Graphics aren't bad, for this game's time.  Models and textures are good enough to get their point across and help lend a sense of atmosphere.  Animations look pretty terrible.  Bodies bend in the wrong places. The main character's sneaking animation belongs in the Ministry of Silly Walks.  The way enemies will suddenly spin their torso around to look right at you, while their legs still point forward, when you fail a stealth check, will haunt my dreams.
Audio is notably good.  For the most part, the voice acting is top quality.  Occasionally a character sounds like their actor phoned it in, but this game is full of memorable dialogue.  If you're playing with good quality headphones, during stealth scenes you can accurately tell where enemy patrols are from the sound of their footsteps.  There's a lot of audio cues to pick up on, like ringing phones, heavy breathing or groaning from hidden characters, and sounds of things breaking. Sometimes the game does get a bit disorienting with ambient city sounds coming from walls and the ceiling.
Storytelling and atmosphere are where the game really stands out.  The story is full of twists and turns, as everyone the main character meets has their own agenda backed by centuries of planning.  The game world feels alive, and full of atmosphere, with many genuinely suspenseful scenes.  There's also a fair amount of humor and satire.
Gameplay requires a balance of combat, diplomacy, and stealth.  This isn't Fallout 1, where every quest had three different ways to finish it, although it often feels like they cut some alternate solutions due to time constraints.
Combat seems deceptively straight forward.  At first it looks like you put your crosshair over the thing you want to hit, and press the attack button, like every other first/third person game.  However, lining up the hit boxes isn't enough.  behind the scenes, the game is doing calculations based on offense and defense stats to determine hits, misses, blocks, knockdowns, glancing hits, and stuff.  One thing the tutorial doesn't tell you is spamming the same melee attack over and over puts enemies into kind of a perma-blocking state.  Early on, when you don't have a lot of points in combat skills, your character feels like a helpless, flailing spaz.   Late in the game, the combat merely feels clunky, instead of completely broken.  Overall, combat is not fun.  Fortunately, you can cheese your way through most combat heavy areas relying entirely on stealthy instakills.  There's also a few cool boss fights.
Stealth feels similarly awkward due to random numbers. Being right in the enemies field of vision only gives them a percentage chance to notice you,  This leads to enemies detecting you when it seems like they shouldn't, or not detecting you when you're literally stealth-killing their buddy right in front of them.  Also the enemy AI has kind of a hive mind.  While one of them can see you, every one of them on the map can see you.
Diplomacy is very well done with skill checks for persuasion, intimidation, seduction, and mind control powers.  Good old fashioned politeness also goes a long way.  Dialogue trees tend to be lengthy with lots of lore to uncover.  There are some parts where it feels like a lot of dialogue was cut or left unfinished.
Replayablility is okay, but could have been a lot better.  Of the seven playable varieties of vampire, only two substantially alter the gameplay.  There's the insane Malkavians, who hallucinate, hear voices, and speak in a mix of riddle, metaphor, allegory, and utter nonsense.  Everyone should play Malkavian on their second playthrough, because they're hilarious.  Then there's the Nosferatu who are too ugly to pass for human and have to be extra stealthy.  Then there's four major factions in the game, but for the majority of the game, you're railroaded into working for one guy.  You don't get to pick a side until you're on your way to the last two missions, so all that really changes is the ending.  I also recommend finding mods for subsequent playthroughs.
Controls are meant for mouse and full-sized keyboard.  This game is from that golden age when devs still made real PC games, instead of just porting console games.  I'm not bitter.  Much.

Trials Evolution Gold Review:
If you have ever used a flash game site, chances are you would have played Trial Bike at least once. Trial Bike was the game that was fun to fail at just to see those amusing ragdoll physics. Besides that, it consisted of the player attempting to get their rider across a two dimensional course. Trials Evolution is merely an extension of this experience, but in a much more polished and intriguing format.

There are two modes; career, as well as online and local multiplayer, all of which have a level of depth that was not realized in the free yet fun to play Trial Bike. Career mode sees your rider climb the tiers of your motorcycle licencing system by running test courses for D, C, B, and A class licences respectively. After you complete a licence, you get to participate in a series of tracks that will test the skills you’ve learned while progressing through your licences. These tracks range from beautiful back country vistas to more classic settings like warehouses and construction sites, each are beautiful in their own way. The game has just built on the foundation that its predecessor has laid, not losing its identity along the way. The level of fun you will have while playing Trials evolution are doubled from Trial Bike, with the inclusion of stellar graphics, a fitting heavy alternative rock sound track, and a deep level of rider and bike customisation. You can also play player modded tracks that can often offer a higher level of challenge. Another thing that is charming in its own way is the way that your rider will shout “YEEEEEEAAAAAAHHHHH!” and exclaims in other ways that’ll put a smile on your face while you pull off big airs and flips.
Trials Evolution Gold Edition on the pc is a dream both visually and in terms of playability. Keyboard and gamepad work perfectly, and it’s likely that you’ll be maxing out all the graphical bells and whistles while maintaining at least sixty frames per second on a decent rig. I played a lot of old LucasArts games as a kid and fell out of point and click adventures by and large after that. I found a lot of them were either lacking a functionality I wanted, or the soul and humor I craved.
This game has both.
The game lays out its general type of humor and narrative style pretty early on, so if you find it's irritating you you'll know quickly and can back out easily. That's one of the great parts about it - this game plays its cards early on and manages to keep up the momentum throughout.
Two of the best functionalities for me were that I could click through dialogue and also skip puzzles if I wanted. I don't really want to listen to the weeaboo girls yell "shing" back and for twenty seconds, nor did all the puzzles seem to be explained adequately. While that in and of itself is a con, the fact that I can skip with no problem helps to not take the wind out of your sails completely at any one point.
I played this game before The Breakout and in short, I can say it's doable. There's a lot of character and location cameos, but I never really felt 100% in the dark. This game has the ability to stand alone (although I did go and play the first one which helped to explain a lot of easter eggs).
It's relatively short for the full price tag, but I don't think point and click fans would really regret their choice nor do I think anyone would be too disappointed by it for a sale price. It's worth it.

I really enjoyed this game and would definitely recommend it to anyone who is into puzzle, humour, or a bit of rpg. The game lures you in with it's child-ish graphics, but quickly drags you into a world of censored death scenes and lots of pink paint. My only regret was not playing The Breakout beforehand.
Pros:
- The game's humour isn't repetitive but had a nice dark twist
- After the recent update, switching between screens was much faster (the double click method works in the beginning too)
- The puzzles weren't too difficult, I only needed the walkthrough for the glyphs
- Storyline was good, the ending (no spoilers) was a nice twist :)
- The art style and color pallette was a nice reminder of Lilli's 'innocent' mindset
- The voice overs were well done
- speedthroughs were easy as long as you can click very fast
Cons:
There were a LOT of bugs in this game before the recent update, I'm not sure how many were fixed but here's what I noticed:
- The menus and save files sometimes took a long time to load, it also took me a while to figure out which keys were for settings and saves
- The esc, 5, and 7 button didn't always work, sometimes you had to repeatedly press the button to trigger it
- There was another bug where if you had the inventory open and moved to another room, the items would still appear, but the inventory background would be invisible
- If you had the brush with honey and moved from the leaf raking room to the swing tree, you couldn't double click into the next room
- Sometimes the inventory/restrictions page didn't show, I had to move back and forth between rooms to be able to trigger it
Non Bug related:
- The instructions for the puzzles could be a bit confusing
- There was minimal characterization for Lilli, even though we follow allong with her through the whole story, we only know her as a quiet and obedient child. This might be a pro if this is what the creater wanted her to be portrayed as.
Even though it's a bit buggy, it's definitely a hidden gem you should play :)

Heavily focused on storyline and action packed game with great attention to detail, which you do not want to miss on.
What can you expect from Mafia II? Beautifully crafted city to experience, '40-50s atmosphere delivered by music, clothing, guns, cars and rest of the visuals overall, well done driving mechanics, where every car handles differently along with the same feeling when it comes to shooting from a variety of guns.
There are so many tiny details, which make the experience even more rewarding, like: driving on a red light can trigger nerby police patrols to start a chase after you, if you drive car long enough it can run out of fuel, no more "every car is open and ready to go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" or packing two magazines of bullets into enemies, before they fall down. It's really easy to immerse into the world.
Strongest point of the game is without a doubt - its plot. Without spoilering anything - life in a family isn't as colorful as one would expect. One day you are rich and without any worries about tommorow, when suddenly you are left out on a street the next day. Story of Vito Scaletta goes through all of the shades, from white to black and all the way around again. You need to remember that being a member of the family has its own set of rules and responsibilities, and all in all - it's like walking on rope. Remember, everything is just a buisness.
Great cutscenes with beautifuly animated characters supports told story strongly.
I can't really put a finger on anything to be honest. If I've really wanted to find any flaws - that would be probably enemies' AI, who sometimes acted really out of place (like running straight on you for no reason), but for the most of the time it wasn't a case.
One thing I would wish for (even though whole package was complete) were moments where you had to make a certain choice. During the game there were more than a few moments which could be resolved by an ablity to decide about their outcome - choosing one or the other way to deal out with the problem at hand. Would call it a perfect game then.
My verdict? This comes as close to a 10/10 as it gets, but since some minor things could be improved 9.5/10 for overall experience.
P.S. Oh, did I mention the collectibles? Gotta find them all Playboy magazines!

Mafia II has a charming 1940s twist to the sandbox style of GTA games. Though similar in many aspects, it's well worth a play through for those details that make it standout amongst it's like.
Visually, it's nothing bad, but nothing great. The style and colour palette work well with the time period. Initially, you start off in the fictional city of Empire Bay. You return from the war to a city blanketed by snow. The landscape is rather bleak at first sight, but primary colours burst out in the form of neon signs or even carlights to counteract it from being too bleak. Slowly as the story, and year(s) progress, you see a change in seasons. The city has much more sunlight and colours are abound. I really enjoyed the art direction 2K Czech took, and I think it worked execellently. It wasn't overly realistic, but just enough so that it didn't turn into something too fake looking.
Gameplay wise is where this game starts to fail. There's a distinct lack of polish in the various mechanics. Shooting is a solid cover based affair. Not bad, but not exactly inspiring. Driving felt incredibly sluggish. Until you get the higher tier cars, driving feels very heavy, slow and ultimately boring to actually do. The episodic structure works well for the story, but it really does ruin it for the flow of the game. Especially towards the end
The side missions are boring and tedious, in particular the collectables (which every sandbox feels like it needs to have to artifically extend game time) are a grind even moreso since some of them can only be picked up within specific story moments. However, picklocking was entertaining to do personally, even though it's pretty much exactly the same as Sleeping Dogs, it felt realistic and tension you had while doing it was fantastic.
The game features a wonderful story which draws from many of the classical gangster films. The Godfather trilogy in particular has numerous parallels and references hidden within the story of Mafia II. Though it doesn't depend on it as a crtuch. By itself, it's an engaging and worthwhile story of the rise of Vito Scalletta, a Sicilian immigrant who rises amongst the ranks of the Mafia in Empire Bay. Mafia II also features a variety of licensed music from the 40s era, which add to the atmosphere but isn't really noteworthy in of itself.
I'd seriously recommend this game to anyone who wants to play a GTA-style sandbox in an interesting setting with a good story. Though it suffers from a distinct lack of polish and mediocre gameplay, the story and setting are well worth playing this game for.

I was doing so well... I evaded asteroids and solar flares (after a few false starts and, er, stops). I took down scummy pirates and lurking drones. I upgraded my ship's mighty shields, and laughed as enemy fire skipped harmlessly off of them. I helped out those in need and put paid to those who were preying on the weak. Just doing my small bit to maintain order in the galaxy, folks.
I must've missed a "last chance for gas" sign at that last outpost, though... I got a bit too generous helping out a stranded ship, took a wrong turn at the Ohek Nebula, and ended up stranded myself. Adrift in the vastness of space, I watched the advancing enemy front loom near on my ship's sensors. I could only watch and curse their unknown names as they spotted me, and mashed my glorious vessel like a gnat.
I mourned for a moment, then hit Restart. :)
Getting serious:
I'm enjoying this game. Playing FTL reminds me a bit of playing UnReal World, in the sense that little stories build up in my mind around the characters' (and ships') progress through the game. Also in the sense of "get used to getting dead a lot and starting over", especially at first, and while learning how best to use new ships as you unlock them. Random generation of playthroughs means that the dreaded RNG can give with both hands, or turn and sting like a stepped-on nest of wasps, without being so harsh or time-and-effort intensive as to suck the fun out of it for me.
The keyboard controls are pretty simple and can be remapped in game options, or you can mouse a lot of it. The game can be paused so your next combat move (or a bio break) can be considered without rushing. Setup of a new game is quick, and if you don't want to change your initial ship selection after the end of a game, you can Restart after your ship's demise. This will start a new game immediately on a new randomly generated map, with the same starting ship setup and starting crew you had last time. That's been a really nice feature.
I wanted a fun little game that wouldn't take up much system power while multitasking, and this ended up being ideal.

This game is more like a simple version of Star Trek.  You command a small crew, which can grow by recruiting through different means other characters of different races.  Your ship has different components needed to travel and fight against other ships.
The weapons vary and can be useful if you know how to deploy them.  For example, the Ion weapon does not cause damage but can disrupt an enemy system.  Target their shields and let a Combat Droid damage their ship.
This game does play hard ball, even in Easy mode.  Your choices feel like it can be 50/50.  Should you help the ailing ship?  Do so and you can be ambushed.  While I do not mind this, what I do mind are the other choices that may cost me a member of my crew in this game.  Replacing them is often difficult.
The biggest draw for me with this game is you constantly want to see what the next star system has.  Will it be a pirate vessel waiting to attack you?  Will it be an ailing Federation ship that has a person inside who will join your crew?  You constantly want to keep playing to see.

I am not normally one for writing reviews but this is one of those games that stands out as one of the all time greats. I picked it up when it first came out and enjoyed it then. Now I have picked it up again and have found it as immersive as ever. Even from the beginning I really enjoy guiding the questions towards the clan that I want. I know you can just pick but you don't get the same thrill.
The dialogue is fantastic and every choice you make has real consequences to the game. I have a special place in my heart for the Malkavians. The dialogue absolutely sings when you are a member of that clan. It dances that line between insanity and genius so well. You only understand half of whats being said as you randomly pluck insights about characters and the future from the air, but the clever thing is you know your character feels exactly the same.
The special vampire abilities promote very different playing styles  which makes you want to play it many times over, sometimes through dialogue options, other times by sneaking and hiding, or brute forcing your way through. The story is exceptional, alluding to the larger vampire world while keeping everything personal. The atmosphere and music make your hair stand on end at some points, especially when you visit a certain hotel early on in the game.
As proved by all the unofficial mods this is a game which while being brilliant also has a lot of potential to be more. If ever there was a candidate for an 'enhanced edition' this would be it. It would make an absolute killing.

The game has a lot of flaws. Bugs, shuddering frame rate, one glitch which straight freezes you in place during dialogue. Weird design sometimes just seems built to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, and it's not clear what the hell you're meant to be doing. Balancing issues can make the game virtually impossible to complete if you put your points in the wrong stats and abilities.  So if you specced into guns and wasted your ammo wandering in circles in a confusing bit of map and you run into a boss fight at the end of it, you get to eat♥♥♥♥♥♥ And don't throw all your points into seduction unless you think you can screw the final boss to death. Awkwardly despite giving us the option to role play and build the character our way, there's some sections and bosses which just can't be beaten without combat.
I ended up using console cheats to finish one of the final bosses because of this combat stuff. In other sections I had to use walkthroughs or guides just to keep up a decent pace and even with them it was hard to make sense of one of the later levels. Yeah it's cheating it's their fault for making this so confusing.
BUT - What the game lacks in its old, weird, broken design it makes up for in making a world that feels beautifully immersive and complex. The world FEELS huge even though there's only a tiny bit of playable map in each region. It feels as though you if you left that map you could just continue on forever in this massive universe the writers have built. The writing is great too, and every npc seems to have an angle, an opinion, a selfish ulterior motive. Every character will have another character either built them up or criticize them, and all of it strained through the filter of their subjective view of their second life. Every line of dialogue has something funny, interesting, or worth reading and decisions have consequences on who lives and dies and what this means for your waning humanity.
So yeah, took me 43 hours (At least 3 of it spent in the ♥♥♥♥ing final boss level) to play through with one character but I know I'm going to return to this, so in the end I think I would recommend it. One of the top games I've ever played.

It is hard to sum up One Way Heroics into just a few words, so let me give you a couple paragraphs. (If you're the sort that likes to go "tl;dr" then just scroll to the bottom, but I mean, then why are you even reading reviews to begin with?)
I picked this game up for <$0.60 when it was sale during the summer. I have to say, those were the best $0.60 I have ever spent. One Way Heroics doesn't appeal to you with stunning graphics, rich storytelling, or intricate gameplay. Instead, it is more retro gaming, silly short tales, and an easy to pick-up set of controls. Now you might be wondering, why would I want something like that? Arguably everything but simplicity of the controls could be considered negative or at least niche.  One Way Heroics doesn't offer high spec gaming while emptying your wallet - what you're buying is meaningless fun and entertainment.
When I first opened this game and started an adventure, I found myself with my silly little 2D character talking to a "Naughty King Victor" about the darkness at the left of my screen that would attempt to eat me until I killed the Demon Lord. Yes, clearly the storyline could use some work, but as I struggled to kill weak mobs and then stronger demons I found myself falling for this game. Everything was fairly straightforward and the desire to complete achievements, "save the world," and become a true hero compels you to play over and over again. It doesn't take several hours to do a run through like a quest in some RPG, just 30 minutes or so if you're short on time. Yet, you can play longer sessions that go for tens of hours depending completely on what you want to do and how much time you have - and those hours? They were some fun hours.
I won't try to tell you that you'll be so entranced with One Way Heroics that you'll spend thousands of hours playing it - you probably won't. But it's easy to lose 10, 20, maybe even 100 hours of your life having fun by sending your hero towards the right of your screen. Was that worth my 60 cents while it was on sale? Definitely. Is it worth the full $3.49? Absolutely. Most of us play games to have fun - and One Way Heroics delivers.
tl;dr?
If you're a hardcore gamer looking for a game with brilliant graphics and intricate/competitive gameplay to drop thousands of hours on, I think you're better off somewhere else.
If you're someone looking to spend 10-100 hours having fun in your spare time? Buy One Way Heroics.

I got this game on a sale, long time ago, for a dumb and extremely low price, something like half an euro, or even less. To tell you the truth, for such a price, I was expecting something horrible, dreadful, like an 8-bit Ride to Hell. Did I got surprised? Yeah! Buuuuuuut as usual, let me explain the BAD things the game has first, so we can take them out of the way:
The game is kind of short. Of course, for such a price, you can understand it, so it's not that big of a deal. Besides, this is a Rogue-like game, and rogue-like games are usually short, but change in every playthrough, this is no different from the standard on that regard.
The other thing that I did not like at all, is the lack of multiplayer. This game had such extreme potential for a Coop experience, but instead you can play the same randomly generated world at the same time as one of your friends, to see who goes further...INSTEAD OF PLAYING TOGETHER, AND HAVING FUN! I was indeed dissapointed by that, by looking at the captures of some friends that got the game, and by looking at the pictures and videos of the Steam-Store, I was expecting to play at least with one friend in a journey to save the world by punching demons on their d#cks.  You know, the usual.
Now, let's talk about the GOOD stuff, pretty much everything else. As I said, it's a Rogue-Like. At the start of the playthrough you select the kind of character you desire to control, and special skills for you: You want to be fast? You want to be strong? You want to use magic? You want to start with a companion? You want to start with insane amoutns of gold? It's your choice, and it's indeed well made. I really did enjoy starting in different ways, and testing different strategies.
The game pretty much goes like this: The world is being taken out by some sort of "Dark Sonic Boom" (Damn Obama, he stole that from Guille!), and ANYTHING NEAR THE LEFT SIDE OF THE SCREEN IS F#CKED. Your goal is to travel to the right, getting stronger, surviving the wilds, getting better gear, meeting other people, saving lives, and if you get far enough, saving the world. It might sound simple enough, but the game mechanics make this journey, a journey to remember: First of all, you have to eat, or your character will get tired. Sounds easy enough? Well, there's not that many free food out there, so you have to make sure to visit any Inn or Town and get supplies before they got suck up into Oblivion (I bet that portal leads to Obama's #sshole, NOW THAT'S ONE SICK WAY TO END UP DEAD). Not only that, but your equipment won't last forever. Your stuff has limited use, for example, 100 uses on a sword. Once you swing it for the 100th time, the thing breaks, and it's lost forever. There are ways to repair it and make it last longer, but you should make sure to AT LEAST CARRY 1 BACKUP WEAPON. Infact, I always try to carry at least 3 weapons on myself. And armor? HAH, THOSE THINGS BREAK TOO, SHIELDS INCLUDED! You're far pass f#cked on these lands, specially later on when enemies start to get dangerous!
For a cheap game, there's a lot of fun to be had in this game, and I do recommend it. The game is worth 3€ WITHOUT sales, and that's already cheap enough, on sales it usually lowers to 1€ or so. It's up to you to buy it or not, but I do recommend that you give it a try.

One Way Heroics is a very nice gem, especially due to its low price.
GAMEPLAY:
The game's gameplay is relatively simple, making it quite easy to learn, a great positive for a more casual game like One Way Heroics. Fortunately, despite its initial simplicity, the gameplay becomes addicting due to its blend of a slow turn-based aspect together with a sense of urgency created by the ever-scrolling screen. The gameplay becomes especially enjoyable inside of the dungeons, where the player must plan out all of the character's moves to kill all the monsters before the darkess reaches you (and maybe take some loot).
SOUND:
Although it didn't strike me as particularly mesmerising, the sound track does a good job at involving the player, and is enjoyable enough to listen to for a long amount of time.
ART:
One Way Heroics seems to be following a recent trend of indie games having pixelated graphics, but despite this I really enjoyed the art, and in this case, it matches the old-school RPG feeling of the game.
In conclusion, this game is a good recommendation for those people who only have a couple minutes available to play games and also to those who have multiple hours to play. The game is very enjoyable,and although the game may seem short at first, it has incredible replay value.
Thumbs up for One Way Heroics
