This game lacks music. Most of your gameplay is filled with digital squeeks and sfx of the character's actions. The sounds get monotonous and boring.
Gameplay
This game is not repetitive for a dungeon crawler. This is good. The game was enjoyable for the first few hours. However, you'll realize that the randomly generated maps are at times impossible to complete. For example, you start a new game, and you spawn right next to a hobgoblin. You'll die. You won't be able to kill it, not with getting artifacts. The chances of getting artifacts are very low, considering that you'll have much more difficulty in trying to survive the first level, let alone trying to find artifacts.
You might be complaining that these "vanilla" gamers don't know what difficult is. Well, if you take the example of spawning next to a hobgoblin, you don't have a chance in playing the game. You could either open doors and run away, not knowing whether the next room would be filled with enemies or weapons to aid in your quest, or you could face the enemy and try killing it, dying in the process. This "fated death" does not represent what difficult is.
The good news is, such situations does not occur frequently. In my opinion, the gameplay does not leave much to be desired. The randomness did not seemed to be well thought of.
Graphics
I had a huge problem with the minimap. At full screen, the mini map was, too mini. You might be thinking, this guy is nuts! It's a mini map, what more do you need? Well, the issue is you can't adjust the size of the minimap. The minimap is important in this game because it shows you the loot, the unopened doors, and the stairs. You can also click on the minimap to move your character to the far side of the room effortlessly. A small minimap was just straining to the eyes.
Overall, information in the hub (or whatever you call it) is dense and it will take you some time to get used to it. This isn't a bad thing. Some players may find that the hub is "busy" because there are a lot of things going on.
You can't really experience this by looking at the screenshots of the game. You have to play it to know what I'm trying to say. When you get into a room with tons of enemies, you may want to choose, say, the easiest to kill/most lethal to take down first. To do that, you gotta hover through each enemy to look at their descriptions, comparing their atk/def with your atk/def to determine the likelihood of you hitting it. This process isn't made easy based on the design of the hub. Again, it takes quite some getting used to.

Pros:
-Driving is solid, especially fun in the winter season.
-Graphics are excellent. Great care was put into the appearance and visual details of this game.
-Gameplay is polished and smooth, as were the cutscenes
-Empire Bay is convincingly alive, especially at first, and the time period is presented very nicely with artwork, music, etc.
Cons:
-Some would say the story would be a "pro" but I found it far less enjoyable, and far more predictable when compared to the previous installment. Still deeper than GTA V, for exmaple, but it just depends on what you like. Only had me for 1 playthrough - the original survived 3. Might be some nostalgia bias at work, I admit.
-The missions. Not bad, but forgettable. I didn't feel the missions added as much to the story as the cutscenes.
-The protagonist. Not as dull as Commander Shepard, but I did not sympathize with him. I think it makes a huge difference on your overall satisfaction when you like the protagonist compared to when you don't.
-A tad too linear. Again, this is not that bad when you consider this is 95% a story driven game, but when the story lets you down there is nothing to fall back on.
Verdict: 8/10. If you like driving around in a 40s-50s New York type setting, you will most likely enjoy this game. It is inevitable to compare it to the GTA series, and the most concise way in which I can do this is as follows: Mafia 2 is more linear than GTA and there is less to do outside the story, but the story drives the game a lot more than it does in GTA, and the gameplay is on par. If you played the original, I would say this game is less interesting overall but it did not let me down. I anticipated it's arrival, and I anticipate the arrival of Mafia III just the same.

This game seemed interesting at first, did have steam cards, and well, overall seemed kind of promising. Not sure if I would ever buy it of the shelve thou. To be honest, probably not, but strangely I wouldn’t mind playing the demo of the second version, as the game is promising if things are improved, and the concept of the game is better. Ok, lets get into it.
The games is a mixture between a puzzle solver and se gravity action game, which very much reminds to games such as Valve's Portal logic, without the graphics and the budget to do most things else. The game is set out as an First Person Shooter ("FPS"). It took some time before the mouse was configured in a playable manner. The first impression was that it moved a bit slow, and the goal or objective of the game was not immediately obvious, at least to me, but I have been known to take more time to understand this kind of games. I hate tutorials as much as the next guy, but when you are an indie, maybe you make things a bit more user friendly at the start of the game. No, it is not that I haven’t played FPS before -I am totally acquainted with the WASD controls- it is more about not exactly knowing what is to be done at the start of the game. Every game has its learning curve, but some clues, some more context to what is going in in the surroundings or in the game’s universe itself would be of great help, if it's not too much to ask, that is.
Some say that giving a game is virtually unimportant and that the story is for dreamers, peeps who are not really into gaming and maybe they are right. I consider myself one of those guys who can just go on with some imagination. I won’t read all the text conversations like a book neither, but I really like the experience a game can deliver, and I play them with some expectancy. So, when there is very little context and intro in a game I am somewhat disappointed. Even when you are creative, even fantastically committed, you will eventually need some support to help your mind wander of deep into a game. This did definitely not happen with me with this game; it was a good concept at the beginning, but it all became a bit repetitive and obvious. The challenges do get more complicated as you advance from level to level, but there is also a sensation that the level design was a bit wary.
For a game of which the basic goal is shifting gravity to move from point A to point B (some variations, of course) it is all right, but I truly think that the game could have been much more if they gave it that little extra. The stability of the game was fine, did not have any problems playing it.
Regarding the music and the graphics, it is fine for an indie, but none are truly remarkable or memorable. Sounds could be improved to give the user an experience when turning gravity, as it feels a bit too simple. It is recognizable that even thou it is an indie, it is always smooth and did not get glitchy, at least for me, as I have read that this was not the case for other reviewers.
With this review I did not mean to diminish the work put into this, it works great, and it is entertaining for a while, but one must measure at first feel, and this was not what I expected it to be.

Summary:
The bad:
- Bad controls
- Bad physics
- Repetative gameplay
- Repetetive levels
- Lack of challenge
- Lacks sound options (mute sound/music)
- Poor choice of music (even recognize one of these songs from other games)
The good:
- Looks OK.
- We get more than 1 color blocks
- It's a good idea
- The basic stuff surrounding the game is just fine as you'd expect of a unity game.
- Very small download size (80mb). Really gets you into the game quickly. I apprechiate it.
This game is more of a gameplay prototype than a game. ALL the levels are extremely similar. The major difference between the classes (groups of 6 levels) is the number of blue blocks you need to touch before the finish.
The game is rather unclear about what the rules actually are, there's a tutorial text on the first level which instructs you to the entire mechanic of the game which is that gravity is pointing towards the ground you last touched and you can rotate segments of blocks.
I wouldn't call this a puzzle game actually. It's certainly what it reaseembles the most but there's no puzzles here. There's no set solution to anything at all. It's simply the nature of the mechanic and level design. The dev should absolutely add walls or some feature that restricts movement, because as is (aside from a slight caveat) you just have to rotate your platform until you can jump down onto another, repeat until you've touched all the blocks and then hit the goal. On the last level (I assume it's a bug) I didn't have to touch the goal, it finished as i touched all the 'checkpoints' (the blue blocks you are supposed to touch before the goal).
I had what I must assume is a bug. The blocks have no indication of being discriminating of what side you're supposed to stand on. So on the last level I played (F6) I had touched all of the checkpoints except one. When I landed on the last checkpoint nothing happened. I couldn't rotate the block (as you're supposed to, the side i was standing on was indicated as a side you can rotate on), nothing happened. After a while of fiddling I discovered a mechanic that wasn't taught at all. If you face up against a perpendicular platform to the one you're standing on and press space you can transfer yourself onto the wall. After a while of fiddling with the box I landed on a side I hadn't landed on before and the game said I completed the level.
The game doesn't let you continue to the next set of levels if you've completed the last level of the group. I didn't realize this until I had played the same level 3 times because they all look so incredibly similar in concept that you actually can't tell easily. That's how incredibly similar they are.
The physics of the game is poorly implemented. You get jerky velocity when falling at terminal velocity (which is very slow in this game). It looks awful. If you look up/down too far you can invert the camera (upside down relative to where your feet are). This is clearly just the most hacky way to get the rotation stuff to work.
Even if you like the concept of this game I can't recommend it. Especially not at 2.99€. It really isn't worth your time even. Plenty of better alternatives.

After playing Vampire the Masquerade completely vanilla besides those mandatory patches to play it on a modern OS and without it crashing every 20 minutes, I can say that the game brings about a lot more positives than negatives to the table. It is one of the most unique settings for an action-RPG I have played, set in the dark drab cities and slums of night-time locales, and brimming with that early 2000s era gothic atmosphere.
It is difficult to encapsulate all thoughts on this game, as there is so much to cover, so I will be rambling about my favourite aspects to the game.
You remember the music video to the song "Bring me to Life" by Evanescence? That is how this game feels visually. It has nailed that perfect atmosphere that is both a product of its time and a testament to good world building. My favourite aspect out of all the atmospherics is by far the nightclubs found in around each city or location. This game has nailed this dark but seductive atmosphere of an early 2000s club scene, reminding me of the intro scene to the movie "Blade" starring Wesley Snipes. Notice how much pop culture references I have been talking about? Well the game is compact full of them; references to bands, music of the era, plenty of movie references from before its original release, and I adore this game for that alone. It shows references to these things without going overboard or coming across as too corny.
The faction system and how each vampire class, without going into too much detail, helps provide a very noticeable and large variety of gameplay styles suited to different players. The game does an excellent job in explaining what each class is capable of doing and what you should be in for should you choose those types of classes/sects of the vampire secret society. The game does an amazing job at immersing you into its world, with its incredible voice acting, damn good facial animations during conversations for a game released in 2004 (put the source engine to good use) and provides a storyline that will seriously make you trudge through even its lowest points due its intrigue and buildup of interest.
The music is incredibly good in my opinion, it will not be to everyone's tastes, as it has that very early 2000s gothic music choice, but it really helps solidify its unique atmosphere and style. In some ways the game has helped immortalise this game as the cult classic it is. Art direction is completely on point from each varying area that you explore, and although completely limited by what you can do by today's action RPG standards, it still has a lot going on to keep you interested.
I have listed off many positives, and the rest would be spoilers, but in fairness, there is a reason this game is a cult classic besides it huge bug problems that will inevitably occur even when patched. Some patience will be needed with this type of game and if you cannot stand the occasional potential crash or glitch messing things up like in plenty of RPGs in this day and age, you might be disappointed. Combat in some classes will leave a lot to be desired, if you play it vanilla, and while the game promotes plenty of playstyles, a lot of the time you WILL be forced to fight in some shape or form. The last major negative I have for this game that I and many, many people have with this game is pretty much the the latter stages of the game, involving a particular sewer, and other aspects that come with following up this part of the game that might put off a lot of people from continuing on.
Despite that last negative, I will say without a doubt, VTM:B is absolutely worth a playthrough in your lifetime if you love RPGs and you are looking for something almost completely unique in experience and setting. It is difficult reviewing a game like this because you would like to explore every part to it, but there is a lot of content to be had in this game, and spoiling it is doing it an injustice.

You Have to Win the Game is an indie platformer blahblah blah blahblahblah. Let's just get to the point. If you don't know what this game is, read the description and watch the trailer.
This game can be extremely frustrating at times. (I'm looking at YOU, Extra Spicy and YOLO Mode. Even you, Playable Cat DLC.) But despite all of its frustrating moments, such as the end room on Extra Spicy (not gonna spoil anything further!) and the entirety of YOLO Mode, this game still turns up on my #1 spot on my personal mentally-memorized best free-to-play indie games list, and takes me back via nostalgia for a time when I wasn't even alive. Quite a feat, am I right?
Its platforming tactics can sometimes be cheap, sometimes annoying, but they're always clever. For instance, take You Have to Flip the Desk (the first room on Extra Spicy) for example. You save OVER the pit of spikes, and in order to try jumping again, you have to first go back to the start of the pit of spikes to retry it. Or how about Nope Nope Nope, where you have to time your jumps literally perfectly to a certain pixel. The first one is quite cheap, and the second is even more annoying, but they're both clever little rooms that take time to complete despite their small size.
And speaking of levels, let's go to level design. You can tell they put a lot of work into the tilesets because there are so many different textures for one tile such as dirt or bricks, and they put the different sprites together so frikkin' well it's almost scary. Then there's the names of each level, which are clever as well, and to top it off, they make bosses unfightable yet STILL enjoyable.
Then there's the different gamemodes. There's infinite ways to play the game, like....wait, no, there's actually about six. The different campaigns are the "Original" campaign, which is for a new player or a seasoned player looking for some chill time, and then there's "Extra Spicy" which is where all the pros go to pass their time. (And it works very, very well.) Then the different characters to play as are a kid (normal, with checkpoints, and you can die an infinite amount of times), a kid with MLG swag YOLO sunglasses (you only live once and when you die you restart the whole game, as the mode suggests, being titled "YOLO Mode"), and a playable cat "DLC" which isn't really a DLC (you have nine lives). They're all equally fun to do, except for YOLO Mode + Extra Spicy, which is living hell on Earth, but that doesn't matter, because you're not forced to do that.
All-in-all, You Have to Win the Game is definitely a great game, it's definitely my top favorite free-to-play indie game on Steam, and I definitely have to recommend it to you. Try this game. It's free. What can you lose? And trust me, it isn't a waste of time either. You will enjoy your time playing this game, that is guaranteed for anyone who wants a good old platformer.

Let me compare this game (EHHNE) to the last two point & click adventure games I played
(and finished, very happily) : Day of the Tentacle (DOTT, 1993) and Anna's Quest (AQ).
Voices:
EHHNE: Your character says "uh uh" or "umm hmm".  Cute.  The voices of other characters
are fine.  The standard response to actions is from a narrator, who gets annoying really
quickly, not because the voice acting is bad, but because it's wholly inappropriate to
expect a narrator to work in every situation.
Say I want to interact with a tree, and instead of your character saying "heck, I dunno
what to do with this tree", you get the narrator saying something like "Your character
wanted to interact with the tree, but the tree didn't need to be interacted with, because
bla bla bla".  It just serves to constantly remind you that you're playing a game, as
opposed to immersing you in the game by hearing _your_ character's voice in _their_
situation.
AQ: Amazing voice acting.  Even if Anna can sound a little nasal sometimes, you can always
relate.
DOTT: Amazing voice acting.  Even if they all sound constipated.
Story:
EHHNE: You're in a convent.... There are some other people.  You're socially awkward.
You've got to do some stuff, cuz hopefully doing stuff will make stuff more interesting.
Oh, some stuff happens, you're kind of dark behind your cute facade, wow, that's so novel ...
yawn.  Stuff.
AQ: You're trapped in a witches house.  The witch has plans for you.  You have
superpowers.  You must save your grandpa.  You meet a teddy bear.  You must help the teddy
bear.  You've got ____ to do!
DOTT: An evil tentacle makes a move to take over the world.  Three friends must
collaborate in the past, present and future to thwart the evil tentacles plans of world
domination.  Hell yea!
Art/graphics:
EHHNE: hi-res cell shading / small characters / cute-centric/ lots of irrelevant
foreground / background graphics / minimal animation
AQ: hi-res cell shading / character dominated / beautiful detailed backgrounds clearly
distinguished from foreground & navigable space
DOTT: cartoony, pixel animation / distorted scale / perspective / saturated colors / most
of the screen is at the scale of the character (not too much foreground / background)

Divide By Sheep is a lazy mobile port. Not a bad mobile port. In fact, its even a good port in some respects. But two glaring errors stuck out to me, the PC user. First one is nitpicking and doesn't affect anything but leaving a "please rate the app" screen at the end of the menus is just bad form. Then there was no resolution/windowed control. And this being a time-filler puzzle game it is primed for being played while consuming other media. Windowed mode (without 3rd party programs) should be considered a must. So alt+tab'ing ensued and I will note I suffered some framerate hiccups upon doing that. The game does look good at 1080p and runs at a solid 60 frames otherwise though.
The port issues aside, this game is great. The wacky theme and art. The tight puzzles. The bright color palette. It all works. The 150 puzzles are all well constructed in their simplicity. Each level features 9 or less platforms with three sets of requirements to clear. It starts with hopping sheep around. But ends up with wolves, pigs, lasers, meat eating octopus, portals, traps, flames, totems, and more. The game regularly provides new wrinkles to the puzzles. Right when one set of mechanics is wearing thin and you are in a groove you run into something new. If you go for all the "stars" on every level you'll find yourself with a solid 7~8+ hours of gameplay. Very much worth the price.

This is a top down retro style dungeon crawler along the lines of an old DOS dungeon crawler with random dungeons, random enemies and everything will kill you. The art style is nice, but really too many games are doing retro. As a game, Hack, Slash, Loot is not fun, it doesn't just feel unfair, but it feels more difficult than fun. You can pick a class or have it random. You can pick a mission / quest or randomly do one. Either way everything is random.
The controls don't feel that good. Everything is grid and turn based. You can use arrow keys to walk around and arrow keys to push into an enemy and attack. You can attack diagonally, but that would mean using the mouse, which is fine if you're using a mouse. You can mouse click square by square to move too. If there are no enemies, you can mouse click to move several tiles. But its all turn based. You go once, the 'active' enemies all need to go before you move. You all go one by one, you don't have 10 units of movement and enemies have 6 moves of unit. You all go 1 space at a time. I had to explain this, because there are other games that feature more movement spaces or real time movement.
The levels generated don't feel balanced, its either you vs 100 or its you + 100 allies vs 1. But hey random is random. This is jut really unpolished. A lot of games would have an easy level first even if its random, but an easy level to get your feet wet so you can get some items. Not this game. Sometimes the only door to go from the start leads to a room laughably full of enemies.
You end up having to bottleneck to survive half a dozen enemies. Luckily the enemy AI is smart enough to go around and flank you on the other side of the room. Not always of course. Most of the time the bottle-necking works well enough, but the attacks miss.... a lot. I could understand enemy attacks missing, for game balance or at least having enemy attacks do minor damage when you just start out. Not this game.
The classes don't even feel that balanced. The melee classes seem to by far be the best. Especially the knight which, just doesn't seem to die at all. It slaughters everything. It may sound fun, but the catch is, there's such little depth to this game that it becomes a chore trying to find the next level to the quest. I'm bored long before I die. The range classes have a difficult task ahead of them, because of 'fog of war,' you don't see what's in a room until you open the door. When you open the door, there are enemies in there and rooms never seem to be large enough to kill enemies before they pile on you and murder you.
Its just not fun, a lot of monotony, room full of enemies, fall back to bottleneck. As the knight you can just run from room to room and not even stop to face enemies, because its just a waste of time. The game is so shallow that you reach your peak pretty quick.
Not just that, some different dungeon graphics would have been nice, its all blue. Every screen shot is blue. I feel like I saw everything the game has to offer within 10 minutes let alone the time I played it for. To top it off, there is no save, but maybe the game expects you to die before you'll ever save. I can't recommend Hack, Slas, Loot. Luckily I bought it for $1, but otherwise there are plenty of free dungeon crawlers out there.

Short Review: It's free, it's short (35-50 mins), and it might do something for you. Give it a try.
Long Review: Where do I start? For a while I was thinking "what box do I check for my recommendation, yes or no?" Well, I ended up picking yes for the reasons explained in my short review but.... but...
First of the game was not completely ineffective on me. There are several times where a mood was imposed, or a feeling, or even a complete idea, just through use of environments, images and music. The game worked I suppose, placing you whiplash style into different mind states using limited resources.
But the game was at its best when it had nothing to say.
I have no issue with self-absorbed art, films like Melancholia benefit from the artist making a film about precisely what THEY feel. It’s sincere, direct. A game however, in many ways, is a different story. Being an interactive and, hopefully, immersive medium, the player is active in the art, not just an observer. There were 3-4 times in the game where the player is made to sit and watch (yeah yeah, I was climbing a ladder, but I was still made to sit) and while one of those moments I did find effective, It took away from the experience. I wasn’t experiencing, snapping from level (dream?) to level and feeling different emotions at a breakneck pace. I was watching. A spectator. I got the distinct feeling this game was not for me, for us.
In a level, there’s only so much time I want to spend looking, I want to experience, move, explore, do. The thing though is that even if that was the point, to share frustration with the player (as one of the sequences makes directly clear, One Step Forward, Two Steps Back) that does not a good game make. Even if it’s intended, that does not excuse it in all cases. Don’t get me wrong, I’m not mad that this game is not Counter Strike, that is in no why what I expected. I’ve played quite a few games like this, Dear Ester, Beginner’s Guide, The Static Speaks My Name to name a few. I’m comparing them to those games. Dear Ester at least allows you to continue exploring at almost all times, and the narration is consistent and punchy. Beginner’s guide is a gestalt experience of narration and gameplay that keeps the player involved as it imparts its message and emotions onto them, putting you in a journey that the artist has(?) taken. Static Speaks is about what the player does, though it also benefits from shorter length and more consistent tone.
Make a game about yourself, that’s fine, but take us WITH you. Guide us. GIVE us something. It doesn’t need to be pleasant, but it needs to be there.
I get the feeling that this guy is going to read almost all his reviews, so I’m just going to address him real quick. I do not hate your game. I don’t dislike your game. But if you ask me things like, well, did you enjoy it? Did it impact you? Was It memorable?
Not quite.
That’s just one phrase that really sums it up for me. Not quite. I actually remember times where I was actively TRYING to feel something, and it just wasn’t there. The times I felt unforced emotion were great, well made, and appreciated. I just think you need to step away from yourself, and make something for the people who will actually be playing. Take us on a trip, don’t drag us with you.
I will be keeping an eye out for your next game, and I genuinely hope you succeed.

Ah, VTMB.
At first, we didn't get along, me and this game. Her graphics were weirding me out, his mannerism of animations was making me uncomfortable and hub areas were laughably small for an RPG. So, I was putting this game down for years, until finally, I convinced myself to give it a run for a couple of hours. And Christ! Did I not expect a story about vampires to resonate with me as much as it did.
You're thrown into this world of vampires. A rookie in a very, very old world of vampires with a rich history, mythos, rules, clans, power figures running things for centuries... And you're living this life of a new vampire whose role is unclear yet. So it feels like you're about to join this somewhat dry world of everyday vampire life, find your place in the vampire society and do errands for older vampires. But at the same time, it seems like something very important is about to happen. And this is the line that VMTB walks beautifully throughout the game. You can't be sure which one it is! I loved this sense of intricacy, even if the ending is... not good.
But! Anyway,
Here is what made this game for me: Bloodlines (probably) has the best ensemble of interwoven characters in the history of games. Now, I shouldn't make such a claim when the number of RPGs I've played is much less than an amount of fingers on my hand (that's less than five). However, I've never played a game in which characters were so engaged in the cast as a whole. Each character has something to say about other characters, their clans, mythos, and anecdotes. This world is totally lived in. None of it is written pretentiously, people do feel like real people, even characters on the joky side of the spectrum. Dialogues in this game are superb, rich in character and charisma and it is such a pleasure that they also happen to be masterfully voiced. Smiling Jack, Gary, LaCroix, and others — these performances are poetry. It really felt like these guys were talking
directly and that's a rare occurrence for a cynical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like me.
I give this game a thumbs up. Play this game if you like good dialogues and quality escapism into fictional worlds.

'Harvey's New Eyes' is the second title in the "Edna & Harvey" series by Daedalic Entertainment.  However, playing the first game will not make this game any less enjoyable.  I am not one who laughs at anything and even when I do it isn't usually genuine.  This game literally had me in stitches, especially in the beginning when I was blind to what the game truly was going to be.  The puzzles require you to think them through, but, I never felt the need to look up a walkthrough to help me through it.  However, the game is worth playing simply for it's comedic value.  The story is about a goody-goody, nieve little girl named Lilli who is trying to help out her mentally unstable friend, Edna, escape from her former psychiatrist.  Lilli is also for the most part mute which keeps you in the dark about what she is thinking, what kind of morals she has, or if she is mentally all-there.  The writing is superb and the narrator did a stellar job.  If you like dark humor (very DARK) and do not get offended easily the game is a must buy, especially when it is on sale.

Well, that was dissapointing. Kinda. Not really. Well. Anyways, it's dissapointing, but only as a port. Ignoring the lie that is "Gold Edition" you have probably THE best racing game ever. No, really. This game is a Redlynx game, so it's harder than titanium and is really less about racing and more about platforming with a bike. The environments are varied and DANG are they beautiful. There's also a really good multiplayer mode that leads to hilarious fun. The game will take a while to complete, even longer to get gold on all tracks, and if you want to 100% it then give up if you're impatient. It cranks up the difficulty 10X from the first game (yes that is possible) and allows for much easier track sharing, so you can have almost impossible tracks to play that probably took 7 years straight to make. But god, are they beautiful. In fact, the only problem I can find is that it's really CPU intensive. Now, as a port..... well. The options are good, but for a "Gold Edition" it lacks the expected DLC and there is no compatibility with the 360 Track Central. However, you do get the entirety of the original first game, which is actually a really nice touch, but honestly the original game wasn't exactly expensive, so having the DLC come with the gold edition and having 360 compatability would have been pretty nice. Anyways, I would give it a buy, and then buy a stress ball or 2... thousand.

In the years since Grand Theft Auto, 'open world' games have become heavily codified. We expect a wealth of collectibles to find and challenges to tackle. We look for satisfying mechanical challenges in vehicles and combat. Some of us just want interesting activities and amusing diversions.  Mafia II, unfortunately has no interest in being noteworthy in any of those things.
Mafia II promises to give players the opportunity to be the star of their own mob tale. However, the journey from street thug to made man lacks any mechanical or dramatic weight: you'll be driving, shooting and punching your way through a story that, although well voiced by dozens of veteran character actors, is largely uninspiring.
All this would be forgivable if the collectibles, diversions and challenges were entertaining and well developed. They're not. Despite the great production values invested into the creation of Empire Bay -- a stand-in for New York not unlike GTA's Liberty City -- there really isn't anything to do outside of the ho-hum story.
Despite the presence of a docking smuggler, a scrapyard mechanic and an arms dealer as NPCs, there're no side missions to speak of. Collectible wanted posters are meaningless historical curios and the Playboy centerfolds are tasteless inclusions with no relevance to the game. Sure you can steal cars and buy clothes, which help you dodge a warrant for your arrest, but outside of that they are perfunctory.
Mafia II is a game that starts out full of promise but degenerates quickly. By providing an 'open' world where there's nothing to do, it shackles you to a story filled with boredom and repetition.

Gameplaywise, it's simple. You have your high and long jumps, you have your wall grapple, a bit further into the game you also get a nice pair of rocket boots. With these you'll have to make it through a series of obstacles - and the game always has some fresh turns to not make it repetitive, from introducing new mechanics to giving you a challenge.
And then there's the scenery. It's beautiful, and I've often just stopped from moving further just to gaze on the pretty cavern walls or breathtaking skies. Flying through those views is quite an experience.
The story is a little straightforward, but heartwarming nonetheless. I'd rather like you to see for yourself and make your own verdict.
Overall, the game is not a very complex or ambitious project at all, and it doesn't even pretend to be one. It's just something to go through and remember for a very long time.

In the years since Grand Theft Auto, 'open world' games have become heavily codified. We expect a wealth of collectibles to find and challenges to tackle. We look for satisfying mechanical challenges in vehicles and combat. Some of us just want interesting activities and amusing diversions.  Mafia II, unfortunately has no interest in being noteworthy in any of those things.
Mafia II promises to give players the opportunity to be the star of their own mob tale. However, the journey from street thug to made man lacks any mechanical or dramatic weight: you'll be driving, shooting and punching your way through a story that, although well voiced by dozens of veteran character actors, is largely uninspiring.
All this would be forgivable if the collectibles, diversions and challenges were entertaining and well developed. They're not. Despite the great production values invested into the creation of Empire Bay -- a stand-in for New York not unlike GTA's Liberty City -- there really isn't anything to do outside of the ho-hum story.
Despite the presence of a docking smuggler, a scrapyard mechanic and an arms dealer as NPCs, there're no side missions to speak of. Collectible wanted posters are meaningless historical curios and the Playboy centerfolds are tasteless inclusions with no relevance to the game. Sure you can steal cars and buy clothes, which help you dodge a warrant for your arrest, but outside of that they are perfunctory.
Mafia II is a game that starts out full of promise but degenerates quickly. By providing an 'open' world where there's nothing to do, it shackles you to a story filled with boredom and repetition.

Este game não será como nenhum outro que jogou. Eu diria que é até mesmo uma historia interativa com dois finais premeditáveis.
1. Você cria o próximo Minecraft. e falha com seus amigos e logo o que te faz humano.
2. Você falha consigo mesmo. Mas, mantém suas amizades assim como as coisas que te fazem feliz.
Agora, o que este jogo tem que nenhum outro tem. E que talvez nem mesmo o desenvolvedor sabia que estava fazendo.. É que esse jogo aborda de leve o tema da Procrastinação. ~~Em palavras baixas, não produzir e só esperar~~
Você deve estar se perguntando como.. E se já jogou principalmente... Bem, o jogo lhe dá algumas opções para se fazer que são "do tipo diversão" ou "deixar o tempo passar." Ou, e a mais importante. Trabalhar em seu jogo. Jogo qual deve ser terminado em 7 dias. E o mais único desse jogo é que, ele aborda diretamente algo que eu sempre senti e achei muito importante e que muitas pessoas também sentem. Que é a ideia de quê~~ Para que vou fazer isso se posso ir me divertir.. Para que vou trabalhar no meu jogo se posso sair com meus amigos. Para que me dedicar nisso, se provavelmente ninguém comprará meu jogo.
Muitos desenvolvedores indie realmente passam por isso. Tanto quando você não tem muitas preocupações, como quando tem várias... Como família para cuidar, ou parentes doentes.
Assim como você está começando e querendo entrar no mercado.
Este jogo é único e me mostrou que não só eu que tenho essa visão sobre desenvolver e sobre como gastar meu tempo.
O único problema deste jogo é que ele não é um jogo em si. E sim, como eu disse acima. Uma forma de história interativa.  Enfim, caso você seja um desenvolvedor ou alguém que goste de uns rocks russos bem♥♥♥♥♥♥ Pode comprar sem medo, vai valer a pena cada moeda. E caso queira confirmar o que eu disse, compre também. E tente ver o jogo com bons olhos e não com os olhos dos haters que largam análises negativas.

"This is a free game after all, what could go wrong?"
That's what I thought to myself before installing this game. It really delivers a continuous sense of exploration. It consists of the obvious inspiration of VVVVV and other plataform jewels.
It's experienced through a computer screen simulating the game you're playing. Pretty crazy, huh? Well. A simple concept that, unexpectedly, brings out some inmersion where I thought there couldn't be.
But what about the game itself? It's a game that consists of many rooms, that, when you reach the edge of the screen, you enter the adjacent room. Each room has an identity, where they have a name below the screen. There are upgrades, which will make your character possible to reach areas that you didn't thought where possible at first. There are a total of 3 modes on each of the two maps.
Wait, but... many rooms!? Some people think this mechanic makes them dizzy, and then they get lost. This is the problem; at first you have no idea where you are, and constantly shifting rooms while creating a path on your mind will, at some point, give you the idea of the whole map. Of course, you could just search on the web the whole map for this game, but that will, for certain, ruin your experience.
This game is pretty fun, try it out.

True to its title, Hack Slash Loot is about as straightforward a rogue-like as you can find. After choosing a hero and a themed dungeon (Goblin fortress! Pharaoh's tomb! Dragon's lair!), you are given a paragraph of exposition and sent straight into mouse-clicky battle. Your goal? To reach the fifth floor of the dungeon and slay the boss monster. There's no leveling to speak of, no skills, no puzzles. Your choice of character only determines your starting gear and your proficiency with melee, ranged, or magic attacks, all of which function identically except that melee can only attack adjacent opponents. That isn't to say there's no strategy involved in the game; HP restoration is very limited, positioning in combat is crucial, and knowing what sorts of monsters and hazards each dungeon contains can make or break your survival. However, the primary method for improving your character is to loot the place, which means endlessly comparing your current items to every item drop you come across in the hopes that one of them might outperform your current outfit. If you're lucky, you'll find something early on which offers tons of resistances or one of the handful of special abilities that can easily carry you through to the end. If you're not lucky, well, keep dying, and eventually you'll turn up something nice.
In the end, HSL suffers from a crummy GUI, tedious mechanics, and a lack of variety in almost every field. It's perfectly playable, and winning is admittedly somewhat satisfying, but you can get better bang for your buck in plenty of other places.

I see most people talking about how this game is too simple and too luck based. Well, for most of us who played Rogue-likes back in the 16-bit era, we took simple games and we learned how to roll with the punches. Guide large groups of enemies through doorways, keep two types of weapons, drink and use all potions/scrolls (except for dispel, trust me.), and take what's given to you and use it to the best of your ability.
And if the game is still too hard, do the Boy with the Mask first. Easiest of all the quests and you can get two artifacts that can really help you.
One of my complaints, however, is that even after being out for two years, there has been no released content for the game. So once you unlock everything, all you have to look forward too is repeating the same quests. I am content with that, but I know a lot of people who wouldn't.
So it's a hit and miss kind of game. If you like challenging, barebone games, then pick it up. If you like games with expansive spells and weapons, this is not the game for you.

If you love Open Worlds with an Olden Day, War Era Style to them, then this is for you!
Many things were enjoyable such as the following:
Positives:
♦ Good Graphics
♦ Good Classic Music from back in the day
♦ Wonderful Olden Day Vibe
♦ Amazing Storyline and incite into the War era
♦ Great Graphics and Sounds
♦ Nice number of Steam Achievements and Findable Content (Such as Magazines and Posters)
♦ Can fight any man you want and rob enterable stores
♦ Police Fights
♦ Map Waypoints (Very Helpful)
♦ Ending left open for Mafia III (This will lead to an amazing sequel if done correctly)
Now don't get me wrong there are many positives, but still not every game is perfect and this one has the following negative points:
Negatives:
♦ Police are too easy (Just kill a few/Drive a short distance in the area and even though you have 3 or 4 Stars they still dissapear)
♦ Map waypoint always tells you to go to Joe's and sleep (Even if you set your own or get a new mission, this is annoying having two waypoints all the time to a mission you don't have to do).
♦ Can't fight Women (Seems Weird).
♦ Fighting randoms doesn't give anything.
♦ Not suitable for kids (Only put this in for those that complain about it)
Other:
♦ Can no-longer buy DLC even if you want to (This sucks as it was nice to have the option of extra addons to this awesome game)
Overall, in my opinion, the game is a great incite into the War period with an awesome Storyline and epic Classical Olden Day styled Cars and Music.  However, due to the slightly crude magazines and posters you can find, this is not suitable for kids... Though I'd highly recommend this to anyone of age that loves an Open World, Olden Day, War era Styled game.
Overall, I'd rate this 4/5!
PS: If the Cops weren't as easy and the Way Point situation wasn't bugged as mentioned in the negatives, it'd be a clear 5/5.

You might call A Story About Mu Uncle a joy-of-movement simulator.  It's focused on jumping and grappling huge distances and the short-form resource conservation puzzles involved.  It's pretty simple--easy to learn, almost as easy to master--but also satisfying to play, pretty to look at, and over well before it's worn out its welcome.
There's also a saccharine-sweet narrative delivered through some charmingly accent-stilted voice acting.  Both can definitely be rather awkward, but ASAMY's story has this comforting sense of earnestness, which helps overcome its stilted delivery and well-tread themes.  It feels entirely divorced from adult self-awareness, both for good and ill.
Definitely give this one a look.  It's a really enjoyable way to spend 2-3 hours.

One Way Heroics is a decidedly different and refreshing take on the rogue genre. Simply put, every decision you make causes the world to end just a little bit more. An existence-destroying void is following you, and the only solution is to constantly push to the right. You'll have to make detours, whether it's shopping for supplies, exploring for dungeons, or going after some great treasure.
As with most other Rogue titles, death is permanent...and expected. Your first game might last several minutes, your second might last a few seconds. Dying tends to result in rewards such as new perks, classes, and the ability to store useful items in a vault for future games. This is all dependent on your hero points, a score received at the end of the game. Surviving as long as possible is just one of many ways to accrue points. The character classes and perks offer a good bit of variety in how you approach the game. There are other awards depending on your in-game actions, so it's always worth trying new things and exploring as much as that rapidly expanding void will allow.
Adding to the replay value is the infinite number of randomly-generated worlds. One Way Heroics has numerous online functions, so it's possible for multiple players to explore the same world. While playing, you'll see the status of other heroes and get a sense of their trials and tribulations. When they die, their cause of death will be displayed. You might even happen upon their remains, and score a nice item for yourself. Despite the game's cheap price, it's still receiving great support by the developer. In fact as of this writing there was an update issued just yesterday. Multiple difficulty settings further add to the replay value.
Really though, the main reason I recommend this game is because staying from the void is such a valuable design-decision. Typical rogue games, with their insistence on dark dungeons, tend to bore me. One Way Heroics is very focused, it's linear, but it retains all of the depth that is consistent with the genre. Every decision in the game carries weight, since the void is never far behind. I never get the sense that I'm just meandering around a dungeon looking for a key or a sword or a set of stairs. Every step is essentially proof of life, and it feels like very real progress(though death remains a very real setback).
All in all, One Way Heroics is an unexpected surprise. I look forward to putting more time into it.

Very fun twist on roguelikes, with streamlined and fast-paced gameplay, pleasant music and a highly addictive concept and progression format.
Basically, this is like a roguelike game (such as Nethack or TOME4: Tales of Maj-Eyal), mixed with one of those old school platformer "scroller" stages where a wall of death is coming towards you. The combination and design makes progression interesting, as gameplay never really stagnates because of the wall keeping you moving forward and requiring you to make decisions. "Is it worth it to enter this dungeon? Will I have a way to get out in time? Can I reach the shopkeeper before the appraiser gets eaten by the darkness?". At the end, you have to battle the boss, the Demon Lord who summoned the wall of death, which packs quite a punch compared to everything else you fight. To aid you, you can find loot, money...all your traditional JRPG elements, but streamlined to be as fast-paced as possible.
The presentation is a mixed bag. Sprites are tiny but appropriate, and look very much like what you'd expect in a Super NES RPG. Music is not the best ever, but makes itself noticeable when needed, and stays out of the way during the less exciting parts. Controls are very simple and consoley, but doesn't really need a pad to be enjoyed, as it controls with mostly 3 keys and directions. The interface is however quite confusing, with vital stats near the middle of the screen, with other stats at the bottom, buffs at the right...it's a bit all over the place and takes a bit to get used to, but at least you can get used to it after a couple rounds.
Larger character artwork is also a mixed bag, with some portraits looking good, others looking kinda bland. Character design is very old-school JRPG medieval fantasy, a bit retro while at it, looks more 90s than 2010s if you get what I mean. I guess it is a good effort at looking old-school.
As for gameplay decisions, it's all quite slick. Weapons have durability, but are usually easy enough to replace, and repairing is possible, while not straightforward. To compensate, the limit on enchantments, buffs and powerups for each individual weapon or armor is quite big, allowing to kind of craft superweapons with a bit of luck or planning, not too much. Dungeons, terrain and towns are terribly simplistic, but then again, you can't really stay more than a dozen turns in most places, so it works out for the best. There's plenty of decent loot lying around as well, although deciding what stuff to keep and what to drop to satisfy your weight limits can bring the action to a temporary halt as you ponder advantages and disadvantages, or wondering if that unidentified item is crap or highly enchanted.
An average game from start to finish can take like 40 minutes. Since it's designed to be played over and over, difficulty is high, and you can store lucky drops for your characters, replay value is pretty good. Specially if you are into beating high scores, a bit of an outdated concept in general, but works pretty well here. Different classes, builds and worlds play quite differently, so there's noticeable variety. Special and shared worlds also have leaderboards, for a slight competitive vibe if you are into it. Could be a good choice for a let's play or speedrunning.
Extra features are quite convenient and welcomed. You don't get a tutorial, but "advice" based on your actions, reminding you of basic tactics and features if you don't use them. Likewise, you have Iris, a little fairy companion, that will give you general advice and specific details of some aspects of the game (such as terrain penalties) on request. At the end of your quest you get rated on a number of aspects, such as looting and combat, and gives you extra advice or praise if it's bad or good. Your general score awards you "hero points", which you can use to make any new playthrough stronger by unlocking perks, player classes or item storages.
This game features a peculiar version of "permadeath", a common roguelike trope, where your character is completely gone after death. You can save your game, but the default would be to start over once you die. However, you can continue a saved game after death, but you aren't awarded hero points if you continue after dying. The game encourages permadeath but doesn't mind very much if you go for the opposite, basically.
You can't play together with other players, however, it has a fairly interesting approach similar to shared Nethack servers of old, where a single-player game gets peppered with messages and other bonuses caused by other players being in the same "Dimension" (a fancy name for random seeds). As well, special events updated daily give special challenges, such as more experience gain in a harder setting; replacing all item drops for money and so on. Or quests with special NPCs, some fairly funny or endearing.
6 months after the latest update, special events are still getting rotated daily, which is a good sign.
A great plus is that, while the game isn't available for Linux, it runs flawlessly on WINE, only having a minimal sound glitch with the conversation sound effect (which echoes a tiny bit), but all online features, replays, input, video, music, all other sound effects and such, works perfectly.

It isn't fast paced action but round-based action, still you can play it as a little morsel when you make a break or when watching TV and again there is this "commercial-time". And the second isn't enervating only a little bit more like - weeeeelllll, in the 1980s we had those nice little breadboxes called C64 that was 8 bit technology and we tried to pull out the most out of this little - homecomputers. An old-school point'n'click adventure game, reminiscent in style of some latter-day LucasArts games, including the amazing Day of the Tentacle. This is actually a sequel to another Edna & Harvey game (also available on Steam), but I played this without first playing the first game, and I can safely say you don't need to play the first game to enjoy this adventure.
It has many of the shortcomings of traditional point'n'click games, including illogical "use item X on Y" problems and an annoying lack of an in-game hint system (EVERY adventure game should have one like Broken Sword 5 recently did!).
No, it doesn't try to be "modern" in any way, but at a time when Telltale has redefined adventure games and turned them into interactive movies, it is refreshing to play something honestly retro and honestly old-school.
Some of the dialogue and humour is not quite as good as it tries to be, and some of the puzzles are a bit illogical, but overall this is a very good retro with gorgeous graphics and some pretty funny, dark scenarios. The best part about it is the overall flow of the game, the inventive dream scenarios and surprisingly touchy adult content. Edna & Harvey does not reinvent the genre, nor cure the inherent mechanical shortcomings in it, but it made me feel good inside, because it feels like a modern day reimagining of Day of the Tentacle, from which it obviously draws a lot of inspiration. Fun stuff.

Mafia II is a fantastic game for those who wish to take a trip back to the 1940s-1950s and witness an awesome story. It might not be of great value to you if you want a GTA clone set in the 1950s. Bear in mind, this game is also quite unlike LA Noire as well.
I'll make this evident from the start, it is not a "free-roam-GTA-shoot-anything" game, although you do have the freedom to walk about, rob stores and do as you wish, the game encourages you to continue on with the story the entire time. There is no "Free ride / Free roam" option, so it's up to you to engage in your own personal errands between quests.
The strongest point of this game by far is the story. Mafia II is more like watching an interactive movie about the protagonist: Vito Scaletta, a Sicilian man who emigrated to the United States in the 1920s with his family. He is brought up in conditions of borderline poverty, and vows to make a name for himself and become one of the "wise guys" who makes it big in the land of opportunity: Empire Bay, USA.
The story follows the odyssey of Vito and his thug friend Joe, as they work to make big names for themselves in the city. The game time period spans from 1943 to 1952, although the majority of the game takes place during the 1950s. The game features plenty of cars dating from the 1920s to the late 1950s (bonus cars). The vehicle handling is incredibly accurate, and the physics are superb as it mimicks the heavy, rockin' feel of cars from the era. You can also customize cars by adding turbo charging, change the color themes, different wheels, and much more.
The City of Empire Bay in which the game takes place is a vivid and bustling city filled with people, cops, car washes, diners, gun stores, clothing stores, shopping malls, hotels, and plenty more to see during the games story. The city feels "real" and lively, with people roaming the streets and going about their business, right down to realistic tidbits such as people sneezing violently during the winter, or slipping over on the pavement.
Unlike Mafia: City of the Lost Heaven, the cars in Mafia II get a lot more speed. The game also features 3 radio stations including a classics channel that plays music from the previous decade. The world is amazing and very detailed, and the graphics are on par with a lot of modern games. There is also plenty of interesting characters involved in the story.
Gameplay wise, Mafia II is a lot of fun. The game will have you driving to most places (Something made much less tiresome than Mafia 1 as the cars are much quicker and handle much better). Other segments may have you drive others around, or simply do errands and odd jobs. Out of the car, your jobs on foot often involve gunfights and getting from A to B. There are hours of cutscenes which narrates the story in great depth and detail. There is also an arsenal of weaponry to choose from, including the classic Colt 1911A1, a Beretta Submachine gun, an MP40, the "Chicago Typewriter" Thompson Machine gun, Mauser pistol, molotov cocktails and much more!
The game focuses more on a linear experience rather than a sandbox find random jobs/do as you wish world. Every day begins with the protagonist waking up and having to deal with another job or event, some not so pleasant. You are given the option to rob stores or crush cars for money in the game, which can be used to buy guns and ammunition, or buy clothes (However, once you have a gun, you can generally rob a store with ease provided there are no police around).
The Downloadable Content that comes with the Digital Deluxe edition (or can be purchased separately) includes access to additional clothing, but also some additional cars which can put you at an advantage, as some are based on experimental / prototype supercars of the 1950s.
All in all, I'd rate it 9/10. I would have given it a 10 if the story were only a big longer and the city larger. The game is heavily underrated, and under-appreciated for its historical accuracy and attention to detail, perhaps because many people were expecting a Grand Theft Auto clone where you could just explore a vast world and do as you wish.
The game is well optimized and is very stable. I have encountered very little in the way of crashes and bugs with this game.
Mafia II is an experience not to be missed! The game has one of the most gorgeous worlds I've seen, and the story will drag you deep into the life of Vito Scaletta and his odyssey to fame, money, fast cars and guns, but the game also has some very deep lessons; the life of a Mafioso doesn't always go as planned.
+ Amazing story
+ Gorgeous visuals, and a bustling 1950s city to explore
+ Authentic music from the era
+ A plethora of weaponry to choose from
+ Incredibly realistic handling of over 40 cars (over 50 if you select the DLC).
+ Detailed characters with in-depth motion-captured cutscenes
- The overall city in which the game takes places feels a tad too small, and most parts of it are underused (see next con)
- A majority of game quests, features and missions were cut down, resulting in, at best, 6-8 hours of gameplay over 15 chapters instead of the initially planned 80.
- No ability to buy the car you want. You must "steal" the one you want during the era in which it is available.
- Uses a checkpoint system which can be frustrating if you are trying to save money/accumulate items (as you can die and lose everything back to the last checkpoint).

Vampire The Masquerade, is a RPG game around supernatual elements (Mainly focusing on vampires hense the title).

There many differnt types of vampires to pick from as well, allowing for differnt styles of play, want to go in and punch everything? Go for it, want to be a lunatic and beat people with an arm? The game hears that and goes sure why not.

There are some saything this game is  'unplayable' without the patch, that could be the case for some people as I have heard of some compatibility issues, however my first playthough was done without the unofficial patch. So if you find this game does not work, please don't just throw it off saying its broken rubbish - its an old game which is doing increabily well for its age. The patch does also have other tweaks, gameplay elements (such as previously removed missions) balaceing with items and skills. I personally like what I have played of the patch.
Reading into the music of the game, it is said they took a risk using licened music. This is due to the fact music they asked permission to use wont always get the feel of the game across, however the music in VTMBL in my opinion fits perfectly into the dark gritty world that is VTMBL.
TL;DR
VTMBL is a story rich game, good sound, good characters and good dialogue between the characters.

A poor mobile port that is still worth playing.
There are 5 worlds, each containing 30 levels. Every 15 levels or so a new gameplay mechanic is introduced, which works well to keep the game interesting as the mechanics are then combined to increase complexity.
Each level is comprised of 3 tasks that need to be accomplished sequentially. The way with which you complete a task affects whether or not it is possible to complete the next one and so on. As such, you often need to plan ahead to make sure you have enough sheep/wolves/pigs to save/kill. While it's not necessary to get 3 stars to advance, I feel without the challenge I'd be bored, particularly because finishing just the first 2 tasks is always easy.
The humorous premise and cute creepy visuals, the overall number of levels and gameplay mechanics, along with the (always acceptable) challenge combine for a worthy experience.
The size of the buttons, the menu navigation, lack of options, no working alt+tab, and no cloud saves make it clear little effort was put into bringing the game to Steam. The controls are also better suited for a touch screen. As such, you may be better off getting it on mobile, but it is good enough that I can recommend it on PC as well.

LISA the Overrated
I might be learning disabled because I can't seem to derive meaning from a lifelong pattern of being disappointed by games that were overwhelmingly praised for their story. On the other hand, it occurs to me that it's this vocal majority that suffers from a learning disability because they don't understand what "story" means. The story is the sequence of actions and events that propels a narrative forward. Of the 5 hours I played, only the first 10 minutes contained any story. The other 4 hours and 50 minutes was a loop of "grind for EXP -> boss -> darn, ya just missed your daughter".
Often, people mistakenly say "story" when they mean "characters" or "atmosphere". Even so, the characters of LISA are absurd caricatures slapped onto disposable damage sponges. They're not charming, deep or endearing. They're just there to even the odds  against your enemies. As for atmosphere...there are the makings of it sprinkled throughout the game...but the disparate elements never converge into a cohesive or coherent whole. You can see the vision the creator had, but the game, unfortunately, fails to manifest it completely. Everything ends up feeling like a cheap parody instead of a genuine post-apocalypse.
Of course, the failing of the story (or perhaps its pacing) might be overlooked if the aforementioned 4 hours and 50 minutes were spent enjoyably. And if I was the sort of man who enjoyed mental/emotional grinds, I suppose they would've been. But I'm not...and they weren't. I will proceed to catalog in detail why that time was not fun:
The combat is pointlessly shallow, rivaling rock-paper-scissors at the height of its strategic apex. If your party isn't composed of the worst characters and you're not dangerously under-leveled, combat consists of pressing Enter until it's over.
The oft touted "dramatic/meaningful choices" chalk up to mild inconveniences for the most part. My personal favorites: "Lose a party member or sacrifice easily obtained items from your inventory" and "A party member has been kidnapped so now you must backtrack for 5 minutes to retrieve him without so much as a confrontation with the guilty party".
The equally oft touted "dark humor" is...there...in some disjointed fashion. There are dark bits that are clearly trying to be funny but aren't. And then there are ridiculous one liners at the end of battles that will either tickle your taint or not. Some of those one liners were surprisingly good.
The music consists of 2 tracks that are pleasant, catchy and original and 3 or 4 additional tracks that are generic and grating. The rest is just ambient noise. However, I can see why the 2 enjoyable tracks would have people raving about the soundtrack. It's a classic case of surpassing a void of expectation. And that about sums up this game and its overwhelmingly positive rating.
The idea of LISA and its Mad Max-ian, deranged-mutant-freakshow-of-a-world is a delightfully refreshing and singular take on the seemingly-beaten-to-death setting of civil collapse. But executing that idea as a parody with generic JRPG mechanics in GameMaker (of all things) was, I think, a mistake. One that lead to disappointment, dissatisfaction, and dullness in the wake of expected refreshment.

A new engine (Deponia’s), a new protagonist, and a lot more serious tone with pitch black humour: this is Harvey’s New Eyes in a nutshell. The sequel of Edna & Harvey is still a lot of fun to play for any casual and hardcore adventure game fan, but only if you are not the type who gets disturbed easily.
Edna & Harvey: Harvey’s New Eyes is more of a spiritual successor to ‘The Breakout’ than an actual sequel, even though you will see many familiar faces and places throughout the story.
From a technical standpoint, it is closer to Deponia: same engine, same user interface, similar multi-chapter story structure and difficulty. This also carries the advantage of using more refined point ‘n’ click mechanics for the small price of sacrificing the charm of a well-made indie game that made ‘The Breakout’ so charismatic.
One of the most defining features of this game is the humour– humour darker than the core of a black hole. Seriously. If you get disturbed about children dying gruesome, horrible deaths, don’t ever buy this one. It may look cartoonish, but that is just one of the clever tools to make the player feel uncomfortable. Another is the narrator who does a perfect job of telling a seemingly innocent tale about a little girl in a way that sends shivers down your spine.
The writing is excellent. Yes, it is disturbing in many places and it is disturbingly cruel with most of the cast, but the characters also fit in their role in the plot perfectly.
It’s the small things though that shows the brilliance. Things like not letting the protagonist say even a single word in any dialogue yet still being able to carry meaningful conversations with everyone. Sure, it sounds insane to essentially cripple your dialogues, one of the main aspects of an adventure game, but sometimes being crazy works. And aren’t we all a little cuckoo in our own ways anyway?

You are Vito Scaletta, Italian war hero who gets saved from the horrors of war by childhood friend and mafioso Joe Barbaro. From that point on, with Joe by your side, you are thrust into a tangled web of Empire baby, divided between three families. Fans of Goodfellas, the Godfather, or any 1940s-50s era gangsters will feel right at home. The game is divided up into "chapter" segments, which can be replayed at any time.
The game engine (while having some hilarious physics glitches) is smooth and beyond optimized. The facial texturing and animation excels at times and falls short at others. Let it also be known that there is no animation for walking up and down stairs, something you spend a surprising amount of time doing. However, to make up for it, the game possesses beautiful fabric physics that can be experienced simply by buying a coat. NVidia card owners with PhysX will appreciate 2K's efforts.
Perfect voice acting, realistic cars and gunfire, more songs from the era in the radio stations than in Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas
, and a stunning orchestral score with a single haunting melody that will visit you both in the game's menu and the game's stunning (albeit mysterious) ending.
Aside from lockpicking and some other interludes, nothing sets the gameplay apart from GTA in terms of driving and a third-person shooter. The game does include a speed limiter on the cars, which locks your highest possible speed at the speed limit, since the cops in this game are actually smart (in a sense) and come after you for speeding. You can also customize any car you procure, including changing the plates.
The vintage Playboy pinups the game uses as collectables add much to the playtime, but the game has no real freeroam. It can be modded in, as the glorious PC Master Race allows, but it does not come available out of the box.

Almost a perfect game but ultimately falls short because of a few glaring issues.
Mafia 2 has the best atmosphere of any game I have played. You play as a gangster in the 1940s-1950s and you feel like you are in the world. Everything about the cars, buildings, stores, and even the radio convinces you that you really are in that city. When you drive around and hear about the remote control being invented or see more powerful and modern cars as time progresses. The attention to detail is very nice with the speedometer being time correct, the radio tuning in on actual music from that era, and the cars being♥♥♥♥♥♥to handle and not going very fast. I have a HD 4000 and I can only run the game on the lowest settings but it still looks good enough to soak in the atmosphere
The story of the game revolves the typical mafia story of a guy who "started from the bottom" and grew his way up until he did something that made him realize that crime never plays. Its cliché but it’s a very good story here. The characters in this game feel real with you feel emotionally invested in your character hoping they make the choices you do.
The mechanics are OK with standard 3rd person shooter stuff. The game relies a lot on realism so you die faster. There is regenerating health but each time it recovers to a lower degree. There are stealth mechanics but you utilize them in maybe 2-3 missions depending on how you count them so they are kind of worthless. You get cool time period weapons with the classic Tommy being the weapon you rely on the most. You almost never have to buy any because you just pick them off the dead guys in missions with shooting. You have to use cover in the game and it feels fluid except when you want to go into covers along walls because Vito can’t figure out which wall (of a corner) to stick to.
A MAJOR issue with the game is that the sandbox is a lie (sort of). There is a large map where you can go and explore but 1) there isn’t anything to do and 2) there is no free roam. Normally, in sandbox games, you explore the world until you choose to start a mission but here, the moment you wake up, you have a mission to do. You can (in certain levels) go out and explore but the problem is that there isn’t anything you can do with that exploration except soak in the atmosphere. There are no side activities and two guys you meet who can give you work never have work for you. You can rob stores but all that happens is that it gives you money. The missions are all linear and they have zones which limit you. Mostly you just drive through the city doing... nothing. There is a mission where you are wanted and you have to get home without being spotted and that is where the city comes alive. With you having to create your own path through a live city trying to avoid the cops. But most of the levels is simply go here, shoot this, go here, shoot this, and drive home, sleep, and repeat. Also, there isn’t a free play mode at the end so you can’t experience the city without the missions.
The story also seemed rushed at the end. There were a lot of betrayals and twists and at the end I was like, "that’s it?" It honestly left me disappointed because the story had been pretty god so far. Speaking of the story, it kind of renders the point of money useless. You use the money to buy clothes and... More clothes but halfway through, you lose all that and you start over... Kind of renders the point of money useless.
In other matters, the cars handle like♥♥♥♥♥♥but that’s probably on purpose. The police are more real meaning that you can hit something and not raise your wanted level if a cop doesn't see you but they are kind of stupid because you can rob a store, steal clothes from the store and walk out without them recognizing you. The character animation is good but they look really plasticy. The camera has trouble in narrow spaces and I only had one bug.
Overall, it’s still a good game. Good mechanics and atmosphere but it lacks in execution and flutters out in the end. I still think it’s a good game but it could have been an amazing game.

I think that this game has been getting unfair negative reviews. I'll admit that my main thematic interests reside in WWII and 40s era material, as well as how the mobster genre has gained my attention as well. However, that did not influence my positive position on this game.
Mafia II has been compared to the Gran Theft Auto series and Saints Row series, but does not seem to stack up against them. That is probably because the people that see the game that way are simply looking for a casual shoot-em-up game where you get into ridiculous scenarios. Mafia II is not so much a shooter (although there is a considerable amount of gunplay), but more of a simulator. The way that the story is structured is meant to show the player what it might be like to work your way up from the bottom to higher tiers within the Italian mob. I read a few of the negative reviews, all of which complain about "boring, pointless missions" like the infamous "stacking crates" and courier missions. However, they failed to note that the purpose of these jobs are to show that the protagonist was faced with the choice of working legit jobs and earning very little, or doing risky, illegal things to earn more, quicker.
There are some fun little details that they put into the game that I cannot help but feel a bit enthralled about. Nothing really important, but more like the ability to open and close the hood/trunk of your car, the police will cite you for speeding or driving recklessly, and general interaction with the environment (light switches, radios, faucets, etc). It should be noted that this is an older game, but it can stand with some of the modern RPGs in terms of playability. It may not have a sprawling and over-populated city like in GTA IV or V, but more like a population of GTA: Vice City.
As far as the game goes in terms of story, mechanics, and playability, I would have to give it an 8.5/10. If you have any interest in era based games or being a REAL gangster, this might be something you'll want to take a gander at.

A Story About My Uncle is a 3D Platformer game that featuring a guy with a suit that has a grapple and can fire up leg boosters in an adventure to find his lost uncle.
Visually impressive, the graphics are so amazing and the environment is too beautiful. And the soundtracks are great too. However, it’s gets repetitive and boring after the first two levels.
It’s the same formula over and over from the beginning to the end, you grab on floating objects to get into tiny rocks or islands then grabble on floating objects to get into other rocks/islands. Because of this, it’s too easy to get lost when no checkpoint is around, and sometimes the checkpoints get far from each other, this is not a problem until the game becomes difficult and frustrating with its mechanics.
I don’t know why the grapple manage to hook up with something from a certain distance, but sometimes refuse on similar-distance objects and/or when they closer. Same story with the jump, every time you do a dash jump, the height of the jump and the trajectory differs, this made some parts very frustrating to be honest if you keep thinking you will get the same results.
Let’s go back to the story, the story is really generic, a guy goes on a journey searching for his uncle, finding a little girl in his way and both share some dialogues that doesn’t give the story any depth or details. After so many swinging and rage quitting, what’s the ending all about? Nothing at all, no twists, no surprises, no sad moments and no actual development, few sentences and the credits begin to roll up. Really disappointed by the ending and the story overall.
Besides, the voice acting of the main protagonist is really bad, it doesn't have character at all.
It feels awkward when he finally finds his uncle, his voice has no sense of joy or emotions, it's too dull.
A Story about my uncle has its good moments, it starts off as a promising game but unfortunately it’s only fun for a while and the story, which hook you up at first is totally nothing to look forward.
Give it a try, not a terrible game, but not a great one either.
