Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is really one of the best RPGs ever made - it's actually like that, not overhyping. The writing in this game is simply amazing. The subject topic - vampires, that is - is not only treated in an incredibly mature way, it's also being satirized upon in true postmodern fashion, since Kindred scoff at superstitious weapons like holy water, garlic, and stakes, and make fun of multiple stereotypes spawned by popular culture. It doesn't end there, however. Bloodlines is probably the best game to read. The dialogue is a wonderful mixture of styles that spawns some of the real-est and deepest characters to grace our computers. Every character feels different, and it's not just because of the textures. They all have their traits, philosophies, values, quirks, filler words and speech impediments. Bloodlines kind of rivals a novel at this point, especially considering how they rewrote ALL of the player lines and added new ones for the NPCs, all of which you'll get to see if you're playing as a Malkavian. The quests in this game are very enjoyable and always offer you a multitude of ways to get them done. Also, prepare to laugh a lot. It's not just because some character cracked a funny joke - sometimes, the way dialogue is delivered in this game is simply hilarious,
I wish I could stop there, but I really have to mention the gameplay. The game itself is nothing difficult - it's really easy to pick up and get going, though it is a bit unorthodox in the sense that melee combat is third person only (that really required some getting used to). However, since Activision doesn't like letting developers finish their games, the player is treated to a very barebones mediocre combat system, full of awkward glitches and bad hit detection. It doesn't really ruin the game - it gets the job done and rarely puts you at a disadvantage, but it's still there. This is also the second game to run on the Source engine, and since the engine itself was a work in progress, Troika had to quickly adapt to the unfamiliar Source. Lack of familiarity, broken code and the unfinished state of the engine itself led to the fact that this game is a glitchy mess even outside of combat. Player animations in cutscenes are weird as hell (not lipsyncing though - that still looks good), random pedestrians sometimes pull a Barry Allen and zoom all over the map, and the physics are borderline broken, with clutter and ragdolls simply too eager to fly around the room if you so much as touch them. Also, don't even think of playing this game without the Unofficial patch (if you somehow missed literally everyone on the web saying this).
I've probably said too much than I'd like about the game's flaws, but, hopefully, they won't stop you from picking up this game. Bloodlines is an experience too good to pass up, and beating this game kind of left a huge hole in my heart that I soon will fill by replaying this again, and again, and again.
Thanks to my homie Zak for giving his cash to Bobby Kotick instead of mine!

To be honest, it is extremely hard to do it justice with a simple review, especially so by keeping it short.
If you can forgive its bugginess and clunky controls/camera, (for the most part solved thanks to the amazing unofficial patch that you MUST install before playing) it offers among the most amazing variety of interesting characters both in written and acting/voiceover that ever graced our computer screens in an rpg.
It has a whole lot of "not hand holding" quests with quite a few different approaches thanks to a very good level design and the different tools at your disposal thanks to your own character skills/traits/clan and how YOU want to play your character.
Yes because this is indeed a role playing game at heart, it's not just about "stats" and "level ups", there are choices to make, characters that can betray you or you can betray before they do.
It will allow you to do things your way, even ignoring most quests, but will reward you (not only with money or experience, but by amusing you) for exploring and trying different approaches and solving also the secondary quests, which in some cases will intertwine beutifully, developing in full branches to be solved as you progress through the different areas of the game.
It's a true masterpiece that deserves to be played, more than once (to experience how different each playthrough can be), I would reccomend it to anyone for how much I love it, but it's not for everyone.
Don't pick it up if you are easily swayed by dated graphics or lack of focus/depth to the combat. In bloodlines you can go gun blazing if you want, but it hardly pays off and it's definitely not the way it's meant to be played.
All of those who like a real rpg, be SURE to grab this one, if you haven't done so already!

One Way Heroics is one hell of an interesting concept - A mix of 'forced scrolling' RPG concept, as said by the developer, Smoking WOLF, himself on his triumphant Playsim product page:
I have to say, it is strangely addicting at the least, and the addition of forced scrolling really adds an extra level of depth to an RPG concept.
The game plays like a rougelike 8-bit top down JRPG, if you can imagine that - every step you take, and every action you take, a turn is made. The game will then play out the rest of the character on the screen's moves - damage taken, monsters moved, status effects applied. There's a catch, though. The world you are in is subjected by an encroaching 'darkness', which will move from the left edge of the screen by one pixel every turn. A cold, chilling touch from this darkness will send your body flying into the air (or so you're told) and your character will die from what I assume to be asyphxiation from the cold vacuum of space. So effectively, you must plan your next moves, and be sure you aren't trapped or caught fighting, or else succumb to a frosty death.
Combat in the game is that of classic rougelike RPGs - press a button to attack, and you will attack in that direction. This makes combat smooth and doesn't impede on the sense of urgency the scrolling darkness imposes. You will soon find yourself trotting along the landscape, uninterupted and fleeting from the ever-infringing darkness. However, it does have the challenge to it - after all, it is a rougelike and will have different layouts if you so choose to play a randomly generated one. Sometimes, the game will throw obstacles in your way that require you to think ahead in order to escape the deathly left edge of the screen - climbing mountains, swimming through water, fighting, breaking down walls will take precious turns, and you must decide weather if you can wing it, or play it safe.
What I love about this game and has kept me intrigued is the progression, not only through one game session but across multiple game sessions - a la Rouge Legacy, at the end of each session you will gain 'Hero Points', points that allow you to unlock various different starting perks, and allow you to purchase new classes if you don't want to meet the objectives for unlocking them. From this, I take away a kind of Dark Souls mentality - your starting class is just what you start with, and what you make of your character during the game is up to you, for example I could start with a knight class, which has low agility, but stack agility starting perks to make him agile and combo more hits in an attack turn. This allowed me to decide right at the start of an adventure what kind of character I wanted to play - the treasure hunter, who has a high lockpicking skill, the ranged hero, who is quick to escape, or the tank, who has high vitality. It also has the allure of getting benifits from NPCs, too. There is a gold system in place, and you'll find yourself picking up strewn items (which are abundant) from the floor and selling them for cash at the next town or city you come across.
Overall, the game definately hits all the right RPG notes whilst still maintaining action. Characters can have party members, different classes, spells, abilities and must actively manage their time, stamina and energy to escape the darkness and ultimately defeat the demon lord. You can also choose the level of challenge you want, each world you choose will give you the option to play 'A Walk In The Park' mode which pits you against the boss at a certain distance travelled, or 'Afternoon Stroll' where the boss will appear at different intervals. Music will change dynamically depending on the terrain you're in, for example in a dungeon or in a town, and the art style is the classic 8-bit sprite look.
If you're a fan of roguelike RPGs like Sword of the Star and Half Minute Hero, then you'll love this game, and the apocalyptic twist of darkness chasing you will add a refreshing approach to the RPG genre. That being said, it is a very unique experience and you'd really have to try it out to understand the game.

I had my eye on this game for a while - thinking it would probably be charming enough for me to pass a few hours on - holy♥♥♥♥♥♥was i wrong. This is a true gem, and at the 70 cents i bought it at it sure is a steal.
You play a nameless (well, you name them) "hero" - you are destined to save the world from the ever spreading darkness - swallowing up the world and creating monsters.
You create a character from one of the starting classes - swordsman, knight etc - all with their own advantages and specialties, and can enhance them further at the start with perks.
Then you pick a world from one of the daily specialties, randomly generate your own to type in some gibberish or word to generate one. (this way if you got a world you like you can get it back again).
The game plays as a kinda turn based action RPG - there are a few different weapon types (which you can use any of, not limited by class - though some classes are better with certain gear) with their own uses - spears can hit two blocks away, axes  are generally less accurate but are strong as sh*t and break walls and boxes easily, swords being a middle ground. All weapons are limited by their durability and all can be upgraded with items you find (and repaired). When you die (or win, or suicide) the game ends and you get an evaluation score of your playthrough - the better you do the more points you get, which can then be spent on permanent upgrades (new classes, perks and increasing your bank size).
The bank is where you can store your most prized items at the end of a playthrough - you can also withdraw from the bank at the start of a playthrough.
There are numerous companions you can get to travel with you, some with hidden or unique ways to access.They can help in battle and protect you from hits - though if they die you lose them... so be careful. There are also a bunch of different endings and ways to finish the game, which i shouldnt really spoil - google them if you want to.
Every few turns the left side of the screen will move to the right and basically force you onwards - so dont go dungeon hunting too long or you might get stuck against a wall as you are swallowed by the darkness.

Divide by Sheep is a pretty simple and straightforward puzzle game. The premise is that Death is lonely, and decides to collect himself some animal friends. Thus, the game centers around killing cute, fuzzy creatures.
Really, the game is at its core about manipulating objects – sheep, wolves, and pigs – around a 2D environment. There are a series of platforms laid out in a grid, and each platform has anywhere between 1 and 9 spaces on it for animals to stand on. If you boot an animal over onto another platform, and there isn’t room for it, it will be ejected from it. If you put wolves onto a platform with sheep or pigs, or vice-versa, the wolves will eat the sheep/pigs and become fat and immobile, locking off spaces from landing on them. If you bounce pigs onto a platform with sheep, the pigs will land on the sheep and kill them. If anything is on a platform with a pig, only the pig will be ejected when you launch from it.
These simple rules, combined with a few other things – a fence preventing ejection between platforms; a laser cutter which chops sheep in half (but not other things), doubling the space they take up; TNT spots, which blow up if nothing is left on the platform, removing it from play; frying spots, which burn up one animal on them per move; burners, which are turned off by buttons on another platform; a portal platform, which teleports back excess animals instead of killing them; a bounce pad, which immediately ejects any animal which lands on it onto one or more adjacent platforms (some will eject onto two, splitting the animals evenly between them); and a totem, which kills anything else on the platform it is on but can be bounced around from platform to platform by the player and is otherwise invincible – make up the gameplay.
The goal is to ship out three sets of animals, in order. Boats come on the top-left of the screen, and your goal is to load exactly the right number of exactly the right kind of animal onto the boats. There are boats for each of the wolves, sheep, and pigs, as well as a boat for Death himself, which requires you to kill X many animals (making their souls appear on his boat), and a sea monster, which just requires X amount of any sort of animal (it isn’t a picky eater). There’s also a boat for a totem on a few of the levels.
The boats won’t leave until they’re filled (or overfilled), and while you only have to get one right to progress, you need to get almost all of the boats filled to unlock consecutive worlds.
Thus, the goal is to get exactly the right number of animals onto the boats using the various platforms and mechanics given to you. The game gradually introduces new mechanics over its length, adding about one new mechanic every 10-15 levels, helping it to keep itself relatively fresh as it adds ever more complexity to its puzzles.
Overall, the game has 150 levels, spanning 5 worlds, and takes somewhere on the order of 6-8 hours to 100%. It isn’t terribly hard, generally speaking, but a few of them levels require quite a bit of cleverness to solve; none of the levels takes more than a minute or so to solve correctly, but you may be stuck on them for ten times that long if you can’t figure out the right trick. It is ultimately very much math-based, and oftentimes the process of elimination is necessary to try and figure out all the ways that clearly won’t work, so you can figure out the one way that will.
This is a fairly decent puzzle game, and the mechanics work well for what it is. However, it is very simple, and unless you really enjoy simple puzzle games without much in the way of story or anything else, there’s nothing else here for you.
That being said, this is really a game you will probably enjoy more on your phone than on your PC; it isn’t a sit down and play it for hours game (though you can do so), it is more of a throwaway thing.
Overall, this is very squarely directed at a puzzle game player – the sort of simple puzzle game you might play on your phone or a similar mobile device. If you like pure puzzle games, this is a decent game, but it is hard for me to muster much enthusiasm for it - while it certainly was clever at times, and its mechanics were simple and clean, I just was never wowed by it. It is just sort of a par for the course game - never quite dull, but never all that interesting, either. If you don’t like pure puzzle games, or if you like plot or purpose or anything else, this game will likely bore you.

Looking for a game you can enjoy for just the story? You're going to be frustrated by the difficulty (but it's not impossible).
Looking for a Challenge? You might find this game a tad easier than you're used too (even if the end is debatable on that aspect).
Looking for a game where all the elements make it enjoyable? Get this one. The story is great the voice acting is surprisingly decent and the enviornments are interesting. The attention to detail in some areas as well is amazing, and everything just looks cool.
I found the platforming to be difficult but this was my first time playing a first person platformer (though I have played other kinds of platformers). I don't recommend using a controller to play this game because of the quick reflexes you need to click on objects to swing yourself from place to place - that reflex is REQUIRED, ESPECIALLY for the last area - trying to whip your head around to nab at falling objects is harder then it sounds.
There are also collectibles to find, both of no story value (if you wanna find them all go ahead) and ones that give more story dialogue (which I recommend you find they're great). Looking around for them can be tedious, but that's only really because there's nothing else to look for besides all of those but if you just want to find the story ones for the extra information there is a guide where you can find em all if you don't feel like scouring the place for them.
Again I'm gonna say the platforming is difficult - I looked up videos after I completed the game and found there were quite a few people saying the game was too hard (which I don't believe myself) or was too irritating to finish (you have to be super precise with your grapple equipment - you can't waste charges unless you know you'll be landing on a platform) but if you think a bit more and try not to hit your head on all the floating boulders it's not that bad... Well for me it wasn't. I still have to agree that this game was frustrating but the pleasant music in some places and the story dialogue (and enviornments) eased my mind off of it for the most part.
If it helps they have been doing fixes to the game occasionally from what I can tell to make some parts that were a bit too punishing easier for players that didn't come just for the challenge.
I think this is when you beat the game only (I didn't honestly check) but there's a time trial where you can speedrun through the areas you previously did in the main game. If you really wanna practice with the platforming or you really liked the gameplay itself feel free to do those - you can also replay stages too, but I'm not 100% sure if you can reget the collectibles that way if you missed them.
..Also as a side note why was there a dead whale that was never brought up in story dialogue who is he why is he not in water where did he come from-
If the price tag concerns you for how long the game actually is (About 2 hours give or take depending on how long it takes you to clear some areas) it's definately a good grab when it's on sale. If it concerns you on anything else (that's price related) I'd still grab it when it's on sale - it's a great game.

I've played this game since it first came out over 10 years ago, and brutha lemme tell you; It. Never. Gets. Old. We have a deep DEEEP story filled with vampire lore and the ability to choose how you maneuver through both the world and combat. Stealth, rambo, manipulation are always on the table for every encounter save a few choice moments where there would clearly be no other choice but to fight.
We have an astounding soundtrack full of big name bands from yesteryear to set the 'gothic' tone of the game. Combine the soundtrack with what I would say is a 98% fully voiced over game with CONVINCING voice acting and you can get swallowed up pretty quickly.
Graphically this game is beyond it's time. for a 2004 title to still be playable and enjoyable in 2017 says something great about it's developers. one or four character models may be a bit wonky (no seriously there's no way that guy's jaw is shaped like that) but with a bit of imagination, they just look like scars or genetic defects
as far as gameplay is concerned, it's up to you brutha. I've gone through whole playthroughs using nothing but powers, fueled by the blood of my enemies and a few bloodpacks in my inventory (I MUST FEEEEEEEEEED). I've done whole melee playthoughs (last boss was tricky af). I've even just used fists (preferred method) the whole way through. Your clan choice helps steer you in a particular direction but in the end it's up to you how you fight.
Additional note about clans: they DO alter conversations and offer specific side quests. And once you can unlock a history, those too add some subtle changes to how you play. You'd think puking from feeding from a bum or rat wouldn't affect you much until you're out of options.
All in all, this game is a for sure buy. Even redemption (think diablo) is worth the purchase. If you want an A-class game without the flowery HD graphics or gimmicks that are in most modern titles, this is it.

*shakes head sadly*  Such a pity.
Look, I like roguelikes.  I really do.  I've played a good few, and I enjoy a desperate struggle with limited resources, where every choice matters and one bad move can ruin an entire run.  I like to have to make hard decisions and cheat death through careful planning, frantic improvisation and the rare lucky break.
Hack Slash Loot is the antithesis of those things.
Unless the game has undergone a  total makeover in terms of design since I last played it, it's a broken, pointless roguelike in which you stand absolutely no chance in hell of surviving (unless you get lucky and get a Holy/Virtue element weapon that boosts your stats with each hit, right at the start of your run).
The most potent strategy you have is "Stand in front of a doorway to fight the enemies one on one, and pray that the guys stuck behind the guy you're hitting don't loop around and flank you before you kill them all one at a time".  You can't even RUN.  The enemies chase you forever like homing missiles and will not stop until you've bopped them on the head enough to kill them.  There's no class-specific skills to use and manage either.  It's all about the items you find and pick up.  And getting them?  Random.  There are virtually no hard choices in the game.  Just roll the dice and pray you make it.
It's like playing russian roulette with a fully loaded gun.  There is no skill.  Only luck.  Winning (Or even PROGRESS) is impossible unless you get insanely lucky.
If you want a roguelike, go play FTL (a much better game), or Dungeons of dredmor.  Hell, if you want an action-based roguelike, Eldritch is pretty good and actually takes skills and quick thinking to beat.  Go play those or the many other good roguelikes out there.  Avoid hack slash loot at all costs.

A Story About My Uncle is a game that instantly popped out to me, when looking through the Steam Specials a couple of weeks ago. For $2 CDN, an adventure game with a cool gimmick? Why not?!
The game features a suit that allows you to "swing" around very open (and beautiful, I might add) environmenta, similar to Spiderman. More features come to the suit later, but I won't go in depth there. The features seem to work very well, even on a controller, where moving your cursor around isn't easy. I found that I was stuck on some parts of some levels, but only because my cursor didn't move fast enough to reach the object with my beam and continue swinging. I'd imagine that this would be at least a little easier with a keyboard and mouse.
While this game does have beautiful graphics, very good voice acting, and wonderful gimmicks to keep users playing through the adventure, there are some quirks in this game, which can be fixed:
I found that, with the energy crystals that are supposed to refill your beam energy, some of them just didn't work. At all. No matter how close or far I got from them, they would not refill my energy. The option didn't even come up. This lead me to reverse-engineering the game's physics, in lack of a better term, to advance through the game in a way that I'm sure the developers did not intend the game to be beaten.
The ability to reach certain objects with your beam from certain distances are also inconsistent. Some objects I can reach when I'm extremely far away from, while other objects, I can't reach when I'm only half as far. This also lead me to just guessing and misusing my abilities, making it harder for me to advance through the game.
The ending. No spoilers, but the ending leaves much to be desired. I wish the game would have gone further; really expanded on what was given to the player. I spent around 4 hours on the game, and the game feels unfinished; like it's just a demo. A $13 (but on sale for $2) demo. It really feels like there should have been more to the story part, to at least make the game FEEL longer. After putting through several, strenuous hours of gameplay, you get to your destination, and it's all over. No going back. The added epilogue was nice, but it still doesn't make the ending any better. It just draws out the feeling of "Is this really it?", which is very dissapointing.
The extras and unlockables are a nice touch to the game. Although I didn't even realize they were a thing until I unlocked the first one. I will most likely go back and scourge the levels again to find the collectibles to unlock the ones I haven't gotten yet.
Overall, the game was worth the money for me. A very good proof-of-concept that should have been expanded on at least a little bit more, but was still very fun to play in it's time. I would 100% recommend someone to get this game,, especially if it goes on sale.

Welcome to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Precise Platforming Theatre.
This game has the most precise platforming with some of the worst accompanying physics that I've ever played. You are expected to make the most pixel-perfect jumps with the strongest gravity in gaming history, and then follow it up with more dumb jumps which you can only just barely make, and if you miss that second jump, you're back to the first one again with no chance to practice the second jump.
The game also requires Battletoads-esque memorization in some parts with many beginner's traps which lead you to get yourself stuck in the wrong places due to a checkpoint in an optional area where you CANNOT GO BACK. So, you end up wasting your time in an area you don't have to go because the game literally trapped you into a side area. Also, due to the copious amount of infinite-corridor type challenges, you can sometimes end up going back into challenges which you've just done (after 10 minutes of brute force) and having to redo something you literally just did, like in the room "You Definitely Shouldn't Go Left", where you might think that you SHOULD go left, and get stuck in the room before it. And before you call me stupid for falling for that, that's just one of many examples of this.
And all of that wouldn't even be so bad if I knew where I was supposed to be going. With no map, no pronounced end goal, and every platform being the same shades of pink (don't even joke about the blue blocks, that's not what I mean and you know it) everything blends together and you don't know where you're going, where you've been, and where you're not supposed to be, meaning you don't even know when you're going the right way. And before someone says that's a stylistic choice and a necessity for a non-linear game, I should point out that this game actually does follow a linear progression in the form of the multiple power-ups, which let you go to the next "area" of the game. Also, there are many non-linear games which do actually let you know where you are and where you've been, like "The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past", where every area of the map has a different aesthetic, not to mention that you do actually have a map which tells you vaguely where you should go to progress.
In short, this game isn't worth your time. You will get frustrated from the platforming and the beginner's traps, and won't even get the pat on the back of getting past it because you don't know if you're going the right way. And it never gets better, only exponentially more unfair and unfun the more you play. And don't tell me I can't complain because it's free, because playing this game did have a price: my time. And this game was not at ALL worth my time.

The presents a very open map with lots of branching baths, but each save point (no, you can't do it manually) disappears upon use. Because your the path forward is so ill-defined and you do so much wandering, it's very easy to explore through a lot of content without any possibility of saving.
And then a game over for any reason, or simply having to leave your computer, means your hosed.
Limited saves like this work for some action games because the content is still kind of fun to repeat, but a game like this with so much focus on dialogue and very plain movement makes for really tedious make-up playing.
I think the save limitations are there to prevent going back on hard choices, and this does make sense, but this was implemented very poorly and ruins what might have been a really interesting game.

You start the game by eaither answering questions and letting the game decide the character that best suits you, or, choose a gender and clan and distribute your stats. You can steal from homes and businesses to sell stuff at pawn shops, pickup side quests from locals, or lure people into alleyways to feed and restore your blood meter. If you can look beyond how dated this game looks and feels, I believe you will enjoy the time you spend in this world.

You're a special forces soldier who seems more interested in his secret crush for his General rather than fighting against the aliens invading Earth: once you've stopped drooling over him you'll be going through several missions where you'll be trying to turn the tide of the war.
Battle for the Sun is a very basic and dull FPS with a gameplay that can be summed up as sprint through bare levels/ shoot a few aliens while getting in cover whenever needed/ look for the next waypoint/ rinse and repeat.
-cutscenes are unintentionally funny in a "so bad/ cheesy it's good" way
-bad graphics, low res textures, blurry environments, lights clip through objects and models look lifeless
-embarassing animations, walking characters seem to be sliding around and their feet will sometimes clip through each other: enemies killed while prone will also sometimes stand up before doing their death animation
-terrible sound, weapons sound extremely weak, voice acting is bad and suffers from awful recording quality
-barebones story and what little can be found is cliched and badly written , most missions even lack an explanation on why you're doing what you're doing
-actual gameplay is poor, weapons are overpowered and extremely precise (even shotguns kill from half a level away), grenades and rpgs have an huge area of effect, aliens are only effective due to homing shots, large areas between alien encounters are just boring to navigate
-basic AI can even have problems navigating stairs or reacting to enemies on different heights
-dull, repetitive level design
-beeped out swearing is as silly as it sounds
-tacked on "skill system" has little to no effect on actual gameplay
-extremely short, took me less than an hour and a half
Battle for the Sun is at least good for a laugh if you got it for free like me, the cutscenes and dialogues alone are so bad and silly- as if they were written by a young overexcited teen- to easily make you laugh. Seriously, just look them up online. Sadly that's all there's to it as once you're done laughing at how terrible everything is you're still left with an hour long game to play through, if you're so inclined.
Gunplay is bad, shotgun trumps everything basically as it can headshot and one shot kill aliens from miles away: on the other hand aliens are extremely weak so the devs decided to give them homing shots that follow the player and can also curve through corners if you dont sidestep fast enough. But don't be worried, if you die you'll restart at the last checkpoint and everything you've killed stays dead so there's basically no challenge whatsoever or penalties for dying. Moving on sounds are bad, voice actors seem to have worked using a potato for a recorder, the skill system does absolutely nothing and the lack of explanation for your objectives makes every mission an uninteresting chore...why am I gathering boxes in a cave? why am I destroying that purple sphere? no one knows.
Even though it can be good for a chuckle if you happen to own it there's no real reason for you to buy this game as there's nothing fun to be found here: even if you can stomach most of the Cons I've listed the game is simply boring and dull.

A Story About My Uncle is a relatively short, but clever, game that focuses on flinging yourself through the air, grappling on to various targets and generally hopping about and traversing large, open areas. You'll fall to your death a lot, but as you get the hang of how the grapple system flows, you'll soon be racing through the air and having a ton of fun.
There are a few hiccups; while the story is well told (as simple as it is), the voice acting is mediocre. While I found the gameplay fun overall, there were certainly spots where there simply weren't enough environmental clues to point you in the direction you were supposed to be heading, making for some pointless deaths as you simply inch forwards and learn the path of the route your supposed to take.
These are minor gripes, though. Overall ASAMU is a fun little game with a clever and well-implemented gameplay mechanic.

The gameplay in this game is the most important start of it. It is what makes this game so amazing. The main premise is you are a player who has access to a suit which let's you swing back and forth between a variety of objects. The settings are interesting where you can explore an overwhelming cave, and mountain encassed in ice, and a city designed in floating rocks. This is the best part of the game, moving between platforms to make it to your destination, with a variety of suit upgrades as your progress. Along with the story mode, you are also given a time trial that is actually extremely difficult to get a gold medal, and this will be the main mode that gives this game a longer life span. This simple element of platforming gives the gameplay a 10/10!
The story is where I feel it is lacking. The story starts out with you doing a simple task: searching for your missing uncle who doubles as an adventurer. This is a unique concept as you are literally flung into a world you know nothing about. The only problem I have with the story is that it is lacking in so many places it makes it hard to follow. It leaves a lot of gaps open that don't explain enough to give your a proper sense, and it has a lackluster ending that is more disappointing then anything. I would give it a 6/10, since the little we are given is really fun.
The games graphics aren't too imporant, but they are nice. The backgrounds of the game are amazing and beautiful, and if you like taking screenshots of games like I do, then you are going to have fun here. The rest of the game is lackluster, however, is bland and I feel this is the only part of the game that I dislike. The player models and animations are very wonky, and it feels like this game could've pushed the graphics and a little further without performance. I would be them a 3/5, since they are bland and boring up close, but the background and looking from the top of a hill is stunning.

Mafia II is an open-world adventure game that takes place in the '40s, '50s, and '60s, following the story of a World War II veteran who gets mixed up in the organized crime world of Empire Bay (New York City).  Seeing the words "open-world crime adventure set in NYC" might lead one to expect a Grand Theft Auto clone, but a GTA clone it is not.  Mafia II's focus is not so much on the freeness of its open world, so much as using the open world as the believable and immersive backdrop for its story.
Mafia II is organized into "chapters" - each starts when protagonist Vito Scaletta wakes up, and usually end when he goes to bed.  Everything that happens in between is the ever-advancing story of Scaletta descending deeper and deeper into the proverbial rabbit hole of the New York mafia, encountering, befriending, and swearing loyalty to a number of characters - some trustworthy, and some not.
The game isn't like GTA where there is lots to do in between missions and the player isn't really actively encouraged to participate in the story; Mafia II's story continues right away at the start of each chapter.  The end of most if not all chapters leave you riveted to your chair, eager to see what happens next - especially as the story progresses and Scaletta starts to find out just how deep the rabbit hole goes.  There's also a great tie-in moment for those who played the original game to completion (and the original is great as well, if not a bit aged).
Shaking the cops off your tail after they witness you commiting a crime can sometimes be a real challenge, as the police will be looking out for not just your vehicle but also your character in the clothes he is wearing.  Find a new car or get your license plate changed at a car shop to lose your car's wanted status - but unless you change your clothes, too, you run the risk of policemen spotting you in the driver's seat, starting the chase all over again.
For those interested in the early to mid 20th century culture, Mafia II is an excellent representation.  From the radio stations and car styles to the interior decor of your home and random peoples' clothing, the three decades the game takes place in are presented wonderfully.  Oldschool weapons like the classic Thompson submachine gun and the police-issue revolver are both a pleasure to see and a pleasure to use, as the combat, cover system, and potent feel of the guns are all very well-done.  Watching your character in a fedora and trench coat in third-person gun down rival gangsters with all these classic weapons feels like nothing short of totally badass.  There is also a complex and interesting fisticuffs combat system; at no point will you find the "press X a bunch of times to do flashy acrobatic combat moves" system employed by the Batman Arkham games.
My only complaint is that the DLC stories aren't nearly as well-done as the main one; you won't be missing much by skipping on them.  I did actually enjoy the Jimmy's Vendetta DLC, the story of an escaped convict in his quest of revenge and his love of driving sports cars way too fast, but it's by no means an essential purchase.  I also didn't get any of the clothing or vehicle DLCs and never really found a want for them as I played the main story.  The base game is very capable of standing on its own two legs.

The world generator while it is random using an 8 digit code that you can even manually control to challenge friends to the same world is fun even if in the end its all the same concept behind things. All in all I give this game a good recommendation.

Ingredients:
- 2 cups enriched white rice
- 4 cups water
- 2/3 cup chopped baby carrots
- 1/2 cup frozen green peas
- 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
- 2 eggs
- soy sauce to taste
- sesame oil, to taste (optional)
Directions:
1. In a saucepan, combine rice and water. Bring to a boil. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes.
2. In a small saucepan, boil carrots in water about 3 to 5 minutes. Drop peas into boiling water, and drain.
3. Heat wok over high heat. Pour in oil, then stir in carrots and peas; cook about 30 seconds. Crack in eggs, stirring quickly to scramble eggs with vegetables. Stir in cooked rice. Shake in soy sauce, and toss rice to coat. Drizzle with sesame oil, and toss again.

Finishing the game and some words that come into mind: beautiful, depth, unpredictable, mature, dark and aged-well. This is one of the best games I've played in a long time. And I'm not letting the fact that it's over 10 years old affect my statement. Not to overstate the appeal of this game or give it unneccessary hype, but this is one of those games where I was personally like, "I am so glad I experienced this game in my lifetime." I really cannot believe how much I would have missed out on if I didn't take a chance on this game. I'm not a goth, emo or vamp fanatic. I like space, spaceships, star wars and sci fi. That being said, this game was really damn cool and such a fresh outtake on a niche theme.
Here's what you need to know first:
Get the patch. The unofficial patch. You must. If you are unwilling to do so, don't buy the game. It needs it. You can look for the link on this game's community page.
There are still bugs in the game. For me, running windows 8.1 it was small things (elevator not working at the "Asylum", gate not opening in Santa Monica, etc.) Google "noclip" and "console" next to the title of the game to understand how to use this if you are playing the game and a door doesn't open or you get stuck in an elevator. Once a boss whipped me so hard I got stuck in a wall.... so just play around with the console command (you have to press the ~ key in-game) to open the console and type commands. It's honestly not as scary as it sounds. Also, I hear typing "money #" gives the females bigger bozangas in the game. Didn't test it as I wanted a legit first run experience.
For all the game's shortcomings (bugs, bugs, bugs), I am very very impressed with how well it's aged in 2017. If you maximize the graphics/textures/shadows... my gosh, it looks amazing. I didn't expect it to look the way it did. I am on an iMac, so glass screen/2,5k resolution. Looks darn impressive at that size. From the sounds and look of the rain drops, to constantly moving clouds in the night sky and even stars that twinkled in the sky independent of whether you moved your character/mouse or not... this game meshed a nostalgic feel with beautiful environmental visuals.
The story(ies) are something I really appreciate. Los Angeles is your playground. Glendale, Santa Monica, Chinatown, Hollywood...they all have their series of side-quests, interesting characters, and uniquely independent stories/quests that are as unpredictable as they are twisted. It felt like going down the rabbit hole and really not knowing how much more gruesome or horrifying it would lead to. But they weren't cheesy jump-scares. It was the environments, ambiance, music, ....the build-up. The endings weren't scary, it was the closer you got, the more everything compounded. I really appreciated the level of depth the devs went into.
The music was pretty bomb. While I absolutely love it and it's the second-most important aspect of this game's awesomeness, it's nothing groundbreaking. I think what makes me love the music in this game so much is the theme. Vampires, kindred, seedy Los Angeles, punk rocker underground clubs with background noise that made you feel you were in a club. The Foley artists did a great job too. The change in tone of the music was in perfect sync with the environment and goal/mission. I loved it.
***I am wondering why it says I've only played so few hours of this game. But then I realized... If you download the unoffical patch, you have to play the game (launch it) from the desktop shortcut that gets created (when you download/install the patch). It doesn't even open steam or launch the game from steam. So, take it from me when I tell you, I've been playing this game several hours a night for the past 2, maybe 2.5 weeks. It's long, its fun, you can run simulataneous missions/quests, and yes... there are katanas in this game.

Upgrade a starship, manage power distribution, and operate airlocks on hours-long missions to save the galaxy from the bad guys.
In FTL you captain a starship on its mission to save the galaxy.  You jump from beacon to beacon, with a wave of powerful enemies slowly taking over the map behind you and driving you forward towards the final boss.  Jumping to a new beacon can result in an encounter (battle / trade / distress call, etc) which can yield resources and equipment for upgrading your ship.  In battle, you target specific subsystems on the enemy ship to degrade their performance.  They do the same to you.  You can pause the game at any time in order to issue commands, which allows you to multitask effectively.  Nothing carries over from one playthrough to another, but you can unlock other ships as you play.  Game sessions usually last about three hours for me.
+ airlocks (it's surprisingly gratifying to vent a fire out into space)
+ artwork
+ music
+ the game state is saved when returning to the main menu (easy to leave when real life interrupts)
+ incremental system upgrades, loot
+ sessions take a few hours to complete
+ map layout and encounters are random, so no two sessions play out the same
+ despite being random, skill is more important than luck
+ ability to pause game at any time and redistribute power to critical systems
+ did I mention airlocks?  (I love those things)
(to be fair, these really only bothered me when I was new to FTL.  Not a problem once I learned the game)
- If you die, you have to start the game over
- The game leading up to the final boss does not prepare you for the final boss

Make That Money is a game about time, money, and energy management. The object is to become a millionaire through hard work, critical thinking, and of course, evaluating risks. The controls are simple, allowing you to focus on the task at hand without the added struggle of learning a bunch of complex menus or control schemes.
The game has an intuitive day and night cycle, and the top down controls / view playing with the bg music and effects remind me of the original GTA days (Pre-GTA IV), granting a lovely salute to the good ol retro days.
In my initial run, playing on Windows 10 I had the bug where the task bar would not leave view, covering the menu options at the bottom of the screen. If this happens to you, the fix is simple: Exit the game (should work on any game that does this), right click on your task bar then select Task Manager, then find Windows Explorer and right click on it, selecting the Reset option. After this, close the windows and restart the game, For me, it was still there until I clicked on the game screen (anywhere will do) and then the task bar went out of view.
Outside of this minor issue, I didn't encounter any game breaking bugs. I know there are said to be some bugs with some users, but the dev is actively updating (just updated yesterday in fact) to fix bug reports and add new features. Unlike many who put games out, this dev seems to be down to earth and up to suggestions, caring about what the user's likes and dislikes are and actively working to integrate those ideas into the game to make it better.
It's a new release, and like all new releases, there are some basic balance issues to deal with and new features to add. It's already a good game. With a few good updates, I can see it easily being a great addition to the strategy / simulation genre of games here on Steam.  I like it, and look forward to the tweaks and additions to come. For $2.99, it's a great game to have some cheap fun and kill a little time with.

There seems to be a lot of great stuff here, but it's ruined by a terrible save system.
The presents a very open map with lots of branching baths, but each save point (no, you can't do it manually) disappears upon use. Because your the path forward is so ill-defined and you do so much wandering, it's very easy to explore through a lot of content without any possibility of saving.
And then a game over for any reason, or simply having to leave your computer, means your hosed.
Limited saves like this work for some action games because the content is still kind of fun to repeat, but a game like this with so much focus on dialogue and very plain movement makes for really tedious make-up playing.
I think the save limitations are there to prevent going back on hard choices, and this does make sense, but this was implemented very poorly and ruins what might have been a really interesting game.

Divide by Sheep is a fun math puzzle game with solid amount of levels. It might look a like cheap mobile port, but underneath there's a very solid and clever puzzle game.
The game starts simple enough. You just need to move groups of sheep between platforms and get the exact right amount of them on the rafts. But the game keeps adding more and more elements to this simple formula and soon enough you are also dealing with wolves, pigs, dynamite platforms, laser fences and many other complications.
The constant introduction of new gameplay elements keeps the game fresh and interesting. There's a good amount of content too, especially if you decide to get full three stars in each level.
Despite the cute art style the game has some seriously dark undertones. Many of the levels actually require you to sacrifice a certain amount of cute animals and using the game's internal logic it makes perfect sense that a sheep cut in half by a laser fence still counts as one if you patch it back together.
The controls are clearly optimized for touch, but the mouse controls work reasonably well too. The game also has a rather prominent "Rate this App" link, which really should have been removed from the Steam release. On a positive note there are no microtransactions or gamebreaking powerups.
Overall Divide by Sheep is a highly enjoyable math puzzle game with lots of clever ideas and interesting levels. I'd recommend it to any puzzle game fans.
The good:
- Great puzzles
- Does a good job of introducing new gameplay elements
- Lots of levels
- Cute art with a dark twist
The bad:
- The tutorials can be somewhat confusing
- Controls are optimized for touch
- Prominent "Rate this App" link

Mafia 2 is an average game. I'd blame it on the lack of time the developpers had to finish it, but that's not really an excuse nowadays.
The atmosphere is decent enough, as you really feel like you're a mobster in an American city in the 40's/50's, but there simply isn't enough to do in the city to make it really feel alive. You can visit restaurants and clothing and gun shops, but your only interaction with them is to either buy something or to rob them. You simply can't really do anything in the city, which makes it pretty boring after a while. Most of the characters are interesting enough, but you only get to see them once or twice in the storyline. The combat is clucky, and feels very unnatural at times.
As for the main part of the game, the story, it's also average. It's simply a typical mafia story, there isn't much else to say about it. There aren't that many great moments in it, and they are vastly outweighted by boring driving sessions that don't really amount to anything.
Anyways, I would say that you can easily skip this game, but you really like (GREAT GREAT SPOILER!) mafia games, you might think it's worth getting.

An interesting and very well done point-and-click game.  Apparently, it's a sequel to "Edna & Harvey: The Breakout."  But, it's independent enough to be played stand-alone.  Because of the age of the main character and some implications from the narrator right at the start, you might be tempted to consider this to be a child's game.  It's not.  It's an adult's game hiding slightly behind a childlike irony.  I bought it on sale for about $4 and that's a no-brainer of a purchase.  Absolutely worth that. I'd say it would still be well worth it at around $10.  It's current list price of about $20 might be a bit high, though.
I do have some issue with the game, too.  First, it's slow to play.  But, that's endemic to these point-and-clicks since you've got to watch the character walk around, interact with the world, and converse.  Mitigating that is the saving grace that a lot of that kind of thing can be ESCaped out of or clicked through.  Second, some of the puzzles are not exactly obvious in what they want you to do.  This is especially true with the mini-games embedded in it.  Heck, the "solutions" from two of those mini-games were still obtuse enough to be of no use to me in the game proper.  And, finally, a lot of the achievements are royal pains.  They're not achievements that enhance gameplay.  Instead, they're of the form of "do some pointless activity enough times for me to say "you win."  But, all-in-all, it's a very good game.

I have played all four of the main titles in the Saints Row series, and this is the one I enjoyed the least. By the third game, they'd gone over the top, and that was fine, that was fun! Then they decided to take it almost as far as they could, which was just a little too much. The problems with this game do not include not being at all fun, no, you can waste some time and enjoy yourself for a while. But it's really not worth it compared to other games, even others in the series.
That's a matter of taste, though. The real reason I can't recommend this game is because of a technical problem. Or rather, several technical problems. I first got this game on the PS3. I played it for a while, progressing through the story, and then my PS3 started to freeze. At first I thought it was the system, because it had been known to freeze occasionally, especially with intensive games or games with large saves. My brother got a PS3 himself, which never had freezing issues. He played it and it did the same thing, but not until late into the game. So then I thought it was the disk. Eventually, I got the game here on Steam on a Windows 10 system that well beats out all the recommended specs. I finally thought I'd finish the game. But no. Around the missions where you start recruiting new lieutenant, my game starts freezing and crashing again. I can't even complete a mission without having to force shut down the game and start it back up again. It's just not worth it to keep trying.

If you're looking for an arcade-depth roguelike, you've found it! While it lacks the depth and intricacies of the pure breeds of the genre, such as the classic ADOM or more recent Dungeons of Dredmor, this game delivers familiar mechanics in a session you can begin AND win within an hour. The gimmick is simple, darkness is literally spreading across the land from the left side of the screen to the right, forcing you to run from it at all times. Every encounter or location you try to explore is an opportunity cost, and time is precious. However, failure to probe enough of the world will result in insufficient necessary medical supplies or a total lack of gear in time for the boss fight, should you survive long enough to hike to it. It follows a lot of the genre's standards, such as the world not moving until you take your actions, but since it is more simplistic, it adds something most roguelikes cannot do comfortably: 360 Controller support. Another fun feature is the world is generated by a key phrase, so you can replay a particular map, or seed a new one by letting your cat walk across your keyboard.

One of the best puzzle games I played this year.
In my opinion it's not a pure math puzzler like other games like Hexcell or Knight. Divide by Sheep has plenty of mechanisms that are more relevant to logic (wolves eating sheeps then blocking cells, pigs taking priority over sheeps, lasers cutting sheeps in half but not wolves, switching platforms, triggered burners, portals, and so on..). Each element appears around every 10 levels, which makes the game never boring and always fun all along the 150 levels.
The longevity is very good, it took me 18h to complete the 150 levels at 100%, which make an average of 7mn per level, please note that I'm very slow, and that around 20% of the levels can be solved in less than 2mn, while some other ones can easily take more than 10mn. One very good point is that the difficulty is not increasing continuously like in most puzzlers, instead, some levels are sometimes more easy than the previous ones, and I never been stuck or felt frustrated. Knowing that the next level can be easier is very motivating. When finishing the game you will be granted with a 100% achievement.
Apart from that, the graphic design is a total success with its colorfull look, animations are smooth and very fun, maybe one bad point is that the screen resolution is locked, but it's really not a problem. The game is also divided in 5 worlds, each one with his own graphic design, mechanisms and music soundtrack (variations on the main theme). The game was made with Adobe Air (which is a very solid engine for such games), and it was designed first for touchscreen (I imagine that a tablet version should exist, I didn't check), but works perfectly with the mouse as well. There is also a parental lock if you want to remove the gore and let your 5yo kid play (it's a fun game for kids too).
If you're into puzzle games, don't hesitate one second.

Let's get this straight: I absolutely adore this game, it is really fun to play and see how you improve over time.
Even better if you have a couple of friends to compete with on the leadersboards or play a bit of multiplayer.
You can even make your own tracks in the editor which is pretty easy to get started in, but advanced enough to make crazy minigames and really slick looking tracks.
If the game will actually run at all for you that is.
It seems to be a coin-toss if this game will work on your system or not, and if it actually does run it might still lag even with really good hardware. I'm running it with a HD7970 and an i7 3770k so it runs well just because of the brute force.
My laptop on the other hand has a decent high end i7 (for a laptop) and a HD8870M and I can't even run the game on low settings in 680x480 (for reference, the laptop can run Battlefield 4 on low sort of okay in 1080p) without having lag.
Other people have problems with the game not starting at all or crashing frequently.
EDIT: Track central is now fixed and works just as well as it does on Xbox 360, removed the "it's not working very well part".
It also has DRM in the form of uPlay, which will start when you try and start the game from Steam. It was pretty terrible in the beginning but seems to have improved a bit over the year (still would rather not have it). uPlay also handles the multiplayer part of the game if you want to make private games with friends and that part is incredibly broken too. Pressing invite from the in-game friendslist just crashes my game and I'm one of the lucky ones that it's the only problem I'm having with it.
To sum things up I would recommend the game if I knew it would work properly, but with all the problems it has it really seems to be dumb luck wether it will work. The infrequent patches haven't done much to remedy the situation in the last few months so I honestly cannot recommend it when it's so broken for a big portion of the people that bought it.

(This review contains some spoilers.)
isn't so much a "quirky" RPG as it is unrelentingly grim and depressing. It's also one of the best indie RPGs made in a long, long time.
Coming off as the love child of
and
,
puts players into the shoes of a man who has been beaten down so thoroughly that he has virtually nothing left, but still perseveres in order to rescue the only woman in the world. More than any other game in a while,
forces you to weigh the consequences of your actions and continue on in the face of nonstop tragedy and tough decisions. Make no mistake - this game
leave you drained by the end of it.
may not be the flashiest RPG out there, but it is a masterwork on how to effectively build tension and uncertainty while utilizing various gameplay elements to the fullest. Every step feels like it could be your last. Enemies will routinely wreck your party, even with planning. Sleeping at a campfire runs the risk of a permanent injury, or worse, one of your companions bailing on you. There is no loyalty between anyone, not even between Brad and Buddy. A choice between chopping your arm off or permanently sacrificing a companion is one of the easier decisions forced upon you. Give something to an innocuous pair of NPCs and an entire village could be wiped out.
Somewhere between the game insinuating that a major character was molested and a decision where I had to choose between sacrificing my current party members or chopping off a minor body part, I had to put the game down and step away for a while. The subject matter is unrelentingly dark, and even the few moments of levity the plot and characters provide aren't really balanced with the grim nature of the world Brad and everyone else inhabit.
The game will flip between moods on a dime - one minute, you're taking part in Russian Roulette that can (and will) cause permadeath for your companions, and the next you're in a village where an amateur magician is asking you to find some playing cards for him. You go from a hilarious wrestling sidequest that riffs on the WWF to a pair of decisions that easily qualify as the darkest moment in the game.
Still,
does have moments of humor and amusement. The various companions you meet throughout the world all have quirky backstories and interesting little comments after battles (which makes it all the more difficult at the end of the game, during a certain cutscene). There are interesting and funny little notes written throughout the world, and some of the ambient locations you run across (like a McDonalds parody, where fast food meals are gifted from the "heavens" above) are quite unique.
The battles are pretty straightforward, but do rely on a lot of strategy, especially if you're playing in "Pain Mode" (where you can only use savepoints once). There is a definite degree of strategy, and even with overleveled characters, you still have to figure out the weaknesses of bosses and attempt to counter them. The game also does a great job of encouraging replayability through multiple endings, alternate choices and different party configurations.
Also, there's a really great fast-travel system that allows you to get to one of the main hubs instantly. It's always something I harp on about longer RPGs not having, but it was pulled off very well here.
If there's anything I didn't like in the game, it's the fact that a certain character that administers the decisions comes off as a bit too "deus ex machina" for my tastes, and some of the bosses either force you to grind or counter them with a really-overpowered companion. I also didn't feel that many of the companions warranted being part of my active party, and they don't do much of consequence after being recruited.
Still, I was more than satisfied after a single playthrough of the game.
is a title that will leave you emotionally drained and weighing the consequences of everything that leads up to that final, nihilistic ending.

This is a very fun rogue-like. Dont be confused about my lack of play time because I have played this before it was released on Steam.
Basically it is a rogue-like game that is different in the fact that there are no real dungeons and the "darkness" follows you across the world. Touching the darkness kills you instantly.
There is still random treasure and random world generation but it has a different spin on it. Instead of dungeons and narrow, dark pathways, it is a large strip of earth with mountains, water and lava. There are random NPC'S and little monster houses that are filled with enemies and treasure.
Each game that you start you choose your characters name, class and up to 3 perks that change the gameplay. Each time that you die (it will happen) you are awarded "Hero Points" based on things like how far your guy got, what level you died at, how many monsters you killed and the like. These Hero Points are used to buy things like more classes, more perks and let you upgrade the amount of slots in this Between-Game inventory. This inventory lets you save OP items and stuff that you got in your last game to be used in your next game. you need to buy the slots though.
It isnt a very difficult game to grasp. On my first game my Hero Point score was 3.  By my second my Hero Point score was 8, and by my third my score was 91 due to killing the final boss and being an all-around nice guy. These were all on the easy mode though. The next mode is much harder.
For $3.50 I recommend this game for being simple, fun and have tons of replayability.

It's not a game per se, but more of an autobiographical installation, centered on the author's abnormal sense of self, of others and of the reality of indie game dev.
Pros:
+ It's short
Cons:
- Everything else
The style of directing constantly attempts to dictate the player's interpretation of the sequences and all thoughts within the piece are conveyed literally, leaving no room for the player to have a genuine experience and reaction of their own. As such, it's a poorly executed piece of art, but it does succeed in revealing something about the dev's personality. The dreams look like they've been plucked out of the dev's head quite directly, but they lack any and all sorts of feeling and exhibit little to no intertextuality either among themselves or outside of the piece, making them very hard to relate to. All throughout the sequences, I never once found myself rooting for the character, and in the last sequence trying to find the way out, I tried killing the character by jumping down several times. It didn't work, and it was sad.
The controls are barely adequate even for a walking simulator, but even if they were flawless the piece is still uninventive at best, drab and repetitive at worst. The dreamscapes are hardly diverse, with each level consisting of either a block building or a scenery with grass or trees, relying entirely on hard contrasts and noise overlays to hide the rushed modeling and texturing work that would be sub-par even on 2006 standards. The music throughout is flat and lacks dynamic range, making it very hard on the ear and they loop pretty quickly. The only level that had music that would change back and forth based on the player's location looked and felt a lot like Jazzpunk, and was by far my favorite sequence.
On the bright side, it's quite short and will only waste less than a half an hour of your life. They say the best things in life are free, but that doesn't mean all free things in life are the best. I clicked thumbs down, but I do recommend checking it out for how to make neither interactive digital art nor games.

Divide by Sheep is math puzzle game disguised with cute critters. Yes, you also divide.
Let me get it out of the way: this is a blatant mobile port that nonetheless ends up working ok with a mouse.
The basic mechanics have you throw groups of critters from one island to the next, with the goal of satisfying 3 requests in each, be it save an exact amount of them or kill a certain number. These requests are tied to the layout of the map and require you to move around the animals until you've satisfied them all in sequence.
You can merge groups on a single island (2 sheeps + 3 sheeps = 5 sheep!) as well as "decrease them" by throwing more than an island can take and drowning the excess. I should also mention that you
divide sheep with laser grids. In half. A bloody half. And two halves make a whole, don't forget!
Things get more complex as the game gives you more critters who interact differently with one another (wolves eat all others, pigs squash sheeps, the golden idol that exists somehow squashes everything...) as well as different types of islands that disappear when left empty or burn any visitor.
While the game is fun, it doesn't have a very good progression; the difficulty varies wildly from one stage and the next, but it somehow manages to be fun for the most part.
I have to point out that it does overstay its welcome by a couple dozen stages; the last world adds slightly uninspired elements that were most likely added just to increase the duration of the game. The achievement structure also suggests this: the "get everything" unlocks after the second-to-last world, with one more "get everything" unlocking after you're done with the last world as well.
All in all, Divide by Sheep is a cute puzzle game, but I wouldn't suggest it to those who don't already love the genre.
To such players, go ahead and get it during a discount for a few hours of fun; feel also free to let go when you get bored though: sadly, there's no majestic puzzle design waiting for you in its last phases.

Let's get this straight: I absolutely adore this game, it is really fun to play and see how you improve over time.
Even better if you have a couple of friends to compete with on the leadersboards or play a bit of multiplayer.
You can even make your own tracks in the editor which is pretty easy to get started in, but advanced enough to make crazy minigames and really slick looking tracks.
If the game will actually run at all for you that is.
It seems to be a coin-toss if this game will work on your system or not, and if it actually does run it might still lag even with really good hardware. I'm running it with a HD7970 and an i7 3770k so it runs well just because of the brute force.
My laptop on the other hand has a decent high end i7 (for a laptop) and a HD8870M and I can't even run the game on low settings in 680x480 (for reference, the laptop can run Battlefield 4 on low sort of okay in 1080p) without having lag.
Other people have problems with the game not starting at all or crashing frequently.
EDIT: Track central is now fixed and works just as well as it does on Xbox 360, removed the "it's not working very well part".
It also has DRM in the form of uPlay, which will start when you try and start the game from Steam. It was pretty terrible in the beginning but seems to have improved a bit over the year (still would rather not have it). uPlay also handles the multiplayer part of the game if you want to make private games with friends and that part is incredibly broken too. Pressing invite from the in-game friendslist just crashes my game and I'm one of the lucky ones that it's the only problem I'm having with it.
To sum things up I would recommend the game if I knew it would work properly, but with all the problems it has it really seems to be dumb luck wether it will work. The infrequent patches haven't done much to remedy the situation in the last few months so I honestly cannot recommend it when it's so broken for a big portion of the people that bought it.

I have played all four of the main titles in the Saints Row series, and this is the one I enjoyed the least. By the third game, they'd gone over the top, and that was fine, that was fun! Then they decided to take it almost as far as they could, which was just a little too much. The problems with this game do not include not being at all fun, no, you can waste some time and enjoy yourself for a while. But it's really not worth it compared to other games, even others in the series.
That's a matter of taste, though. The real reason I can't recommend this game is because of a technical problem. Or rather, several technical problems. I first got this game on the PS3. I played it for a while, progressing through the story, and then my PS3 started to freeze. At first I thought it was the system, because it had been known to freeze occasionally, especially with intensive games or games with large saves. My brother got a PS3 himself, which never had freezing issues. He played it and it did the same thing, but not until late into the game. So then I thought it was the disk. Eventually, I got the game here on Steam on a Windows 10 system that well beats out all the recommended specs. I finally thought I'd finish the game. But no. Around the missions where you start recruiting new lieutenant, my game starts freezing and crashing again. I can't even complete a mission without having to force shut down the game and start it back up again. It's just not worth it to keep trying.

I like that this was ported to Steam, and that I had just as much fun playing through it on PC as I did on PS3, especially with a more steady frame rate. However, controller support is still very limited unless you have a 360 controller or have software to emulate Xinput (I know Steam now has functionality natively in the client, but I prefer using DS4Windows). That being said, even though this was also ported to next-gen consoles, the game will not recognize Dinput. Somewhere with the most recent update, either with Steam or the game itself, it tends to make the game hang on the AMD logo screen, saying that Saints Row IV has stopped working. Also going on that, if it pushes past the AMD logo and gets to the main menu, a plugged in controller will not work unless you unplug and replug it, despite being able to use it to skip those splash screens. A bit ridiculous. During game it seems to be unstable at times, completely hanging and doing a CTD, making any unsaved progress lost. That's not often though. It sometimes feels like the game wasn't written for Windows 7 running under an AMD CPU with all of this. However, if you can push through all of it and get a good streak in, it's an enjoyable gaming experience. Just save early and often. I still recommend this game if you doubt you'll have issues.
